articles.title: How to Install MailClaw on Your Mac in Under 5 Minutes
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: A step-by-step guide to installing MailClaw on your Mac in under five minutes, covering prerequisites, CLI setup, SMTP configuration, and your first campaign — so you can start automating email outreach immediately.
articles.content:
What You're About to Set Up

MailClaw is an open-source, AI-powered email automation platform that runs entirely on your local machine. No cloud subscriptions, no data leaving your laptop, no per-seat pricing. Within a few minutes you'll have a full-featured email automation stack — including AI email agents, a visual sequence builder, contact enrichment, and a live deliverability dashboard — running at localhost:3100 on your Mac.

This guide assumes you're comfortable opening a terminal window. That's really all it takes.

Prerequisites: What You Need Before You Start

MailClaw is built on OpenClaw, which handles the underlying AI orchestration and agent runtime. Before you run the install command, make sure you have the following on your Mac:

  • macOS 12 (Monterey) or later — MailClaw uses system APIs available in recent macOS versions.
  • Node.js 18+ — MailClaw's CLI and dashboard are Node-based. Install via nodejs.org or with Homebrew (brew install node).
  • Git — Already installed on most Macs. Verify with git --version.
  • An SMTP account or OAuth credentials — This can be Gmail, Outlook, or a dedicated sending service like SendGrid or Postmark. You'll connect this in under a minute after install.

That's it. No Docker required, no database server to spin up separately. MailClaw handles its own local SQLite store for contacts, sequences, and campaign data.

Step 1 — Install MailClaw via npm

Open Terminal and run a single command to install the MailClaw CLI globally:

npm install -g mailclaw

This pulls down the MailClaw CLI and the OpenClaw runtime it depends on. The install typically takes 30–60 seconds depending on your connection. Once it finishes, verify the install succeeded:

mailclaw --version

You should see something like mailclaw v1.x.x (OpenClaw runtime: ready). If you see a permissions error, prefix the install command with sudo or, better yet, fix your npm prefix so you don't need sudo for global packages.

Step 2 — Initialize Your MailClaw Workspace

Navigate to the directory where you want MailClaw to store its local data — your home folder works fine — and run:

mailclaw init

The CLI will walk you through a short interactive setup:

  1. Workspace name — A label for this instance (e.g., my-outreach).
  2. AI model preference — MailClaw defaults to a locally-served model via OpenClaw, but you can optionally point it at an OpenAI or Anthropic API key if you prefer a hosted model for heavier agent tasks.
  3. Default sender name and reply-to address — Used as fallbacks across all campaigns.

When init completes, MailClaw creates a ~/.mailclaw config directory with your workspace settings, a local SQLite database, and a default agent configuration file you can edit later.

Step 3 — Connect Your Email Account

This is where MailClaw gets useful fast. Run:

mailclaw accounts add

You'll be prompted to choose a connection method:

Option A: OAuth (Recommended for Gmail and Outlook)

Select OAuth and choose your provider. MailClaw will open a browser window and walk you through the standard OAuth consent screen. Your credentials are stored locally in an encrypted keychain entry — nothing is transmitted to MailClaw servers because there are no MailClaw servers. This is genuinely local-first software.

Gmail and Outlook both work well here. If you're using a Google Workspace account, you may need to enable Less Secure App Access or configure an OAuth client ID in your Google Cloud Console — MailClaw's docs cover this in detail.

Option B: SMTP Credentials

For dedicated sending infrastructure — SendGrid, Postmark, Amazon SES, Mailgun, or a custom SMTP server — select SMTP and enter your host, port, username, and password or API key. For example, a SendGrid configuration looks like this:

SMTP Host: smtp.sendgrid.net
Port: 587
Username: apikey
Password: SG.xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx

MailClaw supports multi-account setups out of the box. You can add as many sending accounts as you need and assign specific accounts to specific campaigns — useful if you're managing outreach across multiple domains or client accounts.

Step 4 — Start the Dashboard

Now the satisfying part. Run:

mailclaw start

MailClaw spins up its local web server and automatically opens your browser to http://localhost:3100. You'll land on the main dashboard, which gives you a real-time view of:

  • Active campaigns and their send/open/reply stats
  • Sequence performance across all enrolled contacts
  • Deliverability health indicators (SPF, DKIM, bounce rates)
  • Your AI email agents and their current task queues

Pro tip: Add mailclaw start to your Mac's Login Items (System Settings → General → Login Items) so the dashboard starts automatically when you boot up. You can also run mailclaw start --background to launch it as a background process without opening a browser window.

Step 5 — Send Your First Test Email

Before building sequences, confirm your sending account is working correctly:

mailclaw send --to you@youremail.com --subject "MailClaw test" --body "It works."

If the email arrives, you're fully operational. If it doesn't, run mailclaw accounts diagnose — this command checks your SMTP connection, validates your authentication, and gives you a human-readable explanation of any issues.

What to Explore Next

With MailClaw installed, you have access to a surprisingly deep feature set. Here are the most valuable things to dig into next:

Build Your First Email Sequence

The sequence builder in the dashboard lets you create multi-step drip campaigns with conditional logic — if a contact opens step one but doesn't reply within 48 hours, send step two; if they reply at any point, remove them from the sequence automatically. No code required for basic flows, but power users can define sequences in YAML for version control.

Use AI Email Agents for Personalization at Scale

MailClaw's AI email agents, powered by the OpenClaw runtime, can research a contact's LinkedIn profile or company website and generate a personalized opening line before sending. You set the rules, the agent does the research. This kind of hyper-personalization used to require a dedicated SDR or expensive third-party tooling.

Enrich Your Contact List

Drop a CSV of names and company domains into MailClaw's contact enrichment pipeline and let it fill in job titles, company size, tech stack, and social profiles. Enriched contacts feed directly into your sequences with all the context your AI agents need to write relevant, specific emails.

Connect Your CRM

MailClaw integrates with HubSpot and Salesforce via the CLI. Run mailclaw integrations add hubspot to sync contacts and log email activity back to your CRM automatically. No more manually updating deal records after a reply comes in.

Monitor Deliverability

The deliverability dashboard inside localhost:3100 tracks your sender reputation metrics, flags high bounce rates before they damage your domain, and gives you actionable recommendations — like warming up a new sending domain gradually or adjusting your daily send volume.

You're Up and Running

Five minutes, one install command, and you have a production-ready email automation platform running locally on your Mac. Because MailClaw is open source and self-hosted, you own your data, your contact lists, and your sending infrastructure completely.

The combination of AI email agents, built-in contact enrichment, and a clean visual dashboard makes MailClaw one of the fastest ways to go from a cold contact list to a running, personalized outreach campaign. And since it runs on OpenClaw, the same agent framework powers everything — so as your needs grow, the tooling grows with you.

Run mailclaw --help to see the full command reference, or browse the dashboard at localhost:3100 to start building your first sequence.

articles.title: MailClaw for Beginners: Complete Getting Started Guide
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Everything you need to get MailClaw up and running — from installation and SMTP setup to building your first AI-powered email sequence and monitoring deliverability from your local dashboard.
articles.content:
What Is MailClaw and Why Run Email Automation Locally?

Most email automation tools live in the cloud — your contacts, your sequences, your API keys, your entire outreach strategy sitting on someone else's server. MailClaw takes a different approach. Built on OpenClaw, it runs entirely on your Mac at localhost:3100, giving you a powerful, AI-driven email automation platform without surrendering your data to a SaaS subscription.

This matters more than it might seem. Cold outreach lists, enriched contact data, and SMTP credentials are sensitive. Running MailClaw locally means you control everything — the database, the AI agent behavior, the sending logic — while still connecting to the external tools and services you already use, like Gmail, Outlook, SendGrid, or HubSpot.

If you've ever wanted the power of a platform like Instantly or Apollo but with full transparency into how it works (and zero monthly fees), MailClaw is worth your time.

Installing MailClaw

MailClaw is open source and installs cleanly on macOS. Before you begin, make sure you have Node.js 18+ and npm installed. You can check with:

node -v
npm -v

Then clone the repository and install dependencies:

git clone https://github.com/openclaw/mailclaw.git
cd mailclaw
npm install

Once dependencies are ready, start the local server:

npm run start

Open your browser and navigate to http://localhost:3100. You'll land on the MailClaw dashboard — a clean, dark-mode interface that surfaces everything you need: campaigns, sequences, contacts, deliverability stats, and your AI agent configuration.

First-Time Configuration

On first launch, MailClaw walks you through a short setup wizard. You'll be prompted to:

  • Set a local admin password (stored securely in your local config)
  • Choose your AI provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, or a local model via Ollama)
  • Connect your first sending account

Your configuration lives in a .env file at the project root. You can edit it directly or use the dashboard UI — both stay in sync.

Connecting Your Email Accounts

MailClaw supports multi-account sending out of the box, which is critical for any serious outreach operation. You can connect accounts via OAuth or raw SMTP — or both simultaneously.

OAuth Integration (Gmail and Outlook)

For Gmail and Outlook, OAuth is the recommended path. In the dashboard, navigate to Settings → Email Accounts → Add Account and select your provider. MailClaw will open a browser-based OAuth flow. Once authorized, the account appears in your sender pool immediately.

The advantage of OAuth here is that MailClaw never stores your password — only the access token, which lives locally on your machine.

SMTP Integration (SendGrid, Mailgun, Custom)

For transactional providers like SendGrid or Mailgun, or for custom mail servers, use SMTP configuration:

SMTP_HOST=smtp.sendgrid.net
SMTP_PORT=587
SMTP_USER=apikey
SMTP_PASS=your_sendgrid_api_key
SMTP_FROM=you@yourdomain.com

You can add multiple SMTP accounts and MailClaw will rotate between them automatically during campaign sends — a simple but effective way to protect individual sender reputation.

Building Your First Email Sequence

The Sequence Builder is where MailClaw earns its keep. Think of sequences as multi-step email workflows that run automatically based on time delays, contact behavior, or AI-driven decisions.

Creating a Sequence

  1. From the dashboard, click Sequences → New Sequence
  2. Give it a name (e.g., "Cold Outreach — SaaS Founders")
  3. Add your first step: choose Email as the step type
  4. Write your subject line and body, or use the AI draft feature
  5. Set a delay before the next step (e.g., 3 days)
  6. Add follow-up steps as needed — most effective sequences have 3–5 touches
  7. Set exit conditions: stop if the contact replies, clicks, or unsubscribes

A typical cold outreach sequence might look like: an initial personalized intro → a value-add follow-up → a gentle bump → a breakup email. MailClaw handles the timing and sending automatically once contacts are enrolled.

Using AI to Draft Emails

Inside any sequence step, click Draft with AI. You'll be prompted to describe your goal, tone, and any personalization variables. MailClaw's AI layer — powered by OpenClaw — generates a draft you can edit, regenerate, or approve in seconds.

Pro tip: Use personalization tokens like {{first_name}}, {{company}}, and {{pain_point}} in your prompts. MailClaw will fill these from your contact data at send time, making every email feel hand-written.

Enriching and Importing Contacts

A sequence without contacts doesn't send anything. MailClaw gives you two paths to build your contact list: import existing data or enrich it on the fly.

Importing Contacts

Navigate to Contacts → Import and upload a CSV. At minimum, MailClaw expects an email column. Everything else — name, company, title, custom fields — is optional but recommended for personalization.

You can also sync contacts directly from HubSpot or Salesforce using MailClaw's CRM integrations. Once connected, you can pull filtered segments (e.g., "all leads in pipeline stage 2 with no email activity in 30 days") directly into a sequence.

AI-Powered Contact Enrichment

This is one of MailClaw's standout features. After importing a list, select contacts and click Enrich. MailClaw will use configured enrichment providers to pull in missing data — job titles, LinkedIn URLs, company size, industry, and more.

Enriched contacts become far more useful for segmentation and AI personalization. A contact who started as just jane@acme.com becomes Jane Smith, VP of Marketing at Acme Inc. (Series B, 120 employees, SaaS) — and your AI email agent can write to her accordingly.

Setting Up AI Email Agents

Beyond scheduled sequences, MailClaw lets you build AI email agents — autonomous agents that can read incoming replies, classify intent, and take action without you lifting a finger.

From Agents → New Agent, you configure:

  • Trigger: What activates the agent (e.g., a reply to a specific sequence)
  • Classification rules: How the agent categorizes replies (interested, not interested, referral, unsubscribe, out of office)
  • Actions: What happens next — send a follow-up, tag the contact, notify you via webhook, push to HubSpot, or pause the sequence

A well-configured agent can handle the majority of reply triage automatically, surfacing only the genuinely interested leads for your attention. For a solo founder or small sales team, this is a meaningful force multiplier.

Monitoring Deliverability

Sending is only half the battle — making sure your emails actually land in inboxes is the other. MailClaw's deliverability dashboard gives you a real-time view of what matters:

  • Open rates, click rates, reply rates per sequence and per sender
  • Bounce tracking (hard and soft) with automatic suppression
  • Spam complaint rates by sending account
  • DNS health checks: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC validation for each connected domain
  • Sending volume pacing recommendations to avoid triggering Gmail or Outlook rate limits

If a sending account starts showing elevated bounce rates or complaints, MailClaw will alert you and optionally pause that account's sends automatically — protecting your domain reputation before it becomes a serious problem.

What to Do After Setup

Once you have accounts connected, contacts imported, and a sequence built, here are the next steps worth prioritizing:

  • Warm up new sending domains before adding them to active campaigns. MailClaw includes a basic warm-up scheduler under Settings → Deliverability.
  • A/B test subject lines in the sequence builder — MailClaw splits sends automatically and promotes the winner after a configurable sample size.
  • Review your AI agent logs after the first few days of replies. Tune the classification prompts if the agent is miscategorizing responses.
  • Set up a webhook to push qualified leads into your CRM the moment an AI agent flags them as interested.

MailClaw is the kind of tool that rewards tinkering. Because it's open source and runs locally, you can inspect every piece of logic, customize behavior, and extend it however you need. The OpenClaw foundation means the AI layer is modular — swap models, adjust prompts, or add entirely new agent behaviors without waiting for a SaaS vendor to ship a feature request.

Start simple: one sending account, one sequence, one AI agent. Get a campaign running end-to-end, see how the dashboard tracks performance, and build from there.

articles.title: Setting Up MailClaw AI Email Agent on localhost:3100
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to install, configure, and launch your first AI email agent in MailClaw running on localhost:3100 — from SMTP setup and contact enrichment to building automated sequences that actually convert.
articles.content:
Why Run an AI Email Agent Locally?

Most email automation platforms ask you to hand over your contact lists, your API keys, and your campaign logic to a third-party server you'll never audit. MailClaw takes a fundamentally different approach. Because it's built on OpenClaw and runs entirely on your machine at localhost:3100, your data never leaves your environment. Your outreach logic, your enriched contacts, your AI prompts — all of it stays local.

This matters more than people realize. Beyond privacy, running locally means zero latency on the dashboard, no subscription tiers throttling your sends, and the freedom to inspect and modify every line of the codebase. If you've been shopping for an alternative to tools like Instantly, Lemlist, or Apollo, and you're comfortable with a terminal, MailClaw is worth a serious look.

This guide walks you through installing MailClaw, connecting your sending accounts, and standing up a fully functional AI email agent — from first command to first sent sequence.

Prerequisites and Installation

Before you start, make sure your Mac has the following:

  • Node.js 18+ — MailClaw's local server and dashboard require it
  • Git — to clone the repo and pull updates
  • A sending account — Gmail with OAuth, Outlook via OAuth, or any SMTP provider like SendGrid, Mailgun, or Postmark
  • Optional but recommended: an OpenAI API key for the AI agent features

With those in place, installation is straightforward:

# Clone the MailClaw repository
git clone https://github.com/openclaw/mailclaw.git
cd mailclaw

# Install dependencies
npm install

# Copy the example environment file
cp .env.example .env

Open .env in your editor and fill in your configuration. At minimum you'll want to set your OPENAI_API_KEY if you're using AI agent features, and your preferred database path for contact storage.

# .env — minimum viable config
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
DATABASE_PATH=./data/mailclaw.db
DASHBOARD_PORT=3100
DEFAULT_FROM_NAME="Your Name"

Then start the server:

npm run start

Open your browser to http://localhost:3100. You should see the MailClaw dashboard — a clean, dark-mode interface showing your accounts, campaign stats, and agent status at a glance.

Connecting Your Sending Accounts

Gmail and Outlook via OAuth

Navigate to Settings → Accounts → Add Account in the dashboard. For Gmail and Outlook, MailClaw supports OAuth 2.0 out of the box. Click the provider, complete the authorization flow in your browser, and MailClaw stores a refresh token locally — no passwords, no plain-text credentials.

For Gmail specifically, you'll want to enable "Less secure app access" if you're on a personal account, or — better — set up a Google Cloud project and use your own OAuth credentials. This gives you full control and keeps you well within Google's sending policies.

SMTP Providers (SendGrid, Postmark, Mailgun)

If you're routing through a dedicated sending infrastructure, head to Settings → Accounts → Add SMTP. Fill in your host, port, and credentials:

Host: smtp.sendgrid.net
Port: 587
Username: apikey
Password: SG.xxxxxxxxxxxx
Encryption: STARTTLS

MailClaw will run a quick deliverability check on save — verifying SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records for the domain you're sending from. This is part of the built-in deliverability monitoring layer, which also tracks bounce rates and spam complaints per account over time.

Pro tip: If you're doing cold outreach at any volume, use a subdomain (like mail.yourdomain.com) and warm it up gradually. MailClaw's sequence builder has a warmup mode that automatically ramps daily sending volume over a configurable period.

Enriching Your Contact List

Before you configure the AI agent, you need contacts to work with. MailClaw's contact enrichment module lets you import a raw CSV — even one with just names and company domains — and fill in the gaps automatically.

From the CLI:

# Import and enrich a CSV
mailclaw contacts import --file ./leads.csv --enrich --source clearbit

Supported enrichment sources include Clearbit, Hunter.io, and Apollo.io (via API key). Once enriched, each contact record in the local database will carry job title, LinkedIn URL, company size, industry, and any custom fields you've mapped from your source CSV.

You can also pipe contacts in from CRM integrations. MailClaw has native sync adapters for HubSpot and Salesforce — both read-only by default so nothing gets written back without your explicit action:

# Sync contacts from a HubSpot list
mailclaw contacts sync --crm hubspot --list-id 1234 --enrich

Once imported, contacts are visible in the dashboard under Contacts → All, where you can filter, tag, and segment before assigning them to a campaign.

Building Your First AI Email Agent

What the AI Agent Actually Does

MailClaw's AI email agent isn't just a mail merge with GPT bolted on. It's a configurable agent loop that reads contact context, selects the right sequence step, personalizes the email body using a prompt template, evaluates the draft against your tone and deliverability guidelines, and only then queues it for sending. You define the rules; the agent executes them consistently at scale.

Creating an Agent

In the dashboard, go to Agents → New Agent. You'll configure four things:

  1. Goal — a plain-English description of what the agent is trying to achieve (e.g., "Book a 20-minute intro call with VP-level engineering leaders at Series B startups")
  2. Persona — the sender voice and style guidelines the AI will follow
  3. Sequence — which email sequence this agent should execute (more on building sequences below)
  4. Audience — a contact segment or saved filter from your contact database

You can also configure the agent from the CLI, which is useful for scripting or version-controlling your campaign setup:

mailclaw agent create \
  --name "SaaS Founder Outreach" \
  --goal "Book discovery calls with SaaS founders" \
  --persona ./personas/founder-friendly.md \
  --sequence cold-saas-v2 \
  --audience "tag:saas AND title:founder"

Building the Sequence

Sequences live under Sequences → New Sequence in the dashboard. Each step is a prompt template plus scheduling logic. A typical 3-step cold outreach sequence might look like this:

  • Step 1 (Day 0): Short intro email — 3 sentences max, one specific insight about their company, one soft CTA
  • Step 2 (Day 4): Follow-up referencing Step 1, add a relevant case study or social proof hook
  • Step 3 (Day 9): Break-up email — low-pressure, leaves the door open

Each step's prompt template has access to contact variables like {{first_name}}, {{company}}, {{job_title}}, and any enriched fields. The AI agent fills these in contextually, not just by string substitution — so the output reads like it was written for that specific person.

Launching the Agent and Monitoring Results

Once your agent is configured and your sequence is built, launching is a single command:

mailclaw agent run --name "SaaS Founder Outreach" --dry-run

The --dry-run flag previews the first batch of emails without sending. Review them in the dashboard under Agents → Queue. When you're satisfied with the output quality, drop the flag and run it live.

The localhost dashboard at http://localhost:3100 gives you real-time visibility into opens, clicks, replies, bounces, and unsubscribes. You can drill into any individual send to see the exact prompt that generated it, the enrichment data used, and the full email rendered — which makes debugging and iteration genuinely fast.

For ongoing campaigns, you can schedule the agent to run on a cron-like interval:

mailclaw agent schedule --name "SaaS Founder Outreach" --interval daily --time 08:00

A Few Things Worth Knowing Before You Scale

MailClaw is powerful, but like any outreach tool it rewards thoughtful use. A few principles that will save you headaches:

  • Respect unsubscribes. MailClaw maintains a global suppression list automatically, but double-check that your sequences include a plain-text unsubscribe option in every footer.
  • Watch your sending velocity. Even with a warmed domain, stay under 200 new contacts per day per inbox when starting out. Use the deliverability dashboard to watch bounce rates — anything above 3% is a signal to slow down.
  • Version control your agents. Because everything is local and config-driven, you can commit your agent definitions, personas, and sequence prompts to a private Git repo. This makes collaboration and rollback trivial.
  • Use multi-account rotation wisely. MailClaw's multi-account support lets you rotate sends across multiple inboxes to distribute volume — but make sure each account has its own warmup history before adding it to a rotation pool.

The combination of local execution, AI personalization, and built-in deliverability tooling makes MailClaw a genuinely capable platform for teams who want to own their outreach stack end to end. Start with one agent, one sequence, one account — and build from there once you've validated the workflow.

articles.title: How to Connect Your Gmail Account to MailClaw
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how to connect your Gmail account to MailClaw using OAuth 2.0 or SMTP, so you can start sending AI-powered email sequences and automating outreach directly from your local dashboard.
articles.content:
Why Connect Gmail to MailClaw?

Gmail is one of the most trusted sending identities you can use for cold outreach and automated email sequences. When you connect it to MailClaw, you get the full weight of Google's sending infrastructure behind your campaigns — combined with MailClaw's AI email agents, contact enrichment, and deliverability monitoring, all running locally on your machine at localhost:3100.

Whether you're a solo founder running outbound sequences, a developer building AI email agents with OpenClaw, or a growth team managing multi-account campaigns, Gmail integration is usually the first thing you'll want to set up. This guide walks you through both methods: OAuth 2.0 (recommended) and manual SMTP configuration.

Before You Begin

Make sure MailClaw is running locally before attempting any account connection. If you haven't started the server yet, run:

mailclaw start

You should see the dashboard available at http://localhost:3100. If you're not yet installed, check the Getting Started guide in the MailClaw docs — installation takes less than two minutes via Homebrew or direct binary download.

You'll also need:

  • A Gmail or Google Workspace account
  • 2-Step Verification enabled on your Google account (required for App Passwords and OAuth flows)
  • Google Cloud Console access if you're setting up your own OAuth credentials (optional — MailClaw includes built-in OAuth for quick setup)

Method 1: Connect Gmail via OAuth 2.0 (Recommended)

OAuth is the cleanest and most secure way to connect Gmail. It doesn't require you to store your Gmail password anywhere, and you can revoke access at any time from your Google account settings. MailClaw handles the entire OAuth handshake locally — no data leaves your machine.

Step 1: Open Account Settings in the Dashboard

Navigate to your MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100, click the Accounts tab in the left sidebar, then click Add Email Account. You'll see a provider selection screen.

Step 2: Select Gmail / Google Workspace

Choose Gmail from the list of providers. MailClaw will display two sub-options: Quick Connect (MailClaw OAuth App) and Custom OAuth Credentials. For most users, Quick Connect is the right choice — it uses MailClaw's pre-registered OAuth application and gets you connected in under a minute.

Step 3: Authorize in Your Browser

Click Connect with Google. Your default browser will open a Google authorization page. Sign in with the Gmail account you want to connect, review the requested permissions (send email, read account info), and click Allow.

Google will redirect back to localhost:3100, and MailClaw will automatically save your credentials. You'll see the account appear in your Accounts list with a green status indicator.

Note: If you're connecting a Google Workspace account managed by your organization, an admin may need to authorize MailClaw's OAuth app in the Google Admin Console under Security → API Controls → App Access Control.

Using Custom OAuth Credentials

If you prefer to use your own Google Cloud project (a good practice for production deployments or team setups), select Custom OAuth Credentials and enter your Client ID and Client Secret from the Google Cloud Console. Set the authorized redirect URI to:

http://localhost:3100/auth/callback/google

Then run the connection via the CLI:

mailclaw accounts add --provider gmail --oauth-client-id YOUR_CLIENT_ID --oauth-client-secret YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET

MailClaw will launch the browser-based authorization flow automatically.

Method 2: Connect Gmail via SMTP

SMTP is the manual alternative — useful if you're in a restricted environment, prefer app-specific passwords, or are connecting a Google Workspace account through a third-party SMTP relay like SendGrid or AWS SES with a Gmail-verified sender identity.

Step 1: Generate a Gmail App Password

Google no longer allows regular passwords for third-party SMTP access. You'll need an App Password:

  1. Go to myaccount.google.com/security
  2. Under How you sign in to Google, click 2-Step Verification
  3. Scroll to the bottom and click App passwords
  4. Select app: Mail, Select device: Other (Custom name) — type "MailClaw"
  5. Copy the 16-character password Google generates

Step 2: Add the SMTP Account in MailClaw

From the dashboard, go to Accounts → Add Email Account → Manual SMTP. Fill in the following settings:

Host:       smtp.gmail.com
Port:       587
Encryption: STARTTLS
Username:   your@gmail.com
Password:   [your 16-character App Password]

Alternatively, configure it via the CLI in one command:

mailclaw accounts add \
  --provider smtp \
  --host smtp.gmail.com \
  --port 587 \
  --encryption starttls \
  --username your@gmail.com \
  --password "abcd efgh ijkl mnop"

MailClaw will send a test message to verify the connection. If it succeeds, the account is live.

Verifying Your Connection and Checking Deliverability

Once connected, MailClaw automatically runs a deliverability check against your Gmail account. Head to localhost:3100 → Accounts → [Your Account] → Deliverability to see:

  • SPF record status — Gmail handles this automatically for @gmail.com addresses; Google Workspace users should verify their domain's SPF record includes Google's mail servers
  • DKIM signing — Enabled by default for all Gmail and Workspace sends
  • DMARC policy — MailClaw will flag if your domain's DMARC policy is missing or too permissive
  • Sending reputation score — Based on bounce rate, spam complaints, and engagement metrics from your prior sends

For Google Workspace accounts sending from a custom domain, MailClaw's deliverability panel will also suggest DNS improvements and link directly to Google's Postmaster Tools for deeper analytics.

Setting Up Your First Sequence with Gmail

With your Gmail account connected, you're ready to build. Open the Sequence Builder from the dashboard and create a new sequence. Select your Gmail account as the sending identity, then use MailClaw's AI-assisted step builder — powered by OpenClaw — to draft your initial email and follow-ups.

A typical cold outreach sequence might look like:

  1. Day 0 — Introduction email (AI-drafted, personalized per contact)
  2. Day 3 — Soft follow-up referencing the first email
  3. Day 7 — Value-add email with a resource or case study
  4. Day 12 — Final breakup email

MailClaw's contact enrichment layer runs automatically on your uploaded leads — pulling in job title, company size, LinkedIn data, and recent news — so each step can be personalized without manual effort. If you're connecting to a CRM like HubSpot or Salesforce, MailClaw's integrations will sync sequence enrollment and reply data back automatically.

Tips for Keeping Your Gmail Account Healthy

Gmail has daily sending limits and spam detection heuristics that can affect deliverability if you push volume too aggressively. MailClaw's built-in sending throttle helps, but here are a few additional best practices:

  • Warm up gradually. If this is a new Gmail account or domain, start with 20–30 emails per day and increase over 3–4 weeks. MailClaw's warmup scheduler can automate this.
  • Use multi-account rotation. MailClaw supports sending across multiple Gmail accounts with round-robin routing. Spread volume across accounts instead of hammering a single inbox.
  • Monitor bounce and reply rates. MailClaw's deliverability dashboard tracks these in real time. A bounce rate above 3–5% is a warning sign worth investigating before your domain reputation suffers.
  • Avoid spam trigger phrases. The AI sequence builder in MailClaw will flag high-risk copy before you schedule sends — take those warnings seriously.
  • Connect Outlook or SendGrid as a fallback. For high-volume campaigns, consider routing transactional emails through SendGrid while keeping Gmail for personalized sequences. MailClaw supports both simultaneously under one dashboard.

You're Ready to Send

Connecting Gmail to MailClaw takes less than five minutes, and once it's done, you have a fully local, AI-powered email automation stack at your fingertips. Your credentials stay on your machine, your sequences run on your schedule, and your AI agents can handle replies, route hot leads, and trigger CRM updates — all without touching a third-party SaaS platform.

Next, explore MailClaw's AI Email Agent builder to create agents that respond to incoming Gmail messages automatically, or dive into the contact enrichment pipeline to turn a raw CSV of leads into a deeply personalized campaign. The full power of OpenClaw is waiting at localhost:3100.

articles.title: MailClaw First Run: Your First Automated Email Sequence
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: A practical walkthrough for getting MailClaw up and running and launching your first automated email sequence — from installation and SMTP setup to building a multi-step drip campaign with AI-assisted copy and contact enrichment.
articles.content:
Getting MailClaw Running in Under Five Minutes

If you've installed MailClaw and are staring at a blank terminal wondering what to do next, this guide is for you. We'll walk through everything from your first mailclaw start command to sending a fully automated, AI-assisted email sequence to a real list of contacts. By the end, you'll have a working drip campaign live on your machine — no SaaS subscriptions, no data leaving your laptop, no surprises on a billing dashboard.

MailClaw runs entirely on localhost:3100, powered by OpenClaw under the hood. That means your contacts, your copy, and your campaign logic stay on your hardware. Let's put it to work.

Starting the Local Server

Once MailClaw is installed, fire up the local dashboard with a single command:

mailclaw start

You'll see the OpenClaw runtime initialize, the local database mount, and finally a confirmation that the dashboard is live. Open your browser to http://localhost:3100 and you'll land on the MailClaw home screen — a clean, dark-mode dashboard showing your accounts, sequences, and deliverability health at a glance.

If this is your first run, most panels will be empty. That's expected. We'll fill them in together.

Step 1 — Connect Your Sending Account

Before you build a sequence, MailClaw needs a sending identity. Head to Settings → Accounts → Add Account. You have a few options here:

  • Gmail / Google Workspace — Connect via OAuth2. MailClaw handles the token refresh automatically. Click "Connect Google Account," authorize the scope, and you're done.
  • Outlook / Microsoft 365 — Same OAuth flow, different provider. Works equally well for enterprise accounts with custom domains.
  • SMTP (SendGrid, Postmark, Mailgun, etc.) — Paste in your host, port, username, and API key. MailClaw will send a test message to confirm the connection.

For a first sequence, a Gmail account connected via OAuth is the fastest path. MailClaw respects Gmail's sending limits automatically — it won't blast 500 emails at 9 AM on a Monday and get you flagged.

Pro tip: Use a dedicated sending subdomain (like outreach.yourdomain.com) rather than your root domain for cold sequences. MailClaw's deliverability monitor will remind you to set up SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records — take that advice seriously before you send to strangers.

Step 2 — Import or Build Your Contact List

Go to Contacts → Import. MailClaw accepts CSV files with flexible column mapping. A minimal contact file looks like this:

email,first_name,last_name,company
jane@example.com,Jane,Smith,Acme Corp
alex@widgetco.io,Alex,Nguyen,WidgetCo

Once imported, you'll see contacts populate in the list view. Each row is clickable — inside you'll find a contact timeline that will eventually show every email sent, opened, clicked, and replied to.

Using Contact Enrichment

If your list is sparse — maybe just emails with no names or company data — run MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment before you build your sequence. From the CLI:

mailclaw enrich --list my-list.csv --output enriched.csv

The enrichment engine pulls publicly available signals to fill in job titles, company size, LinkedIn presence, and more. This matters because MailClaw's AI email agents use contact data as variables when generating personalized copy. The richer the input, the sharper the output.

You can also trigger enrichment on individual contacts from the dashboard by clicking the Enrich button on any contact card. Results come back in seconds for most records.

Step 3 — Build Your First Sequence

Navigate to Sequences → New Sequence. Give it a name — something like Cold Outreach - SaaS Founders Q3 — and assign your sending account.

You're now in the Sequence Builder, a visual node-based editor where each block represents an email step or a wait delay. Here's the structure of a solid three-step cold sequence:

  1. Step 1 — Day 0: Introduction email. Short, value-focused, one clear call to action.
  2. Step 2 — Day 3: Follow-up. Assume they didn't see the first one. Add a new angle or resource.
  3. Step 3 — Day 7: Break-up email. Low-pressure, easy to respond to. "Should I close your file?" converts surprisingly well.

Click Add Step, choose Email, and the composer opens. You can write copy manually or let the AI email agent take a first pass.

Writing with the AI Email Agent

Click the AI Draft button in the composer. A sidebar opens where you describe your goal in plain English:

Draft a cold intro email from a B2B SaaS founder to a VP of Sales.
Goal: book a 20-minute discovery call.
Tone: direct, peer-to-peer, no fluff.
Key differentiator: we cut SDR ramp time by 40%.

The AI email agent — running locally via OpenClaw — generates a draft in seconds. It pulls in {{first_name}} and {{company}} variables automatically if they exist in your contact data. Review the output, tweak the subject line, adjust the CTA, and hit Save Step.

Repeat for Steps 2 and 3, setting the wait delays between each. The sequence builder shows a live timeline so you can see exactly when each email will land relative to enrollment.

Step 4 — Enroll Contacts and Launch

With your sequence built, go back to Contacts, select the contacts you want to target (use the filter bar to narrow by tag, company size, or enrichment status), and click Enroll in Sequence. Choose your sequence from the dropdown and hit Start.

From the CLI, you can do the same thing in one line:

mailclaw sequence run --name "Cold Outreach - SaaS Founders Q3" --list enriched.csv

MailClaw will queue the first batch of emails, stagger sending times to avoid spam filters, and begin tracking opens, clicks, and replies in real time. Switch back to the dashboard at localhost:3100 and you'll see the campaign panel light up with live stats.

Step 5 — Monitor Deliverability

Even a perfectly written sequence fails if emails land in spam. MailClaw's Deliverability Monitor runs passively in the background and surfaces issues before they compound. Check the Deliverability tab in the dashboard for:

  • DNS health: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC record validation for each sending domain.
  • Bounce rate: Hard bounces remove contacts automatically; soft bounces are flagged for review.
  • Spam signals: Reply rate, unsubscribe rate, and engagement trends that correlate with inbox placement.
  • Sending velocity: MailClaw warns you if you're approaching Gmail's daily limits or if your sending pattern looks unnatural to mail servers.

If you're piping campaigns through SendGrid or Postmark, MailClaw reads delivery event webhooks natively — paste your webhook endpoint from the Settings panel and event data flows in automatically.

Connecting to Your CRM

If you're using HubSpot or Salesforce, MailClaw can sync contact activity back without you lifting a finger. Under Settings → Integrations, connect your CRM with an API key. Once linked, every email event — sent, opened, clicked, replied — writes back to the contact record in your CRM. No more manually logging outreach. No more "did we already email this person?" confusion in a shared pipeline.

This is especially useful on teams: MailClaw runs locally for each rep, but CRM sync means activity is visible to everyone with access to HubSpot or Salesforce.

What Comes Next

You've just set up a complete, automated email sequence — AI-drafted copy, enriched contacts, live deliverability monitoring, and CRM sync — all running on your own machine. That's not a small thing.

From here, consider exploring:

  • Multi-account support — Run sequences from multiple sending identities for A/B testing or managing client campaigns.
  • AI email agents — Set up autonomous agents that respond to replies, qualify leads, or route conversations based on intent signals.
  • Branching sequences — Use the sequence builder's conditional logic to send different follow-ups based on whether a contact opened, clicked, or ignored Step 1.

MailClaw is open source and actively developed. If you hit a sharp edge or want a feature that doesn't exist yet, the best place to contribute is the GitHub repository. The architecture is intentionally extensible — adding a new integration or enrichment provider is a matter of writing a single plugin module.

Your first sequence is live. Now go iterate on it.

articles.title: How to Configure MailClaw SMTP Settings for Maximum Deliverability
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to configure MailClaw's SMTP settings step by step to maximize email deliverability, avoid spam filters, and get the most out of your AI-powered outreach sequences.
articles.content:
Why SMTP Configuration Is the Foundation of Deliverability

You can have the most perfectly crafted cold email sequence, a fully enriched contact list, and an AI email agent that writes like a seasoned copywriter — but if your SMTP settings are misconfigured, your emails are going straight to spam. Or worse, they're bouncing entirely.

MailClaw gives you serious flexibility here. Because it runs locally on your machine at localhost:3100, you're not locked into a single sending provider or a SaaS platform's arbitrary limits. You bring your own SMTP credentials — whether that's Gmail, Outlook, SendGrid, Postmark, or your own mail server — and MailClaw handles the rest through its local dashboard and sequence engine.

This guide walks you through everything: connecting your SMTP provider, tuning your sending behavior, authenticating your domain, and using MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring to catch problems before they tank your sender reputation.

Connecting Your SMTP Provider to MailClaw

Open your MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to Settings → Email Accounts → Add Account. You'll see options for SMTP/password auth and OAuth. Here's how each works in practice.

Option 1: SMTP with App Password (Gmail & Outlook)

For Gmail, you'll need to generate an App Password rather than using your main account password. Go to your Google Account → Security → 2-Step Verification → App Passwords. Generate one for "Mail" and copy it.

In MailClaw, fill in the SMTP fields like this:

Host:       smtp.gmail.com
Port:       587
Encryption: STARTTLS
Username:   you@yourdomain.com
Password:   [your 16-character App Password]

For Outlook or Microsoft 365, use:

Host:       smtp.office365.com
Port:       587
Encryption: STARTTLS
Username:   you@yourdomain.com
Password:   [your Microsoft account password or App Password]

If you're using SendGrid as a transactional relay — which is a smart move for high-volume outreach — the config looks like:

Host:       smtp.sendgrid.net
Port:       587
Encryption: STARTTLS
Username:   apikey
Password:   [your SendGrid API key]

Option 2: OAuth (Recommended for Gmail)

OAuth is the more secure and maintainable approach for Gmail. In the MailClaw dashboard under Settings → Email Accounts, click Connect with Google. You'll be redirected through a standard OAuth consent flow and land back at your local dashboard with the account linked. No passwords stored, no manual token management — MailClaw's OpenClaw engine handles token refreshing automatically.

Option 3: Configure via the CLI

If you prefer working in the terminal, MailClaw exposes account management through its CLI. From your project directory:

mailclaw account add \
  --name "Primary Outreach" \
  --host smtp.gmail.com \
  --port 587 \
  --user you@yourdomain.com \
  --pass "your-app-password" \
  --tls starttls

You can verify the connection immediately:

mailclaw account test --name "Primary Outreach"

A successful connection returns a green ✓ SMTP handshake OK in your terminal.

Domain Authentication: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC

This is where most people leave serious deliverability gains on the table. Connecting SMTP is step one — but inbox providers like Gmail and Outlook verify your sending domain before they decide whether your email belongs in the inbox or the spam folder.

SPF (Sender Policy Framework)

SPF tells receiving mail servers which IP addresses are authorized to send email on behalf of your domain. Add a TXT record to your domain's DNS:

Type:  TXT
Host:  @
Value: v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:sendgrid.net ~all

Adjust the include: values to match your actual sending providers. If you're routing through SendGrid and Gmail, include both. The ~all (softfail) is appropriate for most setups; switch to -all (hardfail) only once you're confident you've listed every legitimate sender.

DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail)

DKIM adds a cryptographic signature to every outgoing email. Your sending provider generates a public/private key pair — you publish the public key as a DNS TXT record, and the provider signs outgoing mail with the private key.

In SendGrid, go to Settings → Sender Authentication and follow the domain authentication wizard. You'll get two CNAME records to add to your DNS. With Google Workspace, DKIM setup lives under Admin Console → Apps → Gmail → Authenticate Email.

Once your DNS records propagate, MailClaw's deliverability monitor will automatically detect and validate your DKIM setup from the dashboard.

DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication)

DMARC ties SPF and DKIM together and tells inbox providers what to do when a message fails authentication. Start with a permissive monitoring policy:

Type:  TXT
Host:  _dmarc
Value: v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourdomain.com

After a few weeks of reviewing reports, tighten it to p=quarantine and eventually p=reject. This gradual rollout protects you from accidentally blocking legitimate mail while you tune things.

Tuning Sending Behavior in MailClaw

Authentication is necessary but not sufficient. How you send matters just as much as the technical setup.

Sending Limits and Warmup

Sending 500 cold emails on day one from a brand-new domain is a fast path to blacklisting. MailClaw's sequence builder includes a daily send cap and a warmup ramp setting. Access these under Sequences → [Your Sequence] → Sending Rules.

A sensible warmup schedule for a new domain:

  • Week 1: 10–20 emails/day
  • Week 2: 30–50 emails/day
  • Week 3: 75–100 emails/day
  • Week 4+: 150–200 emails/day (for most outreach use cases)

MailClaw's AI email agents can also help here by varying send times across a natural window rather than blasting all emails at the same timestamp — a pattern that looks robotic to spam filters.

Delays Between Emails

In the MailClaw config file (~/.mailclaw/config.yaml) or directly through the dashboard, set a minimum delay between individual sends:

sending:
  min_delay_seconds: 45
  max_delay_seconds: 180
  randomize_delay: true

Randomizing the delay within a range is key. Fixed delays are another signal that mail is being generated by automation rather than a human.

Bounce and Unsubscribe Handling

MailClaw automatically tracks hard bounces and marks those contacts as suppressed. Make sure your SMTP account has a valid reply-to address configured — some providers require this for bounce processing to work correctly. Navigate to Settings → Sending Defaults → Reply-To to set this globally, or override it per-sequence.

Using MailClaw's Deliverability Monitoring

The local dashboard at localhost:3100 includes a Deliverability tab that gives you a live view of the health of each connected sending account. Here's what to pay attention to:

  • Bounce rate: Keep this below 2%. Above 5% puts your sender reputation at serious risk. Use MailClaw's contact enrichment feature to verify email addresses before adding them to sequences — bad data is the most common cause of high bounce rates.
  • Spam complaint rate: Gmail's Postmaster Tools threshold is 0.1%. If you're approaching that, review your sequence copy, your targeting, and make sure your unsubscribe process works frictionlessly.
  • Authentication checks: The dashboard runs periodic checks against your domain's SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records and flags any misconfigurations with clear, actionable error messages.
  • Blacklist status: MailClaw checks your sending IP and domain against major blacklists (Spamhaus, Barracuda, SURBL) and surfaces alerts if you appear on any of them.

Pro tip: If you're syncing contacts from HubSpot, Salesforce, or a CSV import, run them through MailClaw's contact enrichment step before building a sequence. Enrichment validates email addresses, fills in missing fields, and flags risky domains — all before a single email gets sent.

Multi-Account Strategy for Scale

One of the most underused features in MailClaw is multi-account support. Rather than hammering a single inbox with all your outreach, you can distribute sends across multiple accounts and domains — each with its own SMTP config, warmup schedule, and sending rules.

Add a second account from the dashboard or CLI, then assign it to specific sequences or use MailClaw's round-robin distribution:

mailclaw account add \
  --name "Secondary Outreach" \
  --host smtp.office365.com \
  --port 587 \
  --user outreach2@yourdomain.com \
  --pass "your-password" \
  --tls starttls

mailclaw sequence update "Q4 Campaign" \
  --accounts "Primary Outreach,Secondary Outreach" \
  --distribution round-robin

This approach lets you scale volume while keeping each individual account well within safe sending thresholds.

One Final Check Before You Launch

Before activating any sequence, run MailClaw's pre-launch audit from the dashboard (Sequences → [Your Sequence] → Run Audit) or via CLI:

mailclaw audit --sequence "Q4 Campaign"

The audit checks your SMTP connection, validates authentication records, scores your email copy for spam triggers, confirms your unsubscribe link is functional, and verifies that your daily send limits are within safe ranges for your domain age. Fix anything flagged before you hit send — your future inbox placement will thank you.

Getting SMTP right in MailClaw isn't complicated, but it does require attention to detail. Set it up properly once, keep an eye on the deliverability dashboard, and your AI-powered sequences will land where they're supposed to — in the inbox, starting conversations.

articles.title: Getting Started with OpenClaw Mail: From Install to First Campaign
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: A step-by-step guide to installing MailClaw, connecting your email accounts, enriching your first contact list, and launching a fully automated outreach sequence — all running locally on your Mac.
articles.content:
Why Run Your Email Automation Locally?

Most email automation platforms send your contact data, message drafts, and campaign logic to third-party servers the moment you hit save. If you're running outreach for a startup, managing sensitive B2B relationships, or just uncomfortable with that level of data exposure, the trade-off has always felt uncomfortable.

MailClaw flips that model. Built on the OpenClaw framework, it runs entirely on your Mac at localhost:3100 — your contacts stay local, your AI agents process data on your machine, and your SMTP credentials never leave your control. Open source, auditable, and fast. Let's get you set up.

Installing MailClaw

Before you begin, make sure you have Node.js 18+ and Git installed. You can verify with:

node --version
git --version

Then clone the repository and install dependencies:

git clone https://github.com/openclaw/mailclaw.git
cd mailclaw
npm install

Once dependencies are installed, initialize your local environment:

cp .env.example .env
npm run setup

The setup wizard will walk you through creating a local SQLite database, setting your encryption key for stored credentials, and choosing your preferred AI provider (local Ollama models or an OpenAI-compatible API). After setup completes, start the server:

npm start

Open your browser to http://localhost:3100 and you'll land on the MailClaw dashboard. No accounts, no subscriptions, no tracking pixels phoning home.

Connecting Your Email Accounts

MailClaw supports both SMTP and OAuth connections, so you can wire up virtually any provider. Head to Settings → Email Accounts in the dashboard.

Gmail and Google Workspace

Click Add Account → Google OAuth. MailClaw will open a local OAuth flow — your credentials are exchanged directly with Google and the resulting token is encrypted and stored only on your machine. For Gmail, you'll also want to enable the Gmail API in your Google Cloud Console if you haven't already. Once connected, MailClaw automatically detects your sending limits and adjusts sequence pacing accordingly to protect your sender reputation.

Outlook and Microsoft 365

Select Add Account → Microsoft OAuth. The process mirrors Gmail — authorize via Microsoft's identity platform and MailClaw handles token refresh automatically. This works for both personal Outlook accounts and organizational Microsoft 365 tenants.

SendGrid, Postmark, and Custom SMTP

For transactional email providers or custom SMTP setups, choose Add Account → SMTP and enter your host, port, and credentials. SendGrid users can also paste their API key directly for better deliverability analytics. MailClaw will validate the connection and send a test message before saving.

Pro tip: Add multiple accounts and assign them to different campaigns. MailClaw's multi-account support lets you rotate senders, warm up new inboxes gradually, and isolate cold outreach from transactional mail — all from one dashboard.

Importing and Enriching Your Contacts

With your accounts connected, it's time to bring in contacts. Go to Contacts → Import and upload a CSV. MailClaw accepts any flat CSV with at minimum an email column — everything else is optional and can be filled in later.

Running Contact Enrichment

This is where MailClaw earns its keep. Select your imported contacts and click Enrich. MailClaw's enrichment engine can pull in:

  • Job title and company name from public LinkedIn data and company websites
  • Company size, industry, and tech stack from sources like Clearbit-compatible APIs
  • Verified email status (MX record validation, SMTP handshake checks)
  • Social profiles and recent activity signals

Enrichment runs asynchronously in the background. For a list of 500 contacts, expect it to complete in five to ten minutes depending on your machine and network. Once done, you'll have significantly more personalization data to work with — which the AI sequence builder uses directly.

Syncing with Your CRM

If your team already lives in HubSpot or Salesforce, you don't need to abandon that workflow. MailClaw's integrations panel (under Settings → Integrations) lets you pull contact lists from HubSpot via API key or connect to Salesforce using OAuth. Changes sync bidirectionally — replies and engagement data flow back into your CRM automatically.

Building Your First Email Sequence

Navigate to Sequences → New Sequence. Give it a name, select your sending account, and choose a contact segment to target. Now the fun begins.

Using the AI Sequence Builder

Click Generate with AI and describe your outreach goal in plain English. For example:

"Three-step sequence targeting SaaS founders at companies with 10–50 employees. Goal is to book a 20-minute discovery call. Tone should be direct but not salesy. Reference their company name and industry in step one."

MailClaw's AI agent — running via OpenClaw's local inference layer — will generate a full sequence including subject lines, body copy, and suggested send timing. Because enrichment data is already loaded for your contacts, the AI pulls in real variables like {{contact.company}}, {{contact.title}}, and {{contact.industry}} automatically.

You're not locked into what the AI generates. Every email in the sequence is fully editable in the visual editor. Adjust tone, swap out calls-to-action, or reorder steps with drag-and-drop.

Setting Timing and Conditions

For each step in the sequence, configure:

  1. Send delay — how many days after the previous step (or enrollment) to wait
  2. Send window — limit sending to business hours in the contact's timezone
  3. Exit conditions — stop the sequence if a contact replies, clicks a link, or books a meeting
  4. A/B variants — test two subject lines and let MailClaw auto-select the winner after 100 sends

Monitoring Deliverability Before You Launch

Don't skip this step. Go to Deliverability → Health Check before activating any sequence. MailClaw will run a suite of checks including:

  • SPF, DKIM, and DMARC record validation for each connected domain
  • Blacklist lookups across major RBLs (Spamhaus, Barracuda, etc.)
  • Inbox placement test — sends a probe message and checks which folder it lands in across Gmail, Outlook, and Apple Mail
  • Sending volume warnings — flags if your planned sequence would exceed safe daily limits for a given account's age and reputation

If your domain is missing a DMARC record, MailClaw shows you the exact DNS entry to add. Green across the board? You're ready to launch.

Activating Your Campaign and Reading the Results

Back in your sequence, click Activate. MailClaw will confirm the contact count, estimated completion date, and daily send volume, then begin processing on schedule. You can close your browser — the local server keeps running in the background.

As sends go out, the Campaign Analytics view updates in real time with open rates, click rates, reply rates, and bounce classifications. Click into any individual contact to see their full activity timeline — every send, open, click, and reply, with timestamps.

Setting Up an AI Email Agent

For truly hands-off outreach, enable an AI Email Agent on your sequence. Under Sequences → [Your Sequence] → Agent Settings, you can configure the agent to:

  • Classify incoming replies (interested, not interested, out of office, referral)
  • Auto-respond to common questions using a knowledge base you define
  • Pause the sequence for a contact and flag them for human follow-up when intent signals are high
  • Log meeting requests directly to your calendar integration

The agent runs locally using your chosen model, so no reply content is ever processed by an external API unless you explicitly configure a remote endpoint.

What to Do Next

Once your first campaign is running, explore a few areas that will meaningfully improve your results:

  • Inbox rotation — add two or three warmed-up sending accounts to a sequence and distribute volume across them
  • Custom enrichment sources — MailClaw's plugin architecture lets you write simple JavaScript modules to pull data from internal databases or proprietary APIs
  • Webhook triggers — fire a webhook when a contact replies, clicks, or completes a sequence, then chain that into Zapier, Make, or your own backend
  • Community sequences — the OpenClaw community maintains a library of pre-built sequence templates for common use cases like cold outreach, product onboarding, and re-engagement

MailClaw is genuinely different from hosted platforms — not because it's harder, but because it gives you real control. Your data, your models, your rules. The first campaign is just the beginning.

articles.title: MailClaw Setup Checklist: Everything You Need Before Your First Send
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Before you send your first email campaign with MailClaw, there are a few critical setup steps that can mean the difference between landing in the inbox and disappearing into spam. This checklist walks you through everything — from installation and SMTP configuration to contact enrichment and deliverability hygiene.
articles.content:
Why Setup Matters More Than You Think

Most email tools make it tempting to just hit send. You import a list, write a subject line, and go. But skipping the fundamentals — domain authentication, SMTP warm-up, contact validation — is exactly how campaigns end up flagged, bounced, or silently ignored by spam filters.

MailClaw gives you a serious local-first infrastructure for email automation: AI agents, sequence building, contact enrichment, and deliverability monitoring all running from your machine at localhost:3100. But that power only pays off when your foundation is solid. This checklist makes sure it is.

Step 1: Install MailClaw and Verify Your Local Environment

MailClaw runs locally on your Mac, built on the OpenClaw runtime. Before anything else, confirm your environment is ready.

# Install MailClaw via the official installer
curl -fsSL https://mailclaw.dev/install.sh | bash

# Verify the installation
mailclaw --version

# Start the local server
mailclaw start

Once running, open your browser and navigate to http://localhost:3100. You should see the MailClaw dashboard. If the port is blocked or in use, you can override it:

mailclaw start --port 3200

Check that the following are confirmed before moving forward:

  • Dashboard loads without errors at localhost:3100
  • OpenClaw engine status shows Running in the system panel
  • Node.js version is 18+ (MailClaw's AI agent layer requires it)
  • At least 4GB RAM available for AI enrichment tasks

Step 2: Connect Your Email Sending Account

MailClaw supports both SMTP and OAuth connections, so whether you're sending through Gmail, Outlook, or a dedicated deliverability provider like SendGrid or Postmark, setup is straightforward.

OAuth Integration (Gmail and Outlook)

For Gmail and Microsoft Outlook, OAuth is the recommended path. It avoids storing plain-text passwords and keeps your tokens refreshed automatically. In the MailClaw dashboard, go to Settings → Sending Accounts → Add Account and select your provider.

You'll need to create OAuth credentials in Google Cloud Console or Azure App Registrations. MailClaw's docs walk through both, but the key scopes you need for Gmail are:

https://mail.google.com/
https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.send
https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.modify

SMTP Integration (SendGrid, Postmark, Custom)

For dedicated sending infrastructure, SMTP is the cleaner choice. Add your credentials via the CLI or the dashboard:

mailclaw accounts add \
  --name "SendGrid Production" \
  --type smtp \
  --host smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --port 587 \
  --user apikey \
  --pass YOUR_SENDGRID_API_KEY

Multi-account support means you can rotate between providers, keep cold outreach separate from transactional mail, and protect your primary domain reputation during warm-up phases.

Step 3: Authenticate Your Domain (Non-Negotiable)

This is the step most people skip and the one that causes the most damage. Without proper domain authentication, even beautifully written emails end up in spam or rejected outright.

You need all three of these configured in your DNS before sending a single email:

SPF Record

Tells receiving mail servers which IPs are allowed to send on behalf of your domain.

TXT @ "v=spf1 include:sendgrid.net include:_spf.google.com ~all"

DKIM

A cryptographic signature that proves the email hasn't been tampered with in transit. Your sending provider (SendGrid, Google Workspace, etc.) will generate a DKIM key for you. Add the CNAME or TXT record they provide to your DNS.

DMARC

Tells receiving servers what to do when SPF or DKIM checks fail. Start with a monitoring-only policy:

TXT _dmarc "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com"

Once you've confirmed clean reports over a few weeks, tighten the policy to p=quarantine or p=reject.

MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitor will flag missing or misconfigured records right in the dashboard. Run a check anytime with:

mailclaw deliverability check --domain yourdomain.com

Step 4: Import and Enrich Your Contacts

A clean, enriched contact list dramatically improves personalization — and MailClaw's AI-powered contact enrichment makes this straightforward.

Importing Contacts

You can import contacts from a CSV, pull them directly from HubSpot or Salesforce, or use the MailClaw API to sync from your own systems:

# Import from CSV
mailclaw contacts import --file leads.csv --map "email,first_name,company,title"

# Sync from HubSpot
mailclaw contacts sync --source hubspot --list "Q4 Outreach"

Running AI Enrichment

Before building sequences, run enrichment to fill in missing data like job titles, company size, industry, and LinkedIn URLs. This data feeds directly into MailClaw's AI personalization engine.

mailclaw enrich --list "Q4 Outreach" --fields title,company_size,industry

Enrichment runs locally using the OpenClaw AI layer, so your contact data never leaves your machine. For larger lists, you can also connect external enrichment APIs like Clearbit or Apollo in the integrations panel.

Pro tip: Always run a deduplication pass before enrichment. Use mailclaw contacts dedupe --list "Q4 Outreach" to merge duplicate records and reduce wasted API calls.

Step 5: Build Your First Sequence

With accounts connected and contacts enriched, you're ready to use MailClaw's sequence builder. Head to Sequences → New Sequence in the dashboard, or scaffold one from the CLI:

mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "SaaS Founder Outreach" \
  --steps 4 \
  --interval 3d

Each step in the sequence supports:

  • AI-generated personalized copy (powered by OpenClaw)
  • Dynamic variables pulled from enriched contact fields
  • Conditional branching based on opens, clicks, or replies
  • A/B testing on subject lines and body copy

Let the AI agent draft your initial copy based on your goal, then review and edit. You stay in control — the agent handles the first pass.

Step 6: Run Pre-Send Deliverability Checks

Before activating any sequence, run MailClaw's pre-send checklist. This is one of the most underused features in the tool:

mailclaw sequence validate --name "SaaS Founder Outreach"

This command checks:

  • Spam score — flags high-risk words and excessive link density
  • Authentication status — confirms SPF, DKIM, and DMARC are active
  • Unsubscribe link — verifies one-click unsubscribe is present
  • Sending volume — warns if you're exceeding warm-up safe limits
  • Contact list hygiene — surfaces invalid or risky email addresses

Resolve every warning before your first send. A clean validation output looks like this:

✔ SPF record found and valid
✔ DKIM signature verified
✔ DMARC policy active (p=none)
✔ Spam score: 1.2 / 10 (Low risk)
✔ Unsubscribe link detected
⚠ 14 contacts flagged as high-bounce risk — review recommended

Step 7: Configure Your AI Email Agent

MailClaw's AI email agents can handle reply detection, auto-follow-up pausing when a prospect responds, and even draft suggested replies for your review. Set up your first agent from the dashboard under Agents → New Agent.

At minimum, configure your agent with:

  • Goal context — what the sequence is trying to achieve (demo booking, content download, partnership inquiry)
  • Reply detection rules — stop sequence on positive reply, out-of-office, or unsubscribe language
  • Escalation behavior — notify you via dashboard alert when a hot reply comes in

This is where MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered intelligence really stands out. The agent understands intent, not just keywords, so it won't accidentally stop a sequence because someone replied "thanks, not interested" (which you do want to respect) versus "thanks, sending this to my team" (which is a warm signal worth following up on).

You're Ready to Send

Run through this checklist one more time before activating:

  1. MailClaw running at localhost:3100 ✓
  2. Sending account connected via OAuth or SMTP ✓
  3. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC configured and verified ✓
  4. Contacts imported, deduplicated, and enriched ✓
  5. Sequence built, reviewed, and validated ✓
  6. AI agent configured with reply detection ✓

Good setup isn't glamorous, but it's the difference between a campaign that gets results and one that quietly damages your sending reputation. With MailClaw's local-first architecture, you have more transparency and control over this process than most cloud-based tools will ever give you. Now go send something worth reading.

articles.title: How to Connect Microsoft Outlook to MailClaw
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to connect Microsoft Outlook to MailClaw using OAuth or SMTP, so you can send AI-powered email sequences, enrich contacts, and run automated outreach campaigns — all from your local dashboard.
articles.content:
Why Connect Outlook to MailClaw?

Microsoft Outlook is still the backbone of business email for millions of organizations, particularly in enterprise and mid-market companies running Microsoft 365. If your prospects and customers are expecting email from an Outlook address — or if your domain is managed through Exchange Online — you need your outreach tool to work with that infrastructure, not around it.

MailClaw supports Outlook natively through two methods: OAuth 2.0 via Microsoft Identity Platform and direct SMTP with app passwords. Once connected, your Outlook account becomes a fully active sending channel inside MailClaw's local dashboard at localhost:3100, giving you access to AI email agents, the sequence builder, contact enrichment, and deliverability monitoring — all without routing your data through a third-party cloud.

Before You Begin: What You'll Need

Before connecting Outlook, make sure you have the following ready:

  • MailClaw installed and running locally (mailclaw start from your terminal)
  • A Microsoft 365 or Outlook.com account with sending privileges
  • Access to your Microsoft Azure portal if you're using OAuth (recommended for business accounts)
  • Two-factor authentication enabled on your Microsoft account (required for app passwords)

If you haven't installed MailClaw yet, you can get it running on your Mac in under two minutes. It's open source, built on OpenClaw, and runs entirely on localhost — no accounts, no data leaving your machine.

Method 1: Connect Outlook via OAuth 2.0 (Recommended)

OAuth is the preferred method for Microsoft 365 business accounts. It's more secure than storing credentials directly, and it gives MailClaw a persistent token that can be refreshed automatically — so your campaigns don't stop mid-sequence because a password changed.

Step 1: Register an App in Azure Active Directory

You'll need to register MailClaw as an application in Azure so Microsoft can issue OAuth tokens. This sounds more complex than it is — it takes about five minutes.

  1. Go to portal.azure.com and sign in with your Microsoft 365 admin account.
  2. Navigate to Azure Active Directory → App registrations → New registration.
  3. Give it a name like MailClaw Local.
  4. Under Supported account types, choose Accounts in this organizational directory only (or Personal Microsoft accounts if you're using Outlook.com).
  5. Set the Redirect URI to: http://localhost:3100/auth/microsoft/callback
  6. Click Register.

Once registered, note your Application (client) ID and Directory (tenant) ID from the overview page. Then go to Certificates & secrets → New client secret, create a secret, and copy the value immediately — you won't see it again.

Finally, go to API permissions → Add a permission → Microsoft Graph and add the following delegated permissions:

  • Mail.Send
  • Mail.ReadWrite
  • offline_access
  • User.Read

Grant admin consent if prompted.

Step 2: Add Your Credentials to MailClaw

With your Azure app configured, open your MailClaw config file or use the CLI to add the account:

mailclaw accounts add \
  --provider microsoft \
  --client-id YOUR_CLIENT_ID \
  --client-secret YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET \
  --tenant-id YOUR_TENANT_ID \
  --label "Outlook Work"

MailClaw will open a browser window pointing to localhost:3100/auth/microsoft, walk you through Microsoft's consent screen, and store the resulting token securely in your local config. You'll see the account appear in the Accounts tab of your dashboard within seconds.

Method 2: Connect Outlook via SMTP with an App Password

If you're using a personal Outlook.com or Hotmail account — or if your organization doesn't allow Azure app registrations — SMTP with an app password is a solid fallback. Note that basic authentication is disabled by default on modern Microsoft 365 accounts, so check with your IT admin before going this route.

Step 1: Generate an App Password

  1. Sign in to your Microsoft account at account.microsoft.com.
  2. Go to Security → Advanced security options → App passwords.
  3. Click Create a new app password and copy the generated password.

Note: App passwords are only available if two-step verification is enabled on your account. If you don't see the option, enable 2FA first.

Step 2: Configure SMTP in MailClaw

Run the following command to add your Outlook account via SMTP:

mailclaw accounts add \
  --provider smtp \
  --host smtp-mail.outlook.com \
  --port 587 \
  --encryption starttls \
  --username your@outlook.com \
  --password YOUR_APP_PASSWORD \
  --label "Outlook Personal"

Alternatively, you can enter these details through the Accounts → Add Account form in the local dashboard at localhost:3100. Use the following SMTP settings for Outlook:

  • Host: smtp-mail.outlook.com
  • Port: 587
  • Encryption: STARTTLS
  • Username: Your full Outlook email address
  • Password: Your app password (not your regular login password)

Verifying the Connection

Once your account is added via either method, MailClaw will run a quick connection check. You can also trigger this manually:

mailclaw accounts verify --label "Outlook Work"

A successful response looks like this:

✓ SMTP connection established
✓ Auth handshake complete
✓ Test message sent to postmaster@mailclaw.local
Account "Outlook Work" is ready to send.

If you see authentication errors, double-check that your tenant ID is correct, that admin consent was granted, or that your app password hasn't expired.

Using Your Outlook Account in Campaigns and Sequences

With Outlook connected, it becomes available as a sending account throughout MailClaw. Here's where you'll use it:

Sequence Builder

When building a multi-step email sequence, select your Outlook account as the sending identity in the From dropdown. MailClaw will respect Outlook's sending limits and queue messages accordingly — no more hitting Microsoft's rate limits and getting your account flagged.

AI Email Agents

MailClaw's AI email agents, powered by OpenClaw, can draft and send replies, follow-ups, and nurture messages through your Outlook account. You configure the agent's behavior — tone, goals, reply rules — and it handles the rest, sending from your real Outlook address so replies land back in your actual inbox.

Contact Enrichment

MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment pulls data from public sources and optional integrations like HubSpot, Salesforce, and LinkedIn to fill in job titles, company sizes, and tech stacks. You can trigger enrichment on import or before a sequence launches, so your Outlook-sent emails feel personally researched rather than bulk-blasted.

Deliverability Monitoring

One of the most practical reasons to run MailClaw locally is full visibility into your sending health. The deliverability dashboard shows bounce rates, spam complaints, and open tracking per account — including your Outlook account. If Microsoft flags unusual sending volume, you'll see it in real time and can pause or throttle the sequence before your domain reputation takes a hit.

For teams using Outlook alongside other providers like Gmail, SendGrid, or Amazon SES, MailClaw's multi-account support lets you rotate senders across a campaign, spreading volume and protecting each domain's reputation.

Troubleshooting Common Issues

A few issues come up regularly when connecting Outlook accounts:

  • AADSTS70011 error: The requested scope is invalid. Go back to your Azure app registration and confirm all four API permissions are added and admin consent is granted.
  • 535 Authentication failed (SMTP): You're likely using your regular password instead of an app password, or basic auth is disabled at the tenant level. Switch to OAuth or contact your IT admin.
  • Token expired after 60-90 days: This happens if offline_access scope wasn't granted. Re-authorize the account through localhost:3100/accounts and confirm the scope is included.
