  • Rate limiting (550 errors): Microsoft 365 limits sending volume based on your license tier. Use MailClaw's built-in send throttling (--delay 90s per message) to stay within limits.

Next Steps

Once your Outlook account is live inside MailClaw, you're set up to run serious outreach without touching a third-party platform. From your terminal or the localhost:3100 dashboard, you can build sequences, launch AI agents, enrich contacts, and monitor deliverability — all while keeping your data local and your sending reputation intact.

If you're running multiple accounts — say, Outlook for enterprise outreach and Gmail for startup prospects — check out the MailClaw multi-account rotation guide for tips on balancing volume across senders. And if you want to go deeper on AI agents, the OpenClaw documentation covers how to configure agent personas, reply rules, and escalation logic that works across any connected sending account.

articles.title: MailClaw OAuth Setup: Connecting Email Providers Securely
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to securely connect Gmail, Outlook, and other email providers to MailClaw using OAuth 2.0 — with step-by-step instructions, CLI commands, and best practices for keeping your credentials safe while running powerful AI email automation locally.
articles.content:
Why OAuth Matters for Local Email Automation

If you've ever copy-pasted an app password into a config file and immediately felt a pang of regret, you already understand why OAuth exists. When MailClaw connects to your email provider, it needs a secure, revocable way to send on your behalf — without ever storing your actual password. That's exactly what OAuth 2.0 delivers.

Because MailClaw runs entirely on your local machine at localhost:3100, your credentials never touch a third-party server. The OAuth token exchange happens between your browser, your email provider, and your local MailClaw instance. This architecture is one of the core reasons MailClaw was built on OpenClaw's local-first philosophy — you get enterprise-grade security with zero vendor lock-in.

This guide walks you through connecting Gmail, Microsoft Outlook, and custom SMTP providers using OAuth, so your AI email agents and outreach sequences can fire reliably without compromising your accounts.

Before You Begin: Prerequisites

Make sure MailClaw is running and accessible. If you haven't started it yet:

mailclaw start
# Dashboard available at http://localhost:3100

You'll also want to have the following ready for whichever provider you're connecting:

  • A Google Cloud Console project (for Gmail OAuth)
  • An Azure App Registration (for Outlook/Microsoft 365)
  • Your SMTP credentials or SendGrid API key (for custom providers)
  • MailClaw CLI version 1.2.0 or higher — check with mailclaw --version

Connecting Gmail via OAuth 2.0

Step 1: Create a Google Cloud OAuth App

Head to the Google Cloud Console and create a new project (or use an existing one). Navigate to APIs & Services → Credentials and create an OAuth 2.0 Client ID. Choose Web Application as the application type.

Add the following to your Authorized Redirect URIs:

http://localhost:3100/auth/gmail/callback

Once created, download the JSON credentials file. You'll need the client_id and client_secret values in the next step.

Step 2: Add Gmail to MailClaw

Use the MailClaw CLI to register the account:

mailclaw accounts add \
  --provider gmail \
  --client-id YOUR_CLIENT_ID \
  --client-secret YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET \
  --email you@yourdomain.com

MailClaw will open your browser and prompt you to authorize access through Google's standard consent screen. After approval, the OAuth token is stored locally in your MailClaw keychain — encrypted, never plaintext.

Step 3: Verify the Connection

mailclaw accounts test --email you@yourdomain.com

A successful response looks like:

✓ Gmail connected — SMTP auth via OAuth2
✓ Send quota: 500/day (standard Gmail)
✓ IMAP access: enabled

Your Gmail account now appears in the MailClaw dashboard under Accounts → Connected Providers, ready to be assigned to sequences, AI agents, or bulk campaigns.

Connecting Microsoft Outlook and Microsoft 365

Step 1: Register an Azure App

Sign in to the Azure Portal and navigate to Azure Active Directory → App Registrations → New Registration. Name your app (e.g., "MailClaw Local") and set the redirect URI to:

http://localhost:3100/auth/outlook/callback

Under API Permissions, add the following Microsoft Graph scopes:

  • Mail.Send
  • Mail.ReadWrite
  • offline_access (required for refresh tokens)

Grant admin consent if you're on a managed Microsoft 365 tenant. Copy your Application (client) ID and generate a Client Secret under Certificates & Secrets.

Step 2: Register with MailClaw

mailclaw accounts add \
  --provider outlook \
  --client-id YOUR_AZURE_CLIENT_ID \
  --client-secret YOUR_AZURE_SECRET \
  --tenant-id YOUR_TENANT_ID \
  --email you@company.com

The --tenant-id flag is optional for personal Microsoft accounts but required for Microsoft 365 business tenants. MailClaw handles both the authorization code flow and automatic token refresh so your sequences never drop mid-campaign.

Tip for Microsoft 365 teams: MailClaw's multi-account support lets you connect multiple Outlook inboxes simultaneously. This is particularly powerful when running deliverability rotation across several team members' accounts — each sender gets its own OAuth token, its own warm-up schedule, and its own deliverability score tracked in the dashboard.

Connecting SendGrid and Custom SMTP Providers

Not every workflow needs OAuth. If you're using SendGrid, Mailgun, or a custom SMTP relay, MailClaw supports API key and SMTP credential authentication with the same local-encrypted storage.

mailclaw accounts add \
  --provider sendgrid \
  --api-key YOUR_SENDGRID_API_KEY \
  --from-email outreach@yourdomain.com \
  --from-name "Your Name"

For generic SMTP (useful for services like Zoho Mail, Fastmail, or a self-hosted Postfix server):

mailclaw accounts add \
  --provider smtp \
  --host mail.yourdomain.com \
  --port 587 \
  --username you@yourdomain.com \
  --password YOUR_APP_PASSWORD \
  --encryption tls

Once connected, these accounts are fully interchangeable with OAuth accounts inside the sequence builder and AI agent configuration. MailClaw doesn't care which transport layer you're using — it abstracts that complexity away.

Managing Multiple Accounts in the Dashboard

Open your MailClaw dashboard at http://localhost:3100 and navigate to Settings → Email Accounts. You'll see all connected accounts listed with their health status, daily send limits, OAuth token expiry dates, and deliverability scores.

From here you can:

  • Rotate sending accounts across a sequence to distribute volume and protect sender reputation
  • Re-authorize expired tokens with a single click — MailClaw detects token expiry proactively and alerts you before a campaign fails
  • Assign accounts to AI agents — each agent can have a dedicated inbox for replies, enrichment lookups, and follow-up logic
  • Monitor per-account deliverability including bounce rates, spam complaints, and open rate trends

Security Best Practices for OAuth Tokens

MailClaw's local architecture already gives you a significant security advantage, but there are additional steps worth taking:

Use Scoped Permissions

When configuring your Google or Azure app, request only the permissions MailClaw actually needs. Mail.Send and read access for bounce detection is enough for most campaigns. Avoid requesting calendar or contacts admin scopes unless you're using the contact enrichment features that specifically require them.

Rotate Credentials Regularly

Set a reminder to regenerate your Azure Client Secret and Google OAuth credentials every 90 days. Update MailClaw with:

mailclaw accounts update --email you@yourdomain.com --client-secret NEW_SECRET

Audit Connected Apps

Periodically review the apps connected to your Google and Microsoft accounts. In Google: myaccount.google.com → Security → Third-party apps. In Azure: Enterprise Applications → All Applications. Remove anything you no longer use.

Keep MailClaw Updated

Because MailClaw is open source and built on OpenClaw, security patches move fast. Stay current:

mailclaw update
# or via npm: npm update -g mailclaw

Integrating with CRMs and Enrichment Workflows

Once your email accounts are connected, the real power of MailClaw's OAuth setup becomes clear. Your authenticated accounts can be paired with contact enrichment workflows that pull data from HubSpot, Salesforce, or MailClaw's built-in enrichment engine — and then pass that enriched context directly to AI email agents for hyper-personalized outreach.

For example, a typical sequence might look like this: a contact is imported, enriched with company data, routed through the sequence builder, and then handed off to an AI agent that crafts and sends a personalized email via your OAuth-authenticated Gmail account — all without leaving localhost.

The OAuth layer is what makes this trustworthy. Every email sent by an AI agent is sent as you, through your authenticated provider, with your sender reputation intact — not through some anonymous relay that's already on every blocklist.

Troubleshooting Common OAuth Issues

Token Expired or Revoked

If you see 401 Unauthorized errors in the MailClaw logs, re-run the account add command or use the dashboard re-auth button. Gmail tokens expire after 7 days if the app is in "Testing" mode in Google Cloud — publish your OAuth app to production to get longer-lived refresh tokens.

Redirect URI Mismatch

This is the most common setup error. Double-check that the redirect URI in your Google or Azure app registration exactly matches http://localhost:3100/auth/[provider]/callback — including the protocol, no trailing slash.

Microsoft 365 Admin Consent Required

If your organization's Azure tenant requires admin consent for new app registrations, you'll see a permission error during the OAuth flow. Have your IT admin visit the consent URL or pre-approve the app in the Azure portal under Enterprise Applications → Admin Consent.

OAuth setup is a one-time investment that pays off immediately. Once your providers are connected securely, every feature in MailClaw — from the sequence builder to the AI agents to deliverability monitoring — just works, reliably and safely, from your own machine.

articles.title: How to Set Up Multiple Email Accounts in MailClaw
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how to connect and manage multiple email accounts in MailClaw, from Gmail OAuth to SendGrid SMTP, so you can scale outreach, protect deliverability, and run parallel campaigns without leaving your local dashboard.
articles.content:
Why Multiple Email Accounts Matter for Serious Outreach

If you're running cold outreach at any meaningful scale, a single email account is a liability. Inbox providers like Gmail and Outlook throttle sending volume, flag accounts with sudden spikes in activity, and can suspend senders who push too hard too fast. The solution isn't to send less — it's to spread the load intelligently across multiple accounts, each with its own reputation, warmup history, and sending cadence.

MailClaw's multi-account support is built with exactly this in mind. Because it runs locally on localhost:3100 via OpenClaw, all your account credentials, sequences, and campaign logic stay on your machine — nothing is uploaded to a third-party SaaS platform. You control the data. You control the sending. And with MailClaw's AI email agents, each account can behave like a fully autonomous outreach rep, personalizing and scheduling sends based on real-time signals.

Before You Add Your First Account

Plan Your Account Architecture

Before connecting anything, spend five minutes thinking about structure. The most common setups look like this:

  • Role-based accounts: sales@, hello@, and partnerships@ on your primary domain, each handling a different audience segment.
  • Subdomain accounts: outreach@mail.yourdomain.com keeps cold email separate from transactional mail, protecting your root domain's reputation.
  • Alias domains: Register a secondary domain (e.g., yourdomainhq.com) for cold prospecting so that any deliverability issues never touch your main brand.
  • Provider diversification: Mix Gmail Workspace accounts with SendGrid or Mailgun SMTP so you're not dependent on one provider's policies.

MailClaw's sequence builder lets you assign specific accounts to specific sequences, so this architecture directly affects how you organize campaigns. Getting it right now saves you a painful restructure later.

Authenticate Your Domain First

No matter which provider you use, make sure each sending domain has SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records in place before connecting it to MailClaw. The deliverability monitoring dashboard (accessible at localhost:3100/deliverability) will flag missing records automatically once an account is connected, but it's faster to sort DNS before you start.

Connecting Accounts via the MailClaw Dashboard

Adding a Gmail or Google Workspace Account (OAuth)

OAuth is the recommended method for Gmail and Google Workspace accounts. It avoids storing passwords locally and uses Google's token-based auth, which is more stable for long-running campaigns.

  1. Open your local dashboard at http://localhost:3100
  2. Navigate to Settings → Email Accounts → Add Account
  3. Select Gmail / Google Workspace as the provider
  4. Click Connect with Google and complete the OAuth flow in your browser
  5. Grant MailClaw the required scopes: gmail.send, gmail.readonly, and gmail.modify
  6. Once authorized, the account appears in your accounts list with a green status indicator

MailClaw automatically handles token refresh, so you won't need to re-authenticate unless you explicitly revoke access from Google's security settings.

Adding an Outlook or Microsoft 365 Account (OAuth)

The process for Outlook and Microsoft 365 is nearly identical. Select Outlook / Microsoft 365 as the provider, and MailClaw will redirect you to Microsoft's OAuth consent screen. Make sure your Microsoft 365 admin has enabled third-party app access if you're on a managed corporate tenant — otherwise the OAuth flow will fail at the consent step.

Adding SMTP Accounts (SendGrid, Mailgun, Postmark, Custom)

For transactional email providers or custom SMTP servers, use the manual SMTP configuration path. This works with SendGrid, Mailgun, Postmark, Amazon SES, or any provider that exposes standard SMTP credentials.

# You can also add SMTP accounts via the MailClaw CLI:
mailclaw accounts add \
  --name "SendGrid Outreach" \
  --type smtp \
  --host smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --port 587 \
  --user apikey \
  --pass YOUR_SENDGRID_API_KEY \
  --from "Your Name "

After running this command, the account is immediately available in the dashboard and can be assigned to any sequence. Use mailclaw accounts list to verify the connection and check sending limits pulled from the provider's API.

Managing Multiple Accounts Effectively

Setting Per-Account Sending Limits

One of the most important things you can do with multiple accounts is enforce daily send caps. Blasting at full volume from a fresh account is a fast track to the spam folder. MailClaw respects per-account limits and distributes sequence sends accordingly.

In the dashboard under Accounts → [Account Name] → Sending Rules, configure:

  • Daily send limit: Start at 30–50 for new accounts, scale up 20% per week
  • Send window: Restrict sends to business hours in your target timezone
  • Minimum gap between emails: Set 3–8 minutes to avoid machine-like sending patterns
  • Weekend pause: Enable this for B2B campaigns — decision-makers aren't clearing inboxes on Saturday

Assigning Accounts to Sequences

In the sequence builder, each sequence has an Account Assignment section. You can assign a single account, or enable round-robin mode to rotate sends across multiple accounts automatically. This is particularly powerful when combined with MailClaw's contact enrichment — you can route enterprise leads to your highest-reputation account and cold prospects to a subdomain account, keeping deliverability risks segmented.

Pro tip: If you're integrating MailClaw with HubSpot or Salesforce via the CRM sync feature, you can use contact properties (like company size or lead score) as routing conditions to determine which account handles each contact. This turns your multi-account setup into an intelligent, tiered outreach system.

Using AI Email Agents Per Account

Each connected account can have its own AI email agent with a distinct persona, tone, and response playbook. This matters more than most people realize. An AI agent sending from partnerships@yourdomain.com should sound different from one sending from sales@yourdomain.com — different context, different goals, different level of formality.

In the dashboard under AI Agents → Create Agent, assign the agent to a specific account and configure its:

  • Persona name and role (e.g., "Alex, Head of Partnerships")
  • Tone guidelines (formal, conversational, technical)
  • Response triggers (auto-reply to positive signals, pause on out-of-office, escalate on buying signals)
  • OpenClaw model settings (temperature, max tokens, system prompt)

Because MailClaw is built on OpenClaw and runs locally, your agent prompts and conversation history never leave your machine. That's a meaningful advantage if you're handling sensitive enterprise outreach.

Monitoring Deliverability Across All Accounts

The unified deliverability dashboard at localhost:3100/deliverability gives you a single view across every connected account. Key metrics to watch:

  • Bounce rate: Keep this below 2% per account. MailClaw's contact enrichment can validate email addresses before they enter a sequence, which dramatically reduces hard bounces.
  • Reply rate by account: If one account is consistently underperforming, it may have a reputation issue worth investigating with a tool like Google Postmaster Tools.
  • Spam complaints: Any account with complaints above 0.1% should be paused and reviewed immediately.
  • DKIM/SPF/DMARC status: MailClaw checks these on a rolling basis and surfaces warnings inline.

Rotating and Retiring Accounts

Even well-managed accounts eventually accumulate reputation friction. Build a rotation strategy: when an account hits a certain complaint or bounce threshold (configurable under Settings → Deliverability Alerts), MailClaw can automatically pause it and redistribute active sequences to healthy accounts. You can also archive accounts without deleting them, preserving the sending history for audit purposes.

A Note on Open-Source Flexibility

Because MailClaw is open source, the account management layer is fully extensible. If your team uses a provider not listed in the default integrations — say, a custom on-premise mail server or a regional provider — you can fork the connector module, implement the standard interface, and drop it into your local install without waiting for an official release. The OpenClaw foundation means the AI agent layer is equally extensible: swap models, add custom tools, or wire in your own enrichment APIs with straightforward configuration changes.

Multi-account email outreach, done well, is less about volume and more about precision routing, reputation management, and making each account feel like a real person with a real sending history. MailClaw gives you the infrastructure to do exactly that — and keeps all of it running quietly on your own machine.

articles.title: MailClaw Workspace Configuration: Best Practices for Teams
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how to configure MailClaw workspaces for team environments, covering account separation, shared sequence libraries, permission patterns, and CLI-based setup workflows that keep your outreach organized and your deliverability intact.
articles.content:
Why Workspace Configuration Matters More Than You Think

Most teams install MailClaw, connect a couple of email accounts, and start sending. That works fine for a solo operator running a single outreach sequence. But the moment you add a second sender, a shared contact list, or a colleague who needs access to campaign analytics, the cracks start to show. Sequences overwrite each other. Deliverability scores bleed across accounts. Nobody knows which AI email agent owns which contact segment.

Getting your workspace configuration right from day one isn't busywork — it's what separates teams that scale their outreach cleanly from teams that spend Friday afternoons untangling duplicate contacts and figuring out why their Gmail open rates dropped by 30%.

This guide walks through the practical patterns that work, with real CLI commands and configuration examples you can adapt immediately.

Understanding MailClaw's Workspace Model

MailClaw runs locally on your machine at localhost:3100, which gives you something most SaaS tools can't offer: complete control over your data and configuration. The tradeoff is that you are responsible for structuring it well. MailClaw's workspace model is built on top of OpenClaw's environment abstraction, meaning each workspace is essentially an isolated context with its own:

  • Email account pool (SMTP credentials, OAuth tokens for Gmail and Outlook)
  • Contact database and enrichment history
  • Sequence library and AI agent configurations
  • Deliverability monitoring profiles
  • API integrations (HubSpot, Salesforce, SendGrid, etc.)

Think of workspaces like Git branches — you want a clean separation between contexts, not a single messy main branch where everything lives.

Creating Your First Team Workspace

From the MailClaw CLI, creating a named workspace is a single command:

mailclaw workspace create --name "outbound-sales" --env production

For teams, the convention that works best is to name workspaces after the function, not the person. outbound-sales, partnerships, investor-relations, and product-updates are workspace names that survive team member turnover. jakes-sequences does not.

You can list all workspaces and check their status at any time:

mailclaw workspace list
mailclaw workspace status --name "outbound-sales"

Structuring Email Accounts Across Workspaces

One of the most common mistakes teams make is connecting all their sending accounts to a single workspace. This creates a deliverability liability: if one sequence damages your sender reputation, it affects every campaign running under that account pool.

The Account Isolation Pattern

The recommended approach is to assign dedicated sending accounts per workspace, using MailClaw's multi-account support to bind accounts explicitly:

mailclaw account add \
  --workspace "outbound-sales" \
  --provider gmail \
  --oauth \
  --label "outbound-primary"

mailclaw account add \
  --workspace "outbound-sales" \
  --provider smtp \
  --host mail.sendgrid.net \
  --port 587 \
  --label "outbound-backup"

By giving each account a label, your sequence builder can reference accounts by name rather than credential index — which matters when you're rotating senders or running A/B tests on sending identity.

Warming New Accounts

If you're adding fresh Gmail or Outlook accounts to a workspace, don't connect them to active sequences immediately. Use MailClaw's deliverability tools to run a warm-up profile first:

mailclaw deliverability warmup \
  --account "outbound-backup" \
  --days 21 \
  --daily-ramp 10,20,35,50,75,100

The dashboard at localhost:3100 will show you the warming progress, spam placement rates, and inbox hit percentages in real time. Don't skip this — a cold SendGrid account blasting 500 emails on day one is a quick path to a suspended domain.

Shared Sequence Libraries and Version Control

MailClaw's sequence builder supports exporting sequences as portable YAML files, which is what makes team collaboration actually work. Instead of each person building their own version of the same 5-step cold outreach sequence, you maintain a shared library that everyone pulls from.

Exporting and Importing Sequences

# Export a sequence to share with the team
mailclaw sequence export \
  --workspace "outbound-sales" \
  --name "cold-outreach-v3" \
  --output ./sequences/cold-outreach-v3.yaml

# Import it into another workspace or after a fresh install
mailclaw sequence import \
  --workspace "partnerships" \
  --file ./sequences/cold-outreach-v3.yaml

Store these YAML files in a shared Git repository. This gives you version history, the ability to roll back a sequence change that tanked your reply rates, and a canonical source of truth for what's actually running in production.

AI Agent Configuration Sharing

MailClaw's AI email agents — which handle personalization, follow-up timing, and reply classification — can also be exported and shared. Each agent has a configuration profile that defines its behavior:

mailclaw agent export \
  --workspace "outbound-sales" \
  --agent "sdr-followup-agent" \
  --output ./agents/sdr-followup-agent.json

Pro tip: When sharing AI agent configs, strip out any workspace-specific variables before committing to Git. Use placeholder syntax like {{WORKSPACE_DOMAIN}} and document the required substitutions in a README alongside the config file.

Contact Enrichment and CRM Integration at the Workspace Level

Contact enrichment in MailClaw runs per-workspace, which means your enrichment credits, API keys, and deduplication logic are all scoped appropriately. When connecting to HubSpot or Salesforce, bind the integration to the correct workspace:

mailclaw integration connect \
  --workspace "outbound-sales" \
  --provider hubspot \
  --api-key $HUBSPOT_API_KEY \
  --sync-direction bidirectional

For Salesforce, you'll typically want one-way sync from Salesforce into MailClaw (so your CRM stays the source of truth) rather than bidirectional:

mailclaw integration connect \
  --workspace "outbound-sales" \
  --provider salesforce \
  --client-id $SF_CLIENT_ID \
  --client-secret $SF_CLIENT_SECRET \
  --sync-direction inbound-only

Avoiding Contact Duplication Across Workspaces

MailClaw does not deduplicate contacts across workspace boundaries by default — intentionally so, since a contact might legitimately exist in both your outbound-sales and partnerships workspaces. What you do want to prevent is the same person receiving emails from both workspaces simultaneously.

Use the global suppression list to handle this:

mailclaw suppression add \
  --email "cto@targetcompany.com" \
  --reason "active-in-partnerships" \
  --scope global

The --scope global flag applies the suppression across all workspaces on your MailClaw instance, which is exactly the behavior you want for compliance and relationship hygiene.

Dashboard Access and Team Visibility

Since MailClaw runs locally on localhost:3100, sharing dashboard access requires a bit of setup — but it's straightforward. The cleanest approach for small teams is to run MailClaw on a shared internal machine or a local server that's accessible over your office network or VPN:

mailclaw start --host 0.0.0.0 --port 3100

With this configuration, anyone on your network can access the dashboard at http://[machine-ip]:3100. MailClaw's workspace switcher in the top nav lets team members jump between workspaces they have access to without logging out.

Recommended Team Access Pattern

  • Sequence owners get full access to their assigned workspace(s) and read access to shared sequence libraries
  • Campaign managers get cross-workspace analytics access to compare performance without being able to modify sequences
  • Admins manage account credentials, integration keys, and suppression lists across all workspaces

Backup and Environment Reproducibility

Because MailClaw is open source and runs locally, your configuration is only as durable as your backup habits. Build this into your team workflow:

  1. Export all workspace configurations weekly using mailclaw workspace export --all --output ./backups/
  2. Commit sequence YAML and agent JSON files to version control after every significant change
  3. Document your SMTP and OAuth setup in a secure secrets manager (1Password, Doppler, or AWS Secrets Manager) — never in the repository
  4. Test full restoration from backup at least once per quarter using mailclaw workspace import on a clean instance

That last point sounds tedious, but there is no worse moment to discover your backup process is broken than when you actually need it — usually right before a major campaign launch.

Getting the Most Out of a Well-Configured Workspace

A cleanly structured MailClaw setup pays dividends quickly. Your AI email agents have clear context boundaries and don't inherit noise from unrelated campaigns. Your deliverability monitoring surfaces problems at the workspace level before they cascade. Your team can collaborate on sequences without stepping on each other's work.

The open-source nature of MailClaw and its OpenClaw foundation mean you can inspect, extend, and adapt any of these patterns to fit your team's specific workflow. Start with the workspace separation model described here, instrument your deliverability monitoring from day one, and use the CLI export/import workflow to keep your sequence library in version control. These three habits alone will put your team's outreach operations on a foundation that actually scales.

articles.title: How to Import Contacts into MailClaw from CSV
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to import contacts into MailClaw from a CSV file, including how to format your data, run the import command, map custom fields, and activate AI-powered enrichment to supercharge your outreach campaigns.
articles.content:
Why Contact Imports Matter More Than You Think

Your contact list is the foundation of every campaign you run. Whether you're migrating from HubSpot, exporting a lead list from Salesforce, or pulling a cold outreach sheet together in Google Sheets, the moment you bring those contacts into MailClaw is the moment your email automation strategy begins to take shape. A clean, well-structured import means your AI email agents have better data to work with, your sequences fire at the right people, and your deliverability stays healthy from day one.

MailClaw makes CSV importing straightforward — but there are a few things worth knowing before you hit that command. This guide walks you through the entire process, from formatting your spreadsheet correctly to enriching contacts automatically after they land in your dashboard.

Preparing Your CSV File

Before you import anything, your CSV needs to be in good shape. MailClaw is flexible with column naming, but a few conventions will save you from mapping headaches later.

Required and Recommended Columns

At minimum, every row needs an email address. Everything else is optional but genuinely useful. Here's the structure MailClaw works best with:

email,first_name,last_name,company,title,phone,tags,custom_field_1
jane@acme.com,Jane,Doe,Acme Corp,VP of Marketing,+14155550100,"saas,trial","High intent"
tom@buildco.io,Tom,Reid,BuildCo,Founder,,"cold-outreach",""

A few formatting notes worth keeping in mind:

  • Use UTF-8 encoding. Exports from Excel sometimes default to Windows-1252, which causes character issues with names like José or Müller. Save as CSV UTF-8 explicitly.
  • Wrap multi-value fields in quotes. Tags, for example, should be comma-separated inside a quoted string: "saas,trial,Q3".
  • Avoid merged cells or header rows beyond row 1. MailClaw reads your first row as column headers.
  • Strip trailing whitespace. Emails with a space at the end (jane@acme.com ) will fail validation silently in some tools — MailClaw will flag them, but cleaning beforehand is faster.

Exporting From Common Platforms

If you're pulling contacts from an existing tool, here's the fastest path to a clean CSV:

  • HubSpot: Go to Contacts → All Contacts → Export. Choose CSV, select your properties, and download. The default export maps cleanly to MailClaw's expected columns.
  • Salesforce: Use the Data Export tool under Setup, or run a report with the fields you need and export to CSV. Just rename Email to email (lowercase) before importing.
  • Google Sheets: File → Download → CSV. If your sheet has multiple tabs, export each tab separately.
  • LinkedIn Sales Navigator: Third-party tools like PhantomBuster or Evaboot can help you get a CSV export. Make sure you comply with LinkedIn's terms of service and applicable privacy regulations before importing any scraped data.

Running the Import Command

With MailClaw running locally, open your terminal and navigate to your project directory. The import command follows this structure:

mailclaw contacts import --file ./leads.csv

That's the simplest form. MailClaw will parse the file, attempt to auto-map your columns, and show you a preview before committing anything to the database.

Useful Flags and Options

The import command accepts several flags that give you more control:

# Assign contacts to a specific list on import
mailclaw contacts import --file ./leads.csv --list "Q3 Outreach"

# Skip duplicate emails instead of updating existing records
mailclaw contacts import --file ./leads.csv --on-duplicate skip

# Update existing contacts when a matching email is found
mailclaw contacts import --file ./leads.csv --on-duplicate update

# Dry run — preview results without writing to the database
mailclaw contacts import --file ./leads.csv --dry-run

# Specify a tag to apply to all imported contacts
mailclaw contacts import --file ./leads.csv --tag "csv-import-2024-07"

The --dry-run flag is especially useful when you're importing a large list and want to catch mapping errors or validation issues before they affect your live data. It prints a summary table showing how many records would be created, updated, or skipped — without touching anything.

Mapping Custom Columns

If your CSV uses non-standard column names — say, Email Address instead of email, or Job Title instead of title — MailClaw will prompt you during the import to confirm or correct mappings. You can also define a mapping file ahead of time to skip the interactive prompt entirely:

# mapping.json
{
  "Email Address": "email",
  "First": "first_name",
  "Last": "last_name",
  "Job Title": "title",
  "Organization": "company"
}
mailclaw contacts import --file ./leads.csv --map ./mapping.json

This is particularly handy when you're running recurring imports from the same source — automate the whole thing with a cron job and you've built a lightweight sync pipeline without touching any external infrastructure.

Viewing Imported Contacts in the Dashboard

Once the import completes, open your browser and head to localhost:3100. Under the Contacts section, you'll see your newly imported records with full filtering, search, and tagging capabilities. The dashboard gives you a clean view of contact health — including which emails are valid, which have bounced in previous campaigns, and which have enrichment data attached.

If you applied a list name or tag during import, you can filter directly to those contacts and immediately add them to a sequence or assign them to an AI email agent.

Enriching Contacts After Import

Raw CSV data is a starting point. MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment — powered by OpenClaw — can fill in the gaps automatically: company size, industry, LinkedIn profiles, tech stack, and more. After an import, you can trigger enrichment on your new contacts like this:

# Enrich all contacts added in the last 24 hours
mailclaw contacts enrich --filter "imported_at:last_24h"

# Enrich a specific list
mailclaw contacts enrich --list "Q3 Outreach"

Enriched contacts unlock better personalization in your sequences. Instead of sending "Hi Jane, I wanted to reach out…", your AI email agents can reference Jane's company size, her recent funding round, or the tools her team uses — all pulled automatically and slotted into your templates.

Pro tip: Run a dry-run import first, check the validation report, then enrich only after you're confident the list is clean. Enrichment credits are finite — don't waste them on malformed or duplicate records.

Adding Imported Contacts to a Sequence

Once your contacts are in MailClaw and enriched, the natural next step is putting them into a sequence. From the dashboard at localhost:3100, head to Sequences, open or create a campaign, and use the Add Contacts button to pull from your imported list or tag.

Alternatively, wire it up from the CLI:

mailclaw sequence add-contacts --sequence "Cold Outreach v2" --list "Q3 Outreach"

From there, MailClaw's sequence builder handles the rest — scheduling, follow-up logic, reply detection, and deliverability checks across your connected SMTP accounts or OAuth-linked inboxes like Gmail and Outlook.

Keeping Your List Healthy

Importing contacts is only half the battle. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools flag risky emails before they damage your sender reputation. After any large import, it's worth running a quick validation pass:

mailclaw contacts validate --list "Q3 Outreach" --remove-invalid

This checks for syntax errors, disposable email domains, and known spam traps. Combined with MailClaw's multi-account support and per-domain sending limits, you have a solid foundation for outreach that actually reaches the inbox — not the spam folder.

Clean imports, enriched data, and healthy lists are what separate campaigns that convert from campaigns that bounce. MailClaw gives you the tools to get all three right, entirely on your own machine, without shipping your contact data to a third-party SaaS platform.

articles.title: Migrating from Mailchimp to MailClaw: A Step-by-Step Guide
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: A practical, step-by-step guide to migrating your email marketing from Mailchimp to MailClaw — covering contact exports, sequence rebuilding, SMTP setup, and how to unlock AI-powered automation that runs entirely on your own machine.
articles.content:
Why Developers and Marketers Are Leaving Mailchimp

Mailchimp has been the default choice for email marketing for over a decade. But as pricing has climbed, automation features have been locked behind expensive tiers, and data privacy concerns have grown louder, a lot of teams are looking for something better. Enter MailClaw — an open-source, AI-powered email automation platform built on OpenClaw that runs entirely on your local machine at localhost:3100.

No monthly SaaS fees. No third-party servers holding your contact data. Full control over your sequences, agents, and deliverability stack. If that sounds like a meaningful upgrade, this guide walks you through every step of the migration.

Step 1: Export Your Data from Mailchimp

Before you do anything in MailClaw, get your data out of Mailchimp cleanly. Sloppy exports cause problems downstream — duplicate contacts, missing tags, broken segments.

Exporting Contacts

  1. Log in to Mailchimp and go to Audience → All Contacts.
  2. Click Export Audience and select Export as CSV.
  3. Make sure you include all merge fields: first name, last name, email, tags, subscription status, and any custom fields you've built up over time.
  4. Download and save the file locally — you'll reference it in the next step.

Exporting Campaigns and Sequences

Mailchimp doesn't offer a clean export for automation sequences, so you'll need to manually document your existing flows. Open each active automation and note:

  • Trigger conditions (signup, tag applied, date-based, etc.)
  • Delay intervals between emails
  • Subject lines and body copy for each step
  • Any conditional branches or goal completions

This is actually a good opportunity to audit your sequences. If you haven't looked at them in six months, some of them probably need a rewrite anyway.

Step 2: Install MailClaw and Start Your Local Dashboard

MailClaw runs locally, which means your setup takes minutes and your data never leaves your machine. You'll need Node.js (v18+) and npm installed.

# Clone the MailClaw repo
git clone https://github.com/openclaw/mailclaw.git
cd mailclaw

# Install dependencies
npm install

# Start the local server
npm run start

Once it's running, open your browser and navigate to http://localhost:3100. You'll be greeted by the MailClaw dashboard — a clean, responsive interface where you can manage contacts, build sequences, monitor deliverability, and configure your AI email agents all from one place.

Step 3: Import Your Contacts

MailClaw's contact importer accepts standard CSV files, so the export from Mailchimp drops in cleanly. From the dashboard, go to Contacts → Import and upload your CSV.

During import, you'll map Mailchimp's merge fields to MailClaw's contact schema. For most standard exports this is automatic, but double-check custom fields. Once imported, MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment engine can automatically fill in gaps — job title, company size, LinkedIn profile, industry — using its OpenClaw-powered enrichment pipeline.

You can also trigger enrichment from the CLI after import:

# Enrich all contacts imported in the last 24 hours
mailclaw contacts enrich --since=24h --provider=openclaw
Pro tip: If you're migrating from a HubSpot or Salesforce integration, MailClaw supports direct sync via its CRM connector. You can pull enriched contact records directly rather than going through a CSV intermediary.

Step 4: Rebuild Your Email Sequences

This is where MailClaw starts to feel genuinely different from Mailchimp. The sequence builder is visual and intuitive, but it's backed by a programmable engine that gives you far more control than Mailchimp's automation editor.

Creating a Sequence

From the dashboard, go to Sequences → New Sequence. Give it a name and define your trigger — options include contact import, tag applied, form submission, or a manual trigger via the CLI or API.

Then add your steps. Each step lets you set:

  • Delay (minutes, hours, or days after the previous step)
  • Send conditions (e.g., only send if the contact hasn't replied)
  • Subject line and body (with merge tags and AI-assisted drafting)
  • A/B variant configuration

Using AI to Rewrite Your Copy

Here's where most people have an "aha" moment. MailClaw's AI email agents — powered by OpenClaw — can review your imported Mailchimp copy and suggest rewrites optimized for your audience's engagement patterns. You can accept, reject, or iterate directly in the editor.

You can also invoke the AI agent from the CLI to generate an entire sequence from a prompt:

mailclaw agent run --task="create a 5-step onboarding sequence for a B2B SaaS tool, \
  tone: professional, goal: trial-to-paid conversion"

The agent outputs a complete draft sequence — subject lines, body copy, delays, and send conditions — ready to review and activate. This alone replaces hours of manual work.

Step 5: Configure SMTP and OAuth

MailClaw supports both SMTP and OAuth-based sending, so you can connect whatever sending infrastructure you're already using.

Gmail and Outlook via OAuth

For personal or small-team sending, OAuth integration with Gmail or Outlook is the quickest path. In the dashboard, go to Settings → Sending Accounts and click Add Account. Choose your provider and complete the OAuth flow. MailClaw stores credentials locally — nothing is sent to an external server.

SendGrid and Transactional SMTP

For higher volume or deliverability-critical campaigns, connect a dedicated sending service like SendGrid, Postmark, or AWS SES via SMTP credentials:

# Add a SendGrid SMTP account via CLI
mailclaw accounts add \
  --name="SendGrid Primary" \
  --host=smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --port=587 \
  --user=apikey \
  --pass=YOUR_SENDGRID_API_KEY

MailClaw's multi-account support means you can route different sequences through different sending accounts — for example, using a warmed Gmail account for cold outreach and SendGrid for transactional sequences.

Step 6: Set Up Deliverability Monitoring

One of Mailchimp's real strengths has always been its deliverability infrastructure. When you migrate to a self-managed tool, you need to take deliverability seriously from day one.

MailClaw includes a deliverability monitoring panel that tracks:

  • Open and click rates per sequence and per account
  • Bounce and spam complaint rates
  • DKIM, SPF, and DMARC validation status for each sending domain
  • Reply detection (critical for cold outreach sequences)

Before going live with migrated sequences, run a deliverability check:

mailclaw deliverability check --account="SendGrid Primary" --domain=yourdomain.com

This command validates your DNS records, tests authentication headers, and flags any configuration issues before they affect real sends. Fix everything it surfaces before you activate a single sequence.

Step 7: Go Live and Decommission Mailchimp

With contacts imported, sequences rebuilt, sending accounts connected, and deliverability validated, you're ready to go live. Activate your sequences from the dashboard or CLI:

mailclaw sequence activate --name="Onboarding Flow" --confirm

Run both platforms in parallel for one to two weeks if you have active campaigns. Monitor your open rates, bounce rates, and replies in MailClaw's dashboard to make sure everything is behaving as expected. Once you're confident, pause and archive your Mailchimp automations, export a final backup, and close or downgrade your Mailchimp account.

What You Gain on the Other Side

The practical benefits of completing this migration are significant:

  • Cost: MailClaw is open source. No per-contact pricing, no feature tiers.
  • Privacy: All contact data and campaign logic lives on your machine at localhost:3100.
  • AI automation: OpenClaw-powered agents handle copy, sequencing, and enrichment in ways Mailchimp's editor simply can't match.
  • Flexibility: Programmable via CLI and API — plug it into your existing stack, CI/CD pipeline, or internal tools.
  • Control: You own the codebase. Fork it, extend it, build on it.

Migrating away from a tool you've used for years feels daunting, but the process above is genuinely manageable in a single focused afternoon. And once you've run your first AI-generated sequence through MailClaw and watched it adapt in real time, you'll wonder why you waited.

articles.title: MailClaw Admin Guide: Managing Users and API Keys
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to manage users, roles, and API keys in MailClaw — from adding team members and scoping permissions to rotating credentials and securing your local dashboard against unauthorized access.
articles.content:
Why User and API Key Management Matters in MailClaw

Running MailClaw locally on localhost:3100 doesn't mean security is optional. Whether you're a solo founder automating outreach or a team of five sharing a MailClaw instance over a local network, getting your user roles and API credentials right from day one prevents headaches later — leaked keys, accidental sequence deletions, or a junior hire overwriting your best-performing AI email agent.

This guide walks through everything you need to know: creating and managing users, scoping API keys to specific features, rotating credentials safely, and connecting third-party integrations like SendGrid, HubSpot, and Gmail without exposing sensitive tokens across your team.

Understanding MailClaw's Role System

MailClaw ships with three built-in roles, each designed to match a realistic team structure. You can assign roles during user creation or update them later through the dashboard or CLI.

The Three Default Roles

  • Admin — Full access to everything: user management, API key creation, SMTP/OAuth configuration, deliverability settings, and all campaign data. Treat Admin accounts like production database credentials — limit them.
  • Editor — Can build and launch sequences, manage contacts, run contact enrichment workflows, and configure AI email agents. Cannot manage users or create new API keys. This is the right role for most active team members.
  • Viewer — Read-only access to campaign analytics, sequence performance, and deliverability reports. Ideal for stakeholders or clients who need visibility without the ability to change anything.

A practical rule of thumb: start everyone as a Viewer, promote to Editor when they need to ship work, and keep Admin accounts to one or two people maximum. You can always check who has what role from the dashboard under Settings → Team.

Adding and Managing Users

Creating a New User via the Dashboard

  1. Open your MailClaw dashboard at http://localhost:3100.
  2. Navigate to Settings → Team → Invite User.
  3. Enter the user's email address and select their role (Admin, Editor, or Viewer).
  4. Click Send Invite. MailClaw will generate a one-time setup link — share this securely.

Because MailClaw runs locally, "inviting" a user means generating a setup token rather than sending an automated email (unless you've configured an outbound SMTP account). Copy the link from the confirmation screen and share it directly with your team member.

Creating a User via the CLI

If you prefer the command line — or you're provisioning users as part of a setup script — the OpenClaw CLI makes this straightforward:

# Create an Editor user
mailclaw users create --email "sara@yourcompany.com" --role editor

# Create an Admin user
mailclaw users create --email "admin@yourcompany.com" --role admin

# List all current users
mailclaw users list

# Update a user's role
mailclaw users update --email "sara@yourcompany.com" --role viewer

# Deactivate a user without deleting their data
mailclaw users deactivate --email "sara@yourcompany.com"

Deactivating rather than deleting is the safer move — it preserves sequence history, contact enrichment logs, and audit trails while immediately blocking access.

Working with API Keys

API keys in MailClaw let external tools, scripts, and integrations interact with your instance programmatically. You might use them to push contacts from a HubSpot workflow, trigger a sequence from a Zapier action, or pull campaign analytics into a custom dashboard.

Creating a Scoped API Key

Every API key in MailClaw has a scope — a set of permissions that limits what it can do. Never create a full-access key for an integration that only needs to read data.

# Create a read-only key for analytics integrations
mailclaw apikeys create --name "HubSpot Analytics Sync" --scope "campaigns:read,contacts:read"

# Create a key with permission to add contacts and trigger sequences
mailclaw apikeys create --name "Zapier Outreach Trigger" --scope "contacts:write,sequences:trigger"

# Create a full-access key (Admin only — use sparingly)
mailclaw apikeys create --name "Internal Admin Script" --scope "all"

# List all active API keys
mailclaw apikeys list

Available scopes include: campaigns:read, campaigns:write, contacts:read, contacts:write, sequences:read, sequences:trigger, agents:read, agents:write, enrichment:run, and deliverability:read. Combine them with commas to build exactly the permission set you need.

Viewing and Rotating Keys

From the dashboard, go to Settings → API Keys to see all active keys, their scopes, creation dates, and last-used timestamps. That last-used column is invaluable — if a key hasn't been used in 60 days, it's a candidate for rotation or deletion.

# Rotate a key (invalidates old key, issues new one with same scope)
mailclaw apikeys rotate --name "HubSpot Analytics Sync"

# Delete a key immediately
mailclaw apikeys delete --name "Old Zapier Key"

Best practice: Rotate API keys every 90 days, or immediately after a team member who had access to them leaves. Treat keys the same way you'd treat passwords — don't commit them to version control, don't share them in Slack, and don't hardcode them in scripts.

Connecting Third-Party Integrations Securely

MailClaw supports SMTP and OAuth connections to Gmail, Outlook, and transactional providers like SendGrid and Mailgun. These credentials live in Settings → Email Accounts and are stored encrypted in your local MailClaw database.

Multi-Account Setup for Outreach

If you're running cold outreach across multiple sender identities — common for agencies or teams warming up new domains — each account gets its own credential entry and deliverability profile. This is where MailClaw's multi-account support really shines.

# Add a Gmail account via OAuth
mailclaw accounts add --provider gmail --name "Outreach Account 1"

# Add a SendGrid SMTP account
mailclaw accounts add --provider smtp \
  --name "SendGrid Transactional" \
  --host "smtp.sendgrid.net" \
  --port 587 \
  --user "apikey" \
  --password "your-sendgrid-api-key"

# List connected accounts
mailclaw accounts list

Once connected, you can assign specific email accounts to specific sequences, AI email agents, or campaigns. This prevents your highest-reputation sending domain from being exposed to aggressive cold outreach while keeping warmed-up accounts protected.

CRM Integration Tokens

When connecting MailClaw to Salesforce or HubSpot for contact enrichment and sync, store those OAuth tokens under Settings → Integrations rather than passing them through API keys. This keeps CRM credentials separate from your MailClaw API surface and makes it easier to revoke access if needed without disrupting other integrations.

Auditing Access and Activity

MailClaw logs all user actions and API key activity in a local audit log. This is especially useful when something goes wrong — a sequence fires unexpectedly, a contact list gets overwritten, or an AI email agent sends off-schedule.

# View recent audit log entries
mailclaw audit log --limit 50

# Filter by user
mailclaw audit log --user "sara@yourcompany.com"

# Filter by API key name
mailclaw audit log --apikey "Zapier Outreach Trigger"

# Export audit log to CSV
mailclaw audit export --format csv --output ./audit-$(date +%Y%m%d).csv

Review your audit log monthly as a habit. Look for API keys triggering actions outside their expected scope, users accessing settings they don't normally touch, or enrichment jobs running at unusual times. Catching anomalies early is much easier than untangling them after a campaign goes sideways.

Hardening Your Local MailClaw Instance

Because MailClaw runs on localhost, it's not exposed to the internet by default — but that doesn't mean you can ignore security entirely, especially if your Mac is on a shared network.

  • Bind to localhost explicitly. Confirm your mailclaw.config.json has "host": "127.0.0.1", not "0.0.0.0", unless you intentionally need LAN access.
  • Enable dashboard authentication. Set a strong dashboard password under Settings → Security → Dashboard Auth. Without this, anyone on your machine can open localhost:3100.
  • Use environment variables for secrets. Don't store SMTP passwords or API tokens directly in config files. MailClaw reads from .env automatically — keep your secrets there and add .env to your .gitignore.
  • Back up your encrypted credential store. Run mailclaw backup --output ./mailclaw-backup.enc weekly and store it somewhere safe. Losing your credential store means re-authenticating every integration from scratch.

Quick Reference: Common Admin Commands

# User management
mailclaw users list
mailclaw users create --email "" --role [admin|editor|viewer]
mailclaw users deactivate --email ""

# API key management
mailclaw apikeys list
mailclaw apikeys create --name "" --scope ""
mailclaw apikeys rotate --name ""
mailclaw apikeys delete --name ""

# Account management
mailclaw accounts list
mailclaw accounts add --provider [gmail|outlook|smtp]

# Audit and backup
mailclaw audit log --limit 100
mailclaw backup --output ./backup.enc

Good access management is invisible when it's working — your team ships campaigns, your AI email agents run smoothly, and your contact enrichment workflows sync without a hitch. It only becomes visible when something breaks. A few minutes spent setting up proper roles and scoped API keys today will save you from a much longer investigation later.

articles.title: How to Set Up MailClaw for Multiple Team Members
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to configure MailClaw for your entire team, from shared SMTP credentials and role-based access to syncing AI email agents and sequence templates across multiple workstations — all running locally on OpenClaw.
articles.content:
Why Multi-User Setup Matters More Than You Think

Most teams start with MailClaw the same way: one person installs it, connects their Gmail or Outlook account, builds a few sequences, and starts seeing results. Then someone else on the team wants in. Then another person. Suddenly you're copying config files over Slack and wondering why your contact enrichment data isn't showing up on your colleague's machine.

MailClaw runs locally on localhost:3100, which is one of its greatest strengths — no vendor lock-in, no SaaS subscription fees, no sending your data to a third-party server. But that same architecture requires a bit of intentional setup when multiple team members need access. This guide walks you through exactly how to do it cleanly, from shared credential management to syncing AI email agent configurations across your org.

Understanding MailClaw's Local-First Architecture

Before diving into setup, it helps to understand what you're actually sharing. MailClaw is built on OpenClaw, and its data lives in a structured local directory — typically ~/.mailclaw on each machine. Inside that directory you'll find:

  • accounts.json — SMTP credentials, OAuth tokens for Gmail/Outlook, and SendGrid API keys
  • sequences/ — your email sequence templates and step logic
  • agents/ — AI email agent configurations and prompt templates
  • contacts/ — enriched contact records and list segments
  • config.json — global settings including deliverability rules and sending schedules

When setting up for a team, your goal is to decide which of these assets should be shared across members, and how to keep them in sync without stomping on each other's work.

Step 1: Set Up a Shared Config Repository

The cleanest approach for teams is to version-control your MailClaw configuration using Git. This gives you change history, conflict resolution, and a single source of truth for sequences, agent configs, and deliverability settings.

Initialize the shared repo

On the team member who owns the primary setup, run:

cd ~/.mailclaw
git init
echo "contacts/" >> .gitignore
echo "accounts.json" >> .gitignore
git add .
git commit -m "Initial MailClaw team config"
git remote add origin git@github.com:yourorg/mailclaw-config.git
git push -u origin main

Notice we're ignoring accounts.json and the contacts directory. Account credentials should never be committed to a repo — even a private one. Each team member will set up their own sending accounts. Contact data, depending on your compliance requirements, should also stay off shared repos.

Each team member clones and links the repo

# On each team member's machine
mv ~/.mailclaw ~/.mailclaw.backup
git clone git@github.com:yourorg/mailclaw-config.git ~/.mailclaw
cd ~/.mailclaw
mailclaw init --skip-wizard

Running mailclaw init --skip-wizard regenerates any missing runtime files without overwriting the shared config you just cloned.

Step 2: Configure Individual Sending Accounts

Each team member connects their own sending accounts. MailClaw supports SMTP, Gmail OAuth, Outlook OAuth, and API-based senders like SendGrid or Mailgun. This separation is intentional — it means each person's outreach comes from their own address, with their own sending reputation.

Adding a Gmail account via OAuth

mailclaw account add \
  --type oauth \
  --provider gmail \
  --email yourname@company.com \
  --alias "Primary Work Gmail"

MailClaw will open a browser window to complete the OAuth flow. Once authenticated, the token is stored locally in your personal accounts.json — it never touches the shared repo.

Adding a SendGrid account for high-volume sends

mailclaw account add \
  --type api \
  --provider sendgrid \
  --api-key YOUR_SENDGRID_API_KEY \
  --from-email outreach@company.com \
  --alias "Team SendGrid"

If your team shares a single SendGrid account for bulk campaigns, you can distribute the API key securely through a password manager like 1Password or Doppler, and each member adds it locally using the command above.

Step 3: Share Sequence Templates Across the Team

This is where the Git-based setup pays off immediately. Your MailClaw sequence builder saves sequences as structured JSON files in the sequences/ directory. Once a teammate builds a high-performing 5-step cold outreach sequence, everyone should have access to it.

The workflow is straightforward:

  1. Team member builds or edits a sequence in the MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100/sequences
  2. They commit and push the change: git add sequences/ && git commit -m "Add SaaS demo request sequence" && git push
  3. Other team members pull the update: git pull && mailclaw sequences sync

Running mailclaw sequences sync after a pull tells MailClaw to re-index the sequences directory so the new templates appear in the dashboard immediately.

Step 4: Sync AI Email Agent Configurations

MailClaw's AI email agents are where things get genuinely powerful — and where sharing configurations is most valuable. An agent might be configured to monitor replies, auto-qualify leads based on response sentiment, draft follow-ups, or route hot leads to a Salesforce opportunity. Building that logic once and sharing it across your team saves hours.

Agent configs live in ~/.mailclaw/agents/ and are included in your shared repo. After a teammate pushes a new agent:

git pull
mailclaw agents reload

The reloaded agents will appear in each member's dashboard under Agents → Active. Each person can then assign the agent to their own campaigns without duplicating the underlying logic.

Pro tip: Name your agent config files descriptively — agents/reply-qualifier-saas.json is far more useful than agents/agent1.json when your team has a dozen agents running across different campaigns.

Step 5: Centralize Contact Enrichment Without Sharing Raw Data

MailClaw's contact enrichment features can pull data from sources like Clearbit, Apollo, and Hunter.io. If multiple team members are enriching contacts independently, you risk paying for the same enrichment twice and ending up with conflicting records.

Use a shared enrichment cache

MailClaw supports pointing its enrichment cache at a shared network location. Add this to each team member's config.json:

{
  "enrichment": {
    "cache_dir": "/Volumes/TeamShare/mailclaw-enrichment-cache",
    "cache_ttl_days": 30,
    "providers": ["clearbit", "hunter"]
  }
}

This could point to a shared NAS drive, a mounted S3 bucket via s3fs, or even a Dropbox folder for smaller teams. When one team member enriches a contact, the result is cached and reused by everyone else — no duplicate API calls.

Step 6: Deliverability Monitoring Per Sender

MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools track bounce rates, spam complaints, and domain reputation per sending account. Because each team member runs their own local MailClaw instance, each person gets their own deliverability dashboard at localhost:3100/deliverability — scoped to their accounts.

For team-level visibility, you can export deliverability reports and share them in a weekly review:

mailclaw deliverability export \
  --format csv \
  --range 7d \
  --output ~/Desktop/deliverability-report.csv

Consider creating a shared folder where each team member drops their weekly export. It's a lightweight way to catch issues — like one person's domain drifting toward a spam folder — before they affect the whole team's sender reputation.

Step 7: Establish Team Conventions

The technical setup gets you 80% of the way there. The other 20% is conventions:

  • Branch strategy: Consider having team members work on feature branches for new sequences and agents, then merge to main after a quick review. This prevents half-finished sequences from appearing on everyone's dashboard.
  • Naming conventions: Agree on prefixes for sequences and agents — e.g., cold-, nurture-, follow-up- — so the dashboard stays organized as your library grows.
  • Account aliases: Standardize how sending accounts are named. If one person uses "Gmail" and another uses "Personal Gmail - John," filtering accounts across a shared campaign report becomes unnecessarily annoying.
  • HubSpot/Salesforce sync settings: If your team is syncing contact activity back to a CRM, make sure the field mappings in your shared config.json are agreed upon before multiple people start writing to the same CRM properties.

You're Ready to Scale

MailClaw's local-first, open-source design is a feature, not a limitation. With a shared Git repo, per-user sending accounts, a centralized enrichment cache, and a few team conventions, you get the collaboration benefits of a cloud tool without giving up control of your data or your sending infrastructure.

As your team grows, revisit the mailclaw team namespace in the CLI — it includes utilities for diffing configs between machines, validating sequence JSON before committing, and bulk-reloading agents after a merge. Run mailclaw team --help to see what's available in your current version.

The goal is a setup where every team member has a fully functional local dashboard, shares the same battle-tested sequences and AI agent logic, and can onboard a new colleague in under fifteen minutes. With the steps above, that's entirely achievable.

articles.title: MailClaw Onboarding Checklist for Sales Teams
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: A practical step-by-step onboarding checklist to help sales teams get MailClaw fully configured, connected, and sending high-converting email sequences from day one.
articles.content:
Before Your First Send: Getting the Foundation Right

Most sales teams waste their first week with a new email tool misconfiguring it, sending from a cold domain, or skipping the setup steps that protect deliverability. MailClaw is powerful out of the box — but like any precision instrument, it rewards teams who take ten minutes to set it up correctly. This checklist walks you through everything from first launch to your first live sequence, in the order that actually matters.

If you haven't installed MailClaw yet, spin it up with a single command:

npx mailclaw start

Once it's running, open your local dashboard at localhost:3100. Everything you need — sequences, contacts, agents, deliverability health — lives here, and none of it leaves your machine.

Step 1: Connect Your Email Accounts

MailClaw supports both SMTP and OAuth authentication, so you can connect Gmail, Outlook, or any custom sending domain through providers like SendGrid or Postmark. For most sales teams, we recommend a hybrid approach: OAuth for your primary team accounts, SMTP for dedicated outreach domains.

Connecting Gmail or Outlook via OAuth

  1. Navigate to Settings → Email Accounts in your localhost dashboard.
  2. Click Add Account and select your provider.
  3. Complete the OAuth flow — MailClaw stores your credentials locally and never sends them to an external server.
  4. Set a daily send limit per account. For warmed domains, 80–120 emails/day is a safe starting range.

Adding a SendGrid SMTP Relay

If your team does high-volume outreach from a dedicated sending domain, connect SendGrid as an SMTP relay:

mailclaw accounts add \
  --name "Outreach Domain" \
  --host smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --port 587 \
  --user apikey \
  --pass YOUR_SENDGRID_API_KEY \
  --from outreach@yourdomain.com

Multi-account support means you can rotate sends across accounts within a single sequence — reducing per-account volume and improving deliverability without any manual juggling.

Step 2: Authenticate Your Sending Domain

This is the single most important step that sales teams skip. Without proper authentication, even well-written emails land in spam. Before you import a single contact, confirm these DNS records are live for every domain you're sending from:

  • SPF: Authorizes your sending servers
  • DKIM: Cryptographically signs outgoing mail
  • DMARC: Instructs receiving servers what to do with failures

MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitor checks all three automatically. Head to Deliverability → Domain Health and run a scan on each connected domain. You'll see a pass/fail breakdown with exact DNS records to add if anything is missing.

Pro tip: If you're sending from a subdomain like mail.yourdomain.com, DMARC inheritance rules can be tricky. MailClaw will flag this and suggest the right policy configuration for your setup.

Step 3: Import and Enrich Your Contacts

Don't just dump a CSV into your tool and call it a day. MailClaw's contact enrichment layer — powered by OpenClaw's AI core — can fill in missing fields, normalize job titles, infer company size, and surface intent signals before a single email goes out.

Importing Contacts

From the CLI or the dashboard, import your contact list with:

mailclaw contacts import --file leads.csv --list "Q3 Outreach"

MailClaw accepts CSV files with flexible column mapping. During import, you'll be prompted to match your columns to standard fields like first_name, company, title, and email.

Running Contact Enrichment

Once imported, trigger enrichment on your list:

mailclaw contacts enrich --list "Q3 Outreach" --fields title,company_size,linkedin_url

The enrichment engine cross-references public data sources to fill gaps. For a list of 500 contacts, expect this to take a few minutes. The result is a cleaner, more segmentable list — which directly improves personalization and reply rates.

Syncing with Your CRM

If your team runs HubSpot or Salesforce, connect your CRM under Settings → Integrations. MailClaw can pull existing contacts, push reply data back, and sync sequence enrollment status — keeping your CRM honest without double-entry busywork.

Step 4: Build Your First Sequence

MailClaw's sequence builder is where most of the sales magic happens. A sequence is a timed, conditional series of emails that adjusts based on recipient behavior — opens, clicks, replies, and bounces.

Anatomy of a High-Converting Sequence

For cold outreach, a proven structure looks like this:

  1. Day 1 — Cold intro: Short, personalized, one clear ask. No pitch deck links.
  2. Day 3 — Value add: A case study, relevant stat, or insight specific to their industry.
  3. Day 7 — Soft bump: A single-line reply to your original thread.
  4. Day 14 — Breakup email: Signal you're moving on. Counterintuitively, this often gets the highest reply rate.

Create this in the dashboard under Sequences → New Sequence, or scaffold it from the CLI:

mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "Cold Outreach v1" \
  --steps 4 \
  --interval "1,3,7,14" \
  --list "Q3 Outreach"

Using AI to Write and Personalize Steps

Each sequence step has an AI-assist button that calls MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered writing engine. Give it your context — persona, value prop, tone — and it'll generate a draft you can refine. More usefully, you can insert dynamic personalization tags that pull from enriched contact fields:

Hi {{first_name}},

I noticed {{company}} recently {{recent_signal}} — 
congrats on that. We've helped similar {{industry}} teams 
reduce {{pain_point}} by around 30%.

The {{recent_signal}} and {{pain_point}} fields can be populated manually during import or inferred by the enrichment step — giving you hyper-personalized emails at scale without writing each one by hand.

Step 5: Configure Your AI Email Agent

This is MailClaw's most powerful feature for scaling sales operations. An AI email agent monitors replies in your connected inboxes, categorizes them (interested, not now, unsubscribe, wrong person), and can draft or send follow-up responses based on rules you define.

To create an agent:

mailclaw agent create \
  --name "SDR Agent" \
  --inbox "outreach@yourdomain.com" \
  --mode draft \
  --rules ./agent-rules.json

Start in draft mode — the agent writes responses but queues them for human approval. Once you've reviewed a few dozen and tuned the rules, you can switch to auto mode for specific intent categories like unsubscribes or out-of-office replies, while keeping human review for anything that looks like genuine interest.

A well-configured AI agent can handle 60–70% of reply volume without human intervention, freeing your reps to focus exclusively on warm conversations.

Step 6: Set Deliverability Guardrails

Before launching, configure MailClaw's deliverability safeguards so you don't torch your domain on the first campaign:

  • Bounce threshold: Pause a sequence automatically if bounce rate exceeds 3%
  • Unsubscribe handling: Auto-suppress contacts who reply with opt-out language
  • Send window: Restrict sends to business hours in the recipient's timezone
  • Warm-up schedule: For new domains, ramp send volume gradually over 4–6 weeks

All of these live under Deliverability → Guardrails in the dashboard. MailClaw monitors inbox placement in real-time and will alert you — or pause sending automatically — if something looks off.

Step 7: Launch, Measure, Iterate

Once everything is configured, launch your sequence and let the dashboard do the work. Track the metrics that matter for sales:

  • Open rate (goal: 40–55% for well-warmed domains)
  • Reply rate (goal: 5–10% for cold, 15–25% for warm)
  • Positive reply rate — the one number that actually predicts pipeline
  • Bounce and unsubscribe rates — your canary in the coal mine

After your first sequence completes, use MailClaw's A/B reporting to compare subject lines and step variants. Small copy changes — subject line length, first-line personalization, CTA phrasing — can move reply rates by 2–4 percentage points, which at volume translates directly to meetings booked.

Your Onboarding Is Done — Now Keep Improving

Getting MailClaw set up correctly takes less than an hour. The teams that see the best results aren't the ones who set it up fastest — they're the ones who treat it as a system to iterate on. Review your deliverability health weekly, tune your AI agent rules as reply patterns emerge, and refresh sequences every 60–90 days to avoid list fatigue.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your local machine, you're never locked into a pricing tier or waiting on a vendor to ship a feature. If something doesn't work the way you need it to, the codebase is right there. That's the whole point.

articles.title: How to Test MailClaw with a Sandbox Email Account First
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Before sending real campaigns through MailClaw, learn how to set up a sandbox email environment so you can safely test your AI agents, sequences, and deliverability settings without risking your sender reputation or spamming real contacts.
articles.content:
Why You Should Always Test Before You Send

There's a certain excitement that comes with setting up a new email automation tool — especially one as capable as MailClaw. You've got your sequences drafted, your AI email agents configured, your contact list imported, and your SMTP credentials wired in. Everything looks ready. But hitting "launch" on a live campaign without testing first is one of the fastest ways to damage your sender reputation, confuse real prospects, or surface configuration bugs at the worst possible moment.

Testing with a sandbox account gives you a consequence-free environment to verify that MailClaw is behaving exactly the way you intend — before a single real recipient ever sees your name in their inbox. This guide walks you through exactly how to do that.

What a Sandbox Email Setup Actually Means

A sandbox email environment is an isolated configuration where outgoing emails are either captured without being delivered, routed to a test inbox you control, or processed by a fake SMTP server that logs everything without sending anything to the real world. It lets you:

  • Confirm that your sequence timing and step logic work correctly
  • Verify that contact enrichment data is being merged into email templates properly
  • Check that your AI email agents are generating the right personalized copy
  • Test deliverability headers, DKIM signing, and SPF alignment without touching live mail servers
  • Catch broken links, malformed HTML, or missing unsubscribe footers before they go out

With MailClaw running locally on localhost:3100, you're already in a naturally sandboxed environment — but that doesn't mean emails won't leave your machine unless you explicitly configure a test transport.

Option 1: Use Mailpit as a Local SMTP Trap

Mailpit is the cleanest local option for intercepting outgoing mail. It runs a fake SMTP server on your machine and gives you a web UI to inspect every email MailClaw sends — headers, HTML rendering, text fallback, attachments, the works. Nothing actually gets delivered.

Installing Mailpit on macOS

brew install mailpit
mailpit

By default, Mailpit listens for SMTP on port 1025 and serves its web UI at localhost:8025. Now open your MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to Settings → Sending Accounts, and add a new SMTP account with these values:

Host: localhost
Port: 1025
Encryption: None
Username: (leave blank)
Password: (leave blank)

Label this account something obvious like "Mailpit Sandbox" so you don't accidentally use it on a production campaign. From this point forward, any sequence or one-off send routed through this account will appear instantly in Mailpit's inbox at localhost:8025 — no real delivery, no reputation risk.

Option 2: Use Mailtrap for Cloud-Based Testing

If you prefer a hosted sandbox — especially useful when testing MailClaw's deliverability monitoring features or sharing test results with a teammate — Mailtrap is the industry standard. It captures all outbound mail in a virtual inbox and gives you spam score analysis, HTML previews, and header inspection tools.

Connecting Mailtrap to MailClaw

  1. Create a free account at mailtrap.io and grab your sandbox SMTP credentials from the dashboard.
  2. In MailClaw, go to Settings → Sending Accounts → Add Account → SMTP.
  3. Enter your Mailtrap credentials:
Host: sandbox.smtp.mailtrap.io
Port: 2525
Username: your_mailtrap_username
Password: your_mailtrap_password
Encryption: STARTTLS

Mailtrap also supports an Email Testing API, which is worth exploring if you want to automate sandbox testing as part of a CI workflow or run MailClaw sequence validation programmatically using OpenClaw's underlying agent framework.

Option 3: Create a Dedicated Gmail or Outlook Test Account

Sometimes you want to see exactly what a recipient experiences — how your email renders in Gmail's tabbed inbox, whether Outlook clips your message, how images load. For this, a dedicated test Gmail or Outlook account is the right tool.

Create a throwaway Google account (e.g., yourname.mailclaw.test@gmail.com) and add it as a sending account in MailClaw using OAuth. Then add that same address to a test contact list and send your sequence to yourself.

Pro tip: Gmail's "+" addressing trick is your friend here. If your test account is mailclaw.test@gmail.com, you can use addresses like mailclaw.test+prospect1@gmail.com, mailclaw.test+prospect2@gmail.com, etc. as fake contacts in your sequence — all mail routes to the same inbox, but MailClaw treats each address as a distinct contact.
