This lets you simulate multi-recipient sequences without needing multiple accounts.

Building a Test Sequence in MailClaw

With your sandbox transport configured, let's walk through setting up a real test sequence so you can validate end-to-end behavior.

Step 1: Create a Test Contact List

In the MailClaw dashboard, navigate to Contacts → New List. Name it something like "Sandbox Test Contacts" and import a small CSV with two or three fake entries (or your Gmail "+" aliases). Leave the enrichment toggle off for now — you don't want to burn API credits enriching fake contacts.

Step 2: Build a Short Sequence

Go to Sequences → New Sequence and build a three-step sequence: an initial outreach email, a follow-up at day three, and a breakup email at day seven. Use MailClaw's AI email agent to draft the copy — even in test mode, it's worth validating that the AI-generated personalization tokens resolve correctly against your test contacts' fields.

Step 3: Assign Your Sandbox Sending Account

In the sequence settings, select your Mailpit or Mailtrap account as the sender. This is the single most important step — double-check it before every test run.

Step 4: Launch and Inspect

Activate the sequence and watch your sandbox inbox. In Mailpit or Mailtrap, inspect each captured email and verify:

  • From name and address display correctly
  • Subject lines match what you configured and aren't being truncated
  • Personalization variables like {{first_name}} or {{company}} are resolved, not left as raw tokens
  • HTML rendering looks right in both desktop and mobile preview
  • Plain text fallback is present and readable
  • Unsubscribe link is present in the footer (critical for compliance)
  • Sequence timing advances correctly between steps

Testing MailClaw's Deliverability Features in Sandbox Mode

MailClaw includes built-in deliverability monitoring — but you can also use sandbox testing to audit your technical email setup before going live. Even if Mailpit captures the message without sending it, the generated email will still contain the headers MailClaw constructs, including DKIM-Signature, Message-ID, and List-Unsubscribe.

Copy the raw source of a Mailpit-captured message and paste it into Mail-Tester or MXToolbox's Email Header Analyzer to check for issues before your first real send. If you're planning to use SendGrid or Postmark as your production relay, compare the headers your sandbox run produces against what those services expect to see.

Switching from Sandbox to Production

Once your tests pass — sequences step correctly, personalization resolves cleanly, deliverability headers look healthy — switching to production in MailClaw is just a matter of updating the sending account on your sequence. Everything else stays the same.

If you're connecting a live Gmail or Outlook account via OAuth, or wiring in a transactional relay like SendGrid or Amazon SES, add those credentials under Settings → Sending Accounts and swap the sequence's sender assignment. MailClaw's multi-account support means you can maintain your sandbox SMTP config indefinitely alongside production accounts — it's always there when you need to test a new sequence or troubleshoot a deliverability issue.

Make Sandbox Testing a Habit, Not a One-Time Step

The teams that consistently get strong email performance aren't necessarily the ones with the most sophisticated tooling — they're the ones with disciplined testing habits. Every new sequence, every significant template change, every new AI agent prompt gets run through a sandbox first. It costs you five minutes and saves you from the kind of mistakes that take weeks of inbox warming to recover from.

MailClaw is built to make this easy. The localhost-first architecture means your sandbox and production environments live side by side, your data never leaves your machine, and the OpenClaw-powered agent layer gives you enough programmability to automate your testing workflow as your campaigns scale. Start with Mailpit, graduate to Mailtrap when you need cloud-based inspection, and always keep a test contact list ready to go.

The extra ten minutes you spend testing today is the sender reputation you're not rebuilding next month.

articles.title: MailClaw Free Tier: What You Get with the Open Source Version
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: A complete breakdown of what MailClaw's open source free tier includes — from AI email agents and contact enrichment to the local dashboard and sequence builder — so you can decide if it fits your outreach workflow before spending a dime.
articles.content:
Open Source Doesn't Mean Stripped Down

There's a common assumption with open source software: the free version is a teaser, a taste of something you'll eventually have to pay for. MailClaw flips that assumption. Built on the OpenClaw engine and designed to run entirely on your local machine at localhost:3100, the open source free tier is a fully functional email automation platform — not a trial, not a demo, not a limited sandbox.

This article walks through exactly what you get with the free tier, what's realistically possible from day one, and how to get the most out of it — whether you're a solo founder doing cold outreach, a developer building internal tools, or a growth team that's tired of paying $500/month for a SaaS tool that still doesn't do what you need.

Core Features Included in the Free Tier

AI Email Agents

One of MailClaw's flagship capabilities is its AI email agent system, powered by OpenClaw. In the free tier, you can build and deploy agents that autonomously draft, personalize, and send emails based on contact data, behavioral triggers, or custom logic you define. These aren't simple mail-merge templates — they're context-aware agents that can adapt tone, subject lines, and body copy based on what they know about a recipient.

For example, you might build an agent that checks a contact's job title and company size, then selects from three different email angles — one for enterprise prospects, one for SMBs, and one for freelancers — without you lifting a finger after the initial setup.

Agents are configured via a simple YAML-based spec file:

agent:
  name: outreach-agent-v1
  trigger: contact_added
  model: openClaw-local
  instructions: |
    You are a friendly outreach specialist.
    Personalize the email based on the contact's
    industry and recent activity. Keep it under
    120 words. No fluff.
  sequence: intro-sequence-1

This runs entirely on your machine — no API calls to third-party LLM providers required unless you explicitly configure an external model.

Sequence Builder

The sequence builder lets you design multi-step email campaigns with branching logic, time delays, and conditional follow-ups. From the local dashboard at localhost:3100, you get a visual interface where you can drag, connect, and configure each step in a sequence.

A typical outreach sequence might look like this:

  1. Day 0 — Initial personalized intro email
  2. Day 3 — Follow-up if no reply (different angle)
  3. Day 7 — Value-add email (case study, resource, etc.)
  4. Day 12 — Soft close / breakup email

Each step can reference contact fields, agent outputs, or external data. You can also set exit conditions — if someone replies at any point, they're automatically removed from the sequence and flagged for manual review.

Contact Enrichment

The free tier includes contact enrichment capabilities out of the box. When you import a list of emails or add contacts manually, MailClaw can attempt to fill in missing fields — company name, industry, LinkedIn URL, job title — using its enrichment pipeline.

To kick off enrichment from the CLI:

mailclaw enrich --file contacts.csv --fields company,title,linkedin

Enrichment in the free tier uses open data sources and any custom enrichment providers you configure yourself (such as a self-hosted Clearbit alternative or a simple scraping pipeline). It's not as plug-and-play as a paid SaaS enrichment tool, but it's genuinely powerful if you're willing to spend 20 minutes on configuration.

Multi-Account Support and SMTP/OAuth Integration

You can connect multiple sending accounts in the free tier — Gmail, Outlook, or any SMTP-compatible provider like SendGrid, Mailgun, or Amazon SES. OAuth authentication is supported for Google and Microsoft accounts, which means you don't have to fiddle with app passwords or less-secure app settings.

Setting up a Gmail account takes about two minutes:

mailclaw accounts add \
  --provider gmail \
  --auth oauth \
  --email you@yourdomain.com

MailClaw will open a browser window for the OAuth flow, store the credentials locally (never transmitted to any external server), and you're connected. You can add as many accounts as you want — useful for inbox rotation, team setups, or managing outreach across multiple brands.

Deliverability Monitoring

Bad deliverability kills email programs quietly. MailClaw's free tier includes a deliverability monitoring dashboard that tracks bounce rates, spam complaint rates, open rates (where available), and sending reputation signals for each connected account.

You'll also get warnings when an account's bounce rate crosses a configurable threshold:

mailclaw deliverability status --account you@yourdomain.com

Account: you@yourdomain.com
Bounces (7d): 1.8% ⚠️  (threshold: 2%)
Spam complaints (7d): 0.04%
Open rate (7d): 31.2%
Reputation signal: Good

This kind of visibility is typically locked behind premium tiers in tools like Instantly or Smartlead. In MailClaw, it's standard.

The Local Dashboard: Your Command Center

Everything in MailClaw is accessible through the local dashboard running at localhost:3100. It's clean, fast, and doesn't require an internet connection to use. Campaigns, contacts, sequences, agents, deliverability stats — all of it lives in one place, on your machine.

To start the dashboard:

mailclaw start

✓ OpenClaw engine initialized
✓ Dashboard running at http://localhost:3100
✓ 3 accounts connected
✓ 2 active sequences

The dashboard is particularly useful when you're managing multiple campaigns simultaneously. You can see send volume, reply rates, and agent activity across all accounts in a single view — no context switching between tabs or tools.

What the Free Tier Doesn't Include

Transparency matters, so here's what you won't find in the open source free tier:

  • Native CRM sync — Direct two-way integrations with HubSpot, Salesforce, or Pipedrive are available in the paid tier. In the free tier, you can use CSV import/export or build your own webhook-based sync.
  • Managed cloud hosting — The free tier runs locally. If you want MailClaw hosted on a server with uptime guarantees, that's a paid option.
  • Priority support — Community support via GitHub and Discord is available, but dedicated support channels are paid-only.
  • Advanced analytics exports — Deep reporting exports (PDF reports, Slack digests, etc.) are not included in the free tier.

That said, for most individual users and small teams, these limitations won't be blockers. The CRM gap in particular is easily bridged with a simple webhook or a scheduled CSV sync script.

Practical Setup: Getting from Zero to First Campaign

Here's a realistic end-to-end workflow to get your first campaign live in under 30 minutes:

  1. Install MailClaw — Clone the repo and run the installer. macOS with Homebrew: brew install mailclaw
  2. Connect your sending account — Use the mailclaw accounts add command for Gmail or Outlook OAuth, or drop in SMTP credentials for SendGrid or SES.
  3. Import your contact list — mailclaw contacts import --file leads.csv
  4. Run enrichment — Fill in missing fields before writing your copy.
  5. Build your sequence — Use the visual builder at localhost:3100 to set up your steps and delays.
  6. Configure an AI agent — Drop in a YAML spec to let the agent handle personalization at scale.
  7. Launch — mailclaw campaign start --sequence intro-sequence-1 --list leads

That's it. Your first AI-powered campaign is live, running locally, with no subscription fees and no data leaving your machine.

Who the Free Tier Is Built For

MailClaw's open source tier is genuinely well-suited for:

  • Indie hackers and solo founders who need serious outreach tooling without SaaS pricing
  • Developers who want to extend, modify, or embed email automation into their own products
  • Small sales teams running high-personalization, low-volume outreach where quality beats volume
  • Privacy-conscious organizations that can't send contact data to third-party platforms

If you've ever paid for Apollo, Instantly, or Lemlist and wondered why you were paying so much for something you could barely customize — MailClaw's free tier is the answer you were looking for.

The Bottom Line

The MailClaw free tier isn't a funnel. It's a product. You get AI email agents, multi-step sequence building, contact enrichment, deliverability monitoring, multi-account SMTP/OAuth support, and a full local dashboard — all powered by OpenClaw, all running on your Mac at localhost:3100, all for free.

The best way to evaluate it is to run it. Install MailClaw, connect a Gmail account, import 50 contacts, and launch a three-step sequence with an AI agent doing the personalization. By the time you've done that, you'll know exactly whether you need the paid tier — or whether the open source version already does everything you need.

articles.title: How to Update MailClaw to the Latest Version
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to safely update MailClaw to the latest version, preserve your campaign data and AI agent configurations, and take advantage of new features — all in a few simple terminal commands.
articles.content:
Why Keeping MailClaw Updated Matters

MailClaw moves fast. Because it's built on the open-source OpenClaw engine, improvements ship regularly — new AI email agent capabilities, smarter contact enrichment algorithms, deliverability fixes, and tighter integrations with tools like Gmail, Outlook, SendGrid, and HubSpot. Running an outdated version means you're leaving real functionality on the table, and in some cases, you may be missing critical bug fixes that affect your outreach sequences or SMTP delivery rates.

The good news: updating MailClaw is straightforward. Whether you're on a stable release or tracking the latest commits, the process takes under five minutes and is designed to be non-destructive to your existing campaign data, contact lists, and AI agent configurations.

Before You Update: A Quick Pre-Flight Checklist

A little preparation goes a long way. Before running any update command, work through this checklist:

  • Check your current version. Open your terminal and run mailclaw --version to see exactly what you're running. Compare it against the latest release on the MailClaw GitHub repository.
  • Pause active sequences. Navigate to your local dashboard at localhost:3100, go to Sequences, and pause any live campaigns. This prevents mid-sequence contact states from getting corrupted during the update.
  • Back up your data directory. MailClaw stores campaign data, contact enrichment records, and AI agent configs locally. Run a quick backup before proceeding.
  • Note your active SMTP and OAuth connections. Gmail OAuth tokens and SendGrid API keys are stored securely in your local config — they typically survive updates, but it's worth having them handy just in case.

Backing Up Your MailClaw Data

MailClaw keeps everything in a local data directory. To create a quick snapshot before updating:

# Check where your MailClaw data lives
mailclaw config --show-data-dir

# Create a timestamped backup
cp -r ~/.mailclaw ~/.mailclaw_backup_$(date +%Y%m%d)

This copies your entire MailClaw directory — including sequence definitions, contact enrichment cache, AI agent prompts, and account settings — into a dated backup folder. Takes about three seconds and gives you a clean restore point.

Updating MailClaw: The Standard Method

If you installed MailClaw via the recommended method using npm (the most common setup for the local dashboard running on localhost:3100), updating is a single command:

# Update MailClaw to the latest stable release
npm update -g mailclaw

After the update completes, verify it worked:

mailclaw --version

You should see the new version number printed to your terminal. Then restart the local server:

# Stop any running MailClaw instance first
mailclaw stop

# Start fresh with the new version
mailclaw start

Open localhost:3100 in your browser. The dashboard should load with the updated interface. If you see a first-run migration prompt, that's normal — MailClaw may be applying database schema updates for new features like enhanced deliverability monitoring or updated AI agent tooling.

Updating from a Git Clone (Developer or Power User Setup)

If you cloned the MailClaw repository directly from GitHub — common for developers who want to contribute or run pre-release features — the update process is slightly different:

# Navigate to your MailClaw directory
cd ~/mailclaw

# Stop the running instance
mailclaw stop

# Pull the latest changes from the main branch
git pull origin main

# Install any new or updated dependencies
npm install

# Run database migrations if prompted
mailclaw migrate

# Rebuild the dashboard assets
npm run build

# Start MailClaw again
mailclaw start

Handling Merge Conflicts in Custom Configs

If you've made local modifications to MailClaw config files (for example, customized AI agent prompt templates or bespoke sequence logic), git pull may surface merge conflicts. Don't panic — resolve them carefully:

# See which files have conflicts
git status

# Open conflicted files in your editor and resolve manually
# Then mark them resolved
git add .
git commit -m "Merge upstream MailClaw update"

When in doubt, favor the upstream version for core logic files and preserve your customizations in the designated /custom or /agents directories, which are intentionally gitignored to protect your work.

Post-Update Steps: Reconnect and Reactivate

Once you're running the latest version, a few quick checks will get everything back to full speed.

Verify Your Integrations

Head to localhost:3100 → Settings → Integrations and confirm that your connected accounts are still active:

  • Gmail / Google Workspace — OAuth tokens should persist, but if Google has rotated them, you'll see a "Reconnect" prompt. One click re-authenticates.
  • Outlook / Microsoft 365 — Same OAuth flow. Typically survives updates without issue.
  • SendGrid / Mailgun / Postmark — API keys are stored in your local config and should carry over automatically.
  • HubSpot / Salesforce — If you're syncing contact enrichment data or sequence enrollment status back to your CRM, verify that the webhooks and API connections are still live.

Review AI Agent Configurations

MailClaw's AI email agents are one of its most powerful features, and new versions often introduce updated agent schemas or expanded capabilities. After updating, open Agents in the dashboard and review your active agents. Look for:

  • Any deprecation warnings on older prompt structures
  • New optional parameters that might improve performance (e.g., updated tone controls, richer contact enrichment context, or improved reply-detection logic)
  • Changes to how agents interact with multi-account sending configurations

If an agent prompt references deprecated syntax, MailClaw will usually flag it with an inline warning and suggest a migration path directly in the UI.

Re-Activate Your Sequences

Once you've confirmed integrations and agents look healthy, return to the Sequence Builder and re-activate any campaigns you paused before the update. Check the Deliverability Monitor after a few sends — new versions sometimes include updated bounce handling or spam-signal detection that improves your sending reputation metrics automatically.

Troubleshooting Common Update Issues

Dashboard Won't Load After Update

If localhost:3100 returns an error after updating, the most common cause is a stale process still occupying the port. Fix it:

# Find and kill whatever is on port 3100
lsof -ti:3100 | xargs kill -9

# Start MailClaw fresh
mailclaw start

Migration Errors on Startup

If MailClaw logs a migration error, run migrations manually with verbose output to see exactly what's failing:

mailclaw migrate --verbose

Most migration errors stem from a corrupted local database or a partial previous update. In rare cases, restoring from your pre-update backup and re-running the update cleanly resolves it.

npm Permission Errors on macOS

If you hit permission errors during npm update -g mailclaw, avoid using sudo with npm. Instead, fix your npm global directory ownership:

mkdir ~/.npm-global
npm config set prefix '~/.npm-global'
export PATH=~/.npm-global/bin:$PATH

Add that export line to your ~/.zshrc or ~/.bash_profile to make it permanent, then re-run the update.

Staying Current Going Forward

MailClaw is under active development and the open-source community around it is growing. The best way to stay informed about new releases is to watch the GitHub repository for release notifications — you'll get an email whenever a new version drops, complete with a changelog describing what's new in the AI agent framework, contact enrichment pipelines, or the sequence builder.

Pro tip: Run mailclaw --version at the start of each week as a habit. It takes one second and keeps you aware of how far behind you might be drifting from the latest release.

With your updated MailClaw instance running, your AI email agents dialed in, and your sequences re-activated, you're set up to get the most out of every outreach campaign — with all the latest deliverability improvements, enrichment data sources, and automation intelligence that the newest version has to offer.

articles.title: How to Build a Cold Outreach Sequence with MailClaw AI
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to build a high-converting cold outreach sequence from scratch using MailClaw's AI email agents, contact enrichment, and sequence builder — all running locally on your Mac.
articles.content:
Why Most Cold Outreach Fails (And How AI Changes That)

Cold outreach has a reputation problem. Spray-and-pray campaigns with generic templates, zero personalization, and no follow-up logic have trained inboxes — and humans — to ignore them. The result? Average cold email reply rates hovering around 1–3% for most teams.

The difference between a campaign that converts and one that gets ignored almost always comes down to three things: relevance, timing, and persistence. Nail all three, and reply rates of 15–25% are entirely achievable. MailClaw's AI-powered sequence builder is designed to help you hit all three without the manual overhead that usually makes good outreach feel impossible to scale.

This guide walks you through building a complete cold outreach sequence — from importing contacts to launching your first AI-personalized campaign — using MailClaw running locally on your Mac.

Getting Started: MailClaw on Localhost

MailClaw runs as a local service on localhost:3100, which means your contact data, API keys, and email logic never leave your machine. For teams working with sensitive prospect lists or operating under strict data policies, this is a significant advantage over cloud-only tools.

Once you've installed MailClaw via the OpenClaw CLI, starting the dashboard is a single command:

openclaw start mailclaw

Open your browser to http://localhost:3100 and you'll land on the MailClaw dashboard — a clean interface showing your sequences, active campaigns, deliverability health, and connected accounts at a glance.

Connecting Your Sending Accounts

Before building sequences, connect at least one sending account. MailClaw supports Gmail and Google Workspace via OAuth, Outlook and Microsoft 365 via OAuth, and any custom SMTP provider like SendGrid, Postmark, or Mailgun.

To connect Gmail with OAuth:

mailclaw accounts connect --provider gmail --oauth

For a custom SMTP setup with SendGrid:

mailclaw accounts connect \
  --provider smtp \
  --host smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --port 587 \
  --user apikey \
  --pass YOUR_SENDGRID_API_KEY \
  --label "SendGrid Primary"

MailClaw's multi-account support means you can rotate sending across several addresses — a smart move for warming up new domains and protecting deliverability on your primary account.

Building Your Contact List with AI Enrichment

Good sequences start with good data. MailClaw's contact enrichment layer pulls in professional context — job title, company size, industry, LinkedIn activity, and recent news — that your AI email agents use to personalize outreach at scale.

Importing Contacts

You can import contacts from a CSV, pull them directly from a CRM integration, or add them manually. To import from a CSV file:

mailclaw contacts import --file prospects.csv --map "email,first_name,last_name,company,title"

MailClaw connects natively with HubSpot and Salesforce, so if your SDR team already qualifies leads there, you can sync them into a sequence without any CSV exports:

mailclaw contacts sync --source hubspot --list "Q4 Outbound Targets"

Running Contact Enrichment

Once your contacts are imported, run enrichment to give the AI agents the context they need:

mailclaw contacts enrich --list "Q4 Outbound Targets" --depth full

The --depth full flag triggers a deeper enrichment pass that includes company news, funding rounds, and technology stack signals — all useful inputs for writing timely, relevant first lines. A lighter --depth basic pass covers job title, company size, and industry if you're working with a tight time window.

Pro tip: Enrichment quality directly impacts AI personalization quality. The more signal your contacts carry, the more specific and human your automated emails will sound. Don't skip this step.

Designing Your Sequence with the Sequence Builder

Head to the Sequences tab in the MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100/sequences and click New Sequence. You'll name your sequence, select a sending account, and define the basic cadence logic before writing a single word.

A Proven 5-Step Cold Outreach Cadence

Here's a structure that consistently performs well for B2B outreach. You can build this directly in the sequence builder UI or define it in a YAML config file for version control:

sequence:
  name: "Q4 SaaS Outbound"
  account: "SendGrid Primary"
  steps:
    - day: 1
      type: email
      subject: "ai:generate"
      body: "ai:generate"
      personalization: high
    - day: 3
      type: email
      subject: "Quick follow-up"
      body: "ai:followup"
      personalization: medium
    - day: 7
      type: email
      subject: "One last thought"
      body: "ai:breakup_template"
      personalization: low
    - day: 10
      type: task
      note: "Connect on LinkedIn"
    - day: 14
      type: email
      subject: "Circling back"
      body: "ai:generate"
      personalization: high

The ai:generate directive tells MailClaw's AI email agent to write each email fresh for each contact, drawing on enrichment data. The ai:followup directive generates a contextual follow-up that references the prior message without being robotic about it.

Writing the First Email with AI Assistance

The first touch is the hardest to get right. In the sequence builder, clicking Generate with AI on Step 1 opens the AI email agent panel. You provide a brief on your value proposition and target persona, and the agent drafts an opening email using your contact's enrichment data to write a personalized first line.

For example, given a contact who recently joined a new company as VP of Sales, the AI agent might open with:

"Congrats on the new role at Meridian — joining as VP of Sales right before Q4 is a baptism by fire. I wanted to reach out because we help revenue teams like yours get outbound running fast without hiring a full SDR team..."

That kind of specificity takes 3–4 minutes per email when done manually. With the AI email agent, it happens in seconds, at scale, across your entire list.

Deliverability: Don't Burn Your Domain

Sending volume and spam signals are the silent killers of cold outreach campaigns. MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring tracks your domain reputation, bounce rates, spam complaint rates, and sending velocity in real time — all visible from the dashboard sidebar under Deliverability Health.

Key Settings to Configure Before Launch

  • Daily send limits: Keep new domains under 30–50 emails per day until they're warmed. MailClaw enforces this automatically when you flag an account as warming.
  • Sending windows: Schedule emails to send during business hours in your prospect's timezone using the --timezone-aware flag.
  • Unsubscribe handling: MailClaw automatically processes opt-outs and removes contacts from active sequences — required for CAN-SPAM and GDPR compliance.
  • Bounce management: Hard bounces are suppressed automatically. Soft bounces are retried with configurable backoff logic.

You can run a pre-flight deliverability check on any sequence before it goes live:

mailclaw sequences check --name "Q4 SaaS Outbound" --deliverability

This flags any SPF, DKIM, or DMARC misconfigurations on your sending domain before they become a problem mid-campaign.

Launching and Monitoring Your Campaign

With your sequence built and deliverability checks passed, launching is one command:

mailclaw campaigns launch --sequence "Q4 SaaS Outbound" --list "Q4 Outbound Targets" --start-date 2024-11-04

The campaign dashboard at localhost:3100/campaigns gives you live stats: open rate, click rate, reply rate, bounce rate, and opt-outs — broken down by step, so you can see exactly where contacts are engaging or falling off.

Using AI Agents to Handle Replies

One of MailClaw's most powerful features is the ability to deploy an AI email agent that monitors your inbox for replies and categorizes them — interested, not interested, out of office, referral — and optionally drafts response suggestions for your review. This keeps high-intent replies from going cold while you're focused elsewhere.

Enable reply monitoring for a campaign:

mailclaw agents enable --campaign "Q4 SaaS Outbound" --mode suggest

In suggest mode, the agent drafts replies but waits for your approval. Switch to auto for fully autonomous handling of low-stakes categories like out-of-office responses and referral requests.

Iterating Based on What Works

The best cold outreach programs treat every campaign as a test. After your first sequence completes, use MailClaw's built-in A/B reporting to compare subject line variants, opening line styles, and call-to-action formats. The data lives locally, so you can query it directly:

mailclaw analytics report --campaign "Q4 SaaS Outbound" --export csv

Feed those learnings back into your next sequence — adjust your AI agent prompts, refine your persona brief, tighten your value proposition. Over two or three campaign cycles, you'll have a sequence that reliably converts because it's been tuned on real signal from real prospects.

Cold outreach isn't magic, but with the right tooling, the right data, and a system that handles the repetitive work intelligently, it's one of the highest-leverage growth channels available to any team willing to put in the upfront work to do it well.

articles.title: Creating Drip Email Campaigns with MailClaw Automation
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to build high-converting drip email campaigns using MailClaw's sequence builder, AI email agents, and contact enrichment tools — all running locally on your Mac with full control over your data and deliverability.
articles.content:
What Makes a Great Drip Campaign (And Why Most Fail)

Drip campaigns are one of the highest-leverage activities in any outreach or marketing workflow. Done right, they nurture cold contacts into warm leads, onboard new users without manual effort, and re-engage dormant customers at exactly the right moment. Done wrong, they land in spam, feel robotic, and damage your sender reputation.

Most drip campaigns fail for three reasons: poor timing logic, generic copy that ignores contact behavior, and no feedback loop between campaign performance and future sends. MailClaw was built specifically to solve all three of these problems — locally, privately, and without a monthly SaaS bill eating into your margins.

This guide walks you through building a production-ready drip campaign using MailClaw's sequence builder, AI email agents, and deliverability monitoring tools. Whether you're running cold outreach, a product onboarding flow, or a re-engagement sequence, the principles here apply directly.

Setting Up Your First Campaign in MailClaw

If you haven't already, start MailClaw from your terminal. The local dashboard runs at localhost:3100 and gives you a full visual interface alongside CLI access:

npx mailclaw start

Once the server is running, open http://localhost:3100 in your browser. You'll see the main dashboard with your campaign queue, connected accounts, sequence library, and deliverability health scores — all in one place.

Connecting Your Sending Accounts

Before building sequences, connect at least one sending account. MailClaw supports both SMTP and OAuth authentication, which means you can plug in Gmail, Outlook, or a transactional provider like SendGrid or Postmark in minutes:

# Add a Gmail account via OAuth
mailclaw accounts add --provider gmail --oauth

# Add a SendGrid account via SMTP
mailclaw accounts add --provider sendgrid --smtp --host smtp.sendgrid.net --port 587 --user apikey --pass YOUR_API_KEY

For cold outreach specifically, it's worth adding multiple sending accounts and distributing volume across them. MailClaw's multi-account support lets you set per-account daily send limits, warm-up schedules, and rotation rules — all from the dashboard or CLI.

Building Your Drip Sequence

The sequence builder is where MailClaw really shines. Think of a sequence as a tree of emails with conditional branches driven by contact behavior — opens, clicks, replies, and enrichment data.

Defining Your Sequence Logic

Here's a simple 4-step cold outreach drip you can create via the CLI:

mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "Cold Outreach Q3" \
  --step "Day 0: Initial intro email" \
  --step "Day 3: Follow-up if no reply" \
  --step "Day 7: Value-add email (case study)" \
  --step "Day 14: Soft breakup email" \
  --condition "stop_on_reply"

The --condition stop_on_reply flag tells MailClaw to automatically remove a contact from the sequence the moment they respond. This is critical — nothing burns a relationship faster than continuing to drip on someone who already replied.

You can layer in additional conditions:

  • stop_on_click — pauses the sequence when a contact clicks a tracked link
  • branch_on_open — sends a different follow-up email to contacts who opened but didn't click
  • skip_weekends — reschedules sends that fall on Saturday or Sunday
  • respect_timezone — sends at 9am in the contact's local timezone using enriched location data

Writing Emails That Actually Convert

Paste your email copy directly into the sequence editor on the dashboard, or define it in a local .mjml or plain-text file. For plain-text cold outreach (which tends to outperform HTML in inbox placement), MailClaw handles personalization tokens cleanly:

Hi {{first_name}},

I noticed {{company}} recently {{trigger_event}} — congrats on that.

I work with teams like yours to [value prop in one sentence].

Worth a 15-minute call this week?

{{sender_first_name}}

Token values are pulled from your contact records at send time. If a field is empty, MailClaw's AI fallback system substitutes a contextually appropriate default rather than sending an embarrassing blank field.

Using AI Email Agents to Personalize at Scale

This is where MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered AI layer separates it from traditional sequence tools. Rather than writing one email and blasting it to thousands of contacts, you can instruct an AI email agent to generate a unique variation for each contact based on their enrichment data.

mailclaw agent run \
  --sequence "Cold Outreach Q3" \
  --step 1 \
  --persona "B2B sales rep, concise tone, no buzzwords" \
  --context "Use company industry, recent funding, and LinkedIn headline" \
  --model gpt-4o

The agent reads each contact's enriched profile — job title, company size, recent news, LinkedIn headline — and writes a genuinely personalized opening line before slotting it into your template. This isn't just a first-line spinner; the AI understands the full context of the message and adjusts tone, length, and framing accordingly.

Contact Enrichment Before You Send

Great personalization depends on good data. MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment pipeline lets you enrich a CSV of leads before they ever enter a sequence:

mailclaw enrich --input leads.csv --output enriched_leads.csv --fields "company,title,linkedin,industry,employee_count,funding_stage"

Enriched contacts can also be pushed to or pulled from CRMs like HubSpot or Salesforce via MailClaw's native integrations, so your outreach stays in sync with your pipeline without manual data entry.

Monitoring Deliverability as You Send

Sending a beautifully crafted drip campaign to the spam folder is a silent killer. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring dashboard gives you real-time visibility into:

  • Open rates, click rates, and reply rates per sequence step
  • Bounce rates and spam complaint signals
  • Inbox placement scores across Gmail, Outlook, and Yahoo
  • SPF, DKIM, and DMARC configuration status per sending account
  • Domain blacklist monitoring with alerts

If MailClaw detects a spike in bounce rate or a drop in inbox placement, it will automatically throttle sending on the affected account and flag the issue in the dashboard before it cascades into a reputation problem.

A good rule of thumb: keep bounce rates below 2% and spam complaints below 0.1%. MailClaw's deliverability panel shows a rolling 7-day average of both metrics per account so you always know where you stand.

A/B Testing Your Sequence Steps

MailClaw supports split testing at the step level. You can test two subject lines, two opening approaches, or two entirely different email bodies, and MailClaw will automatically route traffic to the winner once statistical significance is reached:

mailclaw sequence ab-test \
  --sequence "Cold Outreach Q3" \
  --step 1 \
  --variant-a "subject_a.txt" \
  --variant-b "subject_b.txt" \
  --split 50/50 \
  --auto-promote --confidence 95

Integrating With Your Existing Stack

MailClaw is designed to slot into workflows you already have rather than replace them. Common integration patterns include:

  • HubSpot / Salesforce: Pull contact lists from deal stages and push reply events back as activities
  • Zapier / Make: Trigger a MailClaw sequence when a new lead form is submitted, a trial starts, or a deal stage changes
  • Webhooks: POST contact data to http://localhost:3100/api/contacts from any upstream system
  • CSV imports: The simplest path — export from your CRM, enrich with MailClaw, import to a sequence

Because MailClaw runs locally and is fully open source, you can also extend it directly. The OpenClaw core is modular, so adding a custom enrichment provider, a new AI model backend, or a proprietary CRM integration is a matter of writing a plugin rather than waiting for a vendor roadmap.

A Realistic Campaign Timeline

Here's what a complete drip campaign setup looks like end-to-end using MailClaw, from zero to sending:

  1. Day 1: Import your lead list, run contact enrichment, review data quality in the dashboard
  2. Day 1–2: Write your email sequence copy (4–6 steps is a solid starting point)
  3. Day 2: Configure your sequence logic, conditions, and sending schedule in the sequence builder
  4. Day 2: Run AI email agents to generate personalized variants for each contact
  5. Day 3: Verify SPF/DKIM/DMARC for your sending domains using the deliverability panel
  6. Day 3: Launch to a small test segment first (50–100 contacts), monitor for 48 hours
  7. Day 5+: Scale to full list, monitor deliverability daily, A/B test underperforming steps

The Local-First Advantage

Most email automation platforms charge per contact, per email, or per feature. They also store your contact data on their servers, subject to their privacy policies and their uptime. MailClaw runs entirely on your machine. Your contact data never leaves localhost. Your API keys stay in your environment. And because it's open source under the OpenClaw umbrella, you can audit every line of logic that touches your outreach.

For teams that take data ownership seriously — or that simply want to run sophisticated drip campaigns without a growing SaaS tab — that's a meaningful difference. Start with the sequence builder, let the AI agents handle personalization at scale, and use the deliverability tools to protect the sender reputation you've spent time building. That combination is what turns a drip campaign from a spray-and-pray exercise into a repeatable, measurable revenue channel.

articles.title: How to Set Up Follow-Up Sequences That Actually Convert
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to build follow-up email sequences that actually convert, with practical timing strategies, copywriting frameworks, and step-by-step guidance using MailClaw's sequence builder and AI email agents.
articles.content:
Why Most Follow-Up Sequences Fail Before They Even Start

The average cold email gets a response rate somewhere between 1% and 5%. The average follow-up to that cold email? Often higher. Research consistently shows that 80% of sales require at least five touchpoints, yet the majority of outreach campaigns stop after one or two attempts. The math here is brutal: most people are leaving the best part of their sequence on the table.

The problem isn't that follow-ups don't work — it's that most follow-up sequences are built wrong. They're either too aggressive, too generic, or they repeat the same pitch in slightly different words. If you've ever hit "send" on a campaign and watched the reply rate flatline after email one, this guide is for you.

We'll walk through how to structure sequences that genuinely convert, with concrete examples you can implement today using MailClaw's sequence builder and AI email agents — running locally on your machine at localhost:3100.

The Anatomy of a High-Converting Follow-Up Sequence

A well-structured sequence isn't just a series of emails — it's a progression. Each message should serve a distinct purpose and move the prospect incrementally closer to a decision. Think of it less like a drip campaign and more like a conversation you're having over time.

Step 1: Define Your Sequence Goal Before Writing a Single Word

Before you open the MailClaw sequence builder, get specific about what you're trying to accomplish. A sequence built to book a demo call is fundamentally different from one designed to nurture a free trial user toward conversion.

  • Cold outreach: Goal is a reply or a booked meeting
  • Post-demo nurture: Goal is a signed contract or next step
  • Trial activation: Goal is feature adoption or upgrade
  • Re-engagement: Goal is to revive a stalled deal

Each goal demands a different cadence, tone, and value proposition. Mixing them up is one of the most common reasons sequences underperform.

Step 2: Map Your Timing and Touchpoints

Timing is everything in a follow-up sequence. Too fast and you come across as desperate; too slow and you lose momentum. Here's a proven framework for cold outreach sequences:

  1. Day 0: Initial email — lead with value, not your pitch
  2. Day 2: Short follow-up — add a new angle or insight
  3. Day 5: Social proof or case study touchpoint
  4. Day 9: Direct ask — make it easy to say yes or no
  5. Day 14: Break-up email — give them an out, often generates replies

For warmer leads — people who've downloaded a resource, attended a webinar, or started a trial — you can compress this timeline significantly. Someone who just signed up for a free trial should hear from you within hours, not days.

Building Your Sequence in MailClaw

Once you've mapped your strategy, MailClaw makes the actual build straightforward. Fire up your local dashboard and get started:

# Start MailClaw locally
mailclaw start

# Create a new sequence
mailclaw sequence create --name "cold-outreach-q3" --goal "book-demo"

Inside the dashboard at localhost:3100, you'll see the visual sequence builder where you can drag steps, configure delays, set conditions, and preview how emails will render across Gmail, Outlook, and Apple Mail before a single message goes out.

Using AI Email Agents to Write and Personalize at Scale

Here's where MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered AI email agents become genuinely powerful. Writing five unique, non-repetitive emails for hundreds of contacts isn't feasible manually — but it is with an agent.

# Generate sequence copy with AI agent
mailclaw agent run --task "write-sequence" \
  --goal "book-demo" \
  --tone "direct, consultative" \
  --steps 5 \
  --persona "B2B SaaS founder" \
  --output sequences/cold-q3.json

The agent will draft each email with a distinct hook, ensuring you're not just resending the same message with a "just following up" prefix. You can then edit each step in the dashboard, swap in your own voice, and lock the sequence before activating.

Contact Enrichment Before You Send

Personalization without data is just guesswork. Before running any sequence, use MailClaw's contact enrichment pipeline to fill in the gaps. This pulls in company data, role information, LinkedIn signals, and tech stack details so your AI agents and manual edits can reference specifics that actually land.

# Enrich a contact list before launching a sequence
mailclaw enrich --list contacts/leads-q3.csv \
  --fields "company,title,industry,tech_stack" \
  --output contacts/leads-q3-enriched.csv

If you're syncing from HubSpot or Salesforce, MailClaw's native integrations pull contact data directly, so enriched fields flow back into your CRM without manual exports.

Writing Emails That Actually Get Replies

Timing and tooling get you in front of people. Copy is what gets them to respond. Here are the principles that separate high-converting follow-up emails from the ones that get archived.

Each Email Should Earn Its Own Open

Don't rely on your subject line from email one to carry the rest of the sequence. Write a fresh subject line for each follow-up — one that creates enough curiosity or relevance to justify opening. Avoid lazy defaults like "Re: my last email" unless you're intentionally signaling continuity for a warm lead.

The "New Value" Rule

Every follow-up should introduce something new. This might be:

  • A relevant case study or customer result
  • A recent piece of news about their company or industry
  • A different framing of the problem you solve
  • A specific question that requires a short answer
  • A resource (guide, template, calculator) that's genuinely useful

If you can't answer "what new value does this email add?" — it shouldn't be sent.

The Break-Up Email Is Your Secret Weapon

Counterintuitively, the last email in a sequence — where you give the prospect an explicit out — often generates the highest reply rates. A simple version looks like this:

"Hey [Name], I've reached out a few times and haven't heard back — totally understand if the timing isn't right or this isn't relevant. I'll stop following up after this. If things change down the road, feel free to reach out. Either way, good luck with [specific thing about their company]."

This works because it removes pressure and respects the prospect's time. The specificity in the last line ("specific thing about their company") is where contact enrichment pays off — it signals that this isn't a mass blast.

Monitoring Deliverability Without Losing Your Mind

A beautifully written sequence that lands in spam is worthless. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools run alongside your campaigns and surface issues before they compound.

# Check deliverability health for a sending account
mailclaw deliverability check --account outreach@yourcompany.com

# Output includes:
# ✓ SPF record: valid
# ✓ DKIM: configured
# ⚠ Domain age: 6 months (warm up recommended)
# ✓ Blacklist status: clean (checked 42 lists)

If you're using SendGrid, Mailgun, or your own SMTP server, MailClaw's multi-account support lets you distribute sending volume across accounts to protect your domain reputation. You can configure this directly in the dashboard or via the CLI:

# Add a sending account with OAuth (Gmail)
mailclaw account add --provider gmail --oauth --alias "outreach-main"

# Add SMTP account (SendGrid)
mailclaw account add --provider smtp \
  --host smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --port 587 \
  --user apikey \
  --alias "sendgrid-backup"

Sequence-Level Deliverability Rules

Inside the sequence builder, you can set daily send limits, randomize send times within a window (to mimic human behavior), and pause a sequence automatically if reply rates drop below a threshold. These small safeguards dramatically extend the life of your sending domains.

Measuring What Actually Matters

Open rates are vanity. Reply rates are the signal that matters for outreach sequences — but even those need context. In MailClaw's analytics view, focus on these metrics per step:

  • Reply rate per step: Which email in your sequence generates the most responses? Double down on that format.
  • Positive reply rate: Not all replies are good. Track how many are "yes" vs. "not interested" vs. "remove me."
  • Drop-off by step: A sharp drop after email two often means your follow-up copy isn't adding enough value.
  • Time-to-reply: Replies that come in 20 minutes after sending have different intent than replies that come in 4 days later.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs locally, all of this data stays on your machine. No third-party analytics platform is holding your campaign performance data hostage — you own it, export it, and pipe it wherever you need it.

The Mindset Shift That Changes Everything

The most effective follow-up sequences are built with one mental model in mind: you are helping someone make a decision, not pestering them into one. Every email in your sequence should make it easier for the right prospect to say yes — and make it comfortable for the wrong prospect to say no.

When you combine that mindset with the right tooling — enriched contact data, AI-assisted copy, solid deliverability hygiene, and a sequence builder that lets you iterate fast — the results compound quickly. Build the sequence once, watch the data, and sharpen each step over time. The compounding effect of a well-optimized five-email sequence running on autopilot is one of the highest-leverage things you can do in outreach.

Start with your local MailClaw dashboard, build something simple, and let the data tell you what to fix. That's the loop that turns average sequences into ones that actually convert.

articles.title: MailClaw AI Writer: Generating Personalized Email Copy at Scale
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how MailClaw's AI Writer uses OpenClaw-powered intelligence to generate deeply personalized email copy at scale — from first-touch cold outreach to multi-step nurture sequences — without sacrificing the human feel that actually gets replies.
articles.content:
Why "Personalized at Scale" Is No Longer an Oxymoron

For years, email marketers lived with an uncomfortable trade-off: you could send personalized emails, or you could send emails at scale. Doing both at the same time meant hiring a team of copywriters, building elaborate mail-merge templates, or accepting that your "personalization" amounted to nothing more than Hi {{first_name}}, at the top of a generic blast.

MailClaw's AI Writer changes that equation. Built on OpenClaw, the same local inference engine that powers MailClaw's broader automation suite, the AI Writer can generate contextually rich, individually tailored email copy for hundreds of contacts — running entirely on your Mac at localhost:3100, with no data leaving your machine and no per-token API bill eating into your margins.

This article walks through how the AI Writer works, how to feed it the right context, and how to wire it into sequences that actually convert.

How the AI Writer Uses Contact Enrichment Data

Generic AI email tools generate generic email copy. The reason MailClaw's output feels different is that it draws on enriched contact profiles before a single word is written. When you run contact enrichment on a lead — whether imported from a HubSpot export, a Salesforce CSV, or a plain spreadsheet — MailClaw pulls structured signals that the AI Writer uses as writing fuel.

What Gets Enriched

  • Job title and seniority — so the copy doesn't pitch a VP of Engineering like they're an SDR
  • Company size and industry — enabling the writer to reference realistic pain points
  • Recent activity signals — funding rounds, new hires, product launches scraped from public sources
  • Tech stack indicators — useful for positioning your product against tools they already use
  • LinkedIn summary snippets — for genuine first-line personalization that doesn't feel creepy

To kick off enrichment from the MailClaw CLI, run:

mailclaw enrich --list leads.csv --provider clearbit,hunter --output enriched_leads.json

Once enriched, open your dashboard at localhost:3100/contacts and you'll see each contact profile populated with signal data. This is the payload the AI Writer reads when it generates copy.

Writing Your First AI-Generated Sequence

The most common use case is a cold outreach sequence — a 3-to-5 email cadence that moves a prospect from stranger to booked call. Here's how to build one using MailClaw's Sequence Builder with AI Writer enabled.

Step 1: Define Your Sequence Brief

Navigate to localhost:3100/sequences/new and click AI Writer Mode. You'll be prompted to fill out a sequence brief — think of this as the creative brief you'd give a human copywriter:

  • Your offer: What are you selling or offering?
  • Ideal outcome: What action should the reader take? (Book a call, start a trial, reply with interest)
  • Tone profile: Formal, conversational, direct, story-driven
  • Objection set: What are the top 2–3 objections your prospects usually raise?
  • Social proof: A customer name, result, or metric you can reference

The brief doesn't need to be long. A few sharp sentences in each field outperform paragraphs of rambling context. The AI Writer is good at inference — give it the edges of your positioning and it fills in the middle.

Step 2: Generate and Review Email Variants

Once your brief is saved, the AI Writer generates a draft for each step in the sequence. For a five-step cadence targeting SaaS founders, you might see:

  1. Email 1 — The Hook: Personalized first line referencing a recent company signal, followed by a sharp value proposition
  2. Email 2 — The Problem Frame: A short story or industry observation that surfaces the pain your product solves
  3. Email 3 — The Social Proof: A concrete result from a similar customer, kept to two sentences
  4. Email 4 — The Objection Flip: Directly names the most common objection and reframes it
  5. Email 5 — The Soft Close: Low-friction CTA, often a yes/no question

Each email is generated in multiple variants — by default, three — so you can A/B test subject lines, CTAs, or entire approaches without writing anything yourself.

Step 3: Inject Per-Contact Personalization

This is where MailClaw separates itself from tools that just run a prompt in a loop. Rather than generating one email and stamping names into it, the AI Writer re-renders each email against the enriched contact profile. The first line for a VP at a 200-person fintech will read differently than the first line for a founder at a five-person logistics startup — because it actually is different, not just word-swapped.

You can preview per-contact rendering directly in the dashboard, or export a batch preview from the CLI:

mailclaw sequence preview --id seq_482 --contacts enriched_leads.json --limit 10

This outputs a readable HTML file showing the first ten contacts' fully personalized emails, side by side, so you can spot anything that looks off before you send.

AI Email Agents: Beyond Copy Generation

The AI Writer is powerful on its own, but it gets genuinely interesting when you connect it to MailClaw's AI Email Agents. An agent doesn't just write the email — it monitors replies, classifies intent, and triggers follow-up actions automatically.

Setting Up a Reply-Aware Agent

Agents are configured in YAML and live in your MailClaw project directory. A basic reply-handling agent looks like this:

agent:
  name: outreach_agent_v1
  sequence_id: seq_482
  triggers:
    - event: reply_received
      intent: interested
      action: notify_slack + pause_sequence + tag_contact:hot_lead
    - event: reply_received
      intent: not_now
      action: move_to_nurture_sequence:seq_nurture_q2
    - event: reply_received
      intent: unsubscribe
      action: unsubscribe + log_reason
  writer:
    mode: ai
    tone: match_contact_seniority
    personalization: full

Drop this in your agents/ folder and register it with:

mailclaw agent register --file agents/outreach_agent_v1.yaml

The agent connects to your Gmail or Outlook account via OAuth, or to SendGrid if you're sending through a dedicated IP, and begins monitoring the inbox in real time. When a reply comes in, OpenClaw classifies the intent locally — no round-trip to an external API — and the configured action fires within seconds.

Deliverability: Writing Copy That Reaches the Inbox

Even the most perfectly personalized email is worthless if it lands in spam. MailClaw includes a deliverability monitoring layer that works alongside the AI Writer to flag potential issues before you send.

The Pre-Send Deliverability Check

Every AI-generated email passes through a local deliverability scorer before it's queued. The scorer checks for:

  • Spam trigger words and phrases (the AI Writer is already trained to avoid these, but the checker catches edge cases)
  • Subject line length and preview text alignment
  • Link-to-text ratio
  • Sending domain warm-up status
  • DKIM/SPF/DMARC configuration for your connected accounts

You can run a manual check on any sequence step from the CLI:

mailclaw deliverability check --sequence seq_482 --step 1

The output gives you a score out of 100 and a plain-English list of issues to fix — no cryptic codes, no vague warnings.

Practical Tips for Better AI-Written Copy

After running MailClaw across dozens of campaigns, a few patterns consistently produce better output from the AI Writer:

Feed It Specificity, Not Generality

The brief field labeled "Your offer" should not say "we help companies grow." It should say something like: "We cut SaaS churn by an average of 18% in the first 90 days by identifying at-risk accounts before they cancel." The AI Writer amplifies the specificity you give it. Vague inputs produce vague outputs.

Use the Tone Profile Intentionally

Different personas respond to different registers. C-suite contacts often respond better to shorter, more direct emails. Mid-level managers tend to engage more with emails that demonstrate understanding of their day-to-day problems. MailClaw's tone profiles — executive-brief, peer-to-peer, consultative, challenger — are mapped to response data, not just stylistic preferences.

Review the Outliers, Not Just the Averages

When you run a batch preview, don't just skim the first few results. Scroll to the unusual contacts — the ones with incomplete enrichment data, the non-English company names, the edge-case job titles. These are where AI-generated copy tends to break down in ways that are obvious to a human reader but invisible to an automated quality check.

The goal isn't to remove humans from the loop entirely. It's to remove the tedious parts — the blank-page problem, the copy-paste personalization, the manual follow-up tracking — so the humans in the loop can focus on strategy, offer refinement, and the genuine relationship moments that no AI should be handling anyway.

Getting Started Today

If you haven't set up MailClaw yet, the quickest path is through the open-source repo. Clone it, run mailclaw init, and your local dashboard will be live at localhost:3100 in under five minutes. Connect your first sending account — Gmail via OAuth, Outlook, or an SMTP provider like SendGrid or Postmark — and you're ready to build your first AI-written sequence.

The AI Writer isn't a magic button that replaces copywriting judgment. It's a force multiplier that lets one person do the work of a team — and do it with the kind of contextual personalization that, until recently, only the best human writers could pull off at any kind of scale.

articles.title: How to Create Multi-Step Email Sequences with MailClaw
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how to build powerful multi-step email sequences in MailClaw, from configuring your first sequence in the local dashboard to using AI agents for personalization, timing logic, and deliverability best practices.
articles.content:
Why Multi-Step Sequences Win More Replies

Single emails get ignored. That's not pessimism — it's just the reality of a crowded inbox. Studies consistently show that follow-up emails in a sequence outperform standalone sends, with the second or third touchpoint often generating more replies than the first. The challenge has always been orchestrating that sequence without burning hours in a CRM or paying for bloated SaaS tools you barely use.

MailClaw solves this at the command line. Running locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, it gives you a full sequence builder, AI-powered personalization, and deliverability monitoring — without sending your contact data to a third-party cloud. Everything stays on your machine, powered by the OpenClaw engine underneath.

Before You Build: Plan Your Sequence Structure

Good sequences have a clear goal before the first line is written. Are you booking demos? Nurturing leads from a HubSpot export? Re-engaging churned users? The goal determines the cadence, tone, and exit conditions for each step.

A reliable starting framework for cold or warm outreach looks like this:

  • Step 1 — The Hook (Day 0): Short, relevant, no heavy pitch. Establish why you're reaching out.
  • Step 2 — The Value Add (Day 3): Share a resource, insight, or specific result relevant to their industry.
  • Step 3 — The Soft Ask (Day 7): Make a low-friction request — a reply, a quick call, a question.
  • Step 4 — The Breakup (Day 14): A final, honest note that gives them an easy out and often gets the most replies.

You can adapt this to 2 steps or 8 steps depending on your use case. MailClaw's sequence builder has no hard limit on steps, and each step supports its own delay logic, conditions, and AI personalization layer.

Setting Up Your First Sequence in MailClaw

Initialize a New Sequence from the CLI

With MailClaw running, open a terminal and scaffold a new sequence using the mailclaw CLI:

mailclaw sequence create --name "Q4 Outreach" --goal "book-demo" --steps 4

This creates a sequence configuration file at ~/.mailclaw/sequences/q4-outreach.yaml and registers it in your local dashboard. Open the dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to Sequences, and you'll see the new entry ready to edit visually or via the YAML file directly.

Configure Step Timing and Conditions

Each step in the sequence YAML supports a delay, a condition, and an exit_if block. Here's what a two-step sequence configuration looks like:

name: Q4 Outreach
goal: book-demo
steps:
  - id: step_1
    delay: 0
    subject: "Quick question about {{company}}"
    body_template: templates/step1.html
    exit_if:
      - replied
      - booked_meeting

  - id: step_2
    delay: 3d
    subject: "Re: Quick question about {{company}}"
    body_template: templates/step2.html
    condition: not_opened_step_1
    exit_if:
      - replied
      - unsubscribed

The exit_if conditions are evaluated before each step sends. If a contact replies or books a meeting, MailClaw automatically removes them from the sequence — no duplicate follow-ups, no awkward "just checking in" emails to someone who already said yes.

Writing Templates That Actually Convert

Templates live in your ~/.mailclaw/templates/ directory and support Handlebars-style variables. MailClaw's contact enrichment layer can populate fields like {{company}}, {{role}}, {{industry}}, and {{recent_news}} automatically when you run enrichment before launching a sequence.

mailclaw contacts enrich --list q4-prospects.csv --fields company,role,linkedin

Once enriched, those fields are available in every template across all steps. This is where MailClaw's approach pays off — enrichment happens once, locally, and every sequence step can reference the same contact data without repeated API calls.

Using AI Agents to Personalize at Scale

The most powerful feature in MailClaw's sequence builder is the AI email agent layer, powered by OpenClaw. Instead of writing one-size-fits-all templates, you can instruct an AI agent to generate or rewrite each step's body based on the contact's enriched profile.

To attach an AI agent to a sequence step, add an agent block to the step configuration:

  - id: step_1
    delay: 0
    subject: "Quick question about {{company}}"
    agent:
      model: openai/gpt-4o
      tone: conversational
      goal: introduce_and_hook
      context_fields:
        - company
        - role
        - recent_news
        - industry
    exit_if:
      - replied

When the sequence runs, the AI agent reads the contact's enriched data and generates a personalized email body for each recipient. You can review generated drafts in the localhost dashboard before sending, or configure the agent to send automatically once drafts pass a confidence threshold you define.

Pro tip: Set the agent's tone to match your brand voice. Options include formal, conversational, direct, and friendly. For sales sequences targeting VP-level contacts, direct tends to outperform warmer tones.

Connecting Your Email Accounts

MailClaw supports both SMTP and OAuth connections, so you can send through Gmail, Outlook, or a dedicated sending infrastructure like SendGrid or Postmark without changing your sequence setup.

Adding a Gmail Account via OAuth

mailclaw accounts add --provider gmail --oauth

This opens a browser window for Google's OAuth flow. Once authorized, the account appears in your dashboard under Accounts and can be assigned to any sequence as the sending identity.

Adding a SendGrid SMTP Account

mailclaw accounts add \
  --provider sendgrid \
  --smtp-host smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --smtp-port 587 \
  --username apikey \
  --password YOUR_SENDGRID_API_KEY

For high-volume sequences or outreach where deliverability is critical, routing through SendGrid or Postmark gives you dedicated IP options and better reputation management than sending directly from a personal Gmail account. MailClaw's multi-account support means you can rotate sending accounts across a sequence or split a contact list across multiple senders to stay within provider rate limits.

Monitoring Deliverability While Your Sequence Runs

Sequences that nobody sees are just wasted effort. MailClaw's deliverability tools run passively alongside your campaigns and surface issues before they compound. The dashboard at localhost:3100/deliverability shows you:

  • Open rates and click rates per sequence step
  • Bounce rates with categorized reasons (hard vs. soft)
  • Spam complaint signals aggregated from supported providers
  • DKIM and SPF validation status for each connected sending domain
  • Sending volume pacing recommendations based on account warmup status

If MailClaw detects a spike in bounces or complaints on a specific step, it will flag the sequence in the dashboard and optionally pause it automatically if you've configured a deliverability_guard threshold:

mailclaw sequence update "Q4 Outreach" \
  --deliverability-guard \
  --bounce-threshold 5 \
  --complaint-threshold 0.2

Importing Contacts from Your Existing Tools

You don't need to rebuild your contact data inside MailClaw. The CLI supports direct imports from CSV exports, and MailClaw ships with connectors for common platforms:

  • HubSpot: mailclaw contacts import --source hubspot --list-id 12345
  • Salesforce: mailclaw contacts import --source salesforce --query "SELECT Email, Name, Company FROM Lead WHERE Status='New'"
  • CSV: mailclaw contacts import --file prospects.csv --map email:Email,name:Full_Name,company:Company

Imported contacts are stored locally and can be segmented into lists, tagged, and enriched before being enrolled in a sequence. Because MailClaw is open source and runs locally, you maintain full ownership of that data — it never leaves your machine unless you explicitly configure an external integration.

Launching and Managing Your Sequence

Once your steps are configured, templates are written, and contacts are imported and enriched, launching the sequence is a single command:

mailclaw sequence launch "Q4 Outreach" \
  --list q4-prospects \
  --account gmail-work \
  --dry-run

Always use --dry-run first. It processes every step for every contact and logs exactly what would be sent, to whom, and when — without actually sending anything. Review the output in the dashboard, check a few AI-generated drafts for quality, and then launch for real:

mailclaw sequence launch "Q4 Outreach" \
  --list q4-prospects \
  --account gmail-work

From this point, MailClaw handles the rest. Steps fire on schedule, exit conditions are evaluated before each send, AI agents generate personalized copy where configured, and the deliverability monitor watches for problems in the background. You can check progress anytime in the dashboard or with:

mailclaw sequence status "Q4 Outreach"

A Few Things That Make the Difference

Multi-step sequences fail for predictable reasons. Before you launch, run through this checklist:

  1. Test every template with real enriched data — broken variables like {{company}} showing up literally will kill your reply rate immediately.
  2. Keep step one under 100 words — shorter cold emails consistently outperform long ones. Save the detail for step two.
  3. Set realistic exit conditions — if someone opens but doesn't reply, that's not a reason to stop the sequence. Configure exits for meaningful signals: replies, clicks on a calendar link, or explicit unsubscribes.
  4. Warm up new sending accounts — MailClaw's account warmup utility gradually increases sending volume to build domain reputation before you launch at full scale.
  5. Review AI-generated drafts before first launch — even excellent AI output benefits from a human pass on the first run. Once you're confident in the quality, you can increase automation confidence thresholds.

The combination of a local-first architecture, OpenClaw-powered AI agents, and a sequence builder that handles the operational complexity means you can run sophisticated outreach that would otherwise require a full marketing stack — from a single terminal window on your Mac.

articles.title: Building a Welcome Email Series with MailClaw Automation
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how to build a high-converting welcome email series using MailClaw's sequence builder, AI email agents, and contact enrichment tools — all running locally on your Mac without sending a single lead to a third-party SaaS platform.
articles.content:
Why Your Welcome Series Is Your Most Important Automation

The moment someone joins your list, downloads your lead magnet, or signs up for a trial, they're at peak interest. Open rates for welcome emails average 50–60% — roughly four times higher than a standard newsletter blast. That window closes fast. If your first automated touchpoint arrives 48 hours late, generic, or broken, you've already lost the plot.

Most teams cobble together welcome sequences across three or four tools: a form handler, a CRM like HubSpot or Salesforce, an ESP like SendGrid or Mailchimp, and maybe a spreadsheet tracking who fell through the cracks. MailClaw lets you collapse that stack into a single open-source tool running at localhost:3100 on your Mac — with AI baked in at every step.

Planning Your Welcome Series Before You Build It

Before you open the MailClaw dashboard, spend ten minutes mapping the journey. A well-structured welcome series typically follows a three-to-five email arc:

  1. Email 1 (Immediate): Deliver the promised value — the asset, the confirmation, the "you're in."
  2. Email 2 (Day 2–3): Set expectations and introduce your brand story or core differentiator.
  3. Email 3 (Day 5–6): Share a high-value resource, case study, or quick win.
  4. Email 4 (Day 9–10): Soft social proof — a customer story or notable result.
  5. Email 5 (Day 14): A clear, low-friction call to action — a demo, a conversation, a purchase.

The spacing matters as much as the content. Too fast feels spammy. Too slow feels forgettable. MailClaw's sequence builder lets you dial in exact delays in hours or days, with conditional branching based on opens, clicks, or contact data enriched at signup.

Setting Up MailClaw for Your First Sequence

Starting the Local Dashboard

If you haven't already spun up MailClaw, get it running with a single command:

npx mailclaw start

This boots the OpenClaw-powered backend and opens the dashboard at http://localhost:3100. No cloud account required. Your contact data, email content, and API credentials stay on your machine.

Connecting Your Sending Account

MailClaw supports both SMTP and OAuth. For most teams getting started, connecting Gmail or Outlook via OAuth takes about 30 seconds from the Accounts tab in the dashboard. For higher volume or transactional sending, you can drop in your SendGrid or Postmark SMTP credentials:

mailclaw accounts add \
  --name "SendGrid Primary" \
  --type smtp \
  --host smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --port 587 \
  --user apikey \
  --pass YOUR_SENDGRID_API_KEY

MailClaw's multi-account support means you can route different sequences through different senders — keeping cold outreach on a warmed secondary domain while your transactional welcome emails go out through your primary Gmail or Outlook account.

Building the Sequence in the Dashboard

Creating a New Sequence

In the MailClaw dashboard, navigate to Sequences → New Sequence and give it a descriptive name like "SaaS Trial Welcome — 5-Email Arc." You'll see a visual drag-and-drop builder where each node represents an email step or a conditional branch.

Add your first step by clicking + Add Email, then set the delay to 0 minutes (send immediately on trigger). This is your delivery email — the one that confirms the signup and delivers whatever you promised.

Using AI Email Agents to Draft at Scale

Here's where MailClaw pulls ahead of legacy sequence tools. Instead of staring at a blank editor for each step, you can invoke an AI email agent directly from the step editor. Click Generate with AI, describe the goal of that email in plain language, and the OpenClaw-powered agent drafts the full email — subject line, preview text, body, and CTA.

For example, prompting the agent with:

"Write a welcome email for a B2B SaaS product that helps marketing teams automate content repurposing. The subscriber just signed up for a free trial. Tone: friendly and confident. Goal: get them to complete their first project within the app. Keep it under 150 words."

...produces a ready-to-send draft in seconds. You review, tweak the voice, and move on. Across five emails, this saves an hour of staring at cursor blink.

Setting Conditional Branches

A flat sequence treats everyone the same. Smart sequences adapt. In MailClaw's builder, after Email 2, you can insert a conditional node:

  • If opened Email 1: Continue to Email 3 (interest confirmed)
  • If not opened Email 1: Send a re-engagement variant with a different subject line before advancing

You can also branch based on contact properties. Which brings us to enrichment.

Enriching Contacts to Personalize Every Step

Generic personalization — "Hi {first_name}" — stopped impressing anyone around 2015. MailClaw's contact enrichment runs automatically when a contact enters a sequence, pulling in company size, industry, job title, LinkedIn presence, and tech stack signals where available.

You can trigger enrichment manually from the CLI too:

mailclaw contacts enrich --list "trial-signups-june" --fields company,title,industry

Once enriched, you can use those fields inside your email templates with simple merge tags:

Hey {{first_name}},

Given that you're at a {{company_size}}-person company in {{industry}},
you're probably dealing with [specific pain point]...

If you're syncing contacts from Salesforce or HubSpot, MailClaw can pull CRM properties directly, so enrichment isn't duplication — it's augmentation. A contact's HubSpot lifecycle stage can gate which sequence they enter, while MailClaw's own enrichment fills gaps the CRM hasn't captured.

Monitoring Deliverability as You Go

A perfectly crafted welcome series is useless if it lands in spam. MailClaw's deliverability tools surface problems before they compound.

Pre-Send Checks

Before activating any sequence, run the built-in deliverability check from the CLI:

mailclaw deliverability check --sequence "SaaS Trial Welcome"

This audits your sending domain's SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records, scores each email's spam likelihood using content analysis, and flags risky phrases or broken links. It's the equivalent of running your draft through a mail tester — but baked into your workflow, not a separate tab.

Live Monitoring During Active Sequences

The Deliverability panel in the localhost dashboard gives you real-time visibility into bounce rates, spam complaints, and open/click rates per sequence step. If bounce rate on Email 3 spikes above 2%, MailClaw surfaces an alert so you can pause and investigate before the damage reaches your sending reputation.

Keep these benchmarks in mind as you monitor:

  • Hard bounce rate: Keep below 0.5% — anything higher signals a list hygiene problem.
  • Spam complaint rate: Below 0.1% is the safe zone with most ISPs.
  • Unsubscribe rate on Welcome Email 1: Above 1% usually means the expectation set at signup doesn't match what you sent.

Activating and Iterating

Once your sequence is built and deliverability checks pass, activating it is straightforward:

mailclaw sequences activate --name "SaaS Trial Welcome" --trigger signup_form_id:abc123

The trigger parameter connects the sequence to your signup source — a form webhook, a Zapier event, an API call from your app, or a manual import. From that point, every new contact who matches the trigger enters the sequence automatically.

After your first 200–300 contacts have moved through the full arc, export the per-step performance data:

mailclaw sequences report --name "SaaS Trial Welcome" --output csv

Look for the email with the sharpest open-rate drop-off. That's your weakest link. Rewrite the subject line, test a new angle with the AI agent, and iterate. Welcome series optimization isn't a one-time project — it's a compounding return on an hour of setup.

The Case for Running This Locally
