There's a practical case for keeping your email automation off third-party SaaS platforms that rarely gets made explicitly: your contact data is an asset, not a liability. When your welcome series runs in MailClaw at localhost:3100, your subscriber list, enrichment data, and behavioral signals don't feed a vendor's training data or get shared across a multi-tenant infrastructure.

For teams in regulated industries, agencies managing multiple client lists, or founders who've simply had enough of per-seat pricing that scales against you, an open-source, locally-run tool changes the economics entirely. MailClaw's OpenClaw foundation means the entire stack is inspectable, forkable, and yours.

Your welcome series is the first real conversation you have with someone who chose to hear from you. Build it thoughtfully, personalize it intelligently, and monitor it obsessively — and it'll do more for retention and conversion than most campaigns you'll run all year.

articles.title: How to Schedule Email Campaigns by Time Zone in MailClaw
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to schedule email campaigns by time zone in MailClaw, including CLI commands, sequence builder tips, and AI-powered contact enrichment strategies that ensure your outreach lands at the perfect local time for every recipient.
articles.content:
Why Time Zone Scheduling Is a Campaign Killer (If You Get It Wrong)

Sending a "Good morning!" email at 11:47 PM local time is the kind of small detail that quietly destroys open rates. Most email platforms treat time zone scheduling as an afterthought — a dropdown buried in settings that half the team forgets to check. MailClaw takes a different approach: because it runs locally on your machine and gives you direct control over every layer of your outreach stack, time zone logic is something you can build right into your sequences, your contact enrichment pipeline, and even your AI email agents.

This guide walks you through exactly how to do that — from the basics of configuring send-time rules to more advanced techniques using MailClaw's contact enrichment and OpenClaw-powered scheduling logic.

Understanding How MailClaw Handles Time Zones

MailClaw stores all campaign send times in UTC internally, then resolves them against a per-contact timezone field at the moment of dispatch. This means your sequence builder and your actual send behavior are cleanly separated — you define intent ("send this at 9 AM the recipient's time"), and MailClaw resolves delivery.

Before you schedule anything, it's worth understanding the three layers where time zone data lives in MailClaw:

  • Contact-level timezone field — Populated manually, via CSV import, or through contact enrichment
  • Campaign default timezone — A fallback used when the contact field is empty
  • Sequence step offset — Relative delays that respect the resolved send time, not wall-clock UTC

Checking Your Dashboard Settings First

Open your local MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to Settings → Campaign Defaults. Make sure your fallback timezone is set to something sensible for your primary audience — typically your own timezone or the timezone where most of your contacts are located. This fallback fires any time the contact-level field is empty, so it's your safety net.

Enriching Contacts with Timezone Data

The cleanest way to schedule by time zone is to actually know where your contacts are. MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment pipeline can resolve timezone data automatically from IP geolocation, LinkedIn profile data, company domains, or third-party enrichment providers.

Using the CLI to Enrich a Contact List

If you have a CSV of contacts with a city or country column (even partial data), you can run enrichment directly from your terminal:

mailclaw contacts enrich \
  --file ./leads.csv \
  --fields timezone,company,title \
  --provider clearbit \
  --output ./leads-enriched.csv

MailClaw supports multiple enrichment providers — Clearbit, Apollo, Hunter, and a local fallback using OpenClaw's inference engine. When a provider returns a city and country, MailClaw automatically maps that to an IANA timezone string (e.g., America/Chicago or Europe/Berlin) and writes it to the timezone field.

Bulk-Assigning Timezones by Region

If you're working with a list where you know the general geography — say, all contacts are from a HubSpot or Salesforce export covering the US Pacific Coast — you can bulk-assign a timezone without running full enrichment:

mailclaw contacts update \
  --filter "country=US,state=CA" \
  --set timezone="America/Los_Angeles"

This is a quick win for segmented lists where enrichment overhead isn't justified.

Scheduling a Campaign with Per-Contact Time Zone Resolution

Once your contacts have timezone data, you're ready to build a time-zone-aware campaign. Here's how to set that up through both the CLI and the dashboard.

Via the Sequence Builder (Dashboard)

  1. Go to localhost:3100 and open Sequences → New Sequence
  2. Add your first email step and set the send time to 9:00 AM
  3. In the Send Time Mode dropdown, switch from UTC to Recipient Local Time
  4. Under Fallback Behavior, choose either your campaign default timezone or Skip if unknown (recommended for high-deliverability campaigns)
  5. Add follow-up steps using relative delays — e.g., +3 days at 10:00 AM recipient local time

The sequence builder will show you a preview of how sends will be batched across timezones given your current contact list. If you have contacts in New York, London, and Tokyo all set to receive at 9 AM local time, MailClaw queues three separate dispatch windows automatically.

Via the CLI

mailclaw campaign create \
  --name "Q3 Outbound" \
  --sequence ./sequence.json \
  --contacts ./leads-enriched.csv \
  --send-time "09:00" \
  --timezone-mode recipient_local \
  --fallback-tz "America/New_York" \
  --smtp-account primary

The --timezone-mode recipient_local flag is the key argument here. Without it, MailClaw defaults to UTC, which is almost never what you want for a global audience.

Using AI Email Agents to Handle Edge Cases

Here's where MailClaw starts to feel genuinely different from tools like Mailchimp, ActiveCampaign, or even SendGrid. Because it's built on OpenClaw, you can deploy lightweight AI email agents that make scheduling decisions dynamically — not just statically at campaign creation time.

Example: An Agent That Skips Weekends Per Locale

Different regions have different work weeks. Friday afternoon is a send-time blackout in many Middle Eastern markets. Saturday is a normal business day in Israel. You can encode this logic into an agent rather than manually building around it:

// agents/timezone-guard.js
export default {
  name: "timezone-guard",
  trigger: "before_send",
  run: async ({ contact, scheduledAt, mailclaw }) => {
    const tz = contact.timezone || "UTC";
    const localTime = toZonedTime(scheduledAt, tz);
    const day = localTime.getDay();
    const hour = localTime.getHours();

    // Skip weekends and outside 8am-6pm local
    if (day === 0 || day === 6 || hour < 8 || hour >= 18) {
      return mailclaw.reschedule({ days: 1, time: "09:00", tz });
    }

    return mailclaw.proceed();
  }
};

Register the agent with mailclaw agents register ./agents/timezone-guard.js and attach it to any campaign. It runs as a pre-send hook for every outgoing message, silently rescheduling anything that falls outside business hours for that contact's locale.

Monitoring Deliverability Across Time Zones

One underappreciated benefit of time-zone-aware sending is its impact on deliverability. ISPs and spam filters evaluate engagement signals in real time — an email that lands at 3 AM and sits unopened for six hours before the recipient wakes up accumulates negative engagement signals in some filtering models. Sending at the right local time means higher open rates within the first hour, which Gmail, Outlook, and others use as a positive reputation signal.

MailClaw's deliverability dashboard (accessible at localhost:3100/deliverability) breaks down open and click rates by timezone segment, so you can actually see whether your time-zone scheduling is improving performance. Look for the Engagement by Local Send Hour chart — it tells you whether your 9 AM logic is landing correctly or whether certain segments are still receiving mail at suboptimal times.

Pro tip: If you're using OAuth-connected Gmail or Outlook accounts for sending, MailClaw's multi-account manager automatically routes messages through the account with the best recent sender reputation for each timezone batch. This keeps your domain warm across regions without manual rotation.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Ignoring DST transitions — MailClaw uses IANA timezone identifiers (America/New_York, not EST), which handle daylight saving automatically. Never hardcode UTC offsets like UTC-5 in your contact data — they'll break twice a year.
  • Mixing timezone modes within a sequence — If step one uses recipient local time and step two uses UTC, your follow-up delays will be calculated incorrectly. Keep the timezone mode consistent across all steps in a sequence.
  • Empty timezone fields with no fallback — If you skip the fallback timezone setting and 30% of your list has no timezone data, those contacts simply won't send. Always set a campaign fallback.
  • Over-clustering sends — If every contact is set to receive at exactly 9:00 AM, your SMTP server may queue thousands of messages simultaneously. Use MailClaw's send spread setting to distribute dispatch over a 30–60 minute window per timezone batch.

Putting It All Together

Time zone scheduling done well is invisible to your recipients — it just means your emails always show up when they're at their desk, coffee in hand, ready to engage. Done poorly, it's one of those quiet drains on campaign performance that's hard to diagnose without the right tooling.

Because MailClaw runs entirely on your local machine, you have full visibility into every step of this process — from how contact enrichment resolves timezone data to exactly when each message leaves your SMTP queue. The open-source foundation means you can inspect, extend, and customize any part of this pipeline, including the AI agent layer, without being locked into someone else's opinionated workflow.

Start with a simple enrichment run on your next import, flip the recipient_local timezone mode on your next campaign, and check the deliverability dashboard a week later. The difference in engagement metrics is usually obvious — and from there, you can layer in agents and more sophisticated scheduling logic as your needs grow.

articles.title: MailClaw Sequences: A/B Testing Subject Lines with AI
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's AI-powered sequence builder to run statistically meaningful A/B tests on subject lines, automatically promote winners, and continuously improve open rates — all from your local dashboard.
articles.content:
Why Subject Lines Make or Break Your Sequence

You can write the most compelling email body copy in the world, but if the subject line doesn't earn the open, none of it matters. Subject lines are the single highest-leverage variable in any outreach sequence — a 5% improvement in open rate compounds dramatically across a 4-step campaign to thousands of contacts. Yet most teams still rely on gut instinct, picking whichever line "sounds good" and moving on.

MailClaw changes this. Because it runs locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, all your campaign data, contact enrichment signals, and AI-generated variants live in one place with zero round-trips to a third-party SaaS. The result is faster iteration, tighter feedback loops, and A/B tests that actually tell you something useful.

Setting Up an A/B Test in the Sequence Builder

MailClaw's sequence builder ships with native split-testing support. Every step in a sequence can carry multiple subject line variants, and the built-in AI engine — powered by OpenClaw — can generate those variants for you before you even type a single word.

Step 1: Create or Open a Sequence

From your terminal, scaffold a new sequence or open an existing one:

# Create a new sequence
mailclaw sequence create --name "Q3 SaaS Outreach" --steps 4

# Or open the dashboard to manage it visually
mailclaw dashboard
# Then visit http://localhost:3100/sequences

Inside the dashboard, click into any sequence step and you'll see the Subject Line field with an Add Variant button alongside it. This is where the A/B test lives.

Step 2: Generate AI Variants with OpenClaw

Rather than brainstorming manually, let the AI do the heavy lifting. In the sequence step editor, click Generate Variants and MailClaw will use your contact enrichment data — job title, company size, industry vertical, recent funding rounds — to propose subject lines that are contextually relevant, not just generically clever.

You can also trigger this from the CLI if you prefer to stay in your editor:

mailclaw ai subjects \
  --sequence "Q3 SaaS Outreach" \
  --step 1 \
  --count 4 \
  --tone "direct, curiosity-driven" \
  --persona "VP of Engineering at a Series B startup"

This returns something like:

[1] "Quick question about your deployment pipeline"
[2] "How {company} handles on-call burnout (most don't)"
[3] "Saw your team is hiring 3 SREs — timing?"
[4] "{first_name}, cutting incident response time in half"

Variants 3 and 4 pull from enrichment data MailClaw has already gathered on your contacts — a genuinely unfair advantage compared to running blind tests in a tool like HubSpot or a standard Mailchimp campaign where personalization depth is limited.

Step 3: Assign Split Ratios

Back in the dashboard (or via config), assign what percentage of your audience sees each variant. For most tests, an even split works fine with large lists. For smaller lists under 500 contacts, MailClaw recommends a 50/50 split to reach statistical significance faster.

mailclaw sequence ab-config \
  --sequence "Q3 SaaS Outreach" \
  --step 1 \
  --variants "A:25,B:25,C:25,D:25" \
  --winner-metric "open_rate" \
  --confidence 95

The --confidence 95 flag tells MailClaw not to auto-promote a winner until it has reached 95% statistical confidence. You can lower this to 90 for faster iteration or raise it to 99 for high-stakes campaigns.

Reading the Results in Your Local Dashboard

Once sends start going out through your connected accounts — whether that's Gmail via OAuth, Outlook via Microsoft Graph, or a transactional provider like SendGrid or Postmark via SMTP — MailClaw's deliverability layer begins tracking opens, clicks, and replies per variant in real time.

Navigate to localhost:3100/sequences/[id]/analytics to see the live split view. You'll get:

  • Open rate per variant with confidence intervals displayed visually
  • Reply rate and downstream click-through if you're tracking links
  • Deliverability flags — if one variant is triggering spam filters at a higher rate, MailClaw highlights it before it damages your sender reputation
  • Enrichment correlation — which variant performed best with contacts from specific industries, company sizes, or funding stages

That last point is where things get genuinely interesting. You may find that the curiosity-gap subject line crushes it with VP-level contacts but underperforms badly with founders. MailClaw segments this automatically because the enrichment data is already attached to every contact record.

Auto-Promoting Winners and Looping AI Back In

Once a variant clears your confidence threshold, MailClaw can automatically promote it as the default for all remaining sends in the sequence. Enable this in your sequence settings:

mailclaw sequence update "Q3 SaaS Outreach" \
  --auto-promote true \
  --promote-after 95

But don't stop there. After a winner is declared, trigger a new round of AI generation informed by the winner. This is continuous optimization rather than a one-shot test:

mailclaw ai subjects \
  --sequence "Q3 SaaS Outreach" \
  --step 1 \
  --refine-from-winner true \
  --count 3

OpenClaw will analyze what made the winning variant work — length, personalization tokens, question vs. statement framing, urgency cues — and generate a next-generation batch of challengers. Over time, this creates a compounding improvement loop that no static playbook can replicate.

Best Practices for Meaningful Tests

Test One Variable at a Time

It sounds obvious, but it's easy to accidentally test both subject line copy and send time simultaneously when you're moving fast. MailClaw's sequence builder will warn you if you have conflicting variables active in the same step, but be intentional: isolate the subject line first, then run a separate test for send timing or preview text.

Let Enrichment Data Shape Your Hypotheses

Before you generate variants, look at your contact segments. If 60% of your list just raised a Series A, a subject line referencing growth-stage challenges will outperform a generic one almost every time. Use MailClaw's contact enrichment panel — accessible at localhost:3100/contacts/enrichment — to understand your audience before you write for them.

Don't Neglect Deliverability as a Variable

A subject line that contains certain trigger words — excessive punctuation, all-caps phrases, aggressive urgency language — can tank deliverability before the open rate has a chance to be meaningful. MailClaw's deliverability tools run a pre-send lint check on every variant and score it against known spam filter patterns for Gmail, Outlook, and major corporate mail gateways. Fix deliverability issues before you run the test, not after.

Pro tip: Run mailclaw deliverability check --sequence "Q3 SaaS Outreach" --step 1 before activating any A/B test. It takes three seconds and can save you from burning a warm list on a variant that was never going to land in the inbox.

Archive and Learn Across Campaigns

Because MailClaw is open source and stores everything locally, you own your test history completely. Use the export command to build a running spreadsheet of what's worked:

mailclaw sequence export "Q3 SaaS Outreach" \
  --include ab-results \
  --format csv \
  --output ~/email-learnings/q3-saas.csv

Over time, patterns emerge that are specific to your audience and your voice — things no generic best-practices article (including this one) can give you. That accumulated data is genuinely proprietary, and keeping it local rather than siloed in a CRM like Salesforce or locked inside a SaaS platform means you can actually use it across tools and campaigns.

Connecting It to Your AI Email Agent

If you're running AI email agents in MailClaw — autonomous agents that handle replies, qualify leads, and advance contacts through sequences without manual intervention — subject line A/B test results feed directly into the agent's decision layer. An agent managing a multi-account outreach campaign across several Gmail and Outlook inboxes will automatically apply the winning subject line variant to any new contact it enrolls in an active sequence.

This closes the loop between testing and execution in a way that's simply not possible when your testing tool and your sending tool are different products stitched together with Zapier or a leaky API integration.

Getting Started Today

If you haven't set up MailClaw yet, the quickest path is:

  1. Clone the repo and run mailclaw init — the local dashboard spins up at localhost:3100 in under a minute
  2. Connect at least one sending account (Gmail OAuth or SMTP credentials work out of the box)
  3. Import a contact list and let MailClaw's enrichment engine fill in the gaps
  4. Build a 3-step sequence in the visual builder and enable A/B testing on Step 1
  5. Let OpenClaw generate your first round of subject line variants and run the test

The feedback loop is tight, the data is yours, and the AI gets smarter with every campaign you run. Subject line testing stops being a chore and starts being one of the most reliable levers you have for improving outreach performance — one sequence at a time.

articles.title: How to Create Re-Engagement Campaigns with MailClaw
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to build effective re-engagement campaigns in MailClaw using AI email agents, contact enrichment, and automated sequences to win back inactive subscribers and protect your sender reputation.
articles.content:
Why Re-Engagement Campaigns Matter More Than You Think

Every email list has a silent problem: subscribers who stopped opening, stopped clicking, and quietly checked out. Most marketers ignore them until they become a deliverability liability. Gmail, Outlook, and Yahoo's spam filters watch engagement signals closely — a list full of cold contacts drags down your sender reputation and can land your entire campaign in the spam folder, even for people who actually want your emails.

Re-engagement campaigns are your systematic way of either winning those contacts back or gracefully removing them before they hurt you. Done well, they recover real revenue. Done poorly, they accelerate the damage. With MailClaw running locally on your machine, you have a full automation stack — AI email agents, contact enrichment, and a visual sequence builder — to execute this the right way, without shipping your contact data to a third-party SaaS platform.

Step 1: Define Your Inactive Segment

Before you write a single word of copy, you need a clean, honest definition of "inactive." A common threshold is no opens or clicks in the last 90 days, but this varies by your sending frequency and industry. If you send daily, 30 days of silence is significant. If you send monthly, 90–180 days might be more appropriate.

In MailClaw's local dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to the Contacts tab and use the filter builder to create your inactive segment:

# Example: filter contacts with no opens in 90 days using the MailClaw CLI
mailclaw contacts filter \
  --last-open-before "90d" \
  --last-click-before "90d" \
  --tag "inactive-q3" \
  --export inactive_segment.csv

This tags matched contacts and exports them for review. You can also pipe this directly into a sequence without the export step — but reviewing the list first is good hygiene. You'll often find former customers, trial users who churned, or high-value leads who went dark after a sales cycle. Each group needs slightly different messaging.

Step 2: Enrich Your Contacts Before Reaching Out

One of MailClaw's most underutilized features is its built-in contact enrichment engine, powered by OpenClaw. Before you send a single re-engagement email, run enrichment on your inactive segment. This pulls in updated job titles, company changes, LinkedIn activity signals, and firmographic data — all locally, without your contacts' data leaving your machine.

# Enrich the inactive segment
mailclaw enrich \
  --input inactive_segment.csv \
  --sources linkedin,clearbit,hunter \
  --output enriched_inactive.csv

Why does this matter for re-engagement? Because context changes. The contact who went cold six months ago may have changed jobs, received a promotion, or moved to a company where your product is even more relevant. Enrichment lets your AI email agent personalize outreach with current information rather than stale data from when they originally subscribed.

If you're syncing with HubSpot or Salesforce, you can pull enriched data back into those CRMs automatically:

mailclaw sync --crm hubspot --segment inactive-q3 --fields title,company,enriched_at

Step 3: Build Your Re-Engagement Sequence

A re-engagement sequence typically runs 3–5 emails over 2–3 weeks. The goal is to re-establish relevance, offer genuine value, and ultimately ask a direct question: do you still want to hear from us? Here's a proven structure:

Email 1 — The Gentle Nudge (Day 1)

Keep this short and human. No promotions, no pressure. Acknowledge the silence and remind them why they subscribed in the first place. Subject lines like "Still interested in [topic]?" or "We've missed you" perform well because they're honest and low-stakes.

Email 2 — Deliver Value (Day 5)

Give them something genuinely useful — your best blog post, a resource, an insight relevant to their industry. This email should feel like a gift, not a pitch. If your enrichment revealed they changed roles, your AI agent can swap in role-specific content automatically.

Email 3 — Social Proof or a New Angle (Day 10)

Share a customer story, a case study, or a new product update that's relevant to their segment. This is the "here's what you've been missing" email — compelling but not desperate.

Email 4 — The Direct Ask (Day 15)

This is your most important email. Ask plainly whether they want to stay on your list, and make it easy to say yes or no. A clear call-to-action like "Click here to stay subscribed" with an implicit unsubscribe if they don't click is both honest and effective.

Email 5 — The Farewell (Day 21)

For contacts who didn't engage with any of the previous four emails, send a clean goodbye. Let them know you're removing them and give one final easy path back. This email consistently generates surprise re-engagements — people respond to finality.

In MailClaw's Sequence Builder, you can configure this entire flow visually at localhost:3100/sequences. Set branching logic so contacts who open or click any email in the sequence get moved out of the re-engagement flow and tagged as re-engaged automatically:

mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "Q3 Re-engagement" \
  --segment "inactive-q3" \
  --template-dir ./templates/reengagement \
  --interval 5d \
  --exit-on "open,click" \
  --exit-tag "reengaged"

Step 4: Use AI Email Agents to Personalize at Scale

MailClaw's AI email agents — built on the OpenClaw framework — let you move beyond mail-merge-style personalization. Instead of inserting a first name and a company name into a static template, an AI agent can dynamically generate subject lines, adjust the email body tone based on enrichment data, and even choose which social proof example to include based on the contact's industry.

To configure an AI agent for your re-engagement sequence:

# Define your agent persona and personalization rules
mailclaw agent create \
  --name "reengagement-agent" \
  --base-prompt ./prompts/reengagement_base.txt \
  --variables title,company,industry,last_product_used \
  --model openai/gpt-4o \
  --temperature 0.4

Pro tip: Keep your agent's temperature low (0.3–0.5) for re-engagement campaigns. You want consistent, professional tone — not creative variation that might feel off-brand to someone who hasn't heard from you in months.

The agent will reference your enriched contact fields and generate email variants that feel individually written. For a segment of 500 cold contacts, this is the difference between a 4% re-engagement rate and a 14% one — numbers that translate directly to recovered pipeline value.

Step 5: Monitor Deliverability Throughout the Campaign

Re-engagement campaigns carry inherent deliverability risk. You're emailing people who haven't opened in months — which means some percentage have invalid addresses, have marked previous senders as spam, or simply won't interact. Sending to them in bulk without monitoring is how good sender reputations get destroyed.

MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools track bounce rates, spam complaint rates, and inbox placement in real time. Set alert thresholds before you launch:

mailclaw monitor set \
  --campaign "Q3 Re-engagement" \
  --bounce-threshold 2.5 \
  --complaint-threshold 0.08 \
  --alert-email you@yourdomain.com \
  --pause-on-breach

The --pause-on-breach flag automatically pauses sending if either threshold is crossed, protecting your sender reputation with Gmail and Outlook while you investigate. This is especially important if you're sending through SendGrid or another shared infrastructure provider where reputation damage affects your sending IP's reputation globally.

For multi-account setups — common when you're running outreach across multiple team members' Gmail or Outlook accounts via OAuth — MailClaw lets you distribute the re-engagement send across accounts to avoid triggering volume-based spam detection on any single sender:

mailclaw campaign send \
  --campaign "Q3 Re-engagement" \
  --distribute-across-accounts \
  --daily-limit-per-account 150

Handling the Outcomes

After your sequence completes, you'll have three groups to act on:

  • Re-engaged contacts: Move these back into your regular nurture sequence. Tag them in MailClaw and sync back to HubSpot or Salesforce with a note indicating they re-engaged and the date.
  • Partial engagement (opened but didn't click): Consider a follow-up educational sequence. These contacts showed interest but weren't motivated to act. A lower-pressure, content-only sequence for another 30 days is reasonable.
  • No engagement: Suppress them. Archive in MailClaw, remove from active sending lists in your ESP, and document it. Don't delete the records — they're valuable historical data — but stop emailing them.
# Suppress unresponsive contacts after sequence completion
mailclaw contacts suppress \
  --tag "inactive-q3" \
  --exclude-tag "reengaged" \
  --reason "re-engagement-failed" \
  --sync-to hubspot

The Long-Term Play

Re-engagement campaigns shouldn't be quarterly fire drills. The most effective email programs run a lightweight re-engagement sequence on a rolling basis — automatically triggering for any contact that crosses your inactivity threshold. MailClaw's automation layer makes this straightforward to configure as a persistent campaign rather than a one-time event.

When your re-engagement logic runs automatically, your list stays healthier, your deliverability stays strong, and you never again face a massive backlog of cold contacts that feel insurmountable. That's the real value: not just recovering lost contacts, but building the operational discipline to prevent them from accumulating in the first place.

Because MailClaw runs entirely on your local machine — no data sent to third-party servers, no per-seat pricing, no API rate limits on your own contact data — you can run these campaigns as frequently as your list requires without watching a cost meter climb. That's the open-source advantage in action.

articles.title: Building Nurture Sequences for SaaS Onboarding with MailClaw
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to design and deploy effective SaaS onboarding nurture sequences using MailClaw's AI email agents, sequence builder, and contact enrichment — all running locally on your Mac with zero data sent to the cloud.
articles.content:
Why Onboarding Sequences Make or Break SaaS Retention

The window between a user signing up and them becoming a paying, retained customer is razor-thin. Research consistently shows that users who don't experience a meaningful "aha moment" within the first seven days are far more likely to churn. Yet most SaaS teams still rely on a single welcome email and a generic drip campaign cobbled together in whatever marketing tool they inherited.

A well-structured nurture sequence doesn't just deliver information — it guides users toward activation milestones, surfaces the right features at the right time, and builds enough trust that support requests turn into expansion revenue. With MailClaw, you can build these sequences locally on your Mac, enriched with real contact data and powered by AI agents that adapt messaging based on where a user actually is in their journey.

Mapping Your Onboarding Stages Before You Write a Single Email

Before opening the MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100, do the architecture work first. A SaaS onboarding sequence typically moves through four stages:

  • Welcome & orientation — Confirm the signup, set expectations, and point to one clear next step.
  • Activation nudge — Push users toward the core action that defines engagement (connecting an integration, inviting a teammate, creating a first project).
  • Value reinforcement — Show users what's possible once the core action is done. Social proof, use-case walkthroughs, and short tutorials live here.
  • Conversion or expansion — Trial-to-paid prompts, upsell to a higher tier, or referral asks once genuine value has been delivered.

Map each stage to a concrete user behavior (or its absence) and you'll have the skeleton of a branching sequence. MailClaw's sequence builder handles this branching logic natively — no Zapier workarounds required.

Setting Up Your First Sequence in MailClaw

Starting the Local Dashboard

If you haven't already, spin up MailClaw from your terminal:

mailclaw start
# Dashboard available at http://localhost:3100

Connect your sending infrastructure under Settings → Accounts. MailClaw supports Gmail and Google Workspace via OAuth, Outlook via Microsoft OAuth, and any SMTP provider — SendGrid, Postmark, Amazon SES — through standard credential entry. For SaaS onboarding at scale, a dedicated subdomain (e.g., mail.yourapp.com) routed through SendGrid with proper SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records will protect your deliverability from the start.

Creating the Sequence

Navigate to Sequences → New Sequence and give it a descriptive name like SaaS Onboarding — Trial Users. Set the trigger to Contact Added to List so it fires automatically whenever a new signup is imported or synced from your CRM.

MailClaw's sequence builder uses a node-based visual editor. Add your first email node, then use the Branch node to split behavior: one path for users who completed the activation event, another for those who haven't after 48 hours.

Pro tip: Name your branches explicitly — "Activated" and "Not Yet Activated" beats "Branch A / Branch B" when you're debugging at 11pm.

Writing Emails That Actually Get Opened

Subject Lines and Timing

Your welcome email should go out within five minutes of signup — not the next morning. Late delivery is one of the most common and most avoidable onboarding mistakes. In MailClaw, set the delay on your first node to 0 minutes and make sure your sending account has sufficient hourly limits configured under deliverability settings.

For subject lines across the sequence, avoid generic SaaS tropes:

  • ❌ "Welcome to [Product]! Here's how to get started."
  • ✅ "One thing to do in [Product] right now"
  • ✅ "You're 3 minutes away from [core value prop]"
  • ✅ "[First name], your account is ready — here's what most people do first"

Using AI Email Agents to Personalize at Scale

This is where MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered AI agents genuinely change the game. Rather than writing five variations of the same activation nudge email, you can instruct an AI agent to generate personalized copy based on enriched contact data.

In the sequence builder, drop in an AI Agent Node before your email send node. Configure the prompt like this:

You are writing a short, friendly activation email for a SaaS product.
The recipient's name is {{contact.firstName}}.
Their company is {{contact.company}} (industry: {{contact.industry}}).
Their signup date is {{contact.createdAt}}.
They have NOT yet completed the core activation step: {{product.activationEvent}}.

Write a 3-sentence email body that:
1. Acknowledges it's been 48 hours since they signed up
2. Names one specific benefit relevant to their industry
3. Ends with a single clear CTA linking to {{product.activationUrl}}

Tone: conversational, not pushy.

The agent runs locally via OpenClaw — your contact data never leaves your machine. This matters for GDPR compliance and for companies in regulated industries who can't pipe customer data through third-party AI APIs.

Enriching Contacts for Smarter Segmentation

Generic sequences underperform because they treat a solo founder and an enterprise procurement manager identically. MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment engine resolves email addresses to company data, job title, company size, and industry — giving your AI agents and branch logic the context they need.

Trigger enrichment from the CLI before a campaign runs:

mailclaw contacts enrich --list "Trial Users - Q3" --fields company,title,industry,company_size

Once enriched, you can build segments directly in the dashboard. A few high-value segments for SaaS onboarding:

  • Company size > 50 employees — These users often need team-focused messaging. Lead with collaboration features and ROI framing, not individual productivity.
  • Industry = Developer Tools / Engineering — Skip the fluffy copy. Link to your API docs and CLI quickstart on email one.
  • Job title contains "Founder" or "CEO" — Send from a founder email address. Personal outreach converts dramatically better than noreply@ for this segment.

Monitoring Deliverability Without Leaving Your Terminal

A sequence that lands in spam might as well not exist. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring dashboard (available at localhost:3100/deliverability) tracks open rates, bounce rates, spam complaints, and sending reputation across all your connected accounts in real time.

Watch for these thresholds during an onboarding campaign:

  • Bounce rate above 2% — Pause the sequence and clean your list. Run mailclaw contacts validate --list "Trial Users - Q3" to identify invalid addresses before they damage your sender score.
  • Spam complaint rate above 0.1% — Review your unsubscribe flow and frequency. One-click unsubscribe is now required by Gmail and Yahoo for bulk senders.
  • Open rate below 15% on email 1 — Your welcome email is probably delayed or landing in a promotions tab. Check authentication records and consider plain-text format for the first send.

Integrating With Your Existing Stack

MailClaw doesn't replace your CRM — it works alongside it. Use the CLI sync commands to pull contacts from HubSpot or Salesforce into a MailClaw list, run the sequence, and write engagement events back:

# Pull new trial users from HubSpot created in the last 24 hours
mailclaw sync --source hubspot --filter "lifecyclestage=subscriber&created_after=24h" --target-list "Trial Users - Active"

# Push sequence engagement back to Salesforce
mailclaw sync --push-events --destination salesforce --event-types opened,clicked,replied

This two-way sync means your sales team sees email engagement directly in their CRM pipeline without you having to maintain a separate integration layer. Reps working warm trial accounts can see that a lead opened the activation email three times without clicking — a clear signal to reach out personally.

A Sample 7-Day Sequence Structure

  1. Day 0, 0 min — Welcome email: confirm signup, single CTA to activation step
  2. Day 1, 10am — Quick win email: one tip that delivers value in under 5 minutes
  3. Day 2 (branch) — If not activated: nudge with social proof + simplified CTA. If activated: celebrate + introduce next feature.
  4. Day 4 — Use-case spotlight: pick the most relevant one based on enriched industry data
  5. Day 5 (branch) — If activated: invite to webinar or community. If not: personal-tone email from founder alias offering a quick call.
  6. Day 7 — Trial milestone recap: show what they've done (or could have done), soft conversion ask with trial days remaining

This structure is a starting point, not a template to clone blindly. Run it for 30 days, review the branch performance data in your MailClaw dashboard, and iterate on the nodes with the lowest click-through rates first.

Shipping Your Sequence With Confidence

The best onboarding sequence is one that actually ships. MailClaw's local-first architecture removes the usual blockers — no per-seat pricing to justify, no data leaving your infrastructure, no vendor lock-in if your requirements change. Fork the OpenClaw core, extend the agent prompts to match your product's voice, and build something your users will actually thank you for.

Start with two or three emails, get them right, and expand from there. The sequence that converts isn't necessarily the most sophisticated one — it's the one that consistently delivers the right message to the right person at exactly the right moment.

articles.title: How to Automate Post-Demo Follow-Ups with MailClaw
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to build intelligent, personalized post-demo follow-up sequences using MailClaw's AI email agents, sequence builder, and contact enrichment tools — so no warm lead ever goes cold again.
articles.content:
Why Post-Demo Follow-Ups Are Make-or-Break

You spent 45 minutes on a product demo. You nailed the pitch, answered the objections, and left the call feeling good. Then two days pass. Then a week. Then you're sending a "just checking in" email that nobody asked for and nobody will reply to.

Post-demo follow-up is one of the highest-leverage activities in any sales process — and it's also one of the most consistently botched. Timing is off, messaging is generic, and the manual effort of personalizing each follow-up at scale is simply unsustainable. That's exactly the problem MailClaw was built to solve.

In this guide, we'll walk through how to build a complete post-demo follow-up system using MailClaw's sequence builder, AI email agents, and contact enrichment — all running locally on your machine so your data never leaves your environment.

Setting Up Your Post-Demo Workflow in MailClaw

Step 1: Launch the Local Dashboard

If you haven't already, fire up MailClaw from your terminal:

mailclaw start

This spins up the local dashboard at localhost:3100. From here you'll manage everything — sequences, contacts, agents, and deliverability — without touching any third-party SaaS interface. Open your browser and head to http://localhost:3100 to get started.

Step 2: Connect Your Sending Account

MailClaw supports both SMTP and OAuth integrations out of the box. For most sales teams, connecting a Gmail or Outlook account via OAuth is the fastest path:

mailclaw accounts add --provider gmail --oauth

If you're running higher volume outreach or want more control over deliverability, you can route through SendGrid or any custom SMTP server:

mailclaw accounts add --provider sendgrid --api-key YOUR_KEY --from "you@yourdomain.com"

Multi-account support means you can run follow-ups for multiple sales reps or domains from the same MailClaw instance — each with its own sending identity, warm-up schedule, and deliverability profile.

Enriching Your Demo Contacts Automatically

Before you write a single word of follow-up copy, you need context. What does this prospect's company actually do? What's their tech stack? Did they recently raise funding or announce a new initiative? Generic follow-ups fail because they don't reflect what the prospect actually cares about.

MailClaw's contact enrichment layer solves this automatically. After a demo, import your contact — whether that's a manual CSV, a direct pull from HubSpot or Salesforce, or a webhook from your CRM — and let MailClaw enrich the record before your first email goes out.

mailclaw contacts enrich --email prospect@company.com --fields company,title,linkedin,funding,techstack

Enriched fields get stored against the contact and are immediately available as dynamic variables inside your sequence templates. That means your AI email agent can reference the prospect's company size, recent news, or job title without you doing a minute of manual research.

Pro tip: If you're pulling contacts from Salesforce or HubSpot, use MailClaw's native sync commands to keep records in sync and avoid duplicate outreach. Run mailclaw sync --crm hubspot --list demo-completed to pull everyone who's hit a "Demo Completed" stage in your pipeline.

Building the Post-Demo Sequence

The Anatomy of a High-Converting Follow-Up Sequence

A good post-demo sequence isn't a drip campaign. It's a structured conversation that adapts to where the prospect actually is. Here's a framework that consistently performs well:

  • Email 1 (Day 1, within 2 hours): Personalized recap — what you discussed, what problem you're solving for them specifically, and a clear next step.
  • Email 2 (Day 3): Value add — a relevant case study, ROI calculator, or a resource tied to a pain point they mentioned.
  • Email 3 (Day 7): Objection handling — address the most common hesitation for their company profile (pricing, integration complexity, team buy-in).
  • Email 4 (Day 14): The nudge — lighter touch, short, asks for a yes/no on timing.
  • Email 5 (Day 21): The breakup email — honest, no pressure, leaves the door open.

Open the sequence builder in the dashboard at localhost:3100/sequences/new and map this out visually, or build it from the CLI:

mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "Post-Demo Follow-Up" \
  --steps 5 \
  --delays "0h,3d,7d,14d,21d" \
  --tags demo,outbound

Writing Templates with AI Assist

This is where MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered AI engine earns its keep. Instead of writing five emails from scratch, you give the agent context and let it draft. Navigate to the sequence editor in the dashboard, click AI Draft on any step, and describe the goal:

mailclaw agent draft \
  --sequence "Post-Demo Follow-Up" \
  --step 1 \
  --context "B2B SaaS demo, prospect is VP of Engineering at a 200-person fintech, pain point is manual deployment workflows, tone: professional but direct"

The AI agent generates a full draft using enriched contact data as variables. You'll see placeholders like {{company_name}}, {{recent_funding}}, and {{pain_point_summary}} populated dynamically at send time. Review, tweak the voice to match your brand, and move on.

The difference between an AI-drafted follow-up that works and one that sounds robotic is the enrichment layer. Because MailClaw pulled real data about the contact before drafting, the output reads like you did your homework — because effectively, the agent did it for you.

Automating the Send Logic

Triggers and Conditions

Smart automation means sequences respond to behavior, not just time. MailClaw lets you set conditional logic at each step so the sequence adapts:

mailclaw sequence update "Post-Demo Follow-Up" \
  --step 2 \
  --condition "if:email_opened AND link_not_clicked THEN send" \
  --condition "if:link_clicked THEN skip_to:step_3"

If a prospect opens your recap email and clicks the case study link, MailClaw skips the value-add email (they already engaged with it) and jumps straight to the objection-handling message. If they don't open at all, the system can trigger a subject line variation using the AI agent before retrying.

Deliverability Monitoring

Even the best-written sequence fails if your emails land in spam. MailClaw's built-in deliverability tools monitor your sender reputation in real time, flag authentication issues, and surface actionable fixes directly in the dashboard.

  • Check SPF, DKIM, and DMARC status per sending account
  • Monitor open rates, bounce rates, and spam complaints per sequence
  • Get alerts when a sending domain's reputation score drops below your defined threshold
mailclaw deliverability check --account me@company.com

Running locally means this monitoring is continuous and private — no third-party tool is seeing your contact lists or send patterns.

Handing Off to Your CRM

Once a prospect replies or takes a defined action — books a follow-up call, visits your pricing page, responds with a question — you want that signal in your CRM immediately. MailClaw's outbound webhook support makes this straightforward:

mailclaw webhooks add \
  --event reply_received \
  --url https://hooks.salesforce.com/your-endpoint \
  --payload '{"contact": "{{email}}", "status": "replied", "sequence": "{{sequence_name}}"}'

You can push events to Salesforce, HubSpot, Pipedrive, or any tool that accepts a webhook. This keeps your CRM as the source of truth while MailClaw handles the execution layer — no duplicate data entry, no missed updates.

Putting It All Together

The full post-demo automation loop looks like this: demo ends → contact is created or synced from your CRM → MailClaw enriches the record → AI agent drafts a personalized five-step sequence → emails go out on your defined schedule with conditional logic → replies and engagement events sync back to your CRM → your pipeline stays current without manual intervention.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your local machine, you're not locked into a per-seat pricing model, your prospect data never hits a third-party server, and you can extend or modify any part of the system to fit your workflow.

The reps who win deals after demos aren't necessarily the ones with the best pitch — they're the ones who follow up fast, stay relevant, and don't drop the thread. With MailClaw handling the mechanics, that consistency becomes the default rather than the exception.

articles.title: MailClaw for Event Marketing: Automated Invite and Reminder Sequences
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's sequence builder, AI email agents, and contact enrichment tools to automate your entire event marketing funnel — from initial invites to post-event follow-ups — without leaving your local machine.
articles.content:
Why Event Email Marketing Deserves Better Automation

Event marketing is one of the highest-stakes use cases for email. You have a hard deadline, a finite audience, and a sequence of critical touchpoints — save the dates, invitations, registration confirmations, reminders, day-of logistics, and post-event follow-ups — all of which need to land at exactly the right time. Miss one, and attendance drops. Send the wrong message to someone who already registered, and you look disorganized.

Most teams cobble this together manually in HubSpot, Mailchimp, or a spreadsheet-driven nightmare. MailClaw gives you a better option: a locally-running, AI-powered automation engine that handles the entire event email lifecycle from a single command-line interface, with a beautiful dashboard available at localhost:3100.

This guide walks through a practical, end-to-end setup for event email automation using MailClaw's sequence builder, AI email agents, and contact enrichment — whether you're running a webinar for 50 people or a conference for 5,000.

Mapping Your Event Email Funnel

Before you write a single line of automation config, get clear on your funnel stages. A solid event sequence typically has five phases:

  1. Awareness: Early announcement or save-the-date, sent 4–6 weeks out
  2. Invitation: Formal invite with agenda, speakers, and registration CTA, sent 2–3 weeks out
  3. Nurture: Value-add emails (speaker spotlights, agenda previews) for those who opened but didn't register
  4. Pre-event reminders: 1-week, 1-day, and 1-hour reminders to registered attendees
  5. Post-event follow-up: Recording link, survey, next steps, and re-engagement for no-shows

Each phase serves a different audience segment with different intent signals. MailClaw's sequence builder lets you branch logic based on opens, clicks, registrations, and enriched contact data — so the right person gets the right message at every stage.

Setting Up Your Event Sequence in MailClaw

Step 1: Initialize Your Campaign

Start by spinning up MailClaw locally and creating a new campaign from the CLI:

# Start MailClaw (dashboard available at localhost:3100)
mailclaw start

# Create a new event campaign
mailclaw campaign create --name "Q3 Product Summit" --type event

# Set your sending account (supports Gmail OAuth, Outlook, SendGrid, custom SMTP)
mailclaw account add --provider gmail --oauth

MailClaw's multi-account support means you can send transactional reminders via SendGrid for deliverability, while keeping personal invites going through your authenticated Gmail or Outlook account — a common pattern for enterprise events where you want executive-branded outreach.

Step 2: Import and Enrich Your Contact List

Upload your initial invite list and let MailClaw's contact enrichment layer do the heavy lifting before a single email goes out:

# Import contacts from CSV
mailclaw contacts import --file invite-list.csv --campaign "Q3 Product Summit"

# Run enrichment to pull company size, title, industry, LinkedIn data
mailclaw contacts enrich --campaign "Q3 Product Summit" --fields title,company,industry,seniority

This enrichment step is what separates a generic blast from a segmented strategy. Once you know that 30% of your list is C-suite and 40% is mid-level practitioners, you can write different subject lines, different CTAs, and different urgency levels for each group — all within the same sequence.

If your contacts are already in Salesforce or HubSpot, MailClaw can sync directly:

mailclaw contacts sync --source salesforce --filter "list:event-prospects-q3"

Step 3: Build the Sequence with Branching Logic

Open your dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to the Sequence Builder, or define your sequence in YAML for version-controlled campaigns:

sequence:
  name: "Q3 Product Summit - Full Funnel"
  campaign: "Q3 Product Summit"
  steps:
    - id: save_the_date
      type: email
      delay: 0
      template: save-the-date.html
      subject: "You're invited — Product Summit is back"
      segment: all

    - id: formal_invite
      type: email
      delay: 7d
      template: formal-invite.html
      subject: "{{ first_name }}, your seat at Product Summit"
      segment: all

    - id: nurture_opener
      type: branch
      condition: "opened(formal_invite) AND NOT clicked_registration"
      delay: 4d
      steps:
        - type: email
          template: speaker-spotlight.html
          subject: "Meet the speakers at Product Summit"

    - id: reminder_1week
      type: email
      delay: "event_date - 7d"
      template: reminder-week.html
      subject: "One week out — here's what to expect"
      segment: registered

    - id: reminder_1day
      type: email
      delay: "event_date - 1d"
      template: reminder-day.html
      subject: "Tomorrow: Your access link for Product Summit"
      segment: registered

    - id: no_show_followup
      type: email
      delay: "event_date + 1d"
      template: missed-you.html
      subject: "We missed you — here's the recording"
      segment: registered_did_not_attend

The event_date anchor is a first-class concept in MailClaw sequences — all relative delays calculate automatically, so you can reuse the same sequence template for every event just by updating the campaign date.

Using AI Email Agents for Dynamic Personalization

One of MailClaw's most powerful differentiators is its AI email agent system, built on OpenClaw's underlying agent framework. For event marketing, this unlocks two high-value capabilities.

AI-Generated Subject Line Variants

Rather than manually A/B testing subject lines, you can instruct an AI agent to generate and rotate variants based on contact attributes:

mailclaw agent run --task "generate_subject_variants" \
  --template formal-invite.html \
  --segments "executive,practitioner,startup" \
  --variants 3

The agent reads your template, understands the event context, and writes segment-appropriate subject lines. Executives get urgency and exclusivity framing. Practitioners get agenda and learning-outcome framing. Startups get networking and ROI framing.

Intelligent Reply Handling

Configure an AI agent to monitor your sending inbox and handle common replies automatically — confirming dietary requirements, forwarding logistics questions to the right team member, or tagging contacts who request a calendar invite:

mailclaw agent create --name "event-reply-handler" \
  --trigger "inbound_reply" \
  --campaign "Q3 Product Summit" \
  --instructions "Classify replies as: logistics, dietary, cancellation, or other. Auto-respond to logistics and dietary with template responses. Flag cancellations for human review."

This runs entirely on your local machine — no data leaves your environment, which matters when you're handling attendee information for enterprise or regulated-industry clients.

Deliverability: Keeping Your Event Emails Out of Spam

Nothing kills event attendance like an invitation that lands in the Promotions tab. MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring tools help you stay ahead of this.

Pre-Send Checks

# Run deliverability audit before launching sequence
mailclaw deliver audit --campaign "Q3 Product Summit"

This checks SPF/DKIM/DMARC alignment on your sending domain, flags spam-trigger words in subject lines and body copy, and scores your HTML-to-text ratio. For event emails specifically, watch out for over-designed templates — heavy image-to-text ratios are a common spam signal that derails otherwise well-planned campaigns.

Warm-Up Routing for New Domains

If you're sending from an event-specific subdomain (like events.yourcompany.com), use MailClaw's send routing to gradually ramp volume:

mailclaw deliver warmup --domain events.yourcompany.com \
  --daily-limit 200 \
  --ramp-schedule 7d

Pro tip: For large events, split your list so VIP invites go through your primary authenticated domain while general invites route through SendGrid with a warm subdomain. This protects your core domain reputation while scaling volume.

Monitoring Performance from the Local Dashboard

With your sequence running, head to localhost:3100 to track performance in real time. The MailClaw dashboard surfaces the metrics that matter most for events:

  • Registration conversion rate per email step (which touchpoint drove the most sign-ups)
  • Open and click rates by segment (are your executives actually engaging?)
  • Bounce and unsubscribe rates per send (early warning for deliverability issues)
  • No-show rate vs. reminder cadence (did the 1-hour reminder actually help?)

Because MailClaw is open source and built on OpenClaw, you can extend the dashboard with custom metrics or pipe event data into your own analytics stack — something you simply can't do with locked-down SaaS platforms.

A Repeatable Template for Every Event

The real payoff of this setup is reusability. Once you've built and tuned your event sequence, export it as a reusable template:

mailclaw sequence export --campaign "Q3 Product Summit" --output event-template.yaml

Next time you run an event, import the template, update the event date and assets, swap in your contact list, and launch — the entire funnel is live in minutes, not days.

Event marketing has always been time-sensitive and detail-heavy. MailClaw turns that complexity into a repeatable, automated system that runs quietly on your Mac, respects your data, and gives your attendees a consistently professional experience from first invite to post-event follow-up.

articles.title: How to Build a Product Launch Email Sequence with MailClaw
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how to build a high-converting product launch email sequence using MailClaw's AI-powered sequence builder, contact enrichment, and local dashboard — from pre-launch hype to post-launch follow-up.
articles.content:
Why Your Product Launch Deserves More Than a Single Blast

Most product launches fail not because the product is bad, but because the email strategy is lazy. A single announcement email sent to a cold list — even with a great subject line — gets lost in the noise. What actually drives conversions is a coordinated sequence: a series of timed, personalized emails that warm up your audience, build anticipation, handle objections, and close the sale.

MailClaw makes this entire workflow something you can design, test, and deploy from your local machine. No SaaS subscriptions, no vendor lock-in, no data leaving your environment. Just open your terminal, run the command, and your dashboard is live at localhost:3100.

The Anatomy of a High-Converting Launch Sequence

Before touching a single config file, you need to understand the structure. A well-built product launch sequence typically has five distinct phases:

  • Teaser (7–10 days before launch): Build curiosity without revealing everything.
  • Problem/Solution (5–6 days before): Frame the pain point your product solves.
  • Social Proof (3–4 days before): Beta testimonials, early access wins, or case study data.
  • Launch Day: The main announcement with a clear call to action.
  • Follow-Up (2–5 days after): Objection handling, urgency, and a final close.

Each of these phases maps to one or more emails in your MailClaw sequence. The key insight is that timing and personalization do more heavy lifting than copywriting alone. Let's build it.

Setting Up Your First Sequence in MailClaw

Step 1: Start MailClaw and Connect Your Sending Account

If you haven't already, clone MailClaw and start the local server:

git clone https://github.com/openclaw/mailclaw
cd mailclaw
npm install
npm run start

Your dashboard will be available at http://localhost:3100. From there, navigate to Settings → Sending Accounts and connect your email provider. MailClaw supports SMTP (ideal for SendGrid or Postmark), Gmail OAuth, and Outlook OAuth out of the box. For a product launch, we recommend routing through a dedicated sending domain on SendGrid to protect your primary domain's deliverability reputation.

Pro tip: Never send a launch sequence from your main business domain on day one. Use a subdomain like mail.yourproduct.com and warm it up over two weeks beforehand. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring panel shows you real-time send rates, bounce rates, and spam placement data so you can catch problems before they hurt your domain score.

Step 2: Import and Enrich Your Contact List

A launch sequence is only as good as its audience. MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment engine — powered by OpenClaw — lets you take a basic CSV of names and emails and automatically fill in company size, job title, industry, and LinkedIn presence before you ever send a single message.

Upload your list from the Contacts → Import panel, then trigger enrichment via the CLI:

mailclaw contacts enrich --list launch-waitlist.csv --fields company,title,industry

Once enriched, you can segment your list intelligently. For a product launch, you might create three segments:

  1. Waitlist signups — highest intent, deserves the full 5-phase sequence.
  2. Cold prospects — sourced from your CRM (HubSpot, Salesforce, or a direct import), needs a warmer, softer approach.
  3. Existing customers — if this is a new product from an existing brand, these folks need a loyalty-first narrative, not a sales pitch.

Segmenting before you build your sequence means each group gets copy that actually resonates. MailClaw's tagging system makes it easy to route contacts into the right branch of your sequence automatically.

Building the Sequence with MailClaw's Sequence Builder

Creating the Sequence Structure

In the dashboard, go to Sequences → New Sequence. Name it something like "Product Launch — June 2025" and assign it to your waitlist segment. Then add your email steps with their delays:

mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "Product Launch June 2025" \
  --segment waitlist \
  --steps '[
    {"day": 0, "template": "teaser"},
    {"day": 2, "template": "problem-solution"},
    {"day": 4, "template": "social-proof"},
    {"day": 7, "template": "launch-day"},
    {"day": 9, "template": "followup-objections"},
    {"day": 11, "template": "final-close"}
  ]'

Each step references a template. You can write these templates directly in the dashboard's rich-text editor, or use the AI email agent to draft them.

Using the AI Email Agent to Draft Your Copy

This is where MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered AI becomes genuinely useful. Rather than staring at a blank page for each email, you can prompt the AI agent with context about your product and let it generate a first draft you can refine.

Open the AI Agent panel and try a prompt like:

Generate a teaser email for a product launch. The product is a project management 
tool for remote-first engineering teams. Tone: professional but conversational. 
Goal: build curiosity, not reveal the product name yet. Subject line options: 3.
Personalization token: {{first_name}}, {{company}}.

The agent will return a subject line, preview text, and full email body with your personalization tokens already inserted. From there, tweak the voice to match your brand, verify any claims, and save it as a template.

Repeat this process for each step in the sequence. Aim for emails between 80–150 words each — launch sequences perform better when they're concise and punchy, not essay-length.

Deliverability: The Part Most Teams Get Wrong

You can have the best copy in the world and still land in spam. MailClaw includes a deliverability monitoring suite that checks SPF, DKIM, and DMARC alignment on every send, tracks open rates by inbox provider (Gmail vs. Outlook vs. Apple Mail), and flags unusual bounce spikes before they damage your sender reputation.

Before activating your sequence, run a pre-flight check:

mailclaw deliverability check --sequence "Product Launch June 2025"

This command will surface any DNS misconfigurations, spam-trigger words in your subject lines, and HTML rendering issues that could affect placement. Fix the warnings, then run a seed test by sending to a small internal segment first.

Automating Behavior-Based Branching

A static sequence treats every subscriber the same. MailClaw lets you add conditional logic so the sequence adapts based on how contacts engage.

Common branch conditions for a product launch:

  • Opened launch-day email but didn't click: Send a follow-up 24 hours later with a different subject line and CTA.
  • Clicked but didn't purchase: Trigger an objection-handling email with FAQ content or a demo offer.
  • Replied to any email: Pause the automated sequence and route to your sales team or AI email agent for a personalized response.
  • Purchased: Remove from the launch sequence and add to your onboarding sequence immediately.

You can configure these branches in the sequence builder's visual flow editor or via the CLI using conditional step flags. This kind of behavior-based routing is what separates a professional launch from a spam blast.

Multi-Account and Team Workflows

If you're running a launch across multiple products, regions, or sales reps, MailClaw's multi-account support means each sending identity stays isolated. Your SDR's outreach through their Gmail account won't cross-contaminate the marketing sequence running through SendGrid. All of it is visible and manageable from the same localhost:3100 dashboard.

For teams pulling contact data from existing CRMs, MailClaw's HubSpot and Salesforce sync lets you push sequence enrollment status and email events back to the CRM as activities, so your sales team always has context when a prospect calls in hot from a launch email.

Launch Day: Final Checklist

Twenty-four hours before your sequence goes live, run through this checklist in MailClaw:

  1. Verify all personalization tokens have fallback values (e.g., {{first_name | default: "there"}}).
  2. Confirm sending account DKIM and SPF are passing in the deliverability panel.
  3. Send a preview of each template to yourself via Templates → Send Test.
  4. Check segment sizes — make sure no contacts are in overlapping sequences.
  5. Set your sequence to Active and confirm the first send time aligns with your audience's time zone.

Because MailClaw runs locally on your Mac, you stay in full control of the data pipeline at every step. There's no third-party server processing your contact list, no surprise pricing tiers when you hit 10,000 contacts, and no black-box algorithm deciding which emails get throttled. It's your infrastructure, your rules.

Measure, Iterate, and Improve

After your launch sequence completes, the Analytics panel in MailClaw gives you per-email open rates, click-through rates, unsubscribe rates, and revenue attribution if you've connected a webhook to your checkout flow. Use this data to identify which step in the sequence had the highest drop-off, rewrite that template, and A/B test it on your next launch.

Product launches aren't one-and-done events. The sequence you build today becomes the template you refine tomorrow. With MailClaw's open-source foundation, you can fork the project, customize the sequence logic, and build something genuinely tailored to how your business sells.

The best launch email isn't the cleverest one — it's the one that arrives at the right moment, says the right thing, and makes it effortless to say yes.

articles.title: Creating Automated Referral Request Sequences with MailClaw
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to build automated referral request sequences using MailClaw's AI email agents and sequence builder, turning your happiest customers into a steady pipeline of warm, high-converting leads.
articles.content:
Why Referral Sequences Deserve Their Own Automation Strategy

Referrals are the highest-converting lead source most businesses have — and yet the process of actually asking for them is left to chance, memory, or a single awkward email that goes out whenever someone remembers to send it. That's a missed opportunity at scale.

With MailClaw running locally on your machine, you can build a fully automated, AI-assisted referral request sequence that goes out at exactly the right moment, to exactly the right contacts, without ever touching a CRM manually or drafting the same email from scratch again. This guide walks you through the entire setup: from identifying who to ask, to crafting messages that feel personal, to measuring what's actually working.

Step 1: Identify Your Best Referral Candidates

Not every customer is a good referral source. The best candidates are those who have recently experienced success with your product or service, have high engagement, or have already said something positive about you — in a reply, a review, or a support ticket.

Using Contact Enrichment to Score Your List

MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment pulls in data from sources like LinkedIn, Clearbit, and your connected CRM (HubSpot, Salesforce, or any CSV export) to give you a richer picture of who you're emailing. Before building your sequence, run an enrichment pass on your active customer list:

mailclaw enrich --list customers_active.csv --source clearbit --output enriched_customers.json

Once enriched, you can filter contacts by firmographic signals (company size, industry, role) and behavioral signals like open rate, reply rate, or days since last purchase. Customers who have opened more than three of your last five campaigns and haven't submitted a support ticket in 60 days are prime candidates.

From the localhost dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to Contacts → Segments and create a saved segment called "High-Value Referral Ready." Set your conditions, and this list will stay dynamic — automatically updating as new contacts qualify.

Step 2: Build Your Referral Sequence

A referral sequence isn't a single email. It's a short, thoughtful arc — typically three to five touchpoints — that earns the ask before making it, handles non-responses gracefully, and closes the loop regardless of outcome.

The Recommended Sequence Structure

  1. Email 1 (Day 0) — The warm-up check-in: Acknowledge their recent success or milestone. No ask yet. Just demonstrate that you're paying attention.
  2. Email 2 (Day 3) — The soft ask: Introduce the idea of referrals naturally, framed around value — not incentives. Keep it one paragraph.
  3. Email 3 (Day 7) — The direct ask with context: Make the specific request. Give them a frictionless way to respond (a Calendly link, a referral form, or simply "just reply to this email").
  4. Email 4 (Day 14) — The light follow-up: A short, human nudge. Two or three lines max. Assumes they're busy, not uninterested.
  5. Email 5 (Day 21) — The graceful exit: Thank them for their time, let them know the door stays open, and remove them from the sequence automatically.

Creating the Sequence in MailClaw

Open the Sequence Builder from your dashboard or use the CLI to scaffold a new sequence:

mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "Referral Request Q4" \
  --segment "High-Value Referral Ready" \
  --steps 5 \
  --spacing 3,4,7,7 \
  --account gmail_primary

The --spacing flag accepts a comma-separated list of day delays between each step. The --account flag connects this sequence to whichever sending account you've configured — whether that's Gmail via OAuth, Outlook, or a dedicated sending domain through SendGrid or Postmark.

Step 3: Let the AI Email Agent Write the Drafts

This is where MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered AI email agent earns its keep. Rather than writing five variations of the same awkward ask, you give the agent context and let it generate personalized drafts for each step — drafts you can review, edit, and lock in before anything sends.

Prompting the Agent Effectively

From the Sequence Builder, click Generate with AI on any step, or use the CLI:

mailclaw agent generate \
  --sequence "Referral Request Q4" \
  --step 3 \
  --tone "warm, direct, peer-to-peer" \
  --context "B2B SaaS, customer has been active 6+ months, no support issues" \
  --personalization "{{first_name}}, {{company}}, {{last_product_used}}"

The agent will produce a draft that weaves in your personalization tokens naturally. A typical Step 3 output might look like this:

Hey {{first_name}}, quick one — we've loved having {{company}} on board, especially seeing how you've been using {{last_product_used}}. If you know anyone who's dealing with the same challenges you were six months ago, we'd genuinely love an introduction. Even just a "you should talk to these folks" reply works perfectly. No pressure either way — just thought it was worth asking. Thanks!

You can regenerate with different tone settings, swap in your own copy, or mix AI drafts with manual edits on a per-step basis. Nothing sends until you explicitly approve the sequence.

Step 4: Configure Sending and Deliverability

Referral emails feel personal — and that means they should be sent with the deliverability standards of personal email, not mass marketing. A few key settings make a significant difference.

Deliverability Best Practices in MailClaw

  • Send from a warmed domain: If you're using a secondary sending domain (common when protecting your primary domain), make sure it's been warmed for at least 30 days. MailClaw's deliverability monitor at localhost:3100/deliverability shows your domain reputation score and flags any issues with SPF, DKIM, or DMARC alignment.
  • Throttle your sends: Don't blast all 500 contacts on Day 0. Use MailClaw's send-rate controls to drip them out at 50–100 per day, which mimics organic sending patterns and protects your sender reputation.
  • Turn off open tracking for this sequence: Referral emails read better without tracking pixels. You'll still get reply data, which is the signal that actually matters here.
  • Enable reply detection: MailClaw's reply detection will automatically pause or exit a contact from the sequence the moment they respond — no one gets a follow-up after they've already said yes.
mailclaw sequence update "Referral Request Q4" \
  --send-rate 75 \
  --track-opens false \
  --reply-detection true \
  --exit-on-reply true

Step 5: Monitor Results and Iterate

Once your sequence is live, the MailClaw dashboard gives you a real-time view of how each step is performing. From localhost:3100/sequences, you'll see open rates, reply rates, click rates (if enabled), and the number of contacts at each stage of the funnel.

Metrics That Actually Matter for Referral Sequences

Standard open rates are a vanity metric here. What you actually care about:

  • Reply rate per step: Which email is generating the most responses? If Step 2 outperforms Step 3, your soft ask may be working better than your direct one — adjust accordingly.
  • Referral conversion rate: Track how many replies actually resulted in a warm introduction. Tag these contacts manually or connect MailClaw to HubSpot or Salesforce to log the outcome automatically.
  • Unsubscribe rate: If it climbs above 0.5% on any single step, that email needs rewriting. The AI agent can generate a new variant for A/B testing within the same sequence.

Running A/B Tests on Your Ask

MailClaw's sequence builder supports split testing at the step level. For Step 3 (your direct ask), you can test two subject lines or two body variants across a random 50/50 split of your segment:

mailclaw sequence ab-test \
  --sequence "Referral Request Q4" \
  --step 3 \
  --variant-a "referral_ask_direct.txt" \
  --variant-b "referral_ask_story.txt" \
  --split 50

After seven days, MailClaw will flag the winning variant and optionally promote it automatically to all remaining contacts in the sequence.

Putting It All Together

A well-built referral sequence isn't about volume — it's about timing, relevance, and making the ask feel like a natural extension of a real relationship. MailClaw gives you the infrastructure to do all of that from a single tool running on your own machine, with no data leaving your environment and no per-seat SaaS fees eating into your margins.

Start with a small segment of your ten to twenty most engaged customers. Run the five-step sequence, review the replies, and refine the copy before scaling. Most teams that do this see their first referral introduction within the first two weeks — and once the system is tuned, it runs itself.

Since MailClaw is open source and built on the OpenClaw framework, you can also extend the referral sequence logic with custom steps, webhooks, or integrations with tools like Zapier, Notion, or your internal CRM. The defaults get you 90% of the way there; the platform gets out of your way for the rest.

articles.title: How to Set Up Abandoned Cart Email Flows with MailClaw
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to build high-converting abandoned cart email flows using MailClaw's AI email agents, sequence builder, and contact enrichment tools — all running locally on your Mac with full control over your data and deliverability.
articles.content:
Why Abandoned Cart Emails Still Print Money

Somewhere between 70% and 80% of online shoppers abandon their carts before completing a purchase. That's not a rounding error — it's the majority of your potential revenue walking out the door. The good news is that a well-timed, well-written abandoned cart email sequence consistently recovers 5–15% of those sessions, and in some industries considerably more.

Most teams either rely on bloated SaaS platforms that charge per contact, or they stitch together fragile Zapier workflows that break at the worst possible time. MailClaw gives you a third path: a fully local, AI-powered email automation stack that you own completely, runs at localhost:3100, and costs nothing in licensing fees. Let's build an abandoned cart flow from scratch.

What You Need Before You Start

Before touching MailClaw's sequence builder, make sure the following are in place:

  • A webhook or API endpoint on your storefront — Shopify, WooCommerce, and most headless commerce platforms can fire an event when a cart is abandoned (typically after 30–60 minutes of inactivity).
  • MailClaw running locally — If you haven't installed it yet, clone the repo and run mailclaw start. The dashboard will be available at http://localhost:3100.
  • At least one connected sending account — Gmail via OAuth, Outlook, or a dedicated SMTP provider like SendGrid or Postmark all work out of the box.
  • Basic contact fields mapped — You'll want email, first_name, cart_value, and cart_url at minimum.

Connecting Your Store to MailClaw

Sending Cart Data via the Inbound Webhook
