        Just a quick heads-up that invoice {{invoice_number}} 
        for {{amount}} is due on {{due_date}}.

        You can view and pay it here: {{invoice_link}}

        Thanks as always,
        {{sender_name}}

    - name: Due Date Nudge
      delay: +3d
      condition: payment_status != "paid"
      subject: "Invoice {{invoice_number}} is due today"
      body: |
        Hi {{first_name}},

        Invoice {{invoice_number}} for {{amount}} is due today.
        If you've already sent payment, please disregard this note.

        {{invoice_link}}

    - name: 7-Day Overdue
      delay: +10d
      condition: payment_status != "paid"
      subject: "Overdue: Invoice {{invoice_number}} — {{amount}} outstanding"
      body: |
        Hi {{first_name}},

        I wanted to follow up on invoice {{invoice_number}}, 
        which is now 7 days past due. 

        If there's an issue with the invoice or you need 
        to discuss payment terms, I'm happy to help.

        {{invoice_link}}

The condition field is important — it tells MailClaw to check your contact's payment_status field before sending each step. That means clients who pay after the first reminder won't receive the follow-ups. You can update this field manually, via webhook from your invoicing tool (FreshBooks, QuickBooks, Stripe, etc.), or using a sync integration.

Using AI Email Agents to Handle Replies

Here's where MailClaw moves beyond a simple scheduler. MailClaw's AI email agents (powered by OpenClaw) can monitor your billing inbox and respond to common replies automatically — things like:

  • "Can you resend the invoice?" → Agent re-sends the invoice link and logs the interaction
  • "We'll pay by Friday" → Agent acknowledges, pauses the sequence, and flags for review
  • "Who is this?" → Agent identifies the contact context and routes to your attention

To enable an agent on your billing account:

mailclaw agent create \
  --name "Billing Assistant" \
  --account "Billing Account" \
  --sequence "Invoice Follow-Up" \
  --mode auto-reply

Inside the dashboard under Agents, you can review every AI-generated reply before it sends (recommended when you're first getting started), or set the agent to full auto once you're confident in its responses. The agent maintains full conversation context, so it won't awkwardly re-introduce itself to a client you've been working with for two years.

Pro tip: Set your agent's tone to "professional and concise" in the agent config. Invoice reminders should feel like they're coming from a real person — not a debt collection bot. The goal is to make it easy to pay, not make the client feel chased.

Monitoring Deliverability for Billing Emails

Invoice reminders only work if they land in the inbox. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools give you a real-time view of your sender reputation, bounce rates, and spam trigger analysis — all from localhost:3100/deliverability.

A few practices worth following specifically for billing sequences:

  • Authenticate your domain. Make sure SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records are set up for your sending domain. MailClaw will warn you during account setup if anything is missing.
  • Keep list hygiene tight. The contact enrichment step earlier helps here — invalid addresses kill your sender score fast.
  • Watch your subject lines. Words like "URGENT," "OVERDUE," and "FINAL NOTICE" in all-caps can trigger spam filters. MailClaw's AI writing assistant (available in the sequence editor) will flag risky phrasing before you schedule anything.
  • Stagger your sends. If you have 200 overdue invoices, don't blast them all at 9am. Use MailClaw's send-time distribution settings to spread them across a window.

Connecting to Your Invoicing and CRM Tools

MailClaw works best when it's connected to the tools where your invoice data actually lives. A few practical integration patterns:

Stripe Webhooks

Set up a webhook in your Stripe dashboard pointing to http://localhost:3100/webhooks/stripe. When an invoice is paid, Stripe fires an event that MailClaw catches and uses to update payment_status on the matching contact — automatically stopping the reminder sequence.

HubSpot or Salesforce Sync

If your sales team manages accounts in HubSpot or Salesforce, you can sync contact and deal data into MailClaw's contact database using the built-in CRM sync feature. This ensures your billing outreach always uses the right contact name, email, and account context — not a stale CSV from three months ago.

Zapier or n8n (for everything else)

For invoicing tools like FreshBooks, QuickBooks, or Wave, a Zapier or n8n workflow can push invoice data into MailClaw via its REST API whenever a new invoice is created or a payment is received.

# Example: update a contact's payment status via API
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:3100/api/contacts/{{contact_id}} \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"payment_status": "paid", "invoice_number": "INV-0042"}'

The Bigger Picture

Automating invoice reminders isn't just about saving time — it's about removing the emotional friction from chasing money. When the process is systematic, professional, and consistent, clients take it seriously, you follow up every single time (not just when you remember), and awkward conversations become rarer.

Because MailClaw runs entirely on your local machine, your billing data, client names, and payment history never touch a third-party server unless you explicitly connect an external tool. For freelancers and agencies handling sensitive client relationships, that matters.

Start with a simple three-step sequence, watch your overdue rate drop, and build from there. The sequence builder, AI agents, and deliverability tools are all there when you're ready to go deeper — and because MailClaw is open source, you can extend and customize every piece of it to fit exactly how your business works.

articles.title: MailClaw for Newsletters: Setting Up Automated Content Digests
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's AI email agents, sequence builder, and contact enrichment tools to build a fully automated newsletter digest pipeline that runs entirely on your local machine.
articles.content:
Why Newsletters Deserve Better Infrastructure

Most newsletter setups are a patchwork of tools: one platform for sending, another for managing subscribers, a third for analytics, and maybe a spreadsheet holding it all together. The result is friction at every step — segmentation that doesn't sync, deliverability issues you find out about too late, and content personalization that stops at a first name merge tag.

MailClaw takes a different approach. Because it runs locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, you get the full pipeline — subscriber management, AI-assisted content generation, sequence scheduling, and deliverability monitoring — without sending your contact data to a third-party SaaS. Built on OpenClaw, it's open source, auditable, and extensible. For newsletters specifically, that combination unlocks workflows that most commercial tools simply can't replicate.

The Anatomy of an Automated Content Digest

Before touching any configuration, it helps to map out what a digest actually needs to do:

  • Content aggregation: Pulling articles, updates, or curated links from one or more sources
  • Audience segmentation: Sending the right digest to the right subscribers based on their interests or behavior
  • Personalization: Going beyond a name — referencing past reads, job role, company, or engagement history
  • Scheduling and sequencing: Weekly, bi-weekly, or triggered sends based on subscriber actions
  • Deliverability assurance: Making sure your digest actually lands in the inbox

MailClaw has a purpose-built feature for each of these. Let's walk through setting them up end to end.

Step 1: Import and Enrich Your Subscriber List

Start by importing your existing subscribers. MailClaw accepts CSV imports directly from the dashboard, and if you're migrating from tools like HubSpot, Mailchimp, or a Salesforce export, the column mapping wizard handles most common field structures automatically.

# Import subscribers via the MailClaw CLI
mailclaw contacts import --file subscribers.csv --list "Weekly Digest" --dedupe

The --dedupe flag is important for newsletters — if you've been managing subscribers across multiple tools, duplicates are almost inevitable. MailClaw will merge records and flag conflicts for manual review in the dashboard.

Using Contact Enrichment to Improve Segmentation

Raw subscriber lists are often thin: just an email address and maybe a name. MailClaw's contact enrichment feature fills in the gaps using publicly available professional data. For a B2B newsletter, this is transformative. You can automatically append job title, company size, industry, and LinkedIn URL to each contact — giving you the segmentation signals you need without manual research.

# Enrich all contacts in a list
mailclaw contacts enrich --list "Weekly Digest" --fields job_title,company,industry,location

Once enrichment runs, you can slice your subscriber list into meaningful segments directly from the dashboard. A developer-focused digest looks very different from one aimed at marketing directors, and now you have the data to support that distinction.

Step 2: Build Your Content Digest Sequence

MailClaw's sequence builder is where the newsletter logic lives. Think of a sequence as a timeline of emails with conditional branching — if a subscriber opens the first digest, they might get a deeper-dive follow-up two days later. If they haven't opened in three sends, they might enter a re-engagement branch instead.

Creating a Weekly Digest Sequence

Open the sequence builder from the dashboard (localhost:3100/sequences/new) and start with a simple weekly cadence:

  1. Email 1 — Welcome digest: Sent immediately on subscribe, introduces the format and sets expectations
  2. Email 2 — First weekly send: Triggered 7 days after signup, or on the next scheduled send date
  3. Conditional branch: Opened Email 2 → continue normal cadence; Did not open → send a re-subject-line variant at day 9
  4. Ongoing weekly emails: Scheduled sends every 7 days, with dynamic content blocks per segment

You can also define sequences via the CLI using a YAML config, which is especially useful if you're version-controlling your newsletter setup in Git:

# sequences/weekly-digest.yaml
name: Weekly Content Digest
trigger: subscription
steps:
  - delay: 0
    template: welcome-digest
  - delay: 7d
    template: digest-week-1
    conditions:
      - if: opened
        next: digest-engaged
      - if: not_opened
        next: digest-resubject
  - delay: 14d
    template: digest-week-2
# Load the sequence from config
mailclaw sequences load --file sequences/weekly-digest.yaml

Step 3: Let AI Email Agents Handle Content Assembly

This is where MailClaw's capabilities genuinely pull ahead of traditional newsletter tools. AI email agents — powered by OpenClaw — can be configured to automatically assemble your digest content based on rules you define. You're not just writing a template once and blasting it out; the agent can pull from RSS feeds, internal APIs, or structured data sources and compose a fresh digest each send cycle.

Configuring a Digest Agent

# Create an AI agent for content assembly
mailclaw agents create \
  --name "digest-assembler" \
  --type content \
  --sources rss:https://yourblog.com/feed,api:https://api.yourapp.com/featured \
  --template digest-template \
  --segment all \
  --output weekly-digest-sequence

The agent runs on your local machine, so your content sources and subscriber data never leave your environment. You can instruct the agent to prioritize items by recency, engagement score, or topic tags — and it will compose the digest body accordingly, inserting the right content block for each subscriber segment.

For teams with more editorial control, the agent can generate a draft and pause for approval before sending. From the dashboard, you'll see a preview of each week's assembled digest before it goes out — a simple approve/reject workflow that keeps humans in the loop without slowing everything down.

Step 4: Connect Your Sending Infrastructure

MailClaw supports multiple sending options. For newsletters, you'll typically want one of the following:

  • Gmail or Google Workspace via OAuth: Great for low-to-medium volume lists, with native authentication handled through the dashboard's account manager
  • Outlook/Microsoft 365 via OAuth: Ideal for enterprise setups already on the Microsoft stack
  • SendGrid, Postmark, or AWS SES via SMTP: Best for high-volume digests where deliverability infrastructure matters most
# Add a SendGrid SMTP account
mailclaw accounts add \
  --provider sendgrid \
  --api-key YOUR_SENDGRID_API_KEY \
  --from-name "The Weekly Digest" \
  --from-email digest@yourdomain.com

MailClaw's multi-account support means you can send different digest segments from different sender identities — useful if you run multiple newsletters or want to A/B test sender names without duplicating your entire setup.

Step 5: Monitor Deliverability Before and After Sending

A digest that lands in the spam folder is worse than no digest at all — it trains Gmail's filters against you and erodes sender reputation over time. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools run continuous checks so you know your status before each send, not after complaints start rolling in.

Key Deliverability Checks to Run

  • DNS health: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC validation for your sending domain, surfaced directly in the dashboard
  • Blacklist monitoring: MailClaw checks your sending IP and domain against major blocklists on a configurable schedule
  • Engagement scoring: Tracks open rates, click rates, and unsubscribe patterns per segment, flagging lists that may be dragging your sender score down
  • Inbox placement tests: Send test messages to seed accounts across Gmail, Outlook, and Apple Mail to verify placement before a full send
# Run a pre-send deliverability check
mailclaw deliver check --sequence weekly-digest-sequence --segment all

If issues surface — say, a soft DMARC failure or an elevated unsubscribe rate in one segment — MailClaw will surface a plain-language recommendation in the dashboard rather than leaving you to parse raw headers.

Putting It All Together

What you end up with is a newsletter engine that runs entirely on your Mac, costs nothing beyond your sending provider, and gives you more control than most enterprise email platforms. Your subscribers are segmented intelligently using enriched data. Your content is assembled by an AI agent that understands your sources. Your sequences branch based on real behavior. And your deliverability is monitored continuously rather than reactively.

The real advantage of running this locally isn't just privacy or cost — it's that you can iterate fast. Change a template, reload a sequence, test a new agent config, and push to your next send, all without waiting for a SaaS platform to sync or a support ticket to resolve.

For teams already using HubSpot or Salesforce as their CRM, MailClaw's contact sync integrations mean your newsletter subscriber data stays in both places — enriched contacts flow back to your CRM, and CRM activity can trigger or modify digest sequences. It's the kind of tight loop that usually requires a dedicated marketing ops engineer to build. With MailClaw, it's a few CLI commands and a config file.

Start with a single segment and a two-step sequence, get one successful weekly send out the door, and then layer in the AI agent and branching logic. The mailclaw CLI and the local dashboard at localhost:3100 are designed to make that iteration feel low-stakes — because when your infrastructure is open source and runs on your own machine, it actually is.

articles.title: How to Build a Customer Reactivation Email Sequence with MailClaw
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to build a high-converting customer reactivation email sequence using MailClaw's AI email agents, sequence builder, and contact enrichment tools — complete with CLI commands, timing strategies, and deliverability tips.
articles.content:
Why Reactivation Sequences Are Worth Your Time

Dormant customers are one of the most underutilized assets in any business. They already know your product, they've converted once, and re-engaging them costs a fraction of what it takes to acquire someone new. Industry benchmarks consistently show that reactivation campaigns convert at 3–5x higher rates than cold outreach — yet most teams treat lapsed users as a write-off.

The problem isn't motivation. It's execution. Building a thoughtful reactivation sequence that feels personal, times itself correctly, and adapts based on behavior requires tooling that most teams don't have set up. That's exactly where MailClaw comes in. Because it runs locally on your machine and is built on OpenClaw's AI foundation, you get fine-grained control over every message, every trigger, and every send — without pushing sensitive customer data to a third-party SaaS platform.

Step 1: Segment Your Dormant Contacts

Before you write a single word of copy, you need to define what "dormant" actually means for your business. A SaaS product might consider a user dormant after 60 days of inactivity. An e-commerce store might use 90 days since the last purchase. A B2B service might look at 6 months without a reply or meeting.

Start MailClaw and open the contact enrichment panel from your local dashboard at localhost:3100. From there, import your CRM export — MailClaw supports direct sync with HubSpot and Salesforce, or you can drop in a CSV:

mailclaw contacts import --file dormant_customers.csv \
  --tag "reactivation-2024" \
  --enrich true

The --enrich true flag tells MailClaw to run contact enrichment automatically. It will pull in job title changes, company funding rounds, LinkedIn activity signals, and technology stack updates for each contact. This matters because a contact who was a junior developer 18 months ago might now be a VP of Engineering — a very different conversation to have.

Enrichment in Practice

Once enrichment runs, you'll see a refreshed profile for each contact directly in the dashboard. Common enrichment signals that should reshape your segmentation include:

  • Job change: Contact moved to a new company — this is a warm re-introduction opportunity
  • Funding event: Their company just raised a round — budget conversations are more likely
  • Technology change: They swapped a tool your product integrates with — a genuine hook
  • Company growth: Team size expanded significantly — new pain points have emerged

Use these signals to break your dormant list into at least two sub-segments: contextually warm (something has changed that's relevant) and cold dormant (no obvious change, but still worth a shot with a different angle).

Step 2: Build the Sequence in MailClaw

A well-structured reactivation sequence typically runs 4–6 emails over 3–5 weeks. You don't want to bombard someone who's been quiet, but you also need enough touches to break through inbox noise. Here's a framework that works consistently:

  1. Email 1 (Day 0): The gentle check-in — acknowledge the gap, no hard sell
  2. Email 2 (Day 5): Value reminder — what's new or improved since they left
  3. Email 3 (Day 12): Social proof — a customer story or result relevant to their industry
  4. Email 4 (Day 20): A concrete offer — discount, free audit, extended trial
  5. Email 5 (Day 28): The breakup email — low pressure, clear opt-out, genuine

To create this sequence in MailClaw, use the sequence builder CLI or the visual editor in the dashboard:

mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "Customer Reactivation Q1" \
  --tag "reactivation-2024" \
  --ai-assist true \
  --steps 5

The --ai-assist true flag activates MailClaw's AI email agent for this sequence. It will generate draft copy for each step based on the contact's enrichment data, your defined tone of voice, and the sequence goal you provide. You review and approve before anything sends.

Configuring the AI Email Agent

MailClaw's AI agents are where the tool pulls ahead of traditional sequence builders. You're not just filling in {{first_name}} tokens — the agent actually reads the enrichment context and adjusts the message body. Here's how to configure the agent behavior for a reactivation sequence:

mailclaw agent configure \
  --sequence "Customer Reactivation Q1" \
  --goal "reactivate dormant B2B customers" \
  --tone "warm, direct, no fluff" \
  --personalization-depth "high" \
  --avoid "aggressive discounting, urgency pressure"

Once configured, the agent will draft each email using the contact's enrichment signals as context. A contact who recently changed jobs will get a message that acknowledges new beginnings. A contact whose company just grew will get a message about scaling challenges. The draft appears in the dashboard for your review — nothing sends without your sign-off unless you explicitly enable auto-send.

Step 3: Connect Your Sending Infrastructure

MailClaw supports multiple sending methods. For reactivation campaigns, you generally want to choose based on volume and relationship type:

  • Gmail or Outlook OAuth: Best for smaller, high-trust lists under 500 contacts. Uses your real inbox, which maximizes deliverability and reply tracking.
  • SendGrid or Mailgun SMTP: Ideal for larger lists. Add your credentials in the multi-account panel under Settings → Sending Accounts.
  • Custom SMTP: If you're running your own mail server, MailClaw's SMTP integration handles it cleanly with TLS support.
mailclaw accounts add \
  --provider gmail \
  --auth oauth \
  --label "reactivation-primary"

For reactivation specifically, consider using your personal Gmail or Outlook connected via OAuth for the first two emails, then switching to a dedicated sending domain for the offer and breakup emails. MailClaw's multi-account support lets you assign different sending accounts to different steps in the same sequence — a subtle but powerful deliverability lever.

Step 4: Monitor Deliverability Before You Send

Dormant lists are risky from a deliverability standpoint. Contacts may have changed email addresses, become spam traps, or simply not opened anything in months — all of which can hurt your sender reputation if you blast them without care.

Open the deliverability panel in your MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100/deliverability. Before launching, run a pre-send health check:

mailclaw deliverability check \
  --sequence "Customer Reactivation Q1" \
  --verify-emails true \
  --check-blacklists true \
  --preview-spam-score true

This command verifies email addresses for catch-alls and invalid accounts, checks your sending domain against major blacklists, and generates a spam score preview for each email in the sequence. Aim for a spam score below 2.0. If you're above that, the dashboard will highlight which elements — subject line phrasing, link density, missing unsubscribe footer — are pushing the score up.

Warm Up Your Domain If Needed

If you're using a newer sending domain, MailClaw's built-in warmup scheduler will ramp your daily send volume gradually over 2–3 weeks before the campaign goes live. This isn't glamorous, but it's the difference between landing in the primary inbox and getting routed to spam for 40% of your list.

Step 5: Launch, Track, and Iterate

With your sequence built, contacts enriched, sending accounts connected, and deliverability confirmed, you're ready to go live:

mailclaw sequence launch \
  --name "Customer Reactivation Q1" \
  --start-date "2024-02-05" \
  --throttle 50/day \
  --timezone "America/New_York"

The --throttle flag sends no more than 50 emails per day, protecting your sender reputation while the campaign ramps. Monitor results in real time from the dashboard — open rates, click rates, reply rates, and unsubscribes are all tracked per step.

What to watch for: A healthy reactivation sequence typically sees open rates decline from step 1 to step 5, with reply rates peaking at the offer email (step 4) or the breakup email (step 5). If your step 2 open rate drops more than 30% from step 1, the subject lines or send timing need adjustment.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs locally, you can fork the sequence templates, modify the AI agent prompts directly in the OpenClaw config, and version-control your entire outreach system in Git. No vendor lock-in, no per-seat pricing surprises, and no customer data ever leaving your machine.

The Compounding Value of Getting This Right

A well-executed reactivation sequence isn't just about the immediate campaign. Every contact who re-engages gives you fresh behavioral data. Every reply teaches the AI agent something about what resonates with your audience. Every delivered email to a previously dormant contact is a sender reputation data point that makes your next campaign land better.

Build the sequence once, refine it based on real results, and you'll have a reactivation asset that runs reliably every quarter — bringing revenue back from customers your competitors have already written off.

articles.title: How MailClaw AI Enriches Contacts Automatically
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how MailClaw's AI-powered contact enrichment automatically fills in missing data, scores leads, and personalizes outreach — all running locally on your Mac without sending your contacts to third-party servers.
articles.content:
Why Contact Enrichment Is the Hidden Lever in Email Outreach

Most email campaigns fail not because of bad copy or poor timing — they fail because the sender is working with incomplete data. You have a name and an email address, and that's it. No job title, no company size, no industry, no idea whether this person is a decision-maker or an intern. You're essentially firing blind.

Contact enrichment solves this by automatically filling in the blanks. And when that enrichment process is powered by AI and running entirely on your local machine, you get something genuinely powerful: deep, accurate contact profiles built without sacrificing privacy or paying per-seat fees to an external SaaS platform.

This is exactly what MailClaw's AI enrichment engine is designed to do. Built on top of OpenClaw, it pulls from multiple data signals, runs inference locally, and writes enriched data directly back into your contact records — ready to power hyper-personalized sequences.

What MailClaw Enriches (And How)

When you run enrichment on a contact, MailClaw's AI doesn't just do a simple lookup. It builds a profile by cross-referencing multiple signals and making intelligent inferences where hard data isn't available. Here's what gets populated:

  • Job title and seniority level — inferred from email patterns, domain metadata, and public professional signals
  • Company name, size, and industry — resolved from the email domain and augmented with firmographic data
  • LinkedIn and social presence — detected and linked where publicly discoverable
  • Technology stack — identified via domain-level signals (useful for sales targeting)
  • Geographic location — estimated from domain TLD, timezone metadata, and language signals
  • Lead score — an AI-generated score based on ICP fit, engagement history, and profile completeness

All of this happens without your contacts ever leaving your machine. MailClaw's enrichment pipeline runs at localhost:3100, meaning your data stays local. That's a meaningful distinction in a world where most enrichment tools are essentially data brokers in disguise.

Running Enrichment from the CLI

If you prefer working in the terminal, MailClaw gives you a clean command-line interface to kick off enrichment jobs. After installing MailClaw and importing your contacts, enrichment is a single command away:

# Enrich all contacts in a list
mailclaw enrich --list "Q4 Outreach"

# Enrich a single contact by email
mailclaw enrich --contact sarah@acmecorp.com

# Enrich and apply a custom ICP profile
mailclaw enrich --list "Enterprise Leads" --icp ./icp-profiles/saas-cto.json

# Preview enrichment results without writing to database
mailclaw enrich --list "Cold Import" --dry-run

The --dry-run flag is particularly useful when you're onboarding a new list and want to audit what the AI will infer before committing it to your contact records. You'll get a table output in your terminal showing before/after values for every field.

Enrichment via the Local Dashboard

If you're more comfortable with a visual interface, the MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100 gives you a full enrichment workflow with point-and-click controls. Navigate to Contacts → Enrich, select your list, choose which fields to populate, and hit run. A live progress bar shows enrichment status in real time, and you can inspect individual contact cards as they're filled in.

The dashboard also surfaces enrichment confidence scores — a small indicator next to each enriched field that tells you how confident the AI is in that particular inference. Low-confidence fields are flagged for manual review rather than silently written to your records.

Integrating Enrichment with Your Existing Stack

MailClaw doesn't expect you to abandon your existing tools. It's built to sit alongside platforms like HubSpot, Salesforce, and Pipedrive, enriching contacts locally and then syncing the results back to your CRM of choice.

Syncing to HubSpot

Once you've configured your HubSpot API key in MailClaw's settings, enriched fields map automatically to standard HubSpot contact properties. You can run a sync after every enrichment job:

# Sync enriched contacts to HubSpot
mailclaw sync --destination hubspot --list "Q4 Outreach" --fields title,company,lead_score

Custom field mappings are defined in your mailclaw.config.json, so if you've created bespoke properties in HubSpot (like a custom ICP tier field), MailClaw will write to those correctly.

Pulling Contacts from Salesforce

You can also run the pipeline in reverse — import a Salesforce lead list into MailClaw, enrich it locally, and push the results back. This is useful for sales teams that already live in Salesforce but want the enrichment quality of an AI-native tool without paying Salesforce's per-record enrichment fees.

# Import from Salesforce, enrich, and sync back
mailclaw import --source salesforce --query "SELECT Email FROM Lead WHERE Status = 'Open'"
mailclaw enrich --list "Salesforce Import"
mailclaw sync --destination salesforce --list "Salesforce Import"

Using Enriched Data in Sequences

Enrichment only matters if it changes what you send. MailClaw's sequence builder is natively aware of enriched contact fields, so you can build dynamic email templates that pull in the exact data the AI just populated.

Here's a simple example of a first-touch cold email using enriched variables:

Subject: Quick question for {{contact.title}} at {{contact.company}}

Hi {{contact.first_name}},

I noticed {{contact.company}} is in the {{contact.industry}} space —
we've been helping similar {{contact.company_size_label}} companies
reduce churn by about 30% in the first 90 days.

Worth a 15-minute call this week?

The company_size_label field is a good example of AI-enriched data that would be hard to get any other way — MailClaw maps raw employee count estimates into human-readable labels like "small team", "growth-stage startup", or "enterprise org", which you can drop directly into copy without awkward numbers.

Conditional Steps Based on Lead Score

MailClaw's sequence builder also supports conditional branching based on enriched fields. You can build sequences that send different follow-ups depending on a contact's AI-generated lead score:

  • Score 80–100: Aggressive follow-up cadence, direct ask for a call, CC an SDR
  • Score 50–79: Nurture sequence with content-first approach, softer CTA
  • Score below 50: Low-touch newsletter sequence, re-evaluate in 90 days

This is where MailClaw's AI email agents really come into their own. Instead of manually sorting contacts into buckets, you define the scoring thresholds once and let the agent handle routing automatically — including pausing sequences for contacts whose behavior signals they've gone cold.

Keeping Enrichment Fresh Over Time

Contact data decays fast. People change jobs, companies pivot, titles shift. MailClaw handles this with scheduled re-enrichment jobs that you can configure to run on a cadence:

# Re-enrich any contact not updated in the last 60 days
mailclaw enrich --list "All Contacts" --stale-after 60d --overwrite changed-only

The --overwrite changed-only flag ensures that fields you've manually edited are preserved — the AI won't stomp over a correction you made by hand.

You can also wire this into a cron job so it runs automatically in the background, keeping your contact database continuously fresh without any manual intervention.

Deliverability Meets Enrichment

There's a less obvious benefit to enrichment that most people overlook: deliverability. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools use enriched data to flag risky sends before they happen. Contacts with low-confidence email addresses, role-based inboxes (like info@ or support@), or domains known for high bounce rates are automatically surfaced in the deliverability dashboard.

Before any sequence goes live — whether it's sending through Gmail, Outlook, or a dedicated SMTP provider like SendGrid or Mailgun — MailClaw runs a pre-flight check that includes enrichment-informed deliverability scoring. It's one of those features that quietly saves your sender reputation without requiring you to think about it.

"The best enrichment tool is the one that makes your emails feel like they came from someone who actually did their homework — not a mail merge."

Getting Started with Enrichment Today

If you haven't run enrichment on your contact lists yet, here's the fastest path to getting value from it:

  1. Start MailClaw locally with mailclaw start and open the dashboard at localhost:3100
  2. Import your existing contact list from a CSV, HubSpot, or Salesforce
  3. Run a dry-run enrichment to preview what the AI will fill in
  4. Apply enrichment to your list and review confidence scores for key fields
  5. Open the sequence builder and update your templates to use the new enriched variables
  6. Set up a scheduled re-enrichment job to keep data fresh automatically

The whole process — from raw CSV import to enriched, personalized sequence — takes under 30 minutes the first time. After that, it runs itself.

MailClaw is open source and built on OpenClaw, which means the enrichment logic is auditable, extensible, and not locked behind a pricing tier. If your use case requires custom enrichment sources or proprietary data signals, you can extend the enrichment pipeline directly. The codebase is on GitHub, the docs are thorough, and the local-first architecture means you're always in control of your data.

articles.title: Contact Enrichment with MailClaw: Finding Emails, Titles, and Company Data
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment pipeline to automatically find email addresses, job titles, and company data — turning a raw list of names into a fully enriched, ready-to-send outreach campaign.
articles.content:
Why Contact Enrichment Matters Before You Hit Send

Most outreach fails before a single email is written. You have a list of company names, maybe a few LinkedIn URLs, and not much else. You're guessing at job titles, copy-pasting domain names into hunter.io by hand, and hoping the person you're emailing is still at the company. That's not a pipeline — that's a coin flip.

Contact enrichment solves this by filling in the gaps automatically: verified email addresses, current job titles, company headcount, industry tags, and social profiles — all pulled before your sequence even starts. MailClaw's enrichment engine, powered by OpenClaw, handles this natively from your local dashboard at localhost:3100, meaning your contact data never leaves your machine unless you choose to send it somewhere.

Let's walk through exactly how to use it.

Getting Started: Your First Enrichment Run

MailClaw's enrichment pipeline accepts contacts in several formats. The quickest way to kick one off is via the CLI. If you have a CSV with names and company domains, you can pipe it directly into the enrichment command:

# Enrich a CSV of contacts using the default enrichment profile
mailclaw enrich --input contacts.csv --output enriched.csv --profile default

# Enrich a single contact by name and domain
mailclaw enrich --name "Sarah Chen" --domain "acme.com"

# Enrich with a specific data source priority
mailclaw enrich --input contacts.csv --sources hunter,clearbit,linkedin --confidence 0.8

The --confidence flag is worth paying attention to. It filters out results below a certain match threshold — set it to 0.8 and above and you're getting high-confidence email finds only, which protects your sender reputation and keeps your bounce rate low.

What Gets Enriched by Default

Out of the box, MailClaw's enrichment pipeline will attempt to find and validate:

  • Email address — verified against MX records and SMTP handshake where possible
  • Job title and seniority level — mapped to a normalized taxonomy (IC, Manager, Director, VP, C-Suite)
  • Company name, domain, and industry
  • Company headcount range — useful for filtering by company size in sequences
  • LinkedIn profile URL
  • Location (city, country)
  • Technologies used — pulled from BuiltWith and similar sources when available

All of this gets written back to the contact record in MailClaw's local database, and you'll see it reflected in the dashboard under Contacts → Enrichment Status.

Connecting Data Sources

MailClaw doesn't lock you into one data provider. It uses a waterfall enrichment model — it tries each source in priority order and stops when it hits a confident match. You configure your source stack in ~/.mailclaw/config.yaml:

enrichment:
  sources:
    - name: hunter
      api_key: YOUR_HUNTER_KEY
      priority: 1
    - name: clearbit
      api_key: YOUR_CLEARBIT_KEY
      priority: 2
    - name: apollo
      api_key: YOUR_APOLLO_KEY
      priority: 3
    - name: peopledatalabs
      api_key: YOUR_PDL_KEY
      priority: 4
  confidence_threshold: 0.75
  fallback_to_pattern: true

The fallback_to_pattern: true option is a quiet workhorse. When no data source returns a confident match, MailClaw uses known email patterns for the domain (e.g., first.last@, firstlast@) and validates them via SMTP — a surprisingly effective last resort that catches another 10-15% of addresses that paid APIs miss.

Free vs. Paid Enrichment

You don't need paid API keys to get started. MailClaw ships with a built-in lightweight enrichment layer that uses public signals — WHOIS data, structured company pages, and pattern matching — at no cost. It's less complete than Hunter or Clearbit, but it's a solid starting point for smaller lists or testing your setup. Add paid sources as your volume grows.

Enriching Contacts Inside the Dashboard

If you prefer a visual workflow, open your local dashboard at http://localhost:3100 and navigate to Contacts. From there you can:

  1. Upload a CSV or paste a list of names and domains directly
  2. Select an enrichment profile (default, deep, fast, or custom)
  3. Run enrichment in the background while you work on your sequence
  4. Review enrichment results with confidence scores before adding contacts to a campaign
  5. Flag low-confidence results for manual review or exclusion

The enrichment status column shows a color-coded indicator for each contact: green (verified), yellow (pattern-matched, unverified), and red (not found). You can filter your contact list by status and choose to only send to green-status contacts, which is the recommended approach for cold outreach.

Using Enriched Data in Your Sequences

This is where enrichment pays off. Once your contacts are enriched, every piece of data becomes a variable you can reference in your sequence builder. MailClaw uses a double-curly syntax:

Subject: Quick question for {{job_title}}s at {{company_name}}

Hi {{first_name}},

I noticed {{company_name}} is in the {{industry}} space and recently 
expanded to {{employee_count_range}} employees — congrats on the growth.

I work with a few other {{industry}} companies your size and wanted 
to share something that's been relevant for teams like yours...

You can also use enriched data for conditional logic in your sequence steps. MailClaw's AI email agents can branch based on company size, seniority, or tech stack — so a VP at a 500-person SaaS company gets a different version of step two than a founder at a 10-person startup, without you writing two separate sequences:

# Example conditional in a sequence YAML
steps:
  - id: step_2
    type: email
    condition:
      field: seniority
      operator: in
      values: [vp, c_suite]
    template: templates/vp_followup.txt
    fallback_template: templates/standard_followup.txt

CRM Sync: Pushing Enriched Data to HubSpot, Salesforce, and Others

Enriched contacts are most powerful when they flow into the rest of your stack. MailClaw supports native sync to HubSpot and Salesforce, and a generic webhook output for anything else — Pipedrive, Notion databases, Airtable, whatever you're using.

# Push enriched contacts to HubSpot after enrichment
mailclaw sync --destination hubspot --filter "enrichment_status=verified"

# Sync to Salesforce with field mapping
mailclaw sync --destination salesforce --map title=Title,company=Account

Because MailClaw runs locally, this sync is on your terms — it only fires when you tell it to. There's no background data sharing happening without your awareness, which is a meaningful advantage over SaaS enrichment tools that treat your contact data as a resource to be pooled and monetized.

Deliverability and Enrichment: The Hidden Connection

Here's something most people don't connect until it's too late: contact enrichment is a deliverability tool as much as a data tool. Sending to unverified or stale email addresses drives up your hard bounce rate. Once that rate climbs above 2-3%, inbox providers start treating your sending domain as a problem, and your emails start landing in spam — even for contacts who would have engaged.

MailClaw's deliverability monitoring dashboard (under Campaigns → Deliverability) tracks your bounce rate per sending account and per campaign. It integrates with Gmail, Outlook, and SendGrid via OAuth and SMTP, and it will surface a warning if your bounce rate trends upward — prompting you to re-enrich or prune your list before continuing.

A clean, enriched list of 500 contacts will almost always outperform a dirty list of 5,000. Enrichment isn't about volume — it's about precision.

Building an Automated Enrichment Workflow

For teams running continuous outreach, you don't want to manually trigger enrichment every time a new contact comes in. MailClaw supports scheduled enrichment jobs that watch a folder, a CRM segment, or a webhook endpoint and enrich automatically:

# Add a watcher that enriches new contacts from a HubSpot list every 6 hours
mailclaw watch --source hubspot --list-id 1234 --interval 6h --auto-enrich

# Watch a local folder for new CSV drops
mailclaw watch --source folder --path ~/contacts/incoming --auto-enrich --notify

Combine this with MailClaw's AI email agents — which can evaluate enriched profiles and autonomously decide whether to add a contact to a sequence, hold them for manual review, or skip them based on fit criteria you define — and you have a fully automated top-of-funnel that runs on your Mac without any monthly per-seat fees or data leaving your environment.

A Few Enrichment Best Practices Worth Keeping

Before you run your next enrichment batch, a few things that make a real difference in practice:

  • Always enrich before building your sequence, not after. Your personalization variables are only as good as the data behind them.
  • Set a confidence threshold and stick to it. The temptation is to lower it to get more contacts — resist this. Low-confidence contacts hurt deliverability more than they help pipeline.
  • Re-enrich stale contacts. Job titles and email addresses change. Contacts older than 6 months should be re-enriched before being added to a new campaign. MailClaw flags these automatically in the dashboard.
  • Use tech stack data for targeting, not just personalization. If your product competes with or complements Salesforce, filtering for contacts at companies already using Salesforce (via BuiltWith data) is a legitimate shortcut to higher relevance.
  • Review your enrichment logs. Run mailclaw enrich --log-level verbose once in a while to see where your waterfall is failing and adjust your source priority accordingly.

Contact enrichment isn't glamorous, but it's the foundation that everything else in your outreach stack sits on. MailClaw makes it something you can actually own — the data, the process, and the results — without a subscription that scales against you as your list grows.

articles.title: How to Use MailClaw for Lead Scoring Based on Email Engagement
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to implement a practical lead scoring system in MailClaw using email engagement signals like opens, clicks, and replies — so your sales team always knows exactly who to call first.
articles.content:
Why Email Engagement Is Your Best Lead Scoring Signal

Most lead scoring systems are built on demographics and form fills — job title, company size, which whitepaper someone downloaded three months ago. These signals matter, but they go stale fast. Email engagement data is different. When someone opens your sequence for the fourth time in two days, clicks your pricing link, and replies asking about implementation timelines, that behavior is telling you something right now. It's real-time intent data hiding in plain sight.

MailClaw gives you a local-first, open-source environment to capture that signal, score it, and act on it — without shipping your contact data to a third-party SaaS platform. Everything runs on localhost:3100, which means your enrichment logic, scoring rules, and AI agents all execute on your own machine. That's a meaningful advantage if you're handling sensitive prospect lists or just prefer to keep your outreach stack lean and auditable.

Understanding MailClaw's Engagement Tracking Architecture

Before you build a scoring model, it helps to understand what MailClaw actually tracks out of the box. Each contact in your campaign accumulates an engagement record that includes:

  • Open events — timestamped, with client and approximate geo data when available
  • Click events — per-link, so you know if they clicked your case study vs. your pricing page
  • Reply detection — via SMTP polling or Gmail/Outlook OAuth, depending on your integration
  • Bounce and unsubscribe signals — handled automatically by the deliverability monitor
  • Sequence progression — which step triggered a response, and how quickly

This data lives in MailClaw's local SQLite store and is surfaced in the dashboard under Contacts → Engagement Timeline. You can also query it directly via the OpenClaw CLI if you want to build custom exports or push scores into HubSpot or Salesforce.

Building Your Lead Scoring Model

Step 1: Define Your Scoring Dimensions

A practical engagement score doesn't need to be complicated. Start with a simple point system across three dimensions: recency, frequency, and intent depth. Here's a baseline scoring table you can adapt:

# MailClaw Lead Scoring — Baseline Point Values

# Recency (when did they last engage?)
opened_last_24h        = +15
opened_last_7d         = +8
opened_last_30d        = +3
no_open_in_60d         = -10

# Frequency (how often do they engage?)
opened_3_or_more_times = +12
clicked_any_link       = +10
replied_to_sequence    = +25

# Intent Depth (what did they engage with?)
clicked_pricing_link   = +20
clicked_case_study     = +8
clicked_demo_link      = +18
visited_unsubscribe    = -20

These aren't magic numbers — they're starting points. The goal in the first 30 days is to generate enough data to validate whether high-scorers actually convert at a higher rate. Adjust from there.

Step 2: Configure Scoring Rules in the Dashboard

Open your MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to Settings → Lead Scoring. You'll see a visual rule builder where you can define conditions and assign point values. For each campaign or sequence, you can set scoring rules independently — a cold outbound campaign and a post-demo nurture sequence shouldn't share the same score weights.

For link-level intent scoring, make sure you've added UTM parameters or MailClaw's built-in link tagging to your sequence URLs. Tag your pricing page link with ?mc_intent=pricing and MailClaw will automatically bucket that click into the correct scoring category without any extra configuration.

Step 3: Use the CLI for Bulk Score Calculation

If you're importing an existing contact list or retroactively scoring a completed campaign, the OpenClaw CLI makes this fast:

# Score all contacts in a campaign
mailclaw score --campaign="Q3 Outbound" --apply-rules --output=csv

# Score a specific contact list and push to HubSpot
mailclaw score --list="enterprise-prospects.csv" \
  --rules="./scoring-rules.json" \
  --sync=hubspot

# View top-scored contacts in terminal
mailclaw score --campaign="Q3 Outbound" --top=20 --sort=desc

The --sync=hubspot flag uses MailClaw's HubSpot integration to write the computed score back to a custom contact property. You can do the same with --sync=salesforce to update a lead field in your CRM. This keeps your scoring logic in MailClaw while making the output available to your sales team wherever they live.

Using AI Email Agents to Act on Score Changes

Scoring is only useful if it triggers action. MailClaw's AI email agents let you build autonomous response logic that fires when a contact crosses a score threshold — no manual review required.

Setting Up a Score-Triggered Agent

In the dashboard, go to AI Agents → New Agent and select Score Threshold Trigger. Configure it like this:

  1. Set your trigger: "When lead score exceeds 60"
  2. Choose an action: "Send personalized follow-up from sequence step 4" or "Create task in Salesforce"
  3. Add a condition: "Only if contact has not replied in last 7 days"
  4. Set a cooldown period: "Do not retrigger within 48 hours"

The AI agent uses your contact's enrichment data — company size, industry, recent job changes pulled via MailClaw's contact enrichment feature — to personalize the triggered message. A prospect at a 200-person SaaS company who just clicked your pricing page three times in one afternoon gets a different follow-up than someone at an enterprise who opened your introductory email once.

Pro tip: Don't gate your best AI agent behavior behind a single high-score threshold. Build a tiered system: a "warm" agent fires at 40+ points with a light-touch resource share, and a "hot" agent fires at 70+ points with a direct, meeting-focused message. This way you're nurturing the middle of your funnel, not just reacting to the top.

Enriching Contacts to Add Context to Your Scores

Raw engagement scores are powerful, but they're even more useful when layered with firmographic and behavioral context. MailClaw's contact enrichment feature lets you pull in additional data points that can modify your base score or inform how the AI agent responds.

From the CLI, run enrichment before scoring a new list:

# Enrich contacts before scoring
mailclaw enrich --list="new-leads.csv" \
  --fields="company_size,industry,linkedin_url,tech_stack" \
  --provider=clearbit

# Then score with enrichment data as a modifier
mailclaw score --list="new-leads.csv" \
  --rules="./scoring-rules.json" \
  --enrich-modifier="company_size:enterprise=+15,smb=-5"

This lets you apply fit scoring on top of engagement scoring. A contact at a 500-person financial services firm who clicked your pricing link twice is worth a lot more than the same clicks from a solo freelancer — if enterprise is your target market. Combining both signals in a single score gives your outreach a much stronger signal-to-noise ratio.

Monitoring Deliverability So Your Scores Stay Meaningful

One often-overlooked issue with engagement-based scoring: your scores are only as reliable as your deliverability. If your emails are landing in spam, a low open rate doesn't mean low intent — it means low inbox placement. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring panel (under Deliverability → Health Check) shows you per-account inbox rates, spam folder rates, and bounce trends across your SMTP and OAuth connections.

Before drawing conclusions from your engagement data, run a quick health check:

# Check deliverability health across all connected accounts
mailclaw deliverability --check-all --report=summary

# Test a specific sending domain
mailclaw deliverability --domain="yourcompany.com" \
  --test=spf,dkim,dmarc,blacklist

If you're seeing inbox rates below 85% on Gmail or Outlook, your engagement scores are being calculated on a skewed sample. Fix deliverability first, then revisit your scoring baselines.

Connecting the Loop: From Score to Closed Deal

The final piece is making sure your scored leads actually reach the right person at the right time. MailClaw's multi-account support means you can route high-scoring leads to a dedicated sending account with a warmer reputation — keeping your best prospects in a high-deliverability lane separate from early-stage cold outreach.

Combine that with automated CRM sync via the --sync flag, and you have a complete loop: MailClaw scores the engagement, the AI agent sends the right follow-up, the CRM captures the outcome, and your sales team sees a prioritized list of warm contacts without touching the automation layer at all.

Start simple — one campaign, five scoring rules, one threshold agent. Run it for two weeks, then look at whether your high-scorers converted at a higher rate. That validation is what turns a scoring experiment into a repeatable system you can roll out across every sequence in your stack.

articles.title: MailClaw Contact Database: Organizing and Segmenting Your Leads
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to build, organize, and segment your contact database in MailClaw to run smarter outreach campaigns — with practical CLI commands, enrichment tips, and segmentation strategies that actually move the needle.
articles.content:
Why Your Contact Database Is the Foundation of Every Campaign

Every great email campaign starts long before you write a single subject line. It starts with your data. A well-organized contact database isn't just a list of names and email addresses — it's a living, queryable asset that determines who gets what message, when, and why. If your contacts are a mess, your campaigns will be too.

MailClaw treats your contact database as a first-class citizen. Running locally on localhost:3100, it gives you full ownership of your data without shipping it off to third-party servers. No vendor lock-in, no data residency concerns — just clean, structured contact records you control entirely.

Importing Contacts into MailClaw

Getting your existing contacts into MailClaw is the first step. Whether you're migrating from HubSpot, exporting a CSV from Salesforce, or pulling a list together from Gmail and Outlook, MailClaw handles it gracefully.

CSV Import via CLI

The fastest way to bulk-import contacts is through the MailClaw CLI. Your CSV should include at minimum an email column. Everything else — name, company, role, tags — is optional but highly recommended for segmentation later.

# Import a CSV of leads into a named list
mailclaw contacts import --file leads.csv --list "Q3 Outreach" --tag "cold-lead"

# Preview without committing (dry run)
mailclaw contacts import --file leads.csv --dry-run

The --tag flag lets you stamp every imported contact with a label immediately, so you can segment from day one. The dry-run flag is genuinely useful — it validates your CSV structure and flags duplicates before you commit anything to the database.

Syncing from CRMs and Tools

If you're pulling contacts from HubSpot or Salesforce, MailClaw supports OAuth-authenticated syncs. Configure your integration in the local dashboard under Settings → Integrations, then run:

# Sync contacts from a connected HubSpot account
mailclaw contacts sync --source hubspot --filter "lifecycle_stage=lead"

# One-way sync from Salesforce with field mapping
mailclaw contacts sync --source salesforce --map "FirstName:first_name,Title:job_title"

Field mapping is critical here. CRMs often use different naming conventions, and the --map flag lets you align their field names with MailClaw's internal schema so nothing gets lost in translation.

Enriching Your Contacts with AI

Raw import data is rarely enough. Job titles go stale, companies pivot, and a name plus email address tells you almost nothing about intent. This is where MailClaw's AI-powered contact enrichment becomes genuinely powerful.

Powered by OpenClaw under the hood, the enrichment engine can infer or fetch additional context for each contact — company size, industry vertical, LinkedIn presence, tech stack signals, and more — so your segmentation is based on something meaningful rather than arbitrary list membership.

# Enrich all contacts in a list
mailclaw contacts enrich --list "Q3 Outreach"

# Enrich a single contact by email
mailclaw contacts enrich --email jane@acmecorp.com

# Enrich with specific fields only (faster, cheaper on API credits)
mailclaw contacts enrich --list "Q3 Outreach" --fields "company_size,industry,linkedin_url"

After enrichment runs, your contact records will have dramatically more signal. That signal is what makes segmentation actually work.

Segmentation Strategies That Drive Results

Segmentation is the art of sending the right message to the right person. The more precisely you can slice your audience, the more relevant your outreach becomes — and relevance is what separates a 40% open rate from a 4% one.

Tag-Based Segmentation

Tags are the simplest and most flexible segmentation tool in MailClaw. Think of them as labels you apply manually or automatically based on behavior and attributes.

  • Source tags: inbound-website, cold-purchased-list, referral-partner
  • Stage tags: mql, sql, churned, re-engagement
  • Behavior tags: opened-3x, clicked-pricing, replied
  • Campaign tags: sequence-a-complete, webinar-registrant-oct
# Tag contacts who opened an email but never replied
mailclaw contacts tag --filter "opens >= 2 AND replies = 0" --tag "warm-no-reply"

# Remove a tag from a segment
mailclaw contacts untag --filter "tag:cold-lead AND replies >= 1" --tag "cold-lead"

The second command is just as important as the first. When a "cold lead" replies, they're no longer cold — and your database should reflect that automatically.

Attribute-Based Segmentation

With enriched data available, you can build segments based on firmographic and demographic attributes rather than just behavior.

# Build a segment of SaaS companies with 50-200 employees
mailclaw segments create \
  --name "Mid-Market SaaS" \
  --filter "industry=SaaS AND company_size >= 50 AND company_size <= 200"

# Export a segment to CSV for review
mailclaw segments export --name "Mid-Market SaaS" --output mid_market_saas.csv

Pro tip: Create segments before you build sequences. When you wire a sequence to a dynamic segment in MailClaw, any new contact that qualifies for that segment automatically enters the sequence. This is how you build set-and-forget outreach that stays relevant over time.

Engagement-Based Segmentation

MailClaw tracks deliverability and engagement signals at the contact level — opens, clicks, bounces, spam complaints — and you can use all of these as segmentation criteria. This is especially valuable for deliverability hygiene.

# Identify disengaged contacts (no opens in 90 days)
mailclaw contacts query \
  --filter "last_open < 90d AND total_sent >= 3" \
  --output disengaged.csv

# Flag hard bounces for review
mailclaw contacts query --filter "bounce_type=hard" --tag "invalid-email"

Removing or suppressing disengaged contacts before a major send is one of the highest-leverage deliverability moves you can make. Sending to people who never open drags down your sender reputation with providers like Gmail and Outlook, which ultimately hurts deliverability for your engaged contacts too.

Managing Lists vs. Segments: Know the Difference

MailClaw distinguishes between static lists and dynamic segments, and understanding when to use each saves a lot of confusion.

  • Static lists are fixed at the time of creation. Use them for one-time campaigns, event invitees, or manually curated groups. They don't update automatically.
  • Dynamic segments are query-based and always current. Use them for ongoing sequences, re-engagement campaigns, and anything that should automatically include new qualifying contacts.

A common workflow: import contacts into a static list, enrich them, apply tags based on enrichment results, and then feed those tags into dynamic segments that power your sequences. The sequence builder in MailClaw's local dashboard makes this pipeline visual and easy to follow without needing to memorize every CLI command.

Keeping Your Database Clean

A bloated, stale contact database actively hurts you. Duplicate records skew reporting, wasted sends drain API credits with SendGrid or your SMTP provider, and bounces compound over time if you're not pruning.

# Find and merge duplicate contacts by email
mailclaw contacts dedupe --strategy "keep-oldest"

# Remove contacts who have unsubscribed globally
mailclaw contacts purge --filter "status=unsubscribed"

# Archive (not delete) contacts inactive for 6+ months
mailclaw contacts archive --filter "last_activity > 180d"

Set a recurring reminder — monthly or quarterly — to run these cleanup commands. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring dashboard at localhost:3100/deliverability will show you trend lines on bounce rate and complaint rate that make it obvious when your list hygiene is slipping.

Using AI Email Agents to Act on Segments

Once your segments are clean and meaningful, you can wire them directly to MailClaw's AI email agents. These agents don't just send pre-written sequences — they can adapt messaging based on contact attributes, enrichment signals, and prior engagement history.

For example, you might configure an agent to handle your "Mid-Market SaaS" segment with one value proposition, while a separate agent handles "Enterprise Fintech" contacts with entirely different messaging, tone, and call-to-action. Both run autonomously, monitored from the same local dashboard, and both respect the suppression lists and unsubscribe logic you've already configured.

This is the compounding payoff of good database hygiene: when your segments are accurate and your enrichment is current, your AI agents have the context they need to send messages that actually feel personal — because they're based on real information, not guesswork.

Getting Started: A Practical First Step

If you're new to MailClaw, here's a simple sequence to get your contact database into shape today:

  1. Export your existing contacts from your CRM or Gmail/Outlook and save as a CSV.
  2. Run mailclaw contacts import --file contacts.csv --dry-run to validate the data.
  3. Commit the import with a source tag: --tag "import-[month-year]".
  4. Run enrichment on the imported list: mailclaw contacts enrich --list "your-list-name".
  5. Build two or three dynamic segments based on industry or company size.
  6. Open localhost:3100 and wire your first segment to a sequence in the visual builder.

Your contact database is only as useful as the structure you put around it. With MailClaw's combination of CLI power, OpenClaw-driven enrichment, and a local-first architecture, you have everything you need to build a database that's not just organized — but genuinely actionable.

articles.title: How to Deduplicate Contacts in MailClaw Automatically
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to automatically deduplicate contacts in MailClaw using built-in CLI commands, AI-powered enrichment, and smart merge rules — so your outreach stays clean, your deliverability stays high, and your sequences never ping the same person twice.
articles.content:
Why Duplicate Contacts Are Quietly Killing Your Campaigns

Duplicate contacts are one of those problems that starts small and compounds fast. You import a CSV from HubSpot, sync a few leads from Salesforce, manually add a handful from a LinkedIn export — and suddenly you've got john.doe@acme.com, johndoe@acme.com, and j.doe@acme.com all sitting in the same contact list. Your sequence builder fires all three into a drip campaign, the same person gets three emails on the same Tuesday morning, and your unsubscribe rate spikes before noon.

Beyond the annoyance factor, duplicates actively hurt your deliverability scores. MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring tracks bounce rates, spam complaints, and engagement signals per sending account. When duplicates inflate your send volume without adding genuine engagement, those metrics skew — and ISPs notice. Keeping your contact database clean isn't housekeeping, it's a core part of a healthy outreach strategy.

The good news: MailClaw gives you several layers of deduplication tooling, from one-command CLI deduplication to AI-assisted fuzzy matching that catches the tricky cases your spreadsheet formulas never could.

Understanding How MailClaw Stores Contacts

Before you run any deduplication logic, it helps to understand the data model. MailClaw (powered by OpenClaw) stores contacts in a local SQLite database accessible through your localhost dashboard at localhost:3100. Each contact record carries:

  • A unique internal contact_id
  • One or more email addresses (primary + aliases)
  • Enrichment metadata — company, role, social profiles, phone
  • Source tags indicating where the contact originated (e.g., hubspot_sync, csv_import, manual)
  • Sequence membership and engagement history

The source tags are particularly useful during deduplication. If you have a contact from both a Salesforce export and a Gmail OAuth sync, MailClaw can tell you which version has richer data — and use that as the "winner" during a merge.

Method 1: The Built-In CLI Dedup Command

The fastest way to deduplicate is with MailClaw's contacts dedup command. Open your terminal and run:

mailclaw contacts dedup --strategy=email --dry-run

The --dry-run flag is your best friend here. It produces a full deduplication report — showing you exactly which records would be merged and which would be discarded — without actually touching your data. Always start here.

Once you've reviewed the output and you're comfortable, drop the flag and run the merge for real:

mailclaw contacts dedup --strategy=email --merge=keep-richest

The --merge=keep-richest option tells MailClaw to retain whichever duplicate record has the most filled-in fields after enrichment. Alternatively, you can use --merge=keep-oldest to preserve the original record, or --merge=keep-newest if you've been actively updating records and want the latest version to survive.

Deduplicating by Domain

If you're running account-based outreach and you want to identify situations where multiple contacts at the same company have been entered as separate leads, use the domain strategy:

mailclaw contacts dedup --strategy=domain --report-only

This won't merge records (companies genuinely have multiple contacts), but it outputs a grouped report you can use to audit your sequence builder and make sure you're not accidentally enrolling ten people from the same org into the same cold outreach sequence.

Method 2: AI-Powered Fuzzy Matching

Exact email matching catches the obvious duplicates. But what about john.smith@acme.com and jsmith@acme.co? Or a contact you enriched from LinkedIn whose name matches a manually entered record but the emails differ by a single character due to a typo?

This is where MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered AI layer earns its keep. The fuzzy dedup mode runs a similarity analysis across name, company domain, phone number, and LinkedIn URL fields — not just email — and surfaces likely matches for your review:

mailclaw contacts dedup --strategy=fuzzy --confidence=0.85 --dry-run

The --confidence parameter accepts a value between 0 and 1. A threshold of 0.85 is a good starting point — high enough to surface genuine likely duplicates without drowning you in false positives. If you're working with a messy import from a legacy CRM, try dropping it to 0.75 and reviewing manually.

Fuzzy matches are held in a pending review queue inside your localhost dashboard. Navigate to localhost:3100/contacts/dedup-queue to see each candidate pair side by side, with a confidence score and a breakdown of which fields matched. You can approve, reject, or merge-with-edit from this UI — useful for cases where you want to pull the email from one record and the enrichment data from another.

Method 3: Automated Deduplication on Import

The cleanest approach to duplicates is stopping them at the door. MailClaw supports import-time deduplication rules that trigger automatically whenever you bring new contacts in — whether that's via CSV upload, a HubSpot or Salesforce sync, or an OAuth-connected Gmail or Outlook account.

To configure this, open your mailclaw.config.json file (found in your MailClaw install directory) and add the following to your contacts block:

{
  "contacts": {
    "dedup_on_import": true,
    "dedup_strategy": "email",
    "dedup_fallback": "fuzzy",
    "dedup_confidence": 0.88,
    "merge_rule": "keep-richest"
  }
}

With this configuration, every new import first checks for an exact email match. If none is found, it falls back to fuzzy matching at the specified confidence threshold. Anything below the threshold gets imported as a new record but flagged with a needs_review tag for manual inspection later.

Pro tip: If you're syncing contacts from multiple sources — say, both a SendGrid suppression list and a Salesforce CRM export — enable the source_priority option in your config. It lets you rank sources so that when a merge happens, fields from your highest-priority source always win.

Handling Duplicates Already Inside Active Sequences

Here's a scenario that trips people up: you deduplicate your contact database, but some of the merged records were already enrolled in active sequences. What happens to the surviving contact's sequence state?

MailClaw handles this gracefully. When two records merge, the system checks both records' sequence memberships and applies the following logic by default:

  1. If only one record was enrolled in a sequence, that enrollment transfers to the merged record.
  2. If both records were enrolled in the same sequence at different steps, the merge keeps the record at the later step (to avoid re-sending emails the contact already received).
  3. If both were enrolled in different sequences, both enrollments are preserved on the merged record.

You can override this behavior with the --sequence-conflict=pause flag during a manual dedup run, which pauses both enrollments and flags the merged contact for manual review instead of auto-resolving.

Building a Recurring Dedup Schedule

One-time deduplication is a start, but contact databases drift over time — especially when you've got live integrations feeding in new records from Gmail, Outlook, or your CRM. The right move is to schedule deduplication as a recurring task.

MailClaw includes a native task scheduler. To set up a weekly dedup job, run:

mailclaw schedule add \
  --name="weekly-dedup" \
  --command="contacts dedup --strategy=email --merge=keep-richest" \
  --cron="0 2 * * 1"

This runs every Monday at 2:00 AM local time — quietly, in the background, while you're not touching anything. You'll get a summary report in your dashboard each week showing how many duplicates were resolved and what the current state of your contact database looks like.

Pairing Dedup with Contact Enrichment

For best results, run contact enrichment before your deduplication pass. Enrichment fills in missing company names, job titles, LinkedIn profiles, and phone numbers — giving the dedup engine more signals to work with during fuzzy matching, and ensuring that when records merge, the winning record is as complete as possible.

mailclaw contacts enrich --source=clearbit && mailclaw contacts dedup --strategy=fuzzy --merge=keep-richest

Chaining these two commands gives you a clean, enriched contact database in a single terminal session — and your AI email agents will have much better personalization data to work with when building sequences.

Keeping It Clean Going Forward

Deduplication is most effective as a habit, not a one-time fix. The combination of import-time rules, scheduled weekly passes, and the fuzzy review queue in your MailClaw dashboard gives you a layered defense that handles both the obvious cases and the subtle ones. Your deliverability monitoring will reflect the improvement almost immediately — fewer duplicate sends means better engagement rates, cleaner bounce metrics, and a sender reputation that ISPs respect.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your machine, your contact data never leaves localhost. You get enterprise-grade deduplication tooling without handing your lead database to a third-party SaaS — and that's a genuinely rare combination worth taking advantage of.

articles.title: Building Smart Contact Lists with MailClaw AI Segmentation
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's AI-powered segmentation engine to build smarter contact lists that drive higher open rates, better deliverability, and more personalized outreach — all running locally on your Mac.
articles.content:
Why Static Contact Lists Are Killing Your Campaigns

Most email marketers are still working the same way they did a decade ago: export a CSV, import it into a tool, blast everyone with the same message, and hope for the best. The result? Mediocre open rates, spam complaints, and a deliverability reputation that slowly erodes over time.

The problem isn't the list itself — it's the lack of intelligence behind it. A contact database is only as powerful as your ability to understand who's in it and why they should receive a particular message at a particular time. That's exactly where MailClaw's AI segmentation capabilities change the game.

Because MailClaw runs locally on your machine at localhost:3100, your contact data never leaves your environment. No third-party SaaS platforms holding your data hostage. No per-seat pricing that scales against you. Just a clean, fast, open-source tool powered by OpenClaw that puts you in control of how your lists are built and segmented.

Understanding MailClaw's AI Segmentation Engine

MailClaw's segmentation system goes well beyond the standard "filter by tag" approach. Under the hood, the OpenClaw AI engine analyzes behavioral signals, enriched contact attributes, and engagement history to group contacts into meaningful cohorts — automatically.

When you open the MailClaw dashboard, you'll find the Segments panel in the left sidebar. From here, you can create segments manually using rule-based filters, or hand the wheel to the AI agent and let it surface patterns you might have missed entirely.

Rule-Based Segments vs. AI-Generated Segments

There are two modes for building segments in MailClaw, and knowing when to use each one matters:

  • Rule-based segments are great when you know exactly who you're targeting. If you want everyone in your CRM tagged as "SaaS founder" who opened an email in the last 30 days, you define that logic explicitly.
  • AI-generated segments are ideal when you want the system to surface unexpected groupings — high-intent leads who share behavioral patterns, contacts likely to churn, or personas that naturally cluster around a particular product interest.

In practice, the best workflows combine both. Start with AI discovery to find the cohorts worth targeting, then refine them with explicit rules to lock in the boundaries.

Step-by-Step: Building Your First AI Segment

Step 1 — Import and Enrich Your Contacts

Before MailClaw's AI can segment intelligently, it needs rich data to work with. Start by importing your contacts from a CSV, or pull them directly from a connected source like HubSpot, Salesforce, or a custom webhook.

From your terminal, you can kick off an import with the MailClaw CLI:

mailclaw contacts import --file ./leads.csv --enrich true

The --enrich true flag triggers MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment pipeline. It will attempt to fill in missing fields — company size, industry, job title, LinkedIn presence, tech stack — using publicly available signals. For contacts where enrichment returns strong data, you'll see a confidence score in the dashboard.

You can also enrich an existing list in bulk:

mailclaw contacts enrich --segment all --min-confidence 0.75

The --min-confidence flag ensures only high-quality enrichments are applied, keeping your data clean rather than flooding it with low-confidence guesses.

Step 2 — Run the AI Segmentation Analysis

Once your contacts are enriched, run the segmentation analysis from the CLI or directly from the dashboard:

mailclaw segment analyze --model gpt --output-labels true

This command triggers the OpenClaw AI agent to cluster your contacts using a combination of enriched attributes and engagement signals. The --output-labels true flag tells the agent to generate human-readable labels for each segment, so instead of "Cluster 4," you'll see something like "Mid-market SaaS decision makers — high email engagement."

The analysis typically completes in under two minutes for lists under 10,000 contacts, and results appear immediately in the dashboard under AI Segments.

Step 3 — Review and Refine in the Dashboard

Head to localhost:3100/segments to review your AI-generated cohorts. Each segment card shows:

  • Contact count and enrichment coverage percentage
  • Top shared attributes (industry, title, company size)
  • Predicted engagement score based on historical data
  • Suggested sequence type (cold outreach, nurture, re-engagement)

From here, you can click into any segment to inspect individual contacts, remove outliers, or manually add contacts that the AI may have miscategorized. You can also merge two segments if you decide the distinction between them isn't meaningful for your campaign goals.

Step 4 — Connect Segments to Sequences

A segment without a tailored message is just a label. Once your cohorts are defined, connect them to MailClaw's sequence builder to create targeted email flows for each group.

mailclaw sequence create --name "SaaS Founders Outreach" --segment "saas-founders-high-intent" --steps 4

Inside the sequence builder at localhost:3100/sequences, MailClaw's AI email agent will suggest subject lines, opening hooks, and CTAs that align with the segment's profile. For a segment of technical founders, it might lean toward plain-text emails with specific, tangible value propositions. For marketing directors, it might suggest a more formatted email with a clear benefit summary.
