"The best email isn't the most creative one — it's the one that arrives with the right message for the right person at the right moment. Segmentation is how you get there."

Advanced Segmentation Techniques

Behavioral Re-Segmentation

Segments should never be static. As contacts interact with your campaigns — opening emails, clicking links, replying, or going cold — their segment membership should update automatically. MailClaw handles this with re-segmentation triggers.

You can configure re-segmentation rules in your mailclaw.config.json:

{
  "segmentation": {
    "auto_resegment": true,
    "resegment_interval": "7d",
    "triggers": ["email_open", "link_click", "reply", "bounce", "unsubscribe"]
  }
}

With auto_resegment enabled, contacts who engage heavily will automatically migrate toward higher-intent segments, while cold contacts drift into re-engagement cohorts. This keeps your sequences relevant without you having to manually audit lists every week.

Integrating External CRM Data

If your team uses Salesforce or HubSpot, MailClaw can sync CRM properties directly into its contact model. This means pipeline stage, deal size, last activity date, and custom fields can all become segmentation criteria inside MailClaw without any manual export-import cycle.

mailclaw integrations connect --provider hubspot --sync-fields "lifecycle_stage,deal_stage,last_activity"

Once connected, these fields appear as filterable attributes in both your rule-based segment builder and the AI analysis pipeline. A contact who just moved to "Negotiation" in HubSpot can automatically land in a high-priority follow-up segment in MailClaw within minutes.

Deliverability-Aware Segmentation

One of MailClaw's most underrated features is its deliverability monitoring layer, which feeds directly into segmentation decisions. Before sending to a segment, MailClaw checks:

  • Bounce history for contacts in the segment
  • Spam complaint rates from previous sends to similar cohorts
  • Domain health for the sending accounts connected via SMTP or OAuth (Gmail, Outlook, SendGrid)
  • Overall list hygiene score for the segment

If a segment has a hygiene score below a configurable threshold, MailClaw will flag it before you launch a sequence and suggest a cleaning step — removing hard bounces, suppressing complainers, or splitting the segment to warm up higher-risk contacts separately.

This kind of deliverability-first thinking built into the segmentation layer is what separates MailClaw from bolting a separate list-cleaning tool onto a generic email platform.

Multi-Account Segmentation for Agencies and Teams

If you manage outreach across multiple clients or brands, MailClaw's multi-account support means each account has its own isolated contact database, segment library, and sequence history. You can still run global analysis across accounts if you need to, but by default everything stays neatly partitioned.

Switch between accounts from the CLI with:

mailclaw account switch --name "ClientA"

Or use the account selector in the top-right corner of the localhost dashboard to toggle contexts without losing your place.

Putting It All Together

Smart contact lists aren't built once — they evolve continuously as your audience changes and your campaigns generate new behavioral data. MailClaw's AI segmentation engine is designed to make that evolution automatic, intelligent, and transparent, all without sending your data to a cloud platform you don't control.

The practical workflow looks like this: import and enrich your contacts, let the AI surface meaningful cohorts, connect those cohorts to tailored sequences, monitor deliverability as you send, and let re-segmentation keep everything current. Each step compounds on the last, and within a few campaign cycles you'll have a living, breathing contact ecosystem that consistently outperforms anything a static list could achieve.

Because MailClaw is open source and built on OpenClaw, you can extend every part of this pipeline — custom enrichment sources, proprietary scoring models, bespoke segmentation logic — and contribute improvements back to the community. The tool grows with your needs, not against them.

Start with your next import. Run the analysis. See what the AI finds. You might be surprised by the cohorts sitting in your list that you never knew to look for.

articles.title: How to Enrich LinkedIn Leads with MailClaw
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to turn raw LinkedIn leads into fully enriched, campaign-ready contacts using MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment engine — complete with CLI commands, workflow examples, and tips for building AI-powered outreach sequences.
articles.content:
Why LinkedIn Leads Need Enrichment Before You Email Them

LinkedIn is one of the richest sources of B2B leads on the planet. But a raw LinkedIn export — a spreadsheet of names, job titles, and profile URLs — is just a starting point. Before you can run a meaningful outreach campaign, you need verified email addresses, company details, firmographic data, and enough context to personalize your messages beyond "Hi {{first_name}}, I loved your profile."

That's where contact enrichment comes in. MailClaw, the open-source AI-powered email automation tool built on OpenClaw, has a native enrichment pipeline that lets you take a CSV of LinkedIn leads and transform them into campaign-ready contacts — all running locally on your machine at localhost:3100. No third-party SaaS dashboard, no data leaving your infrastructure, no per-seat pricing surprises.

This guide walks you through the full workflow: exporting from LinkedIn, importing into MailClaw, running enrichment, and launching a personalized sequence — step by step.

Step 1: Export Your LinkedIn Leads

LinkedIn gives you two practical ways to get lead data out:

LinkedIn Sales Navigator CSV Export

If you have Sales Navigator, you can export lead lists directly. Go to your saved lead list, click Export, and download the CSV. You'll typically get: first name, last name, job title, company name, LinkedIn URL, and sometimes location.

Manual or Third-Party Scraping

For standard LinkedIn accounts, tools like PhantomBuster, Evaboot, or Apify can extract lead data from searches or Sales Navigator lists. Export to CSV in any case — MailClaw's importer handles both formats cleanly.

A typical raw LinkedIn CSV looks something like this:

first_name,last_name,title,company,linkedin_url,location
Sarah,Chen,Head of Growth,Acme Corp,https://linkedin.com/in/sarahchen,San Francisco CA
Marcus,Webb,VP of Engineering,Loopback AI,https://linkedin.com/in/marcuswebb,New York NY

Notice what's missing: verified email addresses, company domain, employee count, tech stack, and anything else you'd need to write a personalized email. Let's fix that.

Step 2: Import Leads into MailClaw

With MailClaw running locally, open your terminal and use the CLI to import your CSV into a new contact list:

mailclaw contacts import \
  --file ./linkedin-leads.csv \
  --list "LinkedIn Q2 Prospects" \
  --map first_name=first_name \
  --map last_name=last_name \
  --map title=job_title \
  --map company=company_name \
  --map linkedin_url=linkedin_url

The --map flags let you align your CSV column names to MailClaw's internal contact schema. Once imported, open the local dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to Contacts → Lists to confirm your leads are in there. You should see them listed with partial data and a yellow "Needs Enrichment" status badge.

Step 3: Run Contact Enrichment

This is where MailClaw earns its place in your stack. The enrichment engine, powered by OpenClaw's AI core, cross-references your contact data against multiple data sources to fill in the gaps. Depending on your enrichment configuration, it can resolve:

  • Verified email addresses from company domain + name pattern matching and validation
  • Company domain inferred from company name
  • Firmographic data — employee count, industry, funding stage, HQ location
  • Tech stack signals — what tools a company is likely using (great for relevance hooks)
  • Social profile links — Twitter/X, GitHub, personal sites

Running Enrichment from the CLI

mailclaw enrich \
  --list "LinkedIn Q2 Prospects" \
  --fields email,company_domain,employee_count,industry \
  --confidence 0.85

The --confidence flag tells MailClaw to only write enriched values when the internal confidence score meets or exceeds 85%. This keeps your data clean — you won't end up emailing s.chen@acme-inc.biz when the real address is sarah@acmecorp.com.

Enrichment via the Dashboard

Prefer a visual workflow? In the localhost dashboard, open your contact list, select all contacts, and click Enrich Selected. A sidebar lets you toggle which fields to enrich and set your confidence threshold. You can watch enrichment run in real time — each row updates as data resolves.

Pro tip: Run enrichment in batches of 200–500 contacts to keep memory usage stable, especially on machines with less than 16GB RAM. MailClaw's scheduler lets you queue batches to run overnight with mailclaw enrich --list "..." --schedule "02:00".

Step 4: Validate and Clean Your Enriched List

Enrichment gets you far, but validation is the last line of defense before any email goes out. MailClaw's built-in deliverability tools include a syntax checker, MX record validator, and catch-all detector. Run it like this:

mailclaw validate-emails --list "LinkedIn Q2 Prospects" --remove-invalid

The --remove-invalid flag automatically removes contacts where the email fails MX validation. This step alone can save your sender reputation — bouncing more than 3–5% of emails in a campaign is enough to get your sending domain flagged by Gmail and Outlook alike.

After validation, check your list stats in the dashboard under Contacts → List Health. Aim for:

  • Email coverage above 80% of total leads
  • Less than 2% catch-all addresses
  • Zero syntax errors

Step 5: Build a Personalized Outreach Sequence

Now the fun part. With enriched, validated contacts in hand, you can build a sequence that actually references real context about each person.

Using the Sequence Builder

In the dashboard, go to Sequences → New Sequence and give it a name like "LinkedIn Q2 Outreach." Add steps: a cold intro email, a follow-up three days later, and a breakup email on day ten. MailClaw's sequence builder supports dynamic delay logic — you can skip a follow-up if someone opens but doesn't reply, or branch based on link clicks.

Writing Emails with AI Personalization

MailClaw's AI email agent can draft each step using your enriched contact fields as inputs. In the email editor, you have access to merge tags like:

{{first_name}}, {{company_name}}, {{job_title}},
{{industry}}, {{employee_count}}, {{tech_stack_hint}}

You can also prompt the AI agent directly in the editor:

/ai write a two-sentence cold opener for a {{job_title}} at a 
{{employee_count}}-person company in the {{industry}} space, 
referencing their likely challenge with outbound pipeline

The agent drafts copy in seconds. Review it, adjust the tone, and you've got a genuinely personalized cold email — at scale — without sounding like a mail merge from 2009.

Step 6: Connect Your Sending Account and Launch

MailClaw supports multi-account sending via SMTP or OAuth. Connect Gmail or Google Workspace via OAuth in under a minute:

mailclaw accounts add \
  --provider gmail \
  --auth oauth \
  --alias "outreach-primary"

For higher-volume campaigns, connect a dedicated sending domain through SendGrid or Mailgun via SMTP:

mailclaw accounts add \
  --provider smtp \
  --host smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --port 587 \
  --user apikey \
  --alias "sendgrid-bulk"

Once your account is connected, assign it to your sequence in the dashboard and set your daily sending cap. For cold outreach on a new domain, start conservative — 30 to 50 emails per day — and ramp up over two to three weeks as your domain warms.

Syncing Enriched Contacts to Your CRM

If your team uses HubSpot or Salesforce, MailClaw can push enriched contact data back into your CRM after enrichment completes. Use the sync command:

mailclaw sync --list "LinkedIn Q2 Prospects" \
  --destination hubspot \
  --on-conflict update

The --on-conflict update flag means if a contact already exists in HubSpot, their record gets updated with the new enriched fields rather than creating a duplicate. This keeps your CRM clean and your sales team working from fresh data.

Monitoring Deliverability After Launch

Once your sequence is live, MailClaw's deliverability monitoring dashboard gives you a real-time view of open rates, reply rates, bounce rates, and spam complaint signals — all from localhost:3100/deliverability. If you see your bounce rate climbing above 4%, pause the campaign immediately and re-validate the affected segment before resuming.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs locally, all your campaign analytics and contact data stay on your machine. There's no SaaS vendor storing your prospect list or your performance metrics — a genuine advantage if you work in a regulated industry or simply value data ownership.

Putting It All Together

The full LinkedIn enrichment workflow in MailClaw takes under an hour to set up end-to-end. You go from a flat CSV of names and profile URLs to a validated, enriched, personalized outreach sequence — with CRM sync, deliverability monitoring, and AI-assisted copywriting all running locally on your Mac. That's a workflow that used to require three or four separate paid tools, stitched together with Zapier and a lot of copy-paste.

If you haven't already, install MailClaw from the GitHub repo, run mailclaw start, and open localhost:3100 to get started. The contact enrichment pipeline is available out of the box — no API keys required for basic enrichment, with optional integrations available for premium data sources.

articles.title: MailClaw Data Enrichment: Pulling Company Info from Domain Names
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment engine to automatically pull company data, technographics, and firmographics from domain names — turning a bare email list into a fully qualified outreach pipeline.
articles.content:
Why Domain-Based Enrichment Changes Everything

Most email lists start the same way: a spreadsheet with names, email addresses, and not much else. You know who you're reaching out to, but you don't know what they do, how big their company is, what tools they use, or whether they're even worth pursuing right now. That gap between "contact" and "qualified lead" is where most outreach campaigns quietly fall apart.

MailClaw's contact enrichment engine solves this by working backwards from something you almost always have — the domain name embedded in an email address. From that single data point, it can surface company size, industry, location, funding status, technology stack, LinkedIn presence, and more. By the time your AI email agent fires off the first message in a sequence, it's working with a fully fleshed-out picture of the recipient's business context.

This guide walks you through exactly how to set that up, from importing a raw list to triggering enrichment to using the results in personalized sequences — all running locally on your machine at localhost:3100.

How MailClaw Enrichment Works Under the Hood

MailClaw is built on OpenClaw, the open-source automation engine that handles orchestration, data pipelines, and AI agent behavior. The enrichment layer sits inside OpenClaw as a modular provider system. When you trigger enrichment on a contact, MailClaw extracts the root domain from the email address, then fans out requests to whichever data providers you've configured — whether that's a self-hosted lookup, a third-party API like Clearbit or Hunter, or a custom OpenClaw enrichment node you've wired up yourself.

The results are normalized into a standard contact schema and stored locally. Nothing is sent to an external server unless you've explicitly connected a provider. For teams that care about data privacy or work in regulated industries, this local-first architecture is a significant advantage over SaaS enrichment tools that treat your contact data as their own asset.

What Gets Pulled from a Domain

Depending on which providers you have active, a single domain lookup can return:

  • Company name and legal entity
  • Industry and sub-industry classification
  • Employee count range (e.g., 50–200)
  • Annual revenue estimate
  • Headquarters location (city, country)
  • Technology stack (detected via public signals — useful for knowing if a prospect uses HubSpot, Salesforce, Shopify, etc.)
  • Funding stage and total raised
  • LinkedIn company URL
  • Company description (used directly in AI-personalized copy)

That last point matters a lot. When you pass a company description into MailClaw's AI email agent, it has real context to work with — not just a first name and a guess.

Setting Up Enrichment in MailClaw

Step 1: Open the Enrichment Settings Panel

With MailClaw running, navigate to your local dashboard at localhost:3100 and click Settings → Enrichment Providers. You'll see a list of available provider slots. By default, MailClaw ships with a lightweight built-in DNS and WHOIS enricher that works offline. For richer data, you'll want to connect at least one external provider.

Step 2: Connect a Data Provider

MailClaw supports several enrichment providers out of the box. To add one via the CLI, use the following command:

mailclaw enrichment:provider add --name clearbit --api-key YOUR_API_KEY

Or for Hunter.io (useful for finding verified contacts at a domain):

mailclaw enrichment:provider add --name hunter --api-key YOUR_API_KEY --mode domain-lookup

You can chain multiple providers with a priority order. If the first provider returns incomplete data for a given field, MailClaw automatically falls back to the next one. This is configured in your openClaw.config.json file under the enrichment.pipeline key:

{
  "enrichment": {
    "pipeline": ["clearbit", "hunter", "builtin-dns"],
    "fallback": true,
    "cache_ttl_days": 30
  }
}

The cache_ttl_days setting tells MailClaw how long to trust enriched data before re-fetching — useful for keeping company headcount or funding info reasonably fresh without hammering your API quota.

Step 3: Enrich a Contact List

Once providers are configured, you can enrich any contact list from the dashboard or the CLI. To enrich an imported CSV in bulk:

mailclaw contacts:enrich --list "Q1 Prospects" --fields company,industry,size,tech_stack

MailClaw will process each contact, extract the domain from the email address, run it through your provider pipeline, and write the results back to the contact record. You can watch this happen in real time on the Enrichment Monitor tab of the dashboard — it shows provider hits, misses, fallback usage, and estimated API credit consumption.

Pro tip: Run enrichment before building your sequence, not after. The sequence builder's personalization tokens pull directly from enriched contact fields, so the richer your data is upfront, the more personalized your emails can be without any extra manual work.

Using Enriched Data in Your Email Sequences

Personalization Tokens

Every enriched field becomes a usable token inside the MailClaw sequence builder. When writing email copy, you can reference fields like:

  • {{contact.company_name}}
  • {{contact.industry}}
  • {{contact.employee_count}}
  • {{contact.tech_stack}} (returns a comma-separated list of detected tools)
  • {{contact.funding_stage}}
  • {{contact.company_description}}

A simple cold email subject line like "Quick question for [company_name]" becomes "Quick question for Acme Corp" at send time. More usefully, a body that reads "I noticed [company_name] is in the [industry] space and recently [funding_stage]…" suddenly feels like you did your homework — because MailClaw did it for you.

Letting the AI Email Agent Take It Further

MailClaw's AI email agent goes beyond token substitution. When you enable AI personalization on a sequence step, the agent receives the full enriched contact record as context and rewrites the email to feel genuinely tailored. It can pick up on technographic signals — for example, if a contact's company uses Salesforce and your product integrates with it, the agent can work that into the opening line naturally.

To enable this for a sequence step from the CLI:

mailclaw sequence:step update --sequence "Cold Outreach v2" --step 1 \
  --ai-personalize true \
  --ai-context-fields company_description,tech_stack,industry,funding_stage

The agent uses those context fields to generate a unique variation of the email for each contact. You can review a sample batch in the dashboard before committing to a send — which is strongly recommended until you've dialed in the prompt behavior for your specific use case.

Enrichment-Based Segmentation and Filtering

Enriched data isn't just useful for personalization — it's a powerful segmentation layer. In the MailClaw dashboard, the Contact Filters panel lets you build dynamic segments based on any enriched field. Some practical examples:

  • Filter to companies with 50–500 employees in the SaaS industry for an enterprise campaign
  • Target contacts whose tech stack includes HubSpot for a CRM integration pitch
  • Exclude contacts at companies with fewer than 10 employees when promoting a team-tier product
  • Build a priority segment from companies with Series B or higher funding

These filters update dynamically as new contacts are enriched, so you can set them up once and let MailClaw keep the segment fresh as your list grows.

Keeping Deliverability Clean While Enriching at Scale

One thing worth flagging: running enrichment at scale means you're making API calls based on real domain lookups, and some of those domains will belong to free email providers like Gmail or Outlook personal accounts. These contacts won't return meaningful company data, and they're often lower-quality leads in a B2B context anyway.

MailClaw's deliverability tools include a domain quality check that flags free email domains, role-based addresses (like info@ or support@), and disposable domains before enrichment runs. This saves API credits and keeps your list hygiene tight. You can run it as a pre-enrichment step:

mailclaw contacts:validate --list "Q1 Prospects" --filter-free-domains --filter-role-based

After validation, only business-domain contacts move into the enrichment pipeline — which also means your sequences are going to contacts who are far more likely to respond to company-contextualized messaging.

A Practical Workflow to Put It All Together

  1. Import your contact list via CSV or a CRM sync (Salesforce, HubSpot, or a custom integration)
  2. Run domain validation to filter out low-quality addresses
  3. Trigger bulk enrichment with your configured provider pipeline
  4. Build enrichment-based segments in the dashboard to route contacts into the right sequences
  5. Enable AI personalization on your sequence steps, passing enriched fields as context
  6. Review AI-generated email samples before activating the sequence
  7. Monitor deliverability as sends go out using MailClaw's built-in tracking and domain reputation tools

The entire pipeline runs on your machine through localhost:3100. Your contact data never touches a third-party server unless you've explicitly connected a provider — and even then, only the domain name (not the full contact record) is transmitted for the lookup.

When enrichment is wired up properly, MailClaw stops being just an email sender and becomes a genuinely intelligent outreach system — one that knows who it's talking to, what they care about, and how to frame a message that lands. That's the difference between a sequence that gets ignored and one that starts real conversations.

articles.title: How to Tag and Categorize Contacts in MailClaw
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's tagging and categorization system to segment your contacts, personalize outreach sequences, and unlock smarter AI-driven email automation — all from your local dashboard.
articles.content:
Why Contact Organization Matters More Than You Think

Most email outreach fails not because of bad copy or poor timing — it fails because it treats everyone the same. Sending a cold intro sequence to someone who already downloaded your whitepaper, or pitching a SaaS trial to a person who just closed a deal, is the kind of friction that kills deliverability and burns bridges.

MailClaw's tagging and categorization system is your answer to that problem. Because everything runs locally on your machine at localhost:3100, you have complete control over how contacts are labeled, grouped, and routed into sequences — without any data leaving your environment. This guide walks through the full workflow, from basic tag creation to using AI-powered enrichment to auto-tag contacts at scale.

Understanding Tags vs. Categories in MailClaw

Before diving into the how, it helps to understand the distinction MailClaw draws between these two concepts:

  • Tags are flexible, freeform labels you apply to individual contacts. Think of them like sticky notes — a contact can have many tags simultaneously. Examples: warm-lead, saas-founder, replied-once, do-not-contact.
  • Categories are structured groupings that organize contacts into logical buckets, typically used for sequence routing and reporting. Examples: Prospects, Customers, Partners, Churned.

Tags are many-to-many. Categories are typically one-to-one (a contact belongs to one primary category at a time, though this can be overridden). Together, they give you both the granularity of tagging and the clean segmentation of a CRM-style list structure.

Creating and Applying Tags via the Dashboard

Open your MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to the Contacts tab. From here you have two options for tagging: individual contact editing, or bulk tag operations.

Tagging Individual Contacts

  1. Click any contact row to open the contact detail panel.
  2. In the Tags field, type a new tag and press Enter, or select from existing tags in the dropdown.
  3. Tags are saved instantly — no submit button required.
  4. You can also assign or change the contact's Category from the same panel using the category selector dropdown.

Bulk Tagging from the Contact List

  1. Use the filter bar to narrow your contact list (e.g., filter by domain, enrichment data, or existing tag).
  2. Select multiple contacts using the checkboxes on the left.
  3. Click Bulk Actions → Add Tag and type your tag name.
  4. Optionally, use Bulk Actions → Set Category to assign all selected contacts to a category at once.

This is especially useful after importing a CSV from HubSpot, Salesforce, or a LinkedIn export — you can immediately bucket everyone into a starting category before your sequences begin.

Tagging Contacts via the CLI

If you prefer working from the terminal — or you're building automation scripts — MailClaw exposes a clean CLI interface powered by OpenClaw. Here are the most useful tagging commands:

Add a tag to a single contact

mailclaw contacts tag add --email "sarah@example.com" --tag "saas-founder"

Add multiple tags at once

mailclaw contacts tag add --email "sarah@example.com" --tag "saas-founder" --tag "warm-lead" --tag "series-a"

Assign a category

mailclaw contacts category set --email "sarah@example.com" --category "Prospects"

Bulk tag from a CSV file

mailclaw contacts import --file leads.csv --tag "q2-outreach" --category "Prospects"

The --tag and --category flags on the import command are a huge time-saver. Every contact in that CSV gets tagged on the way in, so your sequences can fire immediately without a manual cleanup step.

Remove or replace tags

# Remove a specific tag
mailclaw contacts tag remove --email "sarah@example.com" --tag "cold-lead"

# Clear all tags and reset
mailclaw contacts tag clear --email "sarah@example.com"

Using AI-Powered Contact Enrichment to Auto-Tag

Here's where MailClaw starts to feel genuinely intelligent. The built-in contact enrichment engine — powered by OpenClaw — can analyze a contact's email domain, LinkedIn profile, job title patterns, and firmographic signals to automatically suggest and apply tags.

To run enrichment on a segment:

mailclaw enrich run --category "Prospects" --auto-tag

With --auto-tag enabled, the enrichment engine will apply tags like b2b, enterprise, startup, ecommerce, or agency based on what it finds. You can review and adjust the auto-tag rules in the dashboard under Settings → Enrichment Rules.

You can also define custom enrichment-to-tag mappings:

mailclaw enrich rules add \
  --field "company_size" \
  --condition "gte:200" \
  --apply-tag "enterprise"

Pro tip: Combine enrichment auto-tagging with Gmail or Outlook OAuth sync. When a contact replies to one of your sequences, MailClaw can automatically re-enrich them and update their tags — so a cold-lead becomes a replied tag without you lifting a finger.

Using Tags to Control Sequence Routing

Tags and categories are most powerful when they drive your Sequence Builder logic. Instead of building one giant sequence that tries to handle everyone, you build targeted sequences that only activate for contacts with the right labels.

Tag-based sequence filters

In the Sequence Builder, when you configure the Entry Conditions for a sequence, you'll see a tag filter option:

  • Include if tagged: Only enroll contacts who have specific tags (e.g., warm-lead AND saas-founder)
  • Exclude if tagged: Never enroll contacts with certain tags (e.g., do-not-contact, customer, unsubscribed)
  • Category filter: Restrict the sequence to a single category like Prospects

This means your AI email agents can be context-aware from the very first touchpoint. A contact tagged enterprise gets a different opening email than one tagged startup, even if they're in the same campaign.

Dynamic tag updates mid-sequence

You can also add tag-update steps directly inside a sequence:

mailclaw sequence edit --id seq_29xk \
  --step 3 \
  --on-open add-tag "opened-email-3" \
  --on-click add-tag "clicked-cta" \
  --on-reply move-category "Hot Leads"

This kind of behavioral tagging is what separates a basic drip campaign from a real nurture system. Contacts self-sort based on how they engage.

Syncing Tags with External CRMs and Tools

MailClaw doesn't exist in isolation. If you're already managing contacts in HubSpot, Salesforce, or Notion, you'll want your tagging to stay in sync.

MailClaw supports bidirectional tag sync for connected integrations. For HubSpot, tags map to contact properties. For Salesforce, they map to custom fields or campaign membership. You configure this under Integrations → CRM Sync in the dashboard.

# Pull contacts from HubSpot and preserve their lifecycle stage as a tag
mailclaw sync hubspot --import --map-field "lifecyclestage" --to-tag

# Push MailClaw tags back to Salesforce as a custom field
mailclaw sync salesforce --export --map-tag-to-field "MailClaw_Tags__c"

For teams using SendGrid or Postmark for transactional mail alongside MailClaw for outreach, keeping your suppression lists tagged as transactional-only ensures you never accidentally enroll them in cold sequences.

Best Practices for a Scalable Tagging System

A tagging system that isn't governed tends to collapse under its own weight. Here are the principles that keep things clean:

  • Use lowercase, hyphenated tags consistently. warm-lead not Warm Lead or WarmLead. MailClaw is case-sensitive in CLI filters.
  • Create a tag taxonomy document. Even a simple Notion page listing your approved tags and what they mean prevents tag sprawl.
  • Audit tags quarterly. Run mailclaw contacts tag audit to see unused or duplicate tags and clean them up.
  • Use negative tags liberally. Tags like do-not-contact, bounced, and unsubscribed are as important as positive ones for protecting deliverability.
  • Let enrichment do the heavy lifting. Don't manually tag what the AI can infer — save manual tags for behavioral signals that only you can observe.

Monitoring Deliverability by Segment

One underrated use of tags is in MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools. Because your sequences are tag-filtered, the deliverability dashboard can break down open rates, bounce rates, and spam signals by tag — not just by campaign.

If your enterprise tagged contacts are bouncing at a higher rate than startup contacts, that's a data quality problem in that specific segment, not a systemic issue. You can address it surgically rather than pausing everything.

Navigate to Deliverability → Segment Report in your localhost dashboard, select a tag or category, and you'll see a full breakdown of sending health for that slice of your audience.

Organized contacts aren't just tidier — they're the foundation of email that actually performs.

articles.title: Using MailClaw AI to Find Decision-Maker Email Addresses
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's AI-powered contact enrichment and email agent features to reliably find and verify decision-maker email addresses, so your outreach lands in front of the right people every time.
articles.content:
Why Finding the Right Email Address Is Half the Battle

You can write the most compelling cold email of your career, set up a flawless sequence, and nail your subject line — and still get zero replies if you're sending to info@company.com or a gatekeeper inbox that hasn't been checked since 2019. Getting the right email address for the right decision-maker is foundational to any outreach campaign, and it's where most teams quietly lose hours every week.

MailClaw was built to close this gap. Running locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, it combines AI-powered contact enrichment, intelligent email agents, and a clean dashboard that makes the entire process — from finding a contact to sending a verified sequence — feel like one cohesive workflow rather than a stack of disconnected tools.

Understanding How MailClaw Enriches Contact Data

MailClaw's contact enrichment engine, powered by OpenClaw, doesn't just guess at email patterns. It cross-references multiple data signals to construct and validate addresses before they ever enter your outreach sequences. Here's what happens under the hood when you trigger enrichment:

  • Domain pattern inference: MailClaw analyzes known email formats from a company's domain (e.g., first.last@company.com, f.last@company.com) and applies the most statistically likely pattern to new contacts.
  • Social and public record signals: The AI agent scans publicly available signals — LinkedIn profiles, company websites, press releases, and conference speaker pages — to surface name and role data.
  • SMTP verification: Before a contact is marked as enriched, MailClaw performs a lightweight SMTP handshake to confirm the mailbox exists, without actually sending a message.
  • Deliverability scoring: Each enriched address receives a confidence score visible right in your localhost dashboard, so you can prioritize high-confidence contacts first.

The result is a contact record that isn't just a name and a guessed email — it's a verified, scored, actionable entry ready to drop into a sequence.

Step-by-Step: Finding Decision-Maker Emails with MailClaw

1. Start MailClaw and Open Your Dashboard

If you haven't started MailClaw yet, fire it up from your terminal:

mailclaw start

Then navigate to localhost:3100 in your browser. You'll land on the main dashboard where your campaigns, contacts, and agents all live. No cloud login, no subscription wall — everything runs on your machine.

2. Create a New Contact List or Import Existing Leads

Head to the Contacts tab and either create a new list or import a CSV. MailClaw accepts imports with as little as a first name, last name, and company name — the enrichment engine handles the rest. If you're pulling leads from a CRM, you can connect directly:

mailclaw import --source hubspot --list "Q3 Prospects"
mailclaw import --source salesforce --query "Title LIKE '%VP%' OR Title LIKE '%Director%'"

That second command uses MailClaw's Salesforce integration to pull only senior-level contacts — a quick way to pre-filter for decision-makers before enrichment even begins.

3. Run the AI Enrichment Agent

This is where MailClaw earns its keep. From the CLI, trigger the enrichment agent on your list:

mailclaw enrich --list "Q3 Prospects" --depth full --verify smtp

The --depth full flag tells the OpenClaw-powered agent to go beyond simple pattern matching and pull in contextual signals. The --verify smtp flag ensures every discovered address is checked before it's added to your list. You'll see a live progress feed in your terminal and a real-time update in the localhost dashboard.

Once complete, your contact list will show enriched records with email addresses, confidence scores, job titles, and in many cases LinkedIn URLs — all without leaving your local environment.

4. Review and Filter by Confidence Score

Not every enriched address will come back at 100% confidence. In the dashboard's contact view, use the built-in filter to segment by score:

  • 90–100%: High-confidence, SMTP-verified. Send immediately.
  • 70–89%: Pattern-inferred with some verification signals. Good to use, worth monitoring bounce rates.
  • Below 70%: Treat as unverified. Consider manual review or exclusion from initial sends.

This tiered approach lets you protect your sender reputation — especially important when you're sending through Gmail OAuth or a connected SendGrid account where bounce rates directly affect deliverability.

Using AI Email Agents to Go Deeper

Sometimes standard enrichment isn't enough. If you're targeting a niche industry, a company with an unusual email format, or an executive who's deliberately hard to reach, MailClaw's AI email agents can run more targeted research tasks on your behalf.

You can configure an agent directly from the dashboard or via the CLI:

mailclaw agent create \
  --name "VP Engineering Finder" \
  --task "Find verified email addresses for VP of Engineering and CTO contacts at Series B SaaS companies in the fintech vertical" \
  --output-list "Fintech Decision Makers"

The agent will work asynchronously, enriching contacts as it discovers them and appending results to the specified output list. You can check progress in the Agents tab of your dashboard or stream logs directly:

mailclaw agent logs --name "VP Engineering Finder" --follow

Pro tip: Use the agent's --persona flag to give it additional context about your ICP (ideal customer profile). The more specific the persona, the more targeted the enrichment results. For example, --persona "B2B SaaS companies with 50-200 employees selling to enterprise HR teams" dramatically improves signal quality.

Protecting Deliverability While You Scale

Finding the right email is only useful if your messages actually arrive. MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring tracks key signals across your connected accounts — whether you're using Gmail OAuth, Outlook OAuth, or a transactional provider like SendGrid or Postmark.

Monitor Bounce Rates in Real Time

In the Deliverability section of your dashboard, you'll see bounce rate, spam complaint rate, and open rate per sequence and per sending account. MailClaw will surface a warning automatically if your bounce rate climbs above safe thresholds — a safeguard that matters even more when you're sending to freshly enriched lists.

Warm Up New Addresses Gradually

When adding a new sending account — say a fresh Gmail or a custom domain SMTP — use MailClaw's built-in warmup scheduler:

mailclaw warmup start --account "outreach@yourdomain.com" --days 21 --target 200

This gradually ramps sending volume over 21 days up to 200 emails per day, building domain reputation before your main sequences go live.

From Enriched Contact to Active Sequence in Minutes

Once you've got a verified list of decision-maker emails, the next step is getting them into a sequence. MailClaw's sequence builder makes this a single workflow:

  1. Navigate to Sequences in your dashboard and click New Sequence.
  2. Choose your enriched contact list as the audience.
  3. Use the AI sequence assistant to generate a multi-step email series — initial outreach, follow-up, breakup email — based on your goal and tone.
  4. Assign a sending account (Gmail, Outlook, or SMTP) and set your daily sending limits.
  5. Activate and monitor from the same dashboard.

Because MailClaw is open-source and runs locally, you can customize every part of this pipeline — from the enrichment logic to the sequence templates — by diving into the OpenClaw configuration files in your install directory.

What This Looks Like in Practice

Imagine you're a startup selling a developer tool and want to reach CTOs and VPs of Engineering at mid-sized SaaS companies. Here's the full flow using MailClaw:

  1. Pull a list of target companies from a source like Apollo or a LinkedIn export CSV.
  2. Import into MailClaw: mailclaw import --file targets.csv --list "Dev Tool Prospects"
  3. Run full enrichment with SMTP verification on the list.
  4. Filter to contacts with 85%+ confidence scores.
  5. Launch an AI agent to fill gaps for companies that didn't enrich cleanly.
  6. Build a 4-step sequence with the sequence builder, using a technical but concise tone.
  7. Monitor deliverability live as replies start coming in.

The entire process — from raw company list to active outreach sequence — can happen in a single afternoon, and every piece of it runs on your own machine.

The Open-Source Advantage

Because MailClaw is open-source and built on OpenClaw, you're not locked into a vendor's enrichment database or subject to opaque rate limits. You control the data, the logic, and the infrastructure. That means you can extend the enrichment pipeline with your own data sources, integrate custom verification APIs, or modify the confidence scoring algorithm to match your specific use case.

For teams who take outreach seriously, that level of control isn't just nice to have — it's the difference between a tool you depend on and a tool you've outgrown.

articles.title: How to Build Ideal Customer Profile Lists with MailClaw
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to define, build, and activate Ideal Customer Profile lists using MailClaw's AI-powered contact enrichment, local dashboard, and sequence builder — turning raw prospect data into high-converting outreach campaigns.
articles.content:
Why Your ICP List Is the Foundation of Every Campaign

Most cold email campaigns fail before a single message is sent. The problem isn't the copy, the subject line, or even the sending infrastructure — it's the list. Reaching the wrong people with the right message is still a waste of everyone's time. That's why building a well-defined Ideal Customer Profile (ICP) list is the highest-leverage activity in any outbound strategy.

MailClaw gives you a local-first, AI-powered workflow to define your ICP, enrich raw contact data, score leads, and load them directly into automated sequences — all from your Mac without shipping sensitive prospect data to third-party cloud platforms. Let's walk through how to build one end to end.

Step 1: Define Your ICP Criteria Before You Touch a Tool

Before you run a single CLI command or open the dashboard at localhost:3100, get specific about who you're targeting. An ICP isn't just a persona — it's a set of filterable, verifiable attributes that you can match against real companies and contacts.

The Four Layers of a Strong ICP

  • Firmographic: Industry (e.g., SaaS, logistics, healthcare), company size (headcount, ARR), funding stage, geography.
  • Technographic: Tools they use — HubSpot vs. Salesforce, Shopify vs. Magento, AWS vs. Azure. These signal budget, sophistication, and fit.
  • Behavioral: Hiring patterns (rapidly scaling engineering teams), recent funding announcements, product launches, job postings.
  • Contact-level: Title, seniority, department, reporting structure. A VP of Marketing at a Series B SaaS company is a fundamentally different contact than a Marketing Manager at the same company.

Write these criteria down as a simple JSON object. MailClaw can actually use this structure directly when configuring enrichment jobs:

{
  "icp": {
    "industry": ["SaaS", "B2B Software"],
    "headcount_range": "50-500",
    "funding_stage": ["Series A", "Series B"],
    "technologies": ["HubSpot", "Segment", "Intercom"],
    "target_titles": ["VP of Marketing", "Head of Growth", "CMO"],
    "geography": ["US", "Canada", "UK"]
  }
}

Save this as icp-profile.json. You'll reference it in the next steps.

Step 2: Source Raw Contact Data

You need a starting point. Common sources include:

  • LinkedIn Sales Navigator exports (CSV format, filtered by your ICP criteria)
  • Apollo.io, Clay, or Hunter.io exports for email + company data
  • HubSpot or Salesforce CRM exports for warming up existing leads
  • Manual prospecting lists built from conference attendee rosters, G2 reviewers, or competitor customer pages

The quality of your raw input matters, but don't obsess over perfection here — MailClaw's enrichment engine will fill in gaps, validate emails, and score contacts against your ICP. Get a working CSV with at minimum: first_name, last_name, email (or company_domain), and company_name.

Step 3: Import and Enrich with MailClaw

With MailClaw running locally, open your terminal and import your raw list:

# Start MailClaw if not already running
mailclaw start

# Import a raw CSV prospect list
mailclaw contacts import --file prospects-raw.csv --list "ICP Q1 2025"

# Run AI-powered contact enrichment against your ICP profile
mailclaw enrich --list "ICP Q1 2025" --profile icp-profile.json --score

The --score flag activates MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered scoring model. It evaluates each contact against your ICP criteria and assigns a fit score from 0–100 based on technographic signals, title match, company size alignment, and behavioral indicators pulled from public data sources.

What Enrichment Actually Adds

After enrichment runs, each contact record is augmented with:

  • Verified or inferred work email addresses
  • LinkedIn profile URL and job tenure
  • Company tech stack (pulled from sources like BuiltWith fingerprinting)
  • Headcount and estimated ARR range
  • Recent company news or funding events (used for personalization triggers)
  • ICP fit score and score rationale

You can review enrichment results in the MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100/contacts. Filter by score, sort by fit, and spot-check records before activating any sequences.

Pro tip: Set a minimum ICP score threshold before any contact enters an active sequence. A threshold of 65+ typically filters out the noise while keeping your list large enough to be useful. You can configure this in mailclaw.config.json under sequence.min_icp_score.

Step 4: Segment Your ICP List by Persona and Intent

A single ICP list is rarely one homogeneous group. Within your enriched list, you'll find distinct segments that deserve different messaging. Use MailClaw's tagging system to create sub-segments:

# Auto-tag contacts based on title patterns
mailclaw contacts tag \
  --list "ICP Q1 2025" \
  --rule "title contains 'VP' OR title contains 'Head of'" \
  --tag "senior-decision-maker"

# Tag contacts at companies currently hiring for marketing roles
mailclaw contacts tag \
  --list "ICP Q1 2025" \
  --rule "hiring_signal == true AND department == 'Marketing'" \
  --tag "high-intent-hiring"

Now you have sub-lists you can route to different sequence variants — a more direct, ROI-focused sequence for senior decision-makers and a more educational sequence for high-intent companies still building out their team.

Step 5: Build Sequences Tailored to Each Segment

With your segments defined, head to localhost:3100/sequences to build your outreach flows. MailClaw's sequence builder lets you compose multi-step email campaigns with conditional branching based on opens, clicks, replies, and enrichment data.

A Proven ICP Sequence Structure

  1. Day 1 — The Relevance Hook: Lead with a specific observation about their business (use enrichment data like recent funding or tech stack). No pitch yet.
  2. Day 3 — The Value Bridge: Connect their likely pain point (inferred from ICP criteria) to a concrete outcome you deliver. One sentence of social proof.
  3. Day 7 — The Soft Ask: Low-friction CTA — a quick question or a link to a relevant resource, not a calendar booking.
  4. Day 12 — The Break-Up: Short, respectful close. Leave the door open. These often get the highest reply rates.

MailClaw's AI email agents can draft each step using the enrichment data as context. Run:

mailclaw agent draft-sequence \
  --segment "senior-decision-maker" \
  --tone "direct, peer-to-peer" \
  --steps 4 \
  --goal "book discovery call"

Review the drafts in the dashboard, edit for brand voice, and activate when ready.

Step 6: Configure Sending and Monitor Deliverability

A great ICP list and sharp copy can still get buried in spam folders if your sending infrastructure isn't healthy. MailClaw supports SMTP and OAuth connections to Gmail, Google Workspace, Outlook, and transactional providers like SendGrid and Mailgun.

# Add a sending account via OAuth (Gmail example)
mailclaw accounts add --provider gmail --oauth

# Or configure SMTP manually
mailclaw accounts add \
  --provider sendgrid \
  --smtp-host smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --smtp-port 587 \
  --username apikey \
  --password YOUR_API_KEY

Once connected, MailClaw's deliverability monitor (at localhost:3100/deliverability) tracks your sender reputation, SPF/DKIM/DMARC status, bounce rates, and spam complaint signals in real time. For ICP campaigns specifically, keep your daily send volume under 50 new contacts per sending account until you've established a positive reply signal — this protects your domain reputation while your list proves itself.

Maintaining and Refreshing Your ICP List Over Time

An ICP list isn't a one-time artifact. Companies change, contacts move roles, and your own product positioning evolves. Build a refresh cadence into your workflow:

  • Monthly: Re-enrich contacts who haven't been touched in 30+ days. Job changes and funding events happen fast.
  • Quarterly: Revisit your ICP definition based on win/loss data from closed deals. If your best customers share an unexpected trait, add it to the scoring model.
  • Ongoing: Automatically suppress bounced emails, unsubscribes, and contacts who've been marked as competitors or existing customers. MailClaw handles suppression lists natively — connect your HubSpot or Salesforce CRM via the integrations panel to keep them in sync.

Because MailClaw runs locally and is fully open source, your ICP data and enrichment logic stay on your machine. You can fork the OpenClaw scoring models, customize the enrichment pipeline, and adapt the sequence logic to your exact go-to-market motion — without waiting on a vendor roadmap or paying per-seat fees that scale against you as your list grows.

The best ICP list isn't the biggest one. It's the one where every contact has a legitimate reason to hear from you, and you have something genuinely relevant to say. MailClaw gives you the infrastructure to build that — methodically, repeatably, and entirely under your control.

articles.title: MailClaw Contact Hygiene: Automated Email Verification and Cleanup
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's built-in contact hygiene tools to automatically verify email addresses, remove invalid contacts, and keep your outreach lists clean — so your campaigns land in inboxes, not spam folders.
articles.content:
Why Contact Hygiene Is the Foundation of Deliverability

Every bounced email is a small strike against your sender reputation. Enough of them — whether from stale addresses, typos, or role-based inboxes like info@ or noreply@ — and mailbox providers like Gmail and Outlook start routing your messages straight to spam. By the time you notice the drop in open rates, the damage is already done.

Contact hygiene isn't a one-time cleanup task. It's an ongoing discipline, and the good news is that MailClaw makes it largely automatic. Because it runs locally on your machine at localhost:3100, all your contact data stays under your control — no third-party SaaS sharing your lists, no surprise data caps, no per-seat pricing eating into your budget.

The rule of thumb: A healthy email list has a hard bounce rate below 2% and a spam complaint rate below 0.1%. Anything higher and you're burning your sender domain.

Understanding What "Dirty" Contacts Actually Look Like

Before you can clean a list, you need to know what you're looking for. Problematic contacts generally fall into a few categories:

  • Hard bounces — The address doesn't exist. The mailbox provider rejected delivery permanently.
  • Soft bounces — The inbox is full or the server was temporarily unavailable. A few soft bounces are normal; repeated ones signal an abandoned inbox.
  • Role-based addresses — admin@, support@, sales@, and similar addresses are often shared inboxes or ticketing queues. They have high complaint rates and low engagement.
  • Disposable / temporary addresses — Services like Mailinator or Guerrilla Mail generate these. They're useless for nurture sequences.
  • Syntax errors — Simple typos like user@gmial.com or missing TLDs that slip through form validation.
  • Catch-all domains — Some domains accept every email regardless of whether the mailbox exists. These are risky to send to at scale.

MailClaw's contact enrichment engine, powered by OpenClaw, flags contacts in all of these categories automatically as they flow into your dashboard — whether you're importing a CSV, syncing from HubSpot or Salesforce, or adding leads through an API endpoint.

Setting Up Automated Verification in MailClaw

Step 1: Enable the Hygiene Layer in Your Config

If you're running a fresh MailClaw install, contact verification is available out of the box. Open your local config file and make sure the hygiene module is active:

# ~/.mailclaw/config.yaml

hygiene:
  enabled: true
  auto_verify: true
  bounce_threshold: 2        # hard bounce % before list pause
  complaint_threshold: 0.1   # spam complaint % before alert
  role_address_filter: true
  disposable_filter: true
  catch_all_handling: quarantine  # options: allow, quarantine, reject

Restart the MailClaw server after saving:

mailclaw restart

Your dashboard at localhost:3100 will now show a Hygiene Score for every contact list, updated in real time as verification runs in the background.

Step 2: Run a Bulk Verification Pass on Existing Lists

For contacts already in your system, kick off a manual verification sweep from the CLI:

mailclaw contacts verify --list "Q3 Outreach" --deep

The --deep flag triggers SMTP-level handshake verification in addition to syntax and DNS checks. This takes longer but catches catch-all domains and recently deactivated addresses that simpler tools miss. You can also scope it to a specific segment:

mailclaw contacts verify --tag "imported-2024" --output report.json

The resulting JSON report breaks down every contact into one of five statuses: valid, risky, invalid, disposable, or unknown. From the dashboard, you can bulk-action each category — archive them, tag them for review, or delete them entirely.

Step 3: Configure Auto-Quarantine Rules

You don't want to manually review every new import. Set up quarantine rules so MailClaw automatically holds suspicious contacts before they ever touch a sending sequence:

mailclaw rules create \
  --name "Block Disposables" \
  --trigger contact.created \
  --condition "hygiene.type == disposable" \
  --action quarantine

Rules run at ingestion time, so whether a contact arrives via your HubSpot sync, a Zapier webhook, or a direct API call, the same filters apply consistently.

Using AI Email Agents to Handle Bounce Feedback Loops

One of MailClaw's more powerful features is the ability to deploy AI email agents that monitor delivery feedback in real time and take action without you having to touch a dashboard. This is particularly useful when you're running multi-step sequences through Gmail OAuth or a SendGrid SMTP relay and bounces trickle in asynchronously.

Here's a simple agent configuration that automatically suppresses bounced contacts and pauses sequences when your bounce rate crosses a threshold:

# ~/.mailclaw/agents/bounce-monitor.yaml

name: Bounce Monitor Agent
trigger: delivery.event
conditions:
  - event.type == "hard_bounce"
actions:
  - contact.add_tag: "bounced"
  - contact.suppress: true
  - sequence.check_threshold:
      metric: hard_bounce_rate
      threshold: 2.0
      action: pause_and_notify

Load the agent with:

mailclaw agents load bounce-monitor.yaml

Once active, the agent watches your outbound delivery stream. The moment a hard bounce comes back — whether via Gmail's Postmaster Tools feedback, your SendGrid event webhook, or Outlook's SNDS signal — it suppresses the contact and recalculates your list health score. If the threshold is crossed, it pauses the affected sequence and pushes a notification to your dashboard.

Integrating Enrichment with Verification

Clean contacts are more valuable when they're also complete. MailClaw's contact enrichment pipeline can fill in missing fields — job title, company size, LinkedIn URL, phone — at the same time verification runs. This matters because enriched contacts let you write more personalized sequences, and personalization directly improves deliverability through higher engagement signals.

Enable enrichment alongside verification in one pass:

mailclaw contacts enrich --list "Q3 Outreach" --verify --fields title,company,linkedin

Contacts that fail verification are skipped during enrichment, saving API credits and processing time. Contacts that come back risky (catch-alls, for example) are enriched but tagged so your sequence builder can treat them differently — perhaps skipping them from cold outreach but including them in a lighter-touch newsletter sequence.

Keeping Lists Clean Ongoing: Scheduled Hygiene Jobs

A list verified today will start degrading immediately. Email addresses churn at roughly 2–3% per month as people change jobs, abandon inboxes, or switch providers. A scheduled hygiene job keeps your lists continuously healthy without manual effort.

Setting Up a Weekly Hygiene Cron

mailclaw schedule create \
  --name "Weekly List Hygiene" \
  --cron "0 3 * * 1" \
  --task contacts.verify \
  --args '--tag active --auto-suppress invalid'

This runs every Monday at 3 AM, re-verifies all contacts tagged active, and automatically suppresses any that have gone invalid since the last check. Results are logged to your dashboard with a diff showing what changed since the previous run — useful for spotting patterns like a specific lead source consistently bringing in low-quality addresses.

Monitoring Deliverability Metrics in the Dashboard

The MailClaw deliverability panel at localhost:3100/deliverability surfaces the metrics that matter most:

  • Bounce rate per campaign and per sending domain
  • Spam complaint rate correlated against recent sequence activity
  • Inbox placement estimates by mailbox provider (Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo)
  • Domain health score trends over time
  • Suppression list size and growth rate

If you're sending through multiple accounts — a common setup when you want to warm up a new domain while keeping production sends on an established one — each account's metrics are tracked separately, so a deliverability problem on one doesn't hide behind the averages of another.

Practical List Hygiene Habits That Compound Over Time

Automation handles the heavy lifting, but a few manual habits make a real difference:

  1. Validate at the source. Add real-time verification to your lead capture forms using MailClaw's embeddable API endpoint. A bad address blocked at signup costs nothing. A bad address that survives six months of sending costs your domain reputation.
  2. Sunset inactive contacts deliberately. Build a re-engagement sequence for contacts who haven't opened in 90 days. If they don't engage with the re-engagement email, suppress them. The MailClaw sequence builder makes this a 10-minute setup.
  3. Keep your suppression list portable. Because MailClaw is open source and runs locally, your suppression list is yours — export it any time and apply it across other tools. If you also send through Mailchimp or a Salesforce Marketing Cloud instance, import your suppression list there too.
  4. Review your catch-all handling quarterly. Catch-all policies change. A domain that was safe to send to last year may have switched to a catch-all configuration. Periodic re-verification catches these shifts before they hurt your metrics.

Contact hygiene isn't glamorous work, but it's the unglamorous work that keeps your sender reputation strong enough to actually reach the people you're trying to reach. With MailClaw running locally and automating the verification, suppression, and monitoring loop, you can spend your energy writing better emails instead of cleaning up the fallout from sending to bad ones.

articles.title: How to Import and Enrich Contacts from Google Sheets
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to import contacts directly from Google Sheets into MailClaw, enrich them with AI-powered data, and launch targeted email sequences — all from your local machine.
articles.content:
Why Google Sheets Is Still the Best Starting Point for Contact Lists

Despite the rise of CRMs like HubSpot, Salesforce, and Pipedrive, Google Sheets remains the scrappy workhorse of sales and marketing teams everywhere. It's fast to build, easy to share, and practically universal. Prospect lists, event attendee exports, LinkedIn scrapes, conference leads — they all end up in a spreadsheet at some point.

The problem isn't the data. It's what happens next. Copy-pasting into your CRM, manually enriching emails, trying to remember which column is the company domain versus the personal email — it's tedious and error-prone. MailClaw solves this by letting you pull a Google Sheet directly into your local pipeline, enrich the contacts with AI, and drop them into a live email sequence without ever leaving your terminal or the localhost dashboard at localhost:3100.

This guide walks you through the entire flow: formatting your sheet, importing contacts via the CLI, running enrichment, and launching your first sequence against the enriched list.

Step 1: Prepare Your Google Sheet

MailClaw's importer is flexible, but a well-structured sheet makes everything faster and gives the AI enrichment engine more to work with. Before you export or connect, clean up your columns.

Recommended Column Structure

Your sheet doesn't need to be perfect — MailClaw will map fields during import — but including the following columns will significantly improve enrichment accuracy:

  • email — Required. The primary contact email address.
  • first_name and last_name — Strongly recommended for personalization tokens.
  • company — Used by the enrichment engine to pull company-level data.
  • title or role — Helps AI agents tailor messaging by seniority or function.
  • linkedin_url — Optional but powerful for enrichment context.
  • domain — If you have the company website, include it. MailClaw can infer this from email, but explicit is better.

Remove duplicate rows, clear out any test entries, and make sure your header row uses plain text labels with no special characters. If you have columns you don't recognize or don't need, leave them in — MailClaw will let you skip or map them during import.

Export as CSV or Use the Sheets API

You have two options: export a CSV file manually, or connect MailClaw directly to the Google Sheets API for live syncing. For a one-time import, CSV is fine. For recurring lists that update frequently — like a running lead sheet your sales team populates — the API connection is worth setting up once.

To export manually: File → Download → Comma Separated Values (.csv). Save it somewhere accessible, like ~/mailclaw/imports/leads.csv.

Step 2: Import Contacts via the MailClaw CLI

With your CSV ready, open your terminal. MailClaw's CLI (powered by OpenClaw under the hood) handles imports with a single command. Navigate to your MailClaw directory and run:

mailclaw contacts import --file ~/mailclaw/imports/leads.csv --list "Q3 Outreach"

The --list flag creates or assigns contacts to a named list inside your dashboard. If the list doesn't exist yet, MailClaw creates it automatically. You'll see output like this:

✔ Parsed 247 rows
✔ Validated 241 emails (6 skipped — invalid format)
✔ Deduped against existing contacts (3 merged)
✔ Imported 238 new contacts → list: "Q3 Outreach"

Run `mailclaw contacts enrich --list "Q3 Outreach"` to enrich this list.

MailClaw automatically validates email formats, flags obvious issues (like name@company without a TLD), and deduplicates against contacts already in your database. The skipped rows get logged to ~/.mailclaw/logs/import_errors.log so you can review and fix them without losing track.

Field Mapping During Import

If your column headers don't match MailClaw's expected schema, the CLI will prompt you interactively:

Column "Full Name" not recognized.
Map to: [first_name] [last_name] [display_name] [skip] → display_name

You can also pre-define a mapping file to skip this step on future imports from the same sheet format:

mailclaw contacts import --file leads.csv --map ~/mailclaw/maps/gsheets_default.json

Step 3: Enrich Contacts with AI

This is where MailClaw starts earning its keep. Once your contacts are imported, run the enrichment command against the list:

mailclaw contacts enrich --list "Q3 Outreach" --depth full

The --depth full flag tells the OpenClaw-powered enrichment engine to go beyond basic validation and pull in contextual data for each contact. Depending on your list size, this runs in parallel and typically takes a few minutes for a few hundred contacts.

What Enrichment Actually Does

MailClaw's contact enrichment isn't just appending job titles from a static database. The AI engine cross-references multiple signals to build a richer contact profile:

  • Company data — Industry, employee count, funding stage, tech stack (useful for targeting SaaS or specific verticals).
  • Role inference — If a title is missing, MailClaw infers it from the email pattern, company size, and domain signals.
  • Email validation and deliverability scoring — Each address gets a deliverability risk score so you can filter out likely bounces before they hurt your sender reputation.
  • Social context — Where available, LinkedIn activity or company news is surfaced as personalization context for AI agents.
  • Timezone detection — Company headquarters location is used to suggest optimal send times per contact.

After enrichment, open your dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to Contacts → Q3 Outreach. You'll see each contact card now shows enriched fields, a deliverability badge, and suggested tags the AI applied based on industry and role patterns.

Pro tip: Use the deliverability score filter to exclude contacts with a score below 70 before adding them to a cold outreach sequence. This one habit can cut your bounce rate dramatically and protect your sender reputation across all connected accounts — whether you're sending via Gmail SMTP, Outlook OAuth, or a dedicated provider like SendGrid or Postmark.

Step 4: Connect to Google Sheets for Live Sync (Optional)

If your sheet is a living document — a sales team's running prospect list, for example — you'll want real-time sync instead of periodic CSV exports. MailClaw supports the Google Sheets API through its integrations config.

First, add your Google API credentials to MailClaw's config file:

mailclaw integrations add google-sheets \
  --credentials ~/mailclaw/config/google_service_account.json \
  --sheet-id "1BxiMVs0XRA5nFMdKvBdBZjgmUUqptlbs74OgVE2upms"

Then set a sync schedule using the built-in cron-style scheduler:

mailclaw contacts sync --source google-sheets --list "Q3 Outreach" --interval 6h

Every six hours, MailClaw will pull new rows from the sheet, run them through validation and enrichment, and add net-new contacts to your list. Contacts already in the system are updated if enriched fields have changed — they're never duplicated.

Step 5: Launch an Email Sequence Against Your Enriched List

With a clean, enriched contact list in hand, you're ready to put it to work. In the MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to Sequences → New Sequence and select Q3 Outreach as your audience.

Using AI Email Agents to Personalize at Scale

MailClaw's AI email agents can reference enriched fields to generate genuinely personalized messages — not just {{first_name}} substitutions, but contextually relevant copy that references the contact's industry, company stage, or recent signals picked up during enrichment.

In the sequence builder, enable the AI Agent toggle on any step and give it a prompt like:

Write a 3-sentence cold intro for {{first_name}} at {{company}}.
Reference their industry ({{industry}}) and keep it under 80 words.
End with a specific question about their current {{role}} challenges.

The agent generates a unique variation for each contact at send time, using the enriched fields as context. Combined with MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools — which track open rates, bounce signals, and spam complaints across all connected sending accounts — you get a feedback loop that improves over time.

Keeping Your Data Healthy Over Time

Importing and enriching contacts once is a good start. Keeping that data accurate over weeks and months is the real work. A few practices that help:

  • Run mailclaw contacts audit --list "Q3 Outreach" monthly to surface stale records, changed job titles, or degraded deliverability scores.
  • Use MailClaw's tag system to segment enriched contacts by industry, company size, or engagement level — this makes sequence targeting much more precise.
  • If you're syncing from Salesforce or HubSpot as a secondary source, MailClaw can merge enrichment data from multiple imports without creating duplicates, keeping your master contact database clean across tools.

Because MailClaw runs entirely on your local machine, your contact data never leaves your environment. There's no cloud database syncing your leads to a third-party server — a meaningful advantage if you're working with sensitive prospect lists or operating under data compliance requirements. The open-source foundation means you can inspect exactly how enrichment and storage work, and extend it if your workflow demands something custom.

The Google Sheets → MailClaw pipeline isn't glamorous, but it's one of the highest-leverage workflows you can set up. Clean data in, enriched and sequenced outreach out — with an AI layer that makes personalization genuinely scalable rather than just theoretically possible.

articles.title: Using MailClaw to Build Targeted Account Lists for ABM
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's AI-powered contact enrichment, sequence builder, and local dashboard to build precise account lists for account-based marketing campaigns that actually convert.
articles.content:
Why ABM Starts With the Right Account List

Account-based marketing lives or dies by the quality of your targeting. You can have the most compelling email copy in the world, but if you're sending it to the wrong people at the wrong companies, you're burning budget and goodwill simultaneously. The dirty secret of most ABM failures isn't messaging — it's list building.

Most teams cobble together account lists from a mix of LinkedIn exports, stale CRM data, and the occasional CSV from a vendor who swears their data is "freshly verified." The result is a patchwork of contacts that your sales team won't trust and your email platform will slowly get you blacklisted for sending to.

MailClaw takes a fundamentally different approach. Because it runs locally on your machine at localhost:3100, your contact data never leaves your environment. Powered by OpenClaw, it combines AI-driven enrichment, intelligent deduplication, and a clean dashboard that makes account list hygiene something you'll actually want to do — not dread.

Step 1: Define Your Ideal Customer Profile Before Touching MailClaw

Before you open the MailClaw dashboard, do the thinking work. A well-defined ICP (Ideal Customer Profile) is your filter for every decision downstream. Without it, enrichment and automation just create noise faster.

Your ICP for ABM should specify:

  • Company size — headcount range and revenue band
  • Industry verticals — specific NAICS or SIC codes if you're being precise
  • Technology stack — what tools they already use (e.g., Salesforce, HubSpot, Snowflake)
  • Geographic focus — regions, time zones, or regulatory jurisdictions that matter
  • Buying signals — recent funding, hiring sprees, product launches, leadership changes

Write this down in a plain text file. You'll use it as a prompt context when configuring MailClaw's AI email agents and enrichment filters in the next steps.

Step 2: Import Seed Data Into MailClaw

MailClaw accepts contacts from multiple sources. You can import a CSV directly through the dashboard, sync from a connected CRM, or pull from a previous campaign's engagement data.

Importing a CSV

Start MailClaw from your terminal and navigate to the Contacts panel:

# Start MailClaw on your Mac
mailclaw start

# Open the dashboard
open http://localhost:3100

From the dashboard, go to Contacts → Import and upload your seed CSV. MailClaw will auto-map common fields (first name, last name, email, company, title) and flag any columns it doesn't recognize so you can map them manually.

Pulling From HubSpot or Salesforce

If your team already has account data in a CRM, use MailClaw's native integration to sync it directly:

# Connect HubSpot
mailclaw integrations connect hubspot --api-key YOUR_API_KEY

# Pull contacts matching a list or filter
mailclaw contacts sync --source hubspot --filter "lifecycle_stage=lead&industry=SaaS"

# Connect Salesforce via OAuth
mailclaw integrations connect salesforce --oauth

The OAuth flow for Salesforce opens in your default browser and handles token storage locally. No credentials are sent to any external MailClaw server — this is one of the core advantages of the open-source, self-hosted model.

Step 3: Enrich Contacts With AI-Powered Signals

Raw import data is rarely good enough for ABM. You need enriched signals — job title seniority, verified email addresses, technology stack data, and firmographic context — before you start building segments.

MailClaw's contact enrichment engine, powered by OpenClaw, lets you enrich in bulk from the CLI or trigger enrichment on a per-contact basis through the dashboard.

# Enrich all unverified contacts in a list
mailclaw enrich --list "seed-abm-q3" --fields title,seniority,tech_stack,verified_email

# Enrich a single contact by email
mailclaw enrich --email cto@targetcompany.com --fields all

# Preview enrichment results without writing to database
mailclaw enrich --list "seed-abm-q3" --dry-run

The --dry-run flag is genuinely useful here. Run it before a large enrichment job to see what fields will be populated, what percentage of records will be updated, and what the estimated data confidence scores look like. This saves you from enriching 5,000 records only to find that 60% of them are outside your ICP.

What Enrichment Adds

For ABM specifically, pay attention to these enriched fields:

  • Seniority level — MailClaw maps job titles to a standardized seniority scale (IC, Manager, Director, VP, C-Suite) so you can filter for economic buyers vs. end users
  • Technology stack — whether an account uses Salesforce, Snowflake, AWS, or Stripe matters enormously for personalization
  • Email verification status — removes hard-bounce risk before you ever send a message
  • LinkedIn presence score — a proxy for how reachable a contact is across channels

Step 4: Segment Into Tiered Account Lists

Not all target accounts deserve the same effort. A classic ABM segmentation model uses three tiers:

  1. Tier 1 — High-touch, 1:1 personalization — 10 to 50 accounts where you'll customize every touchpoint
  2. Tier 2 — Moderate personalization by vertical or persona — 100 to 500 accounts grouped by shared characteristics
  3. Tier 3 — Programmatic, intent-driven outreach — 500+ accounts running through automated sequences

Use MailClaw's filter builder to create and save these segments from enriched data:

# Create a Tier 1 list: Series B/C SaaS, 50-500 employees, VP+ seniority
mailclaw lists create "abm-tier1-q3" \
  --filter "industry=SaaS&funding_stage=series_b,series_c&headcount=50-500&seniority=vp,c_suite"

# Create a Tier 2 list by vertical
mailclaw lists create "abm-tier2-fintech" \
  --filter "industry=fintech&seniority=director,vp&tech_stack_includes=stripe"

# Export any list to CSV for review
mailclaw lists export "abm-tier1-q3" --output ./exports/tier1-q3.csv

The dashboard's List Builder view gives you a visual breakdown of each segment — contact count, estimated deliverability score, seniority distribution, and top companies represented. It's worth reviewing this before building sequences so you catch any obvious data quality issues early.

Step 5: Validate Deliverability Before You Launch

A well-built account list means nothing if your emails land in spam. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools let you check domain reputation, DKIM/DMARC alignment, and sending account health — all from the local dashboard.

# Run a deliverability pre-check on your sending domain
mailclaw deliverability check --domain yourdomain.com

# Check health of all connected sending accounts
mailclaw accounts status

# Warm up a new Gmail or Outlook account before using it for ABM
mailclaw warmup start --account outreach@yourdomain.com --days 14

If you're using SendGrid or another SMTP provider for high-volume Tier 3 campaigns, connect it through the SMTP settings in the dashboard and run the same deliverability checks against that sending identity. MailClaw's multi-account support lets you route different tiers through different sending identities — keeping your primary domain reputation clean while scaling programmatic outreach.

Pro tip: For Tier 1 accounts, always send from a Gmail or Outlook account connected via OAuth. The inbox placement rates are meaningfully better than SMTP for small, high-stakes sends. Save SendGrid for Tier 3 volume.

Step 6: Hand Off Lists to Your AI Email Agents and Sequence Builder

Once your lists are validated and segmented, they're ready for MailClaw's sequence builder and AI email agents.

For Tier 1, configure an AI agent with your ICP context and company-specific research prompts:

# Create an AI agent for Tier 1 personalized outreach
mailclaw agents create "tier1-abm-agent" \
  --list "abm-tier1-q3" \
  --model gpt-4o \
  --context-file ./icp-context.txt \
  --personalization-fields company,tech_stack,recent_news \
  --sequence "tier1-5-step"
