The agent will draft personalized first-touch emails for each contact, pulling from the enriched fields you populated earlier. You review and approve drafts in the dashboard before anything sends — MailClaw is designed for humans in the loop, not blind automation.

For Tier 2 and Tier 3, build multi-step sequences in the sequence builder with conditional branching based on opens, clicks, and replies. Connect those sequences to your segmented lists, set your sending schedule, and MailClaw handles the rest — tracking engagement back to the dashboard so you can see which accounts are warming up.

Building Lists Is Ongoing, Not a One-Time Task

The best ABM practitioners treat their account lists as living assets. New funding rounds, executive hires, product announcements, and competitive shifts all change who belongs on your list and at what tier.

Because MailClaw runs locally and is fully open source, you can build cron jobs, webhook triggers, or custom scripts around it to automate list refreshes on whatever cadence makes sense for your business. The data stays yours, on your machine, without vendor lock-in.

Start with a clean ICP, enrich ruthlessly, segment deliberately, and validate before you send. That's the foundation of ABM that actually works — and MailClaw gives you the tooling to do it without stitching together five different SaaS subscriptions.

articles.title: How to Track Contact Engagement History in MailClaw
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how to track, query, and act on contact engagement history in MailClaw — from opening your local dashboard to writing CLI queries that surface your warmest leads automatically.
articles.content:
Why Engagement History Changes Everything About Your Outreach

Most email tools show you aggregate stats — open rates, click rates, bounce percentages. But those numbers lie by averaging. A contact who opened your email seven times in three days is fundamentally different from someone who opened it once six weeks ago, and treating them identically is one of the most common (and costly) mistakes in email marketing.

MailClaw's engagement history system is built around a simple philosophy: every signal a contact sends back to you is a piece of data worth storing, querying, and acting on. Because MailClaw runs locally on your machine at localhost:3100, all of that engagement data lives in your own environment — no third-party platform holding your contact intelligence hostage behind a paywall tier.

This guide walks you through exactly how to access, read, and automate around contact engagement history in MailClaw, whether you're a solo founder doing outreach or a team running multi-account sequences at scale.

Understanding MailClaw's Engagement Data Model

Before you start querying, it helps to understand what MailClaw actually tracks. Each contact in your MailClaw database has an associated engagement timeline that records the following event types:

  • sent — the message left your SMTP/OAuth relay (Gmail, Outlook, SendGrid, etc.)
  • delivered — confirmed delivery, where available via webhook
  • opened — pixel fire or link-based open detection
  • clicked — which links were clicked and how many times
  • replied — reply detected via inbox polling or webhook
  • bounced — hard or soft bounce with classification
  • unsubscribed — opt-out captured from link or manual flag
  • enriched — timestamp when contact enrichment last ran or updated the record

These events are stored as a flat timeline per contact, meaning you can reconstruct a full conversation arc — not just the last touchpoint. That timeline is queryable from both the dashboard and the CLI.

Viewing Engagement History in the Dashboard

Open your browser to localhost:3100 and navigate to the Contacts section. Click any contact to open their detail panel. You'll see two tabs: Profile and Engagement.

The Engagement tab renders a chronological timeline of every event MailClaw has logged for that contact. Each entry shows the event type, the sequence and step it belonged to, the sending account used, and the timestamp. If contact enrichment has run on this person — pulling in data from LinkedIn profiles, company databases, or your connected CRM like HubSpot or Salesforce — the enriched fields appear in the Profile tab alongside the raw engagement data.

Using the Engagement Score Indicator

Next to each contact's name in the list view, you'll notice a small colored dot. This is MailClaw's engagement score indicator, calculated from recency, frequency, and depth of engagement events. Green means recently active, yellow means cooling, and grey means dormant. This visual layer helps you make fast triage decisions without opening individual records.

You can adjust the scoring weights in your mailclaw.config.json file under the engagementScoring key if your use case weights replies more heavily than opens, for example.

Querying Engagement History from the CLI

One of MailClaw's most powerful features is its CLI interface. Because it's open-source and built on OpenClaw, the command layer is fully documented and scriptable. Here are the most useful engagement-related commands:

List All Events for a Contact

mailclaw contacts:engagement --email="sarah@acmecorp.com"

This returns a JSON-formatted timeline of every event recorded for that contact. Pipe it to jq for filtering:

mailclaw contacts:engagement --email="sarah@acmecorp.com" | jq '[.[] | select(.event == "opened")]'

Find Your Most Engaged Contacts

mailclaw contacts:list --sort=engagement_score --order=desc --limit=50

This surfaces your top 50 contacts by engagement score — ideal for identifying who to prioritize for a personal follow-up or a high-touch sequence.

Segment by Last Event Type

mailclaw contacts:list --last-event=replied --since="30d"

This pulls every contact who replied to something in the last 30 days. You can combine filters:

mailclaw contacts:list --last-event=opened --since="7d" --tag=cold-outreach

Export Engagement History for a Sequence

mailclaw sequences:report --id=seq_abc123 --include-engagement --format=csv > q1_outreach_report.csv

This exports a full per-contact engagement breakdown for a given sequence — useful for syncing back to Salesforce, HubSpot, or a spreadsheet for your sales team.

Automating Actions Based on Engagement History

Tracking engagement is only half the value. The real leverage comes from making MailClaw act on what it knows. This is where the sequence builder and AI email agents come together.

Branching Sequences on Engagement Signals

Inside the MailClaw sequence builder, you can add conditional branch steps that evaluate engagement history before deciding what to send next. For example:

  1. Step 1: Send initial outreach email
  2. Step 2 (Day 3): If opened ≥ 2 times → send high-intent follow-up; else → send soft nudge
  3. Step 3 (Day 7): If replied → remove from sequence and tag as hot-lead; else if bounced → flag for re-enrichment

These branches are configured in the sequence YAML file or visually in the dashboard's sequence canvas. Branching on engagement signals means your sequences behave more like conversations than broadcast blasts.

Using AI Email Agents to Respond to Engagement

MailClaw's AI email agents (powered by OpenClaw) can be configured to monitor engagement history and trigger personalized actions autonomously. For example, you can define an agent rule like this in your agent config:

{
  "trigger": {
    "event": "opened",
    "min_count": 3,
    "within_hours": 48
  },
  "action": {
    "type": "send_email",
    "template": "high_intent_followup",
    "personalize": true,
    "enrich_before_send": true
  }
}

When a contact opens an email three or more times within 48 hours, the AI agent fires a personalized follow-up, runs contact enrichment to freshen up their profile data, and sends from the appropriate account based on your multi-account routing rules. All of this happens locally — no data leaves your machine unless you're sending through an external relay like SendGrid or Gmail.

Pro tip: Combine the AI agent trigger with deliverability monitoring so that if a domain starts showing soft bounce signals, the agent pauses outreach automatically rather than burning your sender reputation.

Syncing Engagement History to External CRMs

If your team lives in HubSpot or Salesforce, you'll want engagement events to flow back into those systems so your sales reps have full context. MailClaw supports this through its outbound sync commands:

mailclaw sync:hubspot --events=opened,replied,clicked --since="7d"
mailclaw sync:salesforce --contacts-updated-since="24h" --include-engagement

You can schedule these with a simple cron job on your Mac:

# Sync engagement to HubSpot every morning at 8am
0 8 * * * /usr/local/bin/mailclaw sync:hubspot --events=all --since="24h" >> ~/mailclaw-sync.log 2>&1

For teams using Outlook-connected accounts, engagement events captured through Microsoft Graph webhooks are automatically attributed to the correct contact and appear in the same unified timeline — no separate configuration needed.

Best Practices for Keeping Engagement Data Clean

Engagement history is only as useful as it is accurate. A few habits worth building:

  • Re-enrich dormant contacts before re-engaging them. Run mailclaw contacts:enrich --tag=dormant to refresh stale records before launching a re-engagement sequence. Email addresses change, job titles shift, companies get acquired.
  • Archive, don't delete, bounced contacts. Hard bounces should be flagged and excluded from sends, but keeping the engagement history lets you audit deliverability trends over time. Use mailclaw contacts:archive --filter=hard-bounce rather than deleting records outright.
  • Tag contacts at engagement milestones. Automate tags like replied, high-intent, or at-risk based on engagement thresholds. These tags make segmentation and sequence branching much faster to set up.
  • Review your engagement score weights quarterly. As your outreach evolves, what constitutes a "warm" signal changes. Revisit engagementScoring in your config and calibrate accordingly.

Putting It All Together

Contact engagement history in MailClaw isn't a reporting feature — it's an operational layer. When you wire together the engagement timeline, the sequence builder's branching logic, AI email agent triggers, and CRM sync, you end up with an outreach system that learns from every interaction and responds intelligently rather than on a fixed schedule.

Because everything runs locally and the codebase is open-source, you can extend any piece of this — write custom event listeners, build integrations against the OpenClaw API, or modify the scoring algorithm to fit your specific workflow. That's the core promise of MailClaw: full-stack email intelligence that you actually own.

Start by pulling up a few of your most recent sequences at localhost:3100, opening the Engagement tab on your top contacts, and asking yourself: am I treating these people differently based on what they've shown me? If the answer is no, you now have the tools to fix that.

articles.title: MailClaw Smart Lists: Dynamic Segments That Update Automatically
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how MailClaw's Smart Lists automatically segment your contacts using live behavioral data, enrichment signals, and AI-driven rules — so your outreach always reaches the right people at the right time.
articles.content:
Why Static Lists Are Killing Your Campaigns

Most email tools force you into a familiar ritual: export a CSV, filter by column, import into a list, run your campaign, repeat. It works — until it doesn't. Contacts change jobs. Leads go cold. Someone who ignored your last three emails suddenly opens four in a row. By the time you've manually reshuffled your segments, the moment has passed.

MailClaw's Smart Lists solve this by treating segmentation as a living process rather than a one-time snapshot. Powered by the OpenClaw engine running locally on your machine at localhost:3100, Smart Lists evaluate your contacts continuously against a set of rules you define — and update membership automatically as conditions change. No exports. No re-imports. No stale data.

How Smart Lists Work Under the Hood

Every contact in MailClaw carries a rich profile built from multiple sources: raw import data, SMTP engagement signals (opens, clicks, bounces, replies), enrichment data pulled from third-party APIs, and behavioral tags written by your AI email agents. Smart Lists query this unified profile in real time.

When a contact's profile changes — say, MailClaw's contact enrichment layer detects they've changed their job title to "Head of Engineering" — the Smart List re-evaluates that contact immediately. If the new title matches your rule, they're added. If it no longer matches, they're removed. The whole process happens on your local machine, so there's no latency from cloud sync and no data leaving your environment.

The Evaluation Cycle

By default, Smart Lists refresh on a short polling interval (configurable in your mailclaw.config.json). You can also trigger an immediate re-evaluation from the CLI:

mailclaw lists refresh --list-id=eng-leads --force

Or watch a list in real time during development:

mailclaw lists watch --list-id=eng-leads

This is especially useful when you're testing a new rule set and want to see which contacts fall in or out as you adjust conditions.

Building Your First Smart List

Open your local dashboard at http://localhost:3100, navigate to Lists → New Smart List, and you'll see the rule builder. Rules are structured as condition groups — you can nest AND/OR logic to handle complex scenarios.

A Simple Example: Active Trial Users

Let's say you want a list of contacts who are currently in a free trial, have opened at least one email in the last 14 days, and work at a company with more than 50 employees. In the dashboard, that's three conditions. From the CLI, you can express the same thing in a YAML rule file:

name: "Active Trial Users"
match: all
rules:
  - field: tags
    operator: contains
    value: "trial"
  - field: engagement.last_open_days
    operator: less_than
    value: 14
  - field: enrichment.company_size
    operator: greater_than
    value: 50
mailclaw lists create --from-file=active-trial.yaml

MailClaw's contact enrichment will automatically fill enrichment.company_size for contacts where it's missing, pulling from configured providers — so even if your original CSV didn't include that field, the list will populate correctly as enrichment runs.

Using Engagement Data as a Signal

Engagement-based segmentation is where Smart Lists really shine. You can create a list that captures contacts who've become re-engaged after a long silence — perfect for feeding into a win-back sequence:

name: "Re-Engaged Cold Leads"
match: all
rules:
  - field: engagement.last_open_days
    operator: less_than
    value: 7
  - field: engagement.prior_silence_days
    operator: greater_than
    value: 60
  - field: sequence.status
    operator: not_in
    value: ["active", "completed"]

When a contact from your dormant pool opens an email today, they automatically appear in this list by tomorrow — and if you've wired this list to a sequence in the sequence builder, they'll enter that win-back flow without any manual intervention.

Connecting Smart Lists to Sequences and AI Agents

A Smart List on its own is just a view. The real power comes from connecting it to action.

Triggering a Sequence Automatically

In the sequence builder, any sequence entry point can be set to List Membership as its trigger. When a contact joins the Smart List, they immediately enter step one of the sequence. When they leave the list (because conditions no longer apply), they can be optionally paused or exited.

mailclaw sequences link \
  --sequence-id=win-back-flow \
  --trigger=list_join \
  --list-id=re-engaged-cold-leads \
  --exit-on-leave=true

Feeding Your AI Email Agents

MailClaw's AI email agents are designed to operate on specific audiences. Rather than pointing an agent at your entire contact database, you scope it to a Smart List. This means the agent's context — tone calibration, personalization signals, send-time optimization — is always working with a coherent, current audience.

For example, you might have a Smart List of contacts who've clicked a pricing page link in the last 48 hours. Your AI agent watching this list can draft hyper-relevant follow-ups that reference pricing conversations, then route them for your review or send automatically depending on your confidence threshold settings.

Pro tip: Keep your AI agent scopes narrow. An agent pointed at "clicked pricing link, last 48 hours, not yet replied" will write dramatically better copy than one pointed at your entire prospect pool.

Smart List Recipes Worth Stealing

Here are a few high-value Smart List configurations that work well across most B2B outreach workflows:

  • Champions list: Contacts who've replied positively (sentiment tag: positive), are in a closed-won deal stage synced from HubSpot or Salesforce, and haven't been contacted in the last 90 days. Great for referral or upsell campaigns.
  • Deliverability risk list: Contacts with a bounce history or spam complaint flag. Keep these out of your warm sending pools automatically. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring writes these flags directly to contact profiles.
  • Job-change radar: Contacts whose enriched company_domain has changed since initial import. These people are in a new environment, often with fresh budget and fresh problems — a perfect re-engagement moment.
  • Gmail vs. Outlook segmentation: Contacts whose email domain resolves to Google Workspace or Microsoft 365. Useful for send-time and formatting decisions, since rendering behavior differs between the two clients.
  • SendGrid health filter: If you're routing sends through SendGrid alongside your OAuth accounts, this list surfaces contacts that have historically low deliverability on that sending route, so you can re-route them to a warmer account.

Syncing Smart Lists with External CRMs

If you've connected MailClaw to HubSpot or Salesforce via the integrations panel, Smart List membership can write back as a contact property or list membership on the CRM side. This means your sales team's views in HubSpot stay in sync with the segmentation logic you're running locally — no manual exports, no "which version is current" conversations.

mailclaw integrations sync \
  --provider=hubspot \
  --list-id=active-trial-users \
  --crm-list-name="MailClaw: Active Trial" \
  --direction=bidirectional

Bidirectional sync means that CRM-side changes (a rep marks a contact as "not a fit") can also remove them from your Smart List, preventing unwanted outreach to contacts your sales team has already disqualified.

Keeping Lists Healthy Over Time

Smart Lists can accumulate technical debt just like code. A few habits that will save you headaches:

  1. Name your lists for intent, not content. "Opened last 7 days" is fragile. "Top-of-funnel warm leads" tells you why the list exists, making it easier to audit the rules later.
  2. Set a membership ceiling. Very broad rules can produce massive lists that slow down enrichment and sequence evaluation. Use max_members in your rule file to cap membership and force yourself to be more precise.
  3. Review exit conditions as carefully as entry conditions. A contact who joins a list should have a clear path out — otherwise you'll accumulate stale members over time.
  4. Use the audit log. MailClaw logs every list membership change with a timestamp and the rule that triggered it. From the dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to Lists → [Your List] → Audit to see exactly why a contact was added or removed.

Smart Lists are one of those features that feels like overhead until you've set up two or three of them correctly — and then you can't imagine going back to static CSV segments. The combination of real-time enrichment, engagement signals, AI agent scoping, and sequence triggers means your outreach adapts to your contacts' behavior rather than the other way around. That's the core promise of running an intelligent, open-source email stack locally: the data is yours, the logic is yours, and the system moves at the speed your contacts do.

articles.title: How to Export Enriched Contacts from MailClaw to Your CRM
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to export enriched contact data from MailClaw into HubSpot, Salesforce, and other CRMs using CLI commands, the local dashboard, and custom field mapping — so your outreach intelligence doesn't stay siloed on your Mac.
articles.content:
Why Enriched Contacts Are Worth Exporting

When MailClaw's contact enrichment engine finishes its work, you're not looking at a plain spreadsheet anymore. You're looking at contacts augmented with job titles, company size, LinkedIn profiles, email verification scores, engagement signals, and sequence history — all processed locally on your machine through the OpenClaw-powered backend running at localhost:3100.

The problem is that most teams run their CRM separately. HubSpot, Salesforce, Pipedrive, Notion databases — whatever your team uses as the source of truth, that's where enriched data needs to land. Leaving it inside MailClaw means your sales reps are flying blind, your account managers can't see who opened what, and the intelligence your AI email agents worked hard to surface gets wasted.

This guide walks you through every practical method for getting enriched contacts out of MailClaw and into your CRM cleanly, correctly, and without losing the fields that matter most.

Step 1: Enrich Your Contacts First

Before you export anything, make sure enrichment has actually run. Open your local MailClaw dashboard at http://localhost:3100, navigate to Contacts → Enrichment Queue, and confirm your contacts show a status of Enriched rather than Pending or Partial.

If you're working from the CLI, you can trigger enrichment and check status directly:

# Enrich all contacts in a specific list
mailclaw contacts enrich --list="Q4 Prospects"

# Check enrichment status
mailclaw contacts status --list="Q4 Prospects" --filter=enriched

MailClaw's enrichment pipeline pulls from multiple data sources and validates email deliverability using its built-in deliverability tools before marking a record as fully enriched. Don't skip this step — exporting partial records into a CRM creates messy duplicates and missing fields that are annoying to clean up later.

Step 2: Choose Your Export Format

MailClaw supports several export formats, each suited to different CRM workflows. The right choice depends on how your target CRM ingests data.

CSV Export (Universal)

CSV is the safest universal option. Every major CRM — HubSpot, Salesforce, Pipedrive, Zoho, ActiveCampaign — can import a CSV file. From the dashboard, go to Contacts → Export → CSV and select which fields to include. From the CLI:

# Export enriched contacts from a specific sequence to CSV
mailclaw contacts export \
  --list="Q4 Prospects" \
  --format=csv \
  --fields="email,first_name,last_name,company,title,linkedin_url,phone,enrichment_score,last_opened,sequence_name" \
  --output="./exports/q4-prospects-enriched.csv"

The --fields flag is important. By default, MailClaw exports its full internal schema, which includes fields your CRM won't recognize. Be selective — export only what maps cleanly to your CRM's contact properties.

JSON Export (For Developers)

If you're piping data into a custom integration or building a middleware layer with something like Zapier, Make, or a custom Node script, JSON gives you structured data that's much easier to work with programmatically:

mailclaw contacts export \
  --list="Q4 Prospects" \
  --format=json \
  --enriched-only \
  --output="./exports/q4-prospects.json"

The --enriched-only flag filters out any contacts that didn't complete the enrichment pipeline, keeping your export clean.

Direct API Push (Advanced)

MailClaw's local API, available at http://localhost:3100/api/v1, lets you query enriched contacts programmatically and push them to your CRM's API in real time. This is the most powerful option for teams that want a live sync rather than periodic exports.

Step 3: Map MailClaw Fields to CRM Properties

This is where most exports go wrong. MailClaw uses its own field naming convention internally, and CRMs like Salesforce and HubSpot have their own property keys. Before you import anything, build a field map.

Here's a practical mapping reference for HubSpot:

  • email → email
  • first_name → firstname
  • last_name → lastname
  • company → company
  • title → jobtitle
  • linkedin_url → hs_linkedinid (or a custom property)
  • enrichment_score → custom property: mailclaw_enrichment_score
  • last_opened → custom property: mailclaw_last_email_open
  • sequence_name → custom property: mailclaw_sequence

For Salesforce, the mapping looks slightly different — first_name becomes FirstName, company becomes Account.Name on the Lead object, and so on. Always do a dry-run import with 10–20 records before pushing your full list.

Pro tip: Create a dedicated custom property in your CRM called mailclaw_enrichment_score before importing. This score — generated by MailClaw's deliverability and engagement analysis — is one of the most useful signals for prioritizing follow-up, and you don't want it lost in a notes field.

Step 4: Import Into Your CRM

HubSpot

HubSpot's import flow is forgiving. Go to Contacts → Import → Start an Import → File from computer, upload your CSV, and use HubSpot's column mapping interface to match fields. If you've pre-created custom properties for MailClaw-specific fields, they'll appear in the dropdown. Enable Update existing contacts to avoid duplicates if these contacts already exist in HubSpot.

Salesforce

Use the Data Import Wizard for smaller lists (under 50,000 records) or Data Loader for bulk imports. Choose the Leads or Contacts object depending on your pipeline stage. Salesforce is strict about field types — make sure date fields like last_opened are formatted as YYYY-MM-DD in your export before importing.

# Format date fields correctly on export
mailclaw contacts export \
  --list="Q4 Prospects" \
  --format=csv \
  --date-format="YYYY-MM-DD" \
  --output="./exports/q4-salesforce-ready.csv"

Pipedrive, Zoho, and Others

Most other CRMs follow the same CSV import pattern as HubSpot. The one thing to watch for is how they handle duplicate detection — usually by email address. Make sure your exported emails are clean and de-duplicated, which MailClaw's deliverability tools handle automatically during enrichment.

Automating the Export with a Scheduled Job

If you're running ongoing outreach sequences through MailClaw's sequence builder, you probably don't want to manually export contacts every week. You can automate this with a simple cron job that exports and syncs on a schedule.

# Example cron job — runs every Monday at 8am
0 8 * * 1 mailclaw contacts export \
  --list="Active Sequences" \
  --format=json \
  --enriched-only \
  --output="/path/to/sync/contacts.json" && \
  node /path/to/scripts/push-to-hubspot.js

The companion Node script can use HubSpot's or Salesforce's official SDK to upsert records. Because MailClaw runs entirely on localhost, there are no rate limits or API costs on the MailClaw side — you're only constrained by your CRM's API limits.

What to Do with Engagement Data

One of the most underused exports from MailClaw is engagement data — opens, clicks, replies, and sequence stage — generated by your AI email agents as they run outreach campaigns. This data is gold for CRM segmentation.

When you import enriched contacts into HubSpot or Salesforce, consider creating a workflow or automation rule that triggers when mailclaw_enrichment_score is above a certain threshold, or when mailclaw_last_email_open is within the last 7 days. These signals let your CRM automatically route warm leads to a sales rep or enroll them in a nurture sequence — closing the loop between MailClaw's outreach intelligence and your CRM's pipeline management.

Keeping Your Data in Sync Over Time

Exporting once is a start. The real value comes from keeping MailClaw and your CRM in sync as new contacts are enriched and new sequences run. A few practices that help:

  • Tag contacts by export batch in MailClaw using mailclaw contacts tag --list="Q4 Prospects" --tag="exported-2024-01" so you know what's been synced.
  • Use incremental exports with the --since flag to only pull contacts enriched or updated after a specific date, reducing noise in your CRM imports.
  • Leverage multi-account support in MailClaw to segment exports by sending account — useful when different team members own different CRM territories.
  • Monitor deliverability scores before exporting — contacts with poor deliverability scores from MailClaw's built-in monitoring probably shouldn't be pushed to your CRM at all, and filtering them out keeps your CRM data healthier.
# Incremental export — only contacts enriched in the last 7 days
mailclaw contacts export \
  --list="All Contacts" \
  --enriched-only \
  --since="7d" \
  --format=csv \
  --output="./exports/incremental-$(date +%F).csv"

Because MailClaw is open source and built on OpenClaw, you also have full access to the underlying data models if you want to build a deeper, custom integration. The local dashboard at localhost:3100 exposes a complete API explorer under Settings → Developer → API Reference where you can test endpoints and build your sync logic interactively.

Getting enriched contacts out of MailClaw and into your CRM is one of those workflows that feels like extra work the first time and saves hours every week after that. Do it right once — map your fields carefully, automate the export, and sync engagement signals — and your CRM becomes meaningfully smarter without anyone having to manually update a record again.

articles.title: Using MailClaw AI for Prospect Research Before Outreach
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's AI-powered contact enrichment and email agents to conduct deep prospect research before sending a single outreach email — so every message lands with context, relevance, and a real shot at a reply.
articles.content:
Why Prospect Research Changes Everything About Cold Outreach

Most cold emails fail before they're even opened. Not because of bad subject lines or broken deliverability — but because they were written without knowing anything meaningful about the person receiving them. A generic "Hi [First Name], I wanted to reach out about..." isn't personalization. It's mail merge with a thin disguise.

Real prospect research — understanding someone's role, their company's recent activity, their tech stack, their pain points — is what separates a 2% reply rate from a 20% one. The problem has always been time. Researching 50 prospects manually across LinkedIn, company websites, Crunchbase, and news feeds can take hours. That's where MailClaw changes the equation entirely.

Because MailClaw runs locally on your machine (at localhost:3100), your prospect data never leaves your environment. There's no third-party SaaS storing your contact lists or your research. It's open source, built on OpenClaw, and gives you full control over the AI agents doing the heavy lifting.

Setting Up Your Research Workflow in MailClaw

Step 1: Import Your Raw Contact List

Start by importing your raw prospect list into MailClaw. You can pull in contacts from a CSV, connect directly to HubSpot or Salesforce via the integrations panel, or use the CLI to import in bulk:

# Import contacts from CSV
mailclaw contacts import --file prospects.csv --list "Q3 Outreach"

# Pull contacts from HubSpot CRM
mailclaw contacts sync --source hubspot --list "Q3 Outreach" --limit 200

At this stage, your list might just have names, email addresses, and company names. That's fine — enrichment happens next.

Step 2: Run Contact Enrichment

MailClaw's contact enrichment engine uses AI to fill in the gaps. From the dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to Contacts → Enrich, select your list, and choose what data points you want appended. Alternatively, run it straight from the CLI:

# Enrich a contact list with job title, company size, and tech stack
mailclaw enrich --list "Q3 Outreach" --fields title,company_size,tech_stack,linkedin_url,industry

# Enrich a single contact by email
mailclaw enrich --email sarah@acmecorp.com --fields all

Within minutes, MailClaw will return enriched profiles for each prospect — including their current role, company headcount, funding stage (if available), and in many cases their LinkedIn profile URL and inferred technology stack. This data is stored locally in MailClaw's contact database and is available to every downstream feature, including your AI email agents and sequence builder.

Using AI Email Agents for Deep Research

Enrichment fills in structured data. But the real depth comes from MailClaw's AI email agents — autonomous research assistants that you can instruct to gather contextual intelligence about a prospect or company before you write a single word.

Creating a Research Agent

In the MailClaw dashboard, go to Agents → New Agent and select the Prospect Research template. You'll define the agent's scope — what to look for, where to look, and how to format its findings. Here's an example agent configuration:

{
  "agent_name": "Pre-Outreach Researcher",
  "trigger": "before_sequence_start",
  "tasks": [
    "Find recent news or press releases about the company",
    "Identify the prospect's likely top 3 business priorities based on their role",
    "Check for any recent funding rounds or leadership changes",
    "Note any shared connections or mutual context",
    "Summarize findings in 3 bullet points for use in email personalization"
  ],
  "output_field": "contact.research_summary",
  "model": "openClaw-research-v2"
}

Once saved, this agent runs automatically for every new contact added to your sequence. The output is written to a custom field on the contact record, which you can then reference as a variable in your email templates using {{contact.research_summary}}.

What Good Research Output Looks Like

Here's an example of what the agent might return for a prospect at a Series B SaaS company:

Research Summary — Sarah Chen, VP of Marketing at Acme Corp:
• Acme Corp raised a $22M Series B in March 2024 and is actively expanding into enterprise accounts — marketing team likely under pressure to build pipeline quickly.
• Sarah was promoted to VP from Director 6 months ago; she's likely still establishing her stack and may be open to evaluating new tools.
• The company recently posted 3 job openings for demand generation roles, suggesting they're scaling outbound efforts.

That's the kind of context that turns a cold email into a warm, informed conversation starter. And it was generated in seconds, not hours.

Translating Research Into Sequences That Actually Convert

Using Research Fields in Your Sequence Builder

MailClaw's sequence builder lets you reference any enriched or agent-generated field directly in your email copy. When you're building a sequence step, use the variable picker or type fields manually:

Subject: Quick question about {{contact.company}}'s growth plans

Hi {{contact.first_name}},

Congrats on the recent Series B — scaling enterprise pipeline is exactly the kind
of challenge I work on every day.

{{contact.research_summary}}

That's why I thought it was worth reaching out. Would love to share what's working
for similar VP-level teams right now.

Open to a 15-minute call this week?

This isn't a template with a name swapped in. It's a message that references what's actually happening in their world right now. The research does the personalization work — your sequence builder just delivers it at scale.

Segmenting by Research Signals

Once your contacts are enriched, you can use MailClaw's list segmentation to split your outreach by research signals. For example:

  • Funded in the last 90 days → Lead with growth and scale messaging
  • Hiring for sales or marketing roles → Lead with efficiency and tooling angles
  • Using a competitor's product → Lead with differentiation and switching ease
  • Leadership change in the last 6 months → Lead with fresh-start and quick-win framing

Each segment gets its own sequence, its own angle, and its own tone. All of this is manageable from a single MailClaw dashboard running locally — no extra subscriptions, no data leaving your machine.

Keeping Deliverability Clean During Research-Backed Campaigns

Personalized emails tend to perform better on deliverability too — lower bounce rates, higher engagement signals, fewer spam complaints. But MailClaw also has dedicated deliverability monitoring built in, so you can track domain health as your campaigns run.

From the dashboard, check Deliverability → Inbox Score to see how your sending domains are performing. If you're using multiple accounts — Gmail via OAuth, Outlook, or a dedicated sending domain through SendGrid or Postmark — MailClaw monitors each one independently and flags any warming issues before they compound.

# Check deliverability health for all connected accounts
mailclaw deliverability check --all

# Run inbox placement test for a specific sequence
mailclaw deliverability test --sequence "Q3 Enterprise Outreach" --provider gmail,outlook

A research-backed email campaign only works if the emails actually land in inboxes. Combining strong personalization with proactive deliverability management is the full picture.

The Compounding Advantage of Local, Open-Source Research

Here's what makes the MailClaw approach genuinely different from cloud-based outreach tools: because everything runs locally and the codebase is open source, you can extend it. If you want to connect a custom data source — a niche industry database, a proprietary CRM export, a web scraper you've built — you can wire it into the enrichment pipeline directly.

Your research compounds over time too. Every contact you enrich, every agent output you generate, every sequence result you record builds a richer local database. Over months, you start to see patterns: which signals correlate with replies, which industries respond to which angles, which research fields actually move the needle.

That's the kind of institutional knowledge most sales teams lose when they switch tools or when their CRM data gets stale. With MailClaw, it stays with you — structured, searchable, and AI-ready for the next campaign.

Getting Started Today

If you haven't already, spin up MailClaw locally and run your first enrichment job against a small list of 10–20 prospects. Configure a basic research agent with three or four tasks. Write one sequence step that uses the output. Send it to yourself first and read it back — not as the sender, but as the recipient.

You'll immediately feel the difference between an email that knows something about you and one that's just hoping for a click. That feeling is exactly what your prospects experience too. And once you've felt it, it's very hard to go back to spraying and praying.

articles.title: How to Manage Opt-Outs and Unsubscribes in MailClaw
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to handle opt-outs and unsubscribes properly in MailClaw — from configuring automatic suppression lists to staying compliant with CAN-SPAM and GDPR, so your sender reputation stays clean and your campaigns keep landing in inboxes.
articles.content:
Why Opt-Out Management Is Non-Negotiable

Every email you send carries a legal and ethical obligation: if someone wants off your list, they need a clear, fast, and friction-free way to get there. Under CAN-SPAM, you have 10 business days to honor an unsubscribe request. Under GDPR, it's immediate. Under CASL, the burden is even higher — you need express consent before you send anything in the first place.

But compliance aside, mismanaging opt-outs is a deliverability killer. Gmail and Outlook both use engagement signals — including spam complaints and unsubscribes — as inputs into their filtering decisions. If you're sending to people who've already said no, your open rates drop, your complaint rates climb, and your domain reputation pays the price. When MailClaw is your sending engine, protecting that reputation is built into the workflow.

How MailClaw Handles Unsubscribes Automatically

MailClaw maintains a global suppression list that applies across all your campaigns, sequences, and AI agent outreach. When a contact unsubscribes — whether through a tracked link, a reply, or a manual action — their address is added to this list automatically and excluded from all future sends, regardless of which account or SMTP provider you're using.

You can view and manage the suppression list directly from your localhost dashboard at http://localhost:3100/suppressions. From there you can search, export, bulk-import, and audit every suppressed contact along with the reason and timestamp.

Configuring Your Unsubscribe Link

MailClaw injects a one-click unsubscribe header and a footer link by default for sequences marked as marketing or cold outreach. You can customize the unsubscribe experience in your campaign settings:

# In your sequence config (sequences/welcome-series.yaml)
unsubscribe:
  mode: one_click          # 'one_click' | 'landing_page' | 'reply'
  landing_page_url: ""     # leave blank to use MailClaw's built-in page
  footer_text: "Don't want to hear from us? Unsubscribe instantly."
  suppress_globally: true  # adds to global list, not just this campaign

Setting suppress_globally: true is strongly recommended — it prevents the embarrassing scenario where someone unsubscribes from one sequence and then gets re-enrolled into another by accident.

Reply-Based Opt-Out Detection

One of MailClaw's more useful AI features is reply intent classification, powered by OpenClaw's language model layer. When a contact replies to any email in a sequence, the AI agent reads the reply and classifies its intent. Replies like "please remove me," "stop emailing me," or "unsubscribe" are automatically flagged as opt-out signals, the contact is suppressed, and the sequence is paused — no manual review needed.

You can tune the sensitivity of this detection in your agent config:

# In your agent config (agents/outreach-agent.yaml)
reply_handling:
  opt_out_detection: true
  confidence_threshold: 0.82   # 0.0–1.0, lower = more aggressive detection
  auto_suppress: true
  notify_on_suppress: true     # sends you a dashboard notification
Pro tip: Set confidence_threshold between 0.80 and 0.90. Lower values catch ambiguous replies like "not interested right now" as opt-outs, which is safer for reputation even if it means slightly fewer follow-ups.

Syncing Opt-Outs With Your CRM and Other Tools

If you're running campaigns that feed into HubSpot, Salesforce, or another CRM, keeping your suppression data in sync is critical. Nothing damages a sales team's credibility faster than calling a prospect who just asked to be removed from email outreach.

HubSpot Integration

MailClaw's contact enrichment layer supports two-way sync with HubSpot. When a contact is suppressed in MailClaw, you can push a property update back to HubSpot automatically:

# Run from the MailClaw CLI
mailclaw integrations hubspot configure \
  --api-key YOUR_HUBSPOT_API_KEY \
  --sync-opt-outs true \
  --opt-out-property "hs_email_optout"

Once configured, every suppression event will flip the hs_email_optout property in HubSpot, marking the contact as opted out there too. You can also run a one-time backfill to reconcile existing suppressions:

mailclaw integrations hubspot sync-suppressions --direction push --dry-run

Remove --dry-run once you've confirmed the output looks correct.

Salesforce Integration

For Salesforce users, MailClaw maps suppressions to the HasOptedOutOfEmail field on the Lead or Contact object. Configure it similarly:

mailclaw integrations salesforce configure \
  --client-id YOUR_SF_CLIENT_ID \
  --client-secret YOUR_SF_CLIENT_SECRET \
  --sync-opt-outs true

SendGrid and SMTP Provider Suppression Lists

If you're routing sends through SendGrid, you'll want MailClaw's suppression list and SendGrid's Global Unsubscribe list to stay in sync. MailClaw can pull SendGrid suppression data on a schedule and merge it into your local list:

mailclaw suppressions import --source sendgrid \
  --api-key YOUR_SENDGRID_KEY \
  --merge-strategy union

The --merge-strategy union flag means any address suppressed in either system gets suppressed in both. This is the safest approach.

Manual Opt-Out Workflows

Sometimes opt-outs come through channels you don't control — a phone call, a LinkedIn message, someone emailing your support address. MailClaw's CLI makes it easy to handle these manually:

# Suppress a single address
mailclaw suppressions add --email "jane@example.com" --reason "phone request"

# Suppress a bulk list from a CSV
mailclaw suppressions import --file ./manual-optouts.csv --reason "manual"

# Check if an address is suppressed before sending
mailclaw suppressions check --email "jane@example.com"

The --reason field is logged with a timestamp and your system username, giving you a clean audit trail if you ever need to demonstrate compliance.

Monitoring Opt-Out Rates in the Dashboard

Your MailClaw localhost dashboard at http://localhost:3100 includes a Deliverability panel that surfaces opt-out rate by campaign, sequence, and sending domain. Here's what to watch for:

  • Opt-out rate above 0.5% — investigate the sequence's messaging or targeting before sending more volume
  • Spam complaint rate above 0.1% — Gmail and Yahoo will start throttling or blocking your domain
  • Sudden spike in unsubscribes — often signals a bad contact enrichment source or a message that landed wrong

MailClaw's deliverability tools will also flag if your opt-out rate is trending upward across multiple campaigns, which can indicate a broader list quality issue worth addressing at the source — usually in your contact enrichment settings or import filters.

Setting Up Opt-Out Rate Alerts

You can configure threshold-based alerts that notify you via your dashboard or a webhook when opt-out rates breach a limit:

# In your global MailClaw config (~/.mailclaw/config.yaml)
alerts:
  opt_out_rate:
    warn_threshold: 0.004    # 0.4%
    critical_threshold: 0.01 # 1.0%
    webhook_url: "https://hooks.slack.com/your-webhook-url"

Best Practices to Reduce Opt-Outs in the First Place

The best opt-out management strategy is one you rarely have to use. A few habits that keep opt-out rates low:

  1. Segment before you send. MailClaw's contact enrichment can tag contacts by industry, company size, or role. Use these tags to send relevant messages to the right people instead of blasting your whole list.
  2. Pace your sequences realistically. The sequence builder lets you set delays between steps — don't compress a 5-step sequence into 6 days. Give people room to breathe.
  3. Personalize with AI agents. Generic outreach gets ignored or reported. MailClaw's AI email agents can generate personalized first lines, reference recent company news, and adapt tone based on contact data — all locally, without sending your data to a third-party API.
  4. Make unsubscribing easier than marking as spam. A clean, visible unsubscribe link in every email is table stakes. People who can't find the unsubscribe button hit the spam button instead, and spam complaints hurt you far more than unsubscribes.
  5. Honor preference updates, not just full opt-outs. Consider offering a preference center — MailClaw's landing page builder supports this — where contacts can reduce frequency or opt out of specific topics without leaving your list entirely.

Staying Compliant Long-Term

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your local machine, you have full visibility into and control over how contact data is stored, processed, and deleted. There are no third-party servers holding your suppression list. This matters for GDPR's right to erasure — when someone asks to be deleted, you can run:

mailclaw contacts delete --email "jane@example.com" --purge-all

The --purge-all flag removes the contact from your contact database, all sequence history, and enrichment cache — while preserving their entry in the suppression list (which is required to prevent accidentally re-importing and emailing them in the future). It's a distinction that matters legally: suppression and deletion serve different purposes.

Good opt-out management isn't just a compliance checkbox — it's the foundation of a healthy sender reputation, a more engaged list, and campaigns that actually perform. MailClaw gives you the tooling to do it right, automatically and at scale, without depending on an external platform to get it done.

articles.title: MailClaw for Data Teams: Bulk Email Verification and Enrichment
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how data teams can use MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment and bulk email verification workflows to clean lists, reduce bounce rates, and launch higher-converting outreach campaigns — all from a local dashboard with zero data leaving your machine.
articles.content:
Why Data Quality Is the Foundation of Every Email Campaign

Bad data is expensive. A contact list riddled with invalid addresses, outdated job titles, and missing enrichment fields doesn't just hurt your sender reputation — it wastes hours of sales and marketing time, inflates your bounce rate, and trains inbox providers to distrust your domain. For data teams tasked with maintaining the integrity of CRM exports from HubSpot, Salesforce, or a custom database, email verification and enrichment are table-stakes hygiene steps that often get skipped because the tooling is fragmented, expensive, or requires shipping your data to a third-party SaaS platform.

MailClaw changes that calculus entirely. Because it runs locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, your contact data never leaves your machine. Powered by OpenClaw, MailClaw combines bulk email verification, AI-driven contact enrichment, sequence automation, and deliverability monitoring in a single open-source tool — giving data teams a repeatable, auditable pipeline they actually control.

Understanding MailClaw's Verification and Enrichment Pipeline

Before diving into workflows, it helps to understand what MailClaw is doing under the hood when it processes a contact list. The pipeline has three distinct stages:

  • Syntax and format validation — Catches malformed addresses before any network call is made.
  • MX record and SMTP verification — Confirms the domain accepts mail and probes deliverability without sending a real message.
  • AI enrichment — Uses the OpenClaw AI layer to fill in missing fields like job title, company size, industry, and LinkedIn URL based on the verified email address and any existing context in your contact record.

The result is a cleaned, enriched contact list that flows directly into MailClaw's sequence builder or exports cleanly back to your CRM — no manual reconciliation required.

Setting Up a Bulk Verification Job

Importing Your Contact List

MailClaw accepts CSV imports directly from the local dashboard or via the CLI. If you're pulling a fresh export from Salesforce or HubSpot, save it as a UTF-8 CSV and run:

mailclaw contacts import --file ~/exports/leads_q2.csv --map email:Email,name:FirstName LastName,company:Company

The --map flag lets you align your CSV column names to MailClaw's internal schema without touching the file. For Salesforce exports in particular, column headers are often inconsistent — this saves the cleanup step entirely.

Running Bulk Verification

Once imported, trigger a verification run against the entire contact group:

mailclaw verify --group leads_q2 --mode smtp --concurrency 10 --output verified_leads_q2.csv

Key flags to know:

  • --mode smtp — Performs full MX + SMTP handshake verification (most thorough).
  • --mode syntax — Fast syntax-only pass, useful for a first-pass cleanup of very large lists.
  • --concurrency — Controls parallel verification threads. Keep this under 15 to avoid triggering rate limits on receiving mail servers.
  • --output — Writes results to a new CSV with a verification_status column appended (valid, invalid, risky, catch-all).

The risky and catch-all classifications are especially useful for data teams. Catch-all domains accept mail for any address, so SMTP probing can't confirm individual delivery — MailClaw flags these separately so you can decide your own risk tolerance rather than having a tool silently pass or fail them.

Reviewing Results in the Dashboard

Open localhost:3100 and navigate to Contacts → Verification History. You'll see a breakdown of your run: valid rate, bounce risk score, domain health summary, and a filterable table of every contact. From here you can bulk-archive invalid addresses, move risky contacts to a nurture-only sequence, or flag catch-alls for manual review — all without leaving the dashboard.

Enriching Contacts with the AI Layer

What Enrichment Actually Fills In

Once your list is verified, enrichment adds depth. MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered AI enrichment can populate or update:

  • Job title and seniority level
  • Company name, size bucket, and industry vertical
  • Geographic location (city, country)
  • LinkedIn profile URL
  • Tech stack signals (useful for SaaS and developer-focused outreach)

For contacts already in your CRM with partial data, enrichment is additive — it only fills blank fields by default, preserving any data you've already validated. You can override this with the --overwrite flag if you're doing a full refresh.

Running an Enrichment Job

mailclaw enrich --group verified_leads_q2 --fields title,company_size,industry,linkedin --confidence 0.75

The --confidence flag is one of MailClaw's most practical data quality controls. Any enrichment inference below your threshold (expressed as a 0–1 score) is left blank rather than written — so you're not polluting your CRM with low-confidence guesses. For outbound campaigns where personalization accuracy matters, a threshold of 0.75 or higher is recommended. For broad market research where coverage matters more, 0.55 gives you better fill rates.

Syncing Enriched Data Back to Your CRM

MailClaw includes native sync actions for HubSpot and Salesforce, plus a generic webhook output for any other system. After enrichment, push the updated records back with:

mailclaw sync --group verified_leads_q2 --destination hubspot --field-map title:jobtitle,company_size:numberofemployees

The --field-map argument handles the property name mismatch between MailClaw's schema and HubSpot's internal property names — a small detail that saves a surprising amount of debugging time on real exports.

Building a Verification-First Outreach Sequence

One of MailClaw's most powerful patterns for data teams is chaining verification and enrichment directly into the start of an outreach sequence, so list quality is guaranteed before a single email is sent. Here's how to wire that up:

  1. In the dashboard, go to Sequences → New Sequence and name it something like Q2 Verified Outreach.
  2. Add a Verification Gate as Step 1 — this pauses enrollment for any contact that doesn't pass the SMTP check.
  3. Add an Enrichment Step as Step 2 with your preferred field targets.
  4. Wire your email steps from Step 3 onward, using enriched fields like {{contact.title}} and {{contact.industry}} in your copy for personalization.
  5. Connect your sending account via SMTP or OAuth (Gmail and Outlook both supported) under Settings → Email Accounts.

With this structure, the sequence itself enforces data quality. Contacts that would have bounced never reach the sending step — and the ones that do are personalized with enriched context that meaningfully improves reply rates.

Monitoring Deliverability After Sending

Verification reduces bounce risk, but deliverability monitoring tells you what actually happened. MailClaw's built-in deliverability tools track:

  • Bounce rate by domain and sending account
  • Spam complaint signals from supported providers including SendGrid webhook integration
  • Domain reputation scoring using real-time MX and blacklist checks
  • Open and click tracking with privacy-respecting pixel options

If your bounce rate on a particular domain cluster starts climbing post-send, MailClaw's AI email agent can automatically pause outreach to that domain, alert you via dashboard notification, and suggest a remediation action — like warming up a secondary sending account or scrubbing the remaining contacts in that segment before continuing.

Pro tip for data teams: Run a verification pass on your entire CRM contact database on a monthly schedule, not just before campaigns. Use mailclaw verify --group all_contacts --mode syntax --age-filter 30d to re-check only contacts added or modified in the last 30 days. This keeps your baseline clean without re-processing your entire list every time.

Multi-Account Support for Large Data Operations

Data teams supporting multiple business units or clients often need to manage separate sending identities without cross-contamination of reputation or contact data. MailClaw's multi-account support lets you register distinct SMTP configurations and OAuth connections — separate Gmail or Outlook accounts, a dedicated SendGrid subaccount, or a transactional provider like Postmark — and assign each contact group or sequence to a specific sending identity.

From the CLI, you can switch active accounts or scope a verification job to a specific account's domain baseline:

mailclaw accounts list
mailclaw verify --group enterprise_leads --account sendgrid-primary --mode smtp

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on localhost, data teams can also extend this behavior — the OpenClaw core is designed to be forkable, and the account management module is well-documented for teams that need custom routing logic or compliance-specific data handling.

Putting It All Together

For data teams, the value proposition of MailClaw isn't just feature breadth — it's the combination of local execution, open-source auditability, and a workflow that treats verification and enrichment as first-class pipeline steps rather than afterthoughts. Your contact data stays on your machine. Your enrichment logic is inspectable. Your deliverability outcomes are measurable. And the whole thing runs from one command.

Whether you're maintaining a Salesforce org for an enterprise sales team, building enrichment pipelines for a growth operation, or just trying to stop burning your domain reputation on stale leads — MailClaw gives you the infrastructure to do it right, without the SaaS price tag or the data-sharing tradeoffs that come with it.

Start with a free list import at localhost:3100 and run your first verification job in under five minutes. The dashboard makes it obvious — and the CLI makes it repeatable.

articles.title: How to Use MailClaw Contact Scoring for Sales Prioritization
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's built-in contact scoring system to prioritize your sales outreach, automate high-value sequences, and stop wasting time on leads that aren't ready to buy.
articles.content:
Why Contact Scoring Changes Everything About Sales Outreach

Most sales teams treat their contact list like a flat file — everyone gets the same sequence, the same cadence, and the same generic pitch. The result is predictable: low reply rates, burned domains, and salespeople frustrated that their "best" leads are buried under hundreds of cold contacts.

Contact scoring flips that model. Instead of blasting everyone equally, you assign numerical weights to signals that indicate purchase intent — job title, company size, recent activity, email engagement, funding rounds, tech stack — and let those scores dictate who gets your attention first. MailClaw's contact scoring engine, powered by OpenClaw's local AI layer, does this automatically and keeps everything running on your machine at localhost:3100. No data leaves your system. No SaaS tax. Just clean, prioritized outreach.

Understanding MailClaw's Scoring Model

MailClaw uses a composite scoring model with two layers: static signals and behavioral signals. Static signals are enriched at import time and don't change frequently — things like company headcount, industry vertical, LinkedIn seniority, or whether the contact uses a specific tool in their stack. Behavioral signals are dynamic — they update as contacts interact with your emails, respond to agents, or get re-enriched.

Static Signal Examples

  • Job Title Score: VP or C-Suite titles score higher than manager-level contacts
  • Company Size: Contacts at companies with 50–500 employees might score highest for your ICP
  • Funding Stage: Series A/B companies enriched via Clearbit or Apollo get a funding recency bonus
  • Tech Stack: If a contact's company uses HubSpot or Salesforce, MailClaw can weight them higher for CRM-adjacent pitches
  • Industry Match: Custom weighting for your target verticals

Behavioral Signal Examples

  • Email open (tracked via pixel when deliverability tools are enabled)
  • Link click within a sequence step
  • Reply received — especially positive replies, which AI agents classify automatically
  • Contact re-enriched with new data (e.g., job change detected)
  • Meeting booked or calendar link clicked

Each signal is assigned a point value in your scoring config, and MailClaw recalculates scores in real time as new events come in. The local dashboard at localhost:3100/contacts shows you a live leaderboard of your hottest leads.

Setting Up Your First Scoring Profile

MailClaw manages scoring through a YAML-based configuration file, which makes it easy to version-control and share across your team.

Step 1: Open Your Scoring Config

From the MailClaw CLI, run:

mailclaw scoring init --profile sales-icp

This creates a file at ~/.mailclaw/scoring/sales-icp.yaml. Open it in your editor of choice and you'll see the default template.

Step 2: Define Your Signal Weights

profile: sales-icp
version: 1

static_signals:
  title_keywords:
    - keyword: "VP"
      score: 20
    - keyword: "Director"
      score: 15
    - keyword: "Head of"
      score: 12
    - keyword: "Founder"
      score: 25
  company_size:
    - range: [50, 200]
      score: 20
    - range: [201, 500]
      score: 15
    - range: [1, 49]
      score: 5
  funding_recency_days:
    - within: 180
      score: 30
    - within: 365
      score: 15
  tech_stack_match:
    - tool: "HubSpot"
      score: 10
    - tool: "Salesforce"
      score: 10

behavioral_signals:
  email_opened:
    score: 5
    max_applications: 3
  link_clicked:
    score: 10
  reply_received:
    score: 40
  positive_reply_classified:
    score: 60
  meeting_booked:
    score: 100
  job_change_detected:
    score: 25

decay:
  enabled: true
  half_life_days: 30

The decay block is important — it means a contact who opened your email 90 days ago won't stay artificially hot forever. MailClaw halves their behavioral score every 30 days, keeping your list fresh.

Step 3: Apply the Profile to a Segment

mailclaw scoring apply --profile sales-icp --segment "Q3 Outbound"

MailClaw will process every contact in that segment, calculate their composite score, and write it back to the contact record. You can now filter, sort, and route contacts by score across the entire platform.

Using Contact Enrichment to Supercharge Scores

Raw scoring is only as good as the data behind it. MailClaw's contact enrichment layer pulls in third-party data automatically using your connected providers. You can configure enrichment sources directly from the dashboard under Settings → Enrichment Providers, or via CLI:

mailclaw enrich --segment "Q3 Outbound" --providers clearbit,apollo --fields title,company_size,funding,tech_stack

Once enrichment runs, MailClaw re-scores every contact automatically because static signals are recalculated with the new data. A contact who looked like a mid-level manager might reveal themselves to be a decision-maker at a Series B company — and their score jumps accordingly.

Pro tip: Schedule enrichment to run weekly on your active segments. Job changes alone — especially into new VP roles — are one of the strongest buying signals in B2B sales. MailClaw's AI agent can be configured to trigger a high-priority sequence automatically when a score crosses a threshold after enrichment.

Routing High-Score Contacts to the Right Sequences

Here's where MailClaw's sequence builder and AI email agents work together to create a genuinely automated prioritization engine.

Creating Score-Based Routing Rules

In the dashboard at localhost:3100/sequences, open any sequence and navigate to the Entry Rules tab. You'll see a condition builder where you can set:

  • Score ≥ 80 → Enroll in "Hot Leads — Exec Outreach" (5-step sequence, high personalization)
  • Score 40–79 → Enroll in "Warm Leads — Nurture Track" (8-step sequence, educational content)
  • Score < 40 → Hold in "Cold Pool" for re-enrichment next cycle

You can also trigger these rules from the CLI if you're building custom automation pipelines:

mailclaw sequence enroll \
  --sequence "hot-leads-exec" \
  --filter "score >= 80 AND segment = 'Q3 Outbound'" \
  --dry-run

Always run with --dry-run first. It shows you exactly which contacts would be enrolled without making any changes — a habit worth building.

Letting AI Email Agents Handle the Heavy Lifting

MailClaw's AI email agents, built on OpenClaw, can go beyond static sequence enrollment. You can configure an agent to monitor your contact scores continuously and take action when thresholds are hit:

mailclaw agent create \
  --name "Hot Lead Monitor" \
  --trigger "score_change" \
  --condition "new_score >= 80 AND previous_score < 80" \
  --action "enroll_sequence:hot-leads-exec" \
  --action "notify_slack:#sales-alerts"

This agent watches for the moment a contact crosses from warm to hot — maybe they just clicked a link in step 3 of your nurture sequence, or got re-enriched after a job change — and immediately enrolls them in your best-performing exec outreach. No human review required.

Monitoring Score Health in the Dashboard

MailClaw's local dashboard gives you a real-time view of how your scoring is performing. Navigate to localhost:3100/analytics/scoring to see:

  • Score Distribution: A histogram showing how many contacts fall into each score band. If everything is clustering below 30, your enrichment data might be thin or your ICP definition needs work.
  • Score Velocity: Which contacts are gaining score the fastest over the past 7 days — often your best same-week outreach targets.
  • Signal Attribution: A breakdown of which signals are contributing most to total scores across your database. If "reply_received" is barely registering, your early sequence steps might need a rewrite.
  • Decay Report: Contacts whose scores are actively decaying — useful for deciding whether to re-enrich or archive.

Connecting Scores to Your CRM

If your team uses HubSpot or Salesforce, MailClaw can sync contact scores bidirectionally. Set this up under Settings → Integrations, or push a sync from the CLI:

mailclaw sync --target hubspot --field "mailclaw_score" --segment "Q3 Outbound"

This writes each contact's current MailClaw score to a custom property in HubSpot, where your reps can build views, set task priorities, and build their own score-based workflows inside their familiar CRM — without needing to open MailClaw at all. Same integration is available for Salesforce via the OpenClaw connector, writing to a custom MailClaw_Score__c field.

The Practical Result: Less Volume, More Pipeline

Sales prioritization through contact scoring isn't about sending fewer emails — it's about allocating your best effort where it will actually convert. A rep spending 80% of their time on contacts scoring above 70 will consistently outperform one making their way alphabetically through a flat list.

MailClaw's scoring system, combined with its AI agents and open-source flexibility, gives you a prioritization engine that learns from your actual results, adapts to new data, and runs entirely on your local machine. No vendor lock-in, no per-seat pricing surprises, and no black-box algorithm you can't inspect or modify.

Start with a simple three-band scoring profile, run it for two weeks, and check your reply rate by score band in the analytics dashboard. The data will tell you exactly where to refine your weights — and you'll never go back to flat-list outreach again.

articles.title: Building Lookalike Audiences from Your Best Contacts in MailClaw
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's AI-powered contact enrichment and sequence builder to identify your highest-value contacts, extract their defining traits, and automatically build lookalike audiences that supercharge your outreach results.
articles.content:
Why Lookalike Audiences Belong in Your Email Stack

Paid ad platforms have trained marketers to think of lookalike audiences as a media-buying concept — upload your best customers, let the algorithm find more of them, run ads. But the underlying logic is just as powerful in email outreach. If you can describe exactly what makes your best contacts convert, you can find more people who share those traits and reach them with sequences that already have a proven track record.

MailClaw brings this idea directly into your local email automation workflow. Because it runs on your machine at localhost:3100 and combines AI enrichment with a full sequence builder, you can close the loop between "who converted" and "who should I talk to next" without exporting CSVs to five different tools.

Step 1 — Identify Your Seed Contacts

Before MailClaw can build anything, you need a clear definition of your best contacts. "Best" is intentionally vague — tighten it before you start. Useful definitions include:

  • Contacts who replied positively to a campaign and later converted
  • Customers above a certain lifetime value threshold pulled from HubSpot or Salesforce
  • Subscribers with an open rate above 60% across three or more sequences
  • Trial users who upgraded within the first 14 days

Once you have a definition, export or sync those contacts into MailClaw. If your CRM is HubSpot or Salesforce, the OpenClaw integration layer can pull them in directly:

mailclaw contacts import \
  --source hubspot \
  --filter "lifecycle_stage=customer<v_min=500" \
  --tag seed_audience \
  --enrich true

The --enrich true flag tells MailClaw to immediately run its AI contact enrichment pipeline on every imported record, pulling in firmographic data, tech stack signals, LinkedIn role information, and company funding stage where available. This is the raw material your lookalike model will learn from.

Step 2 — Run Contact Enrichment and Extract Patterns

With your seed list tagged and enriched, open the MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to Contacts → Audience Intelligence. This panel surfaces a statistical breakdown of your seed segment — the traits that appear with statistically unusual frequency compared to your broader contact database.

What the AI Looks For

MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered enrichment engine analyzes dozens of attributes across your seed contacts and weights them by predictive signal strength. The attributes that typically produce the strongest lookalike signals include:

  • Job function and seniority — "Head of Growth at a Series B SaaS company" is far more actionable than just "works in tech"
  • Company headcount range — e.g., 50–200 employees consistently outperforming contacts at enterprise accounts
  • Tech stack overlap — if 70% of your seed contacts use Intercom and Segment together, that's a filter worth building
  • Geographic cluster — certain markets may punch above their weight for your offer
  • Email engagement pattern — open times, device types, reply latency

You can also generate this profile from the CLI if you prefer to work outside the dashboard:

mailclaw audience analyze \
  --tag seed_audience \
  --output profile.json \
  --top-signals 10

The resulting profile.json file is a ranked list of trait clusters with confidence scores. Inspect it, remove anything that looks like noise (industry categories that are too broad, company sizes that basically cover everyone), and save your edited version back as a named audience profile:

mailclaw audience save \
  --profile profile.json \
  --name "high_value_seed_v1"

Step 3 — Build the Lookalike Audience

Now comes the part that makes MailClaw genuinely different from a manual segmentation exercise. Using your saved profile, the tool can search across connected data sources — including your existing un-contacted leads, imported prospect lists, or enrichment APIs — and score every contact against your seed profile in real time.

mailclaw audience build \
  --profile "high_value_seed_v1" \
  --source all_contacts \
  --min-score 0.72 \
  --output lookalike_q3.csv \
  --tag lookalike_q3

The --min-score parameter controls how strict the matching is. A threshold of 0.72 (72% trait overlap) is a reasonable starting point — tight enough to maintain quality, loose enough to generate meaningful volume. Adjust based on your list size and how selective you need to be.

Pulling in Fresh Prospects

If your existing contact database doesn't have enough raw material, MailClaw can reach outward. Connect your Apollo, Clay, or LinkedIn Sales Navigator exports and run the same scoring pass over fresh prospect data:

mailclaw contacts import \
  --source csv \
  --file apollo_export_july.csv \
  --enrich true \
  --score-against "high_value_seed_v1" \
  --min-score 0.70 \
  --tag lookalike_q3

Every contact that clears the threshold gets tagged automatically and is ready to enter a sequence. Contacts that don't make the cut sit in your database enriched but untagged — useful for future campaigns with different seed profiles.

Step 4 — Build a Sequence Tuned to the Lookalike Audience

A lookalike audience performs best when the messaging reflects what you already know about people like them. This is where MailClaw's AI email agents earn their keep.

In the dashboard, go to Sequences → New Sequence and select AI-Assisted Draft. When prompted, reference your seed audience profile:

"My best customers are Heads of Growth at Series B SaaS companies with 50–200 employees who use Intercom and are actively hiring for demand gen roles. They care about pipeline efficiency and have tried and abandoned at least one ABM tool. Write a 4-step cold outreach sequence that leads with operational pain, not product features."

MailClaw's agent will generate a complete multi-step sequence — subject lines, body copy, and follow-up timing — calibrated to the psychographic and firmographic traits you've described. You're not writing blind; you're writing for a version of the audience you've already seen convert.

Personalizing at Scale with Enrichment Fields

Because every lookalike contact was enriched during import, you have a rich set of merge variables available. Use them to make the first touch feel researched rather than blasted:

Hi {{first_name}},

Noticed {{company}} recently {{recent_hiring_signal}} —
usually means the demand gen team is juggling more
tooling than they'd like.

We've helped teams like {{similar_company_1}} and
{{similar_company_2}} cut their outreach stack in half
without losing pipeline visibility.

Variables like {{recent_hiring_signal}} and {{similar_company_1}} are populated from the enrichment data MailClaw collected when you ran the import. The result is personalization that would normally require a researcher — generated automatically from your local install.

Step 5 — Monitor Deliverability Before You Scale

Lookalike audiences are cold contacts. That means deliverability discipline matters more, not less. Before activating your sequence at full volume, use MailClaw's built-in deliverability tools to check your sending infrastructure.

mailclaw deliverability check \
  --account gmail_primary \
  --sequence lookalike_q3_outreach \
  --preview 50

This command runs a pre-flight check: SPF/DKIM/DMARC validation for your connected Gmail or Outlook account, spam score estimation for your sequence copy, and a send-rate recommendation based on your current domain age and warm-up history. If you're routing through SendGrid or another SMTP provider, the same check applies to your API-connected sending accounts.

A few rules of thumb worth building into your process:

  • Cap new cold outreach at 30–50 emails per day per domain until you've established positive reply signals
  • Monitor your reply rate for the first 200 sends before scaling — if it's below 1%, revisit your audience score threshold or your copy
  • Use MailClaw's multi-account support to rotate across sending identities if you're running high-volume sequences in parallel

Iterating: Feed Winners Back Into the Seed

The most durable part of this workflow is its feedback loop. When contacts from your lookalike audience convert — whether that means booking a call, replying positively, or becoming customers — add them back to your seed tag:

mailclaw contacts update \
  --tag lookalike_q3 \
  --filter "reply_sentiment=positive" \
  --add-tag seed_audience

Re-run your audience analysis every four to six weeks. As your seed pool grows and diversifies, the profile sharpens. Traits that were noise at 50 seed contacts become statistically meaningful at 200. Your lookalike audiences get more accurate over time, and the sequences you build from them get tighter — all running locally, all under your control, and all without a SaaS subscription fee attached to every contact record.

That compounding improvement is the real value proposition here. MailClaw isn't just automating outreach — it's building institutional knowledge about who responds to you and why, stored locally and queryable whenever you need it.

articles.title: How to Sync MailClaw Contacts with Your CRM Bidirectionally
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how to set up true bidirectional contact sync between MailClaw and your CRM — covering HubSpot, Salesforce, and custom setups — so your outreach data and enriched contact records stay perfectly in sync across every tool you use.
articles.content:
Why Bidirectional Sync Actually Matters

Most email tools treat CRM sync as a one-way street: contacts flow in, results trickle back out on a delay, and you spend Friday afternoon reconciling duplicate records. If you've ever launched a MailClaw sequence only to discover that half your prospects were already marked "Closed Won" in HubSpot, you know exactly how painful that gap can be.

Bidirectional sync changes the equation entirely. When MailClaw's contact enrichment updates a prospect's job title or phone number, that data should land in Salesforce automatically. When a rep marks a deal as active in your CRM, MailClaw should pull that contact into the right sequence without you touching a keyboard. That's the loop we're going to build.
