Because MailClaw runs locally on localhost:3100 and is built on the open-source OpenClaw engine, you have full control over your data pipeline — no third-party sync service sitting in the middle, no per-seat fees for a connector you barely use.

Understanding MailClaw's Contact Data Model

Before writing a single line of sync logic, it helps to understand how MailClaw stores contacts internally. Every contact record lives in a local SQLite database and carries a set of enriched fields populated by MailClaw's AI contact enrichment layer:

  • Core fields: email, first_name, last_name, company, title, phone
  • Enrichment fields: linkedin_url, company_size, industry, enriched_at
  • Sequence fields: sequence_id, sequence_status, last_sent_at, reply_at
  • Sync metadata: crm_id, crm_source, synced_at, sync_hash

The crm_id and crm_source fields are your anchors. Populate them correctly and you'll always be able to match a MailClaw contact back to its canonical record in HubSpot, Salesforce, or any other CRM without guessing.

Setting Up the MailClaw Contacts API

MailClaw exposes a local REST API at http://localhost:3100/api/v1. You'll use this for both reading and writing contacts during sync. First, generate an API token from your local dashboard under Settings → API Access, then test connectivity:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN" \
  http://localhost:3100/api/v1/contacts?limit=5

You should get a paginated JSON response. If you're scripting the sync in Python, install the lightweight helper:

pip install mailclaw-client

Then initialize a client:

from mailclaw import MailClawClient

mc = MailClawClient(
    base_url="http://localhost:3100",
    token="YOUR_TOKEN"
)

Syncing with HubSpot

Step 1: Create a Private App in HubSpot

In HubSpot, navigate to Settings → Integrations → Private Apps and create a new app. Grant it scopes for crm.objects.contacts.read and crm.objects.contacts.write. Copy the generated token — you'll pass this as your HubSpot bearer token.

Step 2: Pull HubSpot Contacts into MailClaw

The following script fetches recently modified HubSpot contacts and upserts them into MailClaw, preserving the crm_id link:

import requests
from mailclaw import MailClawClient

HS_TOKEN = "YOUR_HUBSPOT_TOKEN"
mc = MailClawClient(base_url="http://localhost:3100", token="YOUR_MC_TOKEN")

def fetch_hubspot_contacts(after=None):
    url = "https://api.hubapi.com/crm/v3/objects/contacts"
    params = {"limit": 100, "properties": "email,firstname,lastname,company,jobtitle,phone"}
    if after:
        params["after"] = after
    resp = requests.get(url, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {HS_TOKEN}"}, params=params)
    return resp.json()

data = fetch_hubspot_contacts()
for contact in data["results"]:
    props = contact["properties"]
    mc.contacts.upsert({
        "email": props.get("email"),
        "first_name": props.get("firstname"),
        "last_name": props.get("lastname"),
        "company": props.get("company"),
        "title": props.get("jobtitle"),
        "phone": props.get("phone"),
        "crm_id": contact["id"],
        "crm_source": "hubspot"
    })

Step 3: Push MailClaw Enrichment Back to HubSpot

This is where the bidirectional part pays off. After MailClaw's AI enrichment layer runs, push the updated fields back:

contacts = mc.contacts.list(crm_source="hubspot", enriched_since="2024-01-01")

for c in contacts:
    url = f"https://api.hubapi.com/crm/v3/objects/contacts/{c['crm_id']}"
    requests.patch(url,
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {HS_TOKEN}"},
        json={"properties": {
            "jobtitle": c.get("title"),
            "company": c.get("company"),
            "hs_linkedin_url": c.get("linkedin_url"),
            "numemployees": c.get("company_size")
        }}
    )

Run these scripts on a cron job every hour and you have a live sync loop. Store synced_at timestamps on both sides to avoid overwriting newer data with stale records.

Syncing with Salesforce

OAuth Setup

MailClaw's multi-account support includes OAuth token management, which makes Salesforce authentication cleaner than managing username/password flows. In your MailClaw dashboard under Integrations → Salesforce, complete the OAuth handshake. MailClaw will store and refresh the access token automatically.

Using the CLI for Bulk Sync

MailClaw ships with a CLI that exposes sync commands directly. For Salesforce, you can trigger a full contact import from the terminal:

# Import Salesforce leads into MailClaw contacts
mailclaw sync import --source salesforce \
  --object Lead \
  --fields "Email,FirstName,LastName,Company,Title,Phone" \
  --filter "LastModifiedDate >= LAST_N_DAYS:7"

And push sequence activity back to Salesforce as activity records:

mailclaw sync export --target salesforce \
  --type activity \
  --sequence-id seq_abc123 \
  --map "reply_at:LastActivityDate,sequence_status:Lead_Status__c"

The --map flag lets you translate MailClaw field names to your custom Salesforce field API names without touching code. This is especially useful when your Salesforce org has non-standard fields built by previous consultants.

Handling Conflicts and Avoiding Data Loops

Bidirectional sync introduces a classic problem: if both systems update the same field, which one wins? Here are the rules we recommend building into any MailClaw sync setup:

  • CRM wins on identity fields (name, email, phone) — your CRM is the system of record for who the person is.
  • MailClaw wins on enrichment fields (LinkedIn URL, company size, industry) — MailClaw's AI enrichment is more current and purpose-built for this.
  • CRM wins on deal/pipeline status — never let outreach tooling overwrite revenue-critical data.
  • Use sync_hash to detect real changes — hash the fields you care about and only sync when the hash changes to avoid infinite update loops.

A sync loop happens when System A updates a record, System B sees the change and writes back, which triggers System A again. Always check whether a field actually changed before writing — don't sync timestamps as content fields.

Keeping Sequences Consistent with CRM Stages

One of the most powerful applications of bidirectional sync is tying MailClaw's sequence builder directly to CRM lifecycle stages. For example, you can configure a rule that automatically enrolls a contact in a nurture sequence when their HubSpot lifecycle stage changes to Lead, and automatically pauses the sequence when it moves to Opportunity:

# In MailClaw's webhook listener config (mailclaw.config.json)
{
  "webhooks": {
    "hubspot_contact_update": {
      "trigger_field": "lifecyclestage",
      "rules": [
        { "value": "lead", "action": "enroll", "sequence_id": "seq_nurture_01" },
        { "value": "opportunity", "action": "pause" },
        { "value": "customer", "action": "complete" }
      ]
    }
  }
}

This configuration means your AI email agents are always working on the right contacts — never sending a cold intro to someone who signed a contract last week.

Monitoring Sync Health from the Dashboard

Open localhost:3100 in your browser and navigate to Contacts → Sync Status. You'll see a live table showing each contact's last sync time, which CRM it's linked to, whether the last sync succeeded, and any field conflicts that were resolved. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring layer also flags contacts whose email addresses bounced in any connected sending account — Gmail, Outlook, or SendGrid — so your CRM doesn't accumulate dead addresses.

For teams running high-volume outreach, the sync error log at localhost:3100/logs/sync is invaluable. Filter by error type, re-queue failed syncs in bulk, and export a report for your ops team — all without leaving your local environment.

A Few Things Worth Getting Right From the Start

Bidirectional sync is one of those infrastructure pieces that's much easier to do correctly at the beginning than to untangle six months later. Before you go live:

  1. Agree on a canonical email field. Every system must treat the email address as the primary key, and that key must never be silently overwritten.
  2. Back up your MailClaw database first. Run mailclaw db backup --output ~/backups/mc_before_sync.db before any bulk import.
  3. Test with a filtered subset. Use --filter flags to sync 50 contacts before touching thousands.
  4. Log everything for 30 days. Set "sync_log_retention_days": 30 in your config so you can audit any unexpected changes.

Done right, a MailClaw-to-CRM sync turns your local outreach tool into the enrichment and sequencing engine your CRM never had natively — and because everything runs on your machine through OpenClaw's open-source core, you own every bit of the pipeline.

articles.title: MailClaw Contact Insights: Understanding Engagement Patterns
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how MailClaw's contact insights and engagement analytics help you decode subscriber behavior, identify high-value leads, and build smarter email sequences that convert — all running locally on your Mac.
articles.content:
Why Engagement Patterns Matter More Than Open Rates

Most email marketers obsess over open rates. It's the metric that gets screenshot, shared in Slack, and celebrated in Monday standups. But a 42% open rate means very little if you don't know who opened, when they opened, and what they did — or didn't do — next.

MailClaw's Contact Insights module is built around a simple but powerful idea: engagement is a pattern, not a moment. When you understand how a contact moves through your sequences over time, you stop guessing and start making decisions grounded in actual behavior. And because MailClaw runs entirely on your machine at localhost:3100, every data point stays private, queryable, and under your control.

What MailClaw Tracks at the Contact Level

When a contact enters a sequence — whether that's a cold outreach chain, a nurture flow, or a re-engagement campaign — MailClaw begins building a behavioral profile. This isn't just click tracking bolted on after the fact. It's woven into the OpenClaw engine that powers every send.

Core Engagement Signals

  • Open timestamps: Not just whether they opened, but when — day of week, time of day, and how quickly after delivery
  • Click depth: Which links were clicked, in what order, and how many times
  • Reply sentiment: When connected to Gmail or Outlook via OAuth, MailClaw's AI email agent can classify inbound replies as positive, neutral, objection, or out-of-office
  • Sequence position drop-off: The exact step where a contact stopped engaging
  • Deliverability signals: Soft bounces, hard bounces, and spam complaints tied to the individual contact record

Together, these signals give you something far more useful than a flat engagement score — they give you a story.

Reading the Dashboard: Patterns to Look For

Open your local dashboard at http://localhost:3100/contacts and navigate to any contact record. You'll see a timeline view that plots every touchpoint across your sequences. Here's what the most actionable patterns look like in practice.

The Late Opener

This contact consistently opens emails 18–36 hours after delivery. They're not ignoring you — they're busy and batch-processing their inbox. If your sequence sends a follow-up at the 24-hour mark assuming silence equals disinterest, you're interrupting someone who was about to respond. MailClaw's sequence builder lets you set smart delay overrides per-contact based on their historical open window, so your follow-up lands after their typical read time, not before.

The Click-Heavy Non-Converter

Opens every email. Clicks multiple links. Never replies, never books, never buys. This pattern usually signals one of two things: genuinely curious but not ready, or a spam filter doing link-checking. MailClaw's deliverability tools can help you distinguish between the two by cross-referencing click timestamps (bot clicks tend to happen within milliseconds of delivery) against your SMTP logs from SendGrid, Postmark, or your own server.

If it's a real human, they need a different kind of nudge — not more emails, but better content at that specific point in the funnel.

The One-Touch Wonder

Opened email one and nothing since. This is your most common drop-off pattern, and it's usually a subject line problem downstream, not an interest problem. Pull the step-level analytics in the sequence builder to see exactly which follow-up subjects correlate with re-engagement for this cohort. Your AI email agent can generate variant subject lines based on what's worked historically for contacts with similar enrichment profiles.

Using Contact Enrichment to Contextualize Behavior

Raw engagement data is useful. Enriched engagement data is actionable. MailClaw's contact enrichment pipeline pulls in firmographic and professional data to add context to every behavioral signal.

Run enrichment from the CLI on a single contact or an entire segment:

# Enrich a single contact by email
mailclaw enrich contact --email jane@example.com

# Enrich all contacts in a segment
mailclaw enrich segment --id seg_coldleads_q4 --provider clearbit

# Review enrichment results in the dashboard
mailclaw open --path /contacts/enrichment-queue

Once enriched, a contact's job title, company size, industry, and LinkedIn activity get layered into their engagement profile. Now that "Late Opener" pattern takes on new meaning when you see they're a VP of Engineering at a 200-person SaaS company — they're not slow, they're strategic. Your outreach should reflect that.

Syncing Enriched Insights to Your CRM

If you're running HubSpot, Salesforce, or Pipedrive alongside MailClaw, you can push enriched contact records and engagement scores back through the native integrations. This closes the loop between your outreach tool and your sales team's workflow without any manual data entry.

# Push engagement scores to HubSpot
mailclaw sync crm --provider hubspot --fields engagement_score,last_open,reply_sentiment

# Preview what will sync before committing
mailclaw sync crm --provider salesforce --dry-run

Your SDRs will thank you when they open a contact in Salesforce and see that someone has opened five emails, clicked the pricing page link twice, and been classified as "high intent" by MailClaw's AI agent — all before the first call is ever booked.

Building Segments from Engagement Patterns

Individual contact insights are powerful. But the real leverage comes from segmenting your list based on behavioral patterns and then feeding those segments into tailored sequences.

In the MailClaw dashboard, navigate to Contacts → Segments → New Segment and use the filter builder to create rule-based cohorts:

  • Contacts who opened 3+ emails but never clicked → Content quality issue segment
  • Contacts who clicked but never replied in the last 60 days → Re-engagement segment
  • Contacts with a positive reply sentiment but no booked meeting → Warm handoff segment for your sales team
  • Contacts with two or more soft bounces → Deliverability review segment

Each segment can be wired directly into a sequence in the sequence builder, so the moment a contact qualifies — or disqualifies — they're automatically routed to the right flow. No manual tagging, no spreadsheet gymnastics.

Letting Your AI Email Agent Act on Insights

This is where MailClaw's architecture starts to feel genuinely different from traditional email tools. Because OpenClaw runs locally, your AI email agent has full access to contact history, enrichment data, and sequence performance without making a single API call to a third-party service.

You can configure an agent to monitor a segment and take action autonomously:

# Create an agent that monitors high-intent contacts and drafts personalized follow-ups
mailclaw agent create \
  --name "warm-lead-watcher" \
  --trigger "engagement_score > 75 AND days_since_reply > 5" \
  --action draft_followup \
  --tone professional \
  --account gmail-primary

The agent watches the segment, detects when a contact crosses the threshold, and drafts a personalized follow-up for your review — or sends it automatically if you've enabled autonomous mode. It pulls in context from the contact's enrichment profile and previous email history to write something that doesn't sound like a template.

Pro tip: Start agents in review mode (--action draft_followup) before switching to autonomous sends. Reviewing the first 20–30 drafts gives you a clear picture of how the agent interprets your tone guidelines, and lets you refine the prompt before it's operating hands-free.

Deliverability and Engagement: The Hidden Connection

There's a feedback loop that most outreach tools don't surface clearly: low engagement hurts deliverability, and poor deliverability depresses engagement. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring ties these two together at the contact and domain level.

If a segment of contacts consistently fails to open — not because of disinterest, but because your emails are landing in spam — your engagement data is lying to you. MailClaw flags this by cross-referencing inbox placement data from your connected SMTP providers (SendGrid, Mailgun, or your own server) with engagement rates per domain.

# Run a deliverability health check across your active sequences
mailclaw deliverability check --sequence seq_outbound_nov

# See per-domain engagement breakdown
mailclaw deliverability report --breakdown domain --format table

When you see that contacts on yahoo.com domains have a 4% open rate versus 38% for gmail.com in the same sequence, that's not a segmentation problem — it's a deliverability problem that needs to be fixed at the infrastructure level before any behavioral analysis will be meaningful.

Turning Insights Into a Continuous Improvement Loop

The most valuable thing you can do with MailClaw's contact insights isn't a one-time audit — it's building a weekly rhythm around the data. Here's a practical 15-minute review process:

  1. Open the dashboard at localhost:3100/analytics and check sequence-level drop-off by step
  2. Pull up the top 10 contacts by engagement score and verify they're in an active sequence or have been handed off to sales
  3. Review any contacts flagged by the deliverability monitor for bounce or complaint activity
  4. Check AI agent drafts in the review queue and approve, edit, or discard
  5. Update one segment rule based on what you observed — small, iterative adjustments compound over time

This isn't a complex workflow. It's 15 minutes of focused attention, informed by data that MailClaw has been collecting and organizing on your behalf all week. Over a quarter, that adds up to a dramatically sharper picture of what your audience actually responds to — and a list that gets healthier, not just bigger.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your infrastructure, you own every piece of this. The data, the models, the integrations — nothing is locked behind a pricing tier or siloed in someone else's cloud. That's not just a philosophical stance; it's a practical advantage when you're building outreach operations that need to scale without the overhead.

articles.title: How to Clean and Validate Your Email List with MailClaw
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to clean and validate your email list using MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment, AI agents, and deliverability tools — so every campaign lands in the inbox, not the spam folder.
articles.content:
Why Email List Hygiene Is Non-Negotiable

Sending to a dirty list is one of the fastest ways to destroy your sender reputation. Bounces pile up, spam complaints roll in, and before long, Gmail, Outlook, and other inbox providers are quietly routing your messages to junk — or blocking them entirely. If you've ever wondered why your open rates are tanking despite great copy, a bloated, unvalidated list is usually the culprit.

The good news: MailClaw gives you everything you need to clean, validate, and enrich your contact list directly from your local machine — no third-party SaaS subscription required, no uploading your contacts to someone else's cloud. Everything runs on localhost:3100, powered by the OpenClaw engine underneath.

This guide walks you through a complete list hygiene workflow using MailClaw's CLI, dashboard, and AI-powered contact enrichment tools.

Understanding What Makes a List "Dirty"

Before you clean anything, it helps to know what you're dealing with. A problematic email list typically contains some combination of the following:

  • Hard bounces — addresses that no longer exist (e.g., departed employees, deleted accounts)
  • Soft bounces — temporary delivery failures that have become chronic
  • Role-based addresses — info@, support@, noreply@ — these rarely convert and often flag campaigns
  • Duplicate contacts — the same person with slight variations in name or email casing
  • Syntax errors — missing @ symbols, extra dots, malformed domains
  • Spam traps — recycled addresses maintained by inbox providers to catch bulk senders
  • Unengaged subscribers — valid addresses that haven't opened or clicked in 6–12+ months

MailClaw's deliverability monitoring dashboard surfaces most of these issues automatically after your first campaign run, but proactive cleaning before sending is always better than reactive cleanup after a deliverability hit.

Step 1 — Import and Audit Your Existing List

Start by importing your contacts into MailClaw. If you're pulling from HubSpot, Salesforce, or a raw CSV, the import command handles all three:

# Import from a CSV file
mailclaw contacts import --file ./my-list.csv --map email:email,name:first_name

# Import from HubSpot via API
mailclaw contacts import --source hubspot --api-key YOUR_HUBSPOT_KEY

# Import from Salesforce
mailclaw contacts import --source salesforce --instance YOUR_INSTANCE_URL

Once your contacts are in, run the built-in audit command to get an immediate health snapshot:

mailclaw contacts audit --output report.json

This generates a structured report flagging syntax errors, duplicates, role-based addresses, and contacts missing key fields. Open your local dashboard at http://localhost:3100/contacts/audit to see a visual breakdown of your list health score alongside actionable fix recommendations.

Step 2 — Validate Email Syntax and Domain Health

Syntax Validation

MailClaw's validation layer checks every address against RFC 5321/5322 rules — catching malformed addresses before they ever touch an SMTP server:

mailclaw contacts validate --rules syntax,mx,disposable --tag validated

The --rules flag lets you stack validation checks. The mx flag performs a live DNS MX record lookup to confirm the domain can actually receive mail. The disposable flag cross-references against known temporary inbox providers like Mailinator and Guerrilla Mail.

MX Record and SMTP Verification

For high-stakes outbound sequences — say, a cold outreach campaign going to 5,000 prospects — you'll want to go one level deeper with SMTP verification:

mailclaw contacts validate --rules smtp --concurrency 10 --dry-run

The --dry-run flag simulates the SMTP handshake (RCPT TO) without actually sending a message, giving you a pass/fail for each address. Keep --concurrency modest (10–20) to avoid rate-limiting from receiving mail servers.

Pro tip: Never run SMTP verification through your primary sending domain. MailClaw lets you assign a separate verification identity in Settings → Accounts so your main sender reputation stays clean.

Step 3 — Enrich Contacts to Fill the Gaps

A clean list is a good list. A clean and enriched list is a great one. MailClaw's contact enrichment engine, powered by OpenClaw's AI layer, can fill in missing fields — job title, company, LinkedIn URL, industry, location — using publicly available signals and integrated data providers.

# Enrich all contacts missing a job title
mailclaw contacts enrich --filter "job_title:missing" --fields job_title,company,linkedin_url

# Enrich a specific segment
mailclaw contacts enrich --tag validated --fields all

Enriched contacts unlock better personalization in your sequences. Instead of "Hi {first_name}", you're writing "Hi Sarah, I saw {company} recently expanded into enterprise — congrats on the Series B." That kind of specificity comes directly from enrichment data feeding into MailClaw's sequence builder variables.

Step 4 — Segment Out the Unengaged

Validation tells you if an address can receive mail. Engagement data tells you if the person wants to. MailClaw tracks opens, clicks, and reply events across every sequence and surfaces engagement scores in the dashboard.

To pull your cold subscribers into a suppression list:

# Find contacts with no opens/clicks in the last 180 days
mailclaw contacts segment \
  --filter "last_engaged:>180d OR last_engaged:never" \
  --tag cold-subscribers \
  --export cold-subscribers.csv

You have a few options for these contacts:

  1. Run a re-engagement sequence — Use MailClaw's sequence builder to craft a short 2–3 email "We miss you" campaign before suppressing. Some will re-engage; the rest self-select out.
  2. Suppress immediately — If the list is old and you've never tracked engagement, it's cleaner to start fresh with verified-only contacts.
  3. Move to a low-frequency nurture track — Keep them in a long-tail sequence with one touchpoint per quarter rather than removing them entirely.

Step 5 — Automate Ongoing Hygiene with AI Email Agents

One-time cleaning is a good start. What you really want is a system that maintains list quality automatically. MailClaw's AI email agents make this possible without manual intervention.

You can configure an agent that monitors incoming bounce events from your SendGrid or SMTP account, automatically suppresses hard bounces, flags soft bounces for review, and triggers re-engagement sequences for chronic non-openers:

# Create a list hygiene agent
mailclaw agent create \
  --name "List Hygiene Agent" \
  --trigger bounce,complaint,inactivity \
  --actions suppress_hard,flag_soft,reengagement_sequence \
  --schedule daily

Once deployed, this agent runs silently in the background — visible in your localhost dashboard under Agents → Active — keeping your list clean without you lifting a finger. You can wire it to any of your connected accounts, whether that's Gmail via OAuth, Outlook through SMTP, or a dedicated sending IP through SendGrid or Mailgun.

Step 6 — Monitor Deliverability Before Every Send

MailClaw's deliverability monitoring panel gives you a pre-send checklist that's easy to overlook but critical to get right. Before launching any campaign:

  • Check your domain reputation score via the dashboard's SPF/DKIM/DMARC validator
  • Review the bounce rate trend from your last 5 campaigns — anything above 2% is a red flag
  • Confirm your unsubscribe link is functional and list-unsubscribe headers are properly set
  • Run a spam score check against your email content before the sequence goes live
# Run pre-send deliverability check
mailclaw deliverability check --sequence "Q4 Outreach" --account primary

Keeping Your List Clean Long-Term

The most important shift you can make is treating list hygiene as infrastructure, not a one-off project. With MailClaw's combination of automated agents, built-in validation, enrichment tools, and deliverability monitoring, you can build a self-maintaining system that protects your sender reputation continuously.

Because MailClaw is open source and built on OpenClaw, you can extend any of these workflows — write custom validation rules, integrate with your own data warehouse, or build bespoke enrichment pipelines — without being locked into a vendor's roadmap. Everything runs locally, your data stays yours, and the full power of the system is always one command away.

Start with the audit, validate what you have, enrich what's worth keeping, and let the AI agents handle the rest. Your inbox placement rates will thank you.

articles.title: How to Connect MailClaw to HubSpot for CRM Sync
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw to HubSpot for seamless CRM sync, so your email sequences, contact enrichment data, and campaign activity flow automatically between your local dashboard and your HubSpot pipeline.
articles.content:
Why Sync MailClaw with HubSpot?

Running your outreach through MailClaw is powerful on its own — you get AI-driven email agents, contact enrichment, a full sequence builder, and deliverability monitoring, all from a clean local dashboard at localhost:3100. But most sales and marketing teams live in a CRM, and HubSpot is often that home base.

Without a sync, you're managing two separate worlds: sequences firing in MailClaw, deal stages updating in HubSpot, and no clean thread connecting them. Contacts fall through gaps. Reps reach out to people already mid-sequence. Marketing has no visibility into what sales is sending.

Connecting MailClaw to HubSpot closes that loop. Contact enrichment data flows into your CRM. Email opens, clicks, and replies update deal records automatically. New HubSpot contacts can trigger MailClaw sequences without any manual intervention. This guide walks you through exactly how to set that up.

What You'll Need Before You Start

  • MailClaw running locally (default: localhost:3100)
  • A HubSpot account with API access (any paid tier, or the free CRM with API enabled)
  • Your HubSpot Private App token — not the legacy API key (HubSpot deprecated those in 2022)
  • Node.js 18+ installed if you plan to use the MailClaw CLI for scripted sync
  • Basic familiarity with MailClaw's config files and the OpenClaw plugin system

If you haven't already, generate a Private App token in HubSpot by navigating to Settings → Integrations → Private Apps → Create a private app. Scope it for crm.objects.contacts.read, crm.objects.contacts.write, crm.objects.deals.read, and timeline access. Copy that token — you'll need it in the next step.

Step 1: Add Your HubSpot Credentials to MailClaw

MailClaw stores integration credentials in its local config file at ~/.mailclaw/config.json. Open it in your editor and add a hubspot block inside the integrations object:

{
  "integrations": {
    "hubspot": {
      "enabled": true,
      "privateAppToken": "pat-na1-xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx",
      "syncDirection": "bidirectional",
      "contactMatchField": "email",
      "dealPipeline": "default"
    }
  }
}

The syncDirection field accepts three values: to_hubspot, from_hubspot, or bidirectional. For most teams, bidirectional is the right choice — it means new contacts enriched by MailClaw flow into HubSpot, and new contacts added to HubSpot can trigger sequences in MailClaw.

Once the config is saved, restart MailClaw or run:

mailclaw integrations reload

You should see a confirmation in the CLI output that the HubSpot connector is active.

Step 2: Test the Connection

Before building any automations, verify that MailClaw can read from and write to your HubSpot account:

mailclaw hubspot test --verbose

This command makes a lightweight API call to fetch your HubSpot portal metadata and checks write permissions by creating and immediately deleting a test contact. A successful output looks like:

✔ HubSpot connection established (portal: 12345678)
✔ Read access confirmed
✔ Write access confirmed
✔ Timeline events: enabled
HubSpot integration is ready.

If you see a 401 Unauthorized error, double-check your token scopes. If you see a timeout, make sure your local network isn't blocking outbound calls on port 443 — MailClaw's HubSpot connector uses HTTPS throughout.

Step 3: Map Contact Fields

MailClaw's contact enrichment engine (powered by OpenClaw) pulls in data points like job title, company size, LinkedIn URL, and tech stack. You need to tell MailClaw how those fields map to HubSpot properties.

Open the field mapping config at ~/.mailclaw/hubspot-fields.json (MailClaw creates this automatically on first run if it doesn't exist):

{
  "fieldMappings": [
    { "mailclaw": "firstName", "hubspot": "firstname" },
    { "mailclaw": "lastName", "hubspot": "lastname" },
    { "mailclaw": "email", "hubspot": "email" },
    { "mailclaw": "company", "hubspot": "company" },
    { "mailclaw": "jobTitle", "hubspot": "jobtitle" },
    { "mailclaw": "linkedinUrl", "hubspot": "hs_linkedin_url" },
    { "mailclaw": "enrichedCompanySize", "hubspot": "numberofemployees" },
    { "mailclaw": "techStack", "hubspot": "technology_stack__c" }
  ]
}

The techStack field assumes you've created a custom HubSpot property called technology_stack__c. You can create custom properties in HubSpot under Settings → Properties → Create property. This is worth doing — having enrichment data like tech stack living in HubSpot means your sales team can filter and prioritize without ever opening MailClaw.

Step 4: Sync Sequences and Engagement Data Back to HubSpot

This is where the integration gets genuinely valuable. When a contact inside a MailClaw sequence opens an email, clicks a link, or replies, you want that activity logged in HubSpot against their contact record — not just sitting in your local dashboard.

Enabling Timeline Events

MailClaw can post engagement events to HubSpot's Timeline API, which surfaces them in the contact activity feed and can trigger HubSpot workflows. Enable this in your config:

{
  "integrations": {
    "hubspot": {
      "timelineEvents": {
        "enabled": true,
        "logOpens": true,
        "logClicks": true,
        "logReplies": true,
        "logBounces": true,
        "sequenceStepLabel": true
      }
    }
  }
}

With sequenceStepLabel enabled, HubSpot will show not just that an email was sent, but which step in which MailClaw sequence triggered it. This makes it easy to understand where in your outreach funnel a contact converted or went quiet.

Triggering HubSpot Deal Stage Updates

If a contact replies to a sequence email, you can configure MailClaw to automatically move their associated deal to a new stage in HubSpot. Add a dealTriggers block to your config:

{
  "dealTriggers": [
    {
      "event": "reply",
      "moveDealToStage": "appointmentscheduled",
      "pipeline": "default"
    },
    {
      "event": "unsubscribe",
      "moveDealToStage": "closedlost",
      "pipeline": "default"
    }
  ]
}

Use the internal HubSpot stage IDs (not the display names) — you can find these via the HubSpot API or in the URL when viewing a pipeline stage in settings.

Step 5: Pull HubSpot Contacts into MailClaw Sequences

The other half of bidirectional sync is pulling contacts from HubSpot into MailClaw sequences. You can do this manually or automate it with a HubSpot workflow.

Manual Import via CLI

mailclaw hubspot import \
  --list "Cold Outreach Q3" \
  --sequence "SaaS Founder Cold Outreach v2" \
  --enrich true \
  --limit 200

This command pulls contacts from a HubSpot list, runs them through MailClaw's enrichment pipeline to fill in any missing fields, and enrolls them in the specified sequence. The --enrich true flag is optional but recommended — it ensures every contact has a full data profile before the first email goes out.

Automating Enrollment with HubSpot Workflows

For a fully automated loop, use a HubSpot workflow to call a MailClaw webhook when a contact meets certain criteria (e.g., a deal is created, a form is submitted, or a lead score crosses a threshold).

In your HubSpot workflow, add a Webhook action with:

  • Method: POST
  • URL: http://localhost:3100/api/webhooks/hubspot/enroll
  • Body: Include contactEmail, sequenceId, and optionally enrichOnEnroll: true
Note: HubSpot webhooks require a publicly accessible URL. If MailClaw is running on your local machine, use a tunneling tool like ngrok or localtunnel to expose your local dashboard temporarily. For production use, consider deploying MailClaw on a small VPS or home server.

Step 6: Monitor Sync Health from the MailClaw Dashboard

Once everything is connected, your MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100 has a dedicated Integrations tab that shows sync status in real time. You can see:

  • How many contacts have been synced to HubSpot in the last 24 hours
  • Failed sync attempts with error details (useful for debugging field mapping issues)
  • Timeline event delivery rates
  • Deliverability metrics from your SMTP providers (SendGrid, Gmail, Outlook, and others) alongside the CRM data

MailClaw's deliverability monitoring becomes especially powerful when paired with HubSpot data. You can see that a sequence has a 42% open rate in MailClaw, cross-reference it with deal conversion data in HubSpot, and use that to inform your AI email agent's messaging — all from a single workflow.

Common Gotchas and How to Avoid Them

  • Duplicate contacts: If a contact exists in both MailClaw and HubSpot with slightly different email formats (e.g., John@company.com vs. john@company.com), MailClaw's deduplication engine will normalize to lowercase before matching. Make sure contactMatchField is set to email in your config.
  • Rate limits: HubSpot's API allows 100 requests per 10 seconds on most plans. MailClaw's sync engine respects these limits automatically with built-in backoff, but if you're importing large lists (1,000+ contacts), use the --batch-size 50 flag to keep things smooth.
  • Sequence enrollment conflicts: If a contact is already active in a MailClaw sequence, a new HubSpot enrollment trigger will be ignored by default. You can override this with --force-enroll, but use it carefully.

Next Steps

With MailClaw synced to HubSpot, you have a genuinely unified outreach stack. Your AI email agents can craft personalized sequences using enrichment data, every touchpoint gets logged in your CRM automatically, and your team works from a single source of truth without manual data entry.

From here, consider building a MailClaw AI agent that monitors deal stage changes in HubSpot and automatically suggests — or sends — follow-up sequences based on where a contact is in your pipeline. That's where the open-source, locally-run architecture of MailClaw really shines: you're not paying per-seat fees for automation logic, and you're not locked into a vendor's opinionated workflow builder. You own the stack.

articles.title: MailClaw + Salesforce Integration: Automating Sales Outreach
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw with Salesforce to automate your sales outreach pipeline — from syncing contacts and triggering email sequences to building AI agents that respond to CRM activity in real time.
articles.content:
Why Salesforce + MailClaw Is a Game-Changer for Sales Teams

Salesforce is where your deals live. MailClaw is where your outreach gets done. The problem most sales teams face is that these two worlds rarely talk to each other without expensive middleware, brittle Zapier chains, or a dedicated RevOps engineer babysitting the integration.

MailClaw changes that equation. Because it runs locally on your machine at localhost:3100 and is built on the open-source OpenClaw framework, you have direct programmatic access to your outreach pipeline — no SaaS middlemen, no per-seat fees for automation, no black-box logic. When you wire MailClaw into Salesforce, you get a tight feedback loop between CRM data and actual email delivery that most teams only dream about.

This guide walks you through exactly how to set that up — from initial configuration to building AI email agents that fire automatically when a Salesforce opportunity changes stage.

Prerequisites and Initial Setup

What You'll Need

  • MailClaw running locally (mailclaw start on port 3100)
  • A Salesforce account with API access (Professional edition or higher)
  • A connected sending account — Gmail via OAuth, Outlook, or an SMTP provider like SendGrid or Postmark
  • Node.js 18+ for the sync scripts below
  • Your Salesforce Connected App credentials (Consumer Key + Secret)

Connecting Your Sending Account

Before anything touches Salesforce, make sure MailClaw has a healthy sending identity. Open your dashboard at http://localhost:3100, navigate to Accounts → Add Account, and connect via OAuth for Gmail or Outlook. If you're sending at volume, configure a dedicated SendGrid or Postmark SMTP account here instead — MailClaw's deliverability monitor will track open rates, bounce rates, and spam complaints per account so you can rotate intelligently.

# Start MailClaw and verify accounts are healthy
mailclaw start
mailclaw accounts list

# Output:
# gmail-sales@yourcompany.com   OAuth    ✓ healthy   reputation: 94
# outreach@yourcompany.com      SMTP     ✓ healthy   reputation: 88

Pulling Salesforce Contacts into MailClaw

Setting Up the Salesforce Connected App

In Salesforce, go to Setup → App Manager → New Connected App. Enable OAuth, add api and refresh_token to the OAuth scopes, and save your Consumer Key and Secret. You'll use these to authenticate against the Salesforce REST API.

Writing the Sync Script

MailClaw exposes a local REST API at localhost:3100/api that accepts contact imports, sequence enrollments, and agent triggers. Here's a minimal Node.js script that pulls Leads from a Salesforce report and pushes them into MailClaw as enriched contacts:

import jsforce from 'jsforce';
import fetch from 'node-fetch';

const sf = new jsforce.Connection({
  oauth2: {
    clientId: process.env.SF_CLIENT_ID,
    clientSecret: process.env.SF_CLIENT_SECRET,
    redirectUri: 'http://localhost:3100/oauth/callback'
  }
});

await sf.login(process.env.SF_USERNAME, process.env.SF_PASSWORD);

// Pull open leads from a specific campaign or stage
const leads = await sf.query(`
  SELECT Id, FirstName, LastName, Email, Company, Title,
         LeadSource, NumberOfEmployees, AnnualRevenue
  FROM Lead
  WHERE Status = 'Open - Not Contacted'
  AND IsConverted = false
  LIMIT 500
`);

// Push to MailClaw contacts API
for (const lead of leads.records) {
  await fetch('http://localhost:3100/api/contacts', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      email: lead.Email,
      firstName: lead.FirstName,
      lastName: lead.LastName,
      company: lead.Company,
      title: lead.Title,
      tags: ['salesforce-lead', lead.LeadSource],
      metadata: {
        sfId: lead.Id,
        employees: lead.NumberOfEmployees,
        revenue: lead.AnnualRevenue
      }
    })
  });
}

console.log(`Synced ${leads.records.length} leads to MailClaw`);

Run this on a cron job — every 15 minutes works well for most teams — and your MailClaw contact list stays in sync with Salesforce automatically.

Enriching Contacts Before Outreach

Once contacts land in MailClaw, let the built-in contact enrichment layer fill in the gaps. From the dashboard, navigate to Contacts → Enrich, select your Salesforce-imported segment, and run enrichment. MailClaw will layer in additional firmographic data, LinkedIn signals, and technographic hints that Salesforce often lacks — giving your AI email agents richer context to personalize from.

# Enrich a tagged segment from the CLI
mailclaw contacts enrich --tag salesforce-lead --provider clearbit,hunter

Building the Outreach Sequence

Designing a Salesforce-Aware Sequence

In the MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100/sequences, create a new sequence. A proven structure for cold-to-warm Salesforce leads looks like this:

  1. Day 0 — Intro email: Short, personalized, one clear ask. Reference their company size or recent trigger if enrichment found one.
  2. Day 3 — Value email: One relevant case study or stat. No fluff.
  3. Day 7 — Soft bump: Two sentences. Reply-based. Keeps it human.
  4. Day 14 — Breakup email: Light humor, low pressure, leaves the door open.

In each step, use MailClaw's AI personalization tokens to reference enriched fields. The sequence builder supports Liquid-style syntax:

Subject: Quick question about {{company}} and {{painPoint}}

Hi {{firstName}},

I noticed {{company}} recently {{recentSignal | default: "expanded your team"}} —
congrats on the growth.

We've helped companies at the {{employees | bucket: "50-200,200-1000,1000+"}}
employee stage cut their outbound setup time by 60%. Worth a 15-minute look?

{{aiClosing}}

The {{aiClosing}} token triggers MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered AI layer to generate a contextual closing line based on the contact's full enrichment profile — a small touch that meaningfully lifts reply rates.

Triggering Sequences from Salesforce Events

Using Salesforce Workflow Rules or Flow

The cleanest way to fire a MailClaw sequence based on a CRM event is to use Salesforce Flow with an outbound HTTP callout. When an Opportunity moves to Proposal Sent, trigger a POST to your local MailClaw instance via a lightweight proxy (since Salesforce can't hit localhost directly — more on that below).

The Localhost Tunnel Approach

Since Salesforce needs a public URL to send webhooks, expose your local MailClaw instance temporarily using ngrok or Cloudflare Tunnel:

# Expose MailClaw to the internet for webhook testing
ngrok http 3100

# You'll get something like:
# Forwarding: https://abc123.ngrok.io -> localhost:3100

# Use this as your Salesforce webhook URL:
# https://abc123.ngrok.io/api/webhooks/trigger-sequence

For production teams, run MailClaw on an internal server or VPN-accessible machine instead of your laptop — then use a stable internal hostname. The architecture is identical; you're just moving from a dev tunnel to a stable host.

The Webhook Payload

Configure your Salesforce Flow to POST this payload when an Opportunity stage changes:

{
  "event": "opportunity_stage_changed",
  "contactEmail": "{!Contact.Email}",
  "sequenceId": "proposal-followup-v2",
  "metadata": {
    "opportunityId": "{!Opportunity.Id}",
    "dealValue": "{!Opportunity.Amount}",
    "stage": "{!Opportunity.StageName}"
  }
}

MailClaw's webhook handler will look up the contact, check enrollment status (so you never double-enroll), and kick off the sequence — all logged in your local dashboard.

Building an AI Email Agent for Salesforce Replies

This is where MailClaw really pulls ahead of traditional outreach tools. Using the AI email agents feature (available under Agents in the dashboard), you can build a responder agent that monitors replies from your Salesforce-synced contacts and takes action automatically.

# Create a new AI agent from the CLI
mailclaw agent create \
  --name "sf-reply-handler" \
  --trigger reply \
  --tag salesforce-lead \
  --model gpt-4o \
  --instructions "agents/sf-reply-handler.md"

Your sf-reply-handler.md instruction file tells the agent how to classify replies — interested, not now, wrong person, unsubscribe — and what to do with each. For interested replies, the agent can automatically update the Salesforce Lead status via the API, pause the sequence, and create a Task for the account owner. For not now, it re-enrolls the contact in a nurture sequence 30 days out.

Pro tip: Keep your agent instructions tight and specific. Tell it explicitly what to do with ambiguous replies rather than letting it improvise — your Salesforce data integrity will thank you.

Monitoring Deliverability Across Your Salesforce Outreach

High-volume Salesforce outreach is a deliverability risk if you're not watching the signals. MailClaw's deliverability monitor at localhost:3100/deliverability tracks bounce rates, spam trap hits, and reply rates per sequence and per sending account. Set alert thresholds so that if bounce rate exceeds 3% on a Salesforce-imported segment, MailClaw pauses the sequence and flags it for review — protecting your sender reputation before it becomes a problem.

# Set a deliverability threshold for a sequence
mailclaw sequence update proposal-followup-v2 \
  --max-bounce-rate 0.03 \
  --max-spam-rate 0.001 \
  --on-breach pause-and-notify

Keeping Salesforce in Sync with MailClaw Outcomes

The loop isn't complete until MailClaw outcomes write back to Salesforce. At its simplest, this means posting engagement events — email opened, link clicked, reply received, unsubscribed — back to the Lead or Contact record as Activity History. Extend your sync script to listen to MailClaw's event webhook and push updates back via the Salesforce Composite API.

With this in place, your sales reps see a real-time feed of email engagement directly inside Salesforce — no tab-switching, no manual logging. Leads that have opened three emails and clicked a link get a visual signal in the CRM, helping reps prioritize their call list without any extra tooling.

The combination of MailClaw's local AI infrastructure and Salesforce's CRM backbone creates an outreach system that's both powerful and genuinely transparent — you can see exactly what's being sent, why, and what's working, all from a single dashboard running on your own machine.

articles.title: How to Connect MailClaw to Slack for Notification Alerts
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw to Slack so your team gets real-time notification alerts for campaign events, deliverability issues, and AI agent activity — all without leaving your local setup.
articles.content:
Why Connect MailClaw to Slack?

Running email outreach locally on your Mac gives you incredible control — no third-party servers, no data leaving your machine, full visibility into every send. But that local-first approach comes with one tradeoff: you're not always staring at the MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100 when something important happens.

That's where Slack integration changes everything. When your AI email agents are firing off sequences, your contact enrichment jobs are completing, or a deliverability issue flags a bounce spike — you want to know immediately, wherever you are. Connecting MailClaw to Slack means your team gets real-time alerts pushed directly to the channels you already live in, without anyone needing to babysit a browser tab.

This guide walks you through setting up Slack notifications for MailClaw step by step, covering webhook configuration, alert types you should monitor, and a few practical patterns that make the integration genuinely useful rather than just noisy.

What You'll Need Before You Start

Before diving into the configuration, make sure you have the following in place:

  • MailClaw running locally — accessible at localhost:3100 with OpenClaw powering the backend
  • A Slack workspace where you have permission to create apps or incoming webhooks
  • Node.js 18+ installed on your Mac (MailClaw's dependency)
  • At least one connected email account — Gmail via OAuth, Outlook, or an SMTP provider like SendGrid

You don't need a paid Slack plan. Incoming webhooks are available on the free tier, which is more than enough for most MailClaw notification setups.

Step 1: Create a Slack Incoming Webhook

Slack's incoming webhooks are the simplest way to push messages from an external app into a channel. Here's how to set one up:

  1. Go to api.slack.com/apps and click Create New App
  2. Choose From scratch, give your app a name like MailClaw Alerts, and select your workspace
  3. In the left sidebar, click Incoming Webhooks and toggle it On
  4. Click Add New Webhook to Workspace and choose the channel you want alerts delivered to (e.g., #email-ops or #outreach-alerts)
  5. Copy the generated webhook URL — it will look something like this:
https://hooks.slack.com/services/YOUR/SLACK/WEBHOOK

Keep this URL secure. Anyone with it can post to your Slack channel.

Step 2: Add the Webhook to MailClaw's Configuration

MailClaw stores its integration settings in a local config file. Open your MailClaw project directory and locate config/integrations.json. If the file doesn't exist yet, create it.

{
  "notifications": {
    "slack": {
      "enabled": true,
      "webhookUrl": "https://hooks.slack.com/services/YOUR/SLACK/WEBHOOK",
      "channel": "#email-ops",
      "alertTypes": [
        "campaign_started",
        "campaign_completed",
        "bounce_spike",
        "sequence_step_sent",
        "enrichment_complete",
        "agent_action",
        "deliverability_warning"
      ]
    }
  }
}

Save the file, then restart MailClaw from your terminal:

mailclaw restart --reload-config

You should see a confirmation in the terminal output indicating the Slack integration loaded successfully. If you get a config validation error, double-check that your JSON is well-formed — a missing comma is the most common culprit.

Step 3: Test the Connection

MailClaw includes a built-in notification test command so you can verify the webhook is working before relying on it in production:

mailclaw notify test --channel slack

This sends a sample payload to your configured Slack channel. You should see a message appear within a few seconds that looks like:

MailClaw · just now
✅ Test notification from MailClaw — your Slack integration is working correctly. Running on localhost:3100.

If nothing arrives, check your webhook URL for typos and confirm the Slack app has permission to post to the target channel. You can also run mailclaw logs --tail to inspect outgoing webhook calls in real time.

Step 4: Configure Alert Types That Actually Matter

One of the easiest mistakes with notification integrations is turning everything on and immediately drowning your team in alerts. The goal is signal, not noise. Here's how to think about which MailClaw events deserve a Slack ping.

High-Priority Alerts (Always Enable)

  • bounce_spike — When your bounce rate crosses a threshold (default: 5%), MailClaw's deliverability monitoring fires this alert. Getting this in Slack immediately lets you pause a campaign before it damages your sender reputation across your Gmail or SendGrid accounts.
  • deliverability_warning — Covers SPF/DKIM failures, blacklist detections, and unusual open-rate drops. These need fast human attention.
  • agent_action — If you're running AI email agents for autonomous outreach, knowing when an agent takes an action (sending a follow-up, pausing a contact, triggering enrichment) keeps your team in the loop without requiring constant dashboard monitoring.

Medium-Priority Alerts (Enable Selectively)

  • campaign_completed — Useful for knowing when a sequence finishes. Good for async teams who hand off campaigns between time zones.
  • enrichment_complete — MailClaw's contact enrichment can run in the background against large lists. A Slack ping when it's done saves you from repeatedly checking the dashboard.
  • sequence_step_sent — Helpful during early testing of a new sequence, but consider disabling this for high-volume campaigns to avoid alert fatigue.

Lower-Priority Alerts (Use Sparingly)

  • campaign_started — Fine for visibility, but if you launched it yourself, this is redundant. More useful when other team members are triggering campaigns.

You can update your active alert types any time by editing config/integrations.json and running mailclaw notify reload.

Step 5: Customize Alert Formatting with Templates

MailClaw supports custom message templates for Slack notifications using a lightweight templating syntax. This lets you include campaign-specific details — like which sequence triggered an alert or which email account is affected — directly in the Slack message.

In your config/integrations.json, add a templates block inside the Slack config:

"templates": {
  "bounce_spike": "🚨 *Bounce spike detected* on campaign `{{campaign_name}}`.\nBounce rate: {{bounce_rate}}% (threshold: {{threshold}}%).\nAffected account: {{email_account}}\nReview at localhost:3100/deliverability",
  "agent_action": "🤖 *AI Agent update*: {{agent_name}} {{action_description}} for contact {{contact_email}} in sequence `{{sequence_name}}`.",
  "enrichment_complete": "✅ *Enrichment complete* — {{contact_count}} contacts processed in {{duration}}s. View results at localhost:3100/contacts"
}

The {{variable}} placeholders are filled in automatically by MailClaw at alert time. This is especially useful when you're running multiple campaigns across different SMTP accounts or managing sequences that sync with tools like HubSpot or Salesforce via MailClaw's CRM connectors.

Routing Alerts to Different Slack Channels

If your team is larger or your workflows are more complex, you might want deliverability alerts going to #ops-critical while routine campaign updates go to #growth-team. MailClaw supports multi-channel routing by defining additional webhook entries with scoped alert types:

"notifications": {
  "slack": [
    {
      "enabled": true,
      "webhookUrl": "https://hooks.slack.com/services/YOUR/SLACK/WEBHOOK.../critical-webhook",
      "channel": "#ops-critical",
      "alertTypes": ["bounce_spike", "deliverability_warning"]
    },
    {
      "enabled": true,
      "webhookUrl": "https://hooks.slack.com/services/YOUR/SLACK/WEBHOOK.../growth-webhook",
      "channel": "#growth-team",
      "alertTypes": ["campaign_completed", "enrichment_complete", "sequence_step_sent"]
    }
  ]
}

This pattern keeps critical operational alerts visible to the people who need to act on them fast, while routine updates land somewhere useful but less urgent.

A Few Practical Tips to Make This Work Long-Term

The technical setup is the easy part. Here's what actually makes Slack alerts valuable in day-to-day outreach work:

  • Set a bounce threshold that matches your sending volume. A 5% bounce rate means something very different on a 50-contact test campaign versus a 5,000-contact sequence. Adjust the deliverability.bounceThreshold setting in MailClaw's config to match your context.
  • Review agent alerts as a team habit. MailClaw's AI email agents are powerful, but having the team glance at agent actions in Slack daily builds trust in what the agents are doing and catches edge cases early.
  • Use Slack's reminder feature on alert messages. For non-urgent alerts like enrichment completions, use Slack's built-in "remind me about this" to revisit them when you have focus time — don't feel pressured to act on every notification immediately.
  • Periodically audit which alerts you're actually acting on. If a certain alert type consistently gets ignored in Slack, disable it. The best notification system is one your team trusts and pays attention to.

You're Now Fully Connected

With Slack notifications wired into MailClaw, your local email automation setup gains a real-time communication layer that keeps your whole team informed without anyone needing to camp out on the dashboard. Whether a deliverability issue surfaces at midnight or an AI agent completes a major enrichment job while you're in a meeting, the right people get the right information exactly when they need it.

From here, consider exploring MailClaw's other integration hooks — including webhooks for HubSpot deal stage changes and Salesforce contact updates — which can be layered on top of the same notification infrastructure you just built. The open-source nature of MailClaw means the config you've set up today is fully yours to extend.

articles.title: Using MailClaw with SendGrid for High-Volume Sending
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw to SendGrid for reliable, high-volume email delivery — including SMTP configuration, API key setup, deliverability best practices, and how to pair SendGrid's infrastructure with MailClaw's AI agents and sequence builder for serious outreach at scale.
articles.content:
Why Pair MailClaw with SendGrid?

If you've been running outreach campaigns through MailClaw and hitting the ceiling on what Gmail or Outlook SMTP can reliably handle, it's time to graduate to a dedicated sending infrastructure. SendGrid is one of the most battle-tested transactional and bulk email platforms in the world, and when you wire it into MailClaw's local dashboard, you get the best of both worlds: the intelligence and automation of an AI-powered tool running on your machine, backed by SendGrid's globally distributed delivery network.

The combination is particularly powerful for teams running sequences at scale — think thousands of contacts, multi-step nurture flows, or outbound campaigns where deliverability isn't just nice-to-have, it's the whole game. MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring will give you real-time visibility into what SendGrid is doing under the hood, and your AI email agents can keep optimizing send times and copy without you babysitting every campaign.

Setting Up Your SendGrid Account

Create an API Key with the Right Permissions

Before you touch MailClaw's configuration, get your SendGrid credentials sorted. Log into your SendGrid dashboard and navigate to Settings → API Keys → Create API Key. For production use, choose Restricted Access and enable at minimum:

  • Mail Send — Full Access
  • Stats — Read Access
  • Suppressions — Full Access
  • Tracking — Full Access

Copy that key immediately — SendGrid won't show it again. Store it somewhere secure before you paste it into MailClaw.

Authenticate Your Sending Domain

This step is non-negotiable if you care about deliverability. In SendGrid, go to Settings → Sender Authentication and authenticate your domain. You'll add CNAME records to your DNS provider (Cloudflare, Route 53, Namecheap — whatever you use). SendGrid will walk you through the specific records. Once verified, your emails will pass DKIM alignment, which dramatically improves inbox placement.

While you're there, set up a dedicated IP address if you're on a Pro plan or higher. Shared IPs are fine for getting started, but at high volumes, your reputation lives and dies on your own IP's history.

Connecting SendGrid to MailClaw

Via SMTP Integration

MailClaw supports both SMTP and API-based sending. For SendGrid, SMTP is the quickest way to get up and running. Open your MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to Settings → Email Accounts → Add Account, and select SMTP / Custom Provider.

Use these SendGrid SMTP credentials:

Host:       smtp.sendgrid.net
Port:       587 (TLS) or 465 (SSL)
Username:   apikey
Password:   YOUR_SENDGRID_API_KEY
Encryption: STARTTLS
Note: The username is literally the string apikey — not your SendGrid account email. This trips people up constantly.

Once saved, MailClaw will run a test send to verify the connection. You should see a green confirmation in the dashboard within a few seconds. If you see an authentication error, double-check that the API key has Mail Send permissions enabled.

Via the CLI

If you prefer working from the terminal, MailClaw's CLI makes account setup scriptable and repeatable across environments. From your project directory:

mailclaw account add \
  --name "SendGrid Production" \
  --type smtp \
  --host smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --port 587 \
  --username apikey \
  --password YOUR_SENDGRID_API_KEY \
  --tls true

You can then set this as the default sending account for a specific campaign or sequence using mailclaw campaign set-account --campaign-id YOUR_ID --account "SendGrid Production". This is especially useful when you're running multi-account setups — for instance, using Gmail OAuth for warm, personal-touch sequences while SendGrid handles your higher-volume broadcast campaigns.

Configuring for High-Volume Sending

Warm Up Your IP Before You Blast

Dumping 50,000 emails through a cold IP on day one is the fastest way to land in spam folders permanently. SendGrid offers an automated IP warmup option in Settings → IP Addresses — enable it. Combined with MailClaw's sequence builder, you can structure your sends to ramp gradually: start with your most engaged contacts (opens, clicks, recent activity), then expand outward as your IP builds reputation.

A practical warmup schedule looks roughly like this:

  1. Days 1–3: 500–1,000 emails/day to highly engaged contacts
  2. Days 4–7: 2,000–5,000 emails/day, expanding to warm segments
  3. Days 8–14: 10,000–25,000 emails/day to broader lists
  4. Week 3+: Full volume, with deliverability monitoring engaged

Use MailClaw's contact enrichment to score your list before you start. Enriched contact data helps you identify which addresses are likely to be active, which reduces your bounce rate from day one — a critical signal to ISPs during warmup.

Set Sending Throttles in MailClaw

Even after warmup, throttling is smart practice. In your campaign settings within the MailClaw dashboard, configure rate limits to stay within SendGrid's recommended guidelines for your plan. For most Pro accounts, staying under 100 emails per minute per IP is a safe ceiling unless you've been explicitly cleared for higher throughput.

mailclaw campaign update YOUR_CAMPAIGN_ID \
  --rate-limit 80 \
  --rate-unit minute \
  --sending-window "08:00-18:00" \
  --timezone "America/New_York"

The --sending-window flag is particularly useful — MailClaw will automatically queue and batch sends to stay within business hours, which improves open rates alongside deliverability.

Using MailClaw's Deliverability Tools with SendGrid

One of MailClaw's strongest features is its built-in deliverability monitoring, and it becomes even more powerful when piped alongside SendGrid's Event Webhook. In SendGrid, go to Settings → Mail Settings → Event Webhook and point it to your local MailClaw webhook endpoint:

http://localhost:3100/webhooks/sendgrid

Enable these event types: delivered, open, click, bounce, spam report, unsubscribe. Once active, MailClaw will ingest these events in real time and surface them in your dashboard. You'll see bounce rates, spam complaint rates, and engagement metrics all in one place — no need to context-switch between SendGrid's UI and your outreach tool.

If your spam complaint rate climbs above 0.08% (Google and Yahoo's current threshold for bulk senders), MailClaw will flag it immediately so you can pause and investigate before you do lasting damage to your sender reputation.

Powering Sequences and AI Agents at Scale

Building Multi-Step Sequences with SendGrid as the Engine

MailClaw's sequence builder lets you chain emails with conditional logic — send follow-up B if the contact didn't open email A within 48 hours, branch to a different track if they clicked a specific link, and so on. With SendGrid handling delivery, these sequences scale without degrading performance. You can run sequences across thousands of contacts simultaneously while MailClaw manages the orchestration logic locally.

If you're syncing contacts from HubSpot or Salesforce, use MailClaw's CRM integrations to pull enriched segments directly into your sequence builder. This means your AI email agents have full context — company size, industry, recent activity, deal stage — when generating and personalizing messages at each step.

Letting AI Agents Optimize in Real Time

MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered AI email agents don't just write emails — they adapt. As SendGrid sends back engagement data through the webhook, your agents can identify which subject lines are landing, which send times correlate with opens for specific contact segments, and which sequence steps are causing drop-off. Set up an agent with:

mailclaw agent create \
  --name "SendGrid Optimizer" \
  --campaign YOUR_CAMPAIGN_ID \
  --goal "maximize_open_rate" \
  --optimize-on "subject_line,send_time" \
  --learning-period 3d

After the learning period, the agent will automatically apply its findings to subsequent sends in the campaign — adjusting copy variations and timing without you lifting a finger.

Managing Suppressions and Compliance

High-volume sending comes with serious compliance obligations. Fortunately, MailClaw and SendGrid both handle suppressions gracefully. When a contact unsubscribes through a SendGrid-tracked link, the event fires to MailClaw's webhook, which immediately marks that contact as suppressed across all your campaigns and sequences. No accidental re-sends, no CAN-SPAM or GDPR violations.

Periodically export your SendGrid suppression lists and cross-reference them with your MailClaw contact database to ensure they stay in sync — especially if you're also sending through other accounts like Gmail or Outlook for different campaign types.

Getting the Most Out of the Stack

The MailClaw and SendGrid combination isn't just a technical integration — it's a genuinely effective outreach stack. SendGrid gives you the infrastructure to send at scale without worrying about IP reputation or rate limiting from personal email providers. MailClaw gives you the intelligence layer: AI agents that personalize and optimize, a sequence builder that handles complex logic, contact enrichment that makes your targeting sharper, and a clean local dashboard at localhost:3100 that keeps everything visible and in your control.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your machine, you're not paying per-seat fees or handing your contact data to a SaaS vendor. Pair that with SendGrid's pay-for-what-you-use pricing model, and you have a high-performance outreach engine that scales economically. Whether you're running 5,000 emails a week or 500,000, the architecture holds up — and your AI agents keep getting smarter the longer you run it.

articles.title: How to Integrate MailClaw with Zapier for Custom Workflows
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw's local email automation engine to Zapier, unlocking powerful custom workflows that bridge your outreach sequences with CRMs, spreadsheets, Slack, and hundreds of other tools — without writing a single line of backend code.
articles.content:
Why Connect MailClaw to Zapier?

MailClaw already handles a remarkable amount of your email automation work natively — building sequences, enriching contacts, monitoring deliverability, and running AI email agents that respond and follow up on your behalf. But no single tool exists in a vacuum. Your sales team lives in HubSpot. Your ops team tracks leads in Google Sheets. Your founder wants a Slack ping every time a prospect books a call.

That's where Zapier comes in. By exposing MailClaw's local API to Zapier via a simple tunnel or webhook setup, you can trigger external workflows from inside MailClaw — or push inbound data from hundreds of apps directly into your contact lists, sequences, and AI agents. The result is a lean, self-hosted automation stack that punches well above its weight class.

Quick note on architecture: MailClaw runs locally on localhost:3100, which means it isn't publicly accessible by default. To connect it to Zapier (which needs a reachable HTTP endpoint), you'll use a lightweight tunnel tool like ngrok or Cloudflare Tunnel. We'll cover the exact setup below.

Step 1: Expose Your Local MailClaw Instance

Before Zapier can talk to MailClaw, your local server needs a public URL. The easiest way to do this is with ngrok.

Install and Start ngrok

If you haven't already, install ngrok from ngrok.com and authenticate with your account token. Then run:

ngrok http 3100

You'll get a forwarding URL that looks something like:

https://a1b2-203-0-113-42.ngrok-free.app

Copy that URL — it's your temporary public endpoint for MailClaw. Keep this terminal window open while you're building your Zaps. For a more permanent setup, consider Cloudflare Tunnel, which gives you a stable, named subdomain that persists across restarts.

Verify the Connection

You can confirm MailClaw is reachable by hitting the health endpoint:

curl https://your-ngrok-url.ngrok-free.app/api/health

If you see a JSON response with "status": "ok", you're good to go. Your MailClaw instance — including the sequence builder, contact enrichment engine, and AI email agents — is now accessible over the web.

Step 2: Understand MailClaw's Webhook and API Surface

MailClaw exposes two integration points you'll use with Zapier:

  • Inbound webhooks: Zapier sends data to MailClaw (e.g., "a new lead just filled out your Typeform — add them to the cold outreach sequence")
  • Outbound webhooks: MailClaw sends data to Zapier when something happens (e.g., "a contact replied to an email — notify the sales team in Slack")

From your MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to Settings → Integrations → Webhooks to configure outbound events. You can subscribe to events like contact.replied, sequence.completed, contact.enriched, and agent.action_taken.

Step 3: Build Your First Zap — New Lead to Outreach Sequence

Let's walk through a practical, end-to-end example: automatically enrolling new HubSpot contacts into a MailClaw sequence.

Trigger: New Contact in HubSpot

  1. In Zapier, click Create Zap and choose HubSpot as your trigger app.
  2. Select the trigger event "New Contact" and connect your HubSpot account.
  3. Test the trigger to pull in a sample contact record.

Action: Add Contact to MailClaw via Webhook

  1. Add a new action step, choose Webhooks by Zapier, and select POST.
  2. Set the URL to your ngrok tunnel plus the contacts endpoint:
https://your-ngrok-url.ngrok-free.app/api/contacts
  1. Set the payload type to JSON and map your HubSpot fields:
{
  "email": "{{contact_email}}",
  "firstName": "{{contact_first_name}}",
  "lastName": "{{contact_last_name}}",
  "company": "{{contact_company}}",
  "sequenceId": "seq_coldoutreach_v2",
  "tags": ["hubspot", "inbound"]
}

MailClaw will receive the contact, run it through the contact enrichment layer (pulling in LinkedIn data, company info, and tech stack signals via the OpenClaw engine), and then automatically enroll the contact in the specified sequence. From that point forward, your AI email agents take over — personalizing subject lines, adjusting send timing, and handling replies based on the rules you've configured.

Step 4: Trigger External Actions When MailClaw Events Fire

Now let's flip the direction. When a contact completes a sequence or replies to your AI agent, you probably want something to happen downstream — update a deal stage, notify a rep, log to a spreadsheet.

Configure an Outbound Webhook in MailClaw

In the MailClaw dashboard, go to Settings → Integrations → Webhooks → Add Webhook. Fill in:

  • Event: contact.replied
  • URL: Your Zapier webhook URL (from the "Webhooks by Zapier" trigger in a new Zap)
  • Secret: A random string you'll use to verify the payload in Zapier

Now, every time a contact replies to any email in your sequence, MailClaw will POST the event payload to Zapier, which can then route it to Slack, Salesforce, Google Sheets, or wherever your team needs it.

Example: Reply Notification in Slack

In Zapier, set Webhooks by Zapier as your trigger (Catch Hook), then add a Slack action with a message template like:

🎯 *New Reply Detected*
Contact: {{first_name}} {{last_name}} ({{email}})
Company: {{company}}
Sequence: {{sequence_name}}
Snippet: {{reply_snippet}}
→ View in MailClaw: http://localhost:3100/contacts/{{contact_id}}

Your sales team gets an instant, context-rich Slack notification with a deep link back into the MailClaw dashboard — no CRM hunting required.

Practical Workflow Ideas Worth Building

Once you've got the core plumbing in place, the possibilities expand quickly. Here are some high-value workflows MailClaw + Zapier users have found genuinely useful:

  • Typeform → MailClaw sequence: When someone fills out a lead magnet form, auto-enroll them in a nurture sequence and trigger contact enrichment to fill in missing fields before the first email goes out.
  • Calendly booked → pause sequence: When a prospect books a meeting, use the Zapier action to call PATCH /api/contacts/:id and set "sequenceStatus": "paused" so they don't receive any more automated emails.
  • Salesforce opportunity stage change → new sequence: When a deal moves to "Negotiation" in Salesforce, enroll the contact in a case study or social proof sequence via MailClaw.
  • Google Sheets row → bulk contact import: Maintain a running sheet of conference leads and use a daily Zap to sync new rows into MailClaw, complete with custom tags for segmentation.
  • Deliverability alert → PagerDuty or email: MailClaw's deliverability monitoring fires a webhook when your sender score drops or bounce rates spike — route that to an alert channel so you catch problems before they damage your domain reputation.
  • SendGrid bounce event → contact suppression: If you're using SendGrid as an SMTP relay, pipe bounce webhooks through Zapier into MailClaw to automatically mark contacts as undeliverable.

Keeping Your Integration Secure

Running a local tool like MailClaw through a public tunnel introduces some surface area worth thinking about. A few quick practices to keep things tight:

  • Use webhook secrets: Always set a secret on outbound MailClaw webhooks and validate the X-MailClaw-Signature header in your Zapier filters to reject spoofed requests.
  • Scope your ngrok exposure: If you're only using ngrok for Zapier, consider adding an ngrok auth policy or using ngrok's IP restrictions to whitelist Zapier's IP ranges.
  • Rotate tokens regularly: MailClaw's API key (found in Settings → API) should be treated like a password. Rotate it if you ever share it or suspect it was exposed in logs.
  • Use Cloudflare Tunnel for production-grade setups: If you're running MailClaw for a team or client, Cloudflare Tunnel gives you TLS, DDoS protection, and access policies without exposing a raw port.

What You've Just Built

With MailClaw acting as your AI-powered outreach engine and Zapier handling the glue between your other tools, you now have a genuinely powerful automation stack — one that runs entirely on your own machine, costs nothing in SaaS fees, and gives you full control over your data and logic.

The open-source foundation of MailClaw (built on OpenClaw) means you can extend the API, add custom webhook events, or fork the contact enrichment pipeline if your use case demands it. And because everything lives at localhost:3100, you're never at the mercy of a vendor's uptime, rate limits, or pricing changes.

Start with one Zap, get comfortable with the webhook format, and then layer on complexity as your workflows mature. The integration patterns above scale from solo founder to full sales team — and the MailClaw AI agents get smarter the more data flows through them.

articles.title: MailClaw + Google Sheets: Importing Leads and Tracking Results
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to connect Google Sheets to MailClaw for seamless lead importing, real-time campaign tracking, and automated outreach — with step-by-step instructions and practical tips for getting the most out of your local email automation setup.
articles.content:
Why Google Sheets Is the Perfect Lead Source for MailClaw

Most sales and marketing teams already live in Google Sheets. It's where leads get collected from webforms, scraped from LinkedIn, exported from CRMs like HubSpot or Salesforce, or manually curated by an SDR over a busy week. Rather than forcing a migration to yet another platform, MailClaw meets you where your data already lives.

Because MailClaw runs entirely on your machine at localhost:3100, your contact data never leaves your environment. There's no third-party SaaS platform ingesting your leads, no privacy gray areas, and no per-seat fees climbing as your list grows. When you combine that local-first philosophy with a live Google Sheet as your lead source, you get a remarkably flexible outreach pipeline that's both powerful and easy to maintain.

Step 1: Preparing Your Google Sheet for Import

Before you pull anything into MailClaw, spend five minutes setting up your Sheet correctly. A clean import saves hours of cleanup later.

Required Column Structure

MailClaw's importer expects a header row in the first row of your Sheet. At minimum, include these columns:
