| first_name | last_name | email           | company        | title             |
|------------|-----------|-----------------|----------------|-------------------|
| Sarah      | Lin       | sarah@acme.io   | Acme Corp      | VP of Engineering |
| Marcus     | Webb      | m.webb@orbit.co | Orbit Labs     | Founder           |

You can include as many custom fields as you like — linkedin_url, phone, city, lead_source — MailClaw will map them to contact properties during import. Columns MailClaw doesn't recognize are stored as custom attributes, which you can reference in sequence templates using {{lead_source}} or any other variable name.

Data Hygiene Tips Before You Import

  • Remove duplicate emails — use Google Sheets' built-in Data → Remove duplicates before exporting.
  • Verify email formats — a quick =ISNUMBER(MATCH("@",SPLIT(A2,""),0)) formula flags obvious malformations.
  • Standardize company names — inconsistent casing (acme vs ACME vs Acme Corp) creates messy segmentation later.
  • Add a status column — values like new, contacted, or replied let you write back results without overwriting your original lead flags.

Step 2: Importing Leads into MailClaw

There are two ways to get your Sheet data into MailClaw: a direct CSV export, or the live Google Sheets sync using MailClaw's built-in connector. Both are fast. The sync option is more powerful if you're running ongoing campaigns.

Option A: CSV Import via the Dashboard

  1. In Google Sheets, go to File → Download → Comma-separated values (.csv).
  2. Open your MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to Contacts → Import.
  3. Drop your CSV file into the upload area. MailClaw will auto-detect your column headers and propose field mappings.
  4. Review the mapping, confirm, and click Import Contacts. A progress indicator shows each record being processed.

For large lists (10,000+ rows), the CLI is faster and gives you more control:

mailclaw contacts import \
  --file ~/Downloads/leads_q2.csv \
  --list "Q2 Outreach" \
  --dedupe-by email \
  --tag "google-sheets-import"

The --dedupe-by email flag ensures existing contacts are updated rather than duplicated, and --tag makes it easy to filter this batch later.

Option B: Live Google Sheets Sync

This is where things get genuinely useful for ongoing campaigns. MailClaw's Google Sheets connector polls your Sheet on a schedule and pulls in new rows automatically.

mailclaw integrations connect google-sheets \
  --sheet-id "1BxiMVs0XRA5nFMdKvBdBZjgmUUqptlbs74OgVE2upms" \
  --tab "Sheet1" \
  --sync-interval 30m \
  --list "Live Pipeline"

Replace the --sheet-id value with the ID from your Sheet's URL. Once connected, any new row added to that Sheet will appear in MailClaw's contact list within 30 minutes (or whatever interval you set). This is perfect for teams where an SDR is continuously adding leads while a campaign is actively running.

Pro tip: Create a dedicated "MailClaw Import" tab in your Sheet rather than syncing from your main data tab. That way your team can clean and stage leads before they enter the campaign pipeline.

Step 3: Enriching Contacts Before Outreach

Raw lead data from a spreadsheet is often incomplete. MailClaw's contact enrichment feature, powered by the OpenClaw engine, can fill in missing details automatically before your sequence fires.

mailclaw contacts enrich \
  --list "Q2 Outreach" \
  --fields title,company_size,linkedin_url,tech_stack

Enrichment pulls from public data sources to add context like company size, industry, tech stack, and LinkedIn profiles. This matters because MailClaw's AI email agents use these enriched fields to personalize outreach at scale — writing genuinely contextual first lines rather than the generic "I noticed you work at {{company}}" approach that everyone can spot immediately.

After enrichment runs, you'll see updated contact cards in the localhost dashboard. From there you can segment your import list into targeted sub-lists before building sequences — for example, separating Founders at companies with 10–50 employees from VPs at Series B+ startups.

Step 4: Building a Sequence for Your Imported Leads

With your contacts imported and enriched, head to the Sequence Builder in the MailClaw dashboard. Create a new sequence and assign your imported list as the audience.

A Simple 3-Step Outreach Sequence

  • Email 1 (Day 0): Personalized cold intro, generated by the AI email agent using enriched contact data.
  • Email 2 (Day 3): A light follow-up referencing the first email, with a different value angle.
  • Email 3 (Day 7): A short "closing the loop" email that gives the prospect an easy out or easy yes.

MailClaw supports multi-account sending, so you can route emails through Gmail via OAuth, Outlook via OAuth, or a dedicated sending domain through SendGrid or Postmark SMTP — all configured under Settings → Sending Accounts. Spreading volume across accounts is one of the most effective deliverability strategies, and MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools will flag any accounts showing engagement drops or spam rate increases before they become a real problem.

Step 5: Writing Results Back to Google Sheets

This is the feature that closes the loop and makes the whole workflow genuinely powerful. MailClaw can write campaign results — opens, clicks, replies, bounces — back to your original Google Sheet in real time.

mailclaw campaigns export \
  --campaign "Q2 Outreach" \
  --destination google-sheets \
  --sheet-id "1BxiMVs0XRA5nFMdKvBdBZjgmUUqptlbs74OgVE2upms" \
  --tab "Results" \
  --fields email,opened,clicked,replied,bounced,last_contact_date

You can run this as a one-time export or schedule it to sync on an interval alongside your import sync:

mailclaw schedule add \
  --task "export-results" \
  --campaign "Q2 Outreach" \
  --interval 1h

What to Track in Your Results Tab

At minimum, add these columns to your results Sheet:

  • email_status — sent, opened, clicked, replied, bounced, unsubscribed
  • open_count — total opens (not unique; useful for gauging interest level)
  • last_opened_at — timestamp of most recent open, great for prioritizing follow-up calls
  • replied — boolean; filter to TRUE for your hottest leads
  • sequence_step — which email in the sequence they last received

With this data flowing back into Sheets, your team can build Looker Studio dashboards on top of it, import results into Salesforce or HubSpot via Zapier, or simply sort by replied = TRUE each morning to prioritize follow-up.

Keeping the Loop Running

The real power of this setup isn't any single step — it's the cycle. Leads enter your Sheet from wherever they originate (webforms, LinkedIn exports, a scraper, a virtual assistant), MailClaw picks them up automatically, enriches and sequences them, and writes outcomes back to the same Sheet your team is already watching. No platform switching, no manual CSV shuffling, no data sitting in a SaaS black box.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs locally, you can customize every part of this pipeline — modify the sync logic, add custom enrichment sources, build your own AI agent prompts, or extend the CLI for your specific workflow. The localhost dashboard gives you full visibility into what's running, and the OpenClaw engine underneath keeps improving with every release.

Start with a small list of 50–100 leads to validate your column mapping and sequence timing, then scale up once you've confirmed results are flowing back correctly. A bit of upfront setup here pays dividends across every campaign you run going forward.

articles.title: How to Connect MailClaw to Pipedrive for Pipeline Automation
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw to Pipedrive and automate your sales pipeline — from syncing contacts and triggering email sequences to building AI agents that respond to deal stage changes in real time.
articles.content:
Why Pipedrive and MailClaw Belong Together

If you're using Pipedrive to manage your sales pipeline, you already know how much manual work sits between a deal moving stages and the right email actually landing in a prospect's inbox. Someone has to notice the stage change, pull up the contact, find the right template, and hit send — often hours later, often inconsistently.

MailClaw changes that equation. Running locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, it connects directly to Pipedrive's API to watch your pipeline in real time, enrich contacts automatically, and fire off precisely timed email sequences the moment a deal moves. Because it's open-source and powered by OpenClaw, you control exactly how the logic works — no black-box automation, no per-seat pricing, no data leaving your machine unless you want it to.

This guide walks you through the full setup: authenticating with Pipedrive, mapping deal stages to sequences, and deploying an AI email agent that handles outreach on autopilot.

Prerequisites

  • MailClaw installed and running (mailclaw start — dashboard at localhost:3100)
  • A Pipedrive account with API access (any paid plan, or the trial)
  • At least one sending account connected (Gmail, Outlook, or an SMTP provider like SendGrid or Postmark)
  • Node.js 18+ if you plan to extend with custom scripts

Step 1: Generate Your Pipedrive API Token

MailClaw communicates with Pipedrive using its REST API. You'll need a personal API token to authenticate.

  1. Log in to Pipedrive and click your avatar in the top-right corner.
  2. Go to Personal Preferences → API.
  3. Copy the API token shown — treat it like a password.

Now open your MailClaw config file. By default it lives at ~/.mailclaw/config.yaml:

integrations:
  pipedrive:
    enabled: true
    api_token: "YOUR_PIPEDRIVE_API_TOKEN"
    poll_interval: 60        # seconds between pipeline checks
    track_stages: true
    enrich_on_sync: true

Save the file and restart the daemon:

mailclaw restart

Open localhost:3100, navigate to Integrations → Pipedrive, and you should see a green connected status with a live count of your deals and contacts.

Step 2: Sync Pipedrive Contacts and Enrich Them

Once connected, MailClaw can pull your Pipedrive contacts and run them through its built-in contact enrichment pipeline. This appends verified email addresses, job titles, company size, and LinkedIn profile data — all sourced and cached locally so you're not paying per-lookup to a third-party tool every time.

To trigger a full sync from the CLI:

mailclaw contacts sync --source pipedrive --enrich

Or set it on a schedule in your config:

sync:
  pipedrive:
    schedule: "0 */6 * * *"   # every 6 hours
    enrich: true
    deduplicate: true
    tag_new_contacts: "pipedrive-import"

Enriched contacts land in your MailClaw contact database with a pipedrive_id field, making two-way updates seamless. Any changes you make to a contact in MailClaw — updated email, added phone number — can be pushed back to Pipedrive automatically.

Step 3: Map Deal Stages to Email Sequences

This is where the real automation lives. MailClaw's sequence builder lets you define multi-step email campaigns and bind them to Pipedrive trigger events — deal stage changes, new deal creation, deal won, deal lost, and more.

Create a Sequence

In the dashboard at localhost:3100, go to Sequences → New Sequence. Build out your steps — each step is an email with a configurable delay, subject line, and AI-assisted body. For a post-demo follow-up sequence, you might use:

  • Step 1 (Day 0): Personalised thank-you after the demo
  • Step 2 (Day 2): Case study relevant to their industry
  • Step 3 (Day 5): Pricing summary with a soft call to action
  • Step 4 (Day 9): Breakup email with a direct question

Bind the Sequence to a Pipeline Stage

In your config, add a trigger block:

triggers:
  - name: "Post-Demo Follow-up"
    source: pipedrive
    event: deal.stage_changed
    condition:
      stage_name: "Demo Completed"
    action:
      type: enroll_sequence
      sequence_id: "post-demo-followup"
      contact_field: deal.person_id
      stop_on_reply: true
      stop_on_stage_change: true

The stop_on_reply flag is important — MailClaw monitors your connected inboxes and automatically halts a sequence the moment a prospect replies, so you never send a follow-up to someone who's already responded. The stop_on_stage_change flag does the same if the deal advances in Pipedrive before the sequence completes.

Step 4: Deploy an AI Email Agent for Pipeline Response

MailClaw's AI email agents go a step further than sequences. Where a sequence fires predefined steps on a timer, an AI agent can read incoming replies, understand context, and craft responses — or flag the conversation for a human when it detects buying signals or objections it shouldn't handle alone.

To create a Pipedrive-aware agent:

mailclaw agent create \
  --name "Pipeline Responder" \
  --model openai/gpt-4o \
  --persona "You are a helpful sales assistant for [Company]. Keep replies concise and professional." \
  --trigger pipedrive:deal.stage_changed \
  --stage "Proposal Sent" \
  --inbox gmail:you@yourcompany.com \
  --escalate-on "pricing objection, legal review, competitor mention"

Once active, this agent monitors replies to emails sent during the Proposal Sent stage. It can answer standard questions about timelines and next steps, and automatically escalates to your inbox when it detects one of the defined phrases. Every conversation the agent handles is logged in the MailClaw dashboard with a full audit trail.

Pro tip: Pair AI agents with MailClaw's deliverability tools to make sure your automated emails are actually landing. The built-in deliverability monitor checks your SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records, tracks bounce rates per domain, and warns you if a sending account starts showing placement issues — all visible from the same local dashboard.

Step 5: Push Activity Back to Pipedrive

Automation only helps if your CRM stays up to date. MailClaw can write activity notes and update deal fields in Pipedrive based on what happens in your email sequences.

In your config, enable writeback:

pipedrive:
  writeback:
    enabled: true
    log_email_sent: true
    log_email_opened: true
    log_reply_received: true
    advance_stage_on_reply: "Replied - Nurture"
    create_activity_on_bounce: true

Now when a prospect opens your case study email and replies, Pipedrive automatically gets a note with the timestamp, the sequence step, and the reply content — and the deal moves to your Replied - Nurture stage without you touching anything. Your pipeline stays clean and current with zero manual data entry.

Managing Multi-Account Outreach

MailClaw's multi-account support is especially useful when your sales team uses different sending domains or when you're running outreach across multiple Pipedrive pipelines. You can assign specific sending accounts — whether Gmail via OAuth, Outlook via OAuth, or a dedicated SMTP provider like SendGrid, Mailgun, or Amazon SES — to specific sequences or agents.

sequences:
  post-demo-followup:
    sending_account: gmail:sales@yourcompany.com
    fallback_account: smtp:sendgrid
    daily_send_limit: 80
    send_window: "08:00-17:00"
    timezone: "America/New_York"

Setting a send_window ensures your automated emails arrive during business hours rather than 2am — a small detail that meaningfully improves reply rates.

Troubleshooting Common Issues

Contacts Not Syncing

Run mailclaw integrations status pipedrive to check the connection. If you see a 401 error, your API token has likely been rotated — regenerate it in Pipedrive and update your config.

Sequences Not Triggering

Check that the stage_name in your trigger config exactly matches the stage name in Pipedrive, including capitalisation. Use mailclaw pipedrive stages list to print all available stage names from your account.

Emails Landing in Spam

Open the deliverability panel at localhost:3100/deliverability and run a quick check. MailClaw will surface any DNS misconfiguration and link you to fix instructions. If you're sending at volume, consider routing through a dedicated SMTP provider with a warmed-up sending IP.

What You've Built

With this setup, your Pipedrive pipeline is no longer a passive record-keeper — it's the trigger layer for a fully automated outreach system. Deals moving stages fire sequences, AI agents handle replies intelligently, enriched contact data keeps your messaging relevant, and every email action writes back to your CRM automatically.

Because MailClaw runs locally and is fully open-source, you can inspect every line of logic, extend it with custom scripts, and integrate it with anything else in your stack — HubSpot, Salesforce, Notion, Slack — using the same pattern. Your sales workflow, running entirely on your own machine, exactly the way you designed it.

articles.title: Using MailClaw with AWS SES for Cost-Effective Email Delivery
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw to AWS SES for high-volume, pennies-per-thousand email delivery — with step-by-step SMTP configuration, IAM setup, and tips for keeping your sequences out of the spam folder.
articles.content:
Why AWS SES Changes the Cost Equation

If you're running cold outreach sequences, nurture campaigns, or transactional email at any kind of volume, delivery costs add up fast. SendGrid's base plan caps you at 100 emails per day on the free tier. Mailgun gets expensive past 5,000 sends per month. Even services built for bulk sending can quietly drain your budget before you've closed a single deal.

AWS Simple Email Service (SES) prices at roughly $0.10 per 1,000 emails sent — and if you're sending from an EC2 instance or other AWS resource, the first 62,000 emails per month are free. For teams using MailClaw to power multi-step sequences, that's a meaningful difference. This guide walks you through exactly how to wire AWS SES into MailClaw as your SMTP backend, so your AI-powered outreach runs on infrastructure that scales without punishing you for it.

Before You Start: What You'll Need

  • An AWS account with SES access (start in sandbox mode — we'll cover getting out of it)
  • A verified sending domain in SES (Route 53 or any DNS provider works)
  • An IAM user with ses:SendEmail and ses:SendRawEmail permissions
  • MailClaw running locally at localhost:3100
  • Your domain's SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records in place

The authentication and DNS work upfront is the most important part. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring will flag issues after the fact, but getting the foundation right means fewer bounces and better inbox placement from day one.

Setting Up AWS SES

Step 1: Verify Your Sending Domain

Log into the AWS console, navigate to Amazon SES → Verified identities, and add your domain. AWS will give you a set of CNAME records to add to your DNS. These enable DKIM signing — a cryptographic signal that tells receiving mail servers your messages are legitimate.

Once the CNAMEs propagate (usually under an hour), your domain status will show Verified. Add your SPF record if you haven't already:

v=spf1 include:amazonses.com ~all

And a basic DMARC policy to start:

v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourdomain.com

Step 2: Create an IAM User for SMTP

In the AWS console, go to IAM → Users → Create user. Attach the managed policy AmazonSESFullAccess, or create a tighter custom policy if you prefer least-privilege:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "ses:SendEmail",
        "ses:SendRawEmail"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}

After creating the user, navigate to Security credentials → SMTP credentials. AWS will generate a unique SMTP username and password — note that these are not the same as your IAM access keys. They're derived credentials specifically for SMTP authentication.

Step 3: Get Your SES SMTP Endpoint

AWS SES SMTP endpoints are region-specific. Common ones:

  • US East (N. Virginia): email-smtp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
  • US West (Oregon): email-smtp.us-west-2.amazonaws.com
  • EU (Ireland): email-smtp.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com

SES uses port 587 with STARTTLS, or port 465 with SSL. Port 587 is generally more reliable across hosting environments.

Connecting AWS SES to MailClaw

Adding the SMTP Account via the Dashboard

Open your MailClaw dashboard at http://localhost:3100 and navigate to Accounts → Add Account → SMTP. Fill in the connection details:

Host:       email-smtp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
Port:       587
Encryption: STARTTLS
Username:   [your SES SMTP username]
Password:   [your SES SMTP password]
From Name:  Your Name or Company
From Email: you@yourdomain.com

Hit Test Connection — MailClaw will fire a test message and confirm authentication succeeded. If you get an authentication error, double-check that you're using the SMTP credentials (not IAM access keys) and that your sending address matches a verified identity in SES.

Adding via the CLI

If you prefer to configure accounts from the terminal, MailClaw's CLI makes this scriptable:

mailclaw account add \
  --type smtp \
  --host email-smtp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com \
  --port 587 \
  --encryption starttls \
  --username YOUR_SES_SMTP_USER \
  --password YOUR_SES_SMTP_PASS \
  --from-email you@yourdomain.com \
  --from-name "Your Name" \
  --label "AWS SES Production"

This is especially useful if you're managing multiple sending accounts — for example, one SES account per domain, or separate accounts for cold outreach versus transactional email.

Getting Out of the SES Sandbox

New AWS SES accounts start in sandbox mode, which means you can only send to verified email addresses. That's fine for testing but useless for real outreach. To request production access, go to SES → Account dashboard → Request production access.

AWS asks you to describe your use case. Be specific and honest: explain that you're sending permission-based outreach, that you maintain suppression lists, and that you monitor bounces and complaints. Approval usually comes within 24 hours.

Important: AWS SES has strict bounce and complaint thresholds. Keep your bounce rate below 5% and complaint rate below 0.1%. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tracks these metrics in real time — use it. A spike in bounces can get your SES account suspended faster than you'd expect.

Building Your First Sequence with SES as the Sender

With your SES account connected, head to MailClaw's Sequence Builder. Create a new sequence, and in the account selector, choose your newly added AWS SES account. From here, the workflow is the same whether you're using SES, Gmail OAuth, or Outlook — the sending infrastructure is abstracted away.

A typical cold outreach sequence might look like:

  1. Day 0: Initial email — personalized intro, one clear ask
  2. Day 3: Follow-up — reference the first email, add value
  3. Day 7: Second follow-up — different angle or social proof
  4. Day 14: Breakup email — low-pressure final touch

Use MailClaw's AI email agents to generate and refine each step. The agents understand sequence context — they won't write a "just following up" email that ignores what was said in step one. You can also pull in enriched contact data (job title, company size, recent news) so each message feels written for that specific person, not blasted to a list.

Deliverability Tips Specific to SES

Warm Up Your SES Sending Identity

Even with a verified domain and clean DNS, jumping straight to high volume will hurt your sender reputation. Start with 50–100 emails per day per domain and ramp up 20–30% each week. MailClaw's sequence scheduler lets you set daily send caps per account — use this to enforce a controlled warmup without manual throttling.

Handle Bounces with SNS Notifications

AWS SES can push bounce and complaint notifications to an SNS topic, which you can then route to a webhook or processing function. Set this up in SES → Configuration sets → Event destinations. Feed that data back into MailClaw's suppression list so you're never re-sending to hard bounces.

Use Configuration Sets for Tracking

SES configuration sets let you enable open and click tracking, plus engagement metrics per campaign. Create a dedicated configuration set for MailClaw sequences:

aws ses create-configuration-set \
  --configuration-set Name=mailclaw-outreach

Then reference it in your MailClaw SMTP account settings under Advanced → SES Configuration Set. This gives you an extra layer of analytics on top of what MailClaw tracks natively.

Multi-Account Strategies for Scale

One of MailClaw's most practical features for high-volume teams is multi-account support. You can add multiple SES accounts — tied to different domains or even different AWS regions — and rotate sending across them within a single campaign. This distributes volume, reduces the blast radius if one account hits a deliverability issue, and lets you A/B test sending domains without running parallel campaigns manually.

A common setup for a small sales team might be:

  • outreach@company.com — primary cold email domain via SES us-east-1
  • hello@company-mail.com — secondary domain for follow-ups via SES us-west-2
  • Personal Gmail or Outlook accounts via OAuth for warm follow-ups and replies

MailClaw manages the routing logic so you don't have to juggle this manually. Set the account rotation rules once in the dashboard and let the sequences run.

Putting It All Together

AWS SES isn't the most glamorous infrastructure choice, but it's one of the most cost-effective and scalable options available — especially when you're running serious outreach volume. Paired with MailClaw's AI agents, contact enrichment, and sequence builder, you get a local-first automation stack that rivals what enterprise teams pay thousands of dollars a month for through HubSpot or Salesforce outreach integrations.

The whole setup — domain verification, IAM credentials, SMTP configuration, and your first sequence — can be done in under two hours. After that, you're sending at scale for fractions of a cent per email, with full visibility into deliverability from your localhost:3100 dashboard. That's a setup worth the afternoon it takes to build it.

articles.title: How to Integrate MailClaw with Linear for Customer Communication Tracking
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw with Linear to automatically track customer communication, sync email sequences with issue workflows, and keep your team aligned without switching between tools.
articles.content:
Why Email and Project Tracking Belong Together

If your team uses Linear to manage work, you already know how good it feels when everything is in one place. Issues get created, assigned, updated, and closed — all with that satisfying speed Linear is known for. But there's a gap that trips up almost every product and customer-success team: email communication lives somewhere else entirely.

A customer replies to your onboarding sequence. A prospect responds to a cold outreach campaign. A churned user replies to a win-back email. Where does that context live? Usually in someone's inbox, disconnected from the issue that tracks the actual work being done to help them. The result is dropped threads, duplicate outreach, and the classic "wait, did anyone respond to them?" Slack message.

Integrating MailClaw with Linear closes that gap. Because MailClaw runs locally at localhost:3100 and exposes a clean webhook and API layer powered by OpenClaw, you can pipe email events directly into Linear issues — without a third-party middleware subscription or a complicated cloud setup.

What You'll Build

By the end of this guide, you'll have a working setup that:

  • Creates or updates a Linear issue when a contact replies to a MailClaw sequence
  • Attaches email metadata (subject, contact name, sequence name) to the issue as a comment
  • Optionally assigns the issue to the right team member based on campaign owner
  • Triggers a MailClaw follow-up sequence when a Linear issue moves to a specific status

This is a two-way sync — not just a one-way fire-and-forget — which is what makes it genuinely useful for customer communication tracking.

Prerequisites

  • MailClaw running locally (localhost:3100) with at least one active sequence
  • A Linear account with API access enabled
  • A Linear API key (generate one at Linear → Settings → API → Personal API Keys)
  • Node.js 18+ installed, or a lightweight webhook relay if you want to expose your local MailClaw instance to Linear's outbound webhooks

Step 1: Enable Webhooks in MailClaw

MailClaw's local dashboard includes a webhook configuration panel under Settings → Integrations → Outbound Webhooks. This is where you tell MailClaw which events to broadcast and where to send them.

Open your browser to http://localhost:3100/settings/integrations and add a new webhook endpoint. For local development and testing, you can use a tool like ngrok or localtunnel to expose your local listener temporarily:

npx localtunnel --port 4000 --subdomain mailclaw-linear

This gives you a public URL like https://mailclaw-linear.loca.lt that forwards to your local webhook receiver running on port 4000.

In MailClaw's webhook settings, select the following events to forward:

  • reply.received — fires when a contact replies to any sequence email
  • sequence.completed — fires when a contact finishes a full sequence without replying
  • contact.bounced — useful for deliverability tracking in Linear

Step 2: Create a Local Webhook Receiver

Create a small Node.js script that receives MailClaw events and forwards them to Linear's GraphQL API:

// mailclaw-linear-bridge.js
const express = require('express');
const axios = require('axios');

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

const LINEAR_API_KEY = process.env.LINEAR_API_KEY;
const LINEAR_TEAM_ID = process.env.LINEAR_TEAM_ID;

app.post('/webhook', async (req, res) => {
  const { event, contact, sequence, email } = req.body;

  if (event === 'reply.received') {
    const mutation = `
      mutation CreateIssue($title: String!, $description: String!, $teamId: String!) {
        issueCreate(input: {
          title: $title,
          description: $description,
          teamId: $teamId
        }) {
          success
          issue { id identifier url }
        }
      }
    `;

    const variables = {
      title: \`Customer reply: \${contact.name || contact.email}\`,
      description: \`**Sequence:** \${sequence.name}\\n**Contact:** \${contact.email}\\n**Subject:** \${email.subject}\\n\\n> \${email.snippet}\`,
      teamId: LINEAR_TEAM_ID
    };

    await axios.post('https://api.linear.app/graphql', {
      query: mutation,
      variables
    }, {
      headers: { Authorization: LINEAR_API_KEY }
    });
  }

  res.sendStatus(200);
});

app.listen(4000, () => console.log('Bridge running on :4000'));

Run it with your credentials:

LINEAR_API_KEY=lin_api_xxxx LINEAR_TEAM_ID=your-team-id node mailclaw-linear-bridge.js

Every time a contact replies to one of your MailClaw sequences — whether it's an onboarding flow, a sales cadence built in the sequence builder, or an AI agent follow-up — a Linear issue gets created automatically with the full context attached.

Step 3: Enrich Contact Data Before Sending to Linear

This is where MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment features earn their keep. Before forwarding a reply event to Linear, you can pull enriched contact data — company, title, LinkedIn profile, estimated deal size — and include it in the Linear issue description.

MailClaw exposes a local enrichment endpoint you can call synchronously inside your webhook handler:

const enriched = await axios.get(
  \`http://localhost:3100/api/contacts/\${contact.id}/enrich\`
);

const { company, title, linkedin } = enriched.data;
const description = \`
**Contact:** \${contact.email}
**Company:** \${company || 'Unknown'}
**Title:** \${title || 'Unknown'}
**LinkedIn:** \${linkedin || 'N/A'}
**Sequence:** \${sequence.name}
**Subject:** \${email.subject}

> \${email.snippet}
\`;

Now your Linear issues arrive pre-loaded with the context your team needs to triage and respond — no manual lookups, no switching to HubSpot or Salesforce to find out who the person is.

Step 4: Trigger MailClaw Sequences from Linear Status Changes

The other half of a real integration is acting on Linear data inside MailClaw. Linear supports outbound webhooks too — you can configure them under Linear → Settings → API → Webhooks.

Set Linear to POST to your bridge whenever an issue changes state. Then add a handler that calls MailClaw's sequence enrollment API:

app.post('/linear-webhook', async (req, res) => {
  const { action, data } = req.body;

  if (action === 'update' && data.state?.name === 'Customer Responded') {
    const contactEmail = extractEmailFromIssue(data.description);

    await axios.post('http://localhost:3100/api/sequences/enroll', {
      email: contactEmail,
      sequenceId: 'your-follow-up-sequence-id'
    });
  }

  res.sendStatus(200);
});

Now when a support agent moves a Linear issue to "Customer Responded", MailClaw automatically enrolls that contact in a follow-up sequence — saving the agent from manually finding the contact and clicking send.

Monitoring Deliverability Across Your Linear-Linked Campaigns

One underrated benefit of this integration is deliverability visibility. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools track open rates, bounce rates, and spam signals across all your connected accounts — whether you're sending through Gmail, Outlook, or SendGrid. When you surface those signals in Linear, your team gets early warnings about campaigns that might be hurting your sender reputation.

Add a handler for contact.bounced events that creates a Linear issue tagged with a "Deliverability" label:

if (event === 'contact.bounced') {
  // Create Linear issue with label 'Deliverability'
  // Include bounce type (hard/soft), sequence name, sending account
}

This gives your team a centralized place to review deliverability incidents alongside all other customer communication issues.

Tips for Keeping the Integration Maintainable

Use MailClaw's Multi-Account Support Wisely

If your team sends from multiple accounts — say, a sales team using individual Gmail addresses and a success team on a shared Outlook mailbox — tag each MailClaw account with a team identifier. Pass that identifier through your webhook payload and use it to assign Linear issues to the right team automatically.

Don't Over-Create Issues

It's tempting to create a Linear issue for every email event, but that gets noisy fast. A good rule: create issues on reply.received and contact.bounced, and use Linear comments (not new issues) for subsequent events on the same contact thread.

Store the Linear Issue ID in MailClaw Contact Notes

After creating a Linear issue, write the issue identifier back to the MailClaw contact record via the contacts API. This creates a durable link — future events for the same contact can update the existing issue instead of creating duplicates.

await axios.patch(\`http://localhost:3100/api/contacts/\${contact.id}\`, {
  notes: \`Linear: \${issue.identifier} (\${issue.url})\`
});

What This Looks Like in Practice

A customer receives your onboarding sequence, built in MailClaw's sequence builder and powered by an AI email agent that personalizes each message. They reply on day three. Within seconds, a Linear issue appears in your Customer Success team's backlog: the contact's name, company, enriched title, the exact email snippet they replied to, and a link to their full MailClaw contact profile. The CS agent triages it, responds, and moves the issue to "Replied" — which automatically enrolls the contact in MailClaw's next nurture sequence. No copy-paste. No manual tracking. No missed follow-ups.

That's the promise of connecting your outreach tooling to your project management workflow. MailClaw's open-source foundation and local-first architecture make it straightforward to build integrations like this without giving a third-party service access to your email data or your contacts — everything stays on your machine until you explicitly push it somewhere.

The full bridge script shown in this guide is a starting point, not a finished product. Fork it, adapt it to your team's Linear workflow, and open a PR back to the MailClaw community if you build something worth sharing.

articles.title: MailClaw + Notion Integration: Documenting Outreach Playbooks
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw with Notion to build a living outreach playbook — documenting sequences, AI agent prompts, contact enrichment logic, and campaign SOPs so your entire team can replicate what works.
articles.content:
Why Your Outreach Playbook Lives and Dies in Documentation

Most email outreach fails not because the sequences are bad, but because no one remembers why they were built that way. You craft a killer cold outreach flow in MailClaw, tune the timing, nail the subject line variants, and then six months later someone on your team runs a completely different campaign with none of that institutional knowledge. The open rates tank. The replies dry up. And you're back to square one.

That's the problem a Notion-based outreach playbook solves. When you pair MailClaw's local-first automation stack with Notion's flexible documentation, you get something genuinely powerful: a living system where every sequence decision, AI agent prompt, enrichment rule, and deliverability insight is documented, searchable, and transferable.

This guide walks you through exactly how to set that up.

The Core Idea: MailClaw as Execution, Notion as Memory

Think of MailClaw as your outreach engine — running locally at localhost:3100, managing your SMTP connections, firing off sequences, enriching contacts, and letting your AI email agents do the heavy lifting. Notion is the brain behind it: the place where you explain why every piece of the engine is configured the way it is.

A well-structured playbook in Notion should answer these questions for any campaign:

  • What is the goal of this sequence and who is the target persona?
  • What enrichment fields are we pulling and why?
  • What prompt is powering the AI email agent for this campaign?
  • What SMTP or OAuth account is sending, and what are the warmup rules?
  • What are the success metrics and what does good deliverability look like here?

When you answer those questions in writing before you build, you ship better campaigns. When you answer them after, you create a reusable playbook for every future rep or collaborator who touches your MailClaw instance.

Setting Up Your Notion Playbook Structure

The Master Campaigns Database

Start with a Notion database — not just a doc. A database gives you filtered views, properties, and the ability to link related pages. Create a database called Outreach Campaigns with these core properties:

  • Campaign Name — text
  • Status — select: Draft, Active, Paused, Archived
  • MailClaw Sequence ID — text (copy this from your sequence builder)
  • Sending Account — select: Gmail, Outlook, SendGrid, custom SMTP
  • Target Persona — text
  • Open Rate / Reply Rate — number fields for tracking
  • AI Agent Enabled — checkbox
  • Last Updated — date

Each row in this database becomes a full campaign page. That page is where your actual playbook documentation lives.

The Campaign Page Template

Create a Notion template for campaign pages so every new campaign starts with the same scaffold. Here's a recommended structure:

  1. Campaign Overview — one paragraph summary of goal, ICP, and expected outcome
  2. Sequence Map — a table or toggle list of each email step, delay, and condition
  3. AI Agent Prompt — the exact prompt used in MailClaw's AI agent for this campaign
  4. Contact Enrichment Rules — what fields you're enriching, from what sources, and how they map to personalization tokens
  5. Sending Configuration — account, warmup status, sending limits, reply-to address
  6. Deliverability Checklist — DKIM, SPF, DMARC status, bounce threshold, spam trap monitoring
  7. Learnings & Retrospective — filled in after the campaign wraps

Documenting MailClaw Sequences Step by Step

Exporting Sequence Structure

Once you've built a sequence in MailClaw's sequence builder, you can document its structure directly. From your local dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to your sequence, open the sequence settings, and copy the sequence ID. Then use the MailClaw CLI to pull a human-readable summary:

# Export a sequence summary to JSON for documentation
mailclaw sequence export --id seq_abc123 --format json > playbook/seq_abc123.json

# Or print a quick summary to terminal
mailclaw sequence describe --id seq_abc123

Paste the output — or a cleaned-up version — into your Notion campaign page under the Sequence Map section. This gives you a snapshot of step count, delays, conditions, and subject line variants that you can refer back to without opening MailClaw.

Documenting AI Agent Prompts

This is the most underrated piece of playbook documentation. MailClaw's AI email agents, powered by OpenClaw under the hood, generate personalized email copy dynamically based on enriched contact data. The quality of that output is almost entirely determined by the quality of your prompt.

Document your agent prompt verbatim in Notion. Include:

  • The full system prompt and user prompt structure
  • Which enrichment fields the prompt references (e.g., {{contact.job_title}}, {{contact.company_size}})
  • Any negative instructions ("do not mention pricing," "avoid casual language for enterprise contacts")
  • The tone and length constraints

Pro tip: Treat your AI agent prompts like source code. Version them in Notion with dates and changelogs. When open rates shift, you'll know exactly what prompt was live at the time.

Recording Contact Enrichment Logic

MailClaw's contact enrichment pulls data from external sources to fill in the gaps — company size, tech stack, LinkedIn role, recent funding, and more. But enrichment logic is invisible once it's configured, which makes it dangerous to leave undocumented.

In your Notion page, create a simple table like this:

| Field              | Source         | Used In                        | Fallback         |
|--------------------|----------------|--------------------------------|------------------|
| job_title          | LinkedIn       | AI agent prompt, Step 1 subject| "your team"      |
| company_size       | Clearbit       | Sequence branching condition   | Skip branch      |
| recent_news        | Google Alerts  | Step 2 personalization line    | Omit line        |
| crm_stage          | HubSpot / SFDC | Suppression list filter        | Assume cold      |

This table alone will save you hours of confusion when you revisit a campaign or hand it off to someone else.

Connecting MailClaw Events to Notion Automatically

Using Webhooks to Update Campaign Stats

MailClaw supports outbound webhooks for sequence events — opens, clicks, replies, bounces, and unsubscribes. You can pipe these into Notion via Make (formerly Integromat) or Zapier to automatically update your campaign database properties without manual entry.

A basic webhook-to-Notion flow looks like this:

  1. In MailClaw, go to Settings → Webhooks and create a new endpoint for your campaign
  2. Point it at a Make or Zapier webhook receiver URL
  3. Map the open_rate and reply_rate fields from the webhook payload to your Notion database properties
  4. Set the trigger to run on each daily summary event

Now your Notion playbook database stays current with live campaign performance — without you manually pulling numbers from the localhost:3100 dashboard.

Logging Deliverability Alerts

MailClaw's deliverability monitoring surfaces alerts when bounce rates spike, spam complaints appear, or sending reputation drops. Set up a second webhook flow that creates a new Notion page in a Deliverability Log database whenever an alert fires. Each log entry should capture:

  • Timestamp and campaign ID
  • Alert type and severity
  • Sending account affected (Gmail, Outlook, SendGrid, etc.)
  • Action taken and resolution notes

Over time this becomes an invaluable audit trail — especially if you're managing deliverability across multiple accounts using MailClaw's multi-account support.

Making Your Playbook Actually Get Used

Build a Pre-Launch Checklist

The best playbooks have enforcement built in. Create a Notion checklist template that every campaign owner completes before activating a sequence in MailClaw:

  • [ ] Sequence exported and mapped in Notion
  • [ ] AI agent prompt documented and reviewed
  • [ ] Enrichment fields verified against contact list
  • [ ] Sending account warmed up and deliverability tools green
  • [ ] Suppression list synced from HubSpot/Salesforce
  • [ ] Unsubscribe handling confirmed active
  • [ ] Campaign page peer-reviewed by one other person

This turns documentation from an afterthought into a launch gate.

Run Monthly Playbook Reviews

Set a recurring monthly task to review your Notion campaign database. Archive anything that's been inactive for 90 days. Pull the top three performing campaigns and extract their patterns into a What Works reference doc. Update your AI agent prompt templates based on what the data shows.

The combination of MailClaw's execution data and Notion's organizational flexibility means you're always building on what worked — not reinventing from scratch every quarter.

The Compounding Value of Documented Outreach

There's a reason great sales and growth teams outperform over time while others plateau: they systematize what works. MailClaw gives you a genuinely powerful local-first platform to run sophisticated, AI-driven outreach without depending on expensive SaaS stacks. But the platform alone isn't the moat — the documented knowledge of how you use it is.

A Notion playbook built on the structure above becomes one of the most valuable assets your outreach operation has. New team members ramp faster. Campaigns improve iteratively rather than randomly. And when something breaks — a deliverability dip, a burnt sending domain, a suddenly underperforming sequence — you have the paper trail to diagnose it in minutes instead of days.

Start with one campaign. Document it thoroughly. You'll never go back to running outreach from memory again.

articles.title: How to Connect MailClaw to Stripe for Customer Lifecycle Emails
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw to Stripe so you can automatically trigger customer lifecycle emails — from welcome sequences to failed payment recovery — using MailClaw's AI email agents and sequence builder running locally on your Mac.
articles.content:
Why Stripe + MailClaw Is a Powerful Combination

If you're running a SaaS product, an e-commerce store, or any subscription-based business, Stripe is probably handling your payments. But Stripe alone doesn't send great emails — it sends transactional emails. What happens after the payment event is entirely up to you.

That's where MailClaw comes in. By connecting your Stripe account to MailClaw, you can build intelligent, AI-powered email sequences that fire based on real payment events: new subscriptions, failed charges, trial endings, refunds, and upgrades. Everything runs locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, so your customer data never leaves your machine unless you explicitly send it.

This guide walks you through the full setup — from Stripe webhook configuration to building your first lifecycle sequence inside MailClaw's dashboard.

Understanding the Architecture

Before diving into commands, it's worth understanding how MailClaw connects to Stripe at a high level.

MailClaw (built on OpenClaw) exposes a local webhook receiver that listens for incoming HTTP POST requests. When Stripe fires an event — say, customer.subscription.created — it sends a signed payload to a URL you define. MailClaw catches that payload, parses the customer data, enriches the contact if needed, and hands it off to a sequence or AI email agent.

Because MailClaw runs locally, you'll need to expose your local server to the internet temporarily during development. The standard approach is to use a tunneling tool like ngrok or Cloudflare Tunnel.

Step 1: Start MailClaw and Open Your Dashboard

Make sure MailClaw is running before you configure anything in Stripe. From your terminal:

mailclaw start

Your dashboard will be available at http://localhost:3100. Open it in your browser and navigate to Integrations → Webhooks. You'll see MailClaw's local webhook endpoint listed — it looks something like:

http://localhost:3100/hooks/stripe

Keep this tab open. You'll need it in a moment.

Step 2: Expose Your Local Endpoint with ngrok

In a separate terminal window, run ngrok to create a public tunnel to your local MailClaw instance:

ngrok http 3100

ngrok will output a forwarding URL like https://a1b2c3d4.ngrok.io. Your Stripe webhook URL will be:

https://a1b2c3d4.ngrok.io/hooks/stripe
Production note: For production deployments, you'll want to run MailClaw on a VPS or dedicated server with a real domain instead of ngrok. The MailClaw docs cover self-hosted deployment with NGINX or Caddy as a reverse proxy.

Step 3: Configure Your Stripe Webhook

Log into your Stripe Dashboard and go to Developers → Webhooks → Add endpoint. Paste your ngrok (or production) URL into the endpoint field.

Next, select the events you want MailClaw to listen for. For a comprehensive customer lifecycle setup, we recommend starting with these:

  • customer.created — New customer added to Stripe
  • customer.subscription.created — New subscription started
  • customer.subscription.updated — Plan change or upgrade
  • customer.subscription.deleted — Cancellation or expiry
  • invoice.payment_failed — Failed charge attempt
  • invoice.payment_succeeded — Successful renewal
  • customer.subscription.trial_will_end — Trial ending in 3 days

After saving, Stripe will display a webhook signing secret (starts with whsec_). Copy it — you'll need it in MailClaw.

Step 4: Add Your Stripe Signing Secret to MailClaw

Back in your MailClaw dashboard, go to Integrations → Stripe and paste your signing secret. MailClaw uses this to verify that incoming webhook payloads are genuinely from Stripe and haven't been tampered with.

Alternatively, you can set it via the CLI:

mailclaw config set stripe.webhook_secret whsec_yourSecretHere

Restart MailClaw to apply the change:

mailclaw restart

You can verify the connection is working by clicking Send test webhook in Stripe. Your MailClaw dashboard should log the event under Integrations → Event Log.

Step 5: Build Your Lifecycle Sequences

Now the fun part. Head to Sequences in your MailClaw dashboard and click New Sequence. You'll see an option to set a trigger — choose Stripe Event and select the event type you want to act on.

Welcome Sequence (customer.subscription.created)

When a new subscriber signs up, you want to onboard them properly — not just send a single "thanks for subscribing" email and disappear. A well-designed welcome sequence might look like this:

  1. Day 0: Warm welcome + what to expect
  2. Day 1: Getting started guide / key feature spotlight
  3. Day 3: Case study or social proof email
  4. Day 7: Check-in + offer to answer questions
  5. Day 14: Advanced tips or upsell opportunity

In MailClaw's sequence builder, you can drag and drop these steps, set delays, and use AI to draft the emails. MailClaw's AI email agent will pull the customer's name and plan details directly from the Stripe payload to personalize each message — no manual field mapping required.

Failed Payment Recovery (invoice.payment_failed)

Failed payments are one of the most recoverable forms of churn, and timing matters enormously. A three-email dunning sequence with MailClaw might look like:

  1. Immediately: Friendly heads-up, link to update payment method
  2. Day 3: Reminder with urgency, highlight what they'll lose
  3. Day 7: Final notice before account suspension

Because MailClaw supports multi-account SMTP and OAuth (including Gmail and Outlook), you can send dunning emails from a dedicated billing address like billing@yourcompany.com while your onboarding sequence sends from hello@yourcompany.com — keeping communication focused and deliverable.

Trial Ending Sequence (customer.subscription.trial_will_end)

Stripe fires this event 3 days before a trial ends. MailClaw can intercept it and kick off a short, sharp conversion sequence. The goal is simple: make the value undeniable before the card is charged. Use MailClaw's contact enrichment feature to pull in LinkedIn data, company size, or industry — then let the AI email agent tailor the message to what that specific customer is likely trying to achieve.

Step 6: Enable Contact Enrichment

MailClaw's contact enrichment layer runs automatically when a new contact is added from a Stripe event. It takes the customer's email address and enriches it with publicly available data — company name, job title, industry, and more. This is especially powerful for B2B SaaS companies where knowing someone's role changes what you say to them.

You can configure enrichment sources in your dashboard under Contacts → Enrichment Settings. MailClaw integrates with enrichment providers and can also pull data from your CRM if you're connected to HubSpot or Salesforce via the OpenClaw connector layer.

Step 7: Monitor Deliverability

Sending lifecycle emails is only half the job. MailClaw's built-in deliverability tools let you monitor open rates, bounce rates, and spam complaints directly from the dashboard. If you're routing through SendGrid, Postmark, or another SMTP provider, MailClaw pulls delivery stats back into your local dashboard so you have a single pane of glass.

Pay particular attention to your dunning emails — billing-related messages have a higher-than-average complaint rate if they feel aggressive. MailClaw's AI email agent can help you A/B test subject lines and tone to find the right balance between urgency and empathy.

Putting It All Together

Once your sequences are live, your Stripe + MailClaw setup essentially runs on autopilot. New customers get onboarded. Failed payments get recovered. Trial users get nudged. Cancellations can trigger a win-back sequence. All of it is configured visually in your local dashboard, all of it is open source and fully auditable, and none of your customer data is sitting in a third-party cloud you don't control.

That's the real value of running MailClaw locally: you get enterprise-grade email automation with the privacy and control of self-hosted infrastructure. And because it's built on OpenClaw, you can extend it, fork it, or contribute to it — the ecosystem grows with your needs.

Start with one sequence, get it dialed in, and build from there. Your Stripe data is a goldmine of behavioral signals — MailClaw helps you turn those signals into revenue.

articles.title: Using MailClaw with Webhooks for Real-Time Event Triggers
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw's webhook system to real-world events from tools like HubSpot, Salesforce, and Stripe — triggering AI-powered email sequences the moment something meaningful happens in your stack.
articles.content:
Why Real-Time Triggers Change Everything About Email Automation

Most email automation tools work on schedules. You define a delay — send this email 3 days after signup, send a follow-up 7 days later — and the tool marches through that queue regardless of what's actually happening with your contacts. It's automation in the loosest sense of the word.

Webhooks flip that model entirely. Instead of polling for changes or relying on fixed timers, your outreach fires the moment something real happens: a deal moves to a new stage in Salesforce, a user upgrades their plan in Stripe, a contact opens a specific landing page, or a support ticket gets resolved in Zendesk. That kind of responsiveness isn't just efficient — it's the difference between an email that feels eerily well-timed and one that feels like noise.

MailClaw's webhook support, built on the OpenClaw engine running locally at localhost:3100, gives you a clean, programmable interface for exactly this kind of event-driven outreach. This guide walks you through how it works, how to set it up, and how to connect it to the tools already living in your stack.

How MailClaw Handles Incoming Webhooks

When you run MailClaw locally, it exposes a webhook endpoint you can point external services at. Every incoming payload is processed by the OpenClaw engine, which parses the event, maps it to a contact record (using email, phone, or a custom identifier), and optionally enriches that contact before deciding what to do next.

The default webhook listener runs at:

http://localhost:3100/api/webhooks/inbound

Because MailClaw runs locally, you'll need to expose this endpoint to the internet during development using a tunneling tool. ngrok is the most common choice:

# Start MailClaw first
mailclaw start

# Then in a new terminal, expose port 3100
ngrok http 3100

ngrok will give you a public URL like https://abc123.ngrok.io. Your full webhook URL becomes:

https://abc123.ngrok.io/api/webhooks/inbound

Paste that URL into any external service that supports webhooks — HubSpot, Salesforce, Stripe, Typeform, Shopify, you name it — and MailClaw will start receiving events immediately. For production deployments, you'd run MailClaw on a server with a fixed domain, but for testing and personal outreach workflows, the ngrok approach is fast and frictionless.

Configuring a Webhook Trigger in MailClaw

Step 1: Create a Webhook Rule

Open the MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to Automations → Webhook Triggers. Click New Trigger and give it a descriptive name — something like "HubSpot Deal Won" or "Stripe Upgrade — Pro Plan".

You'll define three things here:

  • Event filter: A JSON path condition that tells MailClaw which incoming payloads should activate this rule
  • Contact mapping: Which field in the payload maps to a MailClaw contact (usually email)
  • Action: What happens next — enroll in a sequence, send a one-off email, trigger an AI agent, or update a contact property

Step 2: Define Your Event Filter

Say you're listening to HubSpot deal webhooks and you only want to trigger when a deal moves to the "Closed Won" stage. Your filter might look like this in MailClaw's rule editor:

{
  "filter": {
    "path": "properties.dealstage.value",
    "operator": "equals",
    "value": "closedwon"
  },
  "contact_identifier": "properties.email.value"
}

MailClaw evaluates this against every incoming payload. Payloads that don't match are silently ignored — no spam, no accidental triggers.

Step 3: Choose Your Action

This is where MailClaw's sequence builder and AI email agents come in. Once a matching event arrives, you can:

  • Enroll the contact in a pre-built email sequence (onboarding, upsell, re-engagement)
  • Trigger a single personalized email using an AI agent that pulls in live context about the contact
  • Run contact enrichment to fill in missing details before the first email goes out
  • Tag or segment the contact for future campaigns

For the "Closed Won" scenario, you'd typically enroll them in a customer onboarding sequence. Select the sequence from the dropdown, and MailClaw handles enrollment automatically — including respecting send windows, deliverability limits, and any existing sequence membership rules you've set up.

Real-World Integration Examples

Salesforce: Trigger Sequences on Opportunity Stage Changes

Salesforce supports outbound webhooks natively through Workflow Rules and Process Builder (or the newer Flow builder). Set up an outbound message or use a third-party connector like Zapier to POST to your MailClaw endpoint whenever an Opportunity stage changes.

A practical use case: when a prospect moves to "Proposal Sent," automatically start a light-touch follow-up sequence — two or three emails over a week that reference the proposal without being pushy. MailClaw's AI agents can even personalize these emails using enriched contact data, pulling in the company's industry, size, and recent news if your enrichment provider supports it.

Stripe: Trigger Onboarding When a Subscription Starts

Stripe's webhook system is one of the cleanest in the industry. In your Stripe dashboard, add your MailClaw URL as a webhook endpoint and subscribe to the customer.subscription.created event.

# Example Stripe payload (simplified)
{
  "type": "customer.subscription.created",
  "data": {
    "object": {
      "customer_email": "jane@acmecorp.com",
      "plan": {
        "nickname": "Pro Monthly"
      }
    }
  }
}

In MailClaw, map data.object.customer_email as your contact identifier and filter on data.object.plan.nickname equaling "Pro Monthly." The moment that webhook arrives, your onboarding sequence kicks off — no manual intervention, no batch processing delays.

Typeform: Follow Up After Form Completion

If you use Typeform for lead capture, demo requests, or surveys, you can connect it directly to MailClaw via Typeform's built-in webhook support. Every completed submission fires an event with the respondent's answers, including their email address.

Use case: someone fills out a "Request a Demo" form on your site. MailClaw receives the webhook, enriches the contact (pulling in company size, LinkedIn profile, tech stack), and enrolls them in a tailored follow-up sequence — all before you've even seen the notification in your inbox.

Pro tip: MailClaw's contact enrichment runs asynchronously after the webhook is received. You can configure a short delay (e.g., 2 minutes) before the first sequence email sends, giving enrichment time to complete so your AI agent has full context to personalize from.

Securing Your Webhook Endpoint

Leaving a webhook endpoint open without validation is a security risk — anyone who discovers the URL could fire fake events. Most platforms sign their webhook payloads with a secret key, and MailClaw supports signature validation out of the box.

In your MailClaw config file (~/.mailclaw/config.yaml), add your webhook secrets per integration:

webhooks:
  secrets:
    stripe: "whsec_your_stripe_signing_secret"
    hubspot: "your_hubspot_client_secret"
    typeform: "your_typeform_secret"

MailClaw will automatically verify the signature on incoming requests and reject payloads that don't match. For services that don't offer signed webhooks, you can add a static token to the URL itself and configure MailClaw to require it:

https://your-domain.com/api/webhooks/inbound?token=my_secret_token

Monitoring Webhook Activity from the Dashboard

Every incoming webhook event is logged in MailClaw's local dashboard under Automations → Webhook Log. You can see exactly which payloads arrived, whether they matched a rule, what contact was affected, and what action was taken.

If something isn't triggering as expected, the log shows you the raw payload alongside the filter that was evaluated — making debugging fast. You can also replay failed events directly from the dashboard, which is invaluable when you're iterating on a new integration and something breaks mid-test.

MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools sit alongside this — so you can see not just that a sequence was triggered, but how those emails are performing: open rates, click rates, bounce rates, and spam complaints across every connected SMTP account or OAuth-linked Gmail and Outlook inbox.

Combining Webhooks with AI Email Agents

The real power unlocks when you pair webhook triggers with MailClaw's AI email agents rather than static sequences. Instead of a pre-written template, you define a goal and a set of context signals — and the agent composes a unique email for each contact based on the enrichment data available at trigger time.

For example, when a trial user's account shows signs of disengagement (triggered by a webhook from your product analytics tool), the AI agent might craft a check-in email that references the specific features they've used, the ones they haven't, and gently suggest a next step — all personalized, all automated, all running locally on your machine with no data leaving your environment.

This is the value proposition of running on OpenClaw locally: your contact data, your LLM, your rules — none of it passes through a third-party cloud. For teams handling sensitive B2B contact data, that's not a small thing.

Getting Started Today

If you haven't set up MailClaw yet, the quickest path is:

  1. Install via brew install mailclaw or download from the MailClaw GitHub repository
  2. Run mailclaw start and open localhost:3100
  3. Connect your first email account (Gmail OAuth or SMTP — both work)
  4. Create a webhook trigger rule and expose your endpoint with ngrok
  5. Fire a test payload from whatever tool you're integrating and watch it appear in the webhook log

Real-time event-driven outreach isn't a feature reserved for enterprise platforms with six-figure contracts. With MailClaw, it's a Saturday afternoon project — and once it's running, you'll wonder how you ever tolerated the alternative.

articles.title: How to Integrate MailClaw with Segment for Behavioral Email Triggers
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw with Segment to trigger behavioral email sequences based on real user actions — from page views to completed purchases — using webhooks, the MailClaw CLI, and AI-powered agents running locally on your Mac.
articles.content:
Why Behavioral Triggers Beat Scheduled Blasts

Most email campaigns are built around time. You add a contact, wait three days, send a follow-up, wait two more days, close the loop. It's predictable — and that's exactly the problem. Your prospects aren't living on a schedule. They're visiting your pricing page at 11pm, signing up for a trial mid-meeting, or abandoning a cart while distracted on their phone.

Behavioral email triggers solve this by flipping the model: instead of pushing emails based on time, you send them based on intent signals. When a user completes a meaningful action — viewing a key page, activating a feature, upgrading a plan — that action becomes the trigger. The result is email that feels timely, relevant, and almost eerily well-timed.

Segment is one of the best tools for capturing and routing those intent signals. And MailClaw, running locally on your Mac via localhost:3100, is purpose-built to act on them. Here's how to wire the two together.

Understanding the Architecture

Before writing a single line of code, it helps to understand how data flows between these two systems.

Segment collects events from your web app, mobile app, or backend using its SDK. Each event — a track() call like User Signed Up or Plan Upgraded — gets routed to any destination you configure. One of those destinations can be a webhook endpoint exposed by MailClaw.

On the MailClaw side, the OpenClaw-powered engine listens for incoming webhook payloads, matches them to contact records (enriching them if needed), and drops the contact into the appropriate sequence or hands them off to an AI email agent for dynamic follow-up.

The full pipeline looks like this:

User Action (in-app)
  → Segment SDK tracks event
    → Segment Webhook Destination
      → MailClaw Webhook Listener (localhost:3100)
        → Contact Enrichment
          → Sequence Builder trigger
            → AI Email Agent drafts + sends

Step 1 — Expose MailClaw's Webhook Endpoint

MailClaw runs locally, which means Segment can't reach localhost:3100 directly from the internet. You have two good options: use a tunnel during development, or deploy MailClaw to a private server or VPS for production.

Development: Use a Tunnel

The fastest way to get started is with ngrok or Cloudflare Tunnel. With ngrok installed, run:

ngrok http 3100

This gives you a public HTTPS URL like https://abc123.ngrok.io. Use this as your Segment webhook destination during development. Every request Segment sends will be forwarded to your local MailClaw dashboard.

Production: Deploy to a VPS

For production, spin up a small Linux box (DigitalOcean, Hetzner, or Fly.io all work well), clone the MailClaw repo, and run it behind an nginx reverse proxy with SSL. Since MailClaw is fully open source, there are no licensing fees — just your infrastructure costs.

Step 2 — Create the Webhook Listener in MailClaw

Inside the MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to Integrations → Webhooks → New Listener. Give it a name like Segment Behavioral Triggers and copy the generated endpoint path. It will look something like:

POST /webhooks/inbound/seg_a7f3c2

You can also create this via the MailClaw CLI:

mailclaw webhooks create \
  --name "Segment Behavioral Triggers" \
  --source segment \
  --secret YOUR_SIGNING_SECRET

The --secret flag tells MailClaw to validate Segment's webhook signature on every incoming request, so you're not processing spoofed payloads.

Step 3 — Configure Segment's Webhook Destination

In your Segment workspace, go to Connections → Destinations → Add Destination and search for Webhooks (Actions). Connect it to the source that's tracking your user events, then configure a mapping:

  • Trigger: Event Type is track
  • URL: Your MailClaw webhook endpoint (ngrok URL or production domain)
  • HTTP Method: POST
  • Headers: Add X-Segment-Secret: YOUR_SIGNING_SECRET

You can also filter by specific event names — for example, only forward Plan Upgraded and Trial Started events rather than every single Page Viewed call. This keeps your MailClaw instance focused on high-intent signals.

Step 4 — Map Segment Events to MailClaw Sequences

Now for the good part. Inside MailClaw's Sequence Builder, you can define trigger rules that fire when a specific Segment event arrives. Each sequence can have its own entry conditions, timing logic, and email content.

Example: Trial Started Sequence

When Segment fires a Trial Started event, you want to immediately send a warm welcome email, then follow up on days 3 and 7 with onboarding tips tailored to what the user actually did during signup.

mailclaw sequences create \
  --name "Trial Onboarding" \
  --trigger webhook:segment \
  --event "Trial Started" \
  --enrich true \
  --ai-agent onboarding-helper

The --enrich true flag tells MailClaw to run contact enrichment before the first email goes out. Using OpenClaw's enrichment pipeline, it will pull in job title, company size, industry, and LinkedIn data — so your AI email agent has real context to work with when crafting that first message.

Example: High-Intent Page View

Segment can also track page views. If a user visits your pricing page three times in a week without converting, that's a strong signal. Set up a Segment computed trait or audience that fires a custom event — say, Pricing Page High Intent — and map it to a MailClaw sequence that puts a human-feeling email in their inbox within the hour.

Pro tip: Use Segment's Computed Traits to build composite signals (e.g., "visited pricing page AND used core feature AND is on free plan") before forwarding to MailClaw. This prevents over-triggering and keeps your sequences targeted.

Step 5 — Let AI Agents Personalize at Scale

Static email templates only go so far. Once your behavioral triggers are flowing, MailClaw's AI email agents can take over personalization. Instead of writing a single template that says "Hi {first_name}, welcome to your trial!", you define a prompt-based agent that receives the full Segment event payload and the enriched contact profile, then drafts a genuinely personalized email.

In the MailClaw dashboard, create a new AI agent under Agents → New Agent:

mailclaw agents create \
  --name "onboarding-helper" \
  --model gpt-4o \
  --persona "warm SaaS onboarding specialist" \
  --context-fields "event.properties, contact.company, contact.role" \
  --tone "professional, encouraging" \
  --max-length 200

The agent will reference the user's actual event properties — what plan they chose, which features they enabled, what their company does — and write accordingly. Someone who signed up for a developer plan at a fintech startup gets a fundamentally different email than a marketer at a mid-market e-commerce brand, even though both triggered the same Trial Started event.

Step 6 — Monitor Deliverability as Volume Grows

Behavioral triggers can fire frequently. As your Segment event volume grows and MailClaw starts sending hundreds of triggered emails per day, deliverability becomes critical. A single spam complaint spike can hurt your sender reputation across Gmail, Outlook, and every inbox you're trying to reach.

MailClaw's built-in deliverability tools surface the metrics you need to catch problems early:

  • Bounce tracking: Automatically suppress hard bounces from future sends, regardless of which SMTP account or SendGrid sub-user is being used
  • Spam rate monitoring: MailClaw pulls Google Postmaster Tools and Microsoft SNDS data into the local dashboard so you can see reputation scores without switching tabs
  • Sequence-level engagement: See open rates and click rates per trigger sequence, not just per campaign, so you know which Segment events are generating replies and which are generating unsubscribes

If a particular trigger sequence starts seeing elevated unsubscribe rates, that's often a signal that the event itself is too low-intent — worth revisiting your Segment audience definition before scaling further.

Connecting Other Tools in the Stack

The Segment + MailClaw pattern works especially well when you're already using other tools in your stack. A few combinations worth knowing:

  • HubSpot or Salesforce: Use MailClaw's CRM sync to write back engagement data — opens, clicks, replies — so your sales team sees email activity alongside deal stage without manual logging
  • Multi-account outreach: Route different Segment event types through different SMTP accounts or OAuth-connected Gmail and Outlook inboxes. High-intent trial events might go through a personal-looking Gmail; bulk nurture sequences go through SendGrid
  • Slack alerts: When an AI agent sends a reply or a contact hits a specific sequence milestone, MailClaw can post to Slack so your team can jump in manually when the timing is right

Putting It Together

Behavioral email triggers powered by Segment and MailClaw give you something that scheduled campaigns never can: email that arrives at the exact moment a user is thinking about your product. The setup takes an afternoon — expose the webhook, configure the Segment destination, map your events to sequences, enable enrichment and your AI agent — and then it runs continuously in the background while you focus on everything else.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs locally, you own the entire pipeline. No SaaS fees scaling with your contact count, no third-party servers handling your customer data, and no black-box algorithms deciding which emails get sent. Just clean, observable automation that you can inspect, modify, and extend whenever your stack evolves.

Start with two or three high-signal events from Segment, get the sequences dialed in, then expand from there. The infrastructure will scale with you.

articles.title: MailClaw + Airtable: Managing Campaign Data and Contact Sheets
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw with Airtable to build a seamless campaign data pipeline — from syncing contact sheets and enriching records to automating sequence enrollment and tracking deliverability metrics in one place.
articles.content:
Why Airtable and MailClaw Work So Well Together

If you've ever managed a cold outreach campaign, you know the pain: contacts living in one spreadsheet, sequence drafts in another doc, reply tracking in a third tab, and campaign metrics scattered across your email provider's dashboard. It's a mess that slows you down and introduces errors at every handoff.

MailClaw's local-first architecture — running entirely on your machine at localhost:3100 — makes it uniquely suited for deep integrations with tools like Airtable. Because everything stays on your Mac and communicates over local APIs, you get fast, private, and fully controllable data pipelines without pushing sensitive contact data through a dozen third-party cloud services.

Airtable, meanwhile, is the spreadsheet-database hybrid that most growth teams already live in. It's flexible enough to hold your contact lists, campaign briefs, enrichment data, and follow-up notes — and powerful enough to serve as a lightweight CRM when you're not ready to commit to Salesforce or HubSpot.

Together, they form a surprisingly powerful stack. This guide walks you through setting up that connection practically and getting real value out of it fast.

Setting Up Your Airtable Base for Email Campaigns

Before you wire anything to MailClaw, it's worth getting your Airtable base structured correctly. A well-designed base makes automation reliable; a sloppy one creates sync headaches.

Recommended Table Structure

Create a base with at least three linked tables:

  • Contacts — First name, last name, email, company, title, LinkedIn URL, enrichment status, and a linked field to Campaigns.
  • Campaigns — Campaign name, sequence ID (from MailClaw), launch date, goal, status (Draft / Active / Paused / Complete).
  • Events — Contact email, event type (sent, opened, clicked, replied, bounced), timestamp, campaign ID. This is your deliverability log.

Using linked records instead of duplicating data across tables keeps things clean and makes filtering much more useful. When a contact moves from "Contacted" to "Replied," you update one field and every view reflects it instantly.

Adding a Status Field MailClaw Can Write To

Add a single-select field called Outreach Status to your Contacts table with these options: Pending, Enrolled, Active, Replied, Bounced, Unsubscribed. MailClaw will update this field as it processes contacts, giving you a live view of where everyone sits in your funnel.

Pulling Airtable Contacts into MailClaw

MailClaw's CLI makes it straightforward to import contacts from external sources. The quickest path is using the Airtable REST API to export a filtered view and pipe it directly into MailClaw's contact importer.

Step 1: Get Your Airtable API Credentials

Go to airtable.com/create/tokens, create a personal access token with data.records:read and data.records:write scopes, and note your Base ID from the API docs URL.

Step 2: Fetch Contacts from Airtable

Run this from your terminal to pull contacts where Outreach Status is "Pending" and save them as a CSV MailClaw can ingest:

curl "https://api.airtable.com/v0/YOUR_BASE_ID/Contacts?filterByFormula={Outreach Status}='Pending'&maxRecords=500" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN" \
  | jq -r '.records[] | .fields | [.Email, ."First Name", ."Last Name", .Company, .Title] | @csv' \
  > contacts_pending.csv

This uses jq to reshape the JSON response into a flat CSV. If you don't have jq installed, run brew install jq first.

Step 3: Import into MailClaw

mailclaw contacts import \
  --file contacts_pending.csv \
  --map email:0,first_name:1,last_name:2,company:3,title:4 \
  --tag "airtable-import-$(date +%Y%m%d)"
