The --tag flag adds a dated tag so you can filter these contacts in MailClaw's dashboard and know exactly which import batch they came from. Open your local dashboard at localhost:3100/contacts and you should see them appear within seconds.

Enriching Contacts Before You Send

Raw Airtable contact lists are rarely complete enough to power great personalization. MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment engine — powered by OpenClaw — can fill in gaps like job titles, company size, industry, and social profiles before your sequences ever run.

mailclaw contacts enrich \
  --tag "airtable-import-$(date +%Y%m%d)" \
  --fields title,company_size,industry,linkedin \
  --write-back airtable \
  --airtable-base YOUR_BASE_ID \
  --airtable-table Contacts \
  --match-field email

The --write-back airtable flag tells MailClaw to push enriched data back to your Airtable base automatically, keeping both systems in sync. After enrichment runs, open your Airtable base and you'll see the previously blank fields populated — no copy-pasting required.

Pro tip: Run enrichment on a filtered view of contacts who have a LinkedIn URL but are missing a company size. Those are usually the easiest wins — one good data point anchors the rest of the enrichment lookup.

Enrolling Contacts in MailClaw Sequences

Once your contacts are imported and enriched, you can enroll them in a sequence directly from the CLI or the localhost dashboard's sequence builder.

Creating the Sequence

If you haven't built your sequence yet, open localhost:3100/sequences/new. MailClaw's AI email agent can draft the entire sequence for you based on a brief — just describe your offer, target persona, and desired tone, and it'll generate a multi-step sequence with subject line variants and send-time recommendations.

Enrolling from the CLI

mailclaw sequences enroll \
  --sequence-id seq_abc123 \
  --filter tag:airtable-import-$(date +%Y%m%d) \
  --account gmail-primary \
  --start-date tomorrow \
  --dry-run

Always run with --dry-run first. It prints a preview of exactly which contacts would be enrolled, which account they'd send from, and the projected send schedule — without actually queuing anything. Remove the flag when you're confident.

Updating Airtable Status After Enrollment

After enrollment, push the status change back to Airtable so your base stays accurate:

mailclaw contacts list \
  --filter "sequence:seq_abc123,status:enrolled" \
  --format json \
  | jq -r '.[] | {email: .email, status: "Enrolled"}' \
  | mailclaw airtable sync \
  --base YOUR_BASE_ID \
  --table Contacts \
  --match-field email \
  --update-field "Outreach Status"

This pipeline reads enrolled contacts from MailClaw, formats them, and syncs the updated status back to Airtable in one pass. Your team sees live status in Airtable without ever needing to touch MailClaw directly.

Streaming Campaign Events Back to Airtable

The real power of this integration shows up in your Events table. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring captures every send, open, click, reply, and bounce event. You can stream these back to Airtable to build live campaign dashboards using Airtable's native views and automations.

Using a Webhook

MailClaw supports outbound webhooks for campaign events. Set one up to POST to a simple local endpoint (or a tool like Make or Zapier pointing at Airtable's API):

mailclaw webhooks create \
  --events sent,opened,clicked,replied,bounced \
  --url https://hooks.zapier.com/hooks/catch/YOUR_HOOK_ID/ \
  --campaign seq_abc123

On the Zapier or Make side, map the incoming payload fields to your Airtable Events table columns. Each event becomes a new record with a timestamp, letting you query things like "all contacts who opened but haven't replied in 72 hours" and trigger a follow-up step.

What to Track in the Events Table

  • Deliverability rate — Ratio of sent to bounced, filterable by domain to catch blocklist issues early.
  • Engagement timing — Opens and clicks by hour of day to refine future send schedules.
  • Reply rate by sequence step — Reveals which email in your sequence does the heavy lifting.
  • Unsubscribe patterns — If unsubscribes spike on step 2 for a particular segment, that's a signal to rewrite it.

Keeping the Two Systems in Sync Long-Term

One-time syncs are useful; ongoing sync is what makes this integration genuinely powerful. A few practices that keep things clean over time:

  • Schedule nightly imports — Use a cron job to run your Airtable fetch + MailClaw import every night, so new contacts added during the day are ready for the next morning's review.
  • Use Airtable automations to flag records — Set up a native Airtable automation that marks a contact as "Needs Review" if they replied but their Outreach Status hasn't been updated in 48 hours. That catches edge cases where webhook delivery failed.
  • Archive completed campaigns in both tools — When you mark a campaign complete in MailClaw, trigger an Airtable automation to lock the Campaign record and archive the linked contact statuses. Prevents accidental re-enrollment.
  • Version your sequence IDs — Store MailClaw sequence IDs directly in your Airtable Campaigns table. When someone on your team asks "which version of the sequence did this contact receive?", the answer is one lookup away.

MailClaw's open-source codebase means you can also write custom sync scripts and contribute them back to the community — if you build a robust Airtable connector, other teams are one git clone away from using it too.

A Practical Starting Point

The best way to get value from this setup quickly is to start small: pick one active campaign, import its contact list from Airtable into MailClaw, run enrichment, enroll them in a three-step sequence, and stream events back to a single Airtable view. Once you see that loop working end-to-end, expanding it to multiple campaigns and accounts is just repetition with minor configuration changes.

Your MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100 and your Airtable base become two views of the same truth — one optimized for execution, one optimized for visibility. That combination is hard to beat without a much more expensive stack.

articles.title: How to Connect MailClaw to Intercom for Unified Customer Messaging
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw to Intercom so your email sequences, contact enrichment data, and AI-powered outreach all sync seamlessly with your live customer conversations — creating a truly unified messaging workflow.
articles.content:
Why Connecting MailClaw and Intercom Changes Your Outreach Game

Most teams treat email outreach and in-app messaging as two separate worlds. Your cold sequences live in one tool, your customer conversations live in another, and your support team has no idea that a prospect just opened your nurture email three times in the past hour. That disconnect costs you conversions, context, and credibility.

MailClaw, running locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, already gives you a powerful stack: AI email agents, a visual sequence builder, contact enrichment, and deliverability monitoring — all open source, all private, all yours. Intercom gives you real-time chat, in-app messaging, and a rich customer timeline. When you wire them together, every touchpoint your contacts have with your brand becomes visible and actionable from a single source of truth.

This guide walks you through exactly how to connect the two, sync your contacts bidirectionally, and set up automations that trigger the right message in the right channel at the right moment.

What You'll Need Before You Start

  • MailClaw installed and running locally (mailclaw start — dashboard at localhost:3100)
  • An Intercom account with API access (any paid plan includes this)
  • Your Intercom Access Token from Settings → Integrations → Developer Hub → Your App → Authentication
  • Node.js 18+ if you plan to run any custom webhook handlers
  • Optional but recommended: a tunneling tool like ngrok to expose your local MailClaw instance to Intercom webhooks during development

MailClaw's open-source foundation (built on OpenClaw) means you can inspect every integration, modify webhook handlers, and self-host the entire pipeline without routing sensitive contact data through third-party servers. That matters a lot when you're syncing customer conversation history.

Step 1 — Generate Your Intercom API Token

Head to your Intercom Developer Hub and create a new app or use an existing one. Under Authentication, copy your Access Token. This token will allow MailClaw to read and write contacts, tag users, and subscribe to conversation events.

Store it securely in MailClaw's environment config:

# In your MailClaw root directory
mailclaw config set INTERCOM_ACCESS_TOKEN=your_token_here
mailclaw config set INTERCOM_REGION=us  # or eu depending on your workspace

MailClaw encrypts these values locally — they never leave your machine unless you explicitly configure a remote sync target.

Step 2 — Connect the Integration via the MailClaw Dashboard

Open your browser to localhost:3100 and navigate to Settings → Integrations → CRM & Messaging. You'll see first-party connectors for tools like HubSpot, Salesforce, and Intercom listed alongside community-contributed adapters.

  1. Click Intercom and select Connect via API Token
  2. Paste the token you configured above (MailClaw auto-reads it from your config)
  3. Choose your sync direction: MailClaw → Intercom, Intercom → MailClaw, or Bidirectional
  4. Select which contact fields to map (email, name, company, custom attributes)
  5. Hit Test Connection — a green status badge confirms everything is live

For most teams, bidirectional sync is the right choice. Contacts enriched by MailClaw's AI enrichment engine get pushed into Intercom automatically, while conversation events from Intercom flow back into MailClaw's contact timeline.

Step 3 — Map Contact Fields and Custom Attributes

MailClaw's contact enrichment pulls in job title, company size, LinkedIn profile, tech stack, and dozens of other signals. Intercom supports custom attributes on both Users and Companies — you want that enrichment data living in Intercom so your support and success teams can see it during live conversations.

In the integration field mapper (still inside localhost:3100 → Integrations → Intercom → Field Mapping), create mappings like these:

MailClaw Field          → Intercom Attribute
-------------------------------------------------
contact.job_title       → user.job_title
contact.company_size    → company.size
contact.enriched_score  → user.lead_score
contact.tech_stack      → user.tech_stack (custom)
contact.sequence_stage  → user.email_sequence_stage (custom)

The email_sequence_stage custom attribute is particularly powerful. When a contact moves from Day 3 Follow-Up to Booked a Call inside a MailClaw sequence, that update flows to Intercom automatically. Your support agent seeing an incoming chat immediately knows where that person is in your pipeline.

Step 4 — Set Up Intercom Webhooks in MailClaw

Webhooks are how Intercom tells MailClaw when something interesting happens — a new conversation started, a user replied, a lead was tagged. You'll need to expose your local MailClaw instance with ngrok during development:

ngrok http 3100
# Copy the HTTPS forwarding URL, e.g. https://a1b2c3d4.ngrok.io

Then in your Intercom Developer Hub, go to Webhooks and add a new subscription pointing to:

https://a1b2c3d4.ngrok.io/api/webhooks/intercom

Subscribe to these topics to start:

  • conversation.user.created — a new inbound conversation started
  • conversation.user.replied — a prospect replied to your team
  • contact.created — a new lead was added in Intercom
  • contact.tag.created — a tag was applied (useful for triggering sequences)

MailClaw handles incoming webhook payloads at /api/webhooks/intercom out of the box. For production, replace the ngrok URL with your actual MailClaw server hostname if you've deployed it on a VPS or behind a reverse proxy.

Step 5 — Build Cross-Channel Automations

Here's where things get genuinely exciting. With the integration live, you can build automations that respond to behavior across both channels.

Trigger a MailClaw Sequence When an Intercom Tag is Applied

Say your sales team tags a prospect as demo-requested in Intercom. You want MailClaw to automatically enroll them in a post-demo follow-up sequence. In MailClaw's sequence builder:

mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "Post Demo Follow-Up" \
  --trigger intercom:tag:demo-requested \
  --from-account sales@yourcompany.com \
  --smtp sendgrid

MailClaw's AI email agents can then personalize each message in that sequence using the enriched contact data already synced from your CRM — referencing the prospect's company, tech stack, or industry without you writing a single custom line.

Pause a Sequence When a Contact Replies in Intercom

Nothing is more awkward than receiving a canned follow-up email while you're actively chatting with someone in a live Intercom conversation. The conversation.user.replied webhook prevents exactly this:

# MailClaw auto-pauses sequences for contacts with active Intercom threads
mailclaw config set INTERCOM_PAUSE_ON_REPLY=true

This single setting alone will improve your reply rates and protect your sender reputation — one of the deliverability best practices MailClaw's monitoring tools flag when you run a campaign health check.

Enrich New Intercom Contacts Automatically

Every time the contact.created webhook fires, MailClaw can run its enrichment pipeline on the new contact and push the results back to Intercom within seconds. Your team gets a fully profiled lead before they've even responded to the first message.

Step 6 — Validate the Integration End-to-End

Before going live, run a quick smoke test from the MailClaw CLI:

mailclaw integrations test intercom \
  --contact-email test@example.com \
  --simulate-tag demo-requested

This fires a simulated webhook event, checks that the contact syncs correctly, confirms field mappings are working, and verifies that your sequence trigger logic fires as expected. The output is logged in your localhost:3100 dashboard under Integrations → Activity Log so you can see exactly what happened at each step.

Pro Tips for a Healthy Integration

  • Use MailClaw's deliverability monitor to check your sender score before launching any Intercom-triggered sequence. A paused sequence won't help you if your domain is already hurting.
  • Tag contacts in MailClaw with their Intercom conversation ID so you can deep-link directly to the live thread from inside your email campaign view.
  • Leverage multi-account support — if your sales team uses Gmail and your marketing team uses Outlook, MailClaw can route Intercom-triggered emails from the right account based on the contact's assigned owner.
  • Review the OpenClaw integration spec in the MailClaw docs to understand how to extend the Intercom adapter with custom logic specific to your workflow — things like routing based on plan tier or conversation rating.

The goal isn't just to sync data — it's to make every person on your team, whether they're sending a cold outreach email or answering a live chat, feel like they've known the contact for months.

What You've Built

With this integration in place, MailClaw and Intercom stop being parallel tools and start working as a single, context-aware messaging system. Your AI email agents know when to pause. Your support team sees enrichment data the moment a chat opens. Your sequences are smarter because they're informed by live conversation signals — not just email opens and clicks.

And because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your machine, you maintain full ownership of every contact record, every conversation event, and every automation rule. No black boxes, no vendor lock-in, no data leaving your infrastructure without your explicit say-so.

That's a genuinely different way to think about customer messaging infrastructure — and it's available right now at localhost:3100.

articles.title: Using MailClaw with Postmark for Transactional Email
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw with Postmark to deliver reliable transactional emails — from welcome sequences to password resets — using MailClaw's local dashboard, SMTP integration, and AI-powered automation tools.
articles.content:
Why Pair MailClaw with Postmark?

Transactional email is a different beast from marketing email. When someone resets their password, confirms an order, or receives a billing receipt, that message needs to arrive immediately — not sit in a queue, not land in spam, not bounce silently. That's where Postmark earns its reputation. It's purpose-built for transactional delivery, with industry-leading inbox rates and a laser focus on speed.

MailClaw complements Postmark perfectly. As an open-source, locally-run email automation platform built on OpenClaw, MailClaw handles the orchestration — the sequences, the AI agents, the contact enrichment, the logic — while Postmark handles the infrastructure. Together, they give you a production-grade transactional email setup that you control entirely from your own machine at localhost:3100.

This guide walks you through connecting the two, configuring your sending streams, and putting MailClaw's automation features to work on real transactional use cases.

Setting Up Postmark in MailClaw

Getting Your Postmark Server Token

Before touching MailClaw, you need a Postmark server token. Log into your Postmark account, navigate to Servers → Your Server → API Tokens, and copy your server token. Postmark uses separate tokens for transactional and broadcast streams — make sure you're grabbing the one tied to your transactional message stream.

Postmark also supports SMTP as a delivery method, which is what MailClaw uses under the hood. Your SMTP credentials will be:

  • Host: smtp.postmarkapp.com
  • Port: 587 (TLS) or 465 (SSL)
  • Username: Your server token
  • Password: Your server token (same value)

Adding Postmark as an SMTP Account in MailClaw

Open your MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100 and head to Accounts → Add Account. Select SMTP as the connection type and fill in your Postmark credentials. MailClaw's multi-account support means you can have this sitting alongside your Gmail or Outlook accounts without any conflict — useful if you're running marketing sequences from one account and transactional flows from another.

Alternatively, add it via the CLI:

mailclaw account add \
  --name "Postmark Transactional" \
  --type smtp \
  --host smtp.postmarkapp.com \
  --port 587 \
  --user YOUR_SERVER_TOKEN \
  --pass YOUR_SERVER_TOKEN \
  --from "no-reply@yourdomain.com"

Once saved, MailClaw will run a quick deliverability check using its built-in monitoring tools. You should see green lights across the board for SPF, DKIM, and DMARC — Postmark handles all of that automatically for verified domains, which is one of the reasons developers love it.

Verifying Your Domain

If you haven't already verified your sending domain in Postmark, do it now. Postmark will give you DNS records to add — typically a DKIM TXT record and an SPF include. After adding them, MailClaw's deliverability dashboard will confirm they're resolving correctly. This step is non-negotiable for transactional email; without it, even Postmark can't guarantee inbox placement.

Building Transactional Email Sequences

What Counts as Transactional?

Postmark draws a hard line between transactional and marketing email, and so should you. Transactional messages are triggered by a specific user action — a signup, a purchase, a support ticket, a password reset. They're one-to-one, expected, and time-sensitive. Marketing emails are campaigns sent to lists. Mixing them on the same stream is against Postmark's terms and will get you flagged.

MailClaw's sequence builder makes it easy to model both types correctly. When building a transactional sequence, tag it appropriately and assign it to your Postmark account. Your marketing sequences can continue running through Gmail, SendGrid, or whatever other accounts you have configured.

Creating a Welcome Email Sequence

A post-signup welcome flow is the most common transactional sequence. Here's how to build one in MailClaw:

  1. Go to Sequences → New Sequence in the dashboard.
  2. Name it something descriptive: "Post-Signup Welcome — Transactional".
  3. Set the sending account to your Postmark SMTP configuration.
  4. Add your first step: an immediate welcome email (delay: 0 minutes).
  5. Add a second step 24 hours later: a "getting started" guide.
  6. Add a third step at 72 hours: a check-in or feature highlight.

Each step can be written manually or drafted using MailClaw's AI email agents. The AI agents, powered by OpenClaw, can generate personalized copy based on the contact's data, product context, and tone guidelines you set. For transactional email, you typically want a more direct, functional tone — the AI agents handle that constraint well when you specify it in your prompt settings.

mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "Post-Signup Welcome" \
  --account "Postmark Transactional" \
  --steps 3 \
  --ai-draft \
  --tone "helpful, concise, direct"

Triggering Sequences Programmatically

Most transactional sequences need to fire in response to an event in your application — a new row in your database, a webhook from Stripe, a user action in your product. MailClaw exposes a simple local API for exactly this purpose.

Here's an example of triggering the welcome sequence when a new user signs up:

curl -X POST http://localhost:3100/api/sequences/trigger \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "sequence": "post-signup-welcome",
    "contact": {
      "email": "jane@example.com",
      "name": "Jane Doe",
      "plan": "pro",
      "signup_date": "2025-01-15"
    }
  }'

MailClaw will enroll the contact, run contact enrichment if configured, and begin executing the sequence steps through your Postmark SMTP connection. Because everything runs locally, there's no third-party SaaS layer adding latency or logging your data.

Using AI Email Agents for Transactional Flows

MailClaw's AI email agents aren't just for cold outreach. They're genuinely useful for transactional scenarios where personalization matters — onboarding flows, renewal reminders, trial expiration notices.

You can configure an agent to watch a contact segment (say, users on a trial who haven't activated a key feature) and automatically draft and send a targeted nudge through Postmark. The agent uses enrichment data — job title, company size, industry, activity signals — to tailor the message. What would take a team hours to segment and personalize in HubSpot or Salesforce happens automatically, locally, in minutes.

Pro tip: Set up a separate Postmark message stream for each major transactional category (onboarding, billing, notifications). This lets you track performance independently and quarantine any reputation issues without affecting your other streams. In MailClaw, you can map each stream to its own account entry with a distinct server token.

Monitoring Deliverability and Bounces

Postmark provides detailed bounce and delivery webhooks. MailClaw can consume these to keep your contact list clean and your sequences healthy.

Configuring Postmark Webhooks

In your Postmark server settings, navigate to Webhooks and add your MailClaw endpoint. Since MailClaw runs locally, you'll need a tunnel for development — ngrok works well here:

# Expose your local MailClaw instance
ngrok http 3100

# Your webhook URL will look like:
# https://abc123.ngrok.io/api/webhooks/postmark

In production, point the webhook directly at your server. MailClaw will process bounce events, unsubscribes, and spam complaints automatically, flagging contacts in your dashboard and pausing sequences for affected addresses. This keeps your Postmark sender reputation clean — a hard bounce rate above 2% can trigger account review, so automated cleanup is essential.

Reading the Deliverability Dashboard

MailClaw's deliverability dashboard at localhost:3100/deliverability surfaces aggregate metrics across all your accounts. For Postmark specifically, you'll see open rates, delivery speed (Postmark's average is under 10 seconds), bounce classifications, and spam complaints. Cross-reference this with what you see in Postmark's own activity log to catch any discrepancies.

Practical Tips for Transactional Email Success

  • Always use a dedicated sending domain. Don't send transactional email from the same domain you use for cold outreach. Use mail.yourdomain.com or noreply.yourdomain.com and verify it in Postmark separately.
  • Keep sequences short and purposeful. Transactional sequences aren't nurture campaigns. Three to five steps maximum. Every email should have a clear reason to exist.
  • Use MailClaw's contact enrichment to personalize, not spam. Enrichment data should make emails feel more relevant, not more intrusive. A billing reminder that mentions the user's plan name feels helpful. One that mentions their LinkedIn headline does not.
  • Test in staging first. MailClaw supports environment-level account switching. Use a Postmark sandbox account (or a test stream) during development so you're not firing real emails during QA.
  • Review your open-source configuration regularly. Because MailClaw is open source and runs locally, you're in full control of your data and your logic. Audit your sequence configs and agent prompts periodically — especially before major product changes.

Wrapping Up

Postmark and MailClaw are a natural fit. Postmark brings best-in-class transactional delivery infrastructure; MailClaw brings the automation intelligence, contact management, and AI-powered personalization that makes transactional email more than just a utility function. Because MailClaw runs entirely on your machine — no cloud subscription, no vendor lock-in — you maintain full ownership of your sending logic and contact data while still benefiting from Postmark's deliverability reputation.

Whether you're building a simple welcome flow or a sophisticated multi-stream transactional architecture, the combination gives you tools that used to require a full marketing ops stack — now running from a single command on localhost.

articles.title: How to Integrate MailClaw with Calendly for Booking Follow-Ups
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw with Calendly to automatically trigger personalized follow-up email sequences the moment a prospect books, reschedules, or cancels a meeting — saving hours of manual outreach every week.
articles.content:
Why Booking Events Should Trigger Email Sequences Automatically

If you're doing any kind of sales outreach, consulting, or client onboarding, Calendly is probably already baked into your workflow. Someone clicks a link, picks a time, and a meeting appears on your calendar. Clean and simple. But what happens after that booking confirmation email lands? In most setups: nothing automated. You manually send a reminder. You forget to follow up after the call. The deal goes cold.

This is exactly the gap MailClaw was built to close. Because MailClaw runs locally on your machine at localhost:3100, it can respond to webhook events from external tools like Calendly in real time — without shipping your contact data to a third-party SaaS platform. Combine that with MailClaw's AI email agents and sequence builder, and you have a fully autonomous booking follow-up engine running on your Mac.

What You'll Need Before You Start

Before wiring this together, make sure you have the following in place:

  • MailClaw running locally — start it with mailclaw start and confirm the dashboard is live at localhost:3100
  • A Calendly account — any paid plan gives you access to webhooks, which is required for this integration
  • A public webhook URL — since MailClaw runs on localhost, you'll need a tunnel like ngrok or Cloudflare Tunnel to expose it to Calendly during development
  • SMTP or OAuth credentials configured — MailClaw supports Gmail OAuth, Outlook OAuth, and raw SMTP providers like SendGrid or Mailgun

If you haven't connected a sending account yet, open your dashboard at localhost:3100/settings/accounts and add one. For Gmail, click Connect with OAuth. For SendGrid, paste your API key and set the SMTP relay host to smtp.sendgrid.net.

Step 1: Expose Your Local MailClaw Instance

Calendly needs a publicly reachable URL to fire webhook events. Run ngrok to create a tunnel to your local MailClaw server:

ngrok http 3100

Ngrok will give you a forwarding URL like https://a1b2-203-0-113-42.ngrok.io. Copy that — you'll use it in the next step. For a more stable setup in production, consider Cloudflare Tunnel with a custom subdomain pointed permanently at your machine.

Step 2: Create a Webhook in Calendly

Log into Calendly and navigate to Integrations → Webhooks. Click New Webhook and fill in the following:

  1. Subscriber URL: https://your-ngrok-url.ngrok.io/api/webhooks/calendly
  2. Events to subscribe to: Select invitee.created, invitee.canceled, and optionally routing_form_submission.created if you use Calendly routing forms
  3. Signing key: Copy the signing key Calendly generates — you'll add this to MailClaw so it can verify the payload

Save the webhook. Calendly will fire a test ping to your endpoint, and you should see it appear in MailClaw's webhook log at localhost:3100/webhooks/log.

Step 3: Configure the Calendly Integration in MailClaw

MailClaw has a built-in Calendly connector in its integrations panel. Open your terminal and run:

mailclaw integrations add calendly \
  --signing-key YOUR_CALENDLY_SIGNING_KEY \
  --event invitee.created \
  --event invitee.canceled

Or configure it visually from the dashboard at localhost:3100/integrations/calendly. You'll see fields for your signing key and event type mappings. Once saved, MailClaw will begin parsing and validating all incoming Calendly webhook payloads.

What MailClaw Extracts from the Payload

When a Calendly invitee.created event fires, MailClaw automatically extracts and maps the following fields to a contact record:

  • Invitee name and email address
  • Event type name and scheduled start time
  • Any custom questions you've configured in your Calendly event type
  • Cancellation reason (for invitee.canceled events)

That contact is then available for enrichment and sequencing immediately. MailClaw's contact enrichment feature — powered by OpenClaw — can automatically pull in company name, LinkedIn profile, job title, and firmographic data based on the email address alone. No manual research required.

Step 4: Build Your Booking Follow-Up Sequence

This is where the real value kicks in. Navigate to localhost:3100/sequences/new and create a new sequence. Name it something like Calendly — Post-Booking Follow-Up.

Suggested Sequence Structure

Here's a high-performing structure for a sales or discovery call follow-up sequence:

  • Step 1 (Trigger: immediately): Confirmation + value-add email. Thank them for booking, link a relevant case study or resource that maps to what they likely want to discuss.
  • Step 2 (Delay: 24 hours before the meeting): Meeting reminder with agenda. Keep it short. Include a link to reschedule if needed.
  • Step 3 (Delay: 1 hour after the meeting end time): Post-call follow-up. Recap key points discussed, attach a proposal or next steps doc, include a link to book a follow-up call.
  • Step 4 (Delay: 3 days after the meeting): Check-in if no reply. Light-touch message asking if they had any questions.

MailClaw's sequence builder supports conditional branching — so if a contact replies to Step 3, Steps 4 onward are automatically skipped. No awkward "just checking in" emails to someone who already responded.

Letting the AI Email Agent Write the Copy

You don't need to write every email from scratch. In the sequence builder, click Generate with AI on any step. MailClaw's AI email agent — built on OpenClaw — will draft copy based on the event type name, the contact's enriched profile data, and the step's goal (confirm, remind, follow up, etc.).

Pro tip: In the AI prompt field, add context like "This is a 30-minute discovery call for a B2B SaaS product targeting ops teams." The more context you give the agent, the more relevant and personalized the output.

All generated drafts are editable before saving — you stay in full control. The AI handles the blank-page problem; you handle the brand voice.

Step 5: Map the Trigger to Your Sequence

Back in the Calendly integration panel at localhost:3100/integrations/calendly, map each event type to a sequence:

mailclaw trigger create \
  --source calendly \
  --event invitee.created \
  --event-type-name "30 Minute Discovery Call" \
  --sequence "Calendly — Post-Booking Follow-Up" \
  --enrich-contact true

You can create separate triggers for different Calendly event types — a demo call trigger might route to a product-focused sequence, while a consulting intake call routes to an onboarding-flavored one. Multi-account support means you can also route each trigger through a different sending account if needed.

Handling Cancellations Gracefully

Don't ignore the invitee.canceled event. A cancellation is a re-engagement opportunity. Create a short two-step sequence for canceled bookings:

  1. Immediately: "No worries — here's a link to reschedule when you're ready." Include your Calendly link inline, not as a CTA button that looks like a marketing email.
  2. 5 days later (if not rebooked): A softer check-in. Something like: "I know things get busy — happy to jump on a 15-minute call instead if that's easier."

MailClaw's deliverability tools include reply detection and link-click tracking, so if the contact clicks the reschedule link, the second step is automatically suppressed. You're never sending noise.

Monitoring Performance from the Dashboard

Once your integration is live, the MailClaw local dashboard gives you a real-time view of everything. At localhost:3100/campaigns you'll see open rates, click rates, reply rates, and bounce rates broken down by sequence and step. MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring flags issues like rising bounce rates or spam folder placement before they damage your sender reputation.

If you're syncing contacts to a CRM — MailClaw supports native integrations with HubSpot and Salesforce — every email event is written back as a CRM activity automatically, keeping your pipeline data clean without any manual logging.

The Bigger Picture: A Self-Running Outreach Loop

What makes this integration genuinely powerful is that once it's configured, it's invisible. A prospect books a Calendly slot at 11pm on a Tuesday. By the time they wake up Wednesday morning, MailClaw has already enrolled them in a sequence, enriched their contact record, and sent a personalized confirmation email — all from your own machine, using your own SMTP credentials, with no third-party automation platform seeing your contact data.

That's the core promise of MailClaw being open-source and locally run: you get enterprise-grade automation without giving up ownership of your data or paying per-contact SaaS fees. The Calendly integration is one of the fastest ways to see that value in practice.

articles.title: MailClaw + GitHub: Automating Open Source Contributor Outreach
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's AI email agents and sequence builder to automate personalized outreach to open source contributors on GitHub — turning passive repo visitors into active collaborators without leaving your local machine.
articles.content:
Why Open Source Contributor Outreach Is Broken (And How to Fix It)

Most open source projects grow through luck and word of mouth. A developer stumbles across your repo, stars it, maybe opens a PR — and then disappears. The project maintainers never follow up, never nurture that spark of interest, and never convert a curious passerby into a committed contributor.

That's not a community problem. It's a workflow problem.

With MailClaw running locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, you can build a fully automated contributor outreach pipeline that pulls data from GitHub, enriches contact profiles, and sends personalized email sequences — all without shipping your data to a third-party SaaS platform. Everything stays on your machine, powered by OpenClaw under the hood.

This guide walks you through exactly how to do it.

Step 1: Identify the Right Contributors to Reach Out To

Before you write a single email, you need a list of people worth contacting. GitHub is a goldmine for this, but raw data needs context. Here's how to build a qualified contributor list using the GitHub API and MailClaw's contact enrichment engine.

Pull Contributor Signals from GitHub

Start by identifying people who have already shown intent: stargazers who left comments on issues, authors of closed PRs that didn't get merged, or developers who forked your repo but went quiet. These are warm leads, not cold contacts.

Use the GitHub API to export this data. For example, to pull everyone who opened a pull request on your repo:

# Fetch all PR authors from your repo
curl -H "Authorization: token YOUR_GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  "https://api.github.com/repos/YOUR_ORG/YOUR_REPO/pulls?state=all&per_page=100" \
  | jq '[.[] | {login: .user.login, email: .user.email, url: .user.html_url}]' \
  > contributors.json

Many GitHub profiles don't expose emails publicly, which is where MailClaw's contact enrichment feature becomes essential. Import your contributors.json into MailClaw's dashboard and let the enrichment engine cross-reference social profiles, commit metadata, and public developer directories to surface verified email addresses, job titles, and company affiliations.

Segment by Contribution Type

Not all contributors are equal, and your outreach shouldn't treat them that way. Inside MailClaw's contact manager, create segments like:

  • First-time PR authors — needs encouragement and a clear "next step"
  • Issue reporters — engaged users who care about quality
  • Stalwart forkers — developers who cloned but never contributed back
  • Lapsed contributors — past contributors who went silent in the last 90 days

These segments will map directly to different email sequences in the next step.

Step 2: Build Your Contributor Email Sequences

MailClaw's sequence builder lets you design multi-step email workflows with branching logic, time delays, and AI-generated copy — all from the local dashboard at localhost:3100. Here's a battle-tested sequence structure for open source outreach.

The "Welcome to the Community" Sequence (For First-Time PR Authors)

  1. Day 0 — Immediate acknowledgment: Triggered automatically when a PR is opened or merged. Thank them by name, reference their specific contribution, and link to your contributor guide.
  2. Day 3 — The value add: Share something genuinely useful — a technical deep-dive on the area of the codebase they touched, or a link to a related open issue that matches their skill set.
  3. Day 10 — The ask: A short, direct email inviting them to join your Discord, attend your community call, or tackle a "good first issue" that's been sitting unassigned.

In MailClaw's sequence builder, you can configure each step with conditional logic. For example: if email 2 was opened but not clicked, send a follow-up with a different call to action on day 5. This kind of behavioral branching is what separates automated outreach from spam.

The "We Miss You" Re-engagement Sequence (For Lapsed Contributors)

  1. Day 0 — A genuine check-in: Reference their last contribution specifically. Don't be generic. MailClaw's AI email agent can pull the contributor's last PR title or issue number from your contact data and weave it into the email copy automatically.
  2. Day 7 — Share what's changed: Highlight major updates, new features, or architectural decisions that happened since they were last active. Frame it as "we thought you'd find this interesting" — not "please come back."
  3. Day 21 — Last touch: A brief, low-pressure message offering to answer any questions or remove them from future updates. This one almost always gets replies.

Step 3: Configure Your AI Email Agent

This is where MailClaw genuinely earns its keep. Rather than writing static templates that feel robotic, you can configure an AI email agent powered by OpenClaw to generate personalized email copy at send time — pulling from each contact's enriched profile.

Inside the MailClaw dashboard, navigate to Agents → New Agent and configure it with a system prompt like this:

You are a friendly, technical open source maintainer reaching out to a contributor.
Given the contributor's name, their last GitHub contribution, and the project name,
write a warm, concise 3-paragraph email that:
1. Acknowledges their specific contribution authentically
2. Explains why it mattered to the project
3. Invites them to take one clear next step

Tone: collegial, never salesy. Max 150 words. No subject line needed.

The agent runs locally — your contributor data never leaves your machine. This is a significant advantage over cloud-based tools like HubSpot Sequences or Salesforce Pardot, where personalization at this level requires expensive tiers and sends sensitive data to external servers.

Step 4: Connect Your Sending Infrastructure

MailClaw supports SMTP and OAuth integration natively, so you can send through whatever you already use:

  • Gmail or Google Workspace — connect via OAuth in under two minutes from the Settings panel
  • Outlook / Microsoft 365 — supported through OAuth2 with modern authentication
  • SendGrid, Mailgun, or Postmark — paste your API key and set up a custom sending domain for higher deliverability on volume sends

MailClaw's multi-account support means different maintainers on your team can each send from their own address while sharing the same sequence templates and contact database — all coordinated from the local dashboard.

Protecting Your Deliverability

Sending to a list of developers from GitHub is risky if you get it wrong. These are technical people who are quick to mark spam. MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring tools help you stay out of the junk folder:

  • Check your sending domain's SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records directly from the dashboard
  • Monitor open rates, bounce rates, and spam complaint signals per sequence
  • Set automatic send throttles to avoid triggering Gmail or Outlook rate limits
  • Preview emails rendered in dark mode and across common clients before sending

Pro tip: Keep your daily send volume under 100 emails per inbox when warming up a new domain. MailClaw's throttle settings let you ramp up gradually over two weeks — the single most effective thing you can do to protect long-term deliverability.

Step 5: Close the Loop with Tracking and Iteration

The real power of this setup isn't in sending emails — it's in learning from them. After your first sequence completes, review the analytics inside MailClaw's dashboard:

  • Which segment had the highest open rate? (Usually first-time PR authors — they're still excited.)
  • Which email in the sequence drove the most link clicks?
  • Did re-engagement emails for lapsed contributors lead to any new PRs or issue comments?

Feed these learnings back into your AI agent's prompt and your sequence timing. Open source contributor outreach is iterative — the projects that grow the fastest treat their contributor funnel like a product, not an afterthought.

Putting It All Together

Here's a quick summary of the full workflow:

  1. Export contributor data from GitHub using the API
  2. Import and enrich contacts in MailClaw's dashboard (localhost:3100)
  3. Segment contacts by contribution type
  4. Build multi-step sequences with behavioral branching in the sequence builder
  5. Configure an OpenClaw-powered AI email agent for personalized copy generation
  6. Connect Gmail, Outlook, or SendGrid as your sending infrastructure
  7. Monitor deliverability and iterate based on engagement data

Open source projects don't grow because maintainers write better code. They grow because someone decided to treat contributor relationships as something worth investing in. MailClaw gives you the infrastructure to do exactly that — privately, locally, and without a SaaS subscription eating into your project budget.

If you haven't set up MailClaw yet, the installation guide gets you running in about five minutes. Your next contributor is already on GitHub. Go find them.

articles.title: How to Connect MailClaw to Shopify for E-Commerce Email Automation
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw to your Shopify store for fully automated, AI-powered email sequences — from abandoned cart recovery to post-purchase nurture flows — all running locally on your Mac.
articles.content:
Why Shopify + MailClaw Is a Powerful Combination

Most e-commerce store owners are paying $200–$500/month for tools like Klaviyo, Omnisend, or Drip to handle email automation. These are great platforms, but they come with trade-offs: your customer data lives on someone else's servers, pricing scales aggressively with list size, and you're locked into their sequence logic.

MailClaw changes the equation. Because it runs locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, your Shopify customer data — purchase history, abandoned carts, browsing behavior — never leaves your machine. Combine that with OpenClaw-powered AI email agents and a full sequence builder, and you have a genuinely competitive e-commerce automation stack that costs nothing beyond your SMTP bill.

This guide walks you through connecting MailClaw to Shopify, syncing your customer data, and building automated flows for the highest-ROI use cases.

Step 1: Set Up Your Shopify Webhook Integration

MailClaw receives data from Shopify through webhooks — real-time HTTP POST requests that Shopify fires whenever something happens in your store (new order, abandoned checkout, customer creation, etc.).

Create a Shopify Custom App

To get your API credentials, you'll need to create a custom app inside your Shopify admin:

  1. Go to Shopify Admin → Settings → Apps and sales channels → Develop apps
  2. Click Create an app and give it a name like MailClaw Integration
  3. Under Configuration, enable the following API scopes: read_customers, read_orders, read_checkouts
  4. Install the app and copy your Admin API access token

Keep that token handy — you'll paste it into MailClaw in the next step.

Configure MailClaw's Shopify Integration

With MailClaw running, open your local dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to Integrations → E-Commerce → Shopify. You'll see a setup form asking for:

  • Your Shopify store URL (e.g., your-store.myshopify.com)
  • The Admin API access token you just created
  • A webhook secret for request verification

Alternatively, you can configure this directly from the MailClaw CLI:

mailclaw integrations add shopify \
  --store your-store.myshopify.com \
  --token shpat_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx \
  --webhook-secret your_webhook_secret

MailClaw will automatically register the relevant webhooks with Shopify using its built-in tunnel support (powered by ngrok under the hood), so Shopify can reach your local instance during development. For production deployments, you'd point this to your hosted MailClaw instance.

Step 2: Sync and Enrich Your Shopify Contacts

Once the integration is live, MailClaw will begin pulling your existing Shopify customers into its contact database. But raw Shopify data — name, email, order count — only tells part of the story.

Running Contact Enrichment

MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment layer can append firmographic and demographic data to each customer record, pulling from sources like LinkedIn, Clearbit-compatible APIs, and your own historical data. For e-commerce, this is especially useful for B2B stores where you want to know the company size or industry of the person placing orders.

To enrich a segment of your Shopify customers from the CLI:

mailclaw contacts enrich \
  --source shopify \
  --segment "all_customers" \
  --fields company,linkedin,location

You can also trigger enrichment from the dashboard under Contacts → Enrich → Shopify Import. MailClaw will queue the jobs and process them in the background, showing progress in the local dashboard without blocking your other workflows.

Segmenting by Purchase Behavior

After sync, use MailClaw's segment builder to slice your customer list by Shopify-specific properties:

  • Total orders ≥ 3 → VIP customers
  • Last order > 90 days ago → Win-back candidates
  • Checkout created but no order → Abandoned cart targets
  • Product tag contains "subscription" → Renewal sequences

These segments update dynamically as new Shopify events arrive via webhook, so your sequences always target the right people.

Step 3: Build Your First Automated E-Commerce Sequence

Now for the part that actually drives revenue. MailClaw's sequence builder lets you create multi-step email flows triggered by Shopify events. Here are the three highest-value flows to build first.

Abandoned Cart Recovery

Shopify fires the checkouts/create and checkouts/update webhooks when a customer starts but doesn't complete a checkout. MailClaw listens for these and can trigger a sequence automatically.

A simple but effective three-email abandoned cart flow:

  1. Email 1 (1 hour after abandonment): Friendly reminder — "You left something behind." No discount, just the cart contents and a clear CTA.
  2. Email 2 (24 hours later, if no purchase): Address objections — "Questions? We're here." Include social proof or a short FAQ.
  3. Email 3 (72 hours later, if still no purchase): Incentive — offer 10% off with a time-limited code generated dynamically via the Shopify API.

To create this sequence from the CLI:

mailclaw sequences create \
  --name "Abandoned Cart Recovery" \
  --trigger shopify:checkout_abandoned \
  --delay-between-steps "1h,24h,72h"

Then open the sequence in the dashboard to write your email copy or let MailClaw's AI email agent draft it for you (more on that below).

Post-Purchase Nurture Flow

Triggered by orders/paid, this sequence turns one-time buyers into repeat customers. A solid post-purchase flow includes a transactional confirmation (which can still be warm and on-brand), a product tips email 3 days later, a review request at day 10, and a cross-sell recommendation at day 21 based on what they bought.

MailClaw can pull the customer's actual order data into each email using its Shopify merge tags:

Hi {{contact.first_name}},

Your order of {{shopify.order.line_items[0].title}} 
shipped on {{shopify.order.fulfilled_at | date: "%B %d"}}.

Here are a few tips to get the most out of it...

Win-Back Campaign

For customers who haven't purchased in 90+ days, a two or three-email win-back sequence with a personalized subject line based on their last purchase category can recover a meaningful percentage of lapsed buyers. MailClaw's AI email agent can generate subject line variants for A/B testing automatically when you enable the AI Optimize toggle in the sequence builder.

Step 4: Configure Deliverability for E-Commerce Volume

E-commerce email automation can mean high send volumes, especially around sales events. MailClaw's deliverability tools help you stay out of spam folders.

SMTP and OAuth Setup

MailClaw supports multiple sending accounts simultaneously. For e-commerce, a common setup is:

  • Transactional emails (order confirmations, shipping updates) → SendGrid or Postmark via SMTP
  • Marketing sequences (abandoned cart, win-back) → a dedicated Gmail or Outlook account with OAuth, or your own domain via SendGrid

You can configure multiple sender accounts under Settings → Sending Accounts in the MailClaw dashboard and assign specific sequences to specific accounts, keeping your transactional sender reputation separate from your marketing reputation.

Monitor Your Metrics

MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitor tracks open rates, click rates, bounce rates, and spam complaints per sequence and per sending account — all visible from the local dashboard without sending data to a third party. If a sequence starts generating unusual bounce rates after a Shopify import, you'll see it flagged in real time.

Pro tip: Run a deliverability health check before your first large Shopify campaign send using mailclaw deliverability check --account your@domain.com. It will verify your SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records and surface any issues before they affect your sender score.

Step 5: Use AI Email Agents for Dynamic Personalization

This is where MailClaw goes beyond what traditional e-commerce ESPs offer. Because MailClaw is powered by OpenClaw, you can deploy AI email agents that don't just send static sequences — they adapt content based on real-time Shopify data.

For example, you can configure an AI agent that watches for high-value orders above a certain threshold and automatically drafts a personalized thank-you email for your review before sending. Or set up an agent that monitors your win-back segment and suggests revised subject lines when open rates drop below a defined threshold.

To create a simple AI agent that monitors Shopify order events:

mailclaw agents create \
  --name "VIP Order Concierge" \
  --trigger shopify:order_paid \
  --condition "order.total_price > 500" \
  --action draft_and_review \
  --model openai/gpt-4o

The agent will draft an email and surface it in your dashboard's AI Agent Inbox for one-click approval — you stay in control, but the heavy lifting is automated.

Putting It All Together

The Shopify + MailClaw integration isn't a single feature — it's a full local automation stack. You're syncing real-time customer data, enriching contacts, segmenting dynamically, running multi-step sequences through battle-tested SMTP infrastructure, and letting AI agents handle the edge cases that static tools can't anticipate.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your machine, you can extend any part of this stack — write custom webhook handlers, build new trigger types, or modify the sequence logic — without waiting on a vendor roadmap. That's the fundamental advantage of building on open infrastructure.

Start with the abandoned cart sequence. It's the fastest path to measurable ROI, and once you see how cleanly MailClaw handles the Shopify event data, the rest of the flows will come naturally.

articles.title: Using MailClaw with Twilio for SMS + Email Coordinated Outreach
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to combine MailClaw's AI-powered email automation with Twilio's SMS API to build coordinated, multi-channel outreach sequences that dramatically improve response rates and keep prospects engaged across every touchpoint.
articles.content:
Why Multi-Channel Outreach Beats Email Alone

Email is powerful. But even the best-crafted sequence, running through MailClaw's sequence builder with perfectly timed follow-ups, will hit a ceiling on its own. The average professional receives over 120 emails a day. SMS, by contrast, has an open rate above 90% — and most messages are read within three minutes of delivery.

Coordinating SMS and email isn't about bombarding people. It's about meeting prospects where they are, reinforcing your message across channels, and creating natural touchpoints that feel considered rather than automated. When you pair MailClaw's AI email agents with Twilio's programmable SMS, you get a genuinely powerful outreach engine that runs entirely from your local machine.

What You'll Need Before You Start

This guide assumes you have MailClaw running locally at localhost:3100 via its OpenClaw-powered dashboard. If you haven't set it up yet, clone the repo and run:

openclaw start --app mailclaw --port 3100

You'll also need:

  • A Twilio account with a verified phone number and API credentials (Account SID + Auth Token)
  • At least one connected email account in MailClaw (Gmail via OAuth or any SMTP provider like SendGrid or Outlook)
  • Contacts imported into MailClaw with phone numbers — either uploaded via CSV or enriched using MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment
  • Node.js 18+ installed locally for the webhook bridge we'll configure

Step 1: Enrich Your Contacts with Phone Numbers

Before you can send coordinated SMS + email, you need phone numbers alongside your email addresses. MailClaw's contact enrichment feature handles this automatically for many records. From the dashboard at localhost:3100/contacts, select your contact list and click Enrich Contacts.

MailClaw will attempt to fill in missing fields — company name, LinkedIn URL, job title, and phone numbers — using its AI enrichment pipeline. For contacts it can't enrich automatically, you can bulk-import a supplementary CSV or manually add phone numbers inline.

Once enrichment runs, filter your list to contacts with verified phone numbers before building your sequence. You can do this from the CLI as well:

mailclaw contacts filter --has-field phone --export enriched-contacts.csv

Step 2: Configure the Twilio Integration

MailClaw doesn't ship with a native Twilio connector out of the box — but because it's open source and built on OpenClaw, adding one is straightforward. Create a small webhook service that MailClaw can call as a custom action step inside your sequences.

Set Up Your Twilio Webhook Bridge

Create a new file called twilio-bridge.js in your MailClaw extensions folder:

// extensions/twilio-bridge.js
const express = require('express');
const twilio = require('twilio');

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

const client = twilio(
  process.env.TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID,
  process.env.TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN
);

app.post('/send-sms', async (req, res) => {
  const { to, body, from } = req.body;

  try {
    const message = await client.messages.create({
      body,
      from: from || process.env.TWILIO_PHONE_NUMBER,
      to,
    });

    res.json({ success: true, sid: message.sid });
  } catch (err) {
    res.status(500).json({ success: false, error: err.message });
  }
});

app.listen(3101, () => {
  console.log('Twilio bridge running on localhost:3101');
});

Install dependencies and start the bridge alongside MailClaw:

npm install express twilio
TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID=ACxxxx TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN=your_token TWILIO_PHONE_NUMBER=+15550001234 node extensions/twilio-bridge.js

Now MailClaw can POST to localhost:3101/send-sms as a webhook step inside any sequence.

Step 3: Build Your Coordinated Sequence

Head to localhost:3100/sequences and create a new sequence. This is where MailClaw's sequence builder earns its keep. You'll lay out the full timeline of touchpoints — emails and SMS — and define the logic that governs when each fires.

A Proven 7-Day Sequence Structure

Here's a coordinated sequence structure that works well for cold outreach or trial onboarding:

  1. Day 1 — Email (Introduction): Send a personalized cold email using MailClaw's AI email agent. Keep it short, relevant, and focused on one value proposition.
  2. Day 2 — SMS (Soft nudge): Fire a brief SMS via your Twilio bridge: "Hey [First Name], just sent you an email about [topic] — worth a 2-min read when you get a sec."
  3. Day 4 — Email (Follow-up with value): A follow-up email with a relevant case study, article, or specific insight. Let MailClaw's AI agent personalize this based on the contact's company or role.
  4. Day 6 — SMS (Direct CTA): A more direct SMS: "Happy to jump on a quick call this week, [First Name]. Reply here or grab a time: [calendar link]."
  5. Day 7 — Email (Final touch): A short "closing the loop" email. Honest, low-pressure, and leaving the door open.

In MailClaw's sequence builder, add a Webhook Step between your email steps and configure it to POST to localhost:3101/send-sms with a JSON body like this:

{
  "to": "{{contact.phone}}",
  "body": "Hey {{contact.first_name}}, just sent you an email about {{sequence.topic}} — worth a quick look when you're free."
}

MailClaw's templating engine handles variable substitution automatically, pulling values from your enriched contact records.

Step 4: Use AI Agents to Personalize at Scale

One of MailClaw's standout features is its AI email agents — persistent, context-aware agents that can draft, refine, and adapt email content based on contact data, past interactions, and sequence position. For a coordinated SMS + email workflow, you can push this further.

Configure your AI agent to adjust the SMS copy based on whether a contact opened a previous email. In MailClaw's agent settings, enable conditional logic and set rules like:

  • If email_1.opened == true → use a warmer SMS tone referencing the email
  • If email_1.opened == false → send a more context-setting SMS that stands alone
  • If email_1.clicked == true → skip the Day 2 SMS entirely (they're already engaged)

This kind of adaptive logic is the difference between outreach that feels human and outreach that feels like a mail merge.

Step 5: Monitor Deliverability and Compliance

Coordinated outreach raises the stakes on deliverability. If your emails are landing in spam, your SMS nudges lose their context entirely. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools — accessible from localhost:3100/deliverability — give you real-time visibility into bounce rates, spam complaints, and domain health across all your connected accounts.

A quick note on SMS compliance: Twilio requires explicit consent for SMS marketing in most jurisdictions. Make sure your contacts have opted in to receive texts, and always honor opt-out requests immediately. MailClaw lets you tag contacts with consent status; filter your sequence enrollment to only include sms_consent: true records.

For email-side health, connect your SendGrid or Gmail account through MailClaw's multi-account support and let it rotate sending across accounts if you're running high-volume sequences. This protects your domain reputation and keeps open rates clean.

Measuring What's Working

The MailClaw dashboard surfaces per-step analytics for every sequence. For your Twilio webhook steps, you'll see delivery confirmations logged back into the sequence timeline. Cross-reference these with email open and click data to identify which touchpoint combinations drive the highest reply rates.

Common patterns to watch for:

  • SMS-before-email: Some audiences respond better when SMS comes first as a heads-up. Test both orderings.
  • Time-of-day alignment: Schedule SMS steps to fire during business hours in the contact's timezone — MailClaw's scheduler supports timezone-aware delivery.
  • Reply handling: Twilio can forward SMS replies to a webhook so you can log them back into MailClaw's contact timeline, keeping your outreach history unified.

The Bigger Picture

Email automation is table stakes. The teams winning at outreach right now are the ones treating every channel as part of a coherent, intelligent system — not isolated blasts. By running MailClaw locally with full control over your data, extending it with Twilio for SMS, and letting AI agents adapt messaging based on real engagement signals, you're building something most outreach tools can't offer: genuine responsiveness at scale.

The fact that MailClaw is open source means this integration is yours to extend. Add a Slack notification when someone replies via SMS. Pull enrichment data from HubSpot or Salesforce to pre-populate sequence variables. Build a reply-detection agent that pauses the sequence the moment a prospect responds on any channel. The architecture supports it — and your local dashboard at localhost:3100 is the control center for all of it.

articles.title: How to Integrate MailClaw with Clearbit for Real-Time Enrichment
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw with Clearbit to automatically enrich contacts with firmographic and demographic data the moment they enter your sequences, so your AI email agents can personalize outreach at scale without any manual research.
articles.content:
Why Real-Time Enrichment Changes the Outreach Game

Cold outreach fails for one predictable reason: generic messaging. When someone receives an email that could have been sent to anyone, they treat it like it was sent to no one. The fix isn't writing better copy — it's knowing more about your prospect before you write a single word.

Clearbit is one of the most reliable enrichment APIs available. It takes a raw email address and returns company size, industry, funding stage, tech stack, LinkedIn URL, job seniority, and dozens of other data points. When you pipe that directly into MailClaw's contact enrichment layer and let your AI email agents use it to personalize sequences, the result is outreach that feels researched and human — because the data behind it actually is.

This guide walks you through the full integration: setting up your Clearbit API key, configuring MailClaw's enrichment pipeline, mapping fields to your sequence builder, and validating everything from your localhost dashboard at localhost:3100.

Prerequisites

  • MailClaw installed and running locally (openclaw start or mailclaw dev)
  • A Clearbit API key (free tier covers up to 100 enrichments/month; paid plans scale from there)
  • At least one connected sending account — Gmail via OAuth, Outlook, or an SMTP provider like SendGrid works fine
  • Node.js 18+ if you plan to extend the enrichment config with custom scripts

Step 1 — Add Your Clearbit API Key to MailClaw

MailClaw stores third-party API credentials in a local .env file that never leaves your machine. This is one of the core advantages of running on OpenClaw: your enrichment data and API keys aren't sitting on a vendor's cloud server.

Open your MailClaw project root and add the following to your .env file:

# Clearbit enrichment
CLEARBIT_API_KEY=sk_your_clearbit_key_here

# Optional: control enrichment behavior
ENRICHMENT_PROVIDER=clearbit
ENRICHMENT_AUTO_RUN=true
ENRICHMENT_CACHE_TTL=86400

Setting ENRICHMENT_AUTO_RUN=true tells MailClaw to trigger an enrichment lookup automatically whenever a new contact enters any active sequence. The ENRICHMENT_CACHE_TTL value (in seconds) prevents redundant API calls for contacts you've already enriched — 86400 means results are cached for 24 hours.

Restart your local server to apply the changes:

mailclaw restart

Head to localhost:3100/settings/integrations in your browser. You should see Clearbit listed under Enrichment Providers with a green connected indicator.

Step 2 — Configure Field Mapping

Clearbit returns a rich JSON payload. MailClaw needs to know which fields to store and which contact properties to map them to. You configure this in mailclaw.config.js under the enrichment key.

// mailclaw.config.js
module.exports = {
  enrichment: {
    provider: 'clearbit',
    fieldMap: {
      'person.name.fullName': 'contact.fullName',
      'person.title': 'contact.jobTitle',
      'person.linkedin.handle': 'contact.linkedinUrl',
      'person.employment.seniority': 'contact.seniority',
      'company.name': 'contact.companyName',
      'company.domain': 'contact.companyDomain',
      'company.metrics.employees': 'contact.companySize',
      'company.category.industry': 'contact.industry',
      'company.tech': 'contact.techStack',
      'company.location.country': 'contact.country',
      'company.tags': 'contact.companyTags',
    },
    fallbackOnNull: true,
  },
};

The fallbackOnNull: true setting ensures that if Clearbit can't find a value — say, the company size is unknown — MailClaw won't overwrite an existing value you may have imported from HubSpot, Salesforce, or a CSV. This protects data you already have while filling in the gaps.

Storing Tech Stack Data

The company.tech field from Clearbit returns an array. MailClaw stores it as a comma-separated string in the techStack contact property, which your AI email agents can reference directly in prompt templates. If you need it as a filterable tag array instead, set:

enrichment: {
  fieldMap: {
    'company.tech': { target: 'contact.techStack', type: 'tag-array' }
  }
}

Step 3 — Use Enriched Data in Your Sequence Builder

Once fields are mapped, they become available as variables inside the sequence builder at localhost:3100/sequences. MailClaw uses double-brace syntax for merge variables, and enriched fields show up in the variable picker automatically after the first enrichment run.

A simple first-touch email using enriched data might look like this:

Subject: Quick question about {{contact.companyName}}'s {{contact.industry}} stack

Hi {{contact.firstName}},

I noticed {{contact.companyName}} is using {{contact.techStack}} — 
we've helped a few other {{contact.industry}} teams at the 
{{contact.companySize}}-employee stage get more out of that setup.

Worth a 15-minute call this week?

That's a far cry from "Hi [First Name], I wanted to reach out…" — and it took zero manual research to produce.

Conditional Blocks Based on Enriched Fields

The sequence builder supports conditional logic. You can show different copy depending on company size, seniority, or any other enriched field:

{{#if contact.seniority == 'executive'}}
  As someone leading the team at {{contact.companyName}}, you're likely 
  thinking about this from a strategic angle...
{{else}}
  As someone hands-on with the stack at {{contact.companyName}}, you'll 
  appreciate that setup takes under an hour...
{{/if}}

This kind of branching is what separates a sequence from a mail merge. Combined with MailClaw's AI email agents, you can go even further — letting the agent draft the entire email body using the enriched contact record as context, with your tone and angle defined in the agent's system prompt.

Step 4 — Trigger Enrichment Manually or via Webhook

Beyond auto-enrichment on sequence entry, you can trigger enrichment manually from the CLI or set up a webhook to enrich contacts pushed from external tools like HubSpot or Salesforce.

Manual enrichment from the CLI:

# Enrich a single contact by email
mailclaw enrich --email jane@acmecorp.com

# Enrich all unenriched contacts in a list
mailclaw enrich --list enterprise-q3 --unenriched-only

# Dry run to preview what would be fetched
mailclaw enrich --list enterprise-q3 --dry-run

Webhook-based enrichment is useful if your CRM pushes new leads automatically. MailClaw exposes a local webhook endpoint you can tunnel with ngrok or Cloudflare Tunnel during development:

POST http://localhost:3100/api/webhooks/enrich
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "email": "jane@acmecorp.com",
  "listId": "enterprise-q3",
  "triggerSequence": "cold-outreach-v2"
}

This single payload will enrich the contact via Clearbit, add them to the specified list, and enroll them in a sequence — all in one round trip.

Step 5 — Monitor Enrichment Health from the Dashboard

The MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100/enrichment gives you a live view of your enrichment pipeline. You can see enrichment rate by list, which contacts returned null results, how many API credits you've consumed, and whether the Clearbit connection is healthy.

Pay attention to the match rate metric. A match rate below 60% usually means your contact list skews toward personal email addresses (Gmail, Yahoo) rather than professional ones — Clearbit enrichment works best on business domains. If this is an issue, consider pairing Clearbit with a secondary enrichment provider like Apollo or Hunter in a fallback chain:

enrichment: {
  providers: ['clearbit', 'apollo'],
  strategy: 'fallback', // try clearbit first, apollo if no result
}

Deliverability Note: Don't Over-Personalize at Scale

A word of caution that often gets skipped in enrichment tutorials: using highly specific data in every email can trigger spam filters if your sending volume spikes suddenly. MailClaw's deliverability tools include a Spam Score Analyzer and a Sending Warmup module — use them before launching enriched sequences at scale.

Best practice: Warm up new sending accounts for 2–3 weeks using MailClaw's built-in warmup sequences before sending enriched cold outreach. Monitor your open rates and bounce rates from the deliverability dashboard and throttle send volume if you see early warning signs.

Enrichment improves relevance, but relevance only helps if your emails land in the inbox. The two capabilities work best together.

What to Do With Contacts Clearbit Can't Enrich

No enrichment provider has 100% coverage. For contacts that return empty results, MailClaw lets you route them to a separate list or trigger a different sequence — one that asks the recipient to share more about themselves rather than assuming you already know.

enrichment:
  onNullResult:
    action: 'move-to-list'
    listId: 'needs-manual-review'
    # or: trigger a "lightweight" sequence that asks qualifying questions

This keeps your main enriched sequence clean and high-quality while giving unenriched contacts a different, still-thoughtful experience.

Putting It All Together

The Clearbit integration in MailClaw isn't just a data-fetching feature — it's the foundation for running AI-powered outreach that actually feels personal. When your AI email agents have job titles, company size, industry, and tech stack to work with, the output quality improves dramatically. Your sequence builder becomes smarter. Your reply rates go up. And because everything runs locally through OpenClaw, you stay in control of the data the entire time.

Start with a small list, validate your field mappings in the dashboard, check your match rate, and scale from there. Once you've seen an enriched sequence perform against a generic one, you won't go back.

articles.title: MailClaw + Mixpanel: Triggering Emails Based on Product Analytics
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to connect Mixpanel product analytics to MailClaw's AI-powered email automation so you can trigger hyper-personalized outreach based on real user behavior — from feature adoption signals to churn risk events.
articles.content:
Why Behavior-Triggered Email Beats Scheduled Drip Sequences

Most email sequences are built around time. You sign up, you get an email on day one, another on day three, and a "last chance" nudge on day seven. It's predictable, it scales, and it mostly works — until your users stop behaving predictably, which is always.

Mixpanel tells a different story. It shows you exactly what a user did inside your product — what features they touched, where they dropped off, which events preceded a conversion. That data is gold. The problem is that most teams let it sit inside Mixpanel dashboards while their email tool keeps firing generic sequences on a timer.

MailClaw changes that. Because it runs locally on your Mac at localhost:3100 and exposes a clean API built on OpenClaw, you can pipe Mixpanel behavioral data directly into email sequences, AI agents, and contact enrichment workflows — without routing sensitive user data through a third-party SaaS platform.

The Architecture: How Mixpanel and MailClaw Talk to Each Other

There are two primary integration patterns depending on how real-time you need things to be.

Pattern 1: Mixpanel Webhooks → MailClaw API

Mixpanel's Cohort Sync and Warehouse Connectors can push data out, but the fastest path for event-triggered emails is using Mixpanel's Webhooks via Automations (available on Growth and Enterprise plans). When a user hits a defined event — say, feature_activated or trial_day_7_no_upgrade — Mixpanel fires a webhook payload to an endpoint you control.

MailClaw listens on localhost:3100, so for production use you'll want a lightweight tunnel or a small webhook receiver running on your server. Here's a minimal Node.js receiver that forwards Mixpanel events into MailClaw's sequence enrollment API:

// webhook-receiver.js
const express = require('express');
const axios = require('axios');
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

app.post('/mixpanel-hook', async (req, res) => {
  const { event, properties } = req.body;
  const email = properties.$email;
  const distinctId = properties.distinct_id;

  if (!email) return res.status(400).send('No email found');

  // Map Mixpanel event names to MailClaw sequence IDs
  const sequenceMap = {
    'feature_activated': 'seq_onboarding_power_user',
    'trial_day_7_no_upgrade': 'seq_trial_conversion_nudge',
    'invoice_overdue': 'seq_billing_recovery',
    'churned': 'seq_winback_30day'
  };

  const sequenceId = sequenceMap[event];
  if (!sequenceId) return res.status(200).send('Event not mapped');

  await axios.post('http://localhost:3100/api/sequences/enroll', {
    sequenceId,
    contact: {
      email,
      distinctId,
      source: 'mixpanel',
      eventProperties: properties
    }
  });

  res.status(200).send('Enrolled');
});

app.listen(4000, () => console.log('Receiver running on :4000'));

Once enrolled, MailClaw's sequence builder takes over — handling send timing, multi-account routing, deliverability checks, and AI-personalized copy generation.

Pattern 2: Scheduled Cohort Export → Contact Enrichment

For teams that want a batch approach — think daily churn-risk digests or weekly re-engagement sweeps — you can export Mixpanel cohorts as CSVs and feed them into MailClaw's contact enrichment pipeline via the CLI:

# Export a cohort from Mixpanel via their Data Export API
curl -u "YOUR_SERVICE_ACCOUNT:YOUR_SECRET" \
  "https://data.mixpanel.com/api/2.0/export/cohorts?cohort_id=12345" \
  -o at-risk-users.json

# Import and enrich with MailClaw
mailclaw contacts import --file at-risk-users.json \
  --enrich \
  --tag "mixpanel-at-risk" \
  --sequence seq_churn_intervention

The --enrich flag triggers MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment, which augments the Mixpanel data with company info, LinkedIn signals, and firmographic context — giving your AI email agents much richer material to work with when generating personalized outreach.

Building the Sequence in MailClaw's Dashboard

Open your local dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to Sequences → New Sequence. Here's how to structure a trial conversion sequence that responds to Mixpanel signals:

Step 1: Define Enrollment Triggers

Set the enrollment source to API / Webhook and reference the sequence ID you mapped in your receiver script (seq_trial_conversion_nudge). You can also set de-duplication rules here — so if a user converts before the sequence ends, MailClaw automatically unenrolls them.

Step 2: Use Event Properties in Email Copy

This is where it gets powerful. MailClaw's sequence builder supports dynamic variables pulled from the enrollment payload. Since you're passing eventProperties from Mixpanel, you can reference things like the specific feature they used or the number of actions they've taken:

Subject: You're {{eventProperties.feature_count}} steps away from unlocking {{eventProperties.last_feature_used}}

Hi {{contact.firstName}},

We noticed you've been exploring {{eventProperties.last_feature_used}} — 
that's one of the features our power users rely on most.

You're currently on a trial that ends in {{eventProperties.trial_days_remaining}} days.
Here's what you'd lose access to...
