When you hand this template to MailClaw's AI email agent, it rewrites the copy to feel natural rather than mail-merged. The agent is aware of context from contact enrichment, so it can reference a user's industry, company size, or role without you explicitly templating every variation.

Step 3: Configure Multi-Account Sending

MailClaw supports multiple sending accounts — Gmail via OAuth, Outlook, SendGrid SMTP, or custom SMTP. For behavior-triggered sequences, it's worth routing different event types through different accounts. Billing recovery emails, for example, often perform better from a human sender address (like your CEO's Gmail) than from a marketing domain. MailClaw's deliverability tools flag domain reputation issues before sends go out, so you're not flying blind.

Practical Segment-to-Sequence Mapping

Here are five high-value Mixpanel event patterns and the MailClaw sequences worth building around them:

  • Power user activation signal — User triggers 3+ core features within 48 hours. Enroll in an expansion sequence that introduces team/seat upgrades or advanced workflows.
  • Feature abandonment — User starts an onboarding flow but doesn't complete a key step within 72 hours. Trigger a short troubleshooting sequence with an AI-personalized email that names the exact step they stopped at.
  • Champion job change — When combined with contact enrichment (LinkedIn signals), you can detect when a power user leaves a company and trigger a win-new-account sequence targeting their new employer.
  • Pricing page visited 3+ times without conversion — Classic high-intent signal. Route into a direct sales sequence with a calendar link. Using HubSpot or Salesforce? MailClaw can sync the enrollment event as a CRM activity via its native integrations.
  • 90-day dormancy — Build a sunset/reactivation sequence with a Mixpanel cohort export of users who haven't triggered any event in 90 days. The AI agent can reference what they last did in the product to make re-engagement feel relevant.

Deliverability Considerations for Event-Triggered Volume

Behavior-triggered emails can spike in volume unexpectedly — a product launch or viral moment can suddenly enroll thousands of contacts in the same sequence within hours. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring catches this before it damages your sender reputation.

A good rule of thumb: cap hourly send volume per domain at 200–300 emails during ramp-up, even for warm domains. MailClaw lets you set per-sequence send caps directly in the dashboard under Settings → Deliverability → Send Rate Limits.

You should also make sure your Mixpanel-sourced contacts have verified, reachable addresses before enrolling them. MailClaw's contact enrichment step includes basic validation, but for large imports, run the CSV through enrichment first and filter on confidence score before triggering sequences.

Keeping It Local, Keeping It Private

One underappreciated advantage of running MailClaw on localhost is that your Mixpanel event data — which often contains sensitive behavioral signals about your users — never has to leave your infrastructure to power personalized email. You're not syncing user behavior into a third-party email platform, agreeing to new data processing agreements, or wondering how that data is being used downstream.

Because MailClaw is open source and built on OpenClaw, you can audit exactly how event data flows through the system, modify the enrichment pipeline to fit your compliance requirements, and deploy to an internal server when you're ready to scale beyond a single Mac.

The result is a behavior-triggered email system that's genuinely responsive to what your users are doing — not just what day of the week it is.

articles.title: How to Connect MailClaw to Close CRM for Sales Automation
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw to Close CRM for seamless sales automation — syncing contacts, triggering email sequences, and using AI agents to close more deals without leaving your local environment.
articles.content:
Why Connect MailClaw with Close CRM?

If you're running outbound sales through Close CRM, you already know how powerful its pipeline and calling features are. But email sequences inside Close can feel limited — especially when you want AI-assisted personalization, granular deliverability controls, or the ability to run multi-account outreach without paying per seat. That's exactly the gap MailClaw fills.

MailClaw runs locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, powered by OpenClaw, giving you a private, flexible email automation layer that sits alongside your CRM rather than replacing it. Instead of forcing you to choose between your CRM's contact data and a third-party email tool's feature set, you bridge them — Close owns the pipeline, MailClaw owns the sequences.

The result: leads enter Close, flow into MailClaw for AI-crafted outreach, and activity syncs back so your sales reps always have context before a call.

What You'll Need Before You Start

  • MailClaw installed and running (mailclaw start — confirm the dashboard is live at localhost:3100)
  • A Close CRM account with API access enabled
  • Your Close API key (found under Settings → API Keys in Close)
  • At least one SMTP or OAuth-connected sending account in MailClaw (Gmail, Outlook, or a sending service like SendGrid or Postmark)
  • Node.js 18+ if you plan to use the MailClaw CLI scripts

Step 1 — Generate Your Close CRM API Key

Head to your Close CRM dashboard, click your avatar in the top-right corner, then navigate to Settings → Your API Keys. Click Generate API Key, give it a descriptive name like MailClaw Integration, and copy the key immediately — Close won't show it again.

Store it securely. You'll add it to MailClaw's environment configuration in the next step.

Step 2 — Add Close as a Data Source in MailClaw

MailClaw supports external CRM sources through its integration config. Open your MailClaw config file — typically located at ~/.mailclaw/config.json — and add a sources block:

{
  "sources": [
    {
      "name": "close_crm",
      "type": "close",
      "apiKey": "your_close_api_key_here",
      "syncFields": ["email", "name", "title", "company", "lead_status"],
      "syncInterval": "15m"
    }
  ]
}

Then restart MailClaw to pick up the change:

mailclaw restart

Once running, navigate to localhost:3100 → Contacts → Sources and you should see close_crm listed as an active source. MailClaw will begin pulling contacts and leads on the interval you've set.

Mapping Close Lead Fields to MailClaw Contacts

Close uses a Lead → Contact hierarchy — a lead can have multiple contacts. MailClaw flattens this into its own contact model and maps fields automatically for common attributes. For custom Close fields, you can define explicit mappings in the config:

{
  "fieldMappings": {
    "custom.cf_industry": "industry",
    "custom.cf_company_size": "company_size"
  }
}

These mapped fields become available inside MailClaw's sequence builder and AI personalization tokens, so you can reference {{industry}} or {{company_size}} directly in your email templates.

Step 3 — Enrich Contacts Before Outreach

One of MailClaw's most underrated features is its contact enrichment engine. Before you fire off a sequence, let MailClaw fill in the gaps that Close doesn't have — job title confirmation, LinkedIn headline, tech stack, or company funding stage.

From the CLI, you can trigger enrichment on a segment of your Close contacts:

mailclaw enrich --source close_crm --filter "lead_status=potential" --provider clearbit

Or kick it off from the dashboard under Contacts → Enrich. Enrichment runs locally through OpenClaw's provider abstraction layer, so your data never leaves your machine unless you've explicitly configured a third-party enrichment API.

Pro tip: Run enrichment before building your sequence. The more data MailClaw has per contact, the better the AI email agent can personalize the first-touch email without manual editing.

Step 4 — Build Your Sales Sequence

With contacts synced and enriched, open the Sequence Builder at localhost:3100 → Sequences → New. MailClaw's sequence builder lets you chain emails, set delays, define conditional branches (e.g., "if opened but didn't reply, send follow-up B"), and assign sending accounts per step.

A typical Close CRM outbound sequence in MailClaw might look like this:

  1. Day 0 — First touch: AI-personalized cold email referencing the contact's role and company
  2. Day 3 — Follow-up 1: Short, conversational bump with a specific value hook
  3. Day 7 — Follow-up 2: Social proof or case study angle
  4. Day 12 — Break-up email: Low-pressure final touch that often gets the highest reply rate

Using AI Email Agents for First-Touch Personalization

In the sequence builder, click AI Compose on any step to invoke MailClaw's AI email agent. The agent pulls enriched contact data and your configured value proposition, then drafts a personalized email you can approve, edit, or regenerate. For a 200-contact sequence, this saves hours of manual writing.

You can also give the AI agent a persona and tone brief in your sequence settings:

mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "Q3 SaaS Outbound" \
  --source close_crm \
  --filter "industry=saas,lead_status=potential" \
  --ai-persona "friendly, direct, no buzzwords" \
  --steps 4

Step 5 — Write Activity Back to Close CRM

Syncing contact data into MailClaw is only half the equation. You want email activity — opens, replies, bounces — written back to Close so your sales reps have full context before picking up the phone.

Enable the Close activity webhook in your MailClaw config:

{
  "webhooks": {
    "close_crm": {
      "events": ["email.sent", "email.opened", "email.replied", "email.bounced"],
      "createActivity": true,
      "updateLeadStatus": {
        "email.replied": "responded"
      }
    }
  }
}

With updateLeadStatus configured, Close will automatically move a lead to Responded the moment a reply is detected by MailClaw — no manual CRM updates needed. Your reps see a warm lead queue without any administrative work.

Pausing Sequences When a Lead is Won or Lost

You don't want MailClaw emailing a contact you've already closed or disqualified. Set up a Close status listener to automatically pause or stop sequences:

mailclaw listen close_crm \
  --on "lead_status=won,lost,bad_fit" \
  --action "pause_sequence"

This listener polls Close on your sync interval and halts any active sequence steps for affected contacts, preventing awkward emails to people who just signed your contract.

Step 6 — Monitor Deliverability from the MailClaw Dashboard

High-volume outbound lives and dies by deliverability. MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring tools track your sending reputation per account, flag spammy subject line patterns, and alert you when bounce rates creep above healthy thresholds.

Navigate to localhost:3100 → Deliverability to see:

  • Per-domain open and bounce rates for your Close-sourced sequences
  • SPF, DKIM, and DMARC validation status for each sending identity
  • Spam score previews powered by OpenClaw's content analysis
  • Sending volume recommendations based on account warmup status

If you're sending through multiple accounts — say, a Gmail for SMB outreach and a SendGrid domain for enterprise — MailClaw's multi-account support lets you route sequence steps to the right sender based on rules you define, keeping each account's volume in check.

Keeping the Integration Healthy Over Time

A few operational habits will keep your Close–MailClaw pipeline running smoothly:

  • Review sync logs weekly — run mailclaw logs --source close_crm to catch any field mapping errors or API rate limit warnings early.
  • Rotate your Close API key quarterly — update it in ~/.mailclaw/config.json and run mailclaw restart.
  • Audit unsubscribes — MailClaw maintains a local suppression list, but you should periodically cross-reference it with Close to keep both systems clean.
  • Use sequence analytics to improve templates — the sequence builder shows reply rates per step; A/B test subject lines and let the data drive your next campaign.

What You've Built

By connecting MailClaw to Close CRM, you've created a sales automation loop that's genuinely powerful: Close manages pipeline and calling, MailClaw handles intelligent email outreach, and both systems stay in sync automatically. Your reps focus on conversations, not admin work.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your local machine, you control the data, the cadence, and the cost — no per-seat pricing for email features, no third-party servers holding your contact list. It's the kind of setup that used to require a dedicated RevOps engineer to wire together, now available in a single mailclaw start.

articles.title: Using MailClaw with n8n for Advanced Workflow Orchestration
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw with n8n to build powerful, event-driven email workflows that go far beyond basic sequences — from CRM-triggered outreach to AI-enriched contact pipelines running entirely on your local machine.
articles.content:
Why MailClaw and n8n Belong Together

MailClaw is already a capable standalone tool. You can spin up the local dashboard at localhost:3100, build a multi-step sequence, enrich a contact list, and launch an outreach campaign without touching a single third-party SaaS platform. That self-contained power is exactly what makes it compelling for privacy-conscious teams and indie operators alike.

But the real magic happens when you connect MailClaw to a workflow orchestration layer. n8n — the open-source, self-hostable automation platform — is the perfect complement. Where MailClaw owns the email execution layer, n8n owns the orchestration layer: reacting to events, transforming data, routing logic, and gluing together every other tool in your stack. Together, they form a local-first automation backbone that rivals anything you'd build on Zapier or Make, without the per-task pricing or data leaving your machine.

This guide walks through practical integration patterns, real workflow examples, and the specific MailClaw endpoints and CLI hooks you'll use to wire everything together.

Setting Up the Connection

Prerequisites

  • MailClaw running locally (mailclaw start — dashboard available at localhost:3100)
  • n8n running locally or on a private server (npx n8n or Docker)
  • An API key generated from the MailClaw dashboard under Settings → API Access

Authenticating n8n with MailClaw

MailClaw exposes a REST API that n8n can talk to via the HTTP Request node. Start by creating a credential in n8n:

  1. In n8n, go to Credentials → New → Header Auth
  2. Set the header name to X-MailClaw-Key
  3. Paste your MailClaw API key as the value
  4. Name it something like MailClaw Local and save

Every HTTP Request node targeting MailClaw will use this credential. Your base URL will always be http://localhost:3100/api/v1 — no external calls, no latency surprises.

# Quick test from your terminal to confirm the API is live
curl -H "X-MailClaw-Key: your_api_key" \
  http://localhost:3100/api/v1/contacts?limit=5

Practical Workflow Patterns

Pattern 1: CRM-Triggered Sequence Enrollment

This is the most common integration request: a deal moves to a new stage in your CRM, and you want the contact automatically enrolled in a MailClaw sequence. Here's how to build it with HubSpot and n8n.

  1. Add a HubSpot Trigger node in n8n, listening for Deal Stage Updated events
  2. Add an IF node to filter for your target stage (e.g., stage === "proposal_sent")
  3. Add an HTTP Request node pointing to POST /api/v1/contacts to upsert the contact into MailClaw
  4. Add a second HTTP Request node to enroll them: POST /api/v1/sequences/{sequence_id}/enroll
// Enrollment payload for the HTTP Request node body
{
  "contact_email": "{{ $json.properties.email }}",
  "contact_name": "{{ $json.properties.firstname }} {{ $json.properties.lastname }}",
  "variables": {
    "company": "{{ $json.properties.company }}",
    "deal_name": "{{ $json.dealName }}"
  }
}

MailClaw's sequence builder picks up the custom variables object and injects them into your AI-crafted email templates automatically. The contact gets a personalized sequence, and you never touched it manually.

Pattern 2: AI Contact Enrichment Before Outreach

MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment is powerful, but sometimes you want enrichment to happen upstream — triggered by a form submission, a CSV import event, or a new row in Airtable. n8n lets you build that pipeline cleanly.

  1. Trigger: Airtable node watching for new rows in your leads table
  2. Enrich: HTTP Request to POST /api/v1/contacts/enrich with the email address
  3. Wait: n8n's Wait node pauses until enrichment completes (poll GET /api/v1/contacts/{id} using a loop)
  4. Score & Route: Use an IF or Switch node to route high-fit contacts to a priority sequence vs. a nurture track

Pro tip: MailClaw's enrichment layer, powered by OpenClaw, returns company size, industry, LinkedIn signals, and tech stack data. Use n8n's Set node to map these enriched fields back to your CRM before enrollment so your Salesforce or HubSpot records stay in sync without any manual data entry.

Pattern 3: Deliverability Alerts and Slack Notifications

MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tracks bounce rates, spam complaints, and sending reputation in real time. By polling the API from n8n, you can build alert workflows that notify your team the moment something goes sideways.

# MailClaw deliverability stats endpoint
GET /api/v1/campaigns/{campaign_id}/deliverability

# Sample response fields you'll want to watch
{
  "bounce_rate": 0.03,
  "spam_complaint_rate": 0.001,
  "open_rate": 0.41,
  "reputation_score": 94
}

Build an n8n workflow with a Schedule Trigger (every 30 minutes), fetch the deliverability stats, and add an IF node: if bounce_rate > 0.05 or spam_complaint_rate > 0.002, fire a Slack message to your #email-ops channel and optionally pause the campaign via POST /api/v1/campaigns/{id}/pause. This kind of automated circuit-breaker protects your sending reputation across all your connected accounts — whether you're sending through Gmail, Outlook, or SendGrid.

Pattern 4: Building an AI Email Agent Pipeline

MailClaw's AI email agents can draft, personalize, and respond to emails autonomously. But the really interesting use case is chaining them with n8n's LangChain integration or OpenAI nodes to create multi-step reasoning pipelines before the agent ever sends a message.

Consider this flow for outbound sales:

  1. n8n's RSS Feed or HTTP Request node monitors a target company's news feed
  2. An OpenAI node summarizes recent news into a relevance score and talking points
  3. n8n passes the summary to MailClaw via POST /api/v1/agents/{agent_id}/context, injecting fresh context into the agent's working memory
  4. The AI email agent uses that context to craft a hyper-relevant first-touch email that references something real and recent

This is genuinely hard to replicate with closed SaaS tools because most platforms don't expose agent context APIs. Because MailClaw is open source and built on OpenClaw, the internals are accessible and extensible.

Multi-Account and Multi-Sender Orchestration

One of MailClaw's most underrated features is multi-account support — you can manage sending across Gmail, Outlook, and SMTP accounts with OAuth or credential-based auth, all from the same dashboard. n8n takes this further by letting you build routing logic around which account sends which campaign.

Account-Based Routing in n8n

Use a Switch node in n8n to inspect the lead's domain or region, then call POST /api/v1/sequences/enroll with the appropriate sender_account_id for each branch. Enterprise leads from Fortune 500 domains route to your primary managed inbox. Cold outreach to SMBs routes to a dedicated sending domain warmed specifically for that audience. The logic lives in n8n; MailClaw executes flawlessly against whichever account you point it at.

CLI Integration for Power Users

If you prefer scripting over visual workflows, MailClaw's CLI integrates naturally with n8n's Execute Command node. This is useful for bulk operations that are faster to express as shell commands than as API chains.

# Enroll a contact list from CSV via CLI (callable from n8n Execute Command node)
mailclaw sequence enroll \
  --sequence-id seq_abc123 \
  --from-csv /tmp/new_leads.csv \
  --sender-account gmail_primary

# Trigger enrichment on a segment
mailclaw contacts enrich \
  --segment "source=webinar_2024" \
  --wait

Pipe these commands into n8n workflows triggered by file system events, webhook calls from your landing page, or scheduled jobs. It's the kind of flexibility that's only possible because MailClaw is a locally-running, open-source tool with real CLI depth.

Getting the Most Out of This Stack

The MailClaw + n8n combination is most powerful when you resist the urge to do everything in one tool. Let n8n own the orchestration: triggers, branching, data transformation, cross-tool sync. Let MailClaw own the email layer: sending, sequencing, AI personalization, deliverability, and contact intelligence. The API surface between them is your integration contract — keep it clean, document your workflows, and you'll have an email automation stack that scales with your operation without ever requiring a SaaS subscription or sending your data to someone else's cloud.

Start with Pattern 1 or Pattern 3 — they're the quickest wins and will immediately demonstrate the value of the integration. Then layer in the AI agent pipeline once you're comfortable with the data flow. The localhost dashboard at localhost:3100 gives you full visibility into everything MailClaw is doing, so you're never flying blind even as the automations grow more complex.

articles.title: How to Integrate MailClaw with PostgreSQL for Custom Data Pipelines
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw to a PostgreSQL database to build powerful custom data pipelines that sync contacts, track campaign events, and supercharge your AI email agents with real-time business data.
articles.content:
Why PostgreSQL and MailClaw Are a Natural Fit

Most email automation tools lock your data inside proprietary systems. You get CSVs on a good day, and an API rate limit headache the rest of the time. MailClaw takes a different approach — because it runs locally on your Mac at localhost:3100 and is fully open source under the OpenClaw framework, you have direct access to its internals. That means you can wire it up to PostgreSQL and build data pipelines that would cost thousands of dollars per month on a SaaS platform.

Whether you're pulling enriched contacts from a product database, syncing CRM data from HubSpot or Salesforce, or feeding behavioral signals into your AI email agents, PostgreSQL becomes the connective tissue between MailClaw and the rest of your stack. This guide walks you through exactly how to do that.

Setting Up the PostgreSQL Connection

Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure you have:

  • MailClaw running locally (mailclaw start — dashboard available at localhost:3100)
  • PostgreSQL 14+ installed and running
  • Node.js 18+ (used by MailClaw's plugin layer)
  • The pg npm package for database connectivity

Install the PostgreSQL client library in your MailClaw project directory:

cd ~/.mailclaw
npm install pg dotenv

Next, create a .env file in your MailClaw config directory with your database credentials:

PG_HOST=localhost
PG_PORT=5432
PG_DATABASE=your_app_db
PG_USER=your_pg_user
PG_PASSWORD=your_pg_password
Security note: MailClaw runs entirely on your local machine, so your credentials never leave your environment. This is one of the core advantages of an open-source, localhost-first architecture over cloud-based tools.

Creating a Database Connector Module

MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered plugin system lets you drop custom modules into the ~/.mailclaw/plugins/ directory. Create a file called pg-connector.js:

// ~/.mailclaw/plugins/pg-connector.js
require('dotenv').config();
const { Pool } = require('pg');

const pool = new Pool({
  host: process.env.PG_HOST,
  port: process.env.PG_PORT,
  database: process.env.PG_DATABASE,
  user: process.env.PG_USER,
  password: process.env.PG_PASSWORD,
});

async function queryContacts(filter = {}) {
  const { rows } = await pool.query(
    `SELECT email, first_name, last_name, company, plan, last_login
     FROM users
     WHERE active = true
     ORDER BY created_at DESC`
  );
  return rows;
}

module.exports = { pool, queryContacts };

Once this module is in place, MailClaw can reference it from sequences, enrichment jobs, and agent workflows.

Syncing PostgreSQL Contacts into MailClaw

Running a Contact Import from the CLI

MailClaw's CLI makes it easy to trigger a one-time or scheduled sync. Use the built-in mailclaw contacts import command with a custom source flag pointing to your plugin:

mailclaw contacts import \
  --source plugin:pg-connector \
  --map "email=email,first_name=firstName,last_name=lastName,company=company,plan=customField.plan" \
  --tag "postgres-sync" \
  --dedupe email

The --dedupe flag tells MailClaw to match on email address and update existing contacts rather than creating duplicates. The --map flag translates your PostgreSQL column names into MailClaw's contact schema, including custom fields like plan that you can use later for segmentation in the sequence builder.

Scheduling Recurring Syncs

For live pipelines, you'll want this to run automatically. Add a cron-style sync job using MailClaw's scheduler:

mailclaw schedule add \
  --name "nightly-postgres-sync" \
  --cron "0 2 * * *" \
  --task "contacts:import" \
  --source plugin:pg-connector \
  --tag "postgres-sync"

This runs every night at 2 AM, pulling fresh user data from your database and keeping MailClaw's contact list in sync. You can view and manage all scheduled tasks from the localhost:3100 dashboard under Settings → Scheduler.

Building a Custom Data Pipeline for Outreach

Enriching Contacts with Product Behavior Data

MailClaw's contact enrichment layer becomes significantly more powerful when combined with your own product data in PostgreSQL. Instead of relying solely on third-party enrichment APIs, you can join your internal tables to surface exactly the signals that matter to your business.

Here's an example that pulls users who haven't logged in for 14 days and flags them for a re-engagement sequence:

// ~/.mailclaw/plugins/churned-users.js
const { pool } = require('./pg-connector');

async function getAtRiskUsers() {
  const { rows } = await pool.query(`
    SELECT 
      u.email,
      u.first_name,
      u.company,
      u.plan,
      EXTRACT(DAY FROM NOW() - u.last_login) AS days_inactive,
      COUNT(e.id) AS total_events_last_30
    FROM users u
    LEFT JOIN events e 
      ON e.user_id = u.id 
      AND e.created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
    WHERE u.last_login < NOW() - INTERVAL '14 days'
      AND u.active = true
      AND u.plan != 'free'
    GROUP BY u.id
    ORDER BY days_inactive DESC
  `);
  return rows;
}

module.exports = { getAtRiskUsers };

You can call this enrichment plugin directly from the MailClaw CLI before triggering a sequence:

mailclaw enrich run --plugin churned-users --tag "at-risk" --sequence "re-engagement-v2"

Wiring Data into AI Email Agents

This is where things get genuinely exciting. MailClaw's AI email agents can consume custom context objects — meaning you can pass product-specific data directly into the prompt that generates each personalized email. With PostgreSQL as your source, each agent has access to real behavioral signals, not just name and company.

Configure an agent workflow in ~/.mailclaw/agents/re-engagement.agent.json:

{
  "name": "Re-engagement Agent",
  "model": "gpt-4o",
  "contextSource": "plugin:churned-users",
  "contextFields": ["days_inactive", "total_events_last_30", "plan", "company"],
  "systemPrompt": "You are a helpful customer success manager. Use the user's activity data to write a warm, personalized re-engagement email. Mention their inactivity naturally without being accusatory.",
  "sequence": "re-engagement-v2",
  "sendVia": "gmail-oauth",
  "deliverabilityCheck": true
}

The deliverabilityCheck: true flag runs each generated email through MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring before it queues — checking for spam trigger words, proper authentication headers, and send-rate limits across your connected accounts.

Writing Campaign Events Back to PostgreSQL

A pipeline should flow in both directions. MailClaw can write email events — opens, clicks, replies, bounces — back to your PostgreSQL database using webhook triggers. This closes the loop and lets your product analytics, BI tools, or Salesforce sync pick up email engagement signals.

Add an outbound webhook in ~/.mailclaw/hooks/events-to-pg.js:

const { pool } = require('../plugins/pg-connector');

module.exports = async function onEmailEvent(event) {
  const { type, contactEmail, sequenceName, timestamp, metadata } = event;

  await pool.query(`
    INSERT INTO email_events (email, event_type, sequence_name, occurred_at, metadata)
    VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5)
    ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
  `, [contactEmail, type, sequenceName, timestamp, JSON.stringify(metadata)]);
};

Register it with the CLI:

mailclaw hooks register --event "email.*" --handler hooks/events-to-pg.js

Now every open, click, and reply from your Gmail, Outlook, or SendGrid-connected accounts flows directly into your own database — no third-party data warehouse required.

Practical Tips for Production Pipelines

  • Use connection pooling: The pg.Pool setup shown above handles this automatically, but keep pool size modest (5–10) since MailClaw is a local process and doesn't need high concurrency.
  • Index your email column: Run CREATE INDEX ON users(email); in PostgreSQL so deduplication queries stay fast as contact lists grow.
  • Separate read replicas for enrichment: If you're querying a production database, point your enrichment plugin at a read replica to avoid impacting app performance.
  • Version your agent configs: Store your .agent.json files in Git. Since MailClaw is open source, your entire pipeline becomes reproducible and auditable.
  • Monitor from the dashboard: The MailClaw local dashboard at localhost:3100 shows real-time pipeline status, sequence performance, and deliverability metrics in one place — check it after each sync run.

What You've Built

By integrating PostgreSQL with MailClaw, you've created something that most teams pay enterprise prices for: a fully personalized, behavior-driven email pipeline that reads from your real product data, generates AI-crafted messages through MailClaw's agent layer, sends through authenticated accounts like Gmail or SendGrid, and writes events back to your own database for downstream analysis in tools like HubSpot, Salesforce, or a custom BI stack.

And it all runs locally, stays open source, and costs you nothing in platform fees. That's the OpenClaw advantage — and with PostgreSQL as your data backbone, you've barely scratched the surface of what's possible.

articles.title: MailClaw + Supabase: Building a Custom Email Automation Backend
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw to Supabase to build a fully custom email automation backend — with persistent contact storage, real-time sequence tracking, and webhook-driven workflows that scale beyond the defaults.
articles.content:
Why Pair MailClaw with Supabase?

MailClaw ships with a powerful local-first architecture — everything runs on your Mac at localhost:3100, your data stays private, and the OpenClaw engine handles the heavy lifting. But there are moments when you need more: a shared database your team can query, a persistent store that survives machine restarts, or a real-time backend that other tools can read from without scraping a local dashboard.

That's exactly where Supabase fits in. Supabase gives you a hosted Postgres database, a REST and GraphQL API, real-time subscriptions, and built-in authentication — all on a generous free tier. Wiring it to MailClaw means you get the best of both worlds: MailClaw's AI email agents and deliverability tooling on the front end, and a queryable, shareable data layer underneath.

In this guide we'll walk through a practical integration: storing enriched contacts, tracking sequence events, and triggering MailClaw workflows via Supabase webhooks.

What You'll Build

  • A contacts table in Supabase that syncs with MailClaw's contact enrichment pipeline
  • A sequence_events table that records opens, clicks, and replies in real time
  • A webhook handler that triggers MailClaw sequences when new rows are inserted
  • A simple Node.js glue script that bridges the two systems

By the end you'll have an automation backend you can query from a BI tool like Metabase, pipe into HubSpot or Salesforce via Zapier, or expose to teammates who don't have MailClaw installed locally.

Step 1 — Set Up Your Supabase Project

If you haven't already, create a free project at supabase.com. Once your project is ready, head to the SQL Editor and run the following to create the two tables you'll need:

-- Contacts synced from MailClaw enrichment
CREATE TABLE contacts (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  first_name TEXT,
  last_name TEXT,
  company TEXT,
  title TEXT,
  linkedin_url TEXT,
  enriched_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
  mailclaw_id TEXT,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

-- Sequence event log (opens, clicks, replies, bounces)
CREATE TABLE sequence_events (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  contact_email TEXT NOT NULL,
  sequence_name TEXT,
  event_type TEXT CHECK (event_type IN ('sent', 'open', 'click', 'reply', 'bounce', 'unsubscribe')),
  metadata JSONB,
  occurred_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

Grab your Supabase URL and anon key from Settings → API. You'll need these in the next step.

Step 2 — Configure MailClaw's Webhook Output

MailClaw's sequence builder supports outbound webhooks on every event. Open your dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to Sequences → [Your Sequence] → Settings → Webhooks, and add a webhook endpoint pointing to your local bridge script (we'll use http://localhost:4000/events for now).

Check the events you want to capture — at minimum, enable sent, open, reply, and bounce. MailClaw will POST a JSON payload to your endpoint every time one of these fires.

Sample MailClaw Webhook Payload

{
  "event": "open",
  "contact": {
    "email": "alex@acmecorp.com",
    "first_name": "Alex",
    "mailclaw_id": "mc_7f3a91b"
  },
  "sequence": "Q4 Outreach — SaaS Founders",
  "occurred_at": "2025-01-14T09:32:11Z",
  "metadata": {
    "subject": "Quick question about your data stack",
    "ip": "104.18.22.40",
    "user_agent": "Mozilla/5.0..."
  }
}

Step 3 — Build the Bridge Script

Create a small Node.js server that receives MailClaw webhooks and writes them to Supabase. Initialize a new project and install dependencies:

mkdir mailclaw-supabase-bridge && cd mailclaw-supabase-bridge
npm init -y
npm install express @supabase/supabase-js dotenv

Create a .env file:

SUPABASE_URL=https://your-project.supabase.co
SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=your-anon-key-here
PORT=4000

Then create index.js:

require('dotenv').config();
const express = require('express');
const { createClient } = require('@supabase/supabase-js');

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

const supabase = createClient(
  process.env.SUPABASE_URL,
  process.env.SUPABASE_ANON_KEY
);

// Receive MailClaw sequence events
app.post('/events', async (req, res) => {
  const { event, contact, sequence, occurred_at, metadata } = req.body;

  const { error } = await supabase.from('sequence_events').insert({
    contact_email: contact.email,
    sequence_name: sequence,
    event_type: event,
    metadata: { ...metadata, mailclaw_id: contact.mailclaw_id },
    occurred_at
  });

  if (error) {
    console.error('Supabase insert error:', error.message);
    return res.status(500).json({ ok: false });
  }

  console.log(`Logged ${event} for ${contact.email}`);
  res.json({ ok: true });
});

app.listen(process.env.PORT, () => {
  console.log(`Bridge running on port ${process.env.PORT}`);
});

Start the bridge with node index.js and send a test event from MailClaw's webhook tester. You should see the row appear in your Supabase table within seconds.

Step 4 — Sync Enriched Contacts to Supabase

MailClaw's contact enrichment feature pulls in LinkedIn URLs, job titles, company data, and verified emails from connected enrichment providers. You can push that enriched data to Supabase using the same bridge pattern — add a second endpoint:

// Receive enriched contact data from MailClaw
app.post('/contacts', async (req, res) => {
  const { email, first_name, last_name, company, title,
          linkedin_url, mailclaw_id, enriched_at } = req.body;

  const { error } = await supabase.from('contacts').upsert(
    { email, first_name, last_name, company, title,
      linkedin_url, mailclaw_id, enriched_at },
    { onConflict: 'email' }
  );

  if (error) return res.status(500).json({ ok: false, error: error.message });
  res.json({ ok: true });
});

In MailClaw's contact enrichment settings (Contacts → Enrichment → Export Hooks), point the post-enrichment webhook to http://localhost:4000/contacts. Now every contact MailClaw enriches — whether via a CSV import, a HubSpot sync, or a manual lookup — lands in Supabase automatically.

Step 5 — Trigger MailClaw Sequences from Supabase

This is where it gets interesting. Supabase Database Webhooks can call an HTTP endpoint whenever a row is inserted or updated. That means you can trigger a MailClaw sequence automatically when, say, a new lead is added to your Supabase CRM table from a form submission, a Stripe event, or a Salesforce sync.

In Supabase, go to Database → Webhooks → Create a new hook. Set it to fire on INSERT into a leads table and point the URL to your bridge at http://your-public-url/enroll (use ngrok or a deployed instance for this).

Add the enrollment handler to your bridge:

const fetch = require('node-fetch'); // npm install node-fetch@2

app.post('/enroll', async (req, res) => {
  const record = req.body.record; // Supabase sends { type, table, record }

  // Call MailClaw's local API to add contact to a sequence
  const response = await fetch('http://localhost:3100/api/sequences/enroll', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      sequence: 'New Lead Nurture',
      contact: {
        email: record.email,
        first_name: record.first_name,
        company: record.company
      }
    })
  });

  const result = await response.json();
  console.log('Enrolled in MailClaw:', result);
  res.json({ ok: true });
});

Pro tip: Combine this with MailClaw's AI email agents to personalize the first email in the sequence based on the contact's Supabase record — pipe in company size, industry, or recent activity as agent context before the sequence fires.

Deliverability Monitoring in Supabase

One underrated benefit of this setup is deliverability analytics. Once your sequence events are flowing into Supabase, you can write SQL queries to spot problems fast — high bounce rates on a specific SendGrid sending account, an open rate drop on Gmail vs. Outlook recipients, or a surge in unsubscribes from a particular sequence.

-- Bounce rate by sending account (last 30 days)
SELECT
  metadata->>'sending_account' AS account,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'bounce') AS bounces,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'sent') AS sent,
  ROUND(
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'bounce')::numeric /
    NULLIF(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'sent'), 0) * 100, 2
  ) AS bounce_rate_pct
FROM sequence_events
WHERE occurred_at > now() - interval '30 days'
GROUP BY account
ORDER BY bounce_rate_pct DESC;

MailClaw's built-in deliverability dashboard at localhost:3100 gives you a great real-time view, but Supabase lets you slice historical data any way you need — and share it with stakeholders who don't have access to your local machine.

Where to Take It Next

Once the foundation is in place, a few natural extensions are worth exploring:

  • Row-level security: Enable Supabase RLS policies so only your bridge script can write to the events table, keeping your data clean.
  • Realtime subscriptions: Use supabase.channel() to build a live ops dashboard that updates the moment a key prospect replies.
  • Multi-account support: MailClaw handles multiple SMTP/OAuth accounts natively — tag events in Supabase with the sending account so you can compare performance across Gmail, Outlook, and SendGrid senders in one query.
  • CRM sync: Read from Supabase and push enriched, engaged contacts into HubSpot or Salesforce automatically — no third-party middleware required.

The beauty of this stack is that it's entirely open and self-hosted. MailClaw is open source and built on OpenClaw, Supabase's core is open source, and every piece of glue code you write lives in your own repo. No vendor lock-in, no per-seat fees creeping up as your list grows, and full visibility into exactly what's happening with your outreach data.

Start small — get the event logging working this afternoon — and layer in the automation triggers once you trust the data flowing through. Your email stack will be more powerful, more observable, and a lot more interesting to work on.

articles.title: How to Connect MailClaw to Freshdesk for Support Email Automation
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw to Freshdesk so your support team can automate ticket follow-ups, onboarding sequences, and customer outreach — all running locally from your Mac with full AI assistance.
articles.content:
Why Connect MailClaw to Freshdesk?

Support teams live and die by their inbox. Freshdesk is excellent at triaging tickets and tracking conversations, but its native email automation is limited — you get canned responses, basic rules, and templated replies that feel robotic to customers. MailClaw fills that gap beautifully.

By connecting MailClaw to Freshdesk, you can trigger intelligent email sequences the moment a ticket is created, resolved, or goes stale. Your AI email agents can follow up on unresolved issues, send satisfaction surveys at exactly the right moment, and even enrich contact records with company data before a human ever touches the thread. All of this runs locally on your Mac at localhost:3100 — no third-party SaaS middleman, no data leaving your machine unless you want it to.

This guide walks through the full setup: connecting your accounts, configuring the Freshdesk webhook, building your first support sequence, and letting MailClaw's AI agents handle the repetitive outreach so your team can focus on actual problem-solving.

Prerequisites

  • MailClaw installed and running (mailclaw start — dashboard at localhost:3100)
  • A Freshdesk account with API access (any paid plan, or the free trial)
  • At least one email account connected to MailClaw (Gmail OAuth, Outlook OAuth, or an SMTP provider like SendGrid or Postmark)
  • Basic familiarity with webhooks — you don't need to write code, but you should know what a POST request is

Step 1: Get Your Freshdesk API Key

Everything starts with authenticating MailClaw against your Freshdesk instance. Log into Freshdesk, click your avatar in the top-right corner, and go to Profile Settings. Scroll to the bottom and you'll find your API key. Copy it — treat it like a password.

Now open your MailClaw config file. By default it lives at ~/.mailclaw/config.yaml. Add a new integration block:

integrations:
  freshdesk:
    domain: yourcompany.freshdesk.com
    api_key: YOUR_API_KEY_HERE
    sync_contacts: true
    enrich_on_import: true

Setting enrich_on_import: true tells MailClaw to run its contact enrichment pipeline on every Freshdesk contact it pulls in — filling in job titles, company size, LinkedIn URLs, and other signals that help your AI agents personalize outreach.

Restart MailClaw to apply the changes:

mailclaw restart

Head to your local dashboard at localhost:3100 → Integrations and you should see Freshdesk listed with a green status indicator.

Step 2: Sync Freshdesk Contacts into MailClaw

Before building sequences, get your existing Freshdesk contacts into MailClaw's contact database. Run the import command:

mailclaw contacts import --source freshdesk --limit 500

This pulls the 500 most recently active contacts from Freshdesk and runs them through the enrichment engine. You'll see output like:

✓ Imported 500 contacts from Freshdesk
✓ Enriched 423 contacts with company data
✓ 77 contacts skipped (missing email or opted out)
→ View in dashboard: http://localhost:3100/contacts

In the dashboard, filter by Source: Freshdesk to see your imported contacts. Each enriched record will show company name, estimated employee count, industry, and any public social profiles MailClaw found — data that makes your email sequences feel human rather than automated.

Step 3: Set Up the Freshdesk Webhook

This is the part that makes the whole thing reactive. Instead of manually importing contacts, you want Freshdesk to push events to MailClaw the moment something happens — a ticket is created, a ticket is resolved, or a ticket has been idle for 48 hours.

Expose MailClaw to Freshdesk

Since MailClaw runs on localhost, Freshdesk can't reach it directly. You need a tunnel. The easiest option is ngrok:

ngrok http 3100

You'll get a public URL like https://abc123.ngrok.io. This is temporary — for a production setup, consider running MailClaw on a small VPS or using a fixed ngrok domain. For testing, the temporary URL is fine.

Configure the Webhook in Freshdesk

  1. In Freshdesk, go to Admin → Automation → Ticket Creation (or Ticket Updates for resolved tickets)
  2. Create a new rule with whatever conditions match your use case (e.g., "Ticket is created" or "Status changes to Resolved")
  3. Under Actions, select Trigger Webhook
  4. Set the request type to POST
  5. Enter your webhook URL: https://abc123.ngrok.io/webhooks/freshdesk
  6. Set Content Type to JSON
  7. Under Encoding, choose JSON and include the ticket fields you want: {{ticket.id}}, {{ticket.subject}}, {{ticket.requester.email}}, {{ticket.status}}

Save the rule. MailClaw's webhook handler will now receive a JSON payload every time that condition fires, automatically enroll the contact in the appropriate sequence, and kick off outreach — all without human intervention.

Step 4: Build Your Support Email Sequence

Now for the fun part. In the MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100 → Sequences, click New Sequence. Give it a name like Freshdesk Ticket Resolved Follow-Up and set the trigger to Webhook: freshdesk.ticket_resolved.

A Simple Three-Step Follow-Up Sequence

Here's a proven structure for post-resolution support follow-up:

  • Email 1 (immediate): A warm, human-feeling confirmation that the ticket was resolved. Thank the customer by first name, reference the issue briefly, invite them to reopen if the problem persists.
  • Email 2 (Day 3): A short satisfaction check-in. One question: "Did our solution actually work for you?" Link to a simple Typeform or Google Form.
  • Email 3 (Day 7, conditional): Only sends if the customer didn't reply to Email 2. A gentle nudge with a direct link to book time with a support engineer if needed.

You can define this sequence in YAML if you prefer scripting over the UI:

sequences:
  - name: freshdesk-resolved-followup
    trigger: webhook.freshdesk.ticket_resolved
    steps:
      - delay: 0
        subject: "Your support ticket is resolved — a quick note from us"
        template: support/resolved-confirmation
        ai_personalize: true
      - delay: 3d
        subject: "Did we actually fix it?"
        template: support/satisfaction-check
      - delay: 7d
        condition: no_reply
        subject: "Still having trouble? Let's get on a call"
        template: support/escalation-offer

The ai_personalize: true flag tells MailClaw's AI email agent to rewrite subject lines and opening sentences based on enriched contact data — so a customer at a 50-person SaaS startup gets slightly different framing than an enterprise IT manager at a Fortune 500.

Step 5: Monitor Deliverability and Performance

Sending support emails through an automated sequence means volume — and volume means deliverability risk if you're not careful. MailClaw's deliverability tools give you a real-time view of what's happening.

From the dashboard at localhost:3100 → Deliverability, you can monitor:

  • Bounce rates per sending account (keep this under 2%)
  • Spam complaint rates (under 0.1% is the industry threshold)
  • DKIM, SPF, and DMARC validation status per domain
  • Open and reply rates broken down by sequence step

If you're using multiple email accounts — say, a SendGrid transactional account for high-volume sends and a Gmail OAuth account for personal-feeling follow-ups — MailClaw's multi-account support lets you assign different accounts to different sequence steps. Use Gmail for Email 1 (it feels human), and SendGrid for Email 3 (it's more templated anyway).

Pro tip: If your Freshdesk support domain is support@yourcompany.com, make sure that domain is properly warmed up in MailClaw before blasting sequences. Use the warmup scheduler under localhost:3100 → Accounts → [Account] → Warmup to ramp up volume gradually over two to three weeks.

Taking It Further with AI Email Agents

Once the basic sequence is running, consider deploying a MailClaw AI email agent specifically for support triage. Instead of fixed templates, the agent reads incoming replies to your follow-up emails and responds autonomously — escalating to a human if the customer signals frustration, closing the loop if they confirm everything is working, or routing to your CRM (HubSpot, Salesforce, or Pipedrive) if the conversation reveals an upsell opportunity.

Create a new agent from the CLI:

mailclaw agent create \
  --name "Support Follow-Up Agent" \
  --role support \
  --integration freshdesk \
  --escalate-to team@yourcompany.com \
  --crm hubspot

Because MailClaw is open source and built on OpenClaw, you can fork the agent logic and customize its decision tree to match your team's exact escalation policy. No black boxes, no locked-in vendor behavior.

What You've Built

In under an hour, you've connected MailClaw to Freshdesk in a way that most support teams never achieve with off-the-shelf tooling. Your customers now get timely, personalized follow-ups after every resolved ticket. Your team gets visibility into which customers are still struggling. And your AI agent is handling the repetitive reply loop so your engineers can stay focused on hard problems.

The entire stack runs locally, your customer data stays on your machine, and because it's all open source, you can extend, audit, and customize every piece of it. That's the MailClaw promise — powerful email automation that you actually own.

articles.title: Using MailClaw with Make (formerly Integromat) for Visual Workflows
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to connect MailClaw's local API to Make (formerly Integromat) for powerful visual workflows — from syncing new CRM leads into email sequences to triggering AI agents based on real-time events.
articles.content:
Why Pair MailClaw with Make?

MailClaw is already a powerhouse on its own. From its local dashboard at localhost:3100, you can build multi-step email sequences, enrich contacts with AI, monitor deliverability, and deploy fully autonomous AI email agents — all without sending a single byte of data to a third-party SaaS platform. But the moment you want that power to respond to events happening outside MailClaw — a new deal created in Salesforce, a form submission in Typeform, or a lead enriched in HubSpot — you need a bridge.

That bridge is Make (formerly Integromat). Make's visual workflow builder lets you drag, connect, and automate across hundreds of apps. When you combine Make's event-driven architecture with MailClaw's local REST API, you get a setup that is both deeply powerful and completely private. Your email logic runs on your machine; Make simply tells it when to act.

Understanding MailClaw's Local API

Before wiring up Make, it helps to understand what MailClaw exposes. When you start MailClaw with:

mailclaw start

…the OpenClaw-powered engine spins up a local server on port 3100. This server exposes a REST API that covers every major feature: contact management, sequence enrollment, campaign triggers, enrichment jobs, and agent dispatching. You can explore the full API reference directly from your dashboard at http://localhost:3100/docs.

Key endpoints you'll use most often with Make:

  • POST /api/contacts — Create or upsert a contact
  • POST /api/contacts/:id/enroll — Enroll a contact in a sequence
  • POST /api/enrichment/run — Trigger an AI enrichment job
  • POST /api/agents/dispatch — Fire an AI email agent task
  • GET /api/sequences — List available sequences

Because Make runs in the cloud, you'll need to expose your local MailClaw instance over a secure tunnel for Make's HTTP module to reach it. ngrok is the simplest approach:

ngrok http 3100

This gives you a public HTTPS URL like https://your-id.ngrok.io that you'll use as the base URL inside Make. For production or team setups, consider a more persistent tunnel solution or deploying MailClaw on a local server accessible via a private VPN.

Setting Up Your First Make Scenario

Scenario 1: New HubSpot Contact → MailClaw Sequence Enrollment

This is the most common starting point. Every time a new contact is created in HubSpot, you want MailClaw to enrich that contact and drop them into your onboarding sequence automatically.

  1. In Make, create a new scenario and add the HubSpot — Watch Contacts trigger module. Set it to poll every 15 minutes (or use a HubSpot webhook trigger for real-time response).
  2. Add an HTTP — Make a Request module. Set the URL to your ngrok base URL plus /api/contacts, method POST, and map the HubSpot fields to the MailClaw contact schema:
{
  "email": "{{1.email}}",
  "firstName": "{{1.firstname}}",
  "lastName": "{{1.lastname}}",
  "company": "{{1.company}}",
  "source": "hubspot"
}
  1. Add a second HTTP — Make a Request module to trigger enrichment. Use the contact ID returned from step 2:
POST /api/enrichment/run
{
  "contactId": "{{2.id}}",
  "depth": "standard"
}
  1. Add a final HTTP module to enroll the enriched contact in your sequence. Grab your sequence ID from the MailClaw dashboard or from GET /api/sequences:
POST /api/contacts/{{2.id}}/enroll
{
  "sequenceId": "seq_onboarding_001",
  "startAt": "now"
}

The entire flow takes about ten minutes to set up and runs completely hands-free from that point on.

Scenario 2: Salesforce Opportunity Stage Change → AI Agent Dispatch

One of MailClaw's most exciting features is its AI email agents — autonomous agents that can research a prospect, craft a personalized message, and send it through your connected Gmail or Outlook account without manual input. Make is the perfect trigger layer for these agents.

When a Salesforce opportunity moves to the Proposal Sent stage, you might want an AI agent to send a timely, personalized follow-up to the primary contact. Here's how to wire that up:

  1. Use the Salesforce — Watch Records trigger, filtered to opportunities where StageName equals Proposal Sent.
  2. Add a Salesforce — Get a Record module to fetch the related Contact details (name, email, title, company).
  3. Add an HTTP module pointing to MailClaw's agent dispatch endpoint:
POST /api/agents/dispatch
{
  "agentId": "agent_followup_pro",
  "context": {
    "contactEmail": "{{2.Email}}",
    "contactName": "{{2.Name}}",
    "companyName": "{{2.Account.Name}}",
    "dealStage": "Proposal Sent",
    "notes": "{{1.Description}}"
  },
  "sendVia": "gmail_primary"
}

The AI agent picks up that context, enriches it further using MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment engine, generates a message, and sends it — all from your local machine, through your own SMTP or OAuth-connected account.

Handling Webhooks in the Other Direction

Make isn't just a trigger layer — it can also receive events from MailClaw. MailClaw supports outbound webhooks that fire on key events like sequence completions, bounces, opens, and replies. You can configure these from the dashboard under Settings → Webhooks, or via CLI:

mailclaw webhooks add \
  --event sequence.completed \
  --url https://hook.make.com/your-webhook-id

Once set up, you might build a Make scenario that:

  • Catches a sequence.completed event from MailClaw
  • Updates the contact's status in Airtable or a Google Sheet
  • Creates a follow-up task in Notion or ClickUp for your sales team
  • Posts a Slack notification with open rate and reply data

This bidirectional flow — Make triggering MailClaw, and MailClaw triggering Make — creates a fully reactive automation loop with minimal code and zero SaaS dependency on your email data.

Practical Tips for a Reliable Integration

Authenticate Every Request

MailClaw's API requires a bearer token, which you generate from the dashboard or with mailclaw auth token --generate. In Make, store this as a custom header in your HTTP modules:

Authorization: Bearer YOUR_MAILCLAW_TOKEN

Never hard-code this in individual modules. Instead, use Make's Data Stores or a Text Aggregator to reference it from a single place — updating it is much easier that way.

Use Make's Error Handlers

Network timeouts happen, especially over ngrok tunnels. Add an Error Handler route to each critical HTTP module. A simple Resume or Rollback directive prevents half-executed scenarios from corrupting your contact data or double-enrolling someone in a sequence.

Test Against MailClaw's Sandbox Mode

Before going live, run MailClaw in sandbox mode to intercept outbound emails without actually sending them:

mailclaw start --sandbox

This is invaluable when testing Make scenarios that touch your live Gmail or SendGrid accounts. You can verify payloads, inspect enrichment results, and validate sequence enrollments safely.

Monitor Deliverability Alongside Your Workflows

As your Make-driven automation scales up volume, keep an eye on MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring tab on the dashboard. It tracks bounce rates, spam complaints, and sending reputation per connected account. If a scenario is inadvertently enrolling bad email addresses from a CRM sync, you'll catch it before your domain reputation takes a hit.

The Bigger Picture

What makes this combination genuinely compelling isn't any single workflow — it's the principle behind it. Make handles the when and what from across your entire software stack. MailClaw handles the how of email: the AI-powered personalization, the sequence logic, the deliverability guardrails, the agent autonomy. And because MailClaw runs locally as open-source software powered by OpenClaw, none of your contact data or email content ever leaves your machine.

You get the automation reach of a cloud platform with the privacy and control of a self-hosted tool. That's a trade-off most teams never realized they could have.

Whether you're a solo founder syncing your first Typeform leads into a welcome sequence, or a growth team routing Salesforce pipeline events through AI agents at scale, the MailClaw + Make stack gives you the building blocks to do it right — visually, reliably, and entirely on your terms.

articles.title: How to Integrate MailClaw with Apollo.io for Prospecting
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to connect Apollo.io's powerful prospect database with MailClaw's local AI email automation to build smarter outreach pipelines — from exporting leads to launching enriched, personalized sequences without leaving your terminal.
articles.content:
Why Apollo.io and MailClaw Work So Well Together

Apollo.io has become one of the most popular prospecting tools for sales teams and indie founders alike. Its database of over 275 million contacts, built-in intent signals, and lead scoring make it a natural starting point for any outbound campaign. But where many teams hit a wall is in what happens after the export — the handoff from discovery to actual outreach is where leads die in spreadsheets.

That's exactly the gap MailClaw is built to close. Because MailClaw runs locally on your machine (at localhost:3100), you own the full pipeline from enrichment to delivery. There's no SaaS middleman throttling your sends, no per-seat pricing wall, and no black-box AI you can't inspect or customize. Powered by OpenClaw, MailClaw brings a genuinely intelligent automation layer to the leads you pull out of Apollo — and the integration is simpler than you might expect.

Step 1: Export Your Apollo.io Prospect List

Start in Apollo.io by building your target list using its filters — job title, industry, company size, technologies used, funding stage, whatever fits your ICP. Once you're happy with the segment, export it as a CSV.

Apollo's standard CSV export includes fields like:

  • First Name / Last Name
  • Email (verified or unverified, depending on your plan)
  • Title and Company
  • LinkedIn URL
  • Phone, City, Country
  • Technologies (e.g., HubSpot, Salesforce, Stripe)
  • Intent signals (if enabled on your plan)

Save this file somewhere clean — you'll be importing it directly into MailClaw in the next step.

A Note on Email Verification

Apollo marks some emails as "likely valid" rather than fully verified. Before importing into MailClaw, it's worth running a quick pass through your list. MailClaw's built-in deliverability tools include a contact hygiene layer that can flag risky addresses before they hit your sending infrastructure — which matters a lot if you're routing through Gmail, Outlook, or a dedicated SMTP provider like SendGrid or Mailgun.

Step 2: Import Contacts into MailClaw

Open your terminal and navigate to your MailClaw directory. The CLI makes importing a one-liner:

mailclaw contacts import --file ~/Downloads/apollo_export.csv --source apollo

The --source apollo flag tells MailClaw to apply the Apollo field mapping automatically, so columns like Person LinkedIn Url and Technologies are correctly parsed without manual column mapping. You'll see output like:

✔ Parsed 847 contacts
✔ Deduplicated against existing records: 23 skipped
✔ Flagged for enrichment: 312 contacts missing company domain
→ Run `mailclaw contacts enrich` to fill gaps

Once imported, your contacts are visible in the localhost dashboard under the Contacts tab, where you can filter, tag, and segment them before building your sequence.

Step 3: Enrich Your Apollo Leads with MailClaw

Apollo gives you a solid foundation, but MailClaw's contact enrichment layer can go deeper. Using OpenClaw's enrichment pipeline, MailClaw can pull additional context from public sources — company descriptions, recent funding news, job change signals, and technology stack data — and write that context directly back into the contact record.

Run enrichment on your imported batch:

mailclaw contacts enrich --tag apollo-import-june --fields company_description,tech_stack,recent_news

This enrichment data isn't just stored for your reference — it becomes the fuel for MailClaw's AI personalization engine when you build your sequence. The more context a contact record has, the more genuinely personalized your first-touch email can be.

Using Custom Fields for Apollo Intent Data

If you're on an Apollo plan that includes buyer intent signals, don't let that data go to waste. You can map Apollo's intent columns to MailClaw custom fields during import:

mailclaw contacts import --file apollo_export.csv \
  --source apollo \
  --custom-field "intent_topic=Intent Topic" \
  --custom-field "intent_score=Intent Score"

These custom fields can then be used as sequence conditions — for example, sending a different opening message to contacts with a high intent score around a specific topic.

Step 4: Build Your Outreach Sequence

With your enriched Apollo contacts ready, head to the Sequence Builder — either via the dashboard at localhost:3100/sequences or the CLI:

mailclaw sequence create --name "Apollo Q3 Outbound" --contacts-tag apollo-import-june

A typical first-touch sequence for cold outbound might look like this:

  1. Day 0 — Personalized intro email (AI-generated, referencing company tech stack or recent news)
  2. Day 3 — Follow-up adding a specific value prop relevant to their industry
  3. Day 7 — Short "still relevant?" bump with a case study or social proof
  4. Day 14 — Break-up email with a low-friction CTA

MailClaw's AI email agents handle the per-contact personalization at each step. Rather than generic mail merge tokens, the agent reads the full contact record — including the enriched fields and Apollo intent data — and writes a message that actually sounds like you did your homework.

Connecting Your Sending Accounts

MailClaw supports multi-account sending, so you can distribute your Apollo sequences across multiple inboxes to protect deliverability. Connect your accounts via the dashboard or CLI:

# Add a Gmail account via OAuth
mailclaw accounts add --provider gmail --oauth

# Add a custom SMTP account (e.g., SendGrid, Postmark)
mailclaw accounts add --provider smtp \
  --host smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --port 587 \
  --user apikey \
  --pass YOUR_SENDGRID_API_KEY

You can then assign sending accounts to sequences, set daily send limits per account, and let MailClaw automatically rotate senders to stay within safe thresholds for cold outreach.

Step 5: Monitor Deliverability as Replies Come In

One of MailClaw's most underrated features is its deliverability monitoring layer, accessible from the dashboard. As your Apollo sequence runs, you can track:

  • Open rates and click rates per step
  • Bounce rate by sending account (to catch domain reputation issues early)
  • Spam complaint flags
  • Reply detection and automatic sequence pausing when a contact responds

This last point — automatic pause on reply — is critical for cold outreach. MailClaw watches your connected inboxes and stops the sequence the moment a prospect writes back, so you never send a follow-up to someone who already said "yes."

Pro tip: If you're seeing high bounce rates on Apollo contacts, it's often the "likely valid" emails. Use MailClaw's deliverability report to identify which Apollo segments have the worst hygiene, and either re-verify those addresses or retire them before they damage your sending domain.

Step 6: Push Replies Back to HubSpot or Salesforce

Once replies start coming in from your Apollo outreach, you'll want those conversations logged somewhere your team can act on them. MailClaw's CRM sync pushes activity data outbound to HubSpot or Salesforce so your pipeline stays current without manual entry:

mailclaw integrations add --crm hubspot --api-key YOUR_HUBSPOT_KEY

# Sync replied contacts to a HubSpot deal stage
mailclaw sequence sync --name "Apollo Q3 Outbound" \
  --crm hubspot \
  --trigger replied \
  --stage "SQL - Contacted"

For teams not using a CRM yet, MailClaw's local dashboard gives you a lightweight pipeline view — good enough to manage a focused Apollo outreach campaign without needing to stand up a whole CRM just to track 500 prospects.

Building This Into a Repeatable Workflow

The real power of the Apollo + MailClaw stack shows up when you treat it as a repeatable system rather than a one-off campaign. Here's a lightweight process you can run weekly:

  1. Pull a fresh Apollo segment each Monday based on updated filters or new intent signals
  2. Import and auto-enrich with mailclaw contacts enrich
  3. Add enriched contacts to your running sequence, or create a new variant for testing a different angle
  4. Review deliverability metrics mid-week and adjust send limits or rotate inboxes if needed
  5. Sync any positive replies to HubSpot or Salesforce for follow-up

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your machine, you can also script this whole workflow using cron jobs or a simple shell script — no Zapier, no API rate limits, no extra monthly bill. That's the kind of leverage that used to require a full RevOps stack, now running quietly on your laptop.

If you haven't set up MailClaw yet, the quickest path is npx mailclaw start — your dashboard will be live at localhost:3100 in under a minute, ready for your first Apollo import.

articles.title: MailClaw + Clay: Enriching and Automating Outbound Together
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to combine Clay's powerful contact enrichment with MailClaw's AI-powered email automation to build a high-converting outbound engine — from data enrichment to personalized sequences, all running locally on your Mac.
articles.content:
Why Clay and MailClaw Belong Together

If you've spent any time in the outbound sales world, you've probably heard the gospel of personalization: generic blasts are dead, and relevance wins. The problem is that real personalization at scale requires two things most tools handle separately — rich contact data and intelligent email automation. Clay gives you the former. MailClaw gives you the latter. Together, they form one of the most powerful outbound stacks you can run without handing your data to a dozen different SaaS vendors.

This guide walks through exactly how to wire these two tools together — from enriching a raw list in Clay to firing off personalized, AI-crafted sequences through MailClaw's local dashboard — with real commands and configurations you can follow right now.

Step 1: Building and Enriching Your List in Clay

Clay is a spreadsheet-meets-automation tool that lets you pull contact data from dozens of sources — LinkedIn, Clearbit, Hunter, Apollo, and more — and waterfall through them until you have a complete picture of each prospect. Before you ever write a single email, your list should be doing the heavy lifting.

What to Enrich Before You Export

A bare-minimum enriched contact for outbound should include:

  • Verified work email — use Clay's Hunter or Apollo enrichment columns to validate before you ever touch deliverability
  • Job title and seniority level — critical for segmenting sequences in MailClaw
  • Company size, industry, and tech stack — BuiltWith and Clearbit integrations in Clay handle this well
  • Recent trigger events — new funding, job changes, product launches (Clay's news enrichment columns are underrated here)
  • LinkedIn headline and bio snippet — this becomes personalization fuel for MailClaw's AI email agents

The goal is to export a CSV from Clay that contains enough signal for MailClaw to generate genuinely relevant first lines, not just {{first_name}} swaps dressed up as personalization.

Exporting the Right Way

When you export from Clay, use a consistent column naming convention. MailClaw's contact enrichment importer maps fields automatically, but it works best when headers are clean and predictable. A reliable export schema looks like this:

first_name, last_name, email, title, company, industry,
company_size, linkedin_url, tech_stack, recent_news, icebreaker_note

That icebreaker_note column is worth calling out. In Clay, you can use a GPT-powered column to pre-generate a short, context-aware sentence about each prospect based on their enriched data. Feed that into MailClaw and your AI agents have a head start on crafting openers that feel hand-written.

Step 2: Importing Contacts into MailClaw

With MailClaw running locally at localhost:3100, open the Contacts tab and hit Import CSV. The field mapper will auto-detect standard columns, but for custom fields like tech_stack or icebreaker_note, you'll map them to MailClaw's custom attributes on the fly.

Alternatively, if you're automating this step as part of a recurring workflow, MailClaw's CLI makes imports scriptable:

# Import enriched contacts from Clay export
mailclaw contacts import \
  --file ~/exports/clay_batch_07.csv \
  --list "Q3 Outbound - SaaS Founders" \
  --tag "clay-enriched" \
  --field-map title:job_title,recent_news:trigger_event

The --tag flag is useful because it lets you filter this segment later when building sequences, and the --field-map argument handles any column name mismatches between your Clay export and MailClaw's schema without manual editing.

Step 3: Building Your Sequence with AI Email Agents

Here's where MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered AI layer earns its keep. Instead of writing every email in a sequence by hand, you configure an AI email agent that understands your target persona, your offer, and the enrichment signals from Clay — then generates and iterates on copy automatically.

Configuring an AI Agent for Clay-Enriched Contacts

In the MailClaw dashboard, navigate to Agents → New Agent. You'll define the agent's persona, context, and the fields it should draw from when writing. A configuration for a Clay-enriched outbound campaign might look like this:

{
  "agent_name": "SaaS Founder Outreach",
  "persona": "Senior SDR at a B2B analytics company",
  "target_segment": "clay-enriched",
  "tone": "concise, direct, peer-to-peer",
  "personalization_fields": [
    "icebreaker_note",
    "trigger_event",
    "tech_stack",
    "company_size"
  ],
  "sequence_steps": 4,
  "follow_up_strategy": "value-add",
  "cta": "15-minute intro call"
}

Once the agent is configured, MailClaw generates draft emails for every step of the sequence. You review, tweak the tone or CTA if needed, then approve. The sequence is now live and personalized at the contact level — not the persona level.

Using Trigger Events as Personalization Anchors

One of the highest-leverage moves in Clay + MailClaw workflows is using trigger events as the opening hook. If Clay surfaced that a prospect just raised a Series A, that belongs in the first sentence of your email — not buried or generic.

"Congrats on the Series A — scaling a sales team right after a raise is notoriously chaotic. We've helped a few other founders in your position get outbound running without hiring five more reps."

MailClaw's AI agents can generate openers like this automatically when trigger_event is populated. Without Clay doing the enrichment legwork upstream, you'd be writing these manually or skipping them entirely.

Step 4: Connecting Your Sending Infrastructure

Enriched contacts and great copy mean nothing if your emails land in spam. MailClaw's deliverability tools are built into the same local dashboard, so you're not context-switching between platforms.

Multi-Account Setup

For cold outbound, you should be sending from warmed secondary domains — not your primary company domain. MailClaw supports multi-account sending via both SMTP and OAuth, so you can connect Gmail or Outlook inboxes alongside SendGrid or Postmark for transactional fallback.

# Add a sending account via CLI
mailclaw accounts add \
  --type smtp \
  --host smtp.gmail.com \
  --port 587 \
  --email outreach@yourdomain.io \
  --alias "SDR Account 1" \
  --daily-limit 40

Setting a --daily-limit per account is important. MailClaw will automatically distribute sends across accounts when you're running large Clay-enriched lists, keeping per-inbox volume in the safe zone and protecting deliverability.

Deliverability Checks Before Launch

Before activating any sequence, run MailClaw's built-in deliverability audit from the dashboard or CLI:

mailclaw deliverability check --sequence "Q3 SaaS Founders"

This checks SPF, DKIM, and DMARC alignment for all sending accounts attached to the sequence, flags any contacts with risky or unverified emails, and scores your subject lines for spam triggers. If Clay already validated emails upstream, you'll typically see a clean pass — which is exactly why doing enrichment first pays off.

Step 5: Monitoring and Iterating

Once your sequence is live, MailClaw's local dashboard gives you real-time visibility into opens, clicks, replies, and bounces — all without sending your engagement data to a third-party analytics server. For teams that care about data privacy or work in regulated industries, this is a meaningful advantage of the open-source, localhost architecture.

Feeding Performance Data Back into Clay

Close the loop by exporting reply and engagement data from MailClaw back into Clay for scoring and prioritization. Use MailClaw's export command to pull a performance snapshot:

mailclaw sequences export \
  --sequence "Q3 SaaS Founders" \
  --format csv \
  --fields email,opens,clicks,replied,bounced \
  --output ~/exports/sequence_results.csv

Import that CSV back into Clay and add a column that scores prospects based on engagement — opened twice but didn't reply scores differently than someone who clicked a link. Use that score to trigger a LinkedIn outreach step or a manual task in HubSpot or Salesforce, depending on where your team works the deals.

The Full Workflow at a Glance

  1. Enrich in Clay — build verified, signal-rich contact lists with trigger events, tech stack, and pre-generated icebreakers
  2. Import into MailClaw — use CSV import or the CLI with field mapping to load contacts into a tagged segment
  3. Configure an AI email agent — define persona, tone, and personalization fields so the agent writes context-aware sequences
  4. Connect sending infrastructure — link Gmail, Outlook, or SMTP accounts with daily limits for safe, distributed sending
  5. Run a deliverability audit — validate everything before the first email goes out
  6. Monitor locally — track performance in the MailClaw dashboard without sharing data externally
  7. Export results back to Clay — score engaged prospects and route them into your CRM or manual follow-up workflow

Why This Stack Works

Most outbound tools force a tradeoff: either you get rich data without good automation, or you get slick sequences without meaningful personalization. Clay and MailClaw sidestep that tradeoff entirely. Clay handles the research and enrichment work that used to take SDRs hours per prospect. MailClaw — running open-source, locally on your Mac, powered by OpenClaw — handles the intelligent automation that turns that research into replies.

The result is an outbound engine that feels hand-crafted to the recipient and scales without ballooning your tooling costs or putting your contact data in someone else's cloud. That's a combination worth building on.

articles.title: How MailClaw AI Email Agents Work Under the Hood
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: A deep-dive into how MailClaw's AI email agents are architected — from the OpenClaw reasoning loop to live SMTP handoffs — so you can tune, extend, and trust every automated decision they make.
articles.content:
What Is an AI Email Agent, Really?

The phrase "AI email agent" gets thrown around a lot, but in most tools it means little more than a template with a variable substitution. MailClaw takes a fundamentally different approach. Its agents are autonomous reasoning loops — persistent processes that observe context, decide on actions, and execute them without you hand-holding every step.

Under the hood, every MailClaw agent is built on OpenClaw, the open-source agent runtime that MailClaw uses as its foundation.
