OpenClaw provides the primitives: tool calling, memory, state management, and a structured planning layer. MailClaw layers email-specific capabilities on top — SMTP dispatch, inbox monitoring, contact enrichment, deliverability scoring, and sequence orchestration.

Think of OpenClaw as the engine block. MailClaw is the full vehicle — tuned, road-tested, and pointed at your outreach goals.

The Reasoning Loop in Plain English

When you create an agent in MailClaw and give it a goal — say, "Re-engage contacts who opened our last campaign but didn't reply within 5 days" — here's the cycle it runs continuously:

  1. Observe: The agent polls your connected inboxes and MailClaw's internal event stream for relevant signals (opens, clicks, replies, bounces).
  2. Plan: It passes those signals to the OpenClaw planner, which reasons about what action best serves the stated goal right now.
  3. Act: It executes a tool call — send an email, update a contact field, pause a sequence, or fire a webhook.
  4. Reflect: It logs the outcome and updates its working memory, so the next planning step has richer context.

This loop runs locally on your machine at localhost:3100. Nothing leaves your environment unless you explicitly push data to an external CRM like HubSpot or Salesforce via an integration.

How Agents Are Defined: The Agent Config File

Every agent in MailClaw is declared as a YAML config file, which makes them version-controllable, shareable, and easy to audit. Here's a minimal example:

agent:
  name: re-engagement-agent
  goal: >
    Identify contacts who opened the last campaign but have not replied
    within 5 business days. Send a personalized follow-up. If they still
    do not reply after 3 days, mark them as cold and pause outreach.
  triggers:
    - event: contact.opened
    - event: schedule.daily
      cron: "0 9 * * 1-5"
  tools:
    - mailclaw.send_email
    - mailclaw.enrich_contact
    - mailclaw.update_contact_status
    - mailclaw.pause_sequence
  memory: rolling_window_7d
  model: openai/gpt-4o
  smtp_account: gmail-primary

You can deploy this agent from the CLI in one command:

mailclaw agent deploy ./agents/re-engagement-agent.yaml

The dashboard at localhost:3100/agents immediately reflects the new agent, showing its status, last action, memory state, and a full audit log of every decision it's made.

The Tool Layer: What Agents Can Actually Do

An agent is only as powerful as its toolset. MailClaw exposes a rich set of built-in tools that agents can call during the Act phase:

Email Dispatch Tools

  • mailclaw.send_email — Sends a message via any configured SMTP account or OAuth-authenticated inbox (Gmail, Outlook, or a transactional provider like SendGrid or Postmark). The agent automatically selects the best sending account based on deliverability scores.
  • mailclaw.schedule_email — Queues a message for optimal send time based on the recipient's historical engagement window.
  • mailclaw.pause_sequence / resume_sequence — Halts or restarts a contact's position in a sequence without losing their place.

Contact Intelligence Tools

  • mailclaw.enrich_contact — Triggers MailClaw's contact enrichment pipeline to pull company data, job titles, LinkedIn signals, and technographic info before crafting a message.
  • mailclaw.update_contact_status — Writes back to MailClaw's local contact store, or syncs the update to HubSpot, Salesforce, or a custom webhook endpoint.
  • mailclaw.get_engagement_history — Returns a structured timeline of every interaction a contact has had with your campaigns, giving the agent real context for personalization.

Deliverability Tools

  • mailclaw.check_deliverability — Runs a pre-send check against SPF/DKIM/DMARC status, spam score, and domain reputation before any email goes out.
  • mailclaw.rotate_sending_identity — Switches to a secondary sender identity if the primary domain's reputation dips below a configured threshold.

Memory: Why Your Agents Get Smarter Over Time

One of the most underappreciated parts of the OpenClaw architecture is its memory system. MailClaw agents support three memory modes:

  • Rolling window — The agent retains context from the last N days of events. Good for fast-moving campaigns where old context becomes noise.
  • Episodic — The agent stores summaries of past reasoning sessions. Useful for agents that need to recall why a contact was marked cold three months ago.
  • Persistent key-value — Arbitrary facts the agent writes and reads like a scratchpad. Helpful for tracking custom state like "number of follow-ups sent this quarter."

You configure memory mode per-agent in the YAML. All memory is stored locally in MailClaw's SQLite store — no external vector database required, though you can wire in a local Chroma or Qdrant instance if you need semantic search across large contact sets.

How Personalization Actually Happens

When an agent calls mailclaw.send_email, it doesn't just merge a first name into a template. The full call looks more like this internally:

tool_call: mailclaw.send_email
inputs:
  contact_id: "c_48291"
  intent: "re-engagement after open, no reply, day 5"
  tone: "warm, curious, low pressure"
  reference_data:
    - last_opened_subject: "Q3 Partnership Opportunities"
    - company: "Meridian Labs"
    - job_title: "Head of Growth"
    - enrichment_notes: "Recently hired 12 SDRs per LinkedIn"
  constraints:
    - max_length: 120_words
    - no_attachments: true
    - avoid_phrases: ["circle back", "touching base"]

The model composes the email from scratch using all of that structured context. The result is a message that reads like a human wrote it specifically for that person — because the agent actually reasoned about them specifically, not just swapped variables into a pre-written block.

Multi-Account and Multi-Agent Orchestration

MailClaw supports running multiple agents simultaneously, each bound to different sending accounts or contact segments. You might have:

  • A cold outreach agent using a dedicated SendGrid subdomain with aggressive warm-up rules
  • A nurture agent running from your main Gmail via OAuth, handling warm leads
  • A re-engagement agent working a segment of lapsed contacts from Outlook

Each agent runs in its own isolated process within MailClaw, and they coordinate through the shared event bus. If the re-engagement agent marks a contact as cold, the nurture agent picks up that status change and skips them automatically — no manual list hygiene required.

You can see all running agents and their inter-agent signals in real time on the localhost:3100/agents dashboard view.

Practical Tips for Building Reliable Agents

Start With Narrow Goals

Agents with tightly scoped goals outperform generalist ones every time. Instead of "manage all my outreach," write "send one follow-up 48 hours after a first touch if no reply is detected." Narrow goals produce more predictable, auditable behavior.

Always Enable the Audit Log

Every tool call an agent makes is logged to ~/.mailclaw/logs/agent-audit.jsonl by default. Pipe this through mailclaw logs --agent re-engagement-agent --tail 50 during testing to watch exactly what the agent is deciding and why. This is the fastest way to catch unintended behavior before it hits real contacts.

Use Dry-Run Mode Before Deploying

mailclaw agent deploy ./agents/re-engagement-agent.yaml --dry-run

Dry-run mode steps through the agent's first planning cycle and prints every intended action to your terminal without sending anything. It's invaluable before you point an agent at a large segment for the first time.

Set Deliverability Guards

Add a deliverability_threshold to your agent config so it self-pauses if your domain reputation drops:

guards:
  deliverability_threshold: 85
  max_sends_per_day: 200
  bounce_rate_ceiling: 0.02

These guards run before every send call and surface as warnings in the MailClaw dashboard's deliverability panel.

The Open-Source Advantage

Because MailClaw is fully open source and runs locally, you can inspect every layer of this stack — from how OpenClaw constructs its planning prompts to how MailClaw serializes tool call results back into agent memory. If a default behavior doesn't fit your workflow, you can fork it, extend it, or contribute upstream.

This transparency matters for email automation specifically. You're trusting an agent to represent your brand in someone's inbox. Knowing exactly how it reasons — and being able to verify it — is not a nice-to-have. It's the whole point.

articles.title: Building Autonomous Email Agents with OpenClaw and MailClaw
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how to build fully autonomous email agents using OpenClaw and MailClaw — from setting up your local environment to creating AI-driven outreach workflows that research, personalize, and follow up without manual intervention.
articles.content:
What Are Autonomous Email Agents, and Why Do They Matter?

Most email automation stops at scheduling. You write the copy, define the triggers, set the delays, and the tool fires off messages at the right time. That's useful — but it's not intelligent. A sequence that sends the same follow-up to a cold prospect and a warm lead who just visited your pricing page isn't automation doing its job well. It's just a timer.

Autonomous email agents go further. Instead of executing a fixed script, they observe context, make decisions, and adapt — choosing which message to send, when to send it, whether to pause a sequence entirely, or when to escalate a reply to a human. They behave less like a scheduler and more like a thoughtful SDR who never sleeps.

MailClaw, built on the OpenClaw agent framework, gives you the infrastructure to build exactly this kind of system — and because it runs locally at localhost:3100, you maintain full control over your data, your models, and your logic.

The OpenClaw Foundation: How Agents Actually Work

Before diving into MailClaw-specific configuration, it helps to understand what OpenClaw provides under the hood. OpenClaw is an open-source agent runtime that gives tools like MailClaw a structured way to define autonomous workflows. Think of it as the reasoning layer: it handles tool-calling, memory, goal decomposition, and decision loops.

In the context of email, an OpenClaw-powered agent can:

  • Pull enriched contact data and reason about how to personalize an opener
  • Read reply sentiment and decide whether to continue a sequence or trigger a different branch
  • Check deliverability signals before sending and adjust sending time or SMTP account accordingly
  • Write and self-critique draft emails before dispatching them

MailClaw wraps this capability into a clean local dashboard and CLI — so you're not writing raw agent code from scratch unless you want to.

Setting Up Your First Email Agent in MailClaw

Step 1: Install MailClaw and Start the Dashboard

If you haven't already, get MailClaw running locally. Once installed, start the server and open your dashboard:

mailclaw start
# Dashboard available at http://localhost:3100

From the dashboard, navigate to Agents → New Agent. You'll be prompted to name your agent, assign it a goal, and connect it to an email account. MailClaw supports Gmail (via OAuth), Outlook (OAuth or SMTP), SendGrid, and any custom SMTP configuration.

Step 2: Define the Agent's Goal

This is where most people underinvest. A vague goal like "do outreach" produces vague behavior. Be specific. Here's an example of a well-scoped agent goal written in plain language:

"Contact cold leads in the SaaS segment who haven't been emailed in 90+ days. Research each contact using enrichment data, write a personalized three-line opener referencing something specific to their company or role, and follow up twice over 10 days if no reply. If a reply is received, classify intent and either respond directly or flag for human review."

MailClaw parses this goal and maps it to a set of agent tasks: enrichment, drafting, scheduling, reply monitoring, and escalation. You can review and edit each task before activating the agent.

Step 3: Connect Contact Enrichment

An agent is only as smart as the data it has to work with. MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment layer can pull data from your connected sources — including HubSpot, Salesforce, or a local CSV — and augment each contact record with signals like company size, recent news, job title changes, and tech stack.

mailclaw enrich --list prospects.csv --output enriched.json --source clearbit

Once enriched, the agent uses these signals as context when generating personalized copy. A contact who just raised a Series A gets a different opener than one who's been at the same company for six years. The AI isn't guessing — it's working from real data you've already collected or piped in.

Building Agent-Driven Sequences

The Sequence Builder vs. Agent Mode

MailClaw gives you two distinct workflow modes, and it's worth knowing when to use each.

The Sequence Builder is your classic multi-step drip tool — great for nurture campaigns, onboarding flows, or any situation where the logic is deterministic. You define steps, delays, and conditions; the tool executes them reliably.

Agent Mode is for situations where the right action depends on real-time context. Use it for cold outreach, re-engagement campaigns, or any workflow where personalization and adaptability matter more than strict reproducibility.

The two modes aren't mutually exclusive. A common pattern is to use Agent Mode to handle the first-touch and reply handling, then hand off to a Sequence Builder flow for post-meeting nurture or onboarding.

Configuring Agent Branches in YAML

For users who want to go deeper than the UI, MailClaw agents can be defined and versioned as YAML configuration files. Here's a minimal example:

agent:
  name: saas-cold-outreach
  goal: "Reach SaaS founders with personalized cold emails and follow up intelligently"
  model: gpt-4o
  memory: true

steps:
  - id: enrich
    type: contact_enrichment
    source: hubspot

  - id: draft
    type: email_compose
    instructions: "Write a 3-sentence cold email referencing one specific detail from the contact's company. No fluff. Clear CTA."
    tone: professional
    max_words: 120

  - id: send
    type: email_send
    account: gmail-primary
    delay_minutes: 0

  - id: monitor
    type: reply_watch
    window_days: 5
    on_reply:
      classify: true
      if_interested: escalate_to_human
      if_not_interested: stop_sequence
      if_unclear: send_followup

  - id: followup
    type: email_compose
    instructions: "Write a brief 2-sentence follow-up that adds a new data point or insight. Don't repeat the original pitch."
    send_after_days: 5

Save this file and load it into MailClaw with:

mailclaw agent load --file saas-cold-outreach.yaml

You can version-control these files in Git, share them across your team, and iterate on agent behavior the same way you'd iterate on code.

Deliverability: The Variable Most Agents Ignore

An autonomous agent that hammers a single inbox with high volume will end up in spam — or worse, get your domain blacklisted. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools are designed to be part of the agent loop, not an afterthought.

Out of the box, MailClaw monitors:

  • Sending volume per account — automatically throttles if daily limits are approached
  • Bounce rates — pauses sequences when hard bounce rates exceed a configurable threshold
  • Spam placement signals — integrates with tools like Mail-Tester and GlockApps for periodic inbox placement checks
  • Warm-up status — tracks whether a new sending account has been properly warmed before high-volume sends

For multi-account setups — say, rotating across several Gmail addresses or SendGrid subaccounts — MailClaw's agent scheduler distributes sends intelligently based on current deliverability scores, not just round-robin.

mailclaw deliverability report --account gmail-primary
# Outputs: sending score, bounce rate, spam complaints, inbox rate estimate

Practical Patterns That Actually Work

The Researcher-Writer Pattern

Instead of having one agent do everything, split the workload. Create a "Researcher" agent whose only job is to enrich contacts and produce a briefing doc, then a "Writer" agent that reads that briefing and drafts the email. This produces noticeably better output and makes each agent easier to debug and improve independently.

Human-in-the-Loop Escalation

Even the best autonomous agents benefit from a sanity check. MailClaw lets you configure escalation triggers — any reply that the agent classifies as "high intent" or "requires nuance" gets flagged in the dashboard for a human to review before the next action fires. You stay in control of the moments that matter most.

CRM Sync as Agent Memory

Connect MailClaw to HubSpot or Salesforce and the agent treats your CRM as persistent memory. Every email sent, reply received, and enrichment event gets written back to the contact record. The agent can query CRM history before drafting — avoiding the embarrassing mistake of pitching a feature to someone who already churned.

Getting the Most Out of Open Source

Because both MailClaw and OpenClaw are open source, you're never locked into a black box. If the default reply classifier isn't performing well for your use case, you can swap in a custom model. If you need an enrichment source that isn't natively supported, you can write a connector. The agent YAML schema is documented and extensible.

The local-first architecture at localhost:3100 means your contact data and email content never leave your machine unless you explicitly send them — a meaningful advantage if you're handling sensitive B2B relationships or operating under GDPR constraints.

Autonomous email agents aren't a future capability — they're available right now, and MailClaw gives you a practical, production-ready way to build them. Start with a single agent, a narrow goal, and a small contact list. Measure what it does. Iterate. The leverage compounds quickly once you see it working.

articles.title: How to Create a Self-Optimizing Email Agent with MailClaw
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how to build a self-optimizing email agent in MailClaw that automatically tests subject lines, adjusts send timing, rewrites underperforming copy, and improves campaign results over time — all running locally on your Mac.
articles.content:
What a Self-Optimizing Email Agent Actually Does

Most email automation stops at scheduling. You write a sequence, set a schedule, and hope the numbers work out. A self-optimizing email agent goes further — it watches how recipients respond, identifies what's working, adjusts copy and timing on the fly, and feeds those learnings back into future sends. No manual A/B test setup. No waiting for a weekly report before making changes.

MailClaw's AI email agent system, built on the OpenClaw engine, is designed specifically for this loop. Because everything runs locally at localhost:3100, your contact data and behavioral signals never leave your machine — which also means the feedback loop is fast. There's no round-trip to a cloud inference API on every decision.

This guide walks through building one of these agents from scratch: configuring it, connecting it to your sequences, and teaching it what "good" looks like so it can optimize toward real outcomes.

Step 1: Spin Up MailClaw and Create Your Agent

If you haven't already, start the MailClaw server from your terminal:

npx mailclaw start

Once it's running, open http://localhost:3100 in your browser. From the dashboard, navigate to Agents → New Agent. You'll see a configuration panel where you define the agent's role, goals, and the sequences it's allowed to modify.

Give your agent a clear name and set its optimization target. MailClaw supports several built-in targets:

  • Reply rate — prioritizes copy and timing that generates responses
  • Click-through rate — optimizes for link engagement
  • Conversion — tracks downstream outcomes via webhook or CRM sync
  • Deliverability score — focuses on inbox placement and domain health

For most outbound campaigns, start with reply rate. It's the most direct signal and the easiest for the agent to correlate with copy decisions.

Connecting Your Email Accounts

MailClaw supports multi-account sending via SMTP credentials or OAuth. To add a Gmail or Outlook account:

mailclaw accounts add --provider gmail --alias "outreach-main"
mailclaw accounts add --provider outlook --alias "outreach-backup"

For SendGrid or other SMTP providers, use:

mailclaw accounts add --provider smtp \
  --host smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --port 587 \
  --user apikey \
  --alias "sendgrid-primary"

Your agent can distribute sends across accounts automatically, which helps with deliverability by preventing volume spikes on a single domain.

Step 2: Build the Sequence the Agent Will Optimize

Before the agent can optimize anything, you need a base sequence. Open the Sequence Builder in the dashboard and create a simple 3-step outbound flow — a cold intro, a follow-up, and a breakup email. These are the most common patterns for B2B outreach and give the agent enough variation to work with.

Here's the key part: for each email in the sequence, add variant seeds. These are alternative subject lines or opening lines the agent can test. You don't need to write perfect copy — just give it two or three directions:

{
  "step": 1,
  "subject_variants": [
    "Quick question about {{company}}",
    "How {{company}} handles {{pain_point}}",
    "{{first_name}}, saw your post on LinkedIn"
  ],
  "body_variants": [
    "intro_direct",
    "intro_curious",
    "intro_social_proof"
  ]
}

MailClaw's sequence builder accepts this configuration directly in the visual editor or via a .sequence.json file if you prefer to work from the CLI. The agent will begin distributing these variants across your contact list and tracking which combinations drive replies.

Setting Guardrails

Giving an AI agent free rein to rewrite your emails sounds risky — and without guardrails, it can be. In the agent config, set a rewrite threshold: the minimum number of sends before the agent is allowed to retire a variant or promote a new one. A value of 50 is a reasonable starting point for most outbound volumes.

mailclaw agent config \
  --name "outreach-optimizer" \
  --rewrite-threshold 50 \
  --confidence-level 0.85 \
  --max-rewrites-per-cycle 2

The --confidence-level flag tells the agent how certain it needs to be before making a change. At 0.85, it won't swap copy unless it has statistically meaningful evidence — not just noise from a small sample.

Step 3: Enrich Your Contacts for Smarter Personalization

Self-optimization works faster when your personalization signals are strong. MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment pulls in data from public sources and, optionally, your CRM. If you're using HubSpot or Salesforce, connect them now:

mailclaw integrations connect hubspot --api-key YOUR_KEY
mailclaw integrations connect salesforce --instance-url YOUR_URL

Once connected, run enrichment on your contact list before launching the sequence:

mailclaw contacts enrich --list outbound-q3 --fields title,company_size,industry,recent_funding

This gives the agent real signals to work with. When it detects that emails opening with a funding reference get 40% more replies from Series A founders, it can prioritize that variant for contacts who match that profile — even before the local data is statistically significant for those contacts individually.

Step 4: Monitor and Guide the Optimization Loop

Once your sequence is live, the agent starts its work silently in the background. But "self-optimizing" doesn't mean "unsupervised." Open the localhost dashboard and navigate to your agent's activity feed. You'll see a real-time log of every decision it makes:

  • Which variant was sent to which contact segment
  • Reply and click data as it comes in
  • Variant promotions and retirements with the reasoning behind each decision
  • Deliverability signals — open rates, bounce rates, spam complaints per account

This transparency is one of the things that makes MailClaw's open-source design genuinely useful. You can inspect the agent's logic, override a decision if it looks wrong, and even edit the underlying OpenClaw prompt templates in ~/.mailclaw/agents/ if you want to change how the agent reasons about a specific metric.

Reading the Deliverability Panel

A self-optimizing agent that drives replies but tanks your domain reputation is worse than no agent at all. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring runs continuously alongside your campaigns. Watch for:

  • Inbox placement rate dropping below 85% on any sending account
  • Spam complaint rate above 0.08% (Google's threshold for sender reputation damage)
  • Hard bounce rate above 2% — usually a signal that your list needs re-enrichment

If the agent detects a deliverability issue, it will automatically throttle sends on the affected account and flag it in the dashboard. You can configure automatic pausing:

mailclaw agent config \
  --name "outreach-optimizer" \
  --auto-pause-on-spam-rate 0.08 \
  --auto-pause-on-bounce-rate 0.02

Step 5: Close the Loop with Outcome Data

The most powerful version of this setup feeds real conversion data back into the agent — not just replies, but meetings booked, deals created, revenue closed. If you're using Calendly, HubSpot deals, or a custom webhook, you can wire those outcomes into MailClaw's feedback system:

mailclaw webhooks add \
  --event "deal_created" \
  --source hubspot \
  --agent "outreach-optimizer" \
  --weight 10

The --weight parameter tells the agent how much to value this signal relative to a reply (which has a default weight of 1). A booked meeting is worth roughly 5–10 replies in terms of optimization signal — so weight it accordingly.

The goal isn't to automate your judgment — it's to scale it. You decide what outcomes matter. The agent figures out which email patterns produce those outcomes consistently, across hundreds of contacts, faster than any manual process could.

What to Expect After the First Two Weeks

In the first few days, the agent is mostly gathering data. Don't judge it too early. By day 7–10, with a list of 200+ contacts moving through the sequence, you should start seeing the variant distribution shift — low-performers getting retired, winning subject lines getting more volume.

By the end of week two, most users see a 15–30% lift in reply rate compared to their original static sequence — not because the AI wrote magical copy, but because it consistently ran toward what works and away from what doesn't, without waiting for a human to pull a report and make a change.

Because MailClaw is open source, you can also inspect every optimization decision in the ~/.mailclaw/logs/agent/ directory, contribute improvements to the OpenClaw reasoning layer on GitHub, or fork the agent templates for your own use case entirely. The self-optimizing loop is just the beginning of what's possible when your email infrastructure is something you actually own.

articles.title: MailClaw AI Agent: Automating Replies Based on Email Content
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to configure MailClaw's AI email agents to automatically classify incoming messages, trigger intelligent replies, and route conversations — all running locally on your Mac without sending data to the cloud.
articles.content:
Why Automated Email Replies Need More Than Simple Rules

Most email automation tools let you set up rules like "if subject contains 'unsubscribe', remove from list." That works for the obvious cases. But real inboxes are messier. A prospect replies with "Not right now, maybe Q3" — is that a hard no or a soft hold? A lead says "Can you send pricing?" — does your tool know to route that to your sales sequence and not fire back a generic follow-up?

This is exactly the gap MailClaw's AI email agents are designed to fill. Built on the OpenClaw runtime, MailClaw runs entirely on your Mac at localhost:3100, meaning your email content never leaves your machine for classification, enrichment, or decision-making. You get the intelligence of a large language model without the privacy tradeoffs of sending customer conversations to a third-party API endpoint.

In this guide, you'll learn how to configure an AI agent that reads incoming email content, classifies intent, and triggers the right automated response — whether that's a tailored reply, a sequence enrollment, a CRM update, or a human handoff flag.

How MailClaw AI Agents Work

Before diving into configuration, it helps to understand the architecture. Each MailClaw AI agent operates as a pipeline with three stages:

  1. Ingestion — The agent monitors a connected inbox (Gmail via OAuth, Outlook via OAuth, or any SMTP/IMAP account) for new replies or incoming messages matching a trigger condition.
  2. Classification — The OpenClaw-powered model reads the email body, subject, and sender context, then assigns an intent label and confidence score based on your defined schema.
  3. Action Dispatch — Based on the classification result, MailClaw fires one or more actions: send a reply, enroll the contact in a sequence, update a tag, push a field to HubSpot or Salesforce, or escalate to a human queue.

The entire loop runs locally. When you open localhost:3100 in your browser, the dashboard gives you a live view of every agent decision, including which emails were classified, what label was assigned, and what action was taken.

Setting Up Your First AI Reply Agent

Step 1: Connect Your Inbox

If you haven't already connected an account, run the account setup command from your terminal:

mailclaw accounts add --provider gmail --label "outreach-main"

MailClaw will open a local OAuth flow in your browser. For SMTP/IMAP accounts (SendGrid inbound parse, Fastmail, Zoho, etc.), use:

mailclaw accounts add --provider smtp \
  --imap-host imap.fastmail.com \
  --imap-port 993 \
  --label "fastmail-sales"

Once connected, your account appears in the Accounts tab at localhost:3100/accounts.

Step 2: Define Your Intent Schema

This is the most important configuration step. Your intent schema tells the AI agent what categories to look for. Open your project's agents/ directory and create a new agent config file:

# agents/reply-classifier.yaml

agent:
  name: "Reply Intent Classifier"
  account: "outreach-main"
  trigger:
    type: inbound_reply
    sequence: "cold-outreach-q4"

  classification:
    model: openclaw-local
    intents:
      - label: interested
        description: "Prospect expresses interest, asks for more info, or wants to schedule a call"
        confidence_threshold: 0.75
      - label: not_now
        description: "Prospect is busy, wants to reconnect later, or mentions a future date"
        confidence_threshold: 0.70
      - label: pricing_request
        description: "Prospect is asking about cost, plans, or pricing details"
        confidence_threshold: 0.80
      - label: hard_no
        description: "Prospect clearly declines, asks to be removed, or is uninterested"
        confidence_threshold: 0.85
      - label: out_of_office
        description: "Automated OOO reply with no human content"
        confidence_threshold: 0.95

  actions:
    interested:
      - type: enroll_sequence
        sequence: "demo-booking-flow"
      - type: tag_contact
        tag: "hot-lead"
      - type: crm_update
        integration: hubspot
        field: lead_status
        value: "SQL"
    not_now:
      - type: enroll_sequence
        sequence: "nurture-q3-followup"
      - type: tag_contact
        tag: "future-pipeline"
    pricing_request:
      - type: send_reply
        template: "pricing-overview"
        delay_minutes: 0
      - type: notify_human
        channel: slack
        message: "Pricing request from {{contact.first_name}} at {{contact.company}}"
    hard_no:
      - type: unsubscribe_contact
      - type: tag_contact
        tag: "closed-lost"
    out_of_office:
      - type: pause_sequence
        days: 5

Once saved, load the agent with:

mailclaw agents load agents/reply-classifier.yaml

Step 3: Create Your Reply Templates

Templates live in your templates/ folder and support dynamic variables pulled from MailClaw's contact enrichment engine. The enrichment layer automatically fills in company name, role, LinkedIn data, and any custom fields you've synced from Salesforce or HubSpot.

# templates/pricing-overview.txt

Subject: Re: {{original.subject}}

Hi {{contact.first_name}},

Great question — here's a quick overview of how pricing works for 
teams like {{contact.company}}.

{{pricing_block}}

Happy to walk you through it live. You can grab 15 minutes here: 
{{cal_link}}

{{sender.signature}}

The {{pricing_block}} variable can reference a reusable content snippet defined in localhost:3100/snippets, making it easy to update your pricing language in one place without editing every template.

Testing and Monitoring Your Agent

Dry-Run Mode

Before going live, always test with dry-run mode enabled. This runs the full classification pipeline against real emails but does not dispatch any actions:

mailclaw agents run reply-classifier --dry-run --verbose

The verbose output shows you the raw email content, the intent label, the confidence score, and what actions would have fired. This is invaluable for catching edge cases before they hit real leads.

The Live Dashboard

Once you go live, the MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100/agents gives you a real-time feed of agent activity. Each decision log shows:

  • The sender and original message snippet
  • The classified intent and confidence score
  • Every action dispatched and its status (sent, queued, failed)
  • Any manual override flags set by your team

You can click any log entry to review the full email and override the AI's decision if needed — important for edge cases where the model was technically correct but context suggested a different response.

Deliverability Awareness

One thing that distinguishes MailClaw from generic automation frameworks is its built-in deliverability monitoring. When your AI agent sends a reply, it automatically checks against your sending domain's reputation score and applies send-time throttling if your daily reply volume approaches inbox provider thresholds. You can review deliverability health under localhost:3100/deliverability, including DMARC alignment, SPF/DKIM status, and per-domain bounce rates.

Pro tip: If you're running multiple outreach accounts through MailClaw's multi-account support, assign different AI agents to each account. This lets you tune intent schemas per audience — a SaaS sales agent behaves differently than a recruiting outreach agent — without one config bleeding into another.

Advanced Pattern: Human-in-the-Loop Escalation

Not every reply should be fully automated. MailClaw supports a human escalation queue where the AI flags ambiguous or high-value emails for manual review before any action fires. Set a confidence floor in your agent config:

  classification:
    model: openclaw-local
    fallback:
      type: human_queue
      min_confidence: 0.65
      queue_label: "needs-review"

Any email where the highest intent confidence falls below 0.65 gets routed to the review queue at localhost:3100/queue rather than triggering an automated action. This is the right default for early-stage agents before you've had a chance to validate classification accuracy on your specific audience and copy.

Connecting to Your CRM and Stack

MailClaw's agent actions natively support pushes to HubSpot, Salesforce, and Pipedrive via their respective APIs. You configure credentials once in localhost:3100/integrations, and from that point, any agent action with type: crm_update resolves the contact by email address and patches the specified field.

For teams using webhook-based stacks, MailClaw also supports a generic type: webhook action that POSTs the classified intent payload to any endpoint — which means you can pipe decisions into Zapier, Make, n8n, or your own internal tooling without writing a custom integration.

What Makes This Approach Worth It

The combination of local execution, structured intent schemas, and composable actions means your AI reply agent grows with your process rather than fighting it. You're not locked into a vendor's interpretation of what "interested" means — you define it, you refine it, and you own the data.

Because MailClaw is open source and built on OpenClaw, you can inspect exactly how classifications are being made, contribute improvements to the intent pipeline, or swap in a different local model as the ecosystem matures. That transparency matters when the tool is sitting in the middle of your most important sales and customer conversations.

Start with one agent, one inbox, and two or three intent labels. Validate the classifications over two weeks of real replies. Then expand the schema, add CRM actions, and layer in more accounts. That incremental approach consistently produces better results than trying to automate everything on day one.

articles.title: How to Build an AI Email Triaging Agent with MailClaw
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to build a fully autonomous AI email triaging agent using MailClaw — from setting up your local environment to writing agent logic that automatically categorizes, prioritizes, and responds to incoming email.
articles.content:
Why Email Triage Is Broken (And How AI Fixes It)

The average knowledge worker spends 28% of their workweek reading and answering email. For sales teams, support leads, and founders, that number climbs even higher. The irony is that most of that time isn't spent on important email — it's spent on the cognitive overhead of figuring out which emails are important.

That's exactly the problem an AI email triaging agent solves. Instead of you deciding whether an inbound message is a hot lead, a support ticket, a partnership inquiry, or noise, an agent makes that call automatically — and can even take action on your behalf.

MailClaw, built on the OpenClaw agent framework, makes this surprisingly straightforward to set up locally. No cloud dependencies, no per-seat pricing, no vendor lock-in. Just a powerful agent running on localhost:3100 that reads, classifies, and acts on your inbox in real time.

What You'll Build

By the end of this guide, you'll have a working AI triage agent that:

  • Connects to your Gmail or Outlook inbox via OAuth (or any SMTP/IMAP account)
  • Classifies incoming email into categories like Hot Lead, Support Request, Partnership, Spam, and Needs Reply
  • Enriches sender contacts automatically using MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment
  • Routes high-priority emails into a sequence or CRM like HubSpot or Salesforce
  • Drafts or sends templated replies for common categories
  • Surfaces a clean priority queue in your local MailClaw dashboard

Step 1: Get MailClaw Running Locally

If you haven't already, install MailClaw on your Mac. It runs as a local service and exposes a dashboard at localhost:3100.

# Install MailClaw via Homebrew
brew install mailclaw

# Initialize your workspace
mailclaw init

# Start the local server and dashboard
mailclaw start

Once running, open http://localhost:3100 in your browser. You'll see the MailClaw dashboard — your command center for agents, sequences, contacts, and deliverability monitoring.

Connect Your Email Account

Head to Settings → Accounts and connect your inbox. MailClaw supports Gmail and Google Workspace via OAuth, Microsoft Outlook and Exchange, and any provider with standard SMTP/IMAP credentials (SendGrid inbound, Fastmail, Zoho, etc.).

# Or connect via CLI for Gmail OAuth
mailclaw accounts connect --provider gmail --oauth

# For SMTP/IMAP
mailclaw accounts connect \
  --provider smtp \
  --imap imap.yourprovider.com \
  --smtp smtp.yourprovider.com \
  --user you@yourdomain.com

MailClaw stores credentials locally and never sends them to an external service. This is one of the core benefits of the open-source, local-first architecture.

Step 2: Define Your Triage Agent

MailClaw agents are defined in YAML configuration files and powered by the OpenClaw runtime. Create a new agent file in your workspace:

touch ~/.mailclaw/agents/triage-agent.yaml

Here's a complete starter configuration:

name: inbox-triage-agent
description: Classifies and routes inbound email automatically
trigger:
  type: inbound_email
  account: gmail-primary
  poll_interval: 60s

classify:
  model: gpt-4o
  system_prompt: |
    You are an expert email triage assistant. Classify the incoming email
    into exactly one of the following categories:
    - HOT_LEAD: A potential customer or qualified sales prospect
    - SUPPORT: A customer with a problem or question
    - PARTNERSHIP: A business development or collaboration inquiry
    - NEWSLETTER: Marketing or bulk email
    - SPAM: Unwanted or irrelevant email
    - NEEDS_REPLY: Personal or important email requiring a human response

    Return a JSON object with keys: category, priority (1-5), summary (one sentence), suggested_action.

actions:
  - condition: category == "HOT_LEAD"
    steps:
      - enrich_contact: true
      - add_to_sequence: hot-lead-nurture
      - tag: ["lead", "ai-triaged"]
      - notify: slack://sales-channel

  - condition: category == "SUPPORT"
    steps:
      - draft_reply:
          template: support-acknowledgment
          auto_send: false
      - tag: ["support"]
      - webhook: https://hooks.yourcrm.com/support-ticket

  - condition: category == "SPAM" or category == "NEWSLETTER"
    steps:
      - archive: true
      - mark_read: true

  - condition: category == "NEEDS_REPLY"
    steps:
      - pin_to_dashboard: true
      - priority_queue: true

Deploy the agent with a single command:

mailclaw agents deploy triage-agent.yaml

Step 3: Enable Contact Enrichment

One of MailClaw's most powerful features is automatic contact enrichment. When the triage agent identifies a HOT_LEAD, it can look up the sender's company, role, LinkedIn profile, and estimated company size before you've even read the email.

Enable enrichment in your agent config by setting enrich_contact: true (as shown above), then configure your enrichment sources in Settings → Enrichment:

mailclaw enrichment configure \
  --sources clearbit,hunter,apollo \
  --fallback linkedin-scrape

Enriched contact data flows directly into the contact record visible in your dashboard, and can be passed as variables into your email sequences or pushed to HubSpot and Salesforce via the native integrations.

Pro tip: Use enrichment data to personalize your automated reply drafts. A lead from a 500-person SaaS company gets a different opening than one from a solo consultant — your agent can branch on contact.company_size automatically.

Step 4: Build Your Response Templates

For categories where the agent drafts replies, you'll want solid templates. Create these in the MailClaw dashboard under Templates, or via the CLI:

mailclaw templates create support-acknowledgment \
  --subject "Re: {{email.subject}}" \
  --body templates/support-ack.html

Templates support full variable interpolation from both the original email and the enriched contact profile:

<!-- templates/support-ack.html -->
Hi {{contact.first_name | default: "there"}},

Thanks for reaching out. I've received your message about "{{email.ai_summary}}"
and will get back to you within one business day.

{{#if contact.company}}
I see you're with {{contact.company}} — I want to make sure we get this
resolved quickly for your team.
{{/if}}

Best,
{{sender.first_name}}

For hot leads, you can link the template directly into a full MailClaw sequence — a multi-step drip that continues based on whether the contact opens, clicks, or replies.

Step 5: Monitor Agent Activity

Once your agent is live, head to Agents → inbox-triage-agent in your local dashboard. You'll see:

  • A real-time feed of processed emails with their assigned categories
  • Classification confidence scores for each decision
  • Actions taken (sequences enrolled, replies drafted, contacts enriched)
  • Any errors or edge cases flagged for human review

MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools also apply here — if your agent is sending automated replies, you can track reply rates, bounce rates, and spam complaints from the same dashboard to ensure your sending reputation stays healthy.

Reviewing and Overriding Decisions

No AI agent is perfect. MailClaw surfaces a Review Queue for any email the agent classified with low confidence (below a configurable threshold). You can accept the classification, override it, and optionally use your correction to fine-tune the agent's system prompt over time.

# Set the confidence threshold for human review
mailclaw agents config inbox-triage-agent \
  --review-threshold 0.75

Advanced: Chaining Agents for Complex Workflows

Where MailClaw's OpenClaw foundation really shines is in agent chaining. Your triage agent can hand off to specialized sub-agents:

  • A lead scoring agent that queries your HubSpot CRM for existing deal history before deciding on a sequence
  • A reply drafting agent that pulls in context from previous email threads before generating a response
  • A scheduling agent that detects meeting requests and replies with your Calendly link automatically
mailclaw agents chain \
  --primary inbox-triage-agent \
  --on HOT_LEAD lead-scorer-agent \
  --on NEEDS_REPLY reply-drafter-agent

This composable approach lets you build sophisticated email automation without writing a monolithic agent that's hard to debug or maintain.

What This Changes for You

A well-tuned email triage agent doesn't just save time — it changes how you relate to your inbox. Instead of a reactive tool that demands constant attention, email becomes a prioritized queue you check on your terms. Hot leads get followed up faster. Support requests get acknowledged instantly. Noise disappears before it ever reaches your attention.

Because MailClaw runs locally and is fully open source, you're not trusting a third-party SaaS with your email data. The OpenClaw agent runtime, the enrichment pipeline, the sequence builder — all of it runs on your machine, under your control.

Start with the basic config above, run it for a week, and then start tuning. The system prompt, the confidence thresholds, the action conditions — each one is a lever that makes the agent smarter for your specific inbox. Within a few iterations, you'll have something that feels less like automation and more like a genuinely useful collaborator.

articles.title: Using MailClaw Agents to Auto-Categorize Incoming Email
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to set up MailClaw AI agents to automatically sort, tag, and route incoming emails — saving hours of inbox triage and keeping your outreach campaigns running smoothly without manual intervention.
articles.content:
Why Auto-Categorization Changes the Game

If you've ever managed a high-volume outreach campaign, you know the feeling: you send out a thousand emails on Monday, and by Wednesday your inbox is a battlefield. Replies, out-of-office messages, bounces, "unsubscribe me" requests, and genuine sales opportunities are all mixed together in one chaotic pile. Manually sorting through that noise isn't just tedious — it's a bottleneck that slows your entire operation.

MailClaw's AI email agents, powered by OpenClaw, are designed to eliminate that bottleneck entirely. Instead of you reading every reply and deciding what to do with it, a local agent running at localhost:3100 reads, classifies, and routes incoming messages automatically — before you've even had your morning coffee.

The goal isn't to replace your judgment. It's to make sure your judgment is only required for the emails that actually need it.

Understanding MailClaw Agents

MailClaw agents are persistent, event-driven processes that listen to connected mailboxes and act on incoming messages based on rules and AI-powered classification logic you define. Because everything runs locally on your Mac, your email data never leaves your machine — a meaningful advantage over cloud-based automation tools that pipe your correspondence through third-party servers.

Each agent is configured with:

  • A trigger source — a connected Gmail, Outlook, or custom SMTP/OAuth account
  • A classification model — OpenClaw's local LLM or a model you've pointed MailClaw toward
  • Action rules — what happens when a message matches a category
  • Optional integrations — push categorized data to HubSpot, Salesforce, or a webhook

Agents run as background workers that you can monitor, pause, or inspect directly from the MailClaw dashboard or the CLI.

Setting Up Your First Categorization Agent

Step 1: Connect Your Inbox

Before creating an agent, make sure you have at least one mailbox connected. MailClaw supports Gmail via OAuth, Outlook via Microsoft Graph, and any provider via SMTP credentials. Open the dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to Accounts → Add Account, and complete the OAuth flow or enter your SMTP settings.

From the CLI, you can also add an account directly:

mailclaw accounts add \
  --provider gmail \
  --oauth \
  --label "outreach-main"

Step 2: Define Your Categories

This is where most people spend too little time, and it shows in their results. Your categories should reflect the decisions you actually make about incoming email. Generic labels like "positive" and "negative" are a starting point, but a well-designed schema does real work.

A practical category set for outbound sales might look like this:

  • Interested — prospect is engaged, wants more info or a meeting
  • Not Now — prospect asked to follow up later (keep in sequence)
  • Hard No — clear rejection, remove from all sequences
  • Unsubscribe Request — legal and compliance priority, immediate action
  • Out of Office — auto-reply, pause sequence and retry
  • Referral — prospect referred you to someone else
  • Bounce / Delivery Issue — flag for deliverability review

Define these in a YAML config file that your agent will reference:

# categories.yaml
categories:
  - name: interested
    description: "Prospect expresses interest, asks questions, or requests a demo or meeting"
    action: tag_and_notify
    priority: high

  - name: not_now
    description: "Prospect asks to be contacted at a later date or after a specific event"
    action: pause_sequence
    resume_after_days: 30

  - name: hard_no
    description: "Prospect clearly declines and does not want further contact"
    action: remove_from_sequences
    tag: "opted-out"

  - name: unsubscribe
    description: "Prospect explicitly requests to be removed from mailing list"
    action: unsubscribe_contact
    priority: critical

  - name: out_of_office
    description: "Automated out-of-office or vacation auto-reply"
    action: pause_sequence
    resume_after_days: 7

  - name: referral
    description: "Prospect mentions another person or company we should contact"
    action: tag_and_create_lead
    tag: "referral"

  - name: delivery_issue
    description: "Bounce, mailer daemon, or delivery failure notification"
    action: flag_for_deliverability_review

Step 3: Create the Agent

With your categories defined, spin up the agent from the CLI:

mailclaw agents create \
  --name "reply-classifier" \
  --account outreach-main \
  --categories ./categories.yaml \
  --model openclaw-local \
  --watch inbox

Or configure it visually from the dashboard under Agents → New Agent. The UI gives you a live preview of how the model interprets sample emails before you go live — highly recommended for fine-tuning your category descriptions.

Step 4: Configure Actions and Integrations

The real power comes from what happens after classification. MailClaw's action system lets you chain together operations that would otherwise require manual work.

For example, when an email is classified as Interested, you might want to:

  1. Tag the contact in MailClaw's contact database
  2. Pause their current email sequence so they don't receive another automated follow-up
  3. Enrich their contact record using MailClaw's built-in enrichment engine
  4. Push the updated record to HubSpot or Salesforce via the native integration
  5. Send you a Slack or webhook notification so you know to follow up personally

This entire chain is configured in your agent definition:

mailclaw agents edit reply-classifier \
  --on interested \
  --actions "tag:hot-lead,pause-sequence,enrich-contact,sync-crm:hubspot,notify:webhook"

Monitoring Agent Performance

Once your agent is running, the MailClaw dashboard gives you a live feed of classification activity. Under Agents → reply-classifier → Activity Log, you can see every email processed, the category it was assigned, the confidence score the model returned, and the actions that were triggered.

Pay attention to the confidence scores. OpenClaw assigns a probability to each classification decision. You can set a threshold below which emails get flagged for manual review instead of acted on automatically:

mailclaw agents config reply-classifier \
  --confidence-threshold 0.75 \
  --low-confidence-action flag_for_review

This is a sensible default when you're getting started. As you review and confirm low-confidence classifications, you're effectively generating labeled training data that makes your category descriptions — and the model's performance — more accurate over time.

Deliverability Signals From Categorization

Here's an underrated benefit: your classification data is deliverability intelligence. When your agent starts flagging an unusual number of bounce notifications or out-of-office replies from a specific sending domain, that's a signal worth investigating. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools can ingest these signals automatically, correlating reply patterns with your sender reputation health.

A spike in hard bounces from a SendGrid-connected account, for instance, will surface in the Deliverability → Health panel alongside your reply classification data — giving you a complete picture without toggling between tools.

Advanced: Chaining Agents for Full Pipeline Automation

Once you're comfortable with a single classification agent, consider building a chain. MailClaw supports agent-to-agent triggers, so the output of one agent can be the input for another.

A practical example: your reply-classifier agent identifies a Referral email. Instead of just tagging it, it hands off to a second agent — a lead extraction agent — that reads the original email body, extracts the referred contact's name and company, creates a new contact record, runs enrichment, and adds that contact to the top of a targeted sequence. All without you touching a thing.

mailclaw agents create \
  --name "referral-lead-extractor" \
  --trigger "agent:reply-classifier:referral" \
  --model openclaw-local \
  --template extract_referred_contact \
  --on success "create-contact,enrich,add-to-sequence:referral-outreach"

This kind of pipeline is what separates teams running manual outreach at 50 emails a day from teams running intelligent, self-managing campaigns at scale.

Getting the Most Out of Your Agent Setup

A few principles that will save you debugging time and improve classification accuracy:

  • Be specific in your category descriptions. The model uses your description as a prompt. Vague descriptions produce vague classifications. Instead of "positive reply," write "prospect asks a follow-up question, requests pricing information, or suggests a time to meet."
  • Don't over-categorize early on. Start with five to seven categories. You can always split a category later once you understand the actual distribution of replies you receive.
  • Review the flagged queue weekly. Low-confidence flags aren't failures — they're feedback. Use them to refine your category YAML.
  • Test with historical email. Before going live, run the agent against a sample of past replies using mailclaw agents test --inbox-sample 100. Compare the classifications to what you know those emails actually meant.
  • Keep your categories.yaml in version control. Because MailClaw is open-source and runs locally, your entire configuration is just files. Treat it like code.

Auto-categorization isn't magic — it's a well-configured system doing repetitive work so you can focus on the conversations that actually move the needle. With MailClaw agents running locally, you get that automation without surrendering control, privacy, or flexibility.

articles.title: How to Create an AI Agent That Schedules Meetings from Email
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to build an AI agent in MailClaw that reads incoming emails, detects scheduling intent, and automatically books meetings — saving hours of back-and-forth every week.
articles.content:
Why Manual Meeting Scheduling Is Killing Your Productivity

If you've ever spent 20 minutes trading emails just to find a 30-minute slot that works for two people, you already know the problem. Multiply that across dozens of outreach replies, inbound demo requests, or customer follow-ups, and you're looking at hours of low-value work every week. The good news is that this is exactly the kind of repetitive, pattern-based task that AI agents handle exceptionally well.

MailClaw's AI email agent framework — built on top of OpenClaw — gives you the primitives to build a real scheduling agent that runs entirely on your machine. No SaaS subscription. No data leaving your laptop. Just a local agent at localhost:3100 that reads your email, understands intent, and takes action.

What This Agent Will Actually Do

Before writing a single line of config, it helps to be precise about the agent's job. A well-scoped scheduling agent should:

  • Monitor one or more inboxes (Gmail, Outlook, or any SMTP/IMAP account) for replies that signal scheduling intent
  • Extract the contact's name, availability signals, and preferred meeting type from the email body
  • Check your connected calendar for open slots
  • Reply with a personalized scheduling link or propose specific times directly in the email
  • Log the interaction to your CRM — HubSpot, Salesforce, or a local contact store — and update the sequence stage

This isn't a chatbot that mimics scheduling. It's a functional automation that closes the loop without you touching the thread.

Setting Up Your Agent in MailClaw

Step 1: Connect Your Email Accounts

Start by opening your local MailClaw dashboard at http://localhost:3100 and navigating to Settings → Email Accounts. You can connect accounts via OAuth (Google and Microsoft are both supported out of the box) or configure raw SMTP/IMAP credentials for any provider — SendGrid, Postmark, Fastmail, whatever you're using.

From the CLI, you can also add an account directly:

mailclaw account add \
  --provider gmail \
  --oauth \
  --label "outreach-main"

Once connected, MailClaw's deliverability monitor will immediately start tracking open rates, bounce signals, and reply patterns on that account — useful context your agent will use later to prioritize threads.

Step 2: Define the Agent

MailClaw agents are defined in a YAML config file. Create a new file called scheduling-agent.yml in your project directory. Here's a working starting point:

agent:
  name: "MeetingScheduler"
  description: "Detects scheduling intent in email replies and books meetings"
  trigger:
    type: inbound_reply
    accounts:
      - outreach-main
    filters:
      sequence_stage: ["replied", "interested"]

  intent_detection:
    model: openai/gpt-4o
    prompt_template: scheduling_intent_v1
    confidence_threshold: 0.75

  actions:
    - type: enrich_contact
      source: clearbit
      fields: [job_title, company_size, linkedin_url]

    - type: calendar_check
      calendar: google
      duration_minutes: 30
      lookahead_days: 7
      working_hours: "09:00-17:00"

    - type: send_reply
      template: meeting_proposal
      inject_fields: [first_name, proposed_slots, calendar_link]

    - type: crm_update
      provider: hubspot
      stage: "meeting_scheduled"
      log_note: true

Load this config with:

mailclaw agent load scheduling-agent.yml --watch

The --watch flag keeps the agent running and polling for new replies in real time.

Step 3: Customize the Intent Detection Prompt

MailClaw ships with a built-in prompt template called scheduling_intent_v1, but you'll get better results by tailoring it to your context. Override it by creating a file at ~/.mailclaw/prompts/scheduling_intent_v1.txt:

You are analyzing an email reply to determine whether the sender wants to schedule a meeting.

Email body:
{{email_body}}

Sender context:
- Name: {{contact_name}}
- Company: {{contact_company}}
- Previous sequence stage: {{sequence_stage}}

Respond with a JSON object:
{
  "intent": "schedule_meeting" | "more_info" | "not_interested" | "other",
  "confidence": 0.0-1.0,
  "preferred_times": ["extracted time mentions if any"],
  "notes": "brief reasoning"
}

This structured output is what MailClaw uses to decide which action branch to execute. If confidence falls below your threshold (0.75 in the example above), the agent will flag the thread for manual review in the dashboard rather than acting automatically — a sensible safety net.

Enriching Contacts Before You Reply

One of the most powerful things you can do before sending an AI-generated scheduling reply is enrich the contact. MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment can pull data from Clearbit, Hunter, or your own HubSpot/Salesforce records in the same pipeline, before the reply is drafted.

Why does this matter for scheduling? Because the reply template can now be genuinely personalized:

"Hi Sarah — great to hear back. I see you're on the growth team at Acme Corp — I'd love to show you how teams your size are using this. Here are a few times this week that work on my end..."

That's not a mail merge. That's contextual personalization driven by live data. You configure the enrichment fields you care about in the agent YAML, and MailClaw handles the API calls and field injection automatically.

Handling Calendar Integration

Google Calendar and Outlook

MailClaw connects to Google Calendar and Microsoft Outlook Calendar via OAuth. Once connected, the calendar_check action in your agent config will query your actual availability and generate a list of proposed slots. These get injected into the reply template as {{proposed_slots}}.

You can also generate a Calendly-style booking link using MailClaw's local scheduling page, which is served from your dashboard and can be shared externally:

mailclaw schedule create \
  --duration 30 \
  --buffer 15 \
  --title "Quick Intro Call" \
  --public-url https://your-tunnel-url.ngrok.io/schedule/intro

If you need the booking link to be publicly accessible, pair it with a tool like ngrok or Cloudflare Tunnel to expose your local MailClaw instance temporarily.

Proposing Times vs. Sending a Link

There's a strategic choice here. Sending a link asks the recipient to do work. Proposing two or three specific times in the email body often converts better, especially in cold outreach. MailClaw supports both patterns — configure the reply behavior in your template:

template: meeting_proposal
mode: propose_times  # or: booking_link, both

In propose_times mode, the agent writes out specific slots in natural language. In booking_link mode, it appends a self-serve link. The both mode does exactly what it sounds like — a great option for warm leads.

Monitoring and Iterating from the Dashboard

Once your agent is running, open http://localhost:3100/agents/MeetingScheduler to see a live feed of every decision it makes. You'll see:

  • Which emails triggered the agent and what intent was detected
  • Which replies were sent automatically vs. flagged for review
  • Meeting conversion rate (replies that became booked calls)
  • CRM sync status for each contact

This visibility is important. AI agents fail silently when you're not watching them. The MailClaw dashboard gives you a window into every action so you can spot misclassifications early and update your intent detection prompt accordingly.

MailClaw's deliverability tools also run in parallel — so if your scheduling replies start getting flagged as spam (rare, but it happens with high-volume outreach), you'll see the signal immediately and can adjust sending patterns before it damages your sender reputation.

Integrating with Your Existing Workflow

If you're already running outreach sequences in MailClaw's sequence builder, you can attach the scheduling agent as a sequence exit condition. When a contact replies and the agent detects scheduling intent, they're automatically removed from the follow-up cadence — no more sending "just checking in" emails to someone who already said yes.

For teams using HubSpot or Salesforce, the CRM update action in the agent config will move deals to the appropriate pipeline stage and log a timestamped note. This keeps your revenue team's pipeline accurate without anyone manually updating records.

A Few Things to Watch Out For

Building AI agents that act on your behalf requires some discipline. A few practical guardrails worth implementing from day one:

  • Always review before going fully autonomous. Start with confidence_threshold: 0.85 and lower it only after you've validated accuracy on 50+ threads.
  • Cap daily reply volume. Use MailClaw's rate limiting to prevent the agent from flooding threads if something goes wrong: max_actions_per_hour: 20
  • Keep a human-in-the-loop queue. The flagged-for-review queue in the dashboard isn't a fallback — it's a feature. Check it daily until you trust the agent's judgment.
  • Test with a secondary inbox first. Route a test sequence through a non-primary account and manually verify every reply before activating on your main outreach account.

The Bigger Picture

What makes this approach genuinely different from a SaaS scheduling tool is that it's fully yours. The model runs locally, the data doesn't leave your machine, and because MailClaw is open source, you can fork the OpenClaw agent core and customize the scheduling logic as deeply as you need. If your sales process has unusual routing rules, industry-specific language patterns, or a non-standard CRM, you can adapt the agent to fit — not the other way around.

Scheduling meetings is a small problem. But building an agent that solves it end-to-end — reading intent, enriching context, checking availability, replying naturally, and updating your CRM — teaches you the pattern for every other repetitive email task in your workflow. Start here, and the next agent is much easier to build.

articles.title: MailClaw Email Agent: Automatically Summarizing Long Email Threads
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's AI email agents to automatically summarize long, tangled email threads — saving hours of reading time and keeping your outreach context-aware and sharp.
articles.content:
Why Long Email Threads Are Killing Your Productivity

If you've ever opened a sales thread with 47 replies, scrolled to the bottom, and still had no idea what was actually decided — you already understand the problem. Long email threads are one of the most quietly devastating productivity drains in modern work. They bury context, hide decisions, and force you to re-read the same information repeatedly just to stay oriented.

For anyone running outreach campaigns, managing client relationships, or coordinating across teams, this problem compounds fast. You're not just reading one long thread — you're juggling dozens of them across Gmail, Outlook, or multiple SMTP accounts simultaneously. That's where MailClaw's AI email agents change the game entirely.

Introducing the MailClaw Email Agent for Thread Summarization

MailClaw, the open-source AI-powered email automation tool built on OpenClaw, ships with a built-in AI agent framework that you can configure to handle specific, repeatable tasks — including automatically summarizing email threads the moment they cross a certain length or age threshold.

Because MailClaw runs locally on your machine at localhost:3100, your email content never leaves your environment. There's no third-party server processing your sensitive sales conversations or client threads. The AI inference happens on-device, powered by OpenClaw's local model runtime, which makes this approach particularly attractive for teams handling confidential communications.

What the Thread Summarization Agent Actually Does

The summarization agent monitors connected mailboxes for threads that match your defined criteria and generates a structured summary that includes:

  • Key decisions made — any explicit agreements, rejections, or commitments mentioned across the thread
  • Action items — tasks assigned to any participant, with names attached where possible
  • Sentiment trend — whether the conversation is warming up, going cold, or stalling
  • Open questions — unresolved points that might need a follow-up
  • Suggested next step — a recommended reply or action based on thread context

These summaries are surfaced directly in the MailClaw local dashboard, attached to the relevant contact record, and optionally pushed to integrated CRMs like HubSpot or Salesforce as activity notes.

Setting Up the Thread Summarization Agent

Getting this running takes about ten minutes if you already have MailClaw installed. If you don't, spin it up with:

npx mailclaw start

Then open your browser to localhost:3100 and navigate to Agents → New Agent.

Step 1: Connect Your Mailbox

MailClaw supports both OAuth connections (for Gmail and Outlook) and direct SMTP/IMAP configuration. For Gmail, use the OAuth integration to avoid app password friction:

mailclaw accounts add --provider gmail --auth oauth

For Outlook or Microsoft 365:

mailclaw accounts add --provider outlook --auth oauth

You can connect multiple accounts simultaneously — useful if you're running outreach from several sender identities or managing a shared sales inbox alongside a personal account.

Step 2: Define the Agent Trigger

In the dashboard under Agents → Triggers, create a new trigger with the following conditions. You can also do this via the CLI using a YAML config:

agent:
  name: thread-summarizer
  trigger:
    type: thread_watch
    conditions:
      - reply_count: ">= 5"
      - last_activity: ">= 48h ago"
    accounts:
      - all
  actions:
    - summarize_thread:
        model: openclaw-local
        output:
          - dashboard_note
          - contact_record
          - crm_sync: hubspot

Save this as agents/thread-summarizer.yaml in your MailClaw project directory and load it with:

mailclaw agents load ./agents/thread-summarizer.yaml

The agent will begin monitoring immediately and process any existing threads that match your criteria on its first run.

Step 3: Customize the Summary Prompt

One of the biggest advantages of MailClaw being open-source is that you can tune the underlying prompt the AI agent uses to generate summaries. In the dashboard under Agents → [your agent] → Prompt Editor, you'll find the default summarization template. A sales-focused variation might look like:

You are a senior sales analyst reviewing an email thread.
Summarize the following thread in 5 bullet points or fewer.
Focus on: buying signals, objections raised, next steps agreed,
and any deadlines mentioned. Be concise. Use plain language.
Flag if the prospect has gone cold.

Thread:
{{thread_content}}

You can create multiple agent variants — one for inbound support threads, one for outbound sales sequences, one for partnership conversations — and assign them to different labels or folders in Gmail or Outlook.

Connecting Summaries to Your Outreach Workflow

Thread summarization becomes dramatically more powerful when it feeds back into your outreach sequences. MailClaw's sequence builder can use summary data as dynamic variables in follow-up emails.

Using Summary Context in Sequences

Once a thread summary exists on a contact record, you can reference it inside any sequence step using MailClaw's variable syntax:

Subject: Quick follow-up on our conversation

Hi {{first_name}},

Following up on our recent exchange — last we discussed,
{{thread_summary.open_questions[0]}}.

Wanted to make sure that's still top of mind on your end.

{{thread_summary.suggested_next_step}}

This creates follow-ups that feel genuinely context-aware rather than templated, because they literally are context-aware — they're pulling from the AI's understanding of your actual conversation history.

Enriching Contacts Alongside Summaries

MailClaw's contact enrichment layer runs in parallel with thread summarization. When the agent processes a thread, it cross-references participant email addresses against enrichment sources to pull in job titles, company data, LinkedIn profiles, and firmographic signals. This means your summary arrives alongside a fuller picture of who you're actually talking to — without any manual research.

"The combination of thread context and enrichment data is what makes the difference between a generic follow-up and one that actually gets a reply."

Monitoring Deliverability While Agents Run

A common concern when running automated agents against live mailboxes is the risk of triggering spam filters or degrading sender reputation. MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring tools watch for warning signals in real time as your agents operate.

From the dashboard under Deliverability → Health Monitor, you'll see:

  • Bounce rates per sending account
  • Spam complaint trends
  • DMARC and SPF alignment status
  • Reply-to-send ratios across active sequences

The thread summarization agent itself doesn't send any emails — it only reads and processes — so it carries zero deliverability risk. However, if you're feeding summaries into automated follow-up sequences via SendGrid or a direct SMTP connection, those deliverability metrics become essential to watch.

Practical Tips for Getting the Best Summaries

Set a Meaningful Reply Threshold

Triggering on threads with 3+ replies tends to generate summaries that are too thin to be useful. A threshold of 5-7 replies produces summaries with enough substance to actually save you time. For very high-volume inboxes, consider bumping it to 10.

Use Folder Scoping in Gmail

Rather than watching your entire inbox, scope the agent to a specific Gmail label like "Prospects" or "Active Deals." This prevents the agent from churning through newsletter threads and calendar chains, and keeps your dashboard summaries signal-rich.

Review Summaries Before CRM Sync

If you're syncing summaries to Salesforce or HubSpot, consider enabling the review queue in MailClaw's agent settings. This routes every summary through a lightweight approval step in the dashboard before it writes to your CRM. It adds 30 seconds of overhead but prevents AI hallucinations from polluting your deal notes.

Run a Weekly Digest

Beyond real-time summarization, you can schedule the agent to generate a weekly digest of all threads that have gone quiet for more than 7 days. It's an effortless way to resurface deals that slipped through the cracks:

mailclaw agents run thread-summarizer --mode digest --since 7d --output email

What This Unlocks at Scale

When you combine thread summarization with MailClaw's multi-account support, sequence builder, and contact enrichment, you end up with something that functions less like an email client and more like an intelligent sales assistant that never forgets a conversation. You stop spending cognitive energy tracking context across dozens of threads and start spending it on the conversations that actually need your attention.

Because the entire stack is open-source and runs locally, you're also free to extend it — build custom agents, modify the summarization logic, integrate with internal tools, or contribute improvements back to the OpenClaw ecosystem.

Thread summarization is one of the most immediately practical applications of AI email agents, and it's a strong entry point for teams that are new to automation but ready to stop drowning in their own inboxes.

articles.title: How to Build an AI Agent for Lead Qualification via Email
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how to build a fully automated AI agent that qualifies leads through email — from initial outreach to scoring and CRM sync — using MailClaw's local-first AI email agent framework powered by OpenClaw.
articles.content:
Why Lead Qualification via Email Needs an AI Agent

Manual lead qualification is one of the biggest time drains in any sales or marketing workflow. Your team sends dozens of emails, waits for replies, reads responses, updates the CRM, and then decides whether a lead is worth a call. It's slow, inconsistent, and doesn't scale.

An AI agent changes the equation entirely. Instead of a human reading every reply and making a judgment call, an agent can parse intent, score responses, ask follow-up questions autonomously, enrich contact data in real time, and push qualified leads straight into HubSpot, Salesforce, or any CRM — all while you sleep.

In this guide, you'll build a working lead qualification agent using MailClaw, the open-source AI email automation tool that runs locally on your Mac. Because MailClaw runs at localhost:3100 and is powered by OpenClaw, you own the logic, the data, and the entire pipeline. No third-party black boxes, no per-seat pricing, no vendor lock-in.

What a Lead Qualification Agent Actually Does

Before writing a single line of config, it helps to map out what the agent is responsible for:

  • Initial outreach: Send a personalized cold or warm email to a contact list
  • Reply parsing: Detect intent in replies — interested, not interested, objection, question, out of office
  • Follow-up logic: Branch the conversation based on what the lead said
  • Lead scoring: Assign a numeric or categorical score based on signals in the thread
  • Contact enrichment: Pull in company size, industry, job title, LinkedIn profile, and more
  • CRM sync: Push qualified leads to HubSpot, Salesforce, or a webhook
  • Handoff: Notify a human (Slack, email digest) when a lead hits a qualification threshold

MailClaw's AI email agent framework handles all of these steps natively. Let's build it from the ground up.

Step 1: Install MailClaw and Start the Dashboard

If you haven't installed MailClaw yet, it takes about two minutes:

# Clone the repo and install dependencies
git clone https://github.com/mailclaw/mailclaw.git
cd mailclaw
npm install

# Start the local server
npm start

Once it's running, open your browser to http://localhost:3100. You'll see the MailClaw dashboard — a clean, local interface where you can manage agents, sequences, contacts, and deliverability from one place. No cloud account required.

Connect Your Sending Account

Head to Settings → Accounts and connect your sending infrastructure. MailClaw supports:

  • Gmail / Google Workspace via OAuth 2.0
  • Outlook / Microsoft 365 via OAuth
  • SendGrid, Mailgun, Postmark via SMTP or API key
  • Any custom SMTP server

For a lead qualification agent, it's worth using a dedicated sending domain with proper SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records. MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitor will flag any DNS issues before your first send — a small step that makes a big difference in inbox placement.
