Step 2: Import and Enrich Your Contact List

Navigate to Contacts → Import and upload a CSV. At minimum, you need a name, email, and company. But the richer your starting data, the better your agent will personalize outreach.

After import, trigger MailClaw's contact enrichment pass:

# Via CLI
mailclaw contacts enrich --list leads-q1.csv --provider clearbit

The enrichment engine pulls company size, industry vertical, LinkedIn URL, estimated revenue, and tech stack data. This context feeds directly into your agent's personalization layer — so instead of a generic opener, your first email might reference that the prospect just raised a Series B or recently posted a job for a VP of Sales.

Tip: MailClaw supports multiple enrichment providers. Clearbit and Apollo work well for B2B. If you're running on a budget, the built-in OpenClaw enrichment model can infer context from the email domain and LinkedIn data alone.

Step 3: Define Your Agent's Qualification Logic

This is where MailClaw diverges from a simple email sequencer. Instead of a linear drip campaign, you're defining a stateful agent that makes decisions based on what a lead does and says.

In the dashboard, go to Agents → New Agent and give it a name. Then define your qualification criteria — these are the signals the agent uses to score a lead:

# agent.config.yaml
name: "Lead Qualifier v1"
model: openClaw-turbo
qualification_threshold: 70

signals:
  - type: reply_intent
    value: interested
    weight: 40
  - type: reply_intent
    value: asked_question
    weight: 20
  - type: enrichment
    field: company_size
    condition: gte
    value: 50
    weight: 15
  - type: enrichment
    field: title_seniority
    condition: in
    value: ["Director", "VP", "C-Suite", "Head of"]
    weight: 15
  - type: behavior
    event: opened_email
    count: 2
    weight: 10

A lead that replies with interest, works at a company of 50+ people, holds a senior title, and has opened your email twice will score 100 — well above the 70-point qualification threshold. The agent will mark them as SQL (Sales Qualified Lead) and trigger a CRM sync.

Step 4: Build the Email Sequence

With your agent logic defined, head to Sequences → New Sequence and build the conversation flow. The sequence builder uses a branching canvas — not just a linear list of steps.

Touchpoint 1: The Opener

Keep this short. The agent will personalize it using enriched contact data:

Subject: Quick question, {{first_name}}

Hi {{first_name}},

I noticed {{company_name}} recently {{enrichment.recent_signal}} — 
congrats on that.

We help {{enrichment.industry}} teams like yours [one-line value prop].

Worth a quick 15-minute call this week?

— {{sender_name}}

Branch: If They Reply

The agent reads the reply using OpenClaw's intent classifier. Depending on the detected intent, it routes to the right branch:

  • Interested / Positive: Agent replies with a calendar link and marks lead as SQL
  • Has a question / Objection: Agent generates a contextual response, answers the question, and re-engages
  • Not now / Nurture: Contact is moved to a long-term nurture sequence with lower frequency
  • Unsubscribe / Hard no: Agent immediately suppresses the contact and logs the reason

Branch: If No Reply (Touchpoints 2 and 3)

For non-responders, the agent sends two follow-ups over 10 days, each with a different angle — a case study, a relevant insight, or a softer ask. If there's still no reply, the contact is either moved to a low-touch nurture list or suppressed, depending on your config.

Step 5: Connect to Your CRM

When a lead crosses the qualification threshold, you want the data in your CRM instantly. MailClaw ships with native integrations for HubSpot and Salesforce, and a flexible webhook for everything else.

# Push qualified leads to HubSpot
mailclaw integrations connect hubspot --api-key YOUR_KEY

# Or use a webhook for custom CRMs
mailclaw integrations connect webhook \
  --url https://your-crm.com/api/leads \
  --trigger agent.qualified \
  --payload '{"email": "{{email}}", "score": "{{score}}", "company": "{{company}}"}'

You can also set up a Slack notification so your sales team gets a real-time ping whenever the agent qualifies a lead — complete with the lead's score, enrichment summary, and a link to the full email thread in the MailClaw dashboard.

Step 6: Monitor Deliverability and Agent Performance

An agent is only as good as its inbox placement. In the dashboard under Deliverability, MailClaw tracks:

  • Open rates and reply rates per sequence step
  • Bounce and spam complaint rates
  • Domain health (SPF, DKIM, DMARC status)
  • Sending volume and warmup curve

Under Agent Analytics, you'll see how many leads entered the funnel, how many were scored and qualified, what intent categories are most common in replies, and where leads are dropping off. This feedback loop is how you tune your qualification signals over time — raise the weight on a signal that's proving predictive, or drop one that's adding noise.

Putting It All Together

A lead qualification agent built in MailClaw isn't a set-it-and-forget-it tool. It's a living system that gets smarter as you tune the scoring weights, improve your email copy based on reply patterns, and expand enrichment sources.

The real advantage of running this locally with MailClaw is control. Your contact data never leaves your machine. Your agent logic is version-controlled YAML. Your OpenClaw model can be swapped, fine-tuned, or replaced. You're not renting a feature — you're building infrastructure.

Start with a small list of 50–100 contacts, run the agent, read the replies yourself for the first week, and compare your human judgments to the agent's scoring. You'll quickly find where to tighten the logic — and within a few iterations, you'll have an agent that qualifies leads faster, more consistently, and at far greater scale than any manual process could.

articles.title: Using MailClaw to Create Agents That Draft Personalized Responses
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how to build AI email agents in MailClaw that automatically draft personalized responses based on contact data, conversation history, and enrichment signals — so your outreach feels human even at scale.
articles.content:
Why Personalized Responses Still Win (And Why They're Hard to Scale)

Everyone knows personalization drives better email results. Studies consistently show that emails with personalized content see significantly higher reply rates than generic blasts. The problem isn't knowledge — it's execution. Writing a genuinely tailored response to every inbound lead, reply, or inquiry is time-consuming, and most teams simply can't keep up once volume picks up.

This is exactly the gap MailClaw's AI email agents are designed to fill. Rather than replacing your voice, they learn the context around each contact — their role, company, recent activity, pain points, and conversation history — and draft responses that sound like you wrote them, not a template engine. Because MailClaw runs locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, all of that context stays on your machine. No SaaS middleman. No data leaving your environment.

Understanding MailClaw's Agent Architecture

MailClaw is built on OpenClaw, an open-source AI orchestration layer that manages how agents read inputs, reason through context, and generate outputs. When you create a drafting agent in MailClaw, you're essentially configuring an OpenClaw pipeline that connects four things:

  • Trigger: An inbound email, a reply in a sequence, or a manual kick-off
  • Contact enrichment: Data pulled from your enrichment sources (more on this below)
  • Reasoning instructions: Your agent's system prompt and behavioral rules
  • Output: A draft dropped into your outbox or flagged for review in the local dashboard

The key insight is that the draft isn't generated from a template — it's generated from context. The richer the context, the better the draft. That's why contact enrichment is the first thing you should configure before building any agent.

Step 1: Set Up Contact Enrichment

Before your agent can personalize anything, it needs data. MailClaw's contact enrichment layer can pull from multiple sources depending on your stack. Open your MailClaw config file to get started:

# ~/.mailclaw/config.yml

enrichment:
  providers:
    - name: clearbit
      api_key: YOUR_CLEARBIT_KEY
    - name: hunter
      api_key: YOUR_HUNTER_KEY
  crm_sync:
    provider: hubspot
    api_key: YOUR_HUBSPOT_KEY
    fields:
      - company
      - jobtitle
      - recent_activity
      - lifecycle_stage

If you're using Salesforce instead of HubSpot, swap the provider value to salesforce and add your OAuth credentials. MailClaw supports both out of the box. Once enrichment is active, every contact your agent processes gets automatically hydrated with company size, role seniority, industry, and any CRM notes before a single word of the draft is written.

You can verify enrichment is working by visiting your local dashboard at localhost:3100/contacts and clicking into any contact record. You'll see a live enrichment panel showing exactly what data the agent has access to when composing.

Step 2: Create Your First Drafting Agent

MailClaw agents are created via the CLI or directly in the dashboard. Here's the CLI approach, which gives you more control:

mailclaw agent create \
  --name "inbound-reply-drafter" \
  --trigger inbound_reply \
  --account work@yourcompany.com \
  --draft-mode review \
  --enrichment enabled

The --draft-mode review flag is important when you're just getting started. It means every draft the agent produces will appear in your dashboard inbox queue for approval before anything is sent. Once you trust the quality, you can switch to --draft-mode auto for hands-free operation on lower-stakes replies.

After running this command, MailClaw will prompt you to write the agent's system instructions. This is where most of the magic happens.

Writing Effective Agent Instructions

Think of the system instructions as a briefing you'd give a new team member before letting them handle your inbox. Here's a solid starting template:

You are a helpful sales assistant drafting email replies on behalf of [Your Name] at [Company].

Your job is to write a personalized, concise reply to the inbound email below.

Rules:
- Reference the sender's company or role naturally if enrichment data is available
- Match the tone of the original message (formal if they're formal, casual if they're casual)
- Keep replies under 150 words unless the topic demands more
- Never make up facts about the sender's company — only use provided enrichment data
- End with a clear, low-friction next step
- Do not use phrases like "I hope this email finds you well"

Available contact context:
{{contact.name}}, {{contact.jobtitle}} at {{contact.company}}
CRM notes: {{contact.crm_notes}}
Lifecycle stage: {{contact.lifecycle_stage}}

The double-brace variables are MailClaw's templating syntax, which gets populated by the enrichment layer before the prompt is sent to the underlying OpenClaw model. You can preview what a fully-resolved prompt looks like for any contact from the agent detail page at localhost:3100/agents/inbound-reply-drafter.

Step 3: Integrate With Your Email Accounts

MailClaw supports both SMTP configuration and OAuth-based connections. For Gmail and Google Workspace, OAuth is the recommended path because it handles token refresh automatically and respects Gmail's API rate limits properly:

mailclaw account connect \
  --provider gmail \
  --email work@yourcompany.com \
  --oauth

For Outlook and Microsoft 365, the flow is identical — just swap gmail for outlook. If you're routing through SendGrid for deliverability reasons, you can add it as an SMTP relay while still reading inbound replies via your native inbox connection. This separation of sending infrastructure from reading infrastructure is one of MailClaw's more underrated features.

Multi-account support means you can run separate agents for each inbox. A common setup is one agent for your main sales email, a second for a shared hello@ address, and a third monitoring a support alias — each with different instructions and tone settings.

Step 4: Monitor Quality With the Dashboard

Once your agent is running, open localhost:3100/agents to see the drafts queue. Each draft shows:

  • The original inbound message it was responding to
  • The enrichment data that was used
  • The resolved prompt (so you can debug why it said what it said)
  • The draft itself, fully editable before approval

This transparency is one of the biggest advantages of building on an open-source local stack. You're not trusting a black box — you can inspect every step of the reasoning chain.

Deliverability Monitoring

High reply volume from agents can occasionally trigger spam filters if you're not careful. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring panel at localhost:3100/deliverability tracks your domain's sending reputation, bounce rates, and spam complaint signals in real time. If your bounce rate starts creeping up, you'll see a warning before it becomes a problem. Pair this with MailClaw's built-in sending throttle settings to keep your outreach inside safe daily volume windows per account.

Advanced: Chaining Agents With Sequences

Where things get genuinely powerful is combining the drafting agent with MailClaw's sequence builder. Rather than just reacting to inbound replies, you can build proactive sequences where each follow-up is dynamically drafted based on how the previous message was received and what new enrichment data has come in since.

For example, a sequence step configured with --step-type agent_draft will pause before sending, generate a personalized draft for that specific contact at that specific moment in the sequence, and queue it for review. The result is outreach that evolves with the conversation rather than running on rails.

mailclaw sequence add-step \
  --sequence my-outbound-seq \
  --step-number 3 \
  --step-type agent_draft \
  --agent inbound-reply-drafter \
  --delay-days 3

Pro tip: Set different agents for different sequence stages. An early-stage prospecting email needs a different tone and angle than a follow-up to someone who already replied once. Keeping agents specialized makes their output consistently better than trying to handle everything with one general-purpose agent.

What Good Looks Like

After a week of running a well-configured drafting agent, most MailClaw users settle into a rhythm where they spend about ten minutes a day reviewing and approving drafts rather than writing from scratch. The agent handles the research, the context-assembly, and the initial language — you handle the final judgment call and hit send.

That's the right division of labor. The goal isn't to remove humans from the loop. It's to make the human's time in the loop actually worth something, focused on decisions rather than busywork.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your own machine, you also have full control to extend the agent logic, swap in different underlying models through OpenClaw's model configuration, or integrate custom enrichment sources that aren't in the default provider list. The foundation is there — what you build on top of it is up to you.

articles.title: How to Build a Customer Support Email Agent with MailClaw
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to build a fully automated customer support email agent using MailClaw's AI agent framework — from initial setup and SMTP configuration to writing intelligent response logic and monitoring deliverability from your local dashboard.
articles.content:
Why Customer Support Email Agents Are Worth Building

Customer support inboxes are relentless. Whether you're a solo founder handling your own support queue or a small team drowning in repetitive questions about shipping times, refund policies, and account issues, the math is brutal: every hour spent triaging email is an hour not spent on product, growth, or customers who need real human attention.

An AI email agent changes that equation. Instead of routing every message manually, you deploy an agent that reads incoming emails, classifies intent, drafts context-aware replies, and either sends them automatically or queues them for a quick human approval. MailClaw — built on OpenClaw and running entirely on your local machine at localhost:3100 — gives you all the infrastructure to build this without shipping your customer data to a third-party SaaS platform.

This guide walks you through building a working customer support email agent from scratch. By the end, you'll have an agent that handles common support categories, escalates edge cases intelligently, and logs everything to your local dashboard.

What You'll Need Before You Start

MailClaw runs locally, so setup is refreshingly lightweight. Before diving into agent configuration, make sure you have:

  • MailClaw installed on your Mac (brew install mailclaw or pulled from the GitHub repo)
  • A connected email account — Gmail via OAuth or Outlook via OAuth work out of the box; you can also wire in a SendGrid SMTP relay for higher send volumes
  • An OpenAI API key (or a locally hosted model via Ollama if you want to keep everything fully offline)
  • A basic understanding of your support taxonomy — what categories of questions do your customers actually ask?

If you haven't connected an account yet, spin up the dashboard first:

mailclaw start
# Opens automatically at localhost:3100

From the Accounts tab, click Add Account and authenticate with Google or Microsoft OAuth. For SendGrid, paste your API key into the SMTP credentials field — MailClaw will validate the connection before saving.

Designing Your Agent's Intent Structure

Before writing a single line of configuration, map out the intent categories your agent will handle. A well-scoped agent that handles five intents well is far more valuable than a vague agent that handles fifty intents badly.

For a typical SaaS or e-commerce support queue, a solid starting set looks like this:

  • billing_inquiry — questions about invoices, charges, payment methods
  • account_access — password resets, login issues, 2FA problems
  • feature_question — how-to questions about your product
  • refund_request — explicit requests for money back
  • bug_report — something is broken, here's what happened
  • escalation_needed — anything angry, legal, or ambiguous enough to need a human

Write these down. You'll use them as the classification taxonomy in your agent config.

Building the Agent in MailClaw

Step 1 — Create a New Agent

From the Agents section in the localhost dashboard, click New Agent and give it a descriptive name like support-inbox-agent. Alternatively, scaffold it from the CLI:

mailclaw agent create support-inbox-agent \
  --type email \
  --account support@yourcompany.com \
  --trigger inbound

The --trigger inbound flag tells MailClaw to activate this agent whenever a new email arrives in the connected inbox, rather than on a schedule or manual trigger.

Step 2 — Write the Classification Prompt

Open the agent's agent.yaml file. This is where you define the AI behavior. The classify step runs first and assigns an intent label to each incoming email:

name: support-inbox-agent
trigger: inbound
account: support@yourcompany.com
auto_send: false  # Queue for approval by default

steps:
  - name: classify
    type: ai_classify
    prompt: |
      You are a support triage assistant. Read the following customer email 
      and classify it into exactly one of these categories:
      billing_inquiry, account_access, feature_question, 
      refund_request, bug_report, escalation_needed.

      Respond with only the category label. No explanation.

      Email subject: {{email.subject}}
      Email body: {{email.body}}

    output: intent

The {{email.subject}} and {{email.body}} are MailClaw's built-in template variables — they populate automatically from the incoming message.

Step 3 — Add Response Generation

After classification, add a draft_reply step that uses the resolved intent to pull the right context and generate an appropriate response:

  - name: draft_reply
    type: ai_compose
    prompt: |
      You are a friendly and professional customer support agent for Acme Inc.
      The customer's email has been classified as: {{intent}}

      Write a helpful, concise reply. Be warm but efficient. 
      Do not make up specific account details — if you need to look 
      something up, say you'll follow up within one business day.

      If the intent is escalation_needed, do not draft a reply. 
      Instead, output only: ESCALATE

      Customer email:
      Subject: {{email.subject}}
      Body: {{email.body}}

    output: draft

Step 4 — Handle Escalations Separately

Add a conditional branch so that escalations get routed to a human immediately rather than sitting in a draft queue:

  - name: route
    type: conditional
    condition: "{{draft}} == 'ESCALATE'"
    if_true:
      - type: notify
        channel: email
        to: senior-support@yourcompany.com
        subject: "⚠️ Escalation needed: {{email.subject}}"
        body: "Forwarding for human review:\n\n{{email.body}}"
    if_false:
      - type: queue_draft
        to: "{{email.from}}"
        subject: "Re: {{email.subject}}"
        body: "{{draft}}"

With auto_send: false set at the top of the config, all non-escalation drafts land in your MailClaw Drafts Queue on the dashboard. You can review, edit, and approve them with a single click before anything goes out.

Enriching Contacts for Better Context

Generic replies are fine. Personalized replies that reference a customer's plan tier or account history are better. MailClaw's contact enrichment layer can pull data into your agent before the reply step runs.

If you have a HubSpot or Salesforce CRM connected, add an enrichment step between classification and reply drafting:

  - name: enrich_contact
    type: enrich
    source: hubspot
    lookup_field: email
    lookup_value: "{{email.from}}"
    output: contact

Now your prompt can reference {{contact.plan}}, {{contact.signup_date}}, or any other field your CRM tracks. A billing inquiry from an enterprise customer on a $500/month plan should read very differently from one coming from a free tier user — your agent can now make that distinction automatically.

Monitoring Deliverability and Agent Performance

An agent that sends replies no one receives is worse than useless. MailClaw's built-in deliverability tools track bounce rates, spam classification signals, and reply rates right from the localhost dashboard.

Navigate to Analytics → Agent Performance and filter by support-inbox-agent. Key metrics to watch in the first two weeks:

  • Classification accuracy — are intents being tagged correctly? Sample 20 emails per day and spot-check manually
  • Draft approval rate — if you're approving 95%+ of drafts unchanged, consider enabling auto_send: true for low-risk intents like feature_question
  • Escalation rate — if more than 20% of emails are escalating, your prompt taxonomy needs tightening
  • Bounce rate — should stay below 2%; if it creeps up, check your SPF/DKIM records in the Deliverability tab

Iterating Toward Full Automation

The configuration above starts conservative — everything queues for approval. That's intentional. AI agents for customer support should earn autonomy incrementally.

A healthy progression looks like this:

  1. Week 1–2: Full manual approval on all drafts. Review every reply, note where the AI goes wrong.
  2. Week 3: Enable auto_send: true for your two most predictable intents (usually account_access and feature_question).
  3. Month 2: Add canned knowledge base snippets as retrieval context so the agent can quote actual documentation rather than generalizing.
  4. Month 3: Expand to multi-account support if you have regional inboxes or product-specific queues — MailClaw handles multiple accounts from the same dashboard.

The goal isn't to remove humans from support — it's to remove humans from the parts of support that don't require them. Your team's time is better spent on the 10% of tickets that genuinely need empathy and judgment, not the 90% asking how to reset a password.

Going Further with MailClaw's Open Source Foundation

Because MailClaw is open source and built on OpenClaw, none of this is a black box. You can inspect exactly how agent steps are processed, extend the platform with custom step types, or contribute integrations for tools your team already uses. The agent YAML format is designed to be readable by non-engineers, which means your support team lead can adjust triage logic without filing a ticket with engineering.

If you want to explore what else is possible — like building outbound sequences that trigger based on support ticket resolution, or using the sequence builder to send proactive status update emails during incidents — the MailClaw docs and the OpenClaw GitHub repository are both worth an afternoon of reading.

Customer support email is one of the highest-leverage places to apply AI automation precisely because the patterns are so repetitive and the data is so structured. Start with this agent, get it working, then keep pushing the boundary of what it can handle autonomously.

articles.title: MailClaw AI Agent: Detecting Email Sentiment and Escalating Automatically
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to configure MailClaw's AI email agents to automatically detect sentiment in incoming replies and escalate hot leads, angry customers, or urgent requests — without ever writing a complex workflow from scratch.
articles.content:
Why Sentiment Detection Changes Everything in Email Outreach

Most email automation tools treat replies as a binary signal: someone either replied or they didn't. But anyone who has run a cold outreach campaign or a customer success sequence knows that how someone replies matters just as much as the fact that they replied at all. A furious "take me off your list immediately" and an enthusiastic "yes, let's talk this week" both count as replies — but they demand completely different responses.

That's the gap MailClaw's AI email agents are designed to close. Running locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, MailClaw uses its OpenClaw-powered intelligence layer to read incoming replies in context, classify their sentiment, and trigger escalation rules automatically — so your team responds to the right signals at the right time, every time.

How MailClaw's AI Agents Read Incoming Replies

When a reply lands in a connected inbox — whether that's Gmail via OAuth, Outlook via Microsoft's OAuth flow, or a custom SMTP account — MailClaw's agent pipeline intercepts the message before it's processed by your sequence logic. The OpenClaw reasoning engine analyzes the full message thread, not just the latest reply, giving it the context it needs to make accurate classifications.

Each reply gets scored across several dimensions:

  • Sentiment polarity: Positive, neutral, or negative tone
  • Intent signals: Interest, objection, unsubscribe request, complaint, or question
  • Urgency markers: Words and phrasing that suggest time sensitivity
  • Buying signals: Phrases indicating readiness to move forward (pricing questions, availability requests, referrals to decision-makers)

These scores are stored against the contact record inside MailClaw and can be used to trigger escalation rules, pause sequences, update CRM records, or fire webhooks to tools like HubSpot or Salesforce.

Setting Up Sentiment-Based Escalation in MailClaw

Step 1: Connect Your Inbox

Open your local dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to Accounts → Add Account. Choose your provider — Gmail, Outlook, or custom SMTP — and authenticate. MailClaw stores credentials locally; nothing is sent to an external server.

# Or configure via CLI
mailclaw account add \
  --provider gmail \
  --oauth \
  --label "Outreach Primary"

Once connected, incoming replies to any active sequence will automatically flow through the AI agent pipeline.

Step 2: Enable the Sentiment Agent

From the dashboard, go to Agents → New Agent and select the Reply Sentiment Classifier template. This pre-built agent is powered by OpenClaw and requires zero prompt engineering to get started. You can, however, customize its behavior for your specific industry or audience.

# Enable via CLI
mailclaw agent create \
  --template reply-sentiment \
  --account "Outreach Primary" \
  --name "SentimentWatcher"

The agent will begin scoring all new replies immediately. Historical replies can be batch-processed using the --backfill flag.

Step 3: Define Escalation Rules

This is where the real power lives. Navigate to Agents → SentimentWatcher → Escalation Rules and define what should happen when a specific sentiment threshold is crossed. MailClaw gives you a clean rule builder in the dashboard, but you can also define rules in YAML for version control:

# escalation-rules.yaml
rules:
  - name: "Hot Lead Escalation"
    trigger:
      sentiment: positive
      intent: buying_signal
      score_gte: 0.80
    actions:
      - pause_sequence: true
      - notify_slack: "#sales-alerts"
      - update_crm:
          provider: hubspot
          field: lifecycle_stage
          value: "Sales Qualified Lead"
      - assign_to: "sales-team@yourcompany.com"

  - name: "Angry Reply Escalation"
    trigger:
      sentiment: negative
      intent: complaint
      score_gte: 0.70
    actions:
      - pause_sequence: true
      - notify_email: "support@yourcompany.com"
      - tag_contact: "needs-human-review"
      - update_crm:
          provider: salesforce
          field: contact_status
          value: "Escalated"

  - name: "Auto Unsubscribe"
    trigger:
      intent: unsubscribe_request
      score_gte: 0.60
    actions:
      - unsubscribe_contact: true
      - pause_sequence: true
      - log_reason: "AI detected unsubscribe intent"

# Apply rules to your agent
mailclaw agent rules apply \
  --agent SentimentWatcher \
  --file escalation-rules.yaml
Pro tip: Set your unsubscribe intent threshold lower than your other rules (0.60 vs 0.80). It's better to err on the side of caution with opt-out signals — both for compliance and for preserving your sender reputation.

Practical Escalation Scenarios

Scenario 1: The Hot Lead Who Replies on a Friday Afternoon

Your sequence sends a follow-up at 10 AM. By 4 PM Friday, you get: "This looks interesting — do you have any slots next week? We're evaluating a few tools right now." Without sentiment detection, this sits in your inbox over the weekend. With MailClaw's agent active, the sequence pauses instantly, a Slack notification fires to #sales-alerts, and the contact's lifecycle stage in HubSpot updates to SQL — all before you've closed your laptop.

Scenario 2: The Frustrated Customer Mid-Onboarding

A customer in a drip onboarding sequence replies: "I've asked this three times and nobody has helped me. I'm seriously considering canceling." MailClaw classifies this as high-negative sentiment with a complaint intent score of 0.91. The sequence pauses, a priority ticket is created, and your customer success lead gets an email notification with the full reply thread attached. The contact is tagged churn-risk and synced to Salesforce automatically.

Scenario 3: Neutral Replies That Still Need Routing

Not every important reply is emotionally charged. Someone who replies "can you send the pricing PDF?" scores neutral on sentiment but high on buying intent. You can build a separate rule layer for intent-only triggers that routes these contacts into a shorter, more direct sequence — bypassing the educational content they clearly don't need.

Connecting Sentiment Data to Your Contact Records

MailClaw's contact enrichment layer stores sentiment history against each contact profile. Over time, you build a picture of how a given contact engages — not just whether they opened your emails (which deliverability tools already track), but how they feel about your outreach at each stage.

This data becomes especially powerful when you export it. From the dashboard, go to Contacts → Export and include the sentiment_history field in your CSV. Import that into HubSpot, Salesforce, or even a Google Sheet to layer sentiment signals on top of your existing CRM data.

# Export contacts with sentiment data
mailclaw contacts export \
  --fields email,name,sentiment_score,sentiment_label,last_reply_intent \
  --format csv \
  --output enriched-contacts.csv

Deliverability Implications of Sentiment Monitoring

There's a deliverability angle to this that's easy to overlook. When MailClaw detects high negative sentiment or unsubscribe intent and automatically removes those contacts from sequences, you're doing more than protecting relationships — you're actively protecting your sender reputation. Continuing to email disengaged or hostile contacts is one of the fastest ways to spike your spam complaint rate and tank your deliverability with Gmail and Outlook's filtering algorithms.

MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring dashboard (accessible at localhost:3100/deliverability) tracks your complaint rate, bounce rate, and engagement score over time. If you notice a correlation between a particular sequence and rising negative sentiment scores, that's your signal to revisit the copy, timing, or targeting before your sending domain takes the hit.

Customizing the OpenClaw Reasoning Layer

For teams with highly specific use cases — legal, healthcare, enterprise software — the default sentiment model may need tuning. Because MailClaw is open source and built on OpenClaw, you can extend the reasoning layer directly. The agent configuration files live in ~/.mailclaw/agents/ and can be edited to include custom classification prompts, domain-specific vocabulary, or alternative escalation logic.

# View your agent config
cat ~/.mailclaw/agents/SentimentWatcher/config.json

# Reload after editing
mailclaw agent reload --name SentimentWatcher

This is one of the clearest advantages of running locally and open source: you're not waiting for a SaaS vendor to support your edge case. You can ship the customization yourself today.

Getting the Most Out of Automated Escalation

A few principles that separate teams who use sentiment escalation well from those who bolt it on as an afterthought:

  • Always pause before escalating. If the AI triggers an escalation, the sequence should stop immediately. Sending the next scheduled email while a human is handling an angry reply is one of the most avoidable mistakes in outreach automation.
  • Log the reason. Use MailClaw's log_reason action in every rule so you have an auditable trail of why a contact was escalated. This matters for compliance and for training your team.
  • Review your thresholds monthly. As your audience evolves, so does the language they use. Pull your false positive and false negative reports from the dashboard and adjust scoring thresholds accordingly.
  • Don't over-automate the response. Sentiment detection is for routing and escalation — not for generating automated replies to emotionally charged messages. Let the AI surface the right signal, then let a human close the loop.

Sentiment-aware automation isn't about removing the human from email. It's about making sure the human shows up exactly when they're needed — and nowhere else.

articles.title: How to Create an Agent That Extracts Data from Emails into Spreadsheets
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to build a MailClaw AI email agent that automatically reads incoming emails, extracts structured data like leads, orders, or support requests, and pushes it directly into a spreadsheet — no manual copy-pasting required.
articles.content:
Why Manual Email-to-Spreadsheet Work Is Killing Your Productivity

If you've ever spent part of your morning copying contact details from inquiry emails into a Google Sheet, or manually logging order confirmations into an Excel tracker, you already know the pain. It's tedious, error-prone, and — frankly — a waste of time that should be spent on actual work.

The good news is that this is one of the most automatable workflows in existence. With MailClaw's AI email agents (powered by OpenClaw running locally on your machine), you can set up an agent that reads your incoming emails, understands their structure, extracts the fields you care about, and writes them directly to a spreadsheet — all without you lifting a finger.

This guide walks you through building exactly that, step by step.

Understanding MailClaw AI Email Agents

Before we dive into the setup, it helps to understand what a MailClaw agent actually is. Unlike a simple filter or rule (the kind you'd set up in Gmail or Outlook), a MailClaw AI agent is a persistent, intelligent process that can read and reason about email content. It uses the OpenClaw engine running on your localhost to understand natural language, identify structured data inside unstructured text, and take actions based on what it finds.

Think of it like having a very fast, very patient intern whose only job is to read emails and fill in your spreadsheet — except they never make typos and they work 24/7.

Agents in MailClaw can be triggered by:

  • New emails arriving in a connected Gmail or Outlook inbox
  • Emails matching specific subject line patterns or sender filters
  • Replies to sequences built in the MailClaw sequence builder
  • Inbound emails forwarded to your MailClaw SMTP listener

What You'll Need Before You Start

Make sure you have the following ready:

  • MailClaw running locally — accessible at localhost:3100 after running mailclaw start
  • A connected email account (Gmail via OAuth or Outlook via SMTP/OAuth — both are supported out of the box)
  • A destination spreadsheet — this guide covers Google Sheets and CSV output, but the same logic applies to Airtable, Notion databases, or even a HubSpot/Salesforce custom object
  • A Google Sheets API key or service account JSON (if routing to Google Sheets)

Step 1: Connect Your Inbox to MailClaw

Open your local dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to Settings → Email Accounts. Click Add Account and choose your provider. For Gmail, MailClaw will walk you through the OAuth flow. For Outlook or custom SMTP setups, you can paste your credentials directly.

Once connected, you should see your inbox populating under the Inbox Monitor tab. MailClaw's deliverability tools will also begin passively tracking bounce rates and sender reputation data for that account — useful if you're also running outbound sequences from the same address.

Step 2: Create a New AI Agent

From the dashboard, go to Agents → New Agent. Give your agent a name — something like "Lead Form Extractor" or "Order Confirmation Logger" — and select Inbound Email as the trigger type.

Set your trigger filter. For example, if you want to capture all emails with "New Submission" in the subject line from your contact form provider (like Typeform or Webflow), set:

Trigger: Incoming email
Filter: subject contains "New Submission"
Account: your-email@yourdomain.com

You can stack multiple filters — sender domain, label, has-attachment — to be as precise as you need.

Step 3: Define the Extraction Schema

This is the core of the agent. You're going to tell MailClaw exactly what data to pull out of each matching email. Navigate to the Agent Logic tab and select Extract Structured Data as the action type.

You'll see a schema editor. Define the fields you want extracted:

{
  "fields": [
    { "name": "first_name", "type": "string", "description": "Sender's first name" },
    { "name": "last_name", "type": "string", "description": "Sender's last name" },
    { "name": "email", "type": "email", "description": "Sender's email address" },
    { "name": "company", "type": "string", "description": "Company name if mentioned" },
    { "name": "message", "type": "text", "description": "The main body of the inquiry" },
    { "name": "received_at", "type": "datetime", "description": "Timestamp of the email" }
  ]
}

OpenClaw will use this schema to intelligently parse each email — whether the data appears in a structured form dump, a plain paragraph, or a forwarded HTML table. It handles messy real-world formats without you needing to write regex or parsing logic.

Tips for Writing Good Field Descriptions

The description field matters more than it might look. OpenClaw uses it as a hint when the data isn't immediately obvious. For example:

  • "Company name if mentioned, leave blank if not found" is better than just "Company"
  • For ambiguous fields, add context: "The dollar value of the order, numbers only, no currency symbol"
  • You can specify fallback behavior: "Use the sender's email domain as company if no company name is given"

Step 4: Route Extracted Data to a Spreadsheet

Once the extraction schema is defined, add a second action step: Send to Integration. MailClaw supports several output targets natively:

Option A: Google Sheets

Select Google Sheets from the integration list. Paste your Google Sheets spreadsheet ID (found in the sheet URL) and map your extracted fields to column headers. MailClaw will append a new row for each email processed.

Integration: Google Sheets
Spreadsheet ID: 1BxiMVs0XRA5nFMdKvBdBZjgmUUqptlbs74OgVE2upms
Sheet Tab: Leads
Column Mapping:
  A → first_name
  B → last_name
  C → email
  D → company
  E → message
  F → received_at

Option B: CSV Export (Local File)

If you'd rather keep things offline, set the output to Local CSV. MailClaw will append rows to a CSV file at a path you specify on your Mac:

mailclaw agent set-output --agent "Lead Form Extractor" \
  --type csv \
  --path ~/Documents/leads-extracted.csv

You can open this file in Excel, Numbers, or reimport it to any CRM later. It's also a solid staging format before you push data into HubSpot or Salesforce via their import tools.

Option C: Webhook / API Push

For more advanced setups — like feeding data directly into a Salesforce custom object or a HubSpot contact creation endpoint — use the Webhook output type. MailClaw will POST the extracted JSON payload to any endpoint you specify, with support for custom headers and authentication tokens.

Step 5: Test and Activate the Agent

Before going live, use MailClaw's built-in Agent Sandbox to run a test. Paste a sample email into the sandbox and click Run Extraction. You'll see the parsed output in real time, including which fields were found, which were inferred, and which came back empty.

mailclaw agent test --agent "Lead Form Extractor" \
  --sample-email ./sample-inquiry.eml

Review the output, tweak your schema descriptions if anything looks off, then click Activate Agent from the dashboard. From this point on, every matching email that arrives in your connected inbox will be automatically processed and logged.

Real-World Use Cases Worth Building

Once you've built one of these agents, the pattern is reusable. Here are a few workflows teams commonly set up:

  • Inbound sales leads — Extract name, company, and need from contact form emails; push to a Google Sheet that feeds a sales pipeline
  • Order confirmations — Parse order ID, amount, and product from transactional emails; log to an accounting spreadsheet
  • Support ticket triage — Extract issue type and urgency from customer emails; route to the right Slack channel and log to Airtable
  • PR and media inquiries — Capture journalist name, outlet, and deadline from inbound pitches; feed a media tracking sheet
  • Job applications — Pull applicant name, role applied for, and email from submission notifications; create a candidate tracker

Keeping It Running Reliably

MailClaw agents run as background processes tied to the OpenClaw engine on your machine. To make sure your agent survives restarts, add it to your startup routine:

mailclaw start --daemon

You can monitor agent activity, see how many emails have been processed, and check for any extraction failures directly in the Agent Logs section of your localhost dashboard. If an email couldn't be parsed — maybe it was an image-only email or the format was too unusual — MailClaw flags it for manual review rather than silently dropping it.

Pro tip: Use MailClaw's contact enrichment feature alongside your extraction agent. Once an email address is extracted, enrichment can automatically append company size, LinkedIn profile, and job title data before the row hits your spreadsheet — giving you a much richer dataset with zero extra effort.

The Bottom Line

Building an email-to-spreadsheet extraction agent in MailClaw takes about 15 minutes the first time, and once it's running, it just works quietly in the background while you focus on higher-value tasks. Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your local machine, your email data never touches a third-party server — which matters a lot when you're processing customer inquiries or sensitive business correspondence.

The combination of OpenClaw's language understanding, MailClaw's flexible integration layer, and the clean local dashboard makes this one of the most practical things you can set up for any team that lives in their inbox.

articles.title: Using MailClaw AI for Intelligent Email Routing and Assignment
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's AI email agents and routing logic to automatically assign incoming replies, leads, and support threads to the right person or sequence — saving hours of manual triage every week.
articles.content:
Why Intelligent Email Routing Actually Matters

If you've ever watched a shared inbox spiral into chaos — sales replies mixed with support tickets, hot leads sitting unread for three days, and no one quite sure who owns what — you already understand the problem. Email routing sounds like a boring infrastructure concern, but in practice it's often the difference between closing a deal and losing one to a competitor who responded faster.

MailClaw's AI email agents, powered by the OpenClaw engine running locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, bring genuine intelligence to this problem. Instead of relying on brittle keyword filters or manual assignment rules, you can train routing agents that understand context, intent, and priority — and act on that understanding automatically.

Understanding MailClaw's Routing Architecture

Before diving into configuration, it helps to understand how MailClaw thinks about routing. At its core, there are three layers working together:

  • Inbound listeners — connected accounts (Gmail, Outlook, or any SMTP/IMAP inbox) that MailClaw monitors for new messages.
  • AI classification agents — OpenClaw-powered agents that read each incoming message and classify it by intent, sentiment, urgency, and contact attributes.
  • Assignment actions — the downstream actions triggered by classification: assigning to a team member, enrolling in a sequence, tagging in HubSpot or Salesforce, or forwarding to a specialized agent.

All of this runs locally, which means your email content never leaves your machine for classification. That's a meaningful privacy advantage over cloud-based routing tools, especially if you're handling sensitive customer or prospect data.

Setting Up Your First Routing Agent

Step 1: Connect Your Inboxes

Open your MailClaw dashboard at http://localhost:3100 and navigate to Accounts → Add Account. MailClaw supports OAuth for Gmail and Outlook (recommended for deliverability) as well as raw SMTP/IMAP credentials for custom domains and SendGrid-backed inboxes.

For a typical sales team setup, you might connect three accounts: a shared sales@ alias, a personal rep inbox, and a support@ address you want to triage separately.

Step 2: Create a New AI Routing Agent

From the CLI, initialize a new agent:

mailclaw agent create --name "inbound-router" --type routing --watch sales@yourcompany.com

This creates an agent config file at ~/.mailclaw/agents/inbound-router.yaml. Open it in your editor and you'll see the skeleton of your routing logic:

agent:
  name: inbound-router
  type: routing
  watch:
    - sales@yourcompany.com
  classify_on:
    - intent
    - sentiment
    - contact_tier
  actions: []

Step 3: Define Classification Rules with Natural Language

This is where MailClaw's OpenClaw integration genuinely shines. Rather than writing regex patterns or point-scoring systems, you describe your routing logic in plain language inside the actions block:

actions:
  - when: "email expresses interest in pricing or a demo request"
    assign_to: "alice@yourcompany.com"
    tag: "hot-lead"
    enrich_contact: true
    sequence: "demo-followup-5day"

  - when: "email is a reply to an existing thread and sentiment is frustrated or negative"
    assign_to: "support@yourcompany.com"
    priority: high
    notify_slack: "#customer-success"

  - when: "email is from a contact with HubSpot lifecycle stage: customer"
    assign_to: "account-management"
    tag: "existing-customer"
    skip_sequence: true

  - default:
    assign_to: "general-queue"
    tag: "needs-review"

The OpenClaw model reads each incoming email against these conditions in order, picks the best match, and executes the corresponding action. You're not writing code — you're writing intent.

Enriching Contacts Before Routing

One of the most powerful things you can do before routing a message is enrich the sender's contact record. MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment pulls data from connected sources and makes it available to your routing agent at classification time.

Enable enrichment at the agent level:

mailclaw agent update inbound-router --enrich-on-inbound true

Now when a new email arrives from cto@bigcorp.com, MailClaw will pull available firmographic and contact data before the routing agent classifies the message. This means your when conditions can reference enriched fields:

  - when: "contact company size is over 500 employees and email expresses interest in enterprise features"
    assign_to: "enterprise-sales@yourcompany.com"
    tag: "enterprise-icp"
    sequence: "enterprise-outbound"

This kind of context-aware routing is extraordinarily difficult to replicate with traditional rule engines. A contact mentioning "we need to scale this across teams" lands very differently when you know they work at a 2,000-person company versus a 10-person startup — and MailClaw can make that distinction automatically.

Routing Replies Within Active Sequences

If you're running outbound sequences through MailClaw's sequence builder, routing gets even more nuanced. When a prospect replies mid-sequence, you almost certainly want to:

  1. Pause or cancel their active sequence immediately
  2. Notify the rep who owns the outreach
  3. Classify the reply intent (positive, objection, unsubscribe, out-of-office)
  4. Route accordingly — a positive reply goes to the rep, an OOO reschedules follow-up, an unsubscribe triggers compliance handling

MailClaw handles this with reply detection built into the sequence builder. When you create a sequence, set the on_reply behavior:

mailclaw sequence edit demo-followup-5day \
  --on-reply pause \
  --on-reply-route inbound-router

Now every reply to that sequence gets handed off to your routing agent for intelligent handling instead of just sitting in an inbox waiting for someone to notice.

Integrating with Your CRM

Routing assignments are only useful if they actually flow into the tools your team lives in. MailClaw's integrations let you sync routing outcomes to HubSpot, Salesforce, and other platforms.

HubSpot

Connect HubSpot in your dashboard under Integrations → CRM, then reference HubSpot owner IDs or pipeline stages in your routing actions:

  - when: "intent is demo request"
    hubspot:
      set_lifecycle_stage: "salesqualifiedlead"
      create_deal: true
      assign_owner: "alice-hubspot-id"

Salesforce

For Salesforce users, the same pattern applies with lead and opportunity objects. MailClaw can create a new Lead record, assign it to a queue, and log the routing decision as an activity — all in the same action block that fires when the email arrives.

Monitoring Routing Performance

Your localhost dashboard at localhost:3100/agents gives you a live view of every routing decision your agent has made. You can see:

  • Which condition matched each email and why
  • Assignment distribution across team members
  • Classification confidence scores (useful for tuning ambiguous conditions)
  • Emails that fell through to the default rule — a signal that you're missing a condition worth adding

Pay close attention to the default-rule volume. If more than 10–15% of your inbound emails are hitting the catch-all, your routing logic has meaningful gaps. The dashboard makes it easy to spot patterns in those unmatched emails and write new conditions to handle them.

Pro tip: MailClaw's deliverability tools also tie into routing. If a particular sending domain starts seeing elevated bounce rates or spam complaints, the deliverability monitor can flag it and your routing agent can automatically deprioritize or quarantine outbound from that account while you investigate.

Tips for Writing Better Routing Conditions

Since MailClaw's routing conditions are interpreted by an AI model, the quality of your descriptions directly affects classification accuracy. A few guidelines that make a real difference:

  • Be specific about signals, not just topics. "Email mentions pricing" is weaker than "Email asks for a price quote, a custom plan, or mentions budget." The more signal-rich your condition, the more accurate the match.
  • Include negative examples when needed. You can use but not clauses: "email expresses interest in features but not from an existing customer".
  • Order matters. MailClaw evaluates conditions top-to-bottom and stops at the first match. Put your most specific, highest-priority conditions first.
  • Test with real examples. Use mailclaw agent test inbound-router --email path/to/sample.eml to run a specific email through your agent and see exactly which condition it matches before going live.

Going Further: Chaining Agents

For teams with more complex workflows, MailClaw supports chaining multiple agents together. You might have a first-pass triage agent that separates inbound from outbound replies, a second agent that handles enterprise-specific routing, and a third that manages compliance and unsubscribe processing. Each agent in the chain can hand off to the next using the forward_to_agent action.

Because everything runs locally on OpenClaw, this chaining happens in milliseconds with no API rate limits, no per-seat pricing, and no external service dependencies. It's one of the architectural decisions that makes MailClaw genuinely different from hosted alternatives.

Intelligent email routing isn't a luxury feature for large teams — it's the infrastructure layer that lets a small team punch well above their weight. With MailClaw's AI agents handling the triage work automatically, your people can spend their time on the conversations that actually require human judgment.

articles.title: How to Build an AI Agent That Follows Up on Unanswered Emails
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to build a fully automated AI follow-up agent using MailClaw that intelligently tracks unanswered emails, personalizes re-engagement messages, and stops sending the moment a prospect replies — all running locally on your Mac.
articles.content:
Why Manual Follow-Ups Are Killing Your Outreach

Most deals don't close on the first email. Research consistently shows that 80% of sales require at least five follow-up touchpoints, yet the majority of salespeople give up after one or two attempts. The reason isn't laziness — it's that manually tracking who replied, who didn't, and when to follow up again is genuinely exhausting at scale.

The answer isn't a rigid drip sequence that blasts every contact with the same message on a fixed schedule. The answer is an intelligent agent — one that monitors your inbox, detects reply signals, personalizes follow-ups based on context, and knows exactly when to stop. That's precisely what you can build with MailClaw's AI email agent system, powered by OpenClaw, running entirely on your local machine.

What Makes an AI Follow-Up Agent Different from a Drip Sequence

A traditional email sequence fires messages based on time delays. It doesn't care whether the prospect opened your email, visited your website, or replied to a different thread entirely. An AI agent, by contrast, is reactive and contextual. It:

  • Monitors your connected inboxes (Gmail, Outlook, or any SMTP account) for reply activity in real time
  • Reads the thread context before composing a follow-up — so it references your original message intelligently
  • Enriches contact data on the fly to personalize each touchpoint
  • Respects reply detection and suppresses further messages the moment a response arrives
  • Escalates or changes tone based on how many attempts have already been made

MailClaw's AI agent layer sits on top of OpenClaw's reasoning engine, giving you a local, private, API-key-optional system that handles all of this without sending your contact data to third-party servers.

Setting Up Your Follow-Up Agent in MailClaw

Step 1: Connect Your Email Accounts

Open your local MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to Settings → Email Accounts. MailClaw supports OAuth connections for Gmail and Outlook (Microsoft 365), plus raw SMTP/IMAP credentials for providers like SendGrid, Fastmail, or any custom mail server.

For Gmail, click Connect with Google and complete the OAuth flow. MailClaw stores the token locally — nothing leaves your machine. For SMTP-based accounts, enter your credentials directly:

# Alternatively, configure via CLI
mailclaw accounts add \
  --name "Sales Outreach" \
  --smtp-host smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --smtp-port 587 \
  --user apikey \
  --pass YOUR_SENDGRID_API_KEY \
  --imap-host imap.gmail.com

Once connected, MailClaw begins polling your inbox via IMAP for reply signals. You'll see a green Sync Active badge next to each account in the dashboard.

Step 2: Import and Enrich Your Contacts

Before building the agent, give it something to work with. Import your prospect list from a CSV, or pull contacts directly from HubSpot or Salesforce via the built-in CRM sync under Contacts → Import.

Then run MailClaw's contact enrichment to fill in missing context — company size, job title, LinkedIn activity, and recent news about their organization. This data is what lets the AI write follow-ups that feel researched rather than robotic.

# Enrich a contact list from the CLI
mailclaw contacts enrich --list my-prospects.csv --output enriched.json

Enriched contacts are stored locally in MailClaw's contact database and become available as variables inside your agent's prompt templates.

Step 3: Create an AI Email Agent

Navigate to Agents → New Agent in the dashboard. You'll see a configuration panel with several key sections:

  • Trigger: What starts the agent — typically "Email sent, no reply after N days"
  • Reply Detection: The IMAP folder and thread-matching logic MailClaw uses to detect responses
  • Max Attempts: How many follow-ups before the agent marks a contact as cold
  • Prompt Template: The instruction set the OpenClaw AI uses to write each follow-up

Here's an example agent configuration in YAML format (you can also build this visually in the dashboard):

agent:
  name: "Cold Outreach Follow-Up"
  trigger:
    type: no_reply
    after_days: 3
  max_attempts: 4
  reply_detection:
    enabled: true
    stop_on_reply: true
    stop_on_bounce: true
  tone_escalation:
    attempt_1: friendly
    attempt_2: curious
    attempt_3: direct
    attempt_4: breakup
  prompt_template: |
    You are following up on behalf of {{sender_name}} at {{sender_company}}.
    The original email was sent to {{contact_name}} at {{contact_company}}.
    Their role is {{contact_title}}. It has been {{days_since_sent}} days with no response.
    This is follow-up attempt {{attempt_number}} of 4.
    Tone for this attempt: {{tone}}.
    Keep it under 80 words. Do not repeat the original pitch verbatim.
    Reference something specific about {{contact_company}} from enrichment data if available.
    End with a single, low-friction call to action.

The tone_escalation block is particularly powerful. Your first follow-up might be a gentle nudge; by the fourth attempt, the agent sends a classic "breakup email" — which paradoxically tends to generate more replies than almost any other message in the sequence.

Step 4: Monitor Deliverability Before You Launch

An AI agent is only as good as the emails that actually reach the inbox. MailClaw includes a deliverability monitoring panel under Tools → Deliverability that checks your DNS records (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), sender reputation, and blacklist status before you activate any campaign.

Pro tip: If you're sending from a new domain or a fresh SendGrid subaccount, let the agent warm up the account by sending to engaged contacts first. MailClaw's warmup scheduler can handle this automatically — set it under Settings → Warmup and give it 2–3 weeks before running cold outreach at volume.

How the Agent Behaves in Practice

Once activated, the agent runs as a background process on your Mac. You don't need to keep the browser tab open — the MailClaw daemon handles everything. Here's the typical lifecycle for a single contact:

  1. You send the initial email manually or via the sequence builder
  2. MailClaw logs the send event and starts a reply-detection watch on that thread
  3. After 3 days with no reply, the agent generates a personalized follow-up using the OpenClaw model and queues it for sending
  4. If a reply arrives at any point, the agent immediately cancels all pending follow-ups for that contact
  5. If no reply comes after 4 attempts, the contact is tagged cold and removed from active sequences — but preserved in your database for future re-engagement

Every message the agent writes is logged in the dashboard under Agents → Activity Log, including the AI's reasoning for tone and content choices. You can review, edit, or override any queued email before it sends — full transparency and control, because this is your local installation.

Advanced Customizations Worth Exploring

Conditional Logic Based on Enrichment Data

You can tell the agent to behave differently based on what it knows about the contact. For example, if the enrichment data shows the company recently raised a funding round, the prompt can instruct the AI to acknowledge that context. If the contact is a VP-level or above, the agent can skip the "just checking in" softener and lead with value immediately.

Multi-Account Rotation

For high-volume outreach, connect multiple sending accounts and enable Account Rotation in the agent settings. MailClaw will distribute sends across accounts to protect individual sender reputations — a technique that significantly improves inbox placement rates over time.

Webhook Triggers for CRM Sync

When a contact replies and the agent stops its sequence, you probably want that status reflected in HubSpot or Salesforce. MailClaw supports outbound webhooks that fire on reply detection events:

mailclaw webhooks add \
  --event contact.replied \
  --url https://hooks.yourcrm.com/reply-detected \
  --method POST

This keeps your CRM in sync without any manual intervention, and lets your sales team know exactly when a prospect has re-engaged.

The Philosophy: Persistence Without Annoyance

The best follow-up agents aren't the most aggressive ones — they're the most intelligent ones. The goal is to surface your message at the right moment, in the right tone, with enough personalization that it feels like a human wrote it — because in a meaningful sense, it did. You wrote the rules. You set the tone. The AI just executes with consistency you couldn't maintain manually across hundreds of contacts.

MailClaw is open source, which means you can inspect exactly how the OpenClaw reasoning layer generates each message, fork the prompts to match your brand voice, and contribute improvements back to the community. There's no black box, no subscription required for core features, and no contact data leaving your machine.

Start with a small list of 20–30 contacts, watch how the agent performs in the activity log, and iterate on your prompt template until the output consistently matches what you'd write yourself on your best day. That's the benchmark — and with the right setup, your AI agent will clear it reliably, at scale, while you focus on the conversations that actually need a human.

articles.title: MailClaw Agent Skills: Creating Custom Automations for Your Inbox
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how to build and deploy custom agent skills in MailClaw to automate repetitive inbox tasks, enrich contacts on the fly, and trigger intelligent workflows — all running locally on your Mac without sending your data to the cloud.
articles.content:
What Are Agent Skills in MailClaw?

If you've spent any time with MailClaw's AI email agents, you already know they can handle a surprising amount of the tedious work that clogs up your outreach pipeline — drafting follow-ups, scoring leads, flagging replies that need urgent attention. But the real power unlocks when you start writing custom agent skills: small, composable units of logic that teach your agents how to do something new.

Think of a skill as a function your agent can call when it decides the situation warrants it. Out of the box, MailClaw ships with a library of built-in skills covering common tasks like contact enrichment lookups, sequence enrollment, and deliverability checks. Custom skills let you go further — connecting to your own APIs, transforming data in proprietary ways, or encoding business rules that no generic tool would know about.

Everything runs locally through the OpenClaw runtime on localhost:3100, which means your prospect data, your API keys, and your logic stay on your machine. No third-party server ever sees your contacts list.

Anatomy of a MailClaw Skill

A skill is defined as a JavaScript or TypeScript module that exports a standard skill descriptor. The OpenClaw agent runtime picks it up automatically when you drop it into your skills directory. Here's the minimal shape of a custom skill:

// skills/score-reply-sentiment.js

module.exports = {
  name: "score-reply-sentiment",
  description: "Analyzes an inbound reply and assigns a sentiment score from -1 to 1.",
  input: {
    messageId: { type: "string", required: true },
    bodyText:  { type: "string", required: true }
  },
  output: {
    score:   { type: "number" },
    label:   { type: "string" }, // "positive" | "neutral" | "negative"
    summary: { type: "string" }
  },
  async run({ messageId, bodyText }, context) {
    const result = await context.llm.classify(bodyText, {
      labels: ["positive", "neutral", "negative"]
    });
    return {
      score:   result.confidence * (result.label === "negative" ? -1 : 1),
      label:   result.label,
      summary: result.reasoning
    };
  }
};

The context object is injected by OpenClaw and gives you access to the local LLM, the MailClaw database, your connected accounts, and a lightweight HTTP client. You're not reinventing infrastructure — you're just writing the logic that matters to your workflow.

Setting Up Your Skills Directory

Before you write your first skill, make sure MailClaw knows where to look. Open your mailclaw.config.json at the project root and confirm (or add) the skills path:

{
  "skills": {
    "directory": "./skills",
    "autoReload": true
  }
}

With autoReload set to true, the local dashboard at localhost:3100 will pick up changes to your skill files without a restart — essential when you're iterating quickly. Once you've saved a new skill file, navigate to Agents → Skills Library in the dashboard and you'll see it listed alongside the built-ins.

You can also register a skill from the CLI:

mailclaw skill:register ./skills/score-reply-sentiment.js --agent inbox-triage

The --agent flag scopes the skill to a specific agent so you don't accidentally give every agent access to every capability you've built.

Practical Skill Ideas Worth Building

1. CRM Sync on Reply

One of the most common requests from MailClaw users is automatic CRM updates the moment a prospect replies. Here's a condensed skill that pushes activity to HubSpot or Salesforce based on a simple environment flag:

// skills/crm-sync-on-reply.js
const { HubSpotClient } = require("@hubspot/api-client");
const { SalesforceClient } = require("./lib/sf-client");

module.exports = {
  name: "crm-sync-on-reply",
  description: "Logs a reply activity to the configured CRM.",
  input: {
    contactEmail: { type: "string", required: true },
    replySnippet: { type: "string", required: true },
    sentimentLabel: { type: "string" }
  },
  async run({ contactEmail, replySnippet, sentimentLabel }, context) {
    const crm = process.env.CRM_TARGET; // "hubspot" or "salesforce"

    if (crm === "hubspot") {
      const client = new HubSpotClient({ accessToken: process.env.HUBSPOT_TOKEN });
      await client.crm.contacts.basicApi.update(contactEmail, {
        properties: { last_reply_sentiment: sentimentLabel }
      });
    } else if (crm === "salesforce") {
      const sf = new SalesforceClient(process.env.SF_CREDENTIALS);
      await sf.logActivity({ email: contactEmail, note: replySnippet });
    }

    return { synced: true, target: crm };
  }
};

Pair this with MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment — which can pull firmographic data from public sources before the CRM write — and you end up with a record that's already populated with company size, industry, and LinkedIn URL by the time a sales rep opens it.

2. Deliverability Pre-Flight Check

MailClaw's deliverability monitoring surfaces domain reputation scores and spam trigger warnings in the dashboard, but you can push that intelligence into the sequence builder itself by writing a skill that gates sends:

// skills/deliverability-preflight.js
module.exports = {
  name: "deliverability-preflight",
  description: "Blocks a send if the sending domain's reputation score drops below threshold.",
  input: {
    sendingDomain: { type: "string", required: true },
    threshold:     { type: "number", default: 75 }
  },
  async run({ sendingDomain, threshold }, context) {
    const report = await context.mailclaw.deliverability.getDomainScore(sendingDomain);
    const approved = report.score >= threshold;

    if (!approved) {
      await context.mailclaw.alerts.create({
        level: "warning",
        message: `Send blocked: ${sendingDomain} scored ${report.score} (min ${threshold})`
      });
    }

    return { approved, score: report.score, details: report.issues };
  }
};

Drop this into a sequence step and your agent will automatically pause outreach from a domain that's trending toward Gmail spam folders — before you burn a warm list.

3. Smart Unsubscribe Routing

Standard unsubscribe handling suppresses the contact globally. But what if someone opts out of cold outreach but is still a paying customer? A custom skill can route the unsubscribe to the right list segment and fire a Slack notification rather than a blunt suppression:

mailclaw skill:scaffold smart-unsubscribe-router \
  --inputs "contactEmail,currentSequenceId,reason" \
  --outputs "action,targetList" \
  --template conditional-router

The skill:scaffold command drops a boilerplate file into your skills directory with the right structure already in place — just fill in the routing logic.

Chaining Skills Into Agent Workflows

Individual skills become exponentially more useful when you wire them together into a workflow that an agent can reason through. In the MailClaw dashboard under Agents → Workflow Builder, you can define a directed graph of skills with conditional edges:

  • Trigger: Inbound reply received on any connected Gmail or Outlook account
  • Step 1: Run score-reply-sentiment
  • Step 2: If sentiment is positive, run crm-sync-on-reply then enroll in a booking-link sequence
  • Step 3: If sentiment is negative, run smart-unsubscribe-router and flag for human review
  • Step 4: If sentiment is neutral, run deliverability-preflight and queue a follow-up draft for approval

You can export this workflow as a JSON file and commit it to version control alongside your skill files, which is one of the underrated advantages of MailClaw's open-source architecture — your automation logic is auditable, diffable, and portable.

Testing Your Skills Before They Touch Real Contacts

The fastest way to break trust with a prospect list is shipping a skill that hasn't been tested properly. MailClaw provides a sandboxed test runner specifically for this:

mailclaw skill:test score-reply-sentiment \
  --input '{"messageId":"msg_001","bodyText":"Thanks, this looks interesting. Can we set up a call?"}' \
  --dry-run

The --dry-run flag executes the full skill logic but suppresses any writes to your contacts database, CRM, or email accounts. The output is printed to the terminal and also logged in the dashboard under Skills → Test History, so you can compare runs side by side.

Pro tip: Create a fixtures/ folder in your skills directory with sample message payloads for each skill. Check these into Git alongside the skill itself so that anyone cloning your MailClaw setup can run mailclaw skill:test --fixture ./fixtures/positive-reply.json and immediately verify the skill works in their environment.

Sharing Skills With the Community

Because MailClaw is open source and built on OpenClaw, the skills you write are just files — there's no proprietary packaging format to deal with. The community maintains a growing registry of shared skills that you can pull down directly:

mailclaw skill:install @mailclaw-community/linkedin-enrich
mailclaw skill:install @mailclaw-community/sendgrid-bounce-handler

If you've built something useful — a Clearbit enrichment wrapper, a multi-account SendGrid failover skill, a sequence A/B result parser — consider publishing it. The mailclaw skill:publish command handles packaging and pushes to the community registry with your attribution intact.

Custom agent skills are where MailClaw stops being an email tool and starts being the automation layer for your entire outreach operation. Start with one small skill that solves a real annoyance, get comfortable with the context API, and then build outward. The compounding effect of a few well-designed skills running locally — no latency, no data exposure, no per-seat pricing — is hard to overstate once you've felt it in practice.

articles.title: How to Build an Email Agent That Generates Reports from Inbox Data
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how to build a fully automated email agent using MailClaw that reads your inbox, extracts key data, and generates actionable reports — no manual sorting required.
articles.content:
Why Your Inbox Is a Goldmine of Untapped Data

Every day, your inbox accumulates a quiet archive of business intelligence — prospect replies, deal updates, customer sentiment, bounce notifications, and engagement signals. Most people treat this as noise to be managed. The smarter move is to treat it as structured data waiting to be analyzed.

With MailClaw's AI email agents — powered by the OpenClaw engine running locally on your Mac at localhost:3100 — you can build an automated pipeline that reads incoming emails, extracts meaningful signals, and compiles them into clean, scheduled reports. No third-party cloud dependencies. No data leaving your machine. Just a local agent doing the heavy lifting while you focus on what matters.

This guide walks you through building that agent from scratch, step by step.

What You'll Build

By the end of this tutorial, you'll have an email agent that:

  • Monitors one or more connected inboxes (Gmail, Outlook, or any SMTP-connected account)
  • Classifies incoming emails into categories like reply, bounce, out-of-office, or interest signal
  • Extracts structured data from each message using an AI prompt pipeline
  • Aggregates that data into a daily or weekly report
  • Optionally pushes summary data into HubSpot, Salesforce, or a local CSV

Step 1: Connect Your Inboxes

Before the agent can read anything, you need to give MailClaw access to your email accounts. Open your dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to Accounts → Add Account. MailClaw supports both OAuth (for Gmail and Outlook) and manual SMTP/IMAP credentials for everything else.

For Gmail, the OAuth flow is the fastest path:

# From the MailClaw CLI
mailclaw accounts add --provider gmail --oauth

# For Outlook
mailclaw accounts add --provider outlook --oauth

# For custom SMTP/IMAP (e.g., Fastmail, Zoho, custom domain)
mailclaw accounts add --provider custom \
  --imap imap.yourhost.com \
  --smtp smtp.yourhost.com \
  --user you@yourdomain.com

Once connected, MailClaw begins syncing your inbox locally. You can verify the sync status from the dashboard under Accounts → Sync Status, or run mailclaw accounts status in the CLI.

If you're running outreach from multiple domains — a common pattern when managing deliverability across warm and cold sender accounts — you can repeat this process for each account. MailClaw's multi-account support means all of them feed into a single unified agent context.

Step 2: Define Your Agent's Extraction Logic

This is where the real power lives. MailClaw's AI email agents let you define what to look for in each message using a simple YAML-based agent config. Think of it as a prompt template plus a set of extraction rules.

Create a new agent config file:

# agents/inbox-reporter.yaml

name: Inbox Report Agent
description: Reads incoming emails and extracts structured data for reporting
trigger:
  type: inbox_sync
  accounts:
    - all
  filters:
    folder: INBOX
    since: last_run

extraction:
  model: openai/gpt-4o   # or any local model via Ollama
  prompt: |
    Analyze the following email and return a JSON object with these fields:
    - category: one of [reply, bounce, out_of_office, interest, unsubscribe, other]
    - sentiment: one of [positive, neutral, negative]
    - key_topic: a 5-10 word summary of what the email is about
    - action_required: true or false
    - contact_name: the sender's name if identifiable
    - contact_email: the sender's email address

output:
  format: structured_json
  aggregate: daily
  report_template: templates/daily-inbox-report.md

This config tells the agent to run on every inbox sync, process each email through the extraction prompt, and accumulate results into a daily aggregate. The model field is flexible — you can point it at OpenAI's API or run a local model through Ollama if you want fully offline operation.

Customizing Your Extraction Prompt

The prompt is the most important part of your agent. Be specific about what you want. If you're running a sales outreach sequence and want to flag positive replies that mention pricing or timeline, add that to the prompt explicitly:

"If the email mentions pricing, budget, timeline, or a request to schedule a call, set action_required to true and add a field called 'sales_signal' with a brief description."

The more domain-specific your prompt, the more useful your reports become. Generic extraction gives you generic insights.

Step 3: Build the Report Template
