MailClaw uses Markdown templates (rendered to HTML in the dashboard) to format your aggregated output. Create a report template at templates/daily-inbox-report.md:

# Daily Inbox Report — {{date}}

## Summary
- Total emails processed: {{total_count}}
- Action required: {{action_required_count}}
- Positive replies: {{sentiment.positive}}
- Bounces detected: {{category.bounce}}
- Unsubscribes: {{category.unsubscribe}}

## Top Interest Signals
{{#each interest_emails}}
- **{{contact_name}}** ({{contact_email}}): {{key_topic}}
{{/each}}

## Action Items
{{#each action_required_emails}}
- [ ] {{contact_name}} — {{key_topic}}
{{/each}}

This template uses Handlebars-style syntax that MailClaw's report renderer understands. The variables are automatically populated from your agent's aggregated JSON output. You'll find the rendered reports in the dashboard under Reports → Agent Reports every morning.

Step 4: Deploy and Schedule the Agent

With your config and template ready, register and deploy the agent:

# Register the agent
mailclaw agents register ./agents/inbox-reporter.yaml

# Test it against the last 24 hours of inbox data
mailclaw agents run inbox-reporter --dry-run --since 24h

# Schedule it to run daily at 7am
mailclaw agents schedule inbox-reporter --cron "0 7 * * *"

The --dry-run flag is worth using on your first pass. It runs the full extraction pipeline and shows you what the report would look like without writing anything to disk. This is a great way to iterate on your prompt before committing to a schedule.

Step 5: Connect Insights to Your CRM

Raw reports are useful. Reports that automatically update your CRM are transformative. MailClaw supports outbound integrations to HubSpot, Salesforce, and custom webhooks, so you can close the loop between inbox activity and contact records.

Add an integration block to your agent config:

integrations:
  - type: hubspot
    trigger_on: interest
    action: update_contact_property
    properties:
      last_reply_sentiment: "{{sentiment}}"
      last_reply_topic: "{{key_topic}}"
      needs_followup: "{{action_required}}"

  - type: webhook
    url: https://your-internal-tool.com/hooks/email-report
    trigger_on: daily_report
    payload: full_report_json

For Salesforce users, MailClaw's contact enrichment layer can also cross-reference extracted email data against existing records, automatically matching sender emails to Salesforce contacts or leads and appending activity notes. This works especially well when paired with an active outreach sequence in the MailClaw sequence builder — replies from your sequence get parsed, enriched, and logged without you touching a thing.

Monitoring Agent Health and Deliverability

One often-overlooked use case for inbox data reporting is deliverability monitoring. Bounces, spam complaints, and out-of-office ratios in your inbox data are early warning signals that your sending reputation may be under stress.

MailClaw's built-in deliverability tools can be connected to your agent output so that when bounce rates in a reporting window exceed a threshold, you get an automatic alert and your sequence is paused:

alerts:
  - condition: "category.bounce / total_count > 0.05"
    action: pause_sequence
    sequence_id: cold-outreach-q4
    notify: dashboard

This kind of closed-loop automation — where inbox data informs sending behavior — is what separates a smart outreach operation from one that's flying blind.

What to Do with Your Reports

Once your agent is running, you'll have a daily structured view of everything meaningful that hit your inbox. Here's how teams typically use this data:

  • Sales teams use the interest signal feed to prioritize morning follow-ups without digging through threads
  • Growth teams track sentiment trends across outreach campaigns to A/B test messaging effectiveness
  • Operations teams monitor bounce and unsubscribe rates to keep sender domains healthy
  • Founders get a one-glance daily briefing on anything that needs their attention

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your local machine, you also have full control over extending this behavior. The agent YAML format is designed to be hackable — add new extraction fields, chain multiple agents together, or write a custom output formatter in the plugins/ directory.

The Bigger Picture

Building an inbox reporting agent isn't just about saving time on email triage. It's about converting a passive communication channel into an active data source that improves how you sell, support, and operate. When your inbox talks to your CRM, your sequences, and your deliverability monitoring in real time, you're no longer reacting to email — you're using it as infrastructure.

MailClaw's AI agents, running locally through OpenClaw, make this kind of automation accessible without requiring a data engineering team or a cloud subscription. Spin up the dashboard at localhost:3100, build your first agent in under an hour, and start treating your inbox like the asset it's always been.

articles.title: Using MailClaw AI to Auto-Label and Organize Your Inbox
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's AI email agents and automation rules to automatically label, sort, and prioritize your inbox — saving hours of manual triage every week across Gmail, Outlook, and beyond.
articles.content:
Why Manual Inbox Management Is Costing You More Than You Think

The average knowledge worker spends nearly 28% of their workday reading and responding to email. A significant chunk of that time isn't spent actually communicating — it's spent sorting. Deciding what's urgent, what's noise, what belongs in a project folder, and what can wait until Friday. It's cognitive overhead that compounds silently across your team.

MailClaw was built to eliminate exactly this kind of friction. Because it runs locally on your machine at localhost:3100, your email data never has to touch an external server just to get sorted. Powered by OpenClaw's underlying AI engine, MailClaw can read the intent, tone, sender context, and content of incoming messages — then apply labels and routing logic automatically, in real time.

This guide walks you through setting up intelligent auto-labeling from scratch, whether you're connecting a Gmail account, an Outlook inbox, or a custom SMTP source.

How MailClaw's AI Labeling Engine Works

Before diving into configuration, it helps to understand the model. MailClaw's AI email agents don't just match keywords — they classify messages using a combination of:

  • Semantic intent detection — Is this a sales pitch, a support request, a meeting ask, or a newsletter?
  • Sender enrichment signals — MailClaw's contact enrichment layer pulls in company data, domain reputation, and CRM context (including HubSpot and Salesforce integrations) to weight classification decisions.
  • Thread context — Replies and forwards are analyzed in context, not in isolation.
  • Custom label taxonomies — You define the categories that matter to your workflow, not a generic preset list.

The result is a labeling system that gets smarter the longer it runs, because the AI agent learns from the corrections you make through the local dashboard.

Step 1: Connect Your Email Accounts

Open your MailClaw dashboard at http://localhost:3100 and navigate to Settings → Accounts. MailClaw supports both OAuth (recommended for Gmail and Outlook) and direct SMTP/IMAP credentials.

Connecting Gmail via OAuth

# From the MailClaw CLI, run:
mailclaw accounts add --provider gmail --auth oauth

# You'll be prompted to open a browser auth flow.
# After authorization, your account appears in the dashboard.

For Outlook or Microsoft 365 accounts, replace gmail with outlook. MailClaw handles token refresh automatically, so you won't get logged out mid-campaign or mid-sort.

Connecting via SMTP/IMAP

mailclaw accounts add \
  --provider custom \
  --imap-host mail.yourdomain.com \
  --imap-port 993 \
  --smtp-host smtp.yourdomain.com \
  --smtp-port 587 \
  --username you@yourdomain.com

Once connected, MailClaw begins a background sync. You'll see message counts populate in the dashboard within a minute or two depending on inbox size.

Step 2: Define Your Label Taxonomy

Navigate to AI Agents → Inbox Organizer → Labels in the dashboard. This is where you define the categories MailClaw will apply. Think about how your work actually flows — not how you wish it flowed.

A practical starting taxonomy for most professionals looks something like this:

  • @Action — Requires a direct response or decision from you
  • @Waiting — You've sent something and are waiting for a reply
  • @Reading — Newsletters, digests, and articles worth reading later
  • @Sales-Inbound — Cold outreach and vendor pitches
  • @Support — Customer or user requests
  • @Receipts — Order confirmations, invoices, and billing notifications
  • @Internal — Messages from your own team's domain

You can create these labels directly in the dashboard UI or via CLI:

mailclaw labels create \
  --name "@Action" \
  --color "#e74c3c" \
  --description "Needs a direct response or decision"

mailclaw labels create \
  --name "@Reading" \
  --color "#3498db" \
  --description "Low-urgency reading material"

Step 3: Configure the AI Labeling Agent

This is where MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered AI takes over. In AI Agents → Inbox Organizer → Rules, you can configure the agent using natural language instructions — no regex, no filter wizards.

Writing Effective Agent Instructions

Think of writing agent instructions the same way you'd brief a sharp assistant on their first day. Be specific about intent, not just keywords.

"Label any email as @Sales-Inbound if the sender is not in my contacts, the message contains phrases like 'wanted to reach out,' 'quick question,' or 'would love to connect,' and the sender domain doesn't match my company domain."

Compare that to a weak rule: "Label emails with 'quick question' as sales." Your colleagues send quick questions too. Context is everything, and MailClaw's agent handles that nuance well because it combines text classification with contact enrichment data in real time.

Sample Agent Configuration (YAML)

agent:
  name: inbox-organizer
  triggers:
    - event: message.received
  actions:
    - classify:
        model: openclaw-classify-v2
        labels:
          - name: "@Action"
            instruction: >
              Apply when the email is from a known contact and contains
              a direct question, request, or deadline directed at me personally.
          - name: "@Sales-Inbound"
            instruction: >
              Apply when sender is not enriched as a known contact,
              the message has outreach phrasing, and no prior thread exists.
          - name: "@Reading"
            instruction: >
              Apply when the email is from a newsletter domain, contains
              an unsubscribe link, or has a list-unsubscribe header.
        fallback_label: "@Review"
        confidence_threshold: 0.78

Save this as inbox-organizer.yaml and load it with:

mailclaw agents deploy --file inbox-organizer.yaml --account you@gmail.com

The confidence_threshold is important. Setting it too low (below 0.6) creates noisy mislabeling. Too high (above 0.9) and the agent will leave many messages unlabeled. 0.75–0.82 is a solid starting range for most inboxes.

Step 4: Add Contact Enrichment for Smarter Context

Raw email classification improves dramatically when paired with MailClaw's contact enrichment. When a message arrives from alex@momentum-vc.com, enrichment tells the agent: this is a venture capital firm, this sender's LinkedIn title is "Partner," and this domain has a high sender reputation score. That context changes how the email should be labeled.

Enable enrichment from the CLI:

mailclaw enrichment enable --provider clearbit --account you@gmail.com
# or use the built-in OpenClaw enrichment layer (no external API required):
mailclaw enrichment enable --provider openclaw --account you@gmail.com

If you're already using HubSpot or Salesforce, MailClaw can pull contact records from those CRMs to supplement classification. A message from someone already tagged as "Customer — Enterprise" in your CRM gets routed very differently than a cold email from an unknown domain.

mailclaw integrations connect --crm hubspot --sync-contacts true

Step 5: Monitor, Correct, and Improve

The local dashboard at localhost:3100 includes a dedicated Label Review panel where you can see every AI classification decision alongside its confidence score and the reasoning the agent used. This transparency is one of the core advantages of running MailClaw locally — you're not trusting a black box.

When the agent mislabels something, clicking "Correct Label" in the dashboard doesn't just fix that one message — it feeds a correction signal back into the agent's local fine-tuning loop. After 20–30 corrections, classification accuracy on your specific inbox typically improves by 15–25%.

Reviewing Agent Performance via CLI

mailclaw agents stats --name inbox-organizer --period 7d

# Output example:
# Messages processed:    847
# Correctly labeled:     791  (93.4%)
# Low confidence:         38   (4.5%)
# Fallback (@Review):     18   (2.1%)
# Avg confidence score:  0.84

If your fallback rate creeps above 8–10%, that's a signal to revisit your label instructions and add more specificity. Use the AI Agent Logs panel in the dashboard to see which message types are falling through.

Connecting Labeling to Your Outreach Workflow

Auto-labeling isn't just about inbox tidiness — it feeds directly into MailClaw's sequence builder and campaign tools. When an email arrives labeled @Sales-Inbound, you can trigger an automated sequence: acknowledge receipt, add the sender to a nurture track, or flag them for a human follow-up after a delay. When something hits @Support, it can automatically open a thread in your helpdesk workflow.

This is where the open-source architecture of MailClaw genuinely shines. Because everything runs locally and the codebase is fully inspectable, you can wire labeling outputs into any downstream tool — Zapier, Make, a custom webhook, or your own scripts — without worrying about data leaving your environment.

Getting the Most Out of AI Inbox Organization

A few final principles that make the difference between a labeling system that helps and one you abandon after a week:

  • Start with fewer labels. Five well-defined categories beat twenty vague ones. Expand only when you feel friction.
  • Review the fallback queue daily for the first two weeks. Those uncategorized messages are training data you can't afford to ignore early on.
  • Combine labeling with MailClaw's deliverability monitoring. High-confidence @Sales-Inbound detection can help you identify if your own outreach is landing in recipients' "cold email" piles — a useful mirror for your sending reputation.
  • Version control your agent configs. Since agent definitions are YAML files, put them in a git repo. You'll thank yourself when you want to roll back a change that made things worse.

Your inbox reflects how you work. With MailClaw running locally and an AI agent handling the sorting logic, you get back the mental space to focus on the messages that actually need you — not the overhead of figuring out which ones those are.

articles.title: How to Create an AI Agent for Contract Review Emails
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to build an AI agent in MailClaw that automatically reviews contract-related emails, flags key terms, routes responses, and keeps your deals moving — without leaving your local machine.
articles.content:
Why Contract Review Emails Are a Perfect Automation Target

Contract review is one of those workflows that sounds simple but quietly consumes hours every week. You're waiting on redlines, chasing down signatures, forwarding PDFs to legal, and manually updating your CRM every time a thread moves. The emails themselves follow predictable patterns — requests for changes, approval confirmations, deadline nudges — which makes them an ideal candidate for AI agent automation.

With MailClaw's AI email agents (powered by OpenClaw), you can build an agent that monitors your inbox for contract-related threads, extracts key details, routes the right message to the right person, and logs everything to your CRM — all running locally on your Mac at localhost:3100. No cloud dependency. No per-seat pricing. Just a clean, open-source workflow you fully control.

What You'll Build

By the end of this guide, you'll have a MailClaw AI agent that:

  • Detects incoming emails related to contracts (NDAs, MSAs, SOWs, renewals)
  • Extracts entities like contract value, party names, and deadlines
  • Sends acknowledgment replies using a pre-approved template
  • Tags and routes emails to the right internal reviewer
  • Logs contract status updates to HubSpot or Salesforce via enrichment
  • Triggers follow-up sequences when no response arrives within a set window

Step 1: Set Up Your MailClaw Environment

If you haven't already, install MailClaw and start the local server. Make sure you're running Node 18+ and have your SMTP or OAuth credentials ready.

# Install MailClaw globally
npm install -g mailclaw

# Initialize a new project
mailclaw init contract-review-agent

# Start the local dashboard
mailclaw serve
# Dashboard available at http://localhost:3100

From the dashboard, connect your email account under Settings → Accounts. MailClaw supports Gmail (OAuth 2.0), Outlook (Microsoft OAuth), and any SMTP provider like SendGrid or Postmark. For contract review workflows, connecting your primary business Gmail or Outlook account is usually the right call — that's where the threads live.

Step 2: Define the Agent's Trigger Conditions

AI agents in MailClaw are defined in a agent.yaml file inside your project. This is where you tell the agent what to watch for. Open your project directory and create the agent config:

# agents/contract-review.yaml
name: Contract Review Agent
account: primary-gmail
trigger:
  type: inbound_email
  conditions:
    - field: subject
      operator: contains_any
      values: ["contract", "NDA", "MSA", "SOW", "agreement", "redline", "signature"]
    - field: body
      operator: contains_any
      values: ["please review", "attached agreement", "sign by", "legal review"]
  logic: OR
ai:
  model: openai/gpt-4o
  temperature: 0.2
actions:
  - extract_entities
  - send_reply
  - tag_thread
  - enrich_contact
  - log_to_crm

The logic: OR means the agent fires if any of those conditions match. Keep the temperature low (0.2) for contract work — you want consistent, conservative outputs, not creative ones.

Step 3: Write the AI Extraction Prompt

Entity extraction is where the real value lives. You want the agent to pull structured data from unstructured email threads so your team isn't manually reading every message.

# agents/contract-review.yaml (continued)
ai:
  model: openai/gpt-4o
  temperature: 0.2
  extraction_prompt: |
    You are a contract review assistant. From the email below, extract the following fields:
    - contract_type: (NDA, MSA, SOW, Renewal, Amendment, Other)
    - counterparty_name: The other company or individual
    - contract_value: Dollar amount if mentioned, else null
    - deadline: Any signing or review deadline mentioned (ISO 8601 format)
    - action_required: What is being asked (Review, Sign, Approve, Clarify, Other)
    - urgency: (low, medium, high) based on language and deadlines
    - key_concerns: A 1-2 sentence plain English summary of any flagged issues

    Return valid JSON only. Do not include explanation.
    Email: {{email.body}}

This prompt is deliberately structured and low-temperature. For contract contexts, hallucinations are a real risk — you don't want an AI agent confidently inventing a $500,000 contract value. Asking for null when something isn't present, and requesting JSON-only output, dramatically reduces drift.

Step 4: Configure the Reply Template

Once the agent extracts entities, it should send an acknowledgment. Use MailClaw's template system with dynamic fields pulled from the extraction output:

# templates/contract-ack.html
Subject: Re: {{email.subject}}

Hi {{contact.first_name}},

Thanks for sending this over. I've flagged your {{ai.contract_type}} for review
and shared it with the appropriate team member.

{{#if ai.deadline}}
We'll aim to get back to you before {{ai.deadline}}.
{{else}}
You can expect a response within 2 business days.
{{/if}}

If anything changes or you have questions in the meantime, just reply here.

Best,
{{account.sender_name}}

Notice the conditional block around the deadline — if the AI didn't extract a deadline, the fallback copy kicks in automatically. MailClaw's Handlebars-based template engine makes this kind of logic simple without touching code.

Step 5: Route to the Right Reviewer

Most contract types map to specific internal reviewers or teams. You can encode this routing logic directly in the agent:

routing:
  rules:
    - condition: ai.contract_type == "NDA"
      forward_to: legal@yourcompany.com
      tag: nda-review
    - condition: ai.contract_type == "SOW"
      forward_to: ops@yourcompany.com
      tag: sow-review
    - condition: ai.urgency == "high"
      forward_to: cto@yourcompany.com
      tag: urgent-contract
      notify_slack: true
  default:
    forward_to: contracts@yourcompany.com
    tag: general-contract

The Slack notification on high-urgency contracts is wired through MailClaw's webhook integration — add your Slack webhook URL under Settings → Integrations in the dashboard and it just works.

Step 6: Enrich the Contact and Log to Your CRM

MailClaw's contact enrichment layer can take the sender's email address and pull in company data, title, LinkedIn profile, and funding status before logging anything to your CRM. This is especially useful for inbound contracts from prospects you haven't fully profiled yet.

enrichment:
  provider: clearbit   # or hunter, apollo
  fields: [company, title, linkedin, company_size, industry]
  on_failure: skip     # Don't block the workflow if enrichment fails

crm_sync:
  provider: hubspot    # or salesforce, pipedrive
  object: deal
  mapping:
    deal_name: "{{ai.contract_type}} - {{ai.counterparty_name}}"
    deal_stage: "Contract Review"
    close_date: "{{ai.deadline}}"
    amount: "{{ai.contract_value}}"
    custom_field_urgency: "{{ai.urgency}}"

With on_failure: skip, enrichment failures won't block the rest of the workflow. This matters in production — you don't want a bad API key silently halting your entire contract pipeline.

Step 7: Add a Follow-Up Sequence

Contract review threads go quiet all the time. Use MailClaw's sequence builder to automatically nudge the thread if no reply arrives within your defined window:

mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "contract-followup" \
  --trigger "no_reply_after:2d" \
  --linked-agent "contract-review" \
  --steps 3

This opens the sequence builder in your browser at localhost:3100/sequences/contract-followup. From there, drag in your follow-up email steps, set delays (Day 2, Day 5, Day 9 works well for contract threads), and choose whether to stop the sequence on reply or on a specific tag being applied.

Monitoring and Deliverability

Even automated contract emails need to land in the inbox. MailClaw's deliverability dashboard (at localhost:3100/deliverability) shows you open rates, bounce rates, spam signal scores, and DKIM/SPF/DMARC status for each connected account. For contract workflows specifically, keep an eye on:

  • Reply rate — low reply rates on contract threads often mean emails are hitting promotions or spam folders
  • SPF/DKIM alignment — essential if you're sending through SendGrid on behalf of a custom domain
  • Thread continuity — make sure your agent is replying in-thread (same Message-ID chain) rather than opening new threads, which confuses recipients and tanks reply rates

Running and Testing Your Agent

# Dry run against a sample email (no sends, no CRM writes)
mailclaw agent run contract-review --dry-run --sample ./samples/nda-email.txt

# Deploy the agent
mailclaw agent deploy contract-review

# Monitor live activity
mailclaw agent logs contract-review --follow

Always test with --dry-run first. Pass in a few representative email samples — an NDA request, a redline response, a signature confirmation — and verify the extraction output looks right before you point the agent at a live inbox.

Where to Take This Next

Once your contract review agent is running smoothly, a few natural extensions are worth building:

  • PDF attachment parsing: Hook in a document extraction API (like AWS Textract or Reducto) to pull clause summaries directly from attached contracts
  • E-signature integration: Trigger a DocuSign or HelloSign envelope automatically when the agent detects a "ready to sign" confirmation
  • Multi-account routing: Use MailClaw's multi-account support to run the same agent across a legal@ alias, a contracts@ alias, and your personal account simultaneously
  • Analytics reporting: Export agent activity data via MailClaw's API and pipe it into a Notion database or Airtable to track average contract turnaround time

The real power of building this in MailClaw — rather than a SaaS tool — is that all of this runs on your machine. Your contract data, your extracted entities, your CRM credentials — none of it transits through a third-party server. For legal workflows, that's not just a nice-to-have. It's often a requirement.

MailClaw is open source and built on OpenClaw. You can inspect every prompt, every routing rule, and every CRM mapping. When you're automating contract workflows, being able to audit your automation isn't optional — it's the whole point.

articles.title: MailClaw Agent Memory: How Your Email Agent Learns from Past Interactions
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how MailClaw's AI email agent memory system works under the hood, and how to configure persistent context so your agents make smarter, more personalized outreach decisions over time.
articles.content:
Why Agent Memory Changes Everything

Most email automation tools treat every interaction as if it's the first. Your prospect replies saying they're not ready yet, and three weeks later your sequence fires off the exact same opener — oblivious to everything that came before. It's not just inefficient. It's the kind of thing that kills deals before they start.

MailClaw's AI email agents, built on the OpenClaw engine, work differently. They maintain a structured memory of each contact's interaction history, letting them adapt tone, timing, and content based on what's actually happened in the conversation. This isn't a marketing abstraction — it's a real architectural decision that you can inspect, tune, and extend directly from your local dashboard at localhost:3100.

In this post, we'll break down exactly how agent memory works, what gets stored, how to configure it for your use case, and how to avoid the common pitfalls that make memory-enabled agents feel creepy instead of clever.

How MailClaw Stores Contact Memory

When you create an AI email agent in MailClaw, each contact in your campaign gets a dedicated memory context — a structured document that lives locally on your machine alongside your campaign data. This is one of the core advantages of running MailClaw locally: your enriched contact data and interaction history never touch a third-party server unless you explicitly push it to an integration like HubSpot or Salesforce.

The Memory Object Structure

Under the hood, each contact's memory context is a JSON document that your agent reads before composing any message. Here's a simplified example of what that structure looks like:

{
  "contact_id": "claw_c_9f3a2b",
  "email": "maya.chen@acmecorp.com",
  "enrichment": {
    "title": "Head of Growth",
    "company_size": "51-200",
    "tech_stack": ["HubSpot", "Segment", "Slack"],
    "linkedin_activity": "posted about B2B content strategy 4 days ago"
  },
  "interaction_history": [
    {
      "type": "email_sent",
      "subject": "Quick question about your onboarding flow",
      "timestamp": "2024-11-14T09:12:00Z",
      "opened": true,
      "clicked": false
    },
    {
      "type": "reply_received",
      "body_snippet": "Interesting timing — we're actually evaluating tools right now...",
      "sentiment": "positive",
      "timestamp": "2024-11-15T14:33:00Z"
    }
  ],
  "agent_notes": [
    "Contact mentioned evaluating tools — high intent signal",
    "Avoid pressure tactics — responded well to consultative framing"
  ]
}

The agent_notes field is particularly powerful. It's where your agent writes its own observations after each interaction — a scratchpad that persists across the entire sequence. When the agent drafts the next email, it reads these notes first and adjusts accordingly.

Enrichment as a Memory Foundation

Before the first email is ever sent, MailClaw's contact enrichment layer seeds the memory object with structured data pulled from available signals — LinkedIn profiles, company databases, and custom fields you import from tools like Salesforce or a CSV upload. This gives the agent a baseline context so the very first message feels informed, not generic.

To trigger enrichment from the CLI before launching a sequence, run:

# Enrich a contact list before running your agent
mailclaw enrich --list prospects.csv --fields title,company,tech_stack

# Then attach the enriched list to your agent
mailclaw agent create --name "Q1 Outreach" --contacts prospects.enriched.csv

The richer your initial enrichment pass, the smarter the agent's first message will be — and the more useful the memory becomes over time as new signals layer on top of it.

Configuring Memory Behavior for Your Agent

Not all memory is created equal. MailClaw gives you explicit control over what your agent remembers, how long it retains context, and how aggressively it references past interactions. You configure this in your agent's settings file or directly through the dashboard under Agents → Memory Settings.

Memory Depth and Retention Windows

The memory_depth setting controls how many past interactions the agent considers when drafting a new message. A shallow memory (2-3 interactions) keeps emails feeling natural without over-referencing the past. A deeper window is useful for long sales cycles where earlier objections or signals remain relevant.

# In your agent config file (~/.mailclaw/agents/q1-outreach.yaml)
memory:
  depth: 4                  # Number of past interactions to include in context
  retention_days: 90        # How long to keep interaction history active
  sentiment_weighting: true # Prioritize emotionally significant interactions
  note_max_tokens: 200      # Limit agent self-notes to prevent context bloat

Controlling What the Agent References Explicitly

There's an important UX distinction between an agent that uses memory to inform its tone and an agent that mentions memory explicitly in the email body. The first feels smart. The second can feel surveillance-y.

MailClaw lets you control this with the reference_style setting:

  • implicit — The agent uses memory to adjust language, timing, and angle without directly citing past events. Good default for cold outreach.
  • explicit_soft — The agent may reference past interactions naturally, e.g., "Following up on your note last week..." Appropriate once a reply has been received.
  • explicit_full — The agent can cite specific details from previous exchanges. Best reserved for warm sequences or account management workflows.
Pro tip: Set reference_style: implicit for your cold sequence steps and automatically upgrade to explicit_soft after a reply is detected. You can configure this as a conditional branch in MailClaw's sequence builder.

Practical Workflows That Leverage Agent Memory

The Reply-Aware Follow-Up

The most immediately valuable use of agent memory is handling replies intelligently. When a contact replies — even if it's a "not now" — MailClaw logs the sentiment, extracts key phrases, and writes agent notes that shape every subsequent message in the sequence.

Here's how to set up a reply-aware branch in the sequence builder:

  1. Open your sequence in the dashboard at localhost:3100/sequences
  2. Select a step and click Add Branch Condition
  3. Set condition: interaction_history.reply_received == true
  4. On the "true" branch, select Agent Mode: Memory-Informed
  5. Set reference_style to explicit_soft for this branch only

Now contacts who replied get a thoughtful follow-up that acknowledges the previous exchange, while non-responders continue on the standard sequence path.

Long-Cycle Account Nurturing

For deals that span months, agent memory becomes a relationship ledger. Integrate MailClaw with HubSpot or Salesforce via the built-in connectors, and deal stage changes automatically write new context into the contact's memory object. When the agent reaches out again after a product update or pricing change, it knows where the conversation left off.

# Sync CRM deal stage into contact memory
mailclaw sync --source hubspot --map deal_stage:agent_context --contacts active

Deliverability-Aware Pacing

Agent memory also interacts with MailClaw's deliverability monitoring layer. If your open rates drop below a threshold for a given domain, the agent can note this in the campaign-level memory and automatically adjust send timing or switch to an alternate SMTP account or SendGrid routing path — all without manual intervention.

Keeping Memory Honest: Auditing and Resetting

Because agents write their own notes, it's worth periodically auditing what they're learning — especially in early deployments. MailClaw makes this straightforward from the CLI:

# View agent notes for a specific contact
mailclaw memory inspect --contact maya.chen@acmecorp.com --agent "Q1 Outreach"

# Clear and reset memory for a contact (keeps enrichment, removes interaction history)
mailclaw memory reset --contact maya.chen@acmecorp.com --keep-enrichment

# Export full memory log for review
mailclaw memory export --agent "Q1 Outreach" --format json > memory_audit.json

If you're running MailClaw as an open-source deployment and extending the agent with custom OpenClaw plugins, you can also hook into the memory write lifecycle to add validation logic — useful for teams that need to enforce compliance guardrails around what gets stored.

The Bigger Picture: Memory as a Compounding Asset

Individual emails are transient. Memory is cumulative. The longer you run MailClaw's AI email agents, the richer the interaction data becomes — and the better the agents perform. A sequence that launched with generic enrichment data evolves into a nuanced outreach engine that understands which angles resonate with specific personas, which objections tend to surface at which stages, and which send times correlate with replies for contacts at companies using tools like Outlook or Gmail.

This is the compounding advantage of building your outreach on a memory-aware system rather than a static sequence tool. Every reply, every open, every silence teaches the agent something — and because all of that data lives locally on your machine, you own it completely.

Start with a simple sequence, enable enrichment, and let the memory layer build. Within a few weeks, you'll have an agent that feels less like a tool you're configuring and more like a collaborator that's been paying close attention.

articles.title: How to Build an AI Agent That Monitors Competitor Emails
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to build a fully automated AI agent using MailClaw that monitors competitor email campaigns, extracts insights, and helps you craft smarter outreach — all running locally on your Mac.
articles.content:
Why Monitoring Competitor Emails Is a Competitive Advantage

Your competitors are telling you exactly how they sell, what messaging resonates with their audience, and when they run promotions — every time they hit send. Most teams ignore this goldmine entirely. The ones who don't? They iterate faster, write better subject lines, and time their campaigns with surgical precision.

Building an AI agent that automatically monitors, categorizes, and summarizes competitor emails used to require stitching together half a dozen tools and a lot of brittle glue code. With MailClaw's AI agent system — powered by OpenClaw and running entirely on your local machine at localhost:3100 — you can have this running in under an hour.

This guide walks you through the full setup: from creating dedicated inbox listeners to building an OpenClaw-powered agent that extracts actionable intelligence and feeds it directly into your own campaign workflows.

Step 1: Set Up Your Competitor Monitoring Inboxes

Create Dedicated Email Accounts

The cleanest approach is to create throwaway email addresses specifically for competitor subscriptions. Use Gmail or Outlook aliases — something like research+competitor1@yourdomain.com — so all monitoring traffic stays completely separate from your primary outreach accounts.

Once you have your addresses, add them to MailClaw's multi-account manager from the dashboard:

# Start MailClaw locally
mailclaw start

# Add a monitoring account via CLI
mailclaw accounts add \
  --label "Competitor Monitor" \
  --email research+monitor@yourdomain.com \
  --provider gmail \
  --auth oauth

MailClaw supports both SMTP/IMAP credentials and OAuth flows for Gmail and Outlook. For a monitoring inbox, OAuth is the better choice — it stays authenticated without you having to rotate passwords manually.

Subscribe to the Right Lists

Go sign up for every competitor newsletter, drip sequence, and product update list you can find. Also subscribe to SaaS review platforms like G2 and Capterra — their digest emails often contain competitor positioning language that's pure gold for copywriting research. Give it 48–72 hours for the emails to start flowing.

Pro tip: Sign up using a name that sounds like a realistic buyer persona — not an obviously fake name. Some platforms tailor onboarding sequences based on the name or company you provide, and you want to see what a real prospect sees.

Step 2: Build the AI Monitoring Agent in MailClaw

Open the Agent Builder

Navigate to localhost:3100/agents in your browser and click New Agent. MailClaw's agent builder lets you define triggers, connect data sources, write an OpenClaw-powered prompt, and configure outputs — all without leaving the dashboard.

Give your agent a name like Competitor Intel Watcher and set the trigger to New Email Received on your monitoring account.

Write the Agent Prompt

This is where the intelligence lives. OpenClaw processes the raw email content and returns structured output. Here's a solid starting prompt you can paste directly into the agent prompt field:

You are a competitive intelligence analyst. When you receive an email from a competitor, extract and return a JSON object with the following fields:

- sender_brand: The company name sending the email
- email_type: One of [newsletter, promotional, onboarding, feature_announcement, win_back, nurture]
- subject_line: The exact subject line
- preview_text: The preview/preheader text if present
- primary_cta: The main call-to-action text and URL
- key_messaging: 2-3 bullet points summarizing the core value props used
- tone: One of [urgent, educational, casual, formal, story-driven]
- send_time: Day of week and approximate time if available
- notable_tactics: Any interesting copywriting, personalization, or design tactics worth noting
- competitive_angle: Does this email address a pain point or objection that we should be responding to?

Be concise. Focus on what's actionable for a marketing team.

This structured output makes everything downstream much easier — you can sort by email type, filter by competitor, and spot patterns over time.

Configure the Output Destination

MailClaw agents can write their output to several destinations. For a competitive monitoring workflow, the most useful options are:

  • MailClaw's built-in contact notes — Tag each insight entry with the competitor name and email type for easy filtering later
  • HubSpot or Salesforce via webhook — Push structured intel directly into a CRM deal or company record
  • A local JSON log file — Useful if you want to run your own analysis scripts against the data
  • A Slack webhook — Get a daily digest of everything your competitors sent overnight

To add a webhook output, go to the Output tab in the agent builder and paste your endpoint:

mailclaw agents configure competitor-intel-watcher \
  --output webhook \
  --url https://hooks.slack.com/services/YOUR/SLACK/WEBHOOK \
  --format json \
  --trigger on_complete

Step 3: Use Contact Enrichment to Add Context

Raw email content is useful, but it's even more powerful when paired with company context. MailClaw's contact enrichment layer can automatically pull firmographic data — company size, funding stage, tech stack — whenever a new sender appears in your monitoring inbox.

Enable enrichment on the agent by toggling Enrich Sender Domain in the agent settings. This uses the sending domain (e.g., competitor.com) to pull enrichment data and attach it to the intel record. When you're comparing a scrappy Series A startup's messaging against an enterprise player, this context changes how you interpret what you're reading.

Step 4: Turn Insights Into Better Campaigns

Spot Patterns in the Sequence Builder

After a few weeks of collection, you'll have enough data to see patterns. Open MailClaw's sequence builder at localhost:3100/sequences and use your competitive intel as input when designing your own flows. Common things to look for:

  • Which email types do competitors send most frequently? If everyone's doubling down on "educational nurture" and ignoring urgency plays, there may be an opening.
  • What day and time do they typically send? Look for gaps your audience isn't being hit on.
  • Are competitors leaning on social proof (case studies, logos, testimonials) or feature-led messaging? That tells you a lot about where the category is maturing.
  • When do win-back emails appear? This can hint at their average trial length or churn window.

Generate Counter-Positioning Drafts

Here's a workflow that MailClaw users love: once your monitoring agent has collected a batch of emails from a specific competitor, use the sequence builder's AI drafting mode to generate counter-positioning copy.

Select a set of intel entries, click Draft Response Sequence, and MailClaw's OpenClaw backbone will generate an email sequence that directly addresses the gaps or weaknesses in your competitor's messaging — without you having to write from a blank page.

mailclaw sequences draft \
  --source agent:competitor-intel-watcher \
  --competitor "AcmeCorp" \
  --tone consultative \
  --length 3-email \
  --output sequences/acme-counter-positioning.json

Step 5: Monitor Deliverability of Your Own Outreach

There's an irony worth noting: while you're monitoring competitor emails, you should make sure your own emails are actually landing in inboxes. MailClaw's deliverability tools run alongside your agent setup and track open rates, bounce rates, and spam placement across your connected accounts.

Check the Deliverability tab at localhost:3100/deliverability regularly. If you're sending outreach through SendGrid, Mailgun, or your own SMTP server, MailClaw integrates directly and surfaces issues before they become campaigns-destroying problems.

Keeping Your Setup Running and Improving

The real power of this agent compounds over time. A month of data is interesting. Six months is a strategic asset. A few habits that keep the system sharp:

  1. Review the agent's structured output weekly — even 10 minutes of review will surface trends you'd otherwise miss.
  2. Refine your prompt quarterly — as you learn what's actually useful, update the extraction prompt to capture more of it.
  3. Add new competitors as they emerge — subscribe to new lists and add them to your monitoring account. The agent picks them up automatically.
  4. Cross-reference with your own metrics — if a competitor starts hammering a specific message and your own trial-to-paid rate drops, there's likely a connection worth investigating.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your local machine, there are no per-seat fees, no data leaving your environment, and no vendor lock-in. You own the agent logic, you own the data, and you can extend the system any way you want — whether that means writing custom OpenClaw tools, piping output into a local SQLite database, or building a full competitive intelligence dashboard on top of the API.

Competitor intelligence has always been valuable. With an AI agent running 24/7 in the background, it finally becomes effortless.

articles.title: Using MailClaw Agents for Automated Email Compliance Checking
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to configure MailClaw's AI email agents to automatically audit your outbound campaigns for CAN-SPAM, GDPR, and CASL compliance — before a single message ever leaves your inbox.
articles.content:
Why Compliance Checking Belongs in Your Email Automation Stack

Email compliance isn't glamorous, but the consequences of ignoring it are. A single campaign that violates CAN-SPAM, GDPR, or CASL can result in fines that dwarf your entire marketing budget — not to mention the reputational damage of landing on blocklists or having your sending domain blacklisted by Gmail or Outlook.

Most teams treat compliance as a one-time legal review, but outbound email is a living, changing system. New contacts get added through contact enrichment pipelines, sequences get edited under deadline pressure, and A/B test variants get spun up without a second glance at the unsubscribe footer. By the time a compliance issue surfaces, thousands of emails have already gone out.

MailClaw's AI email agents change the calculus entirely. Because everything runs locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, your email content, contact data, and sequence logic never leave your machine — making it a natural fit for compliance workflows that handle sensitive or regulated data. You can configure an agent to act as a persistent compliance auditor, reviewing every draft, sequence step, and contact segment before anything hits your SMTP relay or OAuth-connected account.

What Compliance Checking Actually Involves

Before configuring an agent, it's worth being precise about what automated compliance checking can and should cover. There are three broad layers:

  • Structural compliance: Does the email include a physical mailing address? Is there a functional unsubscribe mechanism? Is the subject line misleading?
  • Data compliance: Are you emailing contacts who have a valid legal basis for contact — opt-in consent, legitimate interest, or an existing business relationship?
  • Content compliance: Does the email body contain claims or language that could trigger regulatory scrutiny (e.g., financial promises, health claims, deceptive urgency)?

MailClaw agents can be configured to audit all three layers automatically, flagging issues before they reach your SendGrid account or your connected Gmail and Outlook senders.

Setting Up Your Compliance Agent in MailClaw

Step 1: Define the Agent's Role and Ruleset

Open your MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to Agents, and create a new agent. Give it a descriptive name like Compliance Auditor and set its role to Reviewer. This prevents the agent from taking autonomous send actions — it only reads and annotates.

In the agent's system prompt, you'll define its compliance ruleset. Here's a solid starting template you can paste directly into the system prompt field:

You are a compliance auditor for outbound email campaigns.

Review every email draft or sequence step provided to you against the following rules:

CAN-SPAM (US):
- Subject line must not be deceptive or misleading
- "From" name must clearly identify the sender
- Physical postal address must be included in the email body or footer
- Opt-out mechanism must be present and clearly labeled
- Honor opt-out requests within 10 business days

GDPR (EU):
- Confirm a lawful basis for processing exists (consent, legitimate interest, contract)
- Do not email contacts flagged as EU-based unless consent field is TRUE
- Do not use pre-ticked consent boxes or bundled consent language

CASL (Canada):
- Express or implied consent must exist before sending
- Sender identification must be complete
- Unsubscribe must function within 10 business days

For each issue found, respond with:
ISSUE: [rule violated]
SEVERITY: [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
SUGGESTION: [specific fix]

If no issues are found, respond with: COMPLIANT

This prompt gives the agent a structured output format that MailClaw can parse and surface in the dashboard's review panel.

Step 2: Attach the Agent to Your Sequence Builder

In the Sequence Builder, open any existing sequence or create a new one. On each step's settings panel, you'll see an Agent Review toggle. Enable it and select your Compliance Auditor agent from the dropdown.

With this enabled, every time a sequence step is saved or edited, the agent runs a compliance audit in the background. If the agent returns any HIGH severity issues, the step is automatically flagged and blocked from sending until a human reviewer clears it. MEDIUM and LOW issues generate warnings visible in the dashboard but don't block delivery.

Step 3: Add Contact-Level Compliance Checks via Enrichment

The contact enrichment pipeline is where data compliance gets enforced. MailClaw's enrichment system can pull in fields from HubSpot, Salesforce, and CSV imports — including consent timestamps, opt-in sources, and geographic region data.

Configure your compliance agent to cross-reference contact metadata before sequence enrollment. In the MailClaw CLI, you can do this with:

mailclaw agent run compliance-auditor \
  --mode contact-check \
  --input contacts/pending-enrollment.csv \
  --rules gdpr,casl \
  --output reports/compliance-check-$(date +%Y%m%d).json

This command runs the agent across your pending contact list, checks each record against your configured rulesets, and writes a dated JSON report to your local reports directory. Any contact flagged as non-compliant is excluded from enrollment automatically when you pass the --enforce flag.

Integrating Compliance Checks Into Your Sending Workflow

Pre-Send Hooks with SMTP and OAuth Senders

MailClaw supports a pre-send hook system that fires before any email is dispatched through your configured senders — whether that's a raw SMTP connection to SendGrid, a Gmail OAuth account, or an Outlook integration. You can attach your compliance agent as a pre-send hook so it acts as a final gate:

# In your mailclaw.config.json
{
  "preSendHooks": [
    {
      "name": "compliance-check",
      "agent": "compliance-auditor",
      "blockOnSeverity": ["HIGH"],
      "notifyOnSeverity": ["MEDIUM", "LOW"],
      "notificationChannel": "dashboard"
    }
  ]
}

With this configuration, HIGH severity findings halt the send and surface an alert in your localhost dashboard. MEDIUM and LOW findings are logged but don't interrupt delivery. You can also route notifications to a Slack webhook or a local log file if you prefer a different alerting pattern.

Using Deliverability Tools to Catch Compliance Signals Early

MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring tracks bounce rates, spam complaints, and unsubscribe spikes across all your connected senders. These metrics are compliance signals in disguise — a sudden spike in spam complaints often means your targeting or consent hygiene has a problem, not just your subject lines.

Configure your compliance agent to ingest deliverability reports as part of its context window. In the Agents panel, enable Deliverability Context for your Compliance Auditor. The agent will then factor in recent complaint rates when scoring new drafts, flagging content that resembles high-complaint patterns from your own sending history.

Building a Compliance Audit Log

Regulators don't just want you to be compliant — they want you to demonstrate that you've been consistently compliant over time. MailClaw's open-source architecture makes this straightforward because everything is stored locally and you control the data.

Set up a scheduled audit job using the MailClaw CLI that runs nightly and archives compliance reports:

mailclaw agent run compliance-auditor \
  --mode full-audit \
  --scope sequences,contacts,sent-last-30d \
  --output audit-logs/$(date +%Y-%m-%d)-audit.json \
  --format structured

Store these JSON reports in a version-controlled directory. Over time, you'll have a complete, timestamped audit trail you can produce quickly if your practices are ever questioned. Because MailClaw runs locally and is built on OpenClaw's extensible agent framework, you can also build a custom export script that formats these logs to match whatever documentation standard your legal team requires.

Practical Tips for Getting the Most Out of Compliance Agents

  • Keep your ruleset versioned. Store your agent's system prompt in a plain text file under version control. When regulations change — and they do — you want a clear record of what rules your agent was enforcing at any given time.
  • Don't treat HIGH severity as infallible. AI agents are powerful reviewers but not lawyers. A HIGH flag should trigger a human review, not an automatic assumption of guilt. Use the agent to surface issues faster, not to replace legal judgment.
  • Run compliance checks on imported lists immediately. Whenever you import contacts from HubSpot, Salesforce, or a CSV, run the contact-check command before those contacts are eligible for any sequence enrollment.
  • Use multi-account support to isolate compliance profiles. If you send to both US and EU audiences, configure separate sender accounts with separate compliance agents tuned to the relevant regulatory frameworks. MailClaw's multi-account support makes this clean and manageable from a single dashboard.
  • Test your agent with known violations. Before trusting the agent in production, seed it with a handful of intentionally non-compliant email drafts and verify it catches every issue. Treat this like a unit test for your compliance pipeline.

The Bottom Line

Compliance checking is exactly the kind of repetitive, rule-based work that AI agents are well-suited for. By configuring MailClaw's agents to audit sequences, validate contact data, and act as pre-send gates, you shift compliance from a periodic review into a continuous, automated layer of your outreach infrastructure.

Because MailClaw runs entirely on your local machine, you get the power of AI-assisted compliance without the privacy trade-offs of sending your email content and contact data to a third-party cloud service. That's a meaningful advantage for anyone operating in regulated industries or handling data subject to GDPR and CASL.

Start with one sequence, one agent, and one ruleset. Once you see how quickly the agent catches issues that would otherwise slip through, you'll wonder how you ever ran outbound campaigns without it.

articles.title: How to Create an AI Agent for Invoice Processing from Email
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how to build a fully automated AI agent that reads, parses, and processes invoice emails directly from your inbox — using MailClaw's local AI agent framework to extract data, update records, and trigger follow-up workflows without manual intervention.
articles.content:
Why Invoice Emails Are a Perfect Use Case for AI Agents

Every finance team, freelancer, and operations manager knows the pain: invoices arrive in dozens of formats — PDFs attached to Gmail threads, inline HTML from Outlook, forwarded chains from vendors, payment confirmations buried under three layers of reply-all. Someone has to open each one, extract the relevant numbers, update a spreadsheet or accounting system, and follow up if something looks wrong.

This is exactly the kind of structured-but-messy workflow that AI agents were built for. The data is predictable in type (amounts, dates, vendor names, invoice IDs) but unpredictable in format — which means rule-based automation breaks constantly, but a language model handles it gracefully.

With MailClaw, you can build an AI email agent that runs locally on your Mac, connects to your real inbox via Gmail or Outlook OAuth, reads incoming invoices, extracts structured data, updates your records in HubSpot or a local database, and triggers follow-up sequences — all without sending a single email to a third-party cloud service for processing.

What You'll Build

By the end of this guide, you'll have a working MailClaw AI agent that:

  • Monitors a connected inbox (Gmail, Outlook, or any SMTP/IMAP account) for invoice emails
  • Uses an OpenClaw-powered AI model to extract invoice fields: vendor, amount, due date, line items, and currency
  • Flags anomalies — duplicate invoice IDs, amounts above a threshold, missing fields
  • Logs structured data to a local JSON file or pushes it to a connected CRM like HubSpot or Salesforce
  • Sends automated acknowledgment or follow-up emails using MailClaw's sequence builder

Step 1: Set Up MailClaw and Connect Your Inbox

If you haven't already, install MailClaw and start the local dashboard:

npx mailclaw start

This spins up the MailClaw interface at localhost:3100. From the dashboard, navigate to Accounts → Add Account and connect your Gmail or Outlook inbox using OAuth. MailClaw never proxies your credentials through external servers — authentication tokens are stored locally and your emails stay on your machine.

For a dedicated invoices inbox (recommended), create a Gmail filter that labels all emails containing "invoice", "payment due", or "remittance" and routes them to a specific label like invoices-inbox. MailClaw can then scope the agent to watch only that label, reducing noise significantly.

Step 2: Create the Invoice Agent

In MailClaw, AI agents are defined as configuration files that describe what the agent watches, what it extracts, and what actions it takes. From your terminal:

mailclaw agent create --name invoice-processor

This scaffolds a new agent config at ~/.mailclaw/agents/invoice-processor.yaml. Open it and configure the trigger and extraction logic:

name: invoice-processor
description: Extracts structured data from incoming invoice emails
trigger:
  type: inbox_watch
  account: finance@yourcompany.com
  filter:
    label: invoices-inbox
    subject_contains:
      - invoice
      - payment due
      - remittance advice

ai:
  model: openclaw-local
  extract:
    - field: vendor_name
      prompt: "What is the name of the company or vendor sending this invoice?"
    - field: invoice_number
      prompt: "What is the invoice number or reference ID?"
    - field: invoice_date
      prompt: "What is the invoice date? Return in YYYY-MM-DD format."
    - field: due_date
      prompt: "What is the payment due date? Return in YYYY-MM-DD format."
    - field: total_amount
      prompt: "What is the total amount due, as a number only?"
    - field: currency
      prompt: "What currency is the invoice in? Return the 3-letter ISO code."
    - field: line_items
      prompt: "List the line items as a JSON array with keys: description, quantity, unit_price, total."

actions:
  - type: log_to_file
    path: ~/invoices/processed.jsonl

  - type: flag_if
    condition: "extracted.total_amount > 10000"
    tag: high-value-review

  - type: flag_if
    condition: "extracted.invoice_number in seen_invoice_ids"
    tag: possible-duplicate

  - type: send_sequence
    sequence: invoice-acknowledgment
    to: "{{ sender_email }}"

Save the file and start the agent:

mailclaw agent start invoice-processor

You'll see live logs in your terminal and in the Agents tab of the localhost:3100 dashboard, showing each email processed, fields extracted, and actions taken.

Step 3: Build the Acknowledgment Sequence

A professional touch — and often a compliance requirement — is sending an automated acknowledgment when an invoice is received. MailClaw's sequence builder makes this straightforward.

Creating the Sequence via CLI

mailclaw sequence create --name invoice-acknowledgment

Edit the generated sequence file to define your email steps:

name: invoice-acknowledgment
steps:
  - delay: 0
    subject: "Invoice Received: {{ extracted.invoice_number }}"
    body: |
      Hi {{ sender_first_name }},

      Thank you — we've received your invoice {{ extracted.invoice_number }}
      for {{ extracted.currency }} {{ extracted.total_amount }}, dated {{ extracted.invoice_date }}.

      Our team will review it and process payment by {{ extracted.due_date }}.
      If you have any questions in the meantime, reply to this email.

      Best,
      The Finance Team

  - delay: 7d
    condition: "invoice.status == 'unpaid'"
    subject: "Following up: Invoice {{ extracted.invoice_number }}"
    body: |
      Hi {{ sender_first_name }},

      Just checking in on invoice {{ extracted.invoice_number }}.
      We want to make sure everything is on track for payment by {{ extracted.due_date }}.

      Please let us know if you need anything from our side.

This sequence fires immediately on receipt and has a built-in 7-day follow-up that only triggers if the invoice is still marked unpaid in your system — a detail MailClaw resolves by checking the invoice.status field you can sync from HubSpot or a local store.

Step 4: Push Data to HubSpot or Salesforce

The extracted invoice data becomes genuinely powerful when it flows into your existing systems. MailClaw supports webhook actions and native CRM integrations for HubSpot and Salesforce.

HubSpot Integration

Add a CRM action to your agent config:

  - type: crm_upsert
    integration: hubspot
    object: deal
    match_on: invoice_number
    fields:
      deal_name: "Invoice {{ extracted.invoice_number }} - {{ extracted.vendor_name }}"
      amount: "{{ extracted.total_amount }}"
      closedate: "{{ extracted.due_date }}"
      pipeline: invoices
      dealstage: received

MailClaw will create or update a Deal in HubSpot every time an invoice is processed, keeping your pipeline current without manual data entry. The contact enrichment engine can also auto-associate the deal with an existing HubSpot contact based on the sender's email domain.

Webhook / Salesforce

For Salesforce or any other system, use the generic webhook action:

  - type: webhook
    url: https://your-internal-api.com/invoices
    method: POST
    payload:
      invoice_number: "{{ extracted.invoice_number }}"
      vendor: "{{ extracted.vendor_name }}"
      amount: "{{ extracted.total_amount }}"
      due_date: "{{ extracted.due_date }}"
      raw_email_id: "{{ email.message_id }}"

Step 5: Monitor Deliverability and Agent Health

Because MailClaw's acknowledgment emails go out from your real account (via Gmail OAuth or a configured SendGrid SMTP connection), deliverability matters. MailClaw's built-in deliverability tools — accessible from the dashboard at localhost:3100 under Deliverability → Monitor — track bounce rates, reply rates, and SPF/DKIM alignment for all outbound agent emails.

If acknowledgment emails start bouncing (common with invoices from auto-generated vendor addresses), the agent will surface those failures in the dashboard and you can configure fallback behavior:

on_bounce:
  action: flag_for_manual_review
  tag: bounced-acknowledgment

Practical Tips for Production Use

Handle PDF Attachments

Many invoices arrive as PDF attachments rather than email body text. MailClaw's agent pipeline includes an attachment extraction step that runs OCR on PDF attachments before passing content to the AI model. Enable it in your agent config with parse_attachments: true — the extracted text is concatenated with the email body for the AI extraction prompt.

Build a Seen Invoice ID Cache

The duplicate detection in the config above relies on a local cache of processed invoice IDs. MailClaw maintains this automatically in ~/.mailclaw/agents/invoice-processor.cache.json, but you can also point it at a shared store for team environments.

Use Contact Enrichment for Vendor Intelligence

MailClaw's contact enrichment feature can automatically look up the sending domain and append company data — industry, size, website — to your invoice records. This is useful for flagging invoices from unknown vendors or auto-populating vendor profiles in your accounting system.

Open source advantage: Because MailClaw is fully open source and built on OpenClaw, you can inspect exactly what the AI extraction prompts look like, modify the parsing logic, and contribute improvements back to the project. There's no black box between your inbox and your data.

What This Replaces

A workflow like this typically requires stitching together Zapier, a cloud OCR service, a form parser, and a CRM integration — each with its own subscription cost, rate limit, and privacy concern. Running the same pipeline locally with MailClaw means your invoice data never leaves your machine until you explicitly push it somewhere, the AI model runs on your hardware via OpenClaw, and the entire system is auditable and version-controlled.

Start with the basic extraction agent, validate that the fields come through cleanly on your real invoice emails, then layer in the CRM sync and sequences. Most teams have a working invoice processor running in under an hour — and a dramatically cleaner accounts payable inbox by end of week.

articles.title: MailClaw AI Agent: Personalizing Outreach at Scale with Context Memory
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how MailClaw's AI email agents use context memory to deliver hyper-personalized outreach at scale — with practical setup steps, CLI commands, and real-world sequencing strategies that go far beyond simple mail merge.
articles.content:
Why "Personalization" Usually Fails at Scale

Most email personalization is a lie. You know the kind — a sequence that swaps in a first name and a company name, then sends the exact same pitch to ten thousand people. Recipients see through it instantly, reply rates crater, and your domain quietly earns a reputation for spam. The problem isn't the intent to personalize; it's that traditional tools treat personalization as a template variable problem rather than a context problem.

Real personalization means knowing that Sarah at Acme Corp just published a LinkedIn post about migrating off Salesforce, that her company grew 40% last quarter, and that three of her colleagues downloaded your pricing page last Tuesday. It means your email speaks to that moment, not to a demographic bucket.

This is exactly the problem MailClaw's AI email agents were built to solve.

What Context Memory Actually Means for Email Agents

MailClaw runs locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, powered by OpenClaw under the hood. One of its most powerful capabilities is the AI agent layer — autonomous agents that don't just fill templates, but reason about each contact's context before composing an email.

Context memory in MailClaw agents works across three dimensions:

  • Contact-level memory: Every enriched data point, prior send, open, click, and reply is stored and available to the agent at compose time.
  • Sequence-level memory: The agent knows what was said in prior steps of the sequence and avoids repeating itself or contradicting earlier messages.
  • Signal-level memory: Real-time signals — job changes, funding announcements, website visits, social activity — feed into the agent's reasoning via MailClaw's enrichment pipeline.

The result is an agent that writes like a thoughtful SDR who actually did their homework, not a mail merge script dressed up with a spinner.

Setting Up Your First AI Email Agent

Step 1: Launch the Dashboard and Configure Your Agent

Start MailClaw from your terminal and open the local dashboard:

mailclaw start
# Dashboard available at http://localhost:3100

From the dashboard, navigate to Agents → New Agent. You'll define the agent's persona, goal, and constraints. A typical outbound agent config looks like this in MailClaw's agent DSL:

# agents/outbound-saas.yaml
name: "SaaS Outbound Agent"
goal: "Book discovery calls with VP-level buyers at Series A-C SaaS companies"
persona:
  tone: professional-friendly
  avoid: ["aggressive follow-ups", "fake urgency", "generic openers"]
memory:
  contact_fields: [job_title, company, recent_news, linkedin_summary, last_open, reply_history]
  sequence_recall: true
  signal_lookback_days: 30
enrichment:
  providers: [clearbit, hunter, linkedin_scraper]
  auto_enrich: true

Save this file and register it with the CLI:

mailclaw agent register agents/outbound-saas.yaml

Step 2: Enrich Your Contact List

Before your agent can personalize intelligently, it needs data. MailClaw's contact enrichment pipeline pulls from multiple sources and normalizes everything into a unified contact record. Import a CSV or connect directly to HubSpot or Salesforce:

# Import from CSV
mailclaw contacts import --file leads.csv --enrich

# Sync from HubSpot
mailclaw contacts sync --source hubspot --filter "lifecycle_stage=lead"

# Sync from Salesforce
mailclaw contacts sync --source salesforce --query "SELECT Id, Email, Title FROM Lead WHERE Status='Open'"

MailClaw will automatically call your configured enrichment providers (Clearbit, Hunter, and others) and backfill missing fields like company headcount, tech stack, recent funding, and LinkedIn headline. You can watch enrichment progress live in the dashboard under Contacts → Enrichment Queue.

Step 3: Build a Context-Aware Sequence

The sequence builder in MailClaw lets you define steps that reference agent-generated content rather than static templates. Here's how a three-step sequence might be configured:

# sequences/discovery-call.yaml
name: "Discovery Call Sequence"
agent: outbound-saas
steps:
  - step: 1
    delay: 0
    subject_strategy: agent_generated
    body_strategy: agent_generated
    context_hints:
      - "Reference a recent company milestone or news item if available"
      - "Tie our value prop to their stated role or team size"
      - "Keep under 120 words"

  - step: 2
    delay: 3d
    condition: "not opened OR not replied"
    subject_strategy: agent_generated
    body_strategy: agent_generated
    context_hints:
      - "Do not repeat the same angle as step 1"
      - "Reference the previous email briefly"
      - "Try a different value prop angle"

  - step: 3
    delay: 5d
    condition: "not replied"
    subject_strategy: agent_generated
    body_strategy: agent_generated
    context_hints:
      - "Short break-up style email"
      - "Low pressure, leave door open"
mailclaw sequence register sequences/discovery-call.yaml
mailclaw sequence launch discovery-call --contacts hubspot-leads

At send time, the agent pulls each contact's full context record, reads the conversation history, checks what signals fired in the last 30 days, and generates a unique email. No two contacts receive identical copy.

Context Signals That Actually Move the Needle

The quality of your agent's output is directly proportional to the richness of your contact context. Here are the signals worth prioritizing:

Job Change Signals

A contact who just started a new role is in "new initiatives" mode. They're evaluating vendors, consolidating tools, and trying to make an early impact. MailClaw's enrichment pipeline watches LinkedIn changes and flags these contacts automatically. Your agent can open with something grounded in that moment — acknowledging the transition and positioning your tool as something worth evaluating fresh.

Funding and Growth Signals

A Series B announcement almost always means headcount growth, new tooling budget, and pressure to scale operations. When MailClaw detects a funding event via Crunchbase enrichment, it tags the contact record with signal:funding_event. Your agent prompt can instruct it to lead with growth-relevant messaging when this tag is present.

Engagement Signals from Prior Sequences

This is where context memory earns its keep. If a contact opened your email three times but never replied, the agent in step 2 knows this. It won't send another generic follow-up — it might try a more direct ask, a different subject line approach, or a softer angle, depending on how you've configured your agent's decision logic.

Pro tip: In your agent config, enable sequence_recall: true and set a signal_lookback_days of at least 14. This gives the agent enough history to avoid redundancy without drowning in stale context.

Deliverability: Keeping Personalization from Backfiring

Hyper-personalized copy only matters if it lands in the inbox. MailClaw includes a built-in deliverability monitoring layer that runs continuously in the background. From the dashboard at localhost:3100/deliverability, you can track:

  • Sender reputation scores per connected account (Gmail, Outlook, custom SMTP via SendGrid or Postmark)
  • SPF, DKIM, and DMARC validation status
  • Bounce and spam complaint rates per sequence
  • Warmup progress for new sending addresses

MailClaw's multi-account support means you can distribute volume intelligently across several sending addresses. The agent is aware of per-account sending limits and routes emails accordingly — no manual rotation required.

# Add a Gmail account via OAuth
mailclaw accounts add --provider gmail --oauth

# Add a custom SMTP account (e.g., SendGrid)
mailclaw accounts add --provider smtp \
  --host smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --port 587 \
  --user apikey \
  --pass YOUR_SENDGRID_API_KEY

# Set send limits per account
mailclaw accounts set-limit --account gmail-1 --daily 80
mailclaw accounts set-limit --account sendgrid-1 --daily 300

Measuring What Your Agent Gets Right

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your machine, you own all your data. The analytics dashboard gives you per-sequence and per-step breakdowns of open rates, reply rates, and conversion events. But more usefully, you can query your agent's reasoning logs to understand why it made specific personalization choices:

mailclaw agent logs --agent outbound-saas --contact sarah@acmecorp.com

This outputs a trace of the context the agent loaded, the signals it weighted, and the copy it generated — making it straightforward to tune your context hints and agent config based on what's actually working.

The Compounding Advantage of Local, Persistent Memory

Because MailClaw runs locally, your contact memory and agent reasoning logs never leave your machine. There's no SaaS vendor holding your enrichment data, no per-seat pricing that scales against you, and no API rate limits throttling your enrichment at the worst moment. The OpenClaw foundation means the agent logic is fully inspectable and extensible — if you want to add a custom signal source or modify how the agent weights job title versus company size, you can.

Over time, as your sequences run and your agent accumulates more reply history, open patterns, and signal data, its personalization gets measurably better. The context memory compounds. A contact who's been in your system for six months carries six months of behavioral signal — and your agent uses all of it.

That's the gap between a mail merge and a genuinely intelligent outreach system. MailClaw closes it, locally, in a single command.

articles.title: How to Build an Agent That Syncs Email Decisions to Project Tools
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to build an AI email agent with MailClaw that automatically syncs reply decisions, deal stages, and follow-up actions to tools like HubSpot, Notion, Linear, and Salesforce — without writing a single manual CRM update.
articles.content:
Why Email Decisions Get Lost in the Noise

Every sales rep, founder, or ops lead knows the feeling: you get a reply, make a mental decision about what to do next, fire off a response — and then forget to update the CRM. Three days later, a deal falls through the cracks because HubSpot still shows the contact as "Contacted" when they've actually said yes to a call.

The problem isn't discipline. It's that email and project tools live in completely separate mental contexts. Bridging them manually is friction, and friction loses deals.

This is exactly the kind of workflow that AI email agents were built to solve. Using MailClaw — the open-source, locally-hosted email automation platform built on OpenClaw — you can build an agent that reads incoming replies, interprets intent, and pushes structured decisions directly to your project and CRM tools, all without leaving your terminal or touching localhost:3100 more than once to set it up.

What "Syncing Email Decisions" Actually Means

Before we build anything, let's be precise about what we're automating. An "email decision" is any inference your agent makes about a reply that should change state somewhere else. Examples include:

  • A prospect replies "let's do it" → move HubSpot deal to Negotiation
  • A lead says "not right now, maybe Q3" → create a follow-up task in Notion or Linear dated for June
  • A customer reports a bug via email → open a GitHub issue and tag the engineering lead
  • A partner confirms availability → update a Airtable row and send a calendar invite
  • Someone unsubscribes or says "remove me" → flag the contact in MailClaw and suppress from all active sequences

The common thread: intent extracted from email → structured action in another tool. That's the pipeline you're building.

Setting Up Your MailClaw Agent Environment

Prerequisites

You'll need MailClaw running locally. If you haven't set it up yet, clone the repo and start the dashboard:

git clone https://github.com/mailclaw/mailclaw
cd mailclaw
npm install
npm run start
# Dashboard available at http://localhost:3100

From the dashboard, connect your email accounts under Settings → Accounts. MailClaw supports Gmail (OAuth), Outlook (OAuth), and any SMTP provider like SendGrid or Postmark. For this workflow, you'll want at least one inbox connected that receives replies from active sequences.

Creating the Agent

MailClaw's AI email agents are defined as YAML config files that combine triggers, a model prompt, and action handlers. Create a new agent file:

touch agents/reply-sync-agent.yaml

Here's a working base configuration:

name: Reply Sync Agent
description: Classifies inbound replies and syncs decisions to project tools
trigger:
  type: inbound_reply
  sequences:
    - outbound-q2-leads
    - partner-outreach-v2
model:
  provider: openai
  model: gpt-4o
  temperature: 0.2
prompt: |
  You are an email classification agent. Given a reply email, extract:
  1. intent (positive, negative, deferral, objection, question, unsubscribe)
  2. next_action (schedule_call, create_task, update_crm, suppress_contact, reply_needed)
  3. urgency (high, medium, low)
  4. notes (a one-sentence summary of what the sender wants)
  Return JSON only.
actions:
  - type: webhook
    label: Push to HubSpot
    url: https://your-n8n-instance.com/webhook/reply-sync
    method: POST
    include_fields: [intent, next_action, urgency, notes, contact_email, sequence_id]
  - type: mailclaw_tag
    label: Tag contact
    tag_map:
      positive: "hot-lead"
      negative: "closed-lost"
      deferral: "nurture-q3"
