      unsubscribe: "do-not-contact"

Load the agent from the CLI:

mailclaw agents:load agents/reply-sync-agent.yaml
mailclaw agents:start reply-sync-agent

Now every inbound reply to those sequences will be classified and routed automatically.

Building the Integration Layer

Option 1: Webhook to n8n or Make

The simplest path is pointing your agent's webhook action at an automation platform like n8n (self-hosted) or Make. Your MailClaw agent POSTs structured JSON on every reply, and n8n routes it based on the next_action field.

A minimal n8n workflow looks like this:

  1. Webhook node receives the MailClaw payload
  2. Switch node branches on next_action
  3. update_crm → HubSpot node updates deal stage using contact_email as lookup key
  4. create_task → Linear or Notion node creates a task with the agent's notes as the description
  5. schedule_call → Calendly or Google Calendar node fires an invite
  6. suppress_contact → calls back to MailClaw's REST API to add a suppression

The MailClaw suppression callback looks like this (useful for step 6):

curl -X POST http://localhost:3100/api/contacts/suppress \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email": "lead@example.com", "reason": "unsubscribe"}'

Option 2: Direct API Integrations via Agent Actions

If you want fewer moving parts, MailClaw's agent action system supports direct HTTP calls with custom headers. You can hit HubSpot or Salesforce APIs directly from the agent config:

actions:
  - type: http
    label: Update Salesforce Opportunity
    condition: "intent == 'positive'"
    url: https://yourinstance.salesforce.com/services/data/v57.0/sobjects/Opportunity/{{salesforce_opp_id}}
    method: PATCH
    headers:
      Authorization: "Bearer {{env.SALESFORCE_TOKEN}}"
      Content-Type: application/json
    body:
      StageName: "Proposal/Price Quote"
      Description: "{{notes}}"

Environment variables are loaded from your .env file in the MailClaw root, so secrets never touch the agent YAML itself. This approach works cleanly for Salesforce, HubSpot, Pipedrive, and any tool with a REST API.

Enriching Contacts Before the Decision Is Made

One underused trick: run MailClaw's contact enrichment as a pre-step before classification. When your agent sees a reply from an unknown sender, enrichment pulls in company size, role, LinkedIn data, and technographics before the model evaluates intent. This means your prompt can include context like "this person is a VP at a 500-person SaaS company" — and the classification becomes significantly more accurate.

Enable enrichment in your agent config:

enrichment:
  enabled: true
  providers: [clearbit, hunter]
  inject_into_prompt: true

With inject_into_prompt: true, MailClaw automatically appends the enriched contact profile to the model context before classification runs. You don't need to write any extra prompt logic — it just works.

Monitoring and Debugging Your Agent

The Localhost Dashboard

Open http://localhost:3100/agents/reply-sync-agent to see a live feed of every reply processed, the raw model output, which actions fired, and any errors. This is invaluable during the first week of running a new agent — you'll quickly spot cases where "let's reconnect sometime" is being classified as positive intent when it should be a deferral.

Refining Your Prompt

Treat your classification prompt like a living document. Keep a prompt-changelog.md alongside your agent YAML and note every correction you make. Common refinements:

  • Add few-shot examples for edge cases your domain sees often (e.g., "out of office" replies should map to deferral, not question)
  • Specify your industry's language patterns — "we're evaluating options" means something different in enterprise sales vs. agency outreach
  • Set temperature: 0.1 for classification tasks — you want deterministic outputs, not creative ones

Deliverability Awareness

MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring tracks reply rates, bounce rates, and spam complaints per sequence. If your reply-sync agent starts seeing a high volume of "remove me" classifications from a specific sequence, that's an early signal that your outreach is landing wrong — before your domain reputation takes a hit. Check the Deliverability tab in the dashboard weekly and cross-reference it with your agent classification logs.

Putting It All Together: A Real Workflow

Here's what a fully wired system looks like in production for a small sales team:

  1. MailClaw runs an outbound sequence via SendGrid SMTP to 200 prospects
  2. Replies come into a connected Gmail inbox
  3. The reply-sync agent classifies each reply within seconds of arrival
  4. Hot leads (positive intent) automatically move to Proposal in HubSpot and create a task in Linear for the AE
  5. Deferrals create a dated Notion reminder with the agent's summary note
  6. Unsubscribes are suppressed in MailClaw and synced back to HubSpot's suppression list via webhook
  7. The team reviews the dashboard each morning, handles only the reply_needed flagged threads

The result: zero manual CRM updates, full audit trail, and a team that spends time on conversations — not data entry.

The best CRM update is the one that happens automatically, the moment the signal exists. MailClaw's agent layer puts that moment at reply-time, not end-of-day.

Because MailClaw is fully open-source and runs on your own machine, you own every piece of this pipeline — the prompts, the data, the integrations. Nothing goes through a third-party black box. Fork it, extend it, and build the exact workflow your team actually needs.

articles.title: Using MailClaw AI Agents for Multi-Language Email Automation
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's AI email agents to build, personalize, and automate multi-language email campaigns — with practical CLI commands, sequence configuration tips, and best practices for reaching global audiences without sacrificing deliverability.
articles.content:
Why Multi-Language Email Automation Is Harder Than It Looks

Sending emails in multiple languages sounds straightforward until you actually try to do it at scale. You need localized copy, culturally appropriate tone, proper character encoding, region-aware sending times, and — if you're running any kind of deliverability monitoring — separate reputation signals per domain or inbox provider. Most commercial platforms bolt on "language support" as an afterthought, leaving you to manage translated templates manually and hope the merge tags survive the copy-paste.

MailClaw takes a fundamentally different approach. Because it runs locally on your machine (at localhost:3100) and is built on the OpenClaw engine, you have full programmatic control over how AI agents generate, translate, and personalize outbound email — without your contact data ever leaving your environment. For teams doing international outreach, this combination of AI flexibility and local-first architecture changes what's actually possible.

Setting Up a Multi-Language AI Agent

MailClaw's AI email agents are configured as agent definitions — YAML or JSON files that tell OpenClaw how to behave when generating or responding to email content. To build a multi-language agent, you'll define language detection logic, per-locale tone profiles, and fallback behavior all in one place.

Step 1: Initialize Your Agent

From your terminal, scaffold a new agent using the MailClaw CLI:

mailclaw agent create --name "global-outreach" --type sequence

This generates a starter agent file at ~/.mailclaw/agents/global-outreach.yaml. Open it in your editor and you'll see the basic structure: model, persona, instructions, and hooks.

Step 2: Define Locale-Aware Instructions

The instructions block is where the real power lives. Here's a working example that supports English, Spanish, French, and German:

name: global-outreach
model: gpt-4o
persona: "You are a professional B2B sales development rep with expertise in international markets."
instructions:
  base: |
    When generating emails, detect the contact's preferred language from
    the `locale` field. If no locale is set, default to English.
    Always match the formality level appropriate for the locale:
    - en: Direct, concise, professional
    - es: Warm but professional, use "usted" for initial contact
    - fr: Formal on first contact, avoid overly casual phrasing
    - de: Precise, structured, avoid unnecessary filler language
  subject_line_rules: |
    Generate subject lines under 50 characters.
    Localize idioms — do not directly translate English metaphors.
  signature: "Use the sender's name and title from the account profile."
hooks:
  on_contact_enrich: true
  on_bounce: escalate_to_human

Notice the on_contact_enrich: true hook — this tells the agent to re-evaluate its personalization logic whenever MailClaw's contact enrichment pipeline updates a record. If a contact's LinkedIn profile reveals they're based in Lyon, the agent will automatically shift to French tone guidance on the next sequence step.

Connecting Contact Enrichment to Language Detection

You can't personalize by language if you don't know what language to use. MailClaw's contact enrichment features can pull signals from multiple sources — including HubSpot properties, Salesforce custom fields, and enrichment APIs — and map them to a locale field that your agents read directly.

To configure enrichment-to-locale mapping, edit your mailclaw.config.js:

module.exports = {
  enrichment: {
    sources: ["hubspot", "salesforce", "clearbit"],
    fieldMappings: {
      locale: ["hs_language", "sf_preferred_locale", "clearbit.geo.countryCode"],
      fallbackLocale: "en"
    }
  }
};

MailClaw will walk down the fieldMappings.locale array in order, using the first non-null value it finds. This means your HubSpot language preference wins if it exists, but you'll still get a sensible fallback for contacts enriched only via Clearbit country data.

Importing Contacts With Locale Metadata

If you're working from a CSV export (say, from a Salesforce campaign or a HubSpot list), make sure your import includes a locale column:

mailclaw contacts import --file prospects.csv --map "language=locale"

The --map flag lets you reconcile column name differences without editing your source file. Once imported, you can verify locale distribution in the localhost:3100 dashboard under Contacts → Segments.

Building Your Multi-Language Sequence

With your agent configured and contacts enriched, it's time to wire everything together in the sequence builder. MailClaw's sequence builder supports conditional branching based on contact fields, which is exactly what you need for multi-language flows.

Creating the Sequence

mailclaw sequence create --name "q4-international" --agent global-outreach --steps 4

In the dashboard at localhost:3100/sequences/q4-international, you'll see four blank steps. For each step, set the generation mode to AI Agent rather than static template. This tells MailClaw to invoke your global-outreach agent at send time, passing the contact's current enriched profile as context.

Adding Locale-Based Delays

One underappreciated aspect of multi-language campaigns is that optimal send times vary significantly by region. A Tuesday morning send that crushes it in New York will land at 9 PM in Berlin. MailClaw lets you set timezone-aware delays per step:

mailclaw sequence edit q4-international --step 2 \
  --delay "3d" \
  --send-time "09:00" \
  --timezone "contact.timezone"

The contact.timezone value is automatically populated during enrichment if you've enabled the timezone resolution feature in your config. If it's missing, MailClaw defaults to the sender account's timezone — never the server's system clock, which is an important distinction when you're running everything locally.

Deliverability Considerations for Multi-Language Campaigns

Here's something most guides skip: sending multilingual email isn't just a content challenge — it's a deliverability challenge. Spam filters in different regions have different sensitivity profiles. French ISPs have historically been stricter about certain HTML patterns. German recipients have high unsubscribe rates if the first email feels too salesy. Japanese email clients render differently from Outlook or Gmail.

Using MailClaw's Deliverability Monitor

MailClaw's built-in deliverability tools let you run pre-send checks per locale. From the CLI:

mailclaw deliverability check --sequence q4-international --locale fr

This runs your French-language generated drafts through spam scoring, checks your DKIM/SPF/DMARC alignment for the sending domain, and flags any HTML encoding issues that might cause rendering problems in common French email clients. Run this for each locale before activating a sequence — it takes under 30 seconds and can save you from a reputation hit.

Multi-Account Sending by Region

For higher-volume international campaigns, consider mapping locale segments to dedicated sending accounts. MailClaw's multi-account support makes this clean to configure:

mailclaw accounts add --alias "eu-outreach" --smtp sendgrid --region eu
mailclaw sequence assign q4-international --locale "fr,de,es" --account eu-outreach

Keeping European contacts on an EU-region SendGrid subaccount (or an Outlook OAuth account with a .eu domain) isn't just good for deliverability — it's also relevant for GDPR compliance, since your data stays within a defined boundary.

Pro tip: Create a dedicated Gmail or Outlook account per language market during the warm-up phase. MailClaw's deliverability monitor will track reputation per account independently, so a problematic German campaign won't drag down your English-language inbox health.

Testing and Iterating With the Local Dashboard

One of the biggest advantages of running MailClaw locally is that your iteration loop is fast. You're not waiting for a cloud platform to sync data or propagate template changes. Open localhost:3100, navigate to your sequence, click Preview with AI, and select a test contact from each locale to see exactly what the agent would generate — subject line, body, and signature — before a single email is sent.

Use the A/B Variants panel to test whether your German contacts respond better to a direct value proposition opener or a case-study-led approach. MailClaw's open-source codebase means you can also extend the dashboard with custom locale-specific reporting if your team needs it — a meaningful advantage over locked-down SaaS platforms.

Practical Checklist Before Going Live

  • Verify locale coverage: Run mailclaw contacts stats --group-by locale to confirm all contacts have a locale assigned before activating.
  • Test every locale path: Use Preview with AI in the dashboard for at least one contact per language to catch awkward phrasing.
  • Check encoding: Ensure your SMTP settings support UTF-8 — critical for French accents, German umlauts, and any CJK characters.
  • Set unsubscribe language: Your unsubscribe link and footer text should also be localized. Configure this in Settings → Compliance → Locale Footers in the dashboard.
  • Monitor the first 48 hours: Watch bounce rates and spam complaints by locale in the deliverability dashboard. Different markets will signal problems differently and early action protects your sending reputation.

Multi-language email automation done right is genuinely complex — but MailClaw's combination of AI agents, enrichment pipelines, and local-first architecture gives you the control to get it right without stitching together five different SaaS tools. Start with two or three locales, nail the agent instructions and deliverability configuration, then expand. The infrastructure will scale with you.

articles.title: How to Create an AI Agent That Tracks Deals from Email Conversations
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to build an AI agent inside MailClaw that automatically extracts deal signals from your email conversations, updates contact records, and triggers the right follow-up sequences — all running locally on your Mac.
articles.content:
Why Your Inbox Is a Gold Mine You're Not Mining

Every sales conversation leaves a trail. A prospect mentions their budget in a reply. A client forwards your proposal to their VP. Someone asks about a specific feature three times in a thread. These are deal signals — and most teams miss them entirely because they're buried in inboxes, scattered across Gmail accounts, or siloed in Outlook folders that nobody checks systematically.

The good news: with MailClaw's AI email agent system, you can build an automated agent that reads your incoming email conversations, extracts deal-relevant information, enriches contact records, and triggers the right follow-up sequences — all without touching a CRM manually. And because MailClaw runs locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, your email data never leaves your machine.

What a Deal-Tracking Email Agent Actually Does

Before we build anything, let's be clear about what we're creating. A deal-tracking agent in MailClaw is not just a filter or a tag. It's a persistent AI process powered by OpenClaw that does the following in real time:

  • Reads incoming replies across your connected accounts (Gmail, Outlook, or any SMTP/OAuth inbox)
  • Classifies intent — is this person interested, objecting, stalling, or ready to close?
  • Extracts deal data — budget signals, decision-maker mentions, timelines, competitor names
  • Updates contact enrichment records inside MailClaw's contact database
  • Triggers or pauses sequences based on what it finds
  • Optionally pushes updates to HubSpot, Salesforce, or any webhook-compatible CRM

Think of it as a tireless SDR that reads every email the moment it lands and takes the right action — no babysitting required.

Setting Up the Agent: Step by Step

Step 1: Connect Your Email Accounts

Open your MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to Accounts → Add Account. MailClaw supports OAuth for Gmail and Outlook, as well as raw SMTP/IMAP credentials for any provider — including SendGrid inbound parse, Fastmail, or custom domains.

For Gmail, the OAuth flow is one click. For Outlook, you'll use Microsoft's OAuth2 endpoint. For SMTP, you'll need your host, port, and credentials:

# MailClaw CLI: add an SMTP account
mailclaw account add \
  --name "deals@yourcompany.com" \
  --type smtp \
  --host mail.yourhost.com \
  --port 993 \
  --user deals@yourcompany.com \
  --password YOUR_PASSWORD \
  --ssl true

Once connected, MailClaw will begin syncing your inbox in the background. You'll see incoming messages appear in the Conversations panel within a few seconds.

Step 2: Create a New AI Email Agent

Navigate to Agents → New Agent in the dashboard. Give your agent a name like "Deal Signal Tracker" and select the account(s) it should monitor. Under Agent Type, choose Inbound Analyzer — this tells the OpenClaw engine to process incoming messages rather than send them.

You'll now define the agent's intelligence using a prompt configuration. MailClaw uses a structured prompt format that gets passed to the underlying OpenClaw model on each new message:

# agent-config.yaml
name: Deal Signal Tracker
type: inbound_analyzer
accounts:
  - deals@yourcompany.com
trigger: on_reply

prompt: |
  You are a deal intelligence agent. When you receive an email reply,
  extract the following if present:
  - Expressed budget or price sensitivity
  - Decision-maker names or titles mentioned
  - Competitor names referenced
  - Timeline or urgency signals
  - Objections or blockers
  - Positive buying signals or next step requests

  Return a structured JSON object with these fields. If a field is not
  present, return null for that field. Do not fabricate information.

output_format: json
update_contact: true
trigger_sequences: true

Save this file and load it via the CLI:

mailclaw agent load ./agent-config.yaml

Step 3: Map Extracted Data to Contact Fields

MailClaw's contact enrichment system lets you define custom fields that agents can write to. Go to Contacts → Custom Fields and add fields like deal_stage, budget_signal, decision_maker, and last_intent_score.

Back in your agent config, add a field mapping section:

field_mappings:
  budget_signal: extracted.budget
  decision_maker: extracted.decision_maker
  objections: extracted.objections
  buying_signal: extracted.positive_signal
  deal_stage:
    logic: |
      if extracted.positive_signal then "warm"
      elif extracted.objections then "needs_nurture"
      else "cold"

Now every time your agent processes a reply, it updates the contact record automatically. You'll see these fields populate in real time on the Contacts panel — no manual CRM entry needed.

Step 4: Trigger Sequences Based on Deal Stage

This is where MailClaw's sequence builder earns its keep. In Sequences → New Sequence, create sequences for each deal stage:

  • Warm Lead Sequence — fast-track follow-up, case studies, demo invite
  • Needs Nurture Sequence — objection-handling content, testimonials, FAQs
  • Re-Engagement Sequence — for contacts who've gone cold

In your agent config, reference these sequences by ID:

sequence_triggers:
  - condition: deal_stage == "warm"
    sequence_id: seq_warm_lead
    pause_existing: true
  - condition: deal_stage == "needs_nurture"
    sequence_id: seq_objection_handler
    pause_existing: false
  - condition: deal_stage == "cold"
    sequence_id: seq_reengagement
    delay_hours: 48

The pause_existing: true flag is important for warm leads — you don't want someone on a slow drip sequence when they're clearly ready to talk.

Pushing Deal Data to Your CRM

If your team lives in HubSpot or Salesforce, you'll want deal signals pushed there automatically. MailClaw supports outbound webhooks on any agent event. In Agents → Integrations, add a webhook destination:

webhooks:
  - event: contact_updated
    url: https://api.hubspot.com/crm/v3/objects/contacts
    method: PATCH
    auth:
      type: bearer
      token: YOUR_HUBSPOT_API_KEY
    payload_template: |
      {
        "properties": {
          "deal_stage": "{{contact.deal_stage}}",
          "budget_signal": "{{contact.budget_signal}}",
          "last_reply_date": "{{event.timestamp}}"
        }
      }

For Salesforce, use the same pattern with the REST API endpoint for your Opportunity or Lead object. MailClaw's template syntax supports dot-notation access to any contact or event field, so mapping to custom Salesforce fields is straightforward.

Monitoring Agent Health and Deliverability

A deal-tracking agent is only useful if it's running reliably. MailClaw's local dashboard includes a dedicated Agent Monitor panel that shows you:

  • Messages processed per hour
  • Extraction success and failure rates
  • Sequence trigger counts by type
  • Webhook delivery status

MailClaw also bundles deliverability monitoring tools so you can track whether your outbound sequences are landing in inboxes or getting routed to spam — a critical factor when your agent is triggering follow-ups at scale. Check the Deliverability tab for DNS health, SPF/DKIM validation, and bounce rate trends across all connected accounts.

Pro tip: Run mailclaw agent status --name "Deal Signal Tracker" --watch in your terminal for a live feed of every message your agent processes. It's satisfying to watch deal data populate in real time.

Common Patterns and What to Watch Out For

Threading and Context Windows

Email replies often only make sense in context of the thread. In your agent config, set context_window: full_thread to pass the entire conversation history to the OpenClaw model, not just the latest reply. This dramatically improves extraction accuracy, especially for budget and timeline signals that often emerge gradually over multiple exchanges.

Avoiding Phantom Triggers

Out-of-office replies, automated confirmations, and newsletter bounces will hit your inbox too. Add a filter layer to your agent:

filters:
  exclude:
    - type: auto_reply
    - subject_contains: ["out of office", "unsubscribe", "delivery failed"]
    - sender_domain_is_own: true

Human-in-the-Loop for High-Value Deals

For enterprise deals above a certain value, you may not want the agent acting autonomously. Set a review_mode: true flag on high-value contacts and the agent will queue suggested actions in the dashboard for a human to approve before executing sequences or pushing CRM updates.

The Bigger Picture: Agents as a Sales Infrastructure Layer

What makes this approach powerful isn't any single automation — it's the compounding effect. When every reply gets analyzed, every contact record stays current, and every sequence fires at exactly the right moment, your sales motion becomes self-correcting. You spend less time on data entry and status updates, and more time on the conversations that actually close deals.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on localhost, you have full control over the logic, the data, and the integrations. There's no black box, no vendor lock-in, and no SaaS subscription eating into your margins. Fork the repo, extend the agent system, and build the exact workflow your team needs.

The deal was always in the email. Now you have an agent that knows how to find it.

articles.title: MailClaw Agent Workflows: Chaining Multiple AI Actions Together
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to chain multiple AI actions together in MailClaw to build powerful, autonomous email workflows that enrich contacts, personalize outreach, and adapt in real time — all running locally on your Mac.
articles.content:
Why Single-Action Agents Fall Short

Most email automation tools give you a simple if-this-then-that model: a contact opens an email, you send a follow-up. It works, but it leaves a lot on the table. Real-world outreach is messy. People respond out of order, go cold for weeks, then re-engage after visiting your pricing page. A single-action agent can't adapt to that — it just fires the next step and moves on.

MailClaw's AI agent system, built on the OpenClaw engine, is designed differently. Instead of linear triggers, you chain multiple AI actions together into a workflow — a graph of decisions, enrichments, lookups, and sends that executes autonomously and adapts based on what it learns at each step. This guide walks you through how that works and how to build workflows that actually reflect the complexity of modern outreach.

Understanding the MailClaw Agent Workflow Model

Before you start chaining actions, it helps to understand how MailClaw structures them under the hood. Every agent workflow is made up of three primitives:

  • Actions — discrete tasks like enriching a contact, generating an email, checking deliverability, or querying an external API.
  • Conditions — branching logic that routes the workflow based on data returned by a previous action.
  • Memory — a short-term context store that passes state between actions in the same workflow run.

When you launch MailClaw at localhost:3100, the local dashboard gives you a visual canvas to wire these together. But the real power comes from defining workflows in code, where you have full control over logic, retries, and data flow.

Building Your First Chained Workflow

Step 1: Define the Workflow in Your Config

MailClaw workflows live in your project's workflows/ directory as YAML files. Here's a minimal example that chains contact enrichment into personalized email generation:

# workflows/enrich-and-send.yaml
name: enrich_and_send
trigger: contact_added
steps:
  - id: enrich
    action: enrich_contact
    inputs:
      email: "{{ contact.email }}"
      sources: [clearbit, linkedin_scrape]

  - id: score
    action: ai_score_lead
    inputs:
      company: "{{ enrich.company }}"
      title: "{{ enrich.job_title }}"
      signals: "{{ enrich.technographics }}"

  - id: branch
    action: condition
    if: "{{ score.value >= 70 }}"
    then: generate_high_intent_email
    else: generate_nurture_email

  - id: generate_high_intent_email
    action: ai_compose
    inputs:
      tone: direct
      goal: book_demo
      context: "{{ enrich }}"

  - id: generate_nurture_email
    action: ai_compose
    inputs:
      tone: educational
      goal: build_awareness
      context: "{{ enrich }}"

  - id: send
    action: send_email
    inputs:
      to: "{{ contact.email }}"
      body: "{{ generate_high_intent_email.body or generate_nurture_email.body }}"
      account: primary_gmail

Run this workflow from the CLI with:

mailclaw workflow run enrich-and-send --contact john@acme.com

The agent will enrich the contact, score them, branch based on that score, generate the right email, and send it — all without you touching a thing.

Step 2: Pass Context Between Actions

Notice the {{ enrich.company }} syntax above. MailClaw uses a lightweight templating layer backed by OpenClaw's memory model. Every action's output is automatically namespaced and available to downstream steps. This means your AI composition step doesn't just know what to write — it knows the prospect's company size, tech stack, and likely pain points because the enrichment step already fetched them.

You can inspect what's in the workflow memory at any point using:

mailclaw workflow debug enrich-and-send --contact john@acme.com --step score

This prints the full memory state up to and including the score step, which is invaluable when something isn't routing correctly.

Real-World Workflow Patterns

The CRM Sync Loop

One of the most practical patterns is syncing agent decisions back to your CRM. After a contact replies, MailClaw can classify the reply sentiment, update a HubSpot or Salesforce record, and branch into a different sequence — all in one workflow:

# On reply received
steps:
  - id: classify_reply
    action: ai_classify
    inputs:
      text: "{{ reply.body }}"
      labels: [interested, not_now, unsubscribe, question]

  - id: update_crm
    action: hubspot_update_contact
    inputs:
      email: "{{ contact.email }}"
      properties:
        lead_status: "{{ classify_reply.label }}"
        last_reply_sentiment: "{{ classify_reply.confidence }}"

  - id: route
    action: condition
    switch: "{{ classify_reply.label }}"
    cases:
      interested: trigger_demo_sequence
      not_now: trigger_30day_nurture
      question: trigger_ai_answer_and_followup
      unsubscribe: trigger_unsubscribe_flow

This pattern effectively turns your inbox into a self-routing decision engine. Replies don't pile up waiting for manual triage — they're classified and acted on immediately.

The Deliverability-Aware Send Chain

MailClaw includes built-in deliverability monitoring, and you can wire it directly into your send chain so the agent checks domain health before committing a send. This is especially important if you're managing multiple SMTP accounts or rotating through SendGrid sub-users:

steps:
  - id: check_deliverability
    action: deliverability_check
    inputs:
      domain: "{{ sender.domain }}"
      checks: [spf, dkim, dmarc, blacklist]

  - id: gate
    action: condition
    if: "{{ check_deliverability.score >= 80 }}"
    then: proceed_to_send
    else: alert_and_pause

  - id: alert_and_pause
    action: notify
    inputs:
      channel: dashboard
      message: "Deliverability score too low for {{ sender.domain }} — workflow paused."

  - id: proceed_to_send
    action: send_email
    inputs:
      account: "{{ sender.account_id }}"

A workflow that pauses itself and fires a dashboard alert when deliverability degrades is the kind of safety net that prevents one bad morning from torching your sender reputation.

The Multi-Touch Research Workflow

For high-value accounts, you might want the agent to do deeper research before composing anything. Chain together multiple enrichment sources before the compose step hits:

  1. Pull company data from your enrichment provider
  2. Scrape recent news mentions for the target company
  3. Check if they're already a CRM contact in Salesforce
  4. Look up mutual connections or existing email history
  5. Pass all of that as context to the AI compose action

The compose action receives a rich, structured context object — and the resulting email reads like it was written by someone who did their homework, because in a sense, the agent did.

Managing Long-Running Workflows

Some workflows aren't instant — they span days or weeks, like a 5-step sequence with time delays between each email. MailClaw handles this with workflow persistence, storing the current state of each active workflow run in a local SQLite database. You can list all running workflows from the CLI:

mailclaw workflow list --status running

And you can manually advance, pause, or cancel any individual run:

mailclaw workflow pause --run-id wf_a3b92f
mailclaw workflow resume --run-id wf_a3b92f
mailclaw workflow cancel --run-id wf_a3b92f

The local dashboard at localhost:3100 also gives you a live timeline view of every active workflow, showing which step each run is sitting on and when the next action is scheduled. It's the kind of visibility that makes handing off to an AI agent feel safe rather than scary.

Tips for Designing Workflows That Scale

Keep Actions Idempotent

If a workflow step fails and retries, you don't want it sending a duplicate email or creating a duplicate CRM record. Design each action so running it twice has the same result as running it once. MailClaw's built-in send_email and CRM actions handle this with deduplication keys, but custom actions you write yourself need to account for it.

Use Named Conditions, Not Inline Logic

Complex inline conditions become unreadable fast. Instead, break branching logic into named condition steps with clear IDs. Your future self — or a teammate reviewing the workflow — will thank you.

Log Generously in Development

During development, add log actions between steps to capture intermediate state. MailClaw writes these to its local log stream, which you can tail in real time:

mailclaw logs --workflow enrich-and-send --follow

Pro tip: Use the --dry-run flag when testing new workflows. It executes every step except the final send, so you can validate logic and inspect composed emails without firing anything live.

Version Your Workflow Files

Since workflows are just YAML files in your project directory, they're naturally version-controlled. Commit them to Git like any other code. When you change a workflow that has active runs, MailClaw will warn you that in-flight runs are still using the previous version — a small but important safety check that prevents silent behavior changes mid-sequence.

What This Makes Possible

Chained agent workflows are what separate MailClaw from a simple email scheduler. When each action can read the output of the last one, make decisions, call external services, and pass enriched context forward, you end up with something that genuinely thinks about what it's doing — rather than just firing pre-written templates on a timer.

The open-source nature of MailClaw means you can inspect exactly what's happening at every layer, extend actions with your own integrations, and trust that your contact data and workflow logic never leave your machine. That combination of autonomy, transparency, and local control is what makes building on top of it feel different from plugging into yet another SaaS platform.

Start with a simple two-step workflow, get comfortable with how context flows between actions, and then layer in the branching and enrichment patterns from this guide. The ceiling is high — but the floor is low enough to get something useful running in an afternoon.

articles.title: How to Build an AI Agent for Recruiting Email Automation
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to build a fully automated AI recruiting agent using MailClaw that sources candidates, enriches contact data, and sends personalized outreach sequences — all running locally on your Mac without expensive SaaS subscriptions.
articles.content:
Why Recruiting Email Automation Needs an AI Agent, Not Just Templates

Traditional recruiting outreach is a numbers game played badly. Recruiters copy-paste the same LinkedIn message to 200 engineers, swap in a first name, and wonder why response rates hover around 3%. The problem isn't volume — it's relevance. Candidates can smell a templated email from the subject line alone.

AI recruiting agents change the equation. Instead of a human writing 200 variations of the same message, an agent reads a candidate's public profile, infers what matters to them, and drafts a message that feels like it was written specifically for them — because, functionally, it was. With MailClaw, you can build that agent locally, on your own machine, without shipping candidate data to a third-party SaaS platform and without paying per-seat pricing that scales painfully as your team grows.

This guide walks you through building a complete recruiting email agent: from ingesting a candidate list, enriching contact data, writing personalized sequences, and monitoring deliverability — all from MailClaw's local dashboard at localhost:3100.

What You'll Build

By the end of this walkthrough, you'll have a MailClaw AI agent that:

  • Accepts a raw list of candidate names and companies
  • Enriches each contact with verified email addresses and professional context
  • Generates a personalized 3-step email sequence for each candidate
  • Sends through your existing Gmail or Outlook account (or a SendGrid SMTP relay)
  • Tracks opens, replies, and bounces from the local dashboard
  • Automatically pauses outreach when a candidate replies

Step 1: Set Up MailClaw and Connect Your Sending Account

If you haven't installed MailClaw yet, it runs on top of OpenClaw and spins up locally with a single command:

npx mailclaw init
mailclaw start

Open http://localhost:3100 in your browser. You'll see the MailClaw dashboard — your command center for everything that follows.

Connecting Gmail or Outlook via OAuth

Navigate to Settings → Connected Accounts and click Add Account. MailClaw supports OAuth for Gmail and Outlook out of the box. Choose your provider, complete the OAuth flow, and your account is connected. No app passwords, no manual IMAP configuration.

If you're sending at higher volume or want to protect your primary domain's sender reputation, connect a SendGrid SMTP relay instead:

mailclaw accounts add \
  --type smtp \
  --host smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --port 587 \
  --user apikey \
  --pass YOUR_SENDGRID_API_KEY \
  --from recruiting@yourdomain.com

For recruiting at scale, using a separate subdomain (like recruiting.yourdomain.com) is a best practice MailClaw's deliverability tools will help you monitor — more on that in Step 4.

Step 2: Import and Enrich Your Candidate List

You probably have candidate data in a spreadsheet, an ATS like Greenhouse or Lever, or exported from LinkedIn Recruiter. MailClaw accepts CSV imports directly from the CLI or dashboard.

mailclaw contacts import candidates.csv \
  --list "Senior Engineers Q3" \
  --enrich

The --enrich flag triggers MailClaw's contact enrichment pipeline, powered by OpenClaw. For each row in your CSV, it will attempt to:

  • Find and verify a professional email address
  • Pull current job title and company from public sources
  • Identify recent professional activity (open source contributions, published articles, conference talks)
  • Detect likely tech stack or domain expertise based on public signals

This enrichment data becomes the fuel for your AI agent's personalization. A candidate who recently gave a talk at a Rust conference should get a different opening line than one who just published a blog post about switching from AWS to bare metal.

Syncing from HubSpot or Salesforce

If your recruiting team tracks candidates in HubSpot or Salesforce, MailClaw can pull contacts directly:

mailclaw contacts sync --source hubspot --list "2024 Pipeline"
mailclaw contacts sync --source salesforce --object Contact --filter "Type='Candidate'"

Two-way sync means reply data and engagement signals flow back into your CRM automatically — so your recruiting ops data stays clean without manual updates.

Step 3: Build Your AI Recruiting Agent

This is where MailClaw's AI email agents shine. An agent isn't just a template with variables — it's a reasoning layer that reads enrichment data and decides how to frame each message.

Creating the Agent

From the dashboard, go to Agents → New Agent and select the Recruiting Outreach base type. Or use the CLI:

mailclaw agent create \
  --name "Senior Engineer Outreach" \
  --type recruiting \
  --tone "professional, direct, no fluff" \
  --goal "Book a 20-minute exploratory call"

Writing the Agent System Prompt

The agent's behavior is governed by a system prompt you define. Here's a strong starting point:

You are a technical recruiter at [Company Name] reaching out to senior software engineers.
Your goal is to write a short, personalized cold email that:
- Opens with a specific, genuine observation about the candidate's work or background
- Briefly explains why [Company Name] is worth their attention (2 sentences max)
- Asks a low-commitment question to start a conversation
- Stays under 120 words
- Never uses phrases like "hope this finds you well", "exciting opportunity", or "rockstar"

Use the following candidate context to personalize:
{{enrichment.summary}}
{{enrichment.recent_activity}}
{{enrichment.skills}}

The {{enrichment.*}} variables are populated automatically from the contact enrichment pipeline. The agent reads this context before generating each email — so every message is grounded in something real about that specific person.

Building the Follow-Up Sequence

Open the Sequence Builder and attach your agent to a 3-step sequence:

  1. Day 1 — Initial outreach: AI-generated, fully personalized. Subject line also AI-generated based on enrichment data.
  2. Day 5 — Light follow-up: Short nudge referencing the first email. Agent checks if a reply was received — if yes, sequence stops automatically.
  3. Day 12 — Final touch: A brief, honest close. Something like: "I'll leave it here — but if the timing ever makes sense, I'd love to connect."

The reply detection is built in. Once a candidate responds at any step, MailClaw removes them from the sequence and flags the contact for human follow-up. No awkward follow-up after a candidate has already said yes.

Step 4: Monitor Deliverability Before You Launch

A recruiting agent is worthless if your emails land in spam. Before activating your sequence, run MailClaw's deliverability check:

mailclaw deliverability check --account recruiting@yourdomain.com

This checks SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records, tests your sending IP against major blocklists, and gives you a deliverability score. From the dashboard, you'll see which issues to fix and how severe they are.

Pro tip: If you're sending from a subdomain for the first time, warm it up gradually. MailClaw's deliverability tools include a warmup scheduler that ramps your daily send volume over 2–3 weeks, mimicking organic sending patterns so inbox providers trust your domain before you go full volume.

Step 5: Launch, Monitor, and Iterate

With your agent configured, sequence built, and deliverability confirmed, you're ready to launch:

mailclaw sequence launch \
  --name "Senior Engineer Outreach" \
  --list "Senior Engineers Q3" \
  --start-at "2024-09-09T09:00:00" \
  --timezone "America/New_York"

The dashboard at localhost:3100 updates in real time. You'll see open rates, click rates, reply rates, and bounce rates broken down by sequence step. If Step 1 has a 40% open rate but only a 2% reply rate, the subject line is working but the body copy isn't converting — a signal to iterate on your agent's system prompt.

What Good Recruiting Benchmarks Look Like

  • Open rate: 45–60% for personalized recruiting cold email (vs. 20–25% for templated)
  • Reply rate: 8–15% is strong for senior passive candidates
  • Bounce rate: Keep below 2% — enrichment helps here significantly

Why Open Source Matters for Recruiting Outreach

Candidate data is sensitive. Names, emails, career histories, and compensation signals are information people haven't explicitly shared with you — you've inferred it. Running your recruiting agent locally with MailClaw means that data never leaves your machine. There's no SaaS vendor storing your candidate pipeline, no third-party with access to your outreach strategy, and no usage-based pricing that penalizes you for being effective.

Because MailClaw is open source and built on OpenClaw, you can inspect exactly what the AI agent is doing, modify the enrichment pipeline, or contribute improvements back to the project. That transparency matters in a recruiting context where trust — with candidates and within your organization — is everything.

Next Steps

Once your first recruiting agent is running, the logical next steps are:

  • Multi-account rotation: Add multiple sending accounts to distribute volume and protect sender reputation across roles or regions
  • Agent specialization: Create separate agents for different roles (engineering, design, sales) with role-specific system prompts and enrichment signals
  • ATS webhook integration: Trigger sequences automatically when a candidate enters a specific stage in your ATS
  • A/B testing: Use MailClaw's sequence builder to test different agent personas or CTAs and let data guide your messaging

Recruiting is fundamentally a human relationship business — but the operational overhead of finding, enriching, and doing first contact at scale doesn't need to be. That's exactly the work an AI agent should handle, so your team can focus on the conversations that actually matter.

articles.title: Using MailClaw to Create Self-Improving Email Campaign Agents
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how to build self-improving email campaign agents with MailClaw that analyze performance data, adapt messaging automatically, and continuously optimize your outreach — all running locally on your Mac.
articles.content:
Why Static Email Campaigns Are Leaving Conversions on the Table

Most email campaigns are built once and left to run. You write a five-step sequence, load it into your tool of choice, and hope the open rates hold. But the reality is that language that worked in Q1 goes stale by Q3, prospect personas shift, and what resonates with a SaaS founder in Austin has no business landing in the inbox of a logistics manager in Munich.

The solution isn't to manually rewrite every sequence every quarter. It's to build agents that do it for you — agents that observe what's working, synthesize patterns, and update their own playbooks. MailClaw, powered by OpenClaw, makes this possible on your local machine without handing your contact data to a third-party SaaS platform.

Understanding MailClaw's Agent Architecture

Before you build a self-improving agent, it helps to understand what MailClaw's AI email agents actually are under the hood. Each agent is a persistent, goal-oriented process that has access to three things:

  • Your contact data — enriched and segmented through MailClaw's contact enrichment pipeline
  • Your campaign history — open rates, click-throughs, reply rates, and bounce signals tracked via the deliverability dashboard
  • A writable sequence context — the ability to propose and apply edits to active email sequences

The agents run inside the OpenClaw runtime and are accessible through MailClaw's local dashboard at localhost:3100. Because everything runs on your machine, you're not rate-limited by an API middleman, and your prospect data never leaves your environment.

Step 1: Setting Up Your First Campaign Agent

Open your terminal and initialize a new agent project inside MailClaw:

mailclaw agent create --name "saas-outbound-optimizer" \
  --goal "Improve reply rate on SaaS founder sequence" \
  --sequence cold-saas-v1 \
  --eval-metric reply_rate

This command scaffolds an agent definition file at ~/.mailclaw/agents/saas-outbound-optimizer.json. Open it and you'll see the core configuration block:

{
  "agent": "saas-outbound-optimizer",
  "goal": "Improve reply rate on SaaS founder sequence",
  "sequence": "cold-saas-v1",
  "eval_metric": "reply_rate",
  "eval_window_days": 7,
  "improvement_threshold": 0.05,
  "actions": ["rewrite_subject", "rewrite_body", "adjust_send_time", "pause_step"],
  "require_approval": true
}

The require_approval flag is worth keeping set to true while you're learning how the agent behaves. Once you trust its judgment, you can flip it to false for fully autonomous operation.

Step 2: Connecting Enrichment Data for Smarter Personalization

A self-improving agent is only as smart as the signals it has access to. MailClaw's contact enrichment pipeline can pull firmographic and behavioral data from several sources, giving your agent real context about who it's writing to.

Configuring Enrichment Sources

In the dashboard at localhost:3100/enrichment, connect your preferred data sources. MailClaw supports direct integrations with HubSpot and Salesforce for CRM sync, and can enrich raw contact lists using built-in web enrichment tools that pull company size, industry, tech stack signals, and job seniority data.

mailclaw enrich --list founders-q3.csv \
  --fields company_size,industry,tech_stack,seniority \
  --output enriched-founders-q3.csv

Once enriched, import the list and tag the segment your agent will target:

mailclaw contacts import enriched-founders-q3.csv \
  --segment "saas-founders-q3" \
  --attach-agent saas-outbound-optimizer

Your agent now has access to richer context when it evaluates why certain messages are or aren't landing. A subject line that underperforms with seed-stage founders at dev-tools companies will be treated differently from one that underperforms with growth-stage founders in fintech.

Step 3: Defining the Feedback Loop

This is the part that makes the agent genuinely self-improving rather than just auto-writing emails. You need to define what "better" means and give the agent a structured way to observe and act on that signal.

Setting Evaluation Windows

In your agent config, eval_window_days: 7 means the agent reviews the last seven days of performance before proposing a change. For high-volume outreach through SendGrid or Mailgun, seven days gives you enough statistical signal. For low-volume sequences sent through Gmail or Outlook OAuth accounts, consider extending this to 14 days to avoid overfitting to noise.

Defining Improvement Thresholds

The improvement_threshold: 0.05 setting means the agent will only propose a change if it believes there's a reasonable path to at least a 5% relative improvement in the target metric. This prevents the agent from churning through rewrites on sequences that are already performing well.

What the Agent Actually Does

When an evaluation cycle runs, the agent performs the following steps automatically:

  1. Pulls performance data for the attached sequence from the deliverability dashboard
  2. Segments results by contact attributes (industry, seniority, company size) to identify underperforming cohorts
  3. Analyzes which email steps in the sequence show the steepest drop-off
  4. Generates rewrite candidates for the weakest-performing step using the OpenClaw language model
  5. Logs proposed changes to localhost:3100/agents/saas-outbound-optimizer/proposals for your review

Pro tip: Run mailclaw agent logs --name saas-outbound-optimizer --tail 50 to see the agent's reasoning in real time. Reading its chain-of-thought output is one of the fastest ways to understand what it's picking up on — and to catch when it's making assumptions you don't agree with.

Step 4: Multi-Account Delivery and Deliverability Monitoring

An optimized sequence means nothing if it's landing in spam. MailClaw's deliverability tools run continuously alongside your agents and feed inbox placement data directly into the feedback loop.

Connect multiple sending accounts — your primary Gmail via OAuth, a warmed SendGrid subaccount, a dedicated Outlook domain for enterprise prospects — through the multi-account manager:

mailclaw accounts add --type gmail --oauth
mailclaw accounts add --type smtp \
  --host smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --port 587 \
  --username apikey \
  --label "sendgrid-warmup"

With multiple accounts configured, MailClaw can rotate sending across identities to protect deliverability while your agent is in the middle of an A/B test. When the deliverability monitor flags a spike in soft bounces or a drop in open rates consistent with inbox filtering, it automatically pauses outreach on that account and alerts your agent — which factors the signal into its next evaluation cycle.

Step 5: Reviewing and Approving Agent Proposals

Head to localhost:3100/agents in your browser. You'll see a clean proposal view that shows the current email copy side-by-side with the agent's proposed rewrite, along with its reasoning:

  • Which cohort underperformed and by how much
  • What pattern it identified in the underperforming copy (too long, weak personalization hook, generic CTA)
  • What change it's proposing and why it expects improvement
  • A confidence score based on the volume of data in the evaluation window

You can approve, reject, or edit the proposal before applying it. When you're comfortable with how the agent thinks, you can enable auto-apply for low-risk changes like subject line rewrites while keeping manual review for full body copy changes.

Building Toward Fully Autonomous Campaign Loops

Chaining Agents Together

One of the most powerful patterns in MailClaw is chaining a prospecting agent that enriches and qualifies new contacts with an optimization agent that continuously improves the sequence those contacts enter. The prospecting agent keeps the top of the funnel full; the optimization agent ensures the sequence gets sharper over time.

mailclaw agent chain \
  --source prospect-enricher \
  --destination saas-outbound-optimizer \
  --handoff-trigger "enrichment_complete"

Exporting Learnings Across Campaigns

Your agent accumulates a body of knowledge — which subject line patterns correlate with high reply rates, which send times underperform with certain industries, which CTAs generate clicks but no replies. Export this as a reusable prompt context that you can apply to new sequences:

mailclaw agent export-learnings \
  --name saas-outbound-optimizer \
  --output saas-founder-playbook.json

Load it into any new campaign and your next sequence starts with the benefit of everything the previous agent learned — rather than starting from zero.

The Compounding Advantage of Local, Open-Source AI Agents

What makes this approach genuinely different from using a hosted email tool with some AI features bolted on is the compounding nature of local, persistent agents. Every campaign you run teaches your agents something. Every proposal you approve or reject calibrates their judgment. Over months, your MailClaw setup becomes a system that reflects your market, your voice, and your hard-won understanding of what makes your prospects respond.

Because MailClaw is open source and built on the OpenClaw framework, you're not locked into someone else's model of what good email looks like. You can inspect the agent logic, modify the evaluation criteria, write custom actions, and build on top of it in ways that a closed SaaS product will never let you do.

That's the real value: not just automation, but compound learning that stays with you.

articles.title: MailClaw Email Deliverability Guide: Getting to the Primary Inbox
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: A practical, no-fluff guide to email deliverability covering DNS authentication, sender reputation, list hygiene, and how MailClaw's built-in tools help you land in the primary inbox instead of spam.
articles.content:
Why Deliverability Is the Foundation of Every Campaign

You can write the most compelling cold email in the world, build a flawless sequence, and nail your timing — and none of it matters if your message lands in the spam folder. Email deliverability isn't a nice-to-have; it's the prerequisite for everything else working.

Most deliverability problems aren't mysterious. They come from a small set of well-understood root causes: missing DNS records, a damaged sender reputation, poor list hygiene, or content patterns that trigger spam filters. This guide walks through each layer, shows you how to diagnose issues, and explains how MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring and AI tooling make the process significantly less painful.

The Authentication Stack: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC

Gmail, Outlook, and every major inbox provider run your sending domain through an authentication checklist before they decide where to route your message. Getting these three records right is the single highest-leverage thing you can do for deliverability.

SPF — Sender Policy Framework

SPF tells receiving mail servers which IP addresses are allowed to send email on behalf of your domain. If you're sending through SendGrid, Google Workspace, or a custom SMTP server configured in MailClaw, each of those needs to be listed in your SPF record.

A typical SPF record in your DNS looks like this:

v=spf1 include:sendgrid.net include:_spf.google.com ~all

The ~all softfail is safer than -all while you're warming up a new domain. Once you're confident in your sending infrastructure, switch to -all for a stronger signal to inbox providers.

DKIM — DomainKeys Identified Mail

DKIM adds a cryptographic signature to your outgoing emails that proves the message wasn't tampered with in transit. When you add a sending account in MailClaw's localhost dashboard at localhost:3100, you'll see a DKIM setup prompt that walks you through generating keys and publishing the correct TXT record for your domain.

After publishing your DKIM record, verify it with a quick DNS lookup:

dig TXT selector._domainkey.yourdomain.com

You should see a p= field containing your public key. If it's missing, your emails are going out unsigned — a significant red flag for modern spam filters.

DMARC — Domain-based Message Authentication

DMARC ties SPF and DKIM together and tells receiving servers what to do when authentication fails. Start permissive, then tighten:

v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourdomain.com

The rua field sends aggregate reports to your inbox — invaluable for catching misconfigurations early. Once your reports show clean authentication for a few weeks, graduate to p=quarantine and eventually p=reject.

MailClaw tip: The deliverability panel in MailClaw's dashboard surfaces SPF, DKIM, and DMARC status for each connected sending account. If something is misconfigured, you'll see a warning before your first send — not after a campaign tanks.

Sender Reputation and Domain Warming

Inbox providers score your sending domain and IP based on engagement history. A brand-new domain sending 2,000 cold emails on day one will almost certainly trigger spam filters, not because of the content, but because the volume spike looks exactly like spam behavior.

How to Warm a New Domain

  1. Start small. Send 20–50 emails per day in week one, targeting your most engaged contacts first.
  2. Ramp gradually. Double your daily volume each week as positive engagement signals accumulate.
  3. Prioritize replies. Getting replies — even short ones — is the strongest positive signal you can generate. Structure your early sequences to invite a response.
  4. Use MailClaw's sequence builder to stagger sends across time windows rather than blasting a list all at once. Drip-style delivery patterns look far more human to filtering algorithms.

If you're managing outreach for multiple clients or brands, MailClaw's multi-account support lets you maintain separate sending identities with isolated reputation pools. A problem with one account doesn't contaminate the others.

Monitoring Your Reputation

Check your domain and IP reputation regularly using these tools:

  • Google Postmaster Tools — essential if Gmail is a significant portion of your recipients
  • Microsoft SNDS — equivalent for Outlook and Hotmail recipients
  • MXToolbox Blacklist Check — scans your domain and IP against major blocklists
  • Talos Intelligence — Cisco's sender reputation database, used by many enterprise mail filters

MailClaw's deliverability monitoring pulls these signals together and surfaces alerts inside the dashboard, so you're not manually checking five different tools before every campaign.

List Hygiene: The Unglamorous Work That Pays Off

Sending to bad email addresses damages your sender score fast. Bounces signal to inbox providers that you're not maintaining your list. High spam complaint rates are even worse — Gmail's threshold before they start throttling your mail is around 0.1%.

Clean Your List Before You Send

Before importing contacts into MailClaw, run them through a verification step. MailClaw's contact enrichment layer (powered by OpenClaw) can flag likely-invalid addresses and surface additional contact data — company size, job title, LinkedIn presence — that helps you segment more precisely and avoid sending irrelevant messages to the wrong people.

From the MailClaw CLI, you can enrich a contact list in one command:

mailclaw contacts enrich --input leads.csv --output enriched.csv --fields email,title,company

The enrichment process validates email syntax, checks domain MX records, and appends any available contact intelligence before you load the list into a sequence.

Remove Unengaged Contacts Regularly

Contacts who haven't opened or clicked in 90+ days are a liability. They drag down your engagement rates, which inbox providers use as a proxy for whether people actually want your mail. Segment them into a re-engagement sequence — one or two emails asking if they still want to hear from you — and suppress anyone who doesn't respond.

Content and Sending Patterns

Authentication and list hygiene get you to the starting line. Content and sending behavior determine where you finish.

Write Like a Human, Not a Marketer

Spam filters in 2025 are trained on billions of messages and are remarkably good at detecting template-speak. Phrases like "Act now," "Limited time offer," and "Click here to learn more" carry real spam weight. So does heavy HTML formatting, large images, and tracking-pixel-heavy templates.

For cold outreach sequences, plain-text or near-plain-text emails consistently outperform heavily designed HTML. MailClaw's AI email agents can generate and A/B test subject lines and body copy variations, helping you find language that resonates without defaulting to high-spam patterns.

Sending Windows and Volume Caps

Set daily sending limits per account and avoid sending large volumes outside of business hours in your recipient's timezone. MailClaw lets you configure timezone-aware sending windows directly in the sequence builder:

mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "Q4 Outreach" \
  --send-window "09:00-17:00" \
  --timezone "recipient" \
  --daily-limit 150

The --timezone recipient flag tells MailClaw to use the timezone inferred from each contact's location during enrichment — a small detail that meaningfully improves open rates and looks more natural to filters.

Integrating with Your Existing Stack

Deliverability doesn't exist in a vacuum. If you're syncing contacts from HubSpot or Salesforce, suppression lists need to flow back in real time — a contact who unsubscribes in your CRM should never receive another email from MailClaw. The same applies to bounce data from SendGrid or any other SMTP provider you've connected.

MailClaw's open-source architecture means you can build these sync integrations yourself using the OpenClaw plugin system, or use the built-in HubSpot and Salesforce connectors to keep suppression lists in sync automatically.

Because MailClaw runs locally on your machine at localhost:3100, your contact data and campaign logic never leave your environment. For teams with strict data handling requirements, this is a meaningful advantage over cloud-based alternatives.

A Pre-Send Deliverability Checklist

Before you launch any campaign, run through this list:

  • SPF record published and includes all sending infrastructure
  • DKIM keys generated and DNS record verified
  • DMARC policy configured with reporting enabled
  • Domain not listed on MXToolbox or Talos blacklists
  • Contact list verified and enriched
  • Unsubscribe link present and functional
  • Daily send volume appropriate for domain age
  • Sending window set to recipient business hours
  • Subject line tested against spam scoring tool (e.g., Mail-Tester)
  • Suppression list synced from CRM

MailClaw's pre-send audit surfaces most of these automatically when you finalize a sequence — but knowing what the tool is checking, and why, puts you in a much better position to fix issues quickly when they come up.

Deliverability isn't a one-time setup. It's ongoing maintenance: watching your reputation scores, cleaning lists after every campaign, and iterating on content based on engagement data. Do it consistently, and the primary inbox becomes the default — not the exception.

articles.title: How to Set Up SPF, DKIM, and DMARC for MailClaw
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to configure SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records correctly so your MailClaw campaigns land in the inbox — with step-by-step DNS instructions, real examples, and tips for using MailClaw's built-in deliverability tools to verify everything is working.
articles.content:
Why Email Authentication Matters Before You Send Anything

You've set up MailClaw, connected your SMTP credentials, built your first sequence in the sequence builder, and your AI email agent is ready to go. But before you fire off a single campaign, there's one foundational task that will determine whether your emails land in the inbox or disappear into the spam folder: email authentication.

SPF, DKIM, and DMARC are three DNS-based protocols that prove to receiving mail servers — Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo, and everyone else — that you are who you say you are. Without them, even beautifully crafted, highly personalized emails sent through MailClaw's outreach engine can get flagged, filtered, or silently dropped. With them properly configured, you're giving your campaigns the strongest possible foundation for deliverability.

This guide walks through each record type, how to set them up for the most common sending configurations, and how to use MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools to confirm everything is working correctly.

Understanding the Three Pillars of Email Authentication

SPF — Sender Policy Framework

SPF tells receiving mail servers which IP addresses and services are authorized to send email on behalf of your domain. It's a TXT record you add to your domain's DNS. When a recipient's mail server gets a message claiming to be from you@yourdomain.com, it checks your DNS to verify the sending server was on your approved list.

DKIM — DomainKeys Identified Mail

DKIM adds a cryptographic signature to every outgoing email. The private key lives on your sending server; the public key is published in your DNS. Receiving servers use the public key to verify the signature, confirming the message wasn't tampered with in transit and genuinely came from your infrastructure.

DMARC — Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance

DMARC ties SPF and DKIM together and tells receiving servers what to do when authentication fails — nothing, quarantine the message, or reject it outright. It also enables aggregate reports sent to your inbox, showing you exactly which servers are sending email using your domain. It's the policy layer that makes SPF and DKIM actionable.

The rule of thumb: SPF says who can send. DKIM proves the message is intact. DMARC enforces the rules and gives you visibility.

Setting Up SPF for MailClaw

Your SPF record depends on which sending infrastructure you've connected to MailClaw. Because MailClaw supports multiple SMTP and OAuth integrations — including Gmail, Outlook, SendGrid, and custom SMTP providers — your SPF record may need to include more than one service.

Basic SPF Record Structure

v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:sendgrid.net ~all

Breaking this down:

  • v=spf1 — declares this as an SPF record
  • include:_spf.google.com — authorizes Google's mail servers (add this if you're using Gmail SMTP or Google Workspace OAuth)
  • include:sendgrid.net — authorizes SendGrid (add this if you're routing through SendGrid's API in MailClaw)
  • ~all — a soft fail; emails from unlisted servers won't be outright rejected but will be marked suspicious. Use -all for a hard fail once you're confident your record is complete.

Common Includes by Provider

  • Gmail / Google Workspace: include:_spf.google.com
  • Outlook / Microsoft 365: include:spf.protection.outlook.com
  • SendGrid: include:sendgrid.net
  • Custom SMTP (VPS/dedicated IP): ip4:YOUR.SERVER.IP.ADDRESS

Add the SPF record as a TXT record on your root domain (@) in your DNS provider — whether that's Cloudflare, Route 53, Namecheap, or GoDaddy. You can only have one SPF record per domain, so if one already exists, edit it rather than creating a new one.

Setting Up DKIM for MailClaw

DKIM setup varies slightly depending on your sending provider, since each one generates its own key pair.

DKIM with SendGrid

  1. In your SendGrid account, go to Settings → Sender Authentication and authenticate your domain.
  2. SendGrid will give you two CNAME records to add to your DNS — typically something like:
s1._domainkey.yourdomain.com  CNAME  s1.domainkey.u12345.wl.sendgrid.net
s2._domainkey.yourdomain.com  CNAME  s2.domainkey.u12345.wl.sendgrid.net
  1. Add both CNAME records to your DNS and click Verify in SendGrid.
  2. In MailClaw's dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to your account's SMTP settings and confirm the sending domain matches what you authenticated in SendGrid.

DKIM with Google Workspace

  1. In Google Admin, go to Apps → Google Workspace → Gmail → Authenticate Email.
  2. Select your domain and click Generate New Record. Choose a 2048-bit key if available.
  3. Add the generated TXT record to your DNS under the host google._domainkey.yourdomain.com.
  4. Return to Google Admin and click Start Authentication once the record has propagated (usually within 15–60 minutes).

Verifying DKIM from the Command Line

Once your record is live, you can verify it quickly with dig:

dig TXT google._domainkey.yourdomain.com +short

You should see a response containing v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=... with a long public key string. No response means the record hasn't propagated yet or was entered incorrectly.

Setting Up DMARC

DMARC is a TXT record added at _dmarc.yourdomain.com. Start with a monitoring-only policy so you can collect data before enforcing anything.

Recommended Starting DMARC Record

v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourdomain.com; ruf=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourdomain.com; fo=1
  • p=none — monitor only; no messages are rejected or quarantined yet
  • rua — where aggregate reports are sent (daily summaries of authentication results)
  • ruf — where forensic reports are sent (individual failure reports)
  • fo=1 — send a forensic report if either SPF or DKIM fails (more visibility)

Tightening Your Policy Over Time

After two to four weeks of monitoring, once you've confirmed all your legitimate sending sources are passing authentication, escalate your policy:

v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; pct=50; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourdomain.com

Then eventually move to full enforcement:

v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourdomain.com

p=reject is the gold standard. It tells receiving servers to outright drop any unauthenticated messages claiming to be from your domain — protecting your brand from spoofing and significantly improving your sender reputation.

Using MailClaw's Deliverability Tools to Verify Your Setup

Once your records are in DNS, MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring panel (accessible from the localhost dashboard at localhost:3100/deliverability) gives you a real-time health check across all your connected sending accounts. It surfaces SPF alignment issues, DKIM signature verification status, and DMARC policy compliance — without needing to leave the app or dig through raw DNS output.

For a quick sanity check before your first campaign, you can also use free external tools like MXToolbox, Mail Tester, or Google's Email Markup Tester. Send a test message from MailClaw to a Mail Tester address and you'll get a full authentication scorecard back.

Things to Check Before Going Live

  • SPF pass: The sending IP is listed in your SPF record
  • DKIM pass: The signature validates against your published public key
  • DMARC alignment: The From domain matches the domain used in SPF/DKIM (this is often where misconfigured setups fail)
  • No SPF record flattening issues: SPF has a 10-lookup limit; if you're including many providers, use an SPF flattening tool to stay under the limit
  • Consistent sending domain: Make sure the domain configured in MailClaw's multi-account settings matches what you authenticated with each provider

A Note on Custom Domains for Outreach

If you're running cold outreach campaigns through MailClaw's sequence builder — leveraging contact enrichment and AI email agents to personalize at scale — consider using a dedicated subdomain like mail.yourdomain.com or a separate root domain entirely for cold email. This protects your primary domain's sender reputation if a campaign generates complaints.

MailClaw's multi-account support makes this straightforward: you can authenticate multiple domains, each with their own SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records, and route different campaign types through the appropriate account. Warm, engaged contacts from your CRM (whether that's HubSpot, Salesforce, or a native MailClaw list) go through your primary domain. Cold outreach sequences get their own domain with a fresh reputation you build carefully over time.

The Bottom Line

Getting SPF, DKIM, and DMARC right isn't glamorous work, but it's the single highest-leverage thing you can do for email deliverability. Done correctly, it tells every major inbox provider — Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo — that your messages are legitimate, authenticated, and worth delivering. Done poorly, even the most sophisticated AI-generated personalization in the world won't save your campaigns from the spam folder.

Set up all three records, start DMARC in monitoring mode, use MailClaw's deliverability panel to track alignment, and tighten your policy once you've confirmed clean results. That's the entire playbook — and it's one most senders still haven't fully executed.

articles.title: MailClaw Analytics Dashboard: Understanding Your Email Metrics
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's local analytics dashboard to track open rates, click-through rates, reply rates, and deliverability signals — and turn those numbers into smarter, higher-performing email campaigns.
articles.content:
Why Email Metrics Actually Matter (And Which Ones to Watch)

Most email marketers track open rates the way people check the weather — habitually, but without really acting on what they see. MailClaw's analytics dashboard, accessible at localhost:3100, is designed to change that habit. Instead of surfacing vanity numbers, it gives you a layered view of campaign health: from top-of-funnel engagement signals all the way down to SMTP-level deliverability diagnostics.

Before diving into the dashboard itself, it's worth grounding yourself in what each core metric actually tells you — because the action you take after seeing a 20% open rate versus a 2% reply rate is completely different.

  • Open Rate: A proxy for subject line quality and sender reputation. Useful for trend analysis, but increasingly noisy after Apple's Mail Privacy Protection.
  • Click-Through Rate (CTR): Measures content relevance and CTA clarity. A low CTR with a high open rate almost always means your email body isn't delivering on the subject line's promise.
  • Reply Rate: The most honest signal in cold outreach. Hard to fake, hard to inflate, and directly tied to revenue.
  • Bounce Rate: A deliverability red flag. Hard bounces above 2% can get your sending domain flagged or blacklisted.
  • Unsubscribe Rate: Measures audience fit. Consistently high unsubscribes often mean your contact enrichment is pulling in the wrong leads.

Navigating the MailClaw Dashboard

When you fire up MailClaw with mailclaw start, the local dashboard spins up at http://localhost:3100. The Analytics tab is split into three panels: Campaign Overview, Sequence Performance, and Deliverability Health. Each panel is independently filterable by date range, sending account, and campaign tag — so you can slice data across your Gmail, Outlook, or SendGrid accounts without switching contexts.

Campaign Overview Panel

The Campaign Overview gives you a bird's-eye view across all active and completed campaigns. You'll see aggregate metrics rendered as time-series charts, making it easy to spot the day a subject line change moved your open rate or when a new sending IP started warming up.

One of the most useful features here is the Benchmark Overlay — powered by MailClaw's OpenClaw AI engine, it compares your metrics against anonymized aggregate data from similar campaign types (cold outreach vs. nurture sequences vs. newsletters) so you're not comparing yourself against irrelevant industry averages.

Sequence Performance Panel

This is where MailClaw's sequence builder really earns its keep. Each step in a multi-touch sequence gets its own row: you can see exactly where contacts are dropping off, which follow-up email is generating the most replies, and how wait times between steps affect engagement.

A common pattern you'll discover here: Step 1 has a solid 40% open rate, Step 2 drops to 18%, and Step 3 barely registers. This usually means your follow-up copy is too repetitive. MailClaw's AI email agent can flag this automatically and suggest revised subject lines or body copy variations to test at each step.

Deliverability Health Panel

This panel is genuinely one of MailClaw's standout features. Most email tools bury deliverability data or charge extra for it. Here, you get real-time visibility into:

  • SPF, DKIM, and DMARC authentication status per sending domain
  • Spam complaint rates broken down by ESP (Gmail vs. Outlook vs. others)
  • Inbox placement estimates based on seed testing
  • Bounce categorization (hard vs. soft, with suggested remediation)

If your spam complaint rate creeps above 0.1% on Gmail, the dashboard surfaces a warning automatically — because at 0.3%, Google will start routing your emails directly to spam for everyone, not just the people who complained.

Turning Metrics Into Action: A Practical Workflow

Step 1: Run a Weekly Metrics Audit

Set aside 15 minutes every Monday to review the previous week's data. MailClaw makes this easy with the CLI report command:

mailclaw analytics report --range 7d --format summary

This outputs a plain-text digest of your key metrics across all campaigns. You can also export to CSV for stakeholders who prefer spreadsheets:

mailclaw analytics export --range 7d --output weekly-report.csv
