Pipe it into your CRM if you're running HubSpot or Salesforce integrations — MailClaw's contact enrichment layer keeps engagement data synced bidirectionally, so your sales team always has fresh context before a call.

Step 2: Diagnose Low Reply Rates with AI Assist

If your reply rate falls below 3% on a cold outreach sequence, don't just rewrite your emails blindly. Use MailClaw's built-in AI email agent to run a diagnostic:

mailclaw agent diagnose --campaign "Q3 Outreach" --metric reply_rate

The agent will analyze subject line patterns, sending times, contact segment characteristics (pulled from enrichment data), and sequence timing — then surface the most likely causes. Common findings include:

  1. Sending at suboptimal times for the recipient's timezone
  2. Using trigger words that increase spam filtering (detectable via the deliverability panel)
  3. Over-personalization that reads as template-generated rather than genuine
  4. Targeting contacts whose job titles don't match the email's assumed pain points

Step 3: A/B Test at the Sequence Level, Not Just the Subject Line

Most people A/B test subject lines and call it done. MailClaw's sequence builder lets you split-test entire sequence variants — different step counts, different wait periods, different CTA structures — and the analytics dashboard tracks variant performance side-by-side with statistical significance indicators.

To set up a sequence-level split test:

mailclaw sequence split --name "Outreach v1" --variant "Outreach v2" --split 50/50

Once you've hit your minimum sample size (MailClaw defaults to 200 contacts per variant, configurable in ~/.mailclaw/config.yaml), the dashboard will highlight the winning variant and let you promote it with a single click.

Reading Deliverability Signals Before They Become Problems

The most expensive email metric is the one you didn't notice until your domain was blacklisted. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring runs continuously in the background, checking your sending domains against major blocklists (Spamhaus, Barracuda, MXToolbox-style checks) and alerting you via the dashboard and optionally via Slack webhook.

Configure alerts in your config file:

# ~/.mailclaw/config.yaml
deliverability:
  alert_thresholds:
    bounce_rate: 0.02
    spam_complaint_rate: 0.001
    blacklist_check: true
  notifications:
    slack_webhook: "https://hooks.slack.com/your-webhook-url"

If you're running multi-account campaigns across multiple Gmail or Outlook accounts (or warming up fresh SendGrid IPs), the dashboard's Account Health view shows each sending identity separately — so a problem with one account doesn't obscure the health of others.

Connecting Analytics to Contact Enrichment

One of MailClaw's most underused features is the feedback loop between campaign analytics and contact enrichment. When a contact segment consistently underperforms — low opens, high unsubscribes, zero replies — that's a signal about who you're targeting, not just how you're writing.

MailClaw can automatically re-enrich underperforming segments to surface updated job titles, company changes, or intent signals:

mailclaw contacts enrich --segment "Low Engagement" --refresh-stale 30d

You'll often find that contacts who went cold have changed roles, moved companies, or their company has undergone funding rounds or layoffs — context that completely changes your outreach angle. Pulling this data back into the sequence builder before your next send dramatically improves relevance and, consequently, reply rates.

Pro tip: Sort your analytics by reply rate descending and look at the top 10% of responding contacts. Use MailClaw's enrichment tools to build an ideal customer profile from that cohort, then let the AI agent generate a new target list that matches those characteristics. It's the fastest path from "what's working" to "doing more of it."

Making the Dashboard Work for Your Team

Because MailClaw runs locally as an open-source tool, there's no data leaving your machine — which matters if you're working with sensitive prospect lists or under data privacy constraints. But "local" doesn't mean "solo." The dashboard supports shareable report links that generate static HTML snapshots you can send to teammates or stakeholders without giving them access to your local instance.

mailclaw analytics share --campaign "Q3 Outreach" --expires 7d

This outputs a self-contained URL (served from your local instance while active) or a downloadable HTML file. Combine this with your HubSpot or Salesforce reporting workflows and you've got a full-stack analytics picture: MailClaw handling the email-layer data, your CRM handling downstream revenue attribution.

The goal of any analytics dashboard isn't more data — it's faster, more confident decisions. MailClaw's local dashboard is built around that principle: surface the signals that matter, automate the diagnosis, and put the controls close enough to the insights that acting on them takes seconds, not days.

articles.title: How to Improve Open Rates with MailClaw AI Subject Line Optimization
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's AI-powered subject line optimization to dramatically improve your email open rates, with practical CLI commands, A/B testing strategies, and real-world examples you can put to work today.
articles.content:
Why Subject Lines Are Your First (and Sometimes Only) Chance

The average professional receives over 120 emails per day. Your subject line has roughly two seconds to convince a real human being — distracted, probably on their phone, definitely skimming — that your message is worth their time. Everything else you've built: the beautifully structured sequence, the personalized body copy, the perfectly timed send — none of it matters if the subject line fails.

The good news is that subject line optimization is no longer a guessing game. MailClaw's AI engine, built on OpenClaw, brings machine learning-driven subject line scoring, variant generation, and real-time deliverability feedback directly to your local machine at localhost:3100 — no cloud subscriptions, no data leaving your system.

Understanding How MailClaw Scores Subject Lines

Before you start generating variants, it's worth understanding what's happening under the hood. When you submit a subject line through MailClaw, the OpenClaw AI model evaluates it across several dimensions:

  • Spam signal density — flags phrases, excessive punctuation, and ALL-CAPS patterns that trigger spam filters in Gmail, Outlook, and SendGrid's filtering layer
  • Emotional resonance score — measures curiosity, urgency, and relevance against your contact segment's historical engagement data
  • Personalization potential — detects opportunities to inject contact-level variables like first name, company, or job title from your enriched contact data
  • Length and preview optimization — ensures the subject renders well on mobile (under 50 characters) and desktop (under 70 characters) without cutting off critical words
  • Deliverability risk score — cross-references against MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring to flag combinations that historically hurt inbox placement

This composite score appears as a 0–100 rating in the dashboard and as a JSON response in the CLI — useful when you're scripting bulk optimization workflows.

Generating AI Subject Line Variants from the CLI

Open your terminal and make sure MailClaw is running. If it isn't, start it with:

mailclaw start

Once the local server is live at localhost:3100, you can use the subject command to generate optimized variants for any sequence step:

mailclaw subject generate \
  --sequence "q4-outreach" \
  --step 1 \
  --tone "professional" \
  --variants 5 \
  --persona "VP of Sales"

This will return five AI-generated subject line options scored and ranked by predicted open rate for that specific persona. The --persona flag leverages your enriched contact data — if you've run contact enrichment on your list, MailClaw already knows job titles, company sizes, and industries, and the AI weights its suggestions accordingly.

Scoring an Existing Subject Line

Already have a subject line you're attached to? Score it before you send:

mailclaw subject score \
  --text "Quick question about your Q4 pipeline" \
  --segment "enterprise-leads"

You'll get output like this:

{
  "subject": "Quick question about your Q4 pipeline",
  "score": 74,
  "spam_risk": "low",
  "personalization_opportunities": ["first_name", "company"],
  "suggested_improvement": "Quick question about {{company}}'s Q4 pipeline",
  "improved_score": 83
}

Notice the AI immediately surfaces a personalization opportunity. Replacing a generic "your" with a company name pulled from enriched contact data consistently lifts open rates — typically between 8 and 15 percentage points in cold outreach sequences.

Running A/B Tests with the Sequence Builder

Generating great subject lines is step one. Knowing which one actually performs better for your audience is step two. MailClaw's sequence builder has native A/B testing built in, and setting it up takes under a minute.

Setting Up a Subject Line Split Test

  1. Open your dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to Sequences
  2. Select the sequence you want to test and click into the step you're optimizing
  3. Toggle A/B Test on the subject line field
  4. Enter your two (or three) variants — or click Generate with AI to pull suggestions directly from OpenClaw
  5. Set your split ratio (50/50 is a solid starting point) and your winning metric: open rate, reply rate, or click rate
  6. Define your test duration — MailClaw will automatically promote the winning variant after the threshold is hit

You can also configure this via CLI if you're managing campaigns programmatically:

mailclaw sequence ab-test \
  --sequence "q4-outreach" \
  --step 1 \
  --variant-a "Quick question about {{company}}'s Q4 pipeline" \
  --variant-b "{{first_name}}, are you hitting your Q4 targets?" \
  --split 50 \
  --win-metric "open_rate" \
  --auto-promote true

Reading Your Results

Results surface in real time on the deliverability dashboard. Pay attention not just to open rates but to the open-to-reply ratio. A subject line that over-promises can inflate opens while cratering replies — a pattern MailClaw flags automatically when it detects a statistically significant gap between the two metrics.

Using AI Email Agents to Personalize at Scale

One of the most underused features in MailClaw is the AI email agent layer. Rather than writing one subject line and applying it to your entire list, you can deploy an agent that crafts a unique, personalized subject line for each contact based on their enriched profile.

mailclaw agent run \
  --agent "subject-personalizer" \
  --list "enterprise-q4" \
  --output-field "subject_line" \
  --context "cold outreach, product is a sales analytics tool"

This agent reads each contact's enriched data — pulled from sources you've connected like HubSpot, Salesforce, or LinkedIn enrichment — and generates a subject line that references something specific and relevant. A VP at a 500-person SaaS company gets a different subject than a founder at a 10-person agency, even if they're in the same sequence.

Pro tip: Combine agent-generated subject lines with MailClaw's multi-account support to send from the most contextually relevant sender address. A subject line from a named human (not a generic company alias) paired with hyper-personalized copy consistently outperforms batch-and-blast approaches by 2–3x in reply rates.

Deliverability: The Subject Line Factor People Forget

A subject line doesn't just influence whether a human opens your email — it influences whether the email reaches the inbox at all. Gmail's filtering algorithms, Microsoft's SmartScreen, and SendGrid's reputation systems all analyze subject lines as part of inbox placement decisions.

MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools run a pre-flight check on every subject line before your sequence activates. This includes:

  • Spam keyword scanning against an up-to-date trigger word database
  • Emoji usage analysis (one emoji: sometimes fine; four emojis: almost always a problem)
  • Domain reputation correlation — if your sending domain has a low reputation score, aggressive subject lines that might otherwise be borderline will push you into the spam folder
  • Historical performance benchmarking against similar subject patterns across the open-source MailClaw community dataset

You can run a standalone deliverability check on any subject line before committing it to a sequence:

mailclaw deliverability check-subject \
  --text "🚀 LAST CHANCE: Unlock your FREE growth audit TODAY!!" \
  --from-domain "yourdomain.com"

Spoiler: that subject line will score poorly. The check will tell you exactly why — and suggest a cleaner alternative.

Building a Subject Line Library Over Time

The real compounding advantage of running MailClaw locally is data ownership. Every open, every reply, every bounce lives in your local instance. Over time, this builds a proprietary performance dataset that makes the AI increasingly accurate for your specific audience and niche.

MailClaw automatically tags and archives high-performing subject lines in your local library:

mailclaw subject library --filter "score>80 AND open_rate>35"

Review this list regularly. Look for patterns: do questions outperform statements for your audience? Does mentioning a specific pain point beat a benefit-led subject? Does personalization with company name outperform personalization with first name? These are insights that no generic best-practices article — including this one — can give you, because they're specific to the relationship between your brand, your product, and your contacts.

The Compounding Effect of Consistent Optimization

Subject line optimization isn't a one-time task. It's a system. Set up your AI agents, run your A/B tests consistently, let MailClaw's deliverability tools catch problems before they become reputation damage, and build your library of what works for your audience.

The teams that see 40–60% open rates on cold outreach aren't using magic words. They're running tighter feedback loops than everyone else — and tools like MailClaw, running entirely on your own machine with no per-seat pricing or data sharing, make that level of discipline accessible to solo operators and small teams who previously couldn't justify the tooling cost.

Start with one sequence, score your existing subject lines today, and let the data tell you what to do next.

articles.title: MailClaw Warm-Up: How to Warm Up a New Email Domain Properly
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to properly warm up a new email domain before launching outreach campaigns — covering DNS setup, sending ramp schedules, inbox rotation, and how MailClaw's built-in deliverability tools automate the entire process from your local dashboard.
articles.content:
Why Domain Warm-Up Is Non-Negotiable

You've registered a fresh domain, configured your DNS records, and you're ready to start sending. It's tempting to fire off your first campaign immediately — but doing so is one of the fastest ways to destroy your sender reputation before it even exists.

Email providers like Gmail, Outlook, and Yahoo maintain complex reputation systems that score every sending domain. A brand-new domain has no history, which means inbox providers treat it with deep suspicion. Send too many emails too fast, and you'll trigger spam filters, get blocklisted, or — worst case — have your domain flagged permanently. Warming up your domain is the process of gradually building that reputation by sending small, consistent volumes of legitimate email over several weeks.

This guide walks through the entire warm-up process step by step, including how to automate much of it using MailClaw's deliverability tools and AI email agents running locally on your machine.

Step 1: Get Your DNS Records Right First

Before you send a single email, your domain's technical foundation must be solid. Inbox providers check these records on every message you send. Missing or misconfigured DNS is an instant credibility killer.

The Three Essential Records

  • SPF (Sender Policy Framework): Declares which mail servers are authorized to send on behalf of your domain. A basic SPF record for SendGrid plus Gmail looks like this:
v=spf1 include:sendgrid.net include:_spf.google.com ~all
  • DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail): Adds a cryptographic signature to every outgoing message. Your ESP (SendGrid, Mailgun, Postmark, etc.) will give you a CNAME or TXT record to add to your DNS. Don't skip this — it's one of the strongest trust signals available.
  • DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication): Tells inbox providers what to do when SPF or DKIM checks fail. Start permissive, then tighten over time:
v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourdomain.com

Once your records are live, verify them before moving on. You can use tools like MXToolbox, or run a quick check directly from the MailClaw CLI:

mailclaw check-dns --domain yourdomain.com

MailClaw's deliverability monitor will flag any missing records and surface warnings directly in your localhost dashboard at localhost:3100.

Step 2: Build a Realistic Warm-Up Schedule

The golden rule of domain warm-up is simple: start low, grow slowly, stay consistent. Here's a proven ramp schedule for a new domain targeting cold outreach:

4-Week Warm-Up Ramp

  1. Week 1: Send 10–20 emails per day. Focus on highly engaged contacts — people who know you, former colleagues, or opt-in subscribers. These early interactions should generate opens and replies, which are the strongest positive signals you can generate.
  2. Week 2: Scale to 40–75 emails per day. Begin mixing in warmed contacts alongside your highest-quality leads. Keep bounce rates below 2%.
  3. Week 3: Increase to 150–200 per day. At this point you can start running light prospecting sequences through MailClaw's sequence builder, but keep messaging highly personalized.
  4. Week 4: Push to 400–500 per day if metrics remain healthy. You're not fully warmed yet — most deliverability experts consider 8–12 weeks the real benchmark — but you're building a solid foundation.

Pro tip: Spread sends throughout the day to mimic natural human behavior. Blasting 200 emails in a 10-minute window is a red flag to spam detection systems regardless of your domain age.

Configuring Your Ramp in MailClaw

MailClaw's sequence builder lets you define per-day sending caps directly in your campaign config. Open your sequence file and set the daily_limit and ramp_schedule fields:

{
  "sequence_name": "Q3 Outreach - New Domain",
  "account": "outreach@yourdomain.com",
  "daily_limit": 20,
  "ramp_schedule": {
    "enabled": true,
    "week_1": 20,
    "week_2": 75,
    "week_3": 200,
    "week_4": 500
  },
  "send_window": { "start": "08:00", "stop": "17:30" },
  "timezone": "America/New_York"
}

Save this config and launch it with:

mailclaw sequence start --config ./sequences/q3-outreach.json

MailClaw will automatically throttle sends according to the schedule and surface real-time delivery stats on your local dashboard. No cloud dependencies, no per-seat pricing — it all runs on your Mac.

Step 3: Use Warm-Up Pools and Inbox Seeding

Automated warm-up networks work by enrolling your email address into a pool of inboxes that automatically receive, open, and sometimes reply to your outgoing messages. This simulates engagement and helps build your reputation passively in the background.

Popular services include Mailreach, Warmbox, and Lemwarm. These integrate with Gmail via OAuth or with custom SMTP. In MailClaw, you can connect any of these accounts through the multi-account panel:

mailclaw account add \
  --name "Warm-Up Account" \
  --provider smtp \
  --smtp-host smtp.yourdomain.com \
  --smtp-port 587 \
  --username outreach@yourdomain.com \
  --password yourpassword \
  --tag warmup

Tag the account as warmup to keep it separate from your active outreach accounts. MailClaw's multi-account support means you can run warm-up traffic and live campaigns side by side without mixing configs.

Step 4: Send Emails That Deserve to Land in the Inbox

Technical setup matters, but content quality is equally important during the warm-up window. Spam filters analyze message content, link-to-text ratios, and engagement patterns together.

Warm-Up Content Best Practices

  • Write in plain text or minimal HTML. Heavy templates with images, tracking pixels, and multiple links look promotional to spam filters.
  • Avoid spam trigger words: "free," "guaranteed," "act now," "no obligation," "limited time." This matters especially in subject lines.
  • Personalize every message. MailClaw's contact enrichment feature pulls LinkedIn data, company info, and technographic signals so your AI email agents can generate genuinely personalized first lines — not just Hi {{first_name}}.
  • Keep your first sequences short: one or two sentences of context, a clear ask, nothing else. Long-form pitches belong in week four and beyond.

Letting MailClaw's AI Agent Write Your Warm-Up Sequences

MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered AI email agents can draft warm-up sequences that are intentionally low-pressure and engagement-optimized. From the dashboard at localhost:3100, open the AI Agent Builder, create a new agent, and set the objective to warm_up_outreach. The agent will generate sequences calibrated for reply rate over conversion rate — exactly what you want during this phase.

Step 5: Monitor Deliverability Continuously

Warm-up isn't a set-and-forget process. You need to track key signals week over week and be ready to pull back if something goes wrong.

Metrics to Watch

  • Bounce rate: Keep hard bounces under 2%. Anything higher suggests your list quality is poor or your DNS records are misconfigured. Use MailClaw's contact enrichment to verify emails before sending.
  • Spam complaint rate: Google's Postmaster Tools provides this directly for Gmail recipients. Aim to stay below 0.08%.
  • Open rate: During warm-up, opens from real engaged contacts matter more than the absolute percentage.
  • Inbox placement rate: Services like GlockApps and MailTester let you send seed messages to test addresses across major providers (Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo) and see whether you land in Primary, Promotions, or Spam.

MailClaw's deliverability dashboard aggregates bounce events, open signals, and SMTP response codes in real time. You can also set up automated alerts:

mailclaw monitor set-alert \
  --metric bounce_rate \
  --threshold 0.02 \
  --action pause_sequence \
  --sequence q3-outreach

This command pauses your active sequence automatically if the bounce rate crosses 2% — protecting your domain reputation without requiring you to babysit the dashboard.

What to Do If You Hit a Problem

Even with a careful warm-up, things can go sideways. Here's how to respond:

  • Blocklisted on Spamhaus or Barracuda? Stop sending immediately. Submit a delisting request, audit your list for spam traps, and don't resume for at least 72 hours.
  • Suddenly landing in spam? Check if a recent batch had unusually high bounces or complaint rates. Review your DMARC reports — MailClaw surfaces these in the deliverability panel if you've configured your rua address to a mailbox it monitors.
  • Low open rates despite good placement? The problem is likely the subject line or preview text, not deliverability. Use MailClaw's A/B testing feature in the sequence builder to test variations systematically.

The Patience Principle

Domain warm-up is fundamentally an exercise in patience. The senders who skip this process and blast 5,000 cold emails on day one are the reason inbox providers have such aggressive filters in the first place. By doing this properly — solid DNS, gradual ramp, quality content, continuous monitoring — you're building an asset that will pay dividends for every campaign you run from this domain for years.

MailClaw exists to make this process less tedious. Because it's open source, runs entirely on your local machine, and is built on the OpenClaw foundation, you get full control over your data, your sequences, and your sending logic — without subscriptions or vendor lock-in. Your warm-up config, your deliverability data, your AI agent prompts: all of it lives on your Mac, accessible from a single dashboard at localhost:3100.

Start slow. Watch the numbers. Let the domain age gracefully. Then scale.

articles.title: How to Monitor Email Bounce Rates with MailClaw
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to monitor and reduce email bounce rates using MailClaw's built-in deliverability tools, CLI commands, and AI-powered contact enrichment — keeping your sender reputation intact and your campaigns performing at their best.
articles.content:
Why Bounce Rates Matter More Than You Think

A single campaign sent to a dirty list can do lasting damage to your sender reputation. Internet service providers like Gmail and Outlook track bounce signals closely — and once your domain or IP lands on a blocklist, recovering takes weeks, not days. Keeping your bounce rate below 2% is the industry benchmark most ESPs enforce before throttling or suspending accounts.

MailClaw treats deliverability as a first-class concern, not an afterthought. Because it runs entirely on your machine at localhost:3100, you get real-time visibility into every bounce event without relying on a third-party SaaS dashboard that hides the details behind paywalls or delayed reporting.

Understanding the Two Types of Bounces

Before you can fix a bounce problem, you need to know which type you're dealing with. MailClaw classifies every bounce automatically in its deliverability log.

Hard Bounces

A hard bounce means the email address is permanently undeliverable — the domain doesn't exist, the mailbox has been deleted, or the server explicitly rejected the message with a 5xx SMTP error code. These contacts must be suppressed immediately. Continuing to send to them is one of the fastest ways to tank your reputation with Gmail, Outlook, and services like SendGrid or Postmark.

Soft Bounces

A soft bounce is a temporary failure — a full inbox, a server that was momentarily down, or a message that exceeded size limits. MailClaw's sequence builder handles soft bounces intelligently: it will retry delivery on a configurable schedule before escalating the contact to a review queue rather than blindly suppressing them.

Monitoring Bounces from the MailClaw Dashboard

Open your local dashboard by navigating to http://localhost:3100 in your browser. From the left sidebar, click Deliverability to access the full bounce monitoring panel. You'll see a live feed of bounce events broken down by campaign, sequence, and sending account.

The dashboard surfaces three key metrics at a glance:

  • Bounce Rate % — hard and soft bounces as a percentage of total sends
  • Suppression List Size — total contacts automatically removed from future sends
  • SMTP Response Codes — the raw server responses so you can diagnose issues at the protocol level

You can filter by date range, sending account (useful when you have multiple SMTP or OAuth connections configured), or by campaign tag. If you're running sequences through Gmail via OAuth or through a dedicated sending infrastructure like SendGrid, each account's bounce data is tracked separately — so a problem with one account doesn't obscure the health of your others.

Using the CLI to Pull Bounce Reports

MailClaw is built on OpenClaw, which means everything you can do in the dashboard you can also do from the terminal. This is especially useful for scheduled reporting or integrating bounce data into other workflows.

To pull a bounce summary for the last 7 days, run:

mailclaw deliverability bounces --range 7d --format table

For a full CSV export you can load into HubSpot, Salesforce, or a spreadsheet:

mailclaw deliverability bounces --range 30d --format csv --output ./reports/bounces-june.csv

To see only hard bounces and immediately add them to your global suppression list:

mailclaw deliverability bounces --type hard --suppress --confirm

The --suppress flag writes those addresses to MailClaw's built-in suppression list, ensuring they're excluded from every future campaign and sequence across all connected accounts. This is critical — suppression needs to be global, not just campaign-level.

Proactive Bounce Prevention with Contact Enrichment

The best time to catch a bad email address is before you send to it. MailClaw's contact enrichment feature, powered by the OpenClaw AI engine, validates and enriches contacts as they enter your pipeline — checking for common patterns associated with disposable addresses, role-based inboxes (like info@ or noreply@), and domains with poor sending history.

To run enrichment on a contact list before launching a sequence:

mailclaw contacts enrich --list ./contacts/outreach-q3.csv --validate-email --flag-risky

This command appends two columns to your contact file: email_valid (true/false) and risk_score (0–100). Contacts with a risk score above 70 are flagged for manual review before MailClaw will include them in an active sequence. You can tune this threshold in your config:

# ~/.mailclaw/config.yaml
enrichment:
  email_risk_threshold: 70
  auto_suppress_invalid: true

Setting auto_suppress_invalid: true means MailClaw will silently drop undeliverable addresses from sequences without throwing errors — keeping your campaigns clean without requiring manual intervention every time.

Setting Up Bounce Alerts

You shouldn't have to check the dashboard manually to know when something is wrong. MailClaw supports webhook-based alerts that fire when your bounce rate crosses a threshold you define.

mailclaw alerts create \
  --metric bounce_rate \
  --threshold 2.0 \
  --window 24h \
  --webhook https://hooks.slack.com/your-slack-url

This creates an alert that fires a Slack notification if your 24-hour bounce rate exceeds 2%. You can also route alerts to email, a custom webhook endpoint, or pipe them into a tool like Zapier to trigger automated cleanup workflows in HubSpot or Salesforce.

Pausing Sequences Automatically on Spike Detection

For higher-stakes campaigns, you can instruct MailClaw to pause a sequence automatically if bounce rates spike:

mailclaw sequence update --id seq_abc123 \
  --bounce-circuit-breaker 3.0 \
  --pause-on-trigger

The circuit breaker monitors that specific sequence in real time. If it hits 3% bounces, it pauses sending and logs an event in the dashboard for your review. This is the kind of safety net that separates professional outreach from spray-and-pray email blasting.

Leveraging AI Email Agents for Ongoing List Hygiene

One of MailClaw's most powerful features is its AI email agents — autonomous workers that run in the background, monitoring your contact database and taking action based on rules you define. You can configure an agent specifically for list hygiene:

mailclaw agent create \
  --name "Bounce Hygiene Agent" \
  --trigger bounce_detected \
  --action suppress_contact \
  --action log_to_crm \
  --crm hubspot

This agent watches for any bounce event across all your campaigns, suppresses the contact globally, and logs the event to HubSpot — keeping your CRM data clean without any manual work. If you're syncing with Salesforce instead, swap hubspot for salesforce in the --crm flag.

Agents run locally, so there's no data leaving your machine. For teams handling sensitive B2B contact data, this is a meaningful advantage over cloud-based tools that process your lists on external servers.

Reading SMTP Bounce Codes Like a Pro

MailClaw surfaces raw SMTP response codes in the deliverability log. Knowing what they mean saves hours of guesswork.

  • 550 / 551 — User does not exist. Hard bounce. Suppress immediately.
  • 552 / 553 — Mailbox full or message rejected by policy. Usually a soft bounce, but worth reviewing if it repeats.
  • 421 — Server temporarily unavailable. Soft bounce — MailClaw will retry automatically.
  • 550 5.7.1 — Message rejected due to spam policy. This is a warning sign — review your sending domain, SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records immediately.

If you're seeing a high volume of 550 5.7.1 responses from Gmail or Outlook, the issue is almost never the email address — it's your sender authentication. Run mailclaw deliverability audit to check your DNS records and get a plain-English diagnosis.

Building a Bounce-Resilient Sending Strategy

Monitoring bounces reactively is important, but the real goal is a proactive strategy that keeps your list clean from day one. Here's a practical framework:

  1. Enrich before you send. Always run new contact lists through mailclaw contacts enrich before adding them to a sequence.
  2. Warm new sending accounts gradually. Use MailClaw's warm-up scheduler to ramp up volume over 2–4 weeks before sending at full scale.
  3. Set circuit breakers on every sequence. A 2–3% bounce threshold is a sensible default for most outreach campaigns.
  4. Sync suppressions to your CRM. A contact suppressed in MailClaw should also be marked as undeliverable in HubSpot, Salesforce, or wherever your source of truth lives.
  5. Review your bounce logs weekly. Schedule a 10-minute dashboard review every Monday. The CLI report can be automated with a cron job.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your machine, you own every piece of this data. There are no usage limits on suppression lists, no per-contact fees for enrichment, and no black-box algorithms deciding what you can and can't see about your own campaigns. That transparency is what makes it possible to build a genuinely healthy sending practice — one that respects your recipients and protects your domain for the long haul.

articles.title: MailClaw Sender Reputation: How to Build and Protect It
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Your sender reputation determines whether your emails land in the inbox or disappear into spam — learn how to build it from scratch, protect it over time, and use MailClaw's built-in tools to stay ahead of deliverability issues.
articles.content:
What Sender Reputation Actually Means (and Why It Controls Your Deliverability)

Every domain and IP address that sends email carries an invisible score. Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo, and every other major inbox provider use this score — your sender reputation — to decide whether your message deserves a place in the inbox, gets quietly routed to spam, or gets blocked entirely before it even arrives.

Sender reputation is calculated from dozens of signals: bounce rates, spam complaints, engagement rates, authentication records, sending volume consistency, and more. The frustrating part is that reputation damage is easy to accumulate and slow to repair. The good news is that with the right habits and tooling, you can build a strong reputation methodically — and MailClaw gives you the infrastructure to do exactly that, running entirely from your own machine.

The Foundation: Authentication Records You Cannot Skip

Before you send a single outreach email, your domain needs proper authentication configured. Without it, inbox providers have no reason to trust that you are who you say you are, and your messages will be treated with deep suspicion.

SPF, DKIM, and DMARC

  • SPF (Sender Policy Framework) — A DNS TXT record that lists the mail servers authorized to send on behalf of your domain. If you're sending through Gmail SMTP, Outlook, or SendGrid, each provider's IP ranges need to be included.
  • DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) — Adds a cryptographic signature to your outgoing messages, letting receiving servers verify the email hasn't been tampered with in transit.
  • DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting & Conformance) — Ties SPF and DKIM together and tells inbox providers what to do when a message fails authentication. It also sends you forensic reports so you can spot abuse early.

A minimal but effective DMARC record looks like this:

v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourdomain.com; pct=100

Start with p=none (monitoring only), review the reports for two to four weeks, then graduate to p=quarantine and eventually p=reject once you're confident legitimate mail is passing cleanly.

MailClaw's deliverability dashboard — accessible at localhost:3100 — surfaces authentication status for every connected sending account. When you add a domain via the multi-account setup, the dashboard flags missing or misconfigured SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records before you ever queue a campaign.

Warming Up: The Process Most People Rush

If you're sending from a new domain or a fresh IP address, jumping straight into high-volume outreach is the fastest way to destroy your reputation before it even exists. Inbox providers flag sudden spikes in sending volume as suspicious behavior — because they usually are.

A Practical Warm-Up Schedule

  1. Week 1: Send 20–50 emails per day to highly engaged contacts — people who are genuinely expecting to hear from you.
  2. Week 2: Double the volume. Monitor open rates and bounce rates closely.
  3. Week 3–4: Continue doubling every 5–7 days, watching for any reputation signals deteriorating.
  4. Month 2 and beyond: You can begin scaling into the hundreds or thousands of sends per day, but only if engagement metrics remain healthy.

MailClaw's sequence builder has rate-limiting controls built directly into the campaign configuration. You can set daily send caps per account and stagger delivery windows so your volume ramp looks natural to receiving servers — not like a script that fired all at once.

# Example: Starting a warm-up sequence via MailClaw CLI
mailclaw sequence start --name "Warm Up - Week 1" \
  --daily-limit 40 \
  --send-window "09:00-17:00" \
  --account founder@yourdomain.com

List Quality: The Single Biggest Lever You Have

A pristine authentication setup and careful warm-up mean nothing if you're sending to a dirty list. High bounce rates and spam complaints are the two metrics that will crater your reputation faster than anything else.

Keep Hard Bounces Below 2%

A hard bounce means the email address doesn't exist. If more than 2% of your sends hard bounce, inbox providers take notice. At 5% or above, you're in serious trouble. MailClaw's contact enrichment layer — powered by OpenClaw — can validate email addresses before they ever enter a sequence, cross-referencing against multiple data sources to flag addresses that are likely invalid, role-based (like info@ or admin@), or associated with known spam traps.

Suppress Unsubscribes and Complaints Immediately

Every sequence in MailClaw automatically processes unsubscribe signals and removes contacts from active campaigns in real time. If you're integrating with a CRM like HubSpot or Salesforce, suppression lists sync bidirectionally so a contact who opts out in either system is honored everywhere.

Segment for Engagement

Sending to people who never open your emails is quietly damaging your reputation. Gmail in particular uses engagement as a major trust signal — a domain that consistently sends to unengaged recipients gets downgraded over time. Use MailClaw's AI email agents to identify contacts who haven't engaged in 90+ days and run a re-engagement sequence before deciding whether to remove them from your active list entirely.

Monitoring Your Reputation in Real Time

Reputation problems are much easier to fix when you catch them early. The following resources should be part of your regular monitoring routine:

  • Google Postmaster Tools — Free dashboard from Google showing your domain reputation, spam rate, and IP reputation for mail delivered to Gmail. Connect your sending domain and check it weekly.
  • Microsoft SNDS (Smart Network Data Services) — The equivalent for Outlook and Hotmail. Shows complaint rates and filtering status for your sending IPs.
  • MXToolbox — Quick checks for blacklist status across dozens of RBLs (real-time blackhole lists). If your IP or domain appears on a blacklist, this surfaces it immediately.
  • MailClaw's deliverability monitor — The localhost dashboard aggregates bounce signals, complaint rates, and open rate trends across all your connected sending accounts (Gmail OAuth, Outlook OAuth, SendGrid API, and custom SMTP) in a single view.

Rule of thumb: If your spam complaint rate climbs above 0.1% in Google Postmaster Tools, stop your campaigns and audit your list and content before sending another message. Google's own documentation now treats 0.3% as the hard threshold for filtering — you want a significant buffer below that.

Content and Sending Behavior Signals

Reputation isn't only about technical configuration and list hygiene. The content of your emails and the behavioral patterns of your sending also feed into how you're perceived.

Avoid Classic Spam Triggers

  • Excessive use of ALL CAPS or multiple exclamation points!!!
  • Overly promotional language in early sequences before trust is established
  • Heavy HTML with lots of images and minimal text — plain-text or lightly formatted emails tend to perform better for cold outreach
  • Misleading subject lines or "RE:" prefixes on cold emails that imply an existing conversation

Send Consistently, Not Erratically

Inbox providers notice when a domain goes quiet for weeks and then suddenly blasts thousands of messages. Even if your volume stays low, sending on a predictable, consistent schedule reinforces that you're a legitimate sender. MailClaw's sequence builder lets you define recurring send cadences with built-in jitter — small random delays between individual sends — so the traffic pattern looks human rather than mechanical.

Using MailClaw's AI Agents to Protect Reputation Proactively

One of the more powerful applications of MailClaw's AI email agents is using them as a reputation watchdog. Because MailClaw runs locally via OpenClaw, you can configure agents that continuously monitor your campaign metrics and trigger automatic actions when thresholds are crossed — without sending your data to a third-party SaaS platform.

For example, you can define an agent that pauses a sequence automatically if the bounce rate for a given batch exceeds 3%, then surfaces a summary in the dashboard explaining which contacts triggered the spike:

# Example agent rule in MailClaw config
agents:
  - name: "Bounce Rate Guardian"
    trigger:
      metric: bounce_rate
      threshold: 0.03
      window: last_200_sends
    action:
      pause_sequence: true
      notify: dashboard
      log: "Bounce threshold exceeded — sequence paused for review"

This kind of automated safety net is especially valuable when you're running multiple campaigns across several accounts simultaneously — a scenario where manual monitoring becomes impractical.

The Long Game: Reputation is Built Over Months, Not Days

Strong sender reputation is a compounding asset. Every campaign that generates high opens, low bounces, and zero complaints adds a small deposit to your trust balance with inbox providers. Every shortcut — buying lists, skipping warm-up, ignoring authentication — makes withdrawals that are painful to recover from.

MailClaw is designed around the philosophy that sustainable outreach is better outreach. The open-source foundation means you can inspect exactly how your sending behavior is managed, the local-first architecture means your contact data and campaign logic stay on your machine, and the built-in deliverability tooling means you're never flying blind.

Start with your authentication records. Warm up your sending domain deliberately. Keep your lists clean using contact enrichment. Monitor your reputation metrics weekly. And let MailClaw's AI agents catch the problems you don't have time to watch for manually. Do those five things consistently, and your inbox placement rates will reflect it.

articles.title: How to Use MailClaw Analytics to Optimize Send Times
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's built-in analytics engine to identify your audience's peak engagement windows, interpret open and click data, and configure your sequences to send at exactly the right moment — all from your local dashboard.
articles.content:
Why Send Time Matters More Than You Think

You can write the perfect subject line, nail the preview text, and craft a sequence that would make David Ogilvy proud — and still watch your open rates flatline because you sent at the wrong time. Send time optimization isn't a nice-to-have. For high-volume outreach, it's often the single highest-leverage variable you can control without touching a word of your copy.

MailClaw's analytics layer, powered by the OpenClaw engine running locally at localhost:3100, gives you the raw data and AI-assisted interpretation to stop guessing and start scheduling with confidence. This guide walks you through exactly how to use it.

Understanding MailClaw's Analytics Dashboard

When you open the MailClaw local dashboard at http://localhost:3100, the Analytics tab surfaces engagement data aggregated across all your connected accounts — whether those are Gmail accounts via OAuth, Outlook mailboxes, or SMTP-configured senders through SendGrid or Postmark.

The core metrics you'll work with for send time optimization are:

  • Open rate by hour of day — broken into your local timezone and, if contact enrichment data is available, the recipient's timezone
  • Click-through rate (CTR) by day of week — useful for sequences that contain links to demos, calendars, or resources
  • Reply rate by send window — arguably the most important metric for cold outreach sequences
  • Time-to-open distribution — how long after delivery recipients typically engage, which reveals habitual email check patterns

Each of these is filterable by campaign, sequence, sender account, and contact list segment. This is where MailClaw's multi-account support pays real dividends — you can compare performance across a personal Gmail sender and a branded domain sender side by side.

Pulling Your Engagement Data via the CLI

For power users, the MailClaw CLI exposes the analytics engine directly. This is especially useful when you want to export data for deeper analysis or pipe it into a script that auto-adjusts your sequence scheduling.

To pull a send-time performance report for a specific campaign:

mailclaw analytics report \
  --campaign "Q3 Outreach" \
  --metric open_rate,reply_rate \
  --group-by hour_of_day \
  --output json > send_time_analysis.json

To see a cross-campaign aggregate for your top-performing send windows:

mailclaw analytics best-windows \
  --accounts all \
  --lookback 90d \
  --min-sample 200 \
  --format table

The --min-sample flag is important. MailClaw won't surface a "best window" recommendation unless it has statistically meaningful data behind it. You can lower this threshold for smaller lists, but be cautious about over-indexing on thin samples.

Interpreting the Data: What Good Looks Like

The Tuesday–Thursday Myth

You've probably read that Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday mornings are universally the best times to send email. That's a population-level average from aggregated industry studies — and it has almost no bearing on your specific audience.

A SaaS founder audience might show peak engagement on Monday mornings when they're planning the week. A retail buying audience might spike on Friday afternoons. MailClaw's contact enrichment features pull in role, industry, and company-size signals from enriched contact records, which means you can segment your timing recommendations by persona rather than applying a one-size-fits-all schedule.

Reading Time-to-Open Distributions

One of the most underused analytics views in MailClaw is the time-to-open histogram. If 60% of your opens happen within 15 minutes of delivery, your audience is checking email in real time — and your send time precision matters enormously. If your distribution is flat over 24 hours, your audience is batching their inbox and the exact send hour is less critical than the send day.

Navigate to Analytics → Campaign → Time-to-Open in the local dashboard to pull this view for any campaign with more than 50 sends.

Configuring Send Time Optimization in Your Sequences

Manual Window Configuration

Once you've identified your best-performing windows from the analytics data, you can hardcode delivery windows into any sequence step inside MailClaw's sequence builder:

mailclaw sequence edit "Cold Outreach v2" \
  --step 1 \
  --send-window "tue-thu:08:00-10:00" \
  --timezone recipient

The --timezone recipient flag tells MailClaw to resolve the window relative to each contact's timezone — inferred from contact enrichment data (city/country fields, or pulled directly from enriched records synced from HubSpot or Salesforce). Without this flag, it defaults to your local system timezone.

AI-Assisted Send Time Recommendations

MailClaw's AI email agent layer can go further than static windows. When you enable Smart Scheduling on a sequence, the OpenClaw-powered agent analyzes your historical engagement data for each contact individually and schedules each email in the optimal window for that specific recipient.

To enable it:

mailclaw sequence edit "Cold Outreach v2" \
  --step 1 \
  --smart-schedule on \
  --fallback-window "tue-thu:09:00-11:00"

The --fallback-window is used for new contacts with no engagement history. As those contacts open, click, or reply, MailClaw's AI agent updates their individual timing profile and applies it to subsequent steps in the sequence automatically.

Pro tip: Smart Scheduling compounds in value across multi-step sequences. By step 3 or 4, the AI agent has enough per-contact data to meaningfully personalize delivery timing — and that's typically where you see the biggest lift in reply rates on longer sequences.

Connecting Analytics to Your Deliverability Health

Send time optimization isn't purely about engagement rates. It also intersects with deliverability. Sending a spike of volume at an unusual hour — say, 3 AM local time for your recipients — can trigger spam filters at providers like Gmail and Outlook that use behavioral anomaly signals in their filtering algorithms.

MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools flag these patterns for you. In the dashboard under Deliverability → Send Pattern Analysis, you'll see a heatmap of your outbound volume by hour. If you're concentrating sends in a narrow window that doesn't match typical human behavior for your audience, MailClaw will surface a warning and suggest redistributing volume across a broader window.

You can also run a quick deliverability check from the CLI:

mailclaw deliverability check \
  --account "outreach@yourcompany.com" \
  --include send-pattern,reputation,authentication

This combines send pattern analysis with SPF/DKIM/DMARC authentication checks and domain reputation signals into a single health report — useful to run before launching any new high-volume campaign.

Building a Continuous Optimization Loop

The real power of MailClaw's analytics isn't in a one-time audit — it's in building a feedback loop that continuously improves your timing over time. Here's a simple workflow to establish that loop:

  1. Run a baseline report after your first campaign with at least 200 sends using mailclaw analytics best-windows
  2. Update your sequence send windows based on the top two or three performing time slots
  3. Enable Smart Scheduling on subsequent sequence steps to let the AI agent personalize at the contact level
  4. Review the analytics dashboard weekly — particularly reply rate by send window, since this lags opens by a few days
  5. Re-run the best-windows report monthly and compare to your previous configuration; audience behavior shifts seasonally and as your list composition changes

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your machine, all of this data stays local. There's no third-party platform holding your engagement analytics hostage behind a paywall or a data export limitation. Your historical performance data is yours, queryable via the CLI or the dashboard whenever you need it.

A Note on List Segmentation and Timing

If you're managing contacts enriched from multiple sources — say, a HubSpot CRM sync, a Salesforce export, and a manually uploaded CSV — it's worth segmenting your timing analysis by source and persona rather than running everything as a single pool.

Enterprise buyers sourced from a Salesforce pipeline often have different inbox habits than SMB leads from an inbound form. MailClaw's contact enrichment layer appends company size, industry, and seniority signals to your contacts, which makes it straightforward to create segments in the sequence builder and configure per-segment send windows rather than a single global schedule.

Send time optimization is one of those areas where marginal gains stack. A 10% lift in open rate from better timing, combined with a better subject line and a stronger sequence, compounds into a meaningfully different outcome at the bottom of your funnel. MailClaw gives you the data and the tooling to pursue those gains systematically — without ever leaving your terminal or sending your data off your machine.

articles.title: MailClaw Deliverability Checklist: 15 Things to Check Before Sending
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Before you hit send on your next email campaign, run through this 15-point deliverability checklist to protect your sender reputation, avoid spam filters, and make sure your messages actually land in the inbox — not the junk folder.
articles.content:
You spent hours crafting the perfect email sequence. The copy is sharp, the subject lines are punchy, and your MailClaw campaign is loaded up and ready to go. Then you hit send — and half your emails never reach the inbox. Open rates tank. Replies dry up. Your domain starts getting flagged.

Deliverability is the silent killer of email campaigns. The good news: most deliverability problems are preventable if you know what to check. This checklist covers the 15 most important things to verify before any campaign goes out — whether you're running a cold outreach sequence, a drip campaign, or an AI-powered agent workflow inside MailClaw.

Authentication: Your Foundation

Email authentication tells receiving servers that you are who you say you are. Without it, you're essentially sending mail without a return address — and spam filters notice.

1. Verify Your SPF Record

Sender Policy Framework (SPF) specifies which mail servers are allowed to send email on behalf of your domain. Check it with a quick DNS lookup:

dig TXT yourdomain.com | grep "v=spf1"

You should see something like v=spf1 include:sendgrid.net include:_spf.google.com ~all. If you're routing through SendGrid, Mailgun, or your own SMTP server configured in MailClaw, make sure those sending sources are included. A missing or broken SPF record is one of the fastest ways to get flagged.

2. Check Your DKIM Signature

DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) adds a cryptographic signature to your outgoing emails. Receiving servers use it to verify the message wasn't tampered with in transit. In MailClaw's dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to Settings → Sending Accounts to confirm DKIM is enabled for each connected account. You can also test it externally:

# Send a test email to mail-tester.com and check your score
# Or use MXToolbox DKIM Lookup:
# https://mxtoolbox.com/dkim.aspx

3. Set Up DMARC

DMARC tells receiving servers what to do when SPF or DKIM checks fail — reject, quarantine, or do nothing. Start with a monitoring-only policy and tighten it over time:

v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourdomain.com

Even a p=none policy signals to inbox providers that you're taking authentication seriously. Google and Yahoo now require DMARC for bulk senders — this is non-negotiable.

Domain and Sender Reputation

4. Warm Up New Sending Domains

If you're using a fresh domain or a recently added sending account, don't blast thousands of emails on day one. Inbox providers trust domains with sending history. MailClaw's sequence builder has a built-in throttling feature — use it. Start with 20–50 emails per day per account, ramp up over 4–6 weeks, and mix in genuine replies to build positive engagement signals.

5. Check Your Domain's Blacklist Status

Before any campaign, run your sending domain and IP address through a blacklist checker. Being listed on Spamhaus, Barracuda, or SORBS will silently kill deliverability with certain email providers.

# Run from your terminal using MailClaw CLI:
mailclaw check-blacklist --domain yourdomain.com --ip 203.0.113.45

MailClaw's deliverability monitoring panel (accessible from the left sidebar at localhost:3100) surfaces blacklist warnings automatically so you're not flying blind.

6. Audit Your Sending IP's Reputation

If you're using a shared SMTP service like SendGrid or Mailgun, you may be sharing IP addresses with other senders. Check your IP reputation at SenderScore.org or Google Postmaster Tools. If scores are consistently low, consider requesting a dedicated IP — most enterprise sending tools support this.

List Quality and Contact Hygiene

7. Remove Invalid and Bounced Addresses

Hard bounces are death for sender reputation. Before importing any list into MailClaw, run it through an email validation service. After every campaign, MailClaw automatically suppresses hard-bounced addresses — but you should also proactively clean your lists using the contact enrichment features powered by OpenClaw.

# Import and validate a contact list via CLI:
mailclaw contacts import --file leads.csv --validate --enrich

The --validate flag checks for syntax errors and known-invalid domains. The --enrich flag uses MailClaw's AI contact enrichment to fill in missing fields and flag suspicious addresses before they ever enter a sequence.

8. Segment Your List — Don't Spray and Pray

Sending irrelevant email to uninterested recipients tanks your engagement rates, which hurts deliverability over time. Use MailClaw's contact enrichment to segment by industry, company size, job title, or intent signals before building your sequences. If you're syncing contacts from HubSpot, Salesforce, or a CSV export, tag them at import time so you can build targeted sequences instead of monolithic blasts.

9. Check for Role-Based and Catch-All Addresses

Addresses like info@, admin@, hello@, and support@ are often shared inboxes managed by multiple people — or no one. They tend to generate spam complaints. Catch-all domains accept every email regardless of whether the mailbox exists, making bounce rates artificially low but complaint rates high. Flag or remove these before launching.

Email Content and Structure

10. Run a Spam Score Check on Your Email Content

Certain words, phrases, and formatting patterns trigger spam filters. Before finalizing any template in MailClaw's sequence builder, test it through a tool like Mail-Tester or SpamAssassin. Common culprits include ALL CAPS subject lines, excessive exclamation marks, free-money language, and broken HTML.

Pro tip: MailClaw's AI email agents (built on OpenClaw) generate copy that's optimized to avoid common spam trigger patterns — but always run a manual check before a large send.

11. Optimize Your Text-to-HTML Ratio

Emails that are pure images or heavily HTML-coded with almost no plain text look suspicious to spam filters. Aim for a healthy ratio of readable text to HTML markup. Always include a plain-text version of your email — MailClaw generates this automatically from your HTML template when you build sequences, but double-check it looks readable in the preview pane.

12. Check Every Link and Unsubscribe Path

Broken links erode trust with both humans and spam filters. Every URL in your email should resolve correctly before sending. More importantly, your unsubscribe link must work — this is a legal requirement under CAN-SPAM and GDPR, and inbox providers like Gmail check for its presence. MailClaw injects a compliant unsubscribe footer automatically, but confirm it's rendering correctly in your template preview.

Technical Sending Configuration

13. Validate Your From Address and Display Name

Mismatches between your From display name, From address, and Reply-To address are a classic spam signal. Your From address should match the domain with valid SPF/DKIM. In MailClaw, go to Settings → Sending Accounts and verify each account's configuration. If you're using Gmail OAuth or Outlook OAuth, MailClaw handles the token flow — but confirm the display name matches what your recipients expect to see.

14. Test Across Major Inbox Providers

An email that lands in Gmail's Primary tab might go straight to Promotions for Outlook users — or spam for Yahoo. Use a tool like Litmus or Email on Acid to preview rendering and inbox placement across providers. At minimum, send test emails to a Gmail account, an Outlook account, and a Yahoo account before any campaign goes live. MailClaw's multi-account support makes it easy to set up dedicated test accounts for this purpose.

15. Review Your Sending Volume and Cadence

Sudden spikes in sending volume are a major red flag for spam filters. If you normally send 100 emails a day and suddenly fire off 5,000, expect deliverability problems. Use MailClaw's sequence builder to spread sends over time with randomized delays between emails:

# Example sequence config with send-time randomization:
mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "Q4 Outreach" \
  --daily-limit 150 \
  --delay-min 90 \
  --delay-max 300 \
  --randomize-send-time true

The --delay-min and --delay-max flags add random pauses (in seconds) between sends, mimicking natural human sending behavior. This alone can meaningfully improve inbox placement for cold outreach campaigns.

Make Deliverability a Habit, Not an Afterthought

Deliverability isn't a one-time setup — it's an ongoing practice. The best campaigns treat inbox placement as a first-class metric alongside open rates and replies. MailClaw's deliverability dashboard gives you a live view of bounce rates, complaint rates, and blacklist status across all your sending accounts in one place at localhost:3100, so you can catch problems before they compound.

Run through this checklist before every new campaign, revisit your authentication records when you add new sending tools, and let MailClaw's AI agents handle the repetitive monitoring work in the background. Your inbox placement — and your sender reputation — will thank you.

articles.title: How to Track Email Reply Rates and Response Times with MailClaw
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to track email reply rates and response times using MailClaw's built-in analytics, CLI tools, and AI-powered insights to optimize your outreach sequences and close more deals faster.
articles.content:
Why Reply Rate and Response Time Actually Matter

Open rates get all the glory, but savvy email marketers know the real signal is in replies. A 45% open rate with a 1% reply rate tells you something is deeply wrong with your message, your timing, or your audience. Reply rate — the percentage of recipients who actually wrote back — and response time — how quickly they did it — are the two metrics that separate high-performing outreach from noise.

Most email platforms bury these numbers in dashboards that take six clicks to reach. MailClaw, running locally on localhost:3100, puts them front and center. Because everything runs on your machine via OpenClaw's engine, your data never leaves your environment, and you get real-time telemetry without waiting for a SaaS platform to sync overnight.

Setting Up Reply Tracking in MailClaw

Before you can measure replies, you need MailClaw configured to listen for them. MailClaw supports both SMTP-based reply detection and OAuth inbox monitoring for Gmail and Outlook, so you can track responses regardless of how your outbound mail is sent.

Connecting Your Inbox for Reply Detection

Start by opening your MailClaw config file and adding your inbound credentials. For Gmail OAuth:

# In your MailClaw config (mailclaw.config.json)
{
  "accounts": [
    {
      "id": "primary-gmail",
      "provider": "gmail",
      "auth": "oauth2",
      "replyTracking": true,
      "replyWebhook": "http://localhost:3100/webhooks/replies"
    }
  ]
}

For Outlook or custom SMTP setups, swap the provider value and add your IMAP credentials. MailClaw polls your inbox on a configurable interval (default: 60 seconds) and matches incoming messages to the originating sequence thread using Message-ID headers — no pixel tracking required.

Enabling Tracking in the Sequence Builder

When building a sequence in MailClaw's sequence builder, reply tracking is a per-sequence setting. Toggle it on from the CLI:

mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "Q4 Outreach" \
  --track-replies true \
  --track-response-time true \
  --account primary-gmail

Or, if you prefer the local dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to Sequences → New Sequence → Tracking Settings and enable both reply tracking and response time logging. Once enabled, MailClaw begins timestamping every sent message and every inbound reply automatically.

Viewing Reply Rate Metrics on the Dashboard

Head to localhost:3100/analytics to access the Analytics module. MailClaw breaks reply metrics down at three levels:

  • Account level — aggregate reply rate across all campaigns for a given sender account
  • Sequence level — reply rate per sequence, broken down by step (Step 1 follow-up vs. Step 3 bump, for example)
  • Contact level — individual reply history, response time, and sentiment classification (powered by MailClaw's AI layer)

The sequence-level view is where most optimization happens. You'll often find that Step 1 has a 4% reply rate and Step 3 has a 9% reply rate — meaning people who don't respond initially often need two nudges before they engage. MailClaw surfaces this visually so you can adjust your sequence cadence accordingly.

Pulling Metrics from the CLI

If you're running MailClaw in a headless environment or want to script your reporting, the CLI exposes full metrics:

# Get reply rate summary for a specific sequence
mailclaw analytics replies --sequence "Q4 Outreach" --format table

# Output example:
# Step | Sent | Replies | Reply Rate | Avg Response Time
# ---- | ---- | ------- | ---------- | -----------------
# 1    | 412  | 18      | 4.4%       | 14h 32m
# 2    | 394  | 31      | 7.9%       | 9h 17m
# 3    | 251  | 24      | 9.6%       | 6h 44m
# Export to CSV for use in HubSpot or Salesforce reporting
mailclaw analytics replies --sequence "Q4 Outreach" --format csv --output ./reports/q4-replies.csv

The exported CSV maps cleanly to custom fields in HubSpot and Salesforce, so you can enrich your CRM records with actual engagement data rather than relying on open-rate proxies.

Understanding Response Time Patterns

Response time is underused as a qualification signal. In practice, contacts who reply within the first two hours of receiving an email are significantly more likely to convert than those who reply three days later. MailClaw's analytics module lets you slice response time by hour of day and day of week, helping you answer the question: when should I send so replies come back during business hours?

Using the Response Time Heatmap

In the dashboard at localhost:3100/analytics/heatmap, MailClaw renders a response time heatmap for each sequence. The X-axis represents send time; the Y-axis represents the lag before reply. Clusters in the upper-left quadrant — early sends that get fast replies — indicate your optimal send window.

For most B2B outreach, MailClaw data tends to show Tuesday and Wednesday morning sends (between 7:30 and 9:00 AM recipient local time) produce the fastest responses. MailClaw's send-time optimization feature can automatically schedule emails in your sequences to hit that window using contact timezone data pulled during enrichment.

Letting AI Agents Optimize Your Sequences

This is where MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered AI layer earns its keep. Rather than manually tweaking subject lines and send times based on intuition, you can hand the optimization loop to a MailClaw AI email agent.

# Spin up an AI agent to monitor and optimize reply rate for a sequence
mailclaw agent create \
  --type reply-optimizer \
  --sequence "Q4 Outreach" \
  --target-reply-rate 8 \
  --optimize subject,send-time,step-delay

The agent monitors reply rate in real time. When it detects a step underperforming against your target, it generates subject line variants, adjusts the send-time window, or modifies the delay between steps — then A/B tests the changes against a holdout group. You approve proposed changes from the dashboard or let the agent run autonomously in autopilot mode.

Pro tip: Set a minimum sample threshold before the agent acts. In the agent config, use --min-sample 50 to ensure the AI isn't reacting to statistical noise in small batches.

Enriching Contacts to Improve Reply Predictions

Raw reply rate tells you how your emails are performing. Enriched reply rate tells you which contacts are most likely to respond — and that's where MailClaw's contact enrichment features come in.

MailClaw can enrich contact records with LinkedIn activity data, company size, tech stack signals, and job change alerts. When you layer enrichment data on top of reply metrics, patterns emerge fast:

  • Contacts at companies using SendGrid for transactional email are 2× more likely to engage with emails about email infrastructure
  • Contacts who changed jobs in the last 90 days reply at significantly higher rates (they're evaluating new vendors)
  • Director-level contacts at companies with 50–200 employees tend to have shorter response times than VP-level at enterprise accounts

Run enrichment before launching a sequence:

mailclaw contacts enrich \
  --list q4-prospects.csv \
  --fields linkedin,company,tech-stack,job-change \
  --output enriched-q4.csv

Then segment your sequence based on enrichment signals to tailor messaging — and watch your reply rates climb.

Keeping Your Reply Rates Honest with Deliverability Monitoring

A drop in reply rate isn't always a content problem. Sometimes it's a deliverability problem: your emails are landing in spam, and you're measuring silence rather than rejection. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools run in the background and surface warnings before they crater your metrics.

From the dashboard sidebar, the Deliverability panel shows your sender reputation, SPF/DKIM/DMARC status, spam complaint rate, and inbox placement estimates across major providers including Gmail, Outlook, and Yahoo Mail. If MailClaw detects a spike in bounce rate or a complaint threshold breach, it pauses the affected sequence automatically and alerts you via the local notification system.

# Run a manual deliverability check before launching a campaign
mailclaw deliverability check --account primary-gmail --test-addresses seed-list.csv

This command fires test emails to a seed list and reports back inbox placement rates by provider. It's the difference between launching confidently and discovering three days in that your entire sequence was going to the Promotions tab.

Building a Reply Rate Reporting Routine

Metrics are only useful if you review them consistently. Here's a lightweight reporting routine that works well with MailClaw's CLI and integrates with tools like HubSpot, Salesforce, or even a simple Notion dashboard:

  1. Weekly sequence audit — run mailclaw analytics replies --period 7d --all-sequences every Monday morning to spot underperforming steps
  2. Response time check — review the heatmap for any shift in reply timing that might indicate audience fatigue or deliverability issues
  3. Agent review — if you're using AI agents, check the change log (mailclaw agent log --id reply-optimizer) to see what the agent modified and whether the changes improved performance
  4. CRM sync — export reply data to your CRM so sales can prioritize follow-up based on actual engagement rather than guesswork

Because MailClaw runs locally, this entire workflow can be scripted and scheduled with a simple cron job — no API rate limits, no monthly data export caps, and no SaaS vendor in the middle of your reporting pipeline.

The Bottom Line

Reply rate and response time are the leading indicators of outreach health, and MailClaw gives you the tools to track them precisely, interpret them intelligently, and act on them automatically. Whether you're a solo founder running cold outreach from your MacBook or a growth team managing multi-account campaigns across dozens of sequences, the combination of MailClaw's local dashboard, CLI-first design, AI agents, and open-source transparency gives you a level of control that hosted platforms simply can't match. Start with tracking enabled on your next sequence, build the review habit, and let the data tell you where to double down.

articles.title: Using MailClaw to Monitor Spam Score Before Sending
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's built-in deliverability tools to check and reduce your spam score before every send, keeping your outreach out of the junk folder and in front of real people.
articles.content:
Why Spam Score Matters Before You Hit Send

You've written a compelling subject line, personalized the body copy, and loaded up your sequence in MailClaw. But if your email lands in spam, none of that work matters. Inbox placement is the silent killer of email outreach — campaigns with a spam score above 5 on the SpamAssassin scale routinely see open rates drop by 60% or more, and some never reach the inbox at all.

The good news is that spam scoring is not a black box. It's a measurable, improvable metric — and MailClaw's deliverability tooling gives you everything you need to catch problems before your sequence fires, not after you've already burned through a contact list.

Rule of thumb: A SpamAssassin score below 2.0 is considered safe. Between 2.0 and 5.0 is a yellow zone worth investigating. Anything above 5.0 is likely headed for the junk folder.

How MailClaw Checks Spam Score Locally

Because MailClaw runs entirely on your Mac at localhost:3100, it performs spam analysis locally through its OpenClaw engine — no third-party API required for the base check. When you open the dashboard and navigate to a draft sequence or individual email, the Deliverability Panel appears in the right sidebar. This panel runs a live analysis of your email content, headers, and sending configuration every time you make a change.

Under the hood, MailClaw pipes your email through a local SpamAssassin-compatible scoring engine, then layers on its own AI-powered heuristics (trained on modern Gmail and Outlook filtering patterns) to give you a composite score. You'll see:

  • A numeric spam score (0–10 scale)
  • A per-rule breakdown explaining why each point was added
  • Header analysis for SPF, DKIM, and DMARC alignment
  • A plain-language AI suggestion for fixing the top offenders

This happens in real time as you edit — no need to send a test email to a scoring service like Mail-Tester or GlockApps (though those are still great for final verification).

Running a Spam Score Check from the CLI

If you prefer working from the terminal — or you're automating pre-send validation inside a script — MailClaw exposes a CLI command for spam scoring:

# Check spam score for a specific sequence step
mailclaw deliverability score --sequence my-outreach-seq --step 1

# Check all steps in a sequence at once
mailclaw deliverability score --sequence my-outreach-seq --all

# Output a full rule breakdown in JSON
mailclaw deliverability score --sequence my-outreach-seq --step 1 --format json

The --all flag is especially useful before launching a multi-step campaign. It loops through every email in your sequence and returns a summary table so you can see at a glance which steps need attention. A typical output looks like this:

Step 1: Score 1.4  ✅ Safe
Step 2: Score 3.1  ⚠️  Review recommended
Step 3: Score 6.8  ❌ High risk — likely spam

From there, you can drill into step 3 with --format json to get the granular rule breakdown and fix each issue systematically.

The Most Common Spam Score Triggers (And How to Fix Them)

1. Spammy Phrases in Subject Lines and Body

Words like "free," "guaranteed," "act now," and "limited time offer" are classic SpamAssassin triggers. MailClaw's AI email agent will flag these inline and suggest alternatives. If you're using the sequence builder's AI-assist mode, it will automatically avoid high-risk phrasing when generating copy — but it's worth reviewing manually, especially if you've imported templates from HubSpot or Salesforce.

2. Broken or Missing Authentication Records

Even perfectly written copy can get flagged if your sending domain lacks proper SPF, DKIM, or DMARC records. MailClaw checks these automatically when you add a sending account — whether you're connecting via OAuth (Gmail, Outlook) or SMTP (SendGrid, Postmark, Mailgun). Navigate to Settings → Sending Accounts and look for the green shield icon. A yellow or red icon means authentication is misconfigured.

To diagnose from the CLI:

mailclaw auth check --account your@domain.com

This returns a report showing whether your SPF record includes your sending IP, whether DKIM is signing correctly, and whether DMARC policy is set to none, quarantine, or reject. If you're routing through SendGrid, MailClaw will also detect whether you've verified your domain inside SendGrid's dashboard — a common oversight that tanks deliverability.

3. High Image-to-Text Ratio

Spam filters still penalize emails that are mostly images with little readable text. If you're sending HTML emails with heavy graphics, MailClaw's deliverability panel will warn you. A good target is at least 60% text to 40% images. Use the plain-text fallback editor in MailClaw (accessible under each sequence step) to ensure every email has a solid plain-text version — this alone can drop your score by 0.5 to 1.5 points.

4. Links to Low-Reputation Domains

If your email contains links to domains with poor sender reputation, that reputation bleeds into your email. MailClaw's deliverability tools check every URL in your draft against known blocklists. You'll see flagged links highlighted in red in the editor. This is particularly relevant when you're linking to landing pages, tracking domains, or shortened URLs — all of which carry additional risk if not configured carefully.

5. Sending Volume Spikes

Spam scoring isn't just about content — sending behavior matters too. If you're warming up a new domain and suddenly blast 500 emails in a day, Gmail and Outlook's filters will notice. MailClaw's sequence builder includes rate-limiting and send-time spreading controls. Under Campaign Settings → Sending Limits, you can configure a daily cap and randomize send windows to mimic natural human behavior.

Setting Up a Pre-Send Spam Score Gate

One of the most powerful workflow patterns in MailClaw is setting a spam score threshold that blocks a sequence from activating until all steps pass. This acts as an automated quality gate so you never accidentally launch a high-risk campaign.

# Set a score threshold gate for a sequence
mailclaw sequence set-gate --sequence my-outreach-seq --max-score 2.5

# Now try to activate — it will fail if any step exceeds 2.5
