mailclaw sequence activate --sequence my-outreach-seq

If any step in the sequence exceeds the threshold, the activation command exits with an error and prints which steps need fixing. You can wire this into a shell script or CI pipeline if you're managing email operations at scale:

#!/bin/bash
mailclaw sequence activate --sequence $SEQUENCE_NAME
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Sequence blocked: spam score threshold exceeded."
  exit 1
fi
echo "Sequence activated successfully."

Using Contact Enrichment to Improve Relevance (and Reduce Spam Risk)

Here's a less obvious tip: highly personalized emails consistently score lower on spam filters because they contain specific, contextual language rather than generic broadcast copy. MailClaw's contact enrichment feature pulls in data points — job title, company size, recent activity, LinkedIn signals — that your AI email agent can use to tailor each message at the individual level.

To enrich a contact list before building a sequence:

mailclaw contacts enrich --list my-contacts.csv --output enriched-contacts.csv

Once enriched, the sequence builder's AI agent can reference these fields to write lines like "I noticed [Company] recently expanded into the European market..." — the kind of specificity that reads as human and legitimate to both recipients and spam filters alike.

Final Verification: Combining MailClaw with External Tools

For campaigns where deliverability is mission-critical, pair MailClaw's local scoring with an external test before launch. Send a test email from your sequence to a service like Mail-Tester.com or GlockApps for a cross-reference score. MailClaw makes this easy — use the Send Test button in the sequence builder to fire a real copy of any step to any address.

If your MailClaw score and your Mail-Tester score are in agreement, you can proceed with confidence. If they diverge significantly, it often points to a sending infrastructure issue (a misconfigured SMTP relay, for example) that only shows up when mail actually transits through real servers.

Deliverability is not a one-time fix — it's an ongoing discipline. With MailClaw's local dashboard, CLI tooling, and AI-powered analysis all working together, you have a complete monitoring stack running on your own machine, under your own control, without shipping your email content to external services. That's the open-source advantage: full visibility, zero compromise.

articles.title: How to Set Up Email Tracking and Click Analytics in MailClaw
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to configure email open tracking, click analytics, and engagement reporting in MailClaw so you can measure campaign performance, trigger AI-powered follow-ups, and optimize your outreach — all from your local dashboard.
articles.content:
Why Email Tracking Actually Matters for Outreach

Sending emails without tracking is like running ads with no conversion data. You're operating on gut instinct when you could be operating on signal. Knowing who opened your email, when they clicked a link, and how many times they revisited your message tells you something fundamental: they're interested, but not yet ready to reply.

MailClaw's built-in tracking layer gives you that signal — and unlike cloud-based tools like HubSpot or Outreach, your data never leaves your machine. Everything is stored locally, processed through the OpenClaw engine, and surfaced in your localhost dashboard at localhost:3100. For teams who care about privacy and data ownership, this is a meaningful advantage.

Good tracking isn't just about vanity metrics. It's the foundation for intelligent follow-up timing, sequence branching, and AI-driven engagement decisions — all of which MailClaw handles natively.

How MailClaw's Tracking Infrastructure Works

Before configuring anything, it helps to understand the mechanics. MailClaw uses two primary tracking methods:

  • Open tracking: A transparent 1×1 pixel image is embedded in outgoing HTML emails. When the recipient's email client loads the image, MailClaw logs the open event with a timestamp and approximate location.
  • Click tracking: Links in your emails are rewritten to pass through a local redirect endpoint before forwarding the recipient to the destination URL. Each click is logged with link identity, timestamp, and contact ID.

Both tracking mechanisms route through MailClaw's local tracking server, which runs as a lightweight sidecar process alongside the main dashboard. This means you need your machine (or a small VPS if you've deployed MailClaw remotely) to be reachable at the time of the tracking event. We'll cover how to handle this in production setups below.

Enabling Tracking in Your MailClaw Configuration

Step 1: Set Your Tracking Domain

Open your mailclaw.config.js file in the root of your MailClaw installation. You'll find a tracking block where you configure the base URL that gets embedded in emails:

// mailclaw.config.js
module.exports = {
  tracking: {
    enabled: true,
    domain: "https://track.yourdomain.com", // or use ngrok for local dev
    openTracking: true,
    clickTracking: true,
    pixelPath: "/t/open",
    redirectPath: "/t/click",
  },
  // ...rest of config
};

For local development, you can use ngrok to expose your localhost tracking server to the public internet. Run the following in a separate terminal:

ngrok http 3100

Then paste the generated HTTPS URL (e.g., https://abc123.ngrok.io) as your tracking.domain value. This is the URL that will be embedded in pixel images and link redirects inside your emails.

For production deployments — if you're running MailClaw on a VPS behind a domain — simply point a subdomain like track.yourdomain.com to your server and use that instead. MailClaw handles the routing internally.

Step 2: Enable Tracking on a Per-Sequence Basis

Once the global config is set, you can toggle tracking on or off for individual sequences inside the MailClaw Sequence Builder. Navigate to your sequence in the dashboard, click Sequence Settings, and enable the tracking toggles:

  • Track Opens
  • Track Clicks
  • Track Replies (via send-time fingerprinting — no pixel required)

You can also control this via the CLI when creating a sequence:

mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "Q4 Outreach" \
  --track-opens true \
  --track-clicks true \
  --from-account gmail:you@yourdomain.com

MailClaw supports multi-account setups, so the --from-account flag lets you specify which connected account — Gmail via OAuth, Outlook via OAuth, or any SMTP provider like SendGrid or Postmark — sends the sequence.

Reading Your Analytics in the Dashboard

Once emails are sending and tracking events are coming in, head to localhost:3100/analytics. You'll see a campaign-level overview with the following metrics:

  • Open rate — percentage of delivered emails with at least one open event
  • Click rate — percentage of delivered emails with at least one click event
  • Click-to-open rate (CTOR) — clicks as a percentage of opens (a better engagement signal than raw click rate)
  • Unique vs. total opens — distinguish genuine re-reads from email client prefetching
  • Per-link breakdown — see which specific links got the most clicks inside a given email

Contact-Level Engagement View

Click into any contact in the MailClaw contact database and you'll see a full engagement timeline: every open, click, and reply event logged chronologically. This is particularly powerful when combined with MailClaw's contact enrichment feature — which pulls in company data, job title, LinkedIn activity, and firmographic signals — because you can correlate engagement with persona type.

For example, you might discover that VP-level contacts at SaaS companies open your emails at a much higher rate on Tuesday mornings, while IC-level engineers engage more on Thursday afternoons. This kind of insight is only possible when tracking data and enriched contact profiles live in the same place.

Using Tracking Data to Power AI Email Agents

This is where MailClaw really separates itself from simpler tools. The OpenClaw-powered AI email agents can consume tracking events as triggers for dynamic sequence behavior.

Trigger-Based Follow-Ups

You can configure an AI agent to watch for specific engagement signals and respond automatically. Here's an example agent rule written in MailClaw's agent config format:

// agents/follow-up-agent.js
export default {
  name: "Hot Lead Follow-Up",
  trigger: {
    event: "link_click",
    linkContains: "pricing",
    withinHours: 24,
  },
  action: {
    type: "send_email",
    template: "pricing-follow-up",
    delay: "2h",
    personalize: true, // uses AI to customize opening line
  },
};

When a prospect clicks your pricing link, the agent automatically schedules a personalized follow-up email two hours later — without you lifting a finger. The personalize: true flag tells the OpenClaw AI layer to generate a custom opening line based on the contact's enriched profile data.

Sequence Branching Based on Engagement

In the Sequence Builder UI, you can add conditional branches after any email step:

  1. Select a step in your sequence
  2. Click Add Branch Condition
  3. Choose "If contact clicked any link" or "If contact did NOT open within 72 hours"
  4. Connect each branch to a different next step

Engaged contacts can receive a more direct CTA-focused email. Non-openers can receive a softer re-engagement message or a subject line variation. This logic runs entirely on your local machine — no webhook configuration, no third-party automation platform required.

Handling Apple MPP and Bot Clicks

Any honest guide to email tracking has to address the elephant in the room: Apple's Mail Privacy Protection (MPP) and bot-generated clicks inflate your open and click metrics if you're not accounting for them.

MailClaw's deliverability tools include basic MPP filtering. When an open event arrives within a few seconds of delivery and originates from Apple's proxy IP range, MailClaw flags it as a suspected MPP open and excludes it from your primary open rate metric (though it's still stored for reference). You can adjust this behavior in your config:

tracking: {
  filterMPP: true,
  mppFlagThresholdSeconds: 10,
  storeFlaggedEvents: true,
}

For click fraud and bot protection, MailClaw checks click events against known bot user agents and flags rapid-fire clicks (multiple clicks within milliseconds) as suspicious. These are excluded from your CTOR calculation by default.

Exporting Tracking Data for External Tools

If your team also uses CRMs like HubSpot, Salesforce, or Pipedrive, you can export MailClaw tracking data as CSV or push events via webhook to keep your CRM activity timelines in sync. Run:

mailclaw export analytics \
  --sequence "Q4 Outreach" \
  --format csv \
  --output ./exports/q4-analytics.csv

Or configure a webhook endpoint in your mailclaw.config.js to POST tracking events to your CRM's inbound webhook URL in real time. This is particularly useful for sales teams who live in Salesforce but want MailClaw's local-first AI outreach layer doing the heavy lifting.

A Quick Checklist Before You Go Live

Before launching a tracked campaign, run through this checklist to make sure your setup is solid:

  • Tracking domain is publicly reachable — test your pixel URL in a browser before sending
  • SSL is configured — many email clients block non-HTTPS tracking pixels
  • MPP filtering is enabled — avoid inflated open rates skewing your AI agent triggers
  • Link redirect is tested — click a tracked link yourself and confirm it logs correctly in the dashboard
  • Unsubscribe handling is active — MailClaw's deliverability tools include auto-unsubscribe list management; make sure it's on

Email tracking done right is one of the highest-leverage investments you can make in your outreach operation. Combined with MailClaw's AI agents, sequence branching, and contact enrichment, it transforms raw engagement data into an intelligent, self-optimizing outreach system — running entirely on your own hardware, entirely under your control.

articles.title: MailClaw AI: Predicting Which Emails Will Get Replies
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how MailClaw's AI engine analyzes subject lines, send timing, contact signals, and sequence structure to predict reply likelihood — and how to use those predictions to dramatically improve your outreach results.
articles.content:
Why Most Cold Email Advice Is Educated Guessing

Most email marketers operate on folklore. "Send on Tuesday morning." "Keep subject lines under 7 words." "Always follow up exactly 3 days later." These rules exist because they worked for someone, somewhere, once — and then got repeated until they became gospel.

The problem is that your audience isn't everyone's audience. A SaaS founder in Austin behaves differently from a procurement manager in Munich. What gets replies from fintech CTOs won't necessarily land with early-stage startup founders. Blanket rules flatten nuance, and nuance is exactly where reply rates live.

MailClaw takes a different approach. Built on OpenClaw and running entirely on your local machine at localhost:3100, it brings machine learning to your outreach without sending your contact data to third-party clouds. The AI doesn't follow rules — it learns patterns from your actual campaigns, your specific contacts, and your writing style, then tells you which emails are likely to get responses before you hit send.

How MailClaw Predicts Reply Probability

The prediction engine inside MailClaw evaluates emails across four signal categories. Understanding what it's looking at helps you write better emails — even when you're not looking at a score.

1. Linguistic Signals

MailClaw's AI parses your email body and subject line for patterns correlated with engagement in your historical data. It's not just sentiment analysis. It looks at:

  • Question density — Emails with exactly one clear question outperform those with zero or three-plus questions in most B2B contexts
  • Personalization depth — Generic openers tank reply rates; references to a contact's recent activity, role change, or company news lift them
  • Reading level — Emails written at a 6th–8th grade reading level consistently outperform complex prose in cold outreach
  • Call-to-action clarity — Vague CTAs ("let me know what you think") underperform specific asks ("would a 15-minute call this week work for you?")

2. Contact Enrichment Signals

MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment layer pulls context about each recipient — job title, company size, tech stack, recent LinkedIn activity, funding events — and feeds that data into the prediction model. A contact who just raised a Series A is statistically more likely to reply to an outreach email than one whose company hasn't had any news signals in 18 months.

When you import contacts or sync from HubSpot, Salesforce, or a CSV, MailClaw automatically enriches each record. You can watch this happen in real time from the localhost dashboard under Contacts → Enrichment Queue.

3. Timing and Sequencing Signals

The sequence builder tracks when contacts open emails, at what point in a sequence they engage, and whether engagement drops off after step 2 or step 4. Over time, the AI learns the optimal send window for each contact segment — not just globally, but for your list.

4. Deliverability and Inbox Placement

An email that lands in spam has a 0% chance of getting a reply. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring checks your domain reputation, SPF/DKIM alignment, and sender score before each campaign run. A predicted reply score above 70% means nothing if your emails aren't reaching the inbox — so deliverability is baked into the overall prediction, not treated separately.

Using the Reply Prediction Score in Practice

Once you've written an email in the sequence builder, you'll see a Reply Prediction Score in the right-hand panel — a number from 0–100 alongside a breakdown of what's dragging the score down or pushing it up.

Here's what a typical CLI check looks like when you're running MailClaw from the terminal:

# Score an email before adding it to a sequence
mailclaw score --file ./emails/follow-up-v2.txt --contact-segment founders

# Output:
# Reply Prediction Score: 68/100
# ✓ Subject line length: optimal (6 words)
# ✓ Personalization tokens detected: 2
# ✗ Reading level: Grade 11 (recommend Grade 7-8)
# ✗ CTA ambiguity: high — consider a time-specific ask
# ✗ Send timing: contact segment active window is 7-9am; scheduled for 2pm

Each flag is actionable. You don't have to guess what to fix — the model tells you. Rewrite the CTA, simplify the language, adjust the send time, and rescore. Most users see their score jump 10–20 points in a single revision pass.

Building Sequences That Learn

The real power isn't scoring individual emails — it's building sequences that adapt over time. MailClaw's AI email agents can manage multi-step sequences autonomously, adjusting follow-up timing and messaging based on engagement signals from earlier steps.

For example, you might configure an agent like this:

mailclaw agent create \
  --name "warm-inbound-sequence" \
  --steps 4 \
  --goal replies \
  --adapt-timing true \
  --stop-on reply,ooo,unsubscribe \
  --accounts gmail-primary,outlook-backup

This agent runs a 4-step sequence, automatically pauses when a reply is detected (pulling from your connected Gmail or Outlook account), adapts send timing based on open data, and falls back to a secondary sending account if deliverability signals degrade on the primary.

Over two or three campaign cycles, the agent accumulates enough signal to make meaningful predictions. After 500+ contacts have moved through a sequence, you'll start to see the model's confidence interval tighten and its recommendations become more specific to your audience.

What the Dashboard Shows You

The MailClaw local dashboard at localhost:3100 has a dedicated Prediction Analytics view that shows:

  • Reply prediction accuracy over time (predicted vs. actual reply rate per campaign)
  • Which subject line patterns are over- or under-performing predictions
  • Segment-level breakdown — founders vs. VPs vs. individual contributors, for example
  • Deliverability trends across sending accounts (SendGrid, Gmail, Outlook, custom SMTP)

Because everything runs locally, you're looking at your data without latency, without subscription tiers, and without anyone else's algorithm deciding what you see. This is one of the core reasons MailClaw is open source — full transparency into how the model works, what data it uses, and how predictions are generated.

"The prediction breakdown told me my subject lines were fine but my CTAs were killing me. I changed one sentence across my entire sequence and reply rates went from 4% to 11% in two weeks." — MailClaw community member, GitHub Discussions

Practical Tips for Improving Your Scores

Prioritize Specificity Over Cleverness

Clever subject lines feel good to write. Specific ones get opened. "Quick question about your onboarding flow" outperforms "You might want to see this" almost every time in MailClaw's aggregate training data. The AI will flag vague subject lines, but it's worth internalizing the principle before you even open the sequence builder.

Segment Before You Score

A reply prediction score is only meaningful relative to a segment. Always specify --contact-segment when running a score check via CLI, or select your segment in the dashboard before reviewing predictions. An email scored against a "cold outreach — enterprise" segment will behave very differently than the same email scored against "warm inbound — SMB."

Let Enrichment Run Before Scoring

Contact enrichment significantly improves prediction accuracy. If you've just imported a fresh list, give MailClaw 10–15 minutes to complete enrichment before scoring your emails against those contacts. You can check enrichment status with:

mailclaw contacts status --list ./imports/q2-prospects.csv
# Shows enrichment progress, data coverage %, and any failed lookups

Run A/B Tests Informed by Predictions

Use the prediction score to narrow your A/B test hypothesis. If version A scores 72 and version B scores 58, the model thinks A will win — but test anyway. When the model is wrong, that mismatch is valuable training data. Feed your actual results back in with mailclaw train --campaign campaign-id to improve future predictions.

The Bigger Picture: From Sending Emails to Understanding Them

Prediction scores are a means to an end. The goal isn't a high number in the dashboard — it's understanding why your audience responds to some messages and not others. MailClaw's AI surfaces those patterns so you can internalize them, not just optimize around them.

Over time, you'll stop needing to check the score on every email because the patterns will be second nature. You'll write shorter sentences by default. You'll ask one question per email automatically. You'll think about timing before you schedule, not after.

That shift — from sending emails to understanding communication — is what separates teams that plateau at 5% reply rates from those that consistently hit 15–20%. MailClaw gives you the feedback loop to get there, running quietly on your Mac, on your terms, with your data staying exactly where it belongs.

articles.title: How to Use MailClaw Heatmaps to Understand Email Engagement
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's built-in heatmap tools to visualize click patterns, identify high-engagement zones in your emails, and make data-driven decisions that improve open rates, CTR, and overall campaign performance.
articles.content:
Why Heatmaps Change the Way You Think About Email

Most email marketers spend hours crafting the perfect subject line, agonizing over CTA button color, and debating whether the hero image should be above or below the fold — only to ship the campaign and stare at a single click-through rate number that tells them almost nothing. Did people click the primary CTA or the footer unsubscribe link? Did the product image actually drive action, or did your plain-text PS line at the bottom steal all the clicks?

That's exactly the gap heatmaps fill. MailClaw's engagement heatmaps let you visualize where subscribers are clicking inside your emails, not just whether they clicked. Running locally through your localhost:3100 dashboard, MailClaw overlays click-density data directly on a rendered preview of your sent email — so the insight is immediate, visual, and deeply actionable.

This guide walks you through setting up heatmap tracking in MailClaw, reading the data correctly, and using those insights to improve every sequence you build going forward.

How MailClaw Heatmap Tracking Works

MailClaw is built on OpenClaw, which means its tracking layer is open source and entirely self-hosted — no third-party pixels sending your subscriber data to an external service. When you enable heatmap tracking on a campaign or sequence, MailClaw automatically wraps each tracked link in a unique, anonymized token and logs click events locally to your SQLite or Postgres store (depending on your config).

Each click event captures:

  • The specific link element that was clicked
  • The position of that link within the email's DOM structure
  • A timestamp and session identifier (no PII stored by default)
  • The contact segment the recipient belongs to
  • Which step in a sequence triggered the email

MailClaw's AI email agent then aggregates this into a heatmap layer that's rendered on top of a live preview in your dashboard. Links with higher click density appear in warmer tones (red/orange), while low-engagement zones cool off to blue or grey. You can filter by date range, contact tag, or sequence step — all from the same view.

Enabling Heatmap Tracking via the CLI

Before you launch a campaign, enable click tracking at the sequence level using the MailClaw CLI:

# Enable heatmap tracking on a specific sequence
mailclaw sequence update --id seq_abc123 --heatmap true --track-clicks true

# Or enable it globally for all new sequences
mailclaw config set tracking.heatmap.enabled true
mailclaw config set tracking.click.granular true

You can verify tracking is active before sending:

mailclaw sequence inspect --id seq_abc123 | grep tracking

This will output the tracking configuration, including whether granular link-position logging is enabled. If you're integrating with SendGrid or Mailgun as your SMTP backend, MailClaw will bypass those providers' native click tracking (to avoid double-counting) and handle all event logging locally.

Reading Your Heatmap in the Dashboard

Once your campaign has at least 50–100 opens (the minimum for statistically meaningful heatmap data), navigate to your local dashboard at http://localhost:3100, open the campaign, and click the Heatmap tab.

The Four Zones to Analyze First

Don't try to absorb everything at once. Train your eye to look at four specific zones in order:

  1. Above the fold (top 300px): This is where first impressions live. High click density here is expected but pay attention to what is getting clicked. Is it your primary CTA or a secondary nav link?
  2. The hero section: If you're using an image with an embedded link, MailClaw tracks the image as a clickable element. Low heat on a visually prominent image often means it isn't communicating value clearly enough.
  3. The body copy zone: Inline text links buried inside paragraphs often surprise you. If subscribers are clicking a hyperlinked phrase mid-paragraph more than your CTA button, that phrase is your real hook — and you should promote it.
  4. The footer: A hot footer is usually a warning sign. Lots of footer clicks often mean people are looking for the unsubscribe link, which signals a relevance or frequency problem worth investigating alongside your deliverability tools.

Filtering Heatmaps by Segment

One of MailClaw's most underused features is segment-filtered heatmaps. The same email can produce radically different click patterns depending on who received it. In the dashboard, use the Segment dropdown to compare heatmaps between:

  • New subscribers vs. contacts in nurture sequences
  • Contacts enriched from HubSpot or Salesforce with a specific job title tag
  • Gmail users vs. Outlook users (rendering differences can shift click behavior)

MailClaw's contact enrichment pipeline pulls firmographic and behavioral data into each contact record, so your segments can get surprisingly granular. A VP of Engineering and a Marketing Manager might be reading the same email completely differently — and your heatmap will show you exactly that.

Turning Heatmap Insights into Better Sequences

Data without action is just noise. Here's how to take what you see in your heatmaps and systematically improve your outreach.

Reorder CTAs Based on Actual Click Gravity

If your heatmap shows that a link in step 2 of your sequence consistently outperforms your primary CTA, promote that link. Use the MailClaw sequence builder to restructure the email:

# Pull the current sequence template
mailclaw sequence export --id seq_abc123 --format html > step2.html

# After editing, reimport the updated template
mailclaw sequence import --id seq_abc123 --step 2 --file step2.html

# Preview the change before activating
mailclaw sequence preview --id seq_abc123 --step 2 --contact contact_xyz

This non-destructive workflow means you can iterate quickly without disrupting contacts who are already mid-sequence.

Let the AI Agent Suggest Copy Changes

MailClaw's AI email agent can analyze your heatmap data and suggest copy or layout adjustments automatically. In the dashboard, navigate to AI Suggestions under your campaign's heatmap view. The agent will flag things like:

  • Links receiving zero clicks despite prominent placement (possible rendering issue or irrelevant anchor text)
  • Multiple competing CTAs splitting click attention
  • Footer over-engagement correlated with a specific email step (suggesting that step has a relevance problem)

Pro tip: Connect MailClaw's AI agent to your HubSpot or Salesforce contact data via the enrichment pipeline, and it can factor in deal stage or lead score when making suggestions. A sequence step that underperforms for cold leads might be perfectly calibrated for warm ones.

A/B Test Layouts Informed by Heatmap Data

Heatmaps tell you what is happening. A/B tests tell you why. Use them together. If your heatmap shows that the left column of a two-column layout is getting significantly more clicks than the right, set up a variant with a single-column layout and see if total CTR improves:

# Create an A/B variant for an existing sequence step
mailclaw ab-test create \
  --sequence seq_abc123 \
  --step 2 \
  --variant-name "single-column-layout" \
  --split 50

MailClaw will automatically split traffic, track click events for both variants, and surface a combined heatmap comparison once you hit statistical significance.

Heatmaps for Deliverability Diagnosis

Here's an angle most marketers miss entirely: heatmaps aren't just a UX tool, they're a deliverability signal. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring layer correlates heatmap engagement patterns with inbox placement data from your SMTP providers — whether that's Gmail via OAuth, Outlook via SMTP, or a transactional provider like SendGrid.

Specifically, watch for these patterns:

  • Near-zero click data on a well-distributed send: If your open rates look reasonable but heatmaps are nearly empty, your emails may be landing in promotions or spam tabs where tracking pixels fire but engagement intent is low.
  • Engagement dropping sharply at sequence step 3 or 4: This can indicate that your sending domain is getting flagged after repeated contact, a signal to review your warm-up schedule in MailClaw's deliverability tools.
  • Footer click spikes correlating with a specific SMTP account: If you're running multi-account outreach, a spike in unsubscribe-area clicks from one account's sends might mean that account is under-warmed or sending at too high a volume.

You can cross-reference this data directly from the CLI:

# Pull deliverability report correlated with heatmap events
mailclaw deliverability report \
  --campaign camp_abc123 \
  --include-heatmap-correlation \
  --output table

Building a Feedback Loop That Compounds Over Time

The real power of MailClaw heatmaps isn't any single insight — it's the compounding feedback loop you build when you treat every campaign as a learning opportunity. After each major send, spend 15 minutes in the heatmap view asking three questions:

  1. Did subscribers click what I intended them to click?
  2. Are there unexpected hot zones that reveal something about what my audience actually wants?
  3. Are there cold zones that represent wasted design or copy effort I can redirect?

Log your answers in MailClaw's campaign notes field (accessible via mailclaw campaign note --id camp_abc123 --add "..."), and you'll build an institutional knowledge base about your audience that gets more valuable with every sequence you run.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your machine, none of this engagement data leaves your environment. You own every click event, every heatmap render, and every AI suggestion — a meaningful differentiator in an era where most email platforms monetize your performance data as much as they help you improve it.

Start with one sequence, enable heatmap tracking today, and let the data show you what your subscribers are actually trying to tell you.

articles.title: MailClaw for Growth Teams: Measuring Email Campaign ROI
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how growth teams can use MailClaw to track, measure, and optimize email campaign ROI — from setting up conversion tracking to interpreting deliverability signals and building feedback loops that compound over time.
articles.content:
Why Email ROI Is Harder to Measure Than It Looks

Every growth team knows email is one of the highest-ROI channels available. But knowing it and proving it are two different things. When a CFO asks you to justify your outreach stack, "our open rates are solid" isn't going to cut it. You need a clear line from send to revenue — and most tools make that line surprisingly hard to draw.

The problem isn't effort. It's instrumentation. Most email platforms treat measurement as an afterthought, burying conversion data behind paywalls, disconnecting from your CRM, or aggregating metrics in ways that obscure what's actually working. MailClaw takes a different approach: because it runs locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, you own your data completely. Nothing is sampled, nothing is hidden, and every event is available for you to query, export, or pipe into your own analytics stack.

This guide walks through how growth teams can build a rigorous ROI measurement framework using MailClaw — from first principles to practical implementation.

Defining the Right Metrics Before You Send

The biggest measurement mistake growth teams make is starting with vanity metrics and working backward. Instead, start from your revenue goal and define a metric hierarchy that flows toward it.

The Email ROI Stack

Think of your metrics in three layers:

  • Activity metrics — sends, opens, clicks, replies. These tell you if your email reached someone and caught their attention.
  • Engagement metrics — click-to-reply rate, sequence completion rate, bounce rate, unsubscribes. These tell you if your messaging resonates.
  • Outcome metrics — demos booked, trials started, deals created, revenue closed. These are the only ones your CFO cares about.

Most teams measure layer one obsessively, layer two occasionally, and layer three almost never in a way that ties back to email. MailClaw's local dashboard surfaces all three simultaneously, so you're not toggling between your ESP, your CRM, and a spreadsheet to get the full picture.

Setting Up Conversion Goals in MailClaw

Before launching any sequence, define what a conversion looks like. In MailClaw's sequence builder, you can tag each campaign with a goal type and a target URL or webhook event:

# Define a conversion goal for a campaign
mailclaw campaign create \
  --name "Q3 SaaS Outreach" \
  --goal "demo_booked" \
  --goal-webhook "https://your-app.com/webhooks/demo-booked" \
  --track-clicks true \
  --utm-source "mailclaw" \
  --utm-medium "email" \
  --utm-campaign "q3-saas-outreach"

When a recipient clicks a tracked link and completes the goal action, MailClaw logs the conversion event locally with a full attribution chain — contact ID, sequence step, send timestamp, and time-to-convert. That data lives in your local SQLite store and can be exported or synced to HubSpot, Salesforce, or any CRM via the OpenClaw connector layer.

Contact Enrichment as a Force Multiplier

ROI measurement is only as good as the data feeding your campaigns. If you're sending to poorly segmented lists, your metrics will be noisy and your conclusions will be wrong. MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment, powered by OpenClaw, fills in the gaps automatically before a contact ever enters a sequence.

Enriching Contacts at Import

# Enrich a CSV of contacts before adding to a sequence
mailclaw contacts import leads.csv \
  --enrich \
  --enrich-fields "company_size,industry,title,linkedin_url,tech_stack" \
  --dedupe true

With enriched contacts, you can segment by company size, industry, or tech stack — which means you can run meaningful A/B tests that actually isolate a variable. Comparing open rates across "fintech companies with 50-200 employees using Salesforce" versus a generic list of emails is the difference between actionable insight and noise.

Enrichment also unlocks better personalization, which directly improves reply rates, which directly improves your pipeline conversion rate. It's the upstream investment that makes downstream measurement more valuable.

Building Sequences That Are Measurable by Design

MailClaw's sequence builder lets you construct multi-step email flows with branching logic, time delays, and AI-generated variants. But from an ROI standpoint, the key is building sequences with measurement baked in — not bolted on afterward.

Best Practices for Measurable Sequences

  1. One goal per sequence. Don't run a sequence that tries to book demos and sell a product and nurture cold leads. Pick one outcome, measure it cleanly.
  2. Use step-level UTM parameters. MailClaw automatically appends step numbers to UTM tags so you can see which email in a sequence drove the conversion — not just which campaign.
  3. Set a sequence expiration. Define a time window (e.g., 30 days) after which a contact who hasn't converted is marked as a loss. This keeps your funnel math clean.
  4. Tag variants explicitly. If you're testing subject lines or CTAs using MailClaw's AI email agent, name your variants clearly in the dashboard so the attribution is unambiguous.

Using AI Email Agents for Smarter Testing

MailClaw's AI email agents — built on the OpenClaw inference layer — can generate and test multiple message variants autonomously. But the real ROI value isn't just better copy. It's the speed of iteration. An AI agent can run a statistically significant subject line test in days rather than weeks, which means you're compounding learnings faster.

Pro tip: Have your AI agent optimize for reply rate rather than open rate. Replies are harder to fake (no pixel-tracking issues) and correlate much more strongly with pipeline outcomes than opens do, especially post-Apple MPP.

Deliverability: The Hidden ROI Killer

You can have the best segmentation, the sharpest copy, and a perfectly instrumented funnel — and still get crushed by deliverability problems you don't know about. Emails landing in spam folders generate zero ROI, but they still inflate your "sent" count and make your metrics look worse than they are.

MailClaw's Deliverability Monitoring

MailClaw's deliverability tools monitor your sender reputation across your connected accounts — whether you're sending through Gmail, Outlook, SendGrid, or a custom SMTP provider. The local dashboard flags:

  • Bounce rate spikes by domain or sending account
  • Spam complaint rates above threshold (typically 0.1% for Google, 0.3% for others)
  • DKIM, SPF, and DMARC misconfigurations
  • Sending volume anomalies that might trigger throttling
# Check deliverability health for all connected accounts
mailclaw deliverability report --all-accounts --format table

# Output:
# Account              Bounce%   Complaint%   DKIM   SPF    Score
# outreach@yourco.com  1.2%      0.04%        ✓      ✓      94/100
# sales@yourco.com     4.8%      0.12%        ✓      ✗      61/100  ← needs attention

Catching a deliverability issue early — before it tanks your sender score — can be worth more than any copy optimization. A 10% improvement in inbox placement across a 5,000-contact sequence is 500 more people actually seeing your email.

Connecting MailClaw to Your Revenue Stack

Measuring email ROI in isolation is useful. Measuring it in the context of your full revenue stack is transformative. MailClaw's multi-account support and OpenClaw connector layer make it straightforward to sync attribution data to the tools your team already uses.

Syncing to HubSpot or Salesforce

# Sync conversion events to HubSpot
mailclaw integrations connect hubspot \
  --api-key YOUR_HUBSPOT_KEY \
  --sync-events "email_sent,email_opened,email_replied,conversion" \
  --map-contact-field "email:email" \
  --create-deals-on-conversion true

# Sync to Salesforce
mailclaw integrations connect salesforce \
  --client-id YOUR_SF_CLIENT_ID \
  --client-secret YOUR_SF_SECRET \
  --sync-to-object "Lead" \
  --update-campaign-member-status true

Once connected, every email event MailClaw tracks flows into your CRM as a timestamped activity. Your sales team sees the full engagement history before a call. Your revenue ops team can build attribution reports that span email, sales activity, and closed-won data in a single view.

Calculating True Campaign ROI

With conversion events flowing into your CRM, the math becomes straightforward:

  • Revenue attributed: Sum of deal value for contacts who converted via the campaign
  • Campaign cost: Time spent (at blended hourly rate) + any third-party sending costs (SendGrid, etc.)
  • ROI: (Attributed Revenue - Campaign Cost) / Campaign Cost × 100

Because MailClaw is open source and runs locally, your "tool cost" is effectively zero — which means more of the ROI calculation goes in your favor compared to teams paying $500-2,000/month for a hosted outreach platform.

Building a Measurement Cadence That Compounds

The teams that consistently drive email ROI aren't the ones who measure best at launch — they're the ones who build a regular review cadence that turns data into decisions.

A simple weekly cadence with MailClaw looks like this:

  1. Monday: Pull the weekly sequence performance report from the local dashboard. Flag any sequences with reply rates below 3% or bounce rates above 3%.
  2. Wednesday: Review AI agent test results. Promote winning variants. Pause underperformers.
  3. Friday: Update your CRM attribution data. Calculate week-over-week pipeline contribution from email. Share with the team.

Over time, this cadence builds an institutional knowledge base about what works for your specific audience — which is something no off-the-shelf AI tool can replicate, because it's grounded in your data, your contacts, and your market.

The ROI Case for Running Email Locally

There's one final ROI consideration that often gets overlooked: data ownership. When your email automation runs on a hosted platform, your contact data, engagement data, and campaign learnings live in someone else's database. When you switch tools — and you will switch tools — that institutional knowledge is hard to export and even harder to query.

Because MailClaw runs locally at localhost:3100 on your Mac, your data is always yours. You can query it directly, back it up, version it, and carry it forward regardless of what tools you use in the future. For growth teams building long-term competitive advantage, that's not a small thing — it's a structural edge.

Start with one campaign, instrument it properly, and let the numbers make the case. The ROI of doing email right is self-evident once you can actually see it.

articles.title: How to Reduce Unsubscribe Rates with MailClaw Smart Sending
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how MailClaw's smart sending features — from AI-powered timing and contact enrichment to sequence-level engagement scoring — can dramatically cut your unsubscribe rates and keep your audience genuinely interested in what you send.
articles.content:
Why People Unsubscribe (And Why It's Not Always Your Fault)

Unsubscribes are one of the most misunderstood metrics in email marketing. Most senders treat them as a content problem — "if only I wrote better subject lines" — when the real culprits are usually timing, frequency, and relevance. Someone who opted in to hear about your SaaS product three months ago may have already solved their problem, changed roles, or simply moved on. Sending them your standard five-step nurture sequence anyway is almost guaranteed to generate a click on that unsubscribe link.

MailClaw's smart sending layer is designed to address exactly this gap. Because it runs locally on your machine at localhost:3100, all of your contact data, behavioral signals, and sending logic stay in one place — no stitching together three different SaaS tools to get a coherent picture of what's actually happening with your list.

Start With Smarter Segmentation Using Contact Enrichment

The fastest way to reduce unsubscribes is to stop sending everyone the same thing. MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment engine pulls job title, company size, industry, and tech stack data directly into your contact profiles before a sequence ever fires. This means you can build segments that are actually meaningful — not just "opened last email" but "opened last email AND works at a Series B SaaS company AND uses Salesforce."

Enriching Contacts Before a Sequence Runs

From the MailClaw CLI, enriching a contact list before launching a campaign takes a single command:

mailclaw enrich --list "q4-outbound.csv" --fields title,company,industry,tech --output enriched-q4.json

Once enriched, those fields are available as dynamic variables in any sequence template and as filter criteria in the sequence builder. You can now route a DevOps engineer at a 500-person company down a completely different branch than a solo founder — with zero manual sorting on your end.

Building Segments That Reduce Noise

In the local dashboard, navigate to Contacts → Segments → New Segment and layer conditions like:

  • Industry is "Financial Services" AND Company Size is greater than 200
  • Last Engaged is within 30 days
  • Sequence Status is not "Converted"

Contacts who don't meet your engagement threshold get automatically excluded from new sequences — they won't receive another email until they re-engage, which dramatically reduces the "why are you still emailing me?" unsubscribes that tank deliverability over time.

Use AI Email Agents to Personalize at Scale

Generic personalization — inserting a first name and calling it a day — stopped working years ago. MailClaw's AI email agents, powered by OpenClaw, go several layers deeper. Instead of static templates, each agent can analyze a contact's enrichment profile, previous engagement history, and even the content of their company's website to generate a message that genuinely feels like it was written for that specific person.

Configuring an Agent for a Cold Outreach Sequence

Here's a minimal agent configuration that instructs MailClaw to generate the first email in a cold sequence with real context:

mailclaw agent create \
  --name "cold-outreach-agent" \
  --model openclaw-v2 \
  --persona "helpful SaaS consultant" \
  --context-fields "title,company,industry,pain_point" \
  --tone "professional, concise, no fluff" \
  --max-length 120

Assign this agent to any step in your sequence builder and it will dynamically generate the email body at send time — not at template creation time. That means a contact added to the list next Tuesday gets messaging that reflects their current context, not the context you imagined when you wrote the template three weeks ago.

Pro tip: Set --max-length 120 (words) deliberately. Shorter, more focused emails consistently outperform long-form cold outreach, and they leave less room for off-key sentences that make readers feel like they're reading a mail merge.

Control Frequency With Sequence-Level Send Rules

One of the most common causes of unsubscribes is pure volume — too many emails in too short a window. MailClaw's sequence builder lets you set send rules at the sequence level, the step level, and even globally across all accounts. This is particularly useful if you're running multiple campaigns simultaneously through Gmail, Outlook, and a dedicated SendGrid account at the same time.

Setting Global Frequency Caps

In your mailclaw.config.json, you can enforce a hard cap on how many times any single contact can receive an email across all active sequences:

{
  "sending": {
    "global_contact_cap": {
      "max_emails_per_contact": 2,
      "window_days": 7,
      "exclude_transactional": true
    }
  }
}

This one setting alone can cut unsubscribes significantly for teams running overlapping campaigns. A prospect in both a product launch sequence and a re-engagement drip won't receive four emails in five days — MailClaw will queue and prioritize based on sequence weight you assign, ensuring the more critical message gets through first.

Step-Level Timing Optimization

Beyond frequency caps, when you send matters. MailClaw's deliverability tools include engagement-time analysis per contact. If someone consistently opens emails on Tuesday mornings, the sequence builder will hold a queued message until that window — rather than blasting at 9am your local time and hoping for the best.

Enable this in the sequence builder UI under Step Settings → Send Timing → Optimize for Recipient, or via the CLI when creating a step:

mailclaw sequence add-step \
  --sequence-id "sq_abc123" \
  --delay "3d" \
  --timing-mode "recipient-optimized" \
  --fallback-time "10:00" \
  --fallback-tz "America/New_York"

Monitor Deliverability Before Problems Compound

High unsubscribe rates and poor deliverability feed each other in a vicious cycle. When your emails land in spam, the only people who see them are the ones hunting through their junk folder — and they're already annoyed. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring dashboard surfaces domain reputation, DKIM/SPF alignment, and bounce rates in real time across all connected accounts, whether those accounts use SMTP, Gmail OAuth, or Outlook OAuth.

Reading the Deliverability Health Panel

Open your local dashboard at http://localhost:3100 and navigate to Deliverability → Health Overview. You'll see a per-account breakdown including:

  • Spam complaint rate — anything above 0.1% is a red flag with most providers
  • Bounce rate — hard bounces above 2% will get your SendGrid or SMTP account flagged
  • DKIM/SPF/DMARC status — misconfiguration here causes silent deliverability failures that look like low engagement
  • Inbox placement estimate — derived from test sends through MailClaw's seed list integration

If complaint rates start climbing on a specific sequence, you can pause it directly from this panel with one click — no digging through campaign dashboards or logging into SendGrid separately.

Use Behavioral Branching to Exit Disengaged Contacts Early

The sequence builder supports conditional branching based on engagement behavior. Rather than letting a disengaged contact grind through all eight steps of a sequence and eventually unsubscribe, you can exit them gracefully after a defined number of non-opens — and optionally move them into a low-frequency "stay warm" sequence instead.

mailclaw sequence add-branch \
  --sequence-id "sq_abc123" \
  --after-step 3 \
  --condition "opens == 0 AND clicks == 0" \
  --action "exit_to_sequence" \
  --target-sequence-id "sq_warmkeep"

This approach is far more respectful of your contacts' inboxes than pushing forward blindly. It also protects your sender reputation — ISPs and inbox providers like Gmail and Outlook track engagement signals at the domain level. Consistently sending to people who never open hurts everyone on your list, not just your metrics.

Bringing It All Together

Reducing unsubscribe rates isn't a single tactic — it's the compound result of sending the right message, to the right person, at the right time, with the right frequency. MailClaw's smart sending stack gives you the tools to execute on all four dimensions from a single open-source platform running entirely on your local machine.

Because MailClaw is built on OpenClaw and fully open source, you can extend any part of this pipeline — custom enrichment providers, bespoke agent personas, integrations with HubSpot or Salesforce contact data — without waiting for a vendor to add the feature to their roadmap. Your sending logic, your data, your rules.

Start with enrichment and frequency caps if you're new to MailClaw — those two changes alone tend to produce measurable reductions in unsubscribe rates within the first two or three campaigns. Then layer in AI agents and behavioral branching as you get comfortable with how the system works. The goal isn't to trick people into staying subscribed — it's to make sure every email you send is actually worth receiving.

articles.title: MailClaw A/B Testing: Optimizing Email Content with AI
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's AI-powered A/B testing features to systematically optimize your email subject lines, body copy, and send timing — with real CLI examples and a step-by-step workflow you can run locally today.
articles.content:
Why A/B Testing Email Content Still Matters (And Why Most People Do It Wrong)

Most email marketers run A/B tests the same way they did a decade ago: change one subject line, wait a week, pick the winner, move on. It works, technically. But it's slow, it wastes sends on losing variants, and it rarely surfaces why something performed better — which means you can't generalize the insight to future campaigns.

MailClaw takes a different approach. Because it runs locally on your Mac and is powered by OpenClaw's AI engine, it can do the pattern recognition work for you — analyzing performance signals in real time, generating new variants based on what's working, and feeding those learnings back into your sequence builder automatically. The result is a compounding optimization loop instead of a one-off test.

This guide walks you through exactly how to set that up, from your first CLI command to interpreting results in your localhost dashboard at localhost:3100.

Setting Up Your First A/B Test in MailClaw

Step 1: Define Your Test in the Sequence Builder

Every A/B test in MailClaw lives inside a sequence. If you already have a sequence running, you can add a split variant to any step. If you're starting fresh, initialize a new sequence first:

mailclaw sequence create --name "Q3 Outbound" --account gmail-primary

Once your sequence exists, add a test to a specific step using the --split flag. The following command creates a two-variant subject line test on step one of the sequence:

mailclaw sequence step add \
  --sequence "Q3 Outbound" \
  --step 1 \
  --subject-a "Quick question about your pipeline" \
  --subject-b "Saw your post on LinkedIn — had to reach out" \
  --split 50/50 \
  --test-metric open_rate

MailClaw supports four primary test metrics: open_rate, click_rate, reply_rate, and conversion_rate. For cold outreach sequences, reply_rate is almost always the right choice. Open rate is a vanity metric in most outbound contexts — especially post-iOS 15, where Apple Mail pre-fetches pixels and inflates open counts across Gmail, Outlook, and others.

Step 2: Let AI Generate Your Variants

Here's where MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered AI agents start earning their keep. Instead of manually writing variants, you can ask the AI email agent to generate them based on your contact segment's enrichment data:

mailclaw agent run --task "generate_subject_variants" \
  --sequence "Q3 Outbound" \
  --segment "SaaS founders, Series A, 10-50 employees" \
  --tone "direct, peer-to-peer" \
  --variants 5

The agent pulls context from your enriched contact data — industry, company size, recent funding signals, job title — and generates subject lines tuned to that specific audience. You can review the output directly in the dashboard under Sequences → AI Suggestions, or pipe it to a file:

mailclaw agent run --task "generate_subject_variants" \
  --sequence "Q3 Outbound" \
  --segment "SaaS founders, Series A, 10-50 employees" \
  --tone "direct, peer-to-peer" \
  --variants 5 \
  --output variants.json

Pick your two strongest candidates and plug them back into the sequence step. This workflow typically takes under three minutes and produces significantly more targeted copy than brainstorming from scratch.

What to Test (And in What Order)

One of the most common A/B testing mistakes is testing too many things at once, or testing in a random order with no cumulative strategy. Here's a prioritized framework based on impact:

  1. Subject line — Highest leverage. Controls whether the email gets opened at all. Test this first, always.
  2. Opening line / hook — The first sentence determines whether the reader continues. Personalized openers consistently outperform generic ones.
  3. Call to action (CTA) — Soft ask vs. direct ask. "Would this be worth a 15-minute call?" vs. "Book time here: [link]" can produce dramatically different reply rates.
  4. Email length — Short (3-5 sentences) vs. medium (8-12 sentences). Shorter almost always wins in cold outreach; longer can win in nurture sequences where trust already exists.
  5. Send timing — Day of week and hour. MailClaw's deliverability tools track engagement windows per contact domain, so you can test time-based variants with actual signal rather than generic best-practice advice.

Pro tip: Don't move to the next test until you have statistical significance on the current one. MailClaw flags significance at 95% confidence by default, but you can adjust this threshold in ~/.mailclaw/config.yaml under ab_testing.confidence_threshold.

Reading Results in the Local Dashboard

Once your test is live and sends have gone out, head to localhost:3100 and navigate to Analytics → A/B Tests. You'll see a live breakdown for each variant including:

  • Send count and delivery rate per variant
  • Primary metric performance (the metric you set in --test-metric)
  • Confidence score and estimated sends-to-significance
  • AI-generated insight summarizing why the leading variant is winning based on copy analysis

That last item is particularly useful. Most A/B testing tools tell you what won. MailClaw's AI layer tries to tell you why — for example, "Variant B's subject line contains a specific social proof trigger (LinkedIn mention) that resonates with this segment's self-reported preference for peer validation." You can use that insight to inform copy across your entire campaign, not just the winning variant of this one test.

Promoting a Winner Automatically

Once MailClaw detects a statistically significant winner, it can automatically promote that variant and stop sending the loser — without you having to check in manually:

mailclaw ab promote --sequence "Q3 Outbound" --step 1 --auto --threshold 95

This is especially useful for high-volume sequences connected to SendGrid or multi-account SMTP setups where waiting costs real deliverability budget. You can also set up Slack or webhook notifications when a winner is declared:

mailclaw config set ab_testing.notify_on_winner true
mailclaw config set ab_testing.webhook_url "https://hooks.slack.com/your-webhook-url"

Integrating A/B Insights with Your CRM

If you're syncing contacts from HubSpot, Salesforce, or a CSV import, MailClaw can write A/B test outcomes back to contact records as custom properties. This lets your sales team see which message variant a prospect responded to — context that's genuinely useful when they pick up the phone.

mailclaw sync crm \
  --provider hubspot \
  --write-ab-outcomes true \
  --sequence "Q3 Outbound"

For Salesforce users, the same flag works with --provider salesforce. The sync writes the winning variant label, the metric value, and a timestamp to the contact's activity log. It's a small thing, but it closes the loop between your email performance data and your broader go-to-market intelligence.

Building a Compounding Testing System

The real power of running A/B tests through MailClaw isn't any single test — it's the institutional memory that builds up over time. Because MailClaw is open source and stores all test results locally in a SQLite database (~/.mailclaw/data/results.db), you own your data completely. Nothing is shipped to a third-party analytics platform.

You can query your historical test results directly:

mailclaw results query \
  --metric reply_rate \
  --segment "SaaS" \
  --winner-only \
  --export winning_patterns.csv

Feed that CSV back into your AI agent with a prompt like "analyze these winning email patterns and generate a best-practice style guide for this segment" — and you've got a self-improving playbook that gets smarter with every campaign you run.

Scheduling Recurring Tests

Markets change. What worked in January for enterprise IT buyers might not work in September. Set up quarterly re-tests on your best-performing sequences so your baselines stay current:

mailclaw ab schedule \
  --sequence "Q3 Outbound" \
  --interval quarterly \
  --auto-generate-variants true \
  --notify team@yourcompany.com

With --auto-generate-variants enabled, MailClaw's AI agent will draft new challengers based on recent top performers and any updated enrichment data on your contact segment — so the test runs itself, and you just review the results.

The Bottom Line

A/B testing email content isn't a one-time optimization project — it's an ongoing system. The teams that consistently outperform in email outreach aren't the ones who found the perfect subject line in 2022 and stuck with it. They're the ones who built a process for continuous experimentation and made it cheap enough to run regularly.

MailClaw's local-first architecture, OpenClaw AI layer, and tight integration between contact enrichment, sequence building, and deliverability monitoring make that kind of systematic testing genuinely accessible — without needing a data science team or an expensive SaaS contract. You run it on your Mac, you own the data, and it gets smarter every time you use it.

Start with one sequence, one step, and one subject line test. The compounding takes care of itself from there.

articles.title: How to Set Up Custom Email Tracking Domains in MailClaw
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to configure custom email tracking domains in MailClaw to boost deliverability, protect your sender reputation, and get accurate open and click data — without relying on shared tracking infrastructure.
articles.content:
Why Custom Tracking Domains Matter for Cold Email

If you're running email sequences through MailClaw and relying on default or shared tracking domains, you're leaving serious deliverability gains on the table. Shared tracking domains are used by thousands of senders simultaneously — and if even one of those senders gets flagged for spam, your emails suffer for it. Spam filters evaluate tracking links as part of their scoring, and a link pointing to a domain with a bad reputation will drag your whole campaign down.

Custom tracking domains solve this by routing all your open-tracking pixels and click-redirect links through a subdomain you control — something like track.yourdomain.com or click.yourdomain.com. This means your reputation is yours alone, your analytics stay clean, and recipients don't see generic third-party URLs in the links they hover over.

MailClaw's built-in deliverability tools make this setup straightforward, and since everything runs locally on localhost:3100, you have full visibility into how tracking is being handled without any data leaving your machine until it's time to send.

Understanding How MailClaw Handles Email Tracking

Before diving into configuration, it helps to understand what MailClaw is actually doing under the hood. When you build a sequence in the Sequence Builder and enable tracking, MailClaw — powered by the OpenClaw engine — rewrites two types of links in your outgoing emails:

  • Open tracking pixels: A 1×1 transparent image served from your tracking domain. When the recipient's email client loads the image, MailClaw registers an open event.
  • Click tracking redirects: Your original links are replaced with redirect URLs on your tracking domain. When a recipient clicks, they're redirected to the original destination and MailClaw logs the click.

All of this is managed through the local dashboard at localhost:3100. You can see exactly which contacts in your enriched contact list have opened or clicked, which sequences are performing, and how individual AI email agents are contributing to engagement — all in real time.

Step 1: Choose and Configure Your Tracking Subdomain

Start by deciding on a subdomain. Most senders use something like track.yourdomain.com, click.yourdomain.com, or em.yourdomain.com. Avoid anything that sounds suspicious to spam filters — subdomains like redirect.yourdomain.com can occasionally raise flags with more aggressive filters.

Once you've chosen your subdomain, you need to add a CNAME DNS record pointing it to MailClaw's tracking endpoint. If you're using a hosted SMTP provider like SendGrid or Mailgun for delivery, they often provide their own tracking hostnames to point to. For a fully self-managed setup, you'll point your CNAME to your own publicly accessible server or a lightweight proxy.

A typical DNS entry looks like this:

Type:  CNAME
Host:  track
Value: tracking.mailclaw-proxy.yourdomain.com
TTL:   3600

If you're running MailClaw purely locally and routing through SendGrid's SMTP, you'd use their provided CNAME target instead — usually something like sendgrid.net with a specific prefix they assign to your account.

Step 2: Add the Custom Domain in MailClaw

Open your MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to Settings → Deliverability → Tracking Domains. Click Add Custom Domain and enter your full subdomain:

track.yourdomain.com

MailClaw will prompt you to verify ownership. It does this by checking for the CNAME record you set up in the previous step. DNS propagation can take anywhere from a few minutes to 48 hours, but in practice most modern DNS providers propagate changes within 15–30 minutes.

You can also configure this via the MailClaw CLI if you prefer working from the terminal:

# Add a custom tracking domain
mailclaw domains:tracking add track.yourdomain.com

# Check verification status
mailclaw domains:tracking verify track.yourdomain.com

# List all configured tracking domains
mailclaw domains:tracking list

Once verified, you'll see a green status indicator in the dashboard. MailClaw will automatically begin using your custom domain for all new sequences assigned to that account.

Step 3: Enable SSL for Your Tracking Domain

This step is non-negotiable. Email clients and security tools have become increasingly aggressive about flagging mixed-content or insecure links. If your tracking domain serves links over HTTP instead of HTTPS, you'll see drops in deliverability and potentially broken redirects in clients like Gmail and Outlook.

If you're proxying through a provider like Cloudflare, enabling SSL is as simple as toggling "Full SSL" in your Cloudflare dashboard for the subdomain. If you're managing your own proxy server, use Certbot to provision a free Let's Encrypt certificate:

sudo certbot --nginx -d track.yourdomain.com

Once SSL is live, return to the MailClaw Tracking Domains settings and confirm the HTTPS option is selected for your domain. MailClaw will then generate all tracking links with the https:// scheme.

Step 4: Assign the Tracking Domain to Campaigns and Sequences

MailClaw supports multi-account setups, which means you might be sending from different email addresses — a Gmail account for warm outreach, an Outlook account for enterprise prospects, and a dedicated cold-outreach domain connected via SMTP or OAuth. You can assign different tracking domains to each sending account, which is excellent practice for keeping your tracking reputation segmented.

To assign a tracking domain to a specific sequence, open the sequence in the Sequence Builder, click Settings, and select your verified domain from the Tracking Domain dropdown. This overrides the account-level default for that specific sequence — useful when running A/B tests or managing campaigns for multiple clients.

Assigning via CLI

# Assign tracking domain to a specific sequence by ID
mailclaw sequences:update <sequence-id> --tracking-domain track.yourdomain.com

Step 5: Validate Tracking Is Working Correctly

Before you let your AI email agents loose on a full campaign, validate that tracking is firing correctly. MailClaw includes a built-in link tester in the deliverability panel:

  1. Go to Deliverability → Link Tester in the dashboard.
  2. Send a test email to yourself using the Send Test button in any sequence.
  3. Open the email in Gmail or Outlook, hover over a link, and confirm it shows your custom tracking domain rather than a generic third-party URL.
  4. Click the link and verify you're redirected to the correct destination.
  5. Return to the MailClaw dashboard and confirm the click event was recorded under Analytics → Events.

You can also run a quick audit from the CLI:

# Run a tracking validation check on a sequence
mailclaw sequences:validate <sequence-id> --check tracking

Common Issues and How to Fix Them

CNAME Not Resolving

Use dig or an online DNS checker to confirm your CNAME is live before attempting verification in MailClaw:

dig CNAME track.yourdomain.com +short

If it returns your expected target, the record is live. If it returns nothing, the change hasn't propagated yet or there's a typo in your DNS configuration.

Links Showing as HTTP Instead of HTTPS

Double-check that SSL is provisioned and that MailClaw's HTTPS setting is enabled for the domain in Settings → Tracking Domains. If you're using Cloudflare, make sure the SSL mode is set to "Full" and not "Flexible" — Flexible can cause redirect loops.

Open Tracking Not Firing in Outlook

Outlook, particularly in corporate environments, often blocks external images by default, which prevents open pixels from loading. This is normal behavior and not a configuration error. Focus on click tracking as a more reliable engagement signal for Outlook-heavy audiences. MailClaw's AI email agents can be configured to weight click events more heavily than opens for these segments.

Integrating with CRM and Enrichment Workflows

Once your custom tracking domain is live, the engagement data it captures becomes significantly more useful when paired with MailClaw's contact enrichment features. As contacts open and click through your sequences, MailClaw can push those events to connected CRMs like HubSpot or Salesforce, enriching contact records with behavioral data automatically.

This creates a feedback loop where your AI email agents can adapt follow-up timing and messaging based on real engagement signals — not guesswork. A contact who clicked three links in your sequence but never replied gets treated very differently from one who never opened at all, and that nuance lives entirely within your local MailClaw instance, not a third-party SaaS platform.

Pro tip: Create a separate tracking subdomain for each major campaign or client if you're managing outreach at scale. This keeps your reputation data clean and makes it trivial to identify which campaign is causing deliverability issues if something goes wrong.

Custom tracking domains are one of those foundational configurations that pay dividends across every campaign you run. Set it up once, validate it thoroughly, and MailClaw will handle the rest — giving you clean, trustworthy engagement data that actually reflects how your prospects are interacting with your emails.

articles.title: MailClaw Reporting: Creating Weekly Campaign Performance Reports
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to set up automated weekly campaign performance reports in MailClaw, from configuring your metrics dashboard to scheduling AI-generated summaries that surface actionable insights across all your email sequences.
articles.content:
Why Weekly Reporting Is the Backbone of Smarter Email Outreach

Most email marketers check their stats reactively — something tanks, they notice, they scramble. Weekly reporting flips that dynamic entirely. Instead of chasing fires, you're spotting trends before they become problems: a deliverability dip on your SendGrid account, a sequence step that's hemorrhaging opens, a contact segment that's quietly outperforming everything else.

MailClaw's local-first architecture makes this unusually powerful. Because everything runs on your machine at localhost:3100, your reporting pipeline has zero latency, no API rate limits on analytics calls, and complete data ownership. Your campaign intelligence never leaves your environment unless you explicitly push it somewhere.

This guide walks through building a weekly reporting system in MailClaw — from configuring the metrics you actually care about, to scheduling automated summaries, to using AI email agents to surface the insights buried in your numbers.

Setting Up Your Reporting Baseline

Connecting Your Sending Accounts

Before any report is meaningful, MailClaw needs a complete picture of your outreach. If you're running campaigns across multiple accounts — a Gmail workspace for warm outreach, Outlook for enterprise sequences, SendGrid for high-volume sends — make sure each account is connected through the Accounts panel in your local dashboard.

From the CLI, you can verify your connected accounts with:

mailclaw accounts list --status

You should see each account flagged with its integration type (SMTP or OAuth), its current sending health score, and any deliverability alerts. Accounts with degraded health will skew your weekly metrics, so resolve those before pulling your first report.

Defining Your Core Metrics

MailClaw tracks a wide range of signals, but for weekly reporting you want a focused scorecard. Open the Reporting tab in your dashboard and configure your primary metrics. The most actionable set for most teams is:

  • Open rate — by sequence, by account, and by contact segment
  • Click-to-open rate (CTOR) — a more honest engagement signal than raw clicks
  • Reply rate — especially for outreach sequences
  • Bounce rate — hard and soft, broken out separately
  • Unsubscribe rate — with trend comparison to prior week
  • Deliverability score — pulled from MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring

Resist the urge to track everything. A weekly report with fifteen metrics trains you to read past the important ones.

Building Your Weekly Report in MailClaw

Using the Sequence Builder for Report Segmentation

MailClaw's sequence builder isn't just for outreach — it's also how you scope your reporting. Each sequence you've built becomes a natural reporting unit. If you're running a cold outreach sequence to SaaS founders, a re-engagement sequence for dormant HubSpot contacts, and a nurture sequence for inbound leads, you want separate metric breakdowns for each.

In the dashboard, navigate to Sequences → Reports → Weekly Snapshot and select which sequences to include. You can also set this via config:

# In your mailclaw.config.yaml
reporting:
  weekly_snapshot:
    sequences:
      - saas-founders-cold-outreach
      - hubspot-dormant-reengagement
      - inbound-nurture-q3
    metrics:
      - open_rate
      - reply_rate
      - bounce_rate
      - deliverability_score
    compare_to_prior_week: true

The compare_to_prior_week: true flag is what transforms a snapshot into a trend report. Without week-over-week context, a 28% open rate is just a number. With it, you know whether you're moving in the right direction.

Scheduling Automated Report Generation

MailClaw's scheduler lets you generate and deliver reports on a cadence. The cleanest setup for weekly reporting is a Sunday evening generation, so your report is waiting for you Monday morning.

mailclaw report schedule \
  --type weekly \
  --sequences all \
  --cron "0 20 * * 0" \
  --output pdf,json \
  --deliver email:your@email.com

The --output pdf,json flag gives you both a human-readable PDF for stakeholders and a structured JSON file you can pipe into other tools — a Salesforce dashboard, a Notion database, a Slack webhook. The --deliver flag supports email addresses, webhook URLs, and local file paths.

If you'd rather generate on demand, the one-liner is:

mailclaw report generate --type weekly --format pdf

Letting AI Do the Heavy Lifting

Configuring AI Email Agents for Report Analysis

Raw metrics tell you what happened. MailClaw's AI email agents, powered by OpenClaw under the hood, tell you why — and what to do about it. You can configure an agent specifically for report analysis that reads your weekly data and generates a plain-English summary with prioritized recommendations.

Set up your analysis agent in the dashboard under Agents → New Agent → Report Analyst, or define it in your config:

agents:
  report_analyst:
    role: "Weekly campaign performance analyst"
    data_sources:
      - weekly_snapshot
      - deliverability_logs
      - contact_enrichment_history
    output:
      format: executive_summary
      max_length: 500_words
      include_recommendations: true
      priority_threshold: high

When the agent runs, it produces an output like this alongside your metrics:

"Open rates on the SaaS founders sequence dropped 6 points this week, driven primarily by Step 3 subject lines underperforming on Outlook accounts. Reply rates remain strong at 11.4%. Recommend A/B testing shorter subject lines on Step 3. Deliverability on your SendGrid account shows a mild SPF alignment warning — review DNS records before next send."

That's the difference between a report and an insight. The agent surfaces the signal without you having to dig for it.

Enriching Contact Data Before You Report

MailClaw's contact enrichment feature adds another layer of intelligence to weekly reports. When you enrich your contact list — pulling in company size, industry, job title, and intent signals — your reports can segment performance not just by sequence, but by who you're sending to.

Run enrichment on your active contacts before generating your report:

mailclaw contacts enrich --segment active --source clearbit,apollo

After enrichment, your weekly report can answer questions like: "Are enterprise contacts responding better than SMB contacts on this sequence?" or "Which industries are driving the most replies this week?" That kind of segmentation is what separates teams that iterate intelligently from teams that guess.

Reading Your Report: What to Actually Act On

Deliverability Signals Come First

Whatever else your report shows, start with deliverability. A beautiful open rate means nothing if 15% of your sends are landing in spam. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tracks inbox placement, spam complaints, bounce patterns, and authentication health (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) across every connected account.

If your report flags a deliverability warning, investigate before sending anything else that week. The dashboard's Deliverability tab gives you a per-account breakdown with specific remediation steps.

Sequence Step Dropout Is Your Biggest Lever

Your weekly report will show per-step performance within each sequence. Look for where contacts stop engaging — a sharp drop between Step 2 and Step 3 almost always means your Step 3 email isn't earning the click. This is exactly where MailClaw's sequence builder pays off: you can clone the underperforming step, edit the copy or subject line, and run it as a variant without rebuilding the whole sequence.

Reply Rate Benchmarks Worth Knowing

For cold outreach sequences, a reply rate above 8% is strong. Between 3-8% is workable. Below 3% means your targeting, messaging, or both need attention. For warm sequences to existing contacts or inbound leads, you should expect significantly higher — a nurture sequence that can't crack 15% replies is leaving opportunity on the table.

Use your weekly report's week-over-week comparison to trend these numbers, not to judge any single week in isolation.

Sharing Reports With Your Team

Because MailClaw runs locally, sharing reports means exporting them explicitly — which is actually a feature, not a limitation. You control exactly what gets shared and where. The most common patterns:

  • PDF via email — use the --deliver flag to auto-send the PDF summary to stakeholders every Monday
  • JSON to a shared dashboard — pipe your JSON output into a Notion database, a Google Sheet via Zapier, or a custom internal tool
