  • Slack summary — configure a webhook to post the AI agent's executive summary to your team's #email-performance channel
mailclaw report generate \
  --type weekly \
  --format json \
  | curl -X POST https://hooks.slack.com/services/YOUR/SLACK/WEBHOOK \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @-

Being open source, MailClaw's reporting output is fully documented — if you need a custom integration with Salesforce, HubSpot, or an internal BI tool, the data schema is right there in the MailClaw repository to build against.

Making Weekly Reporting a Habit That Compounds

The teams that get the most out of email automation aren't the ones with the most sophisticated setup — they're the ones who review their numbers consistently and act on them quickly. Weekly reporting in MailClaw is designed to lower the friction on both sides of that equation: automated generation removes the excuse not to review, and AI-powered summaries make the review fast enough to actually happen.

Start simple. Get one report running, review it for two weeks, make one change based on what you see. That loop — measure, understand, adjust — is what compounds into meaningful results over a quarter. MailClaw gives you the infrastructure. The habit is yours to build.

articles.title: How to Use MailClaw Analytics for Sales Pipeline Attribution
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to leverage MailClaw's built-in analytics to trace every closed deal back to the exact email sequence, agent action, or touchpoint that drove it — turning your local dashboard into a full-stack sales attribution engine.
articles.content:
Why Email Attribution Matters More Than You Think

Most sales teams track opens and clicks. Fewer track replies. Almost none can answer the question that actually matters: which email sequence, sent on which day, to which segment, ultimately contributed to a closed deal?

That gap between "we sent some emails" and "we closed $40k this quarter" is where pipeline attribution lives — and it's where most outreach tools quietly give up. MailClaw's analytics layer, powered by OpenClaw's event tracking engine, is built specifically to close that gap. Because everything runs locally on localhost:3100, you own every event, every timestamp, and every attribution path. Nothing is abstracted away behind a SaaS pricing tier.

This guide walks you through setting up attribution tracking in MailClaw, connecting it to your CRM, and reading the data in a way that actually informs sales decisions.

Understanding MailClaw's Attribution Model

Before touching the dashboard, it helps to understand how MailClaw thinks about attribution. The system uses a multi-touch weighted model by default, which means credit for a conversion is distributed across all meaningful touchpoints in a sequence — not just the first or last email.

Each tracked event falls into one of three categories:

  • Engagement events — opens, clicks, link hovers, reply detection
  • Sequence events — step completions, branch triggers, AI agent actions taken on behalf of a contact
  • Outcome events — CRM stage changes, deal created webhooks, manual conversion flags

When you connect MailClaw to HubSpot or Salesforce (more on that shortly), outcome events are pulled in automatically and stitched to the engagement history already living in your local database. The result is a complete picture: contact enriched → sequence enrolled → reply detected → deal created → closed won.

Setting Up Conversion Tracking

Step 1: Enable Analytics in Your MailClaw Config

Out of the box, MailClaw tracks engagement events. To enable full pipeline attribution, you need to turn on outcome tracking in your config file:

# ~/.mailclaw/config.yaml

analytics:
  enabled: true
  attribution_model: multi_touch   # options: first_touch, last_touch, multi_touch, linear
  conversion_window_days: 30
  track_crm_outcomes: true
  crm_provider: hubspot            # or: salesforce, pipedrive, none

Restart the MailClaw server after saving:

mailclaw restart --reload-config

You should see confirmation in your terminal that analytics is running with the new model, and the Analytics tab in your dashboard at localhost:3100/analytics will now show a Pipeline Attribution section.

Step 2: Connect Your CRM

MailClaw supports native webhook listeners for HubSpot and Salesforce, and a generic webhook endpoint for any other tool (Pipedrive, Close, Attio, etc.).

For HubSpot, run the built-in OAuth setup wizard:

mailclaw integrations connect hubspot

This opens a browser window, walks you through the OAuth flow, and registers a deal stage webhook that fires whenever a contact moves to a new pipeline stage. MailClaw automatically matches incoming HubSpot contact IDs to enriched contacts in your local database using email address as the join key.

For Salesforce, the flow is similar:

mailclaw integrations connect salesforce --instance-url https://yourorg.my.salesforce.com

Once connected, you can verify the integration is receiving events:

mailclaw integrations status
# Output:
# ✔ HubSpot       connected  (last event: 4 minutes ago)
# ✔ SendGrid      connected  (last event: 12 seconds ago)
# ✗ Salesforce    not connected

Step 3: Tag Your Sequences with Campaign Metadata

Attribution is only as good as your tagging. Every sequence you build in MailClaw's sequence builder should include campaign metadata so you can slice results later by campaign, persona, or channel.

mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "Q3 SaaS Founders Outreach" \
  --campaign "q3-2025-saas" \
  --persona "founder-smb" \
  --channel "cold-outbound"

These tags become filterable dimensions in the analytics dashboard. Without them, you're left with aggregate numbers that can't tell you which campaign drove pipeline — only that pipeline exists.

Reading the Analytics Dashboard

The Pipeline Attribution View

Navigate to localhost:3100/analytics/attribution. The default view shows a waterfall chart breaking down pipeline value by sequence, with each bar segmented by attribution weight across touchpoints.

The columns you care most about in the underlying table:

  • First Touch Sequence — the sequence that first engaged the contact
  • Conversion Sequence — the sequence active when the deal was created
  • Weighted Pipeline Value — deal value multiplied by this sequence's attribution share
  • Reply-to-Meeting Rate — what percentage of replies from this sequence resulted in a meeting booked
  • Days to Opportunity — average time from sequence enrollment to deal creation

Pro tip: Sort by Weighted Pipeline Value descending, then filter to sequences with at least 50 contacts enrolled. This removes statistical noise and shows you what's actually working at scale.

AI Agent Attribution

If you're using MailClaw's AI email agents to handle follow-up replies, personalize sequences on the fly, or re-engage dormant contacts, those actions are tracked as first-class attribution events. In the dashboard, you'll see an Agent Actions column that credits the specific AI-generated touchpoint.

This matters because in many campaigns, an AI agent's personalized re-engagement email — sent three days after a contact went cold — ends up being the touchpoint that turns a dead lead into a booked call. Without agent-level attribution, that win gets misattributed to the original sequence, and you never learn that your re-engagement logic is your strongest asset.

Deliverability's Impact on Attribution

MailClaw's deliverability monitoring feeds directly into attribution accuracy. If a sequence shows low pipeline contribution but high enrollment numbers, the first thing to check is deliverability: are those emails actually landing in inboxes?

Run a deliverability audit scoped to a specific campaign:

mailclaw deliverability audit --campaign "q3-2025-saas" --output table

This checks DKIM/DMARC alignment, inbox placement rates across Gmail and Outlook (using seed testing), bounce rates, and spam trap hits. Poor deliverability silently poisons your attribution data by making low-performing sequences look like they have no impact — when really, the emails just never arrived.

Building Attribution Reports for Your Team

Exporting Data

MailClaw can export attribution reports in CSV, JSON, or as a live-updating HTML report you can share with stakeholders who don't have access to your local instance:

mailclaw analytics export \
  --type attribution \
  --format csv \
  --date-range 2025-01-01:2025-03-31 \
  --output ./reports/q1-attribution.csv

The CSV includes one row per contact-sequence combination, with full event history, attribution weights, and CRM outcome data. Drop it into a Google Sheet or import it into your BI tool of choice.

Setting Up Automated Weekly Reports

You can schedule attribution digests to be emailed to your team using MailClaw's built-in scheduler. This uses whatever SMTP account or OAuth connection you've already set up — Gmail, Outlook, SendGrid, whatever you prefer:

mailclaw report schedule \
  --type attribution-digest \
  --frequency weekly \
  --day monday \
  --time 08:00 \
  --recipients sales@yourcompany.com,ceo@yourcompany.com \
  --smtp-account work-gmail

Every Monday morning, your team gets a clean summary of which sequences drove pipeline last week, which AI agent actions had the highest conversion correlation, and which campaigns need attention — without anyone having to log into a dashboard.

Common Attribution Mistakes to Avoid

Even with good tooling, attribution analysis goes wrong in predictable ways. Watch out for these:

  • Ignoring the conversion window. If your sales cycle is 60 days but your conversion window is set to 30, deals will appear unattributed. Match your window to your actual cycle length.
  • Attributing to sending account, not sequence. If you use multi-account support to warm up domains, make sure you're filtering attribution by sequence, not sending account — otherwise account rotation skews your results.
  • Not enriching contacts before analyzing. MailClaw's contact enrichment fills in firmographic data (industry, company size, tech stack) that unlocks segmentation. Without it, you can see that a sequence works, but not for whom it works.
  • Treating last-touch as ground truth. The last email before a deal is created is rarely the reason the deal was created. Stick with multi-touch or linear attribution unless you have a specific reason to do otherwise.

Putting It All Together

Pipeline attribution isn't a reporting exercise — it's a feedback loop. The goal is to run a sequence, measure its actual contribution to revenue, learn which steps and agent behaviors correlate with closed deals, and use that to build better sequences next time.

Because MailClaw runs locally and is fully open source, you're not fighting with a vendor's data model or waiting for a product team to ship the feature you need. If you want to extend the attribution logic — custom models, new event types, deeper CRM integrations — the codebase is there to fork and modify.

Start with the basics: enable multi-touch attribution, connect your CRM, tag your sequences, and spend 15 minutes each week in the attribution view. Within a quarter, you'll have enough data to make confident, evidence-based decisions about where your outreach budget and attention should go.

That's the difference between sending emails and running a sales engine.

articles.title: MailClaw Domain Health Monitor: Keeping Your Sending Reputation Clean
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how MailClaw's Domain Health Monitor helps you track SPF, DKIM, DMARC, blacklist status, and sender reputation so your cold outreach actually lands in the inbox — not the spam folder.
articles.content:
Why Domain Health Is the Foundation of Email Deliverability

You can write the most compelling cold email sequence in the world, enrich your contacts with perfect firmographic data, and build a beautifully timed multi-step campaign — and still watch your open rates crater. Nine times out of ten, the culprit isn't your copy. It's your domain health.

Inbox providers like Gmail, Outlook, and Yahoo Mail make millisecond decisions about where your email goes based on a complex cocktail of signals: DNS record integrity, sending IP reputation, historical bounce rates, spam trap hits, and domain age. If any of those signals look off, your message gets quietly rerouted to spam — or rejected outright — before a human ever sees it.

MailClaw's built-in Domain Health Monitor gives you a real-time, consolidated view of everything that affects your sending reputation, surfaced directly in your local dashboard at localhost:3100. No third-party dashboards to juggle, no manual DNS lookups, no waiting for bounce reports to tell you something already went wrong.

The Core Signals MailClaw Monitors

SPF, DKIM, and DMARC Validation

These three DNS records form the trust triangle of modern email authentication. MailClaw continuously validates all three for every sending domain you've connected — whether that's through a Gmail OAuth integration, an Outlook account, or a raw SMTP connection via SendGrid, Mailgun, or Postmark.

  • SPF (Sender Policy Framework) — Declares which mail servers are authorized to send on behalf of your domain. A missing or misconfigured SPF record is one of the fastest ways to trigger spam filters.
  • DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) — Adds a cryptographic signature to your outgoing mail so receiving servers can verify the message hasn't been tampered with in transit.
  • DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting & Conformance) — Tells receiving servers what to do when SPF or DKIM checks fail, and routes aggregate reports back to you so you can spot spoofing attempts early.

To check your current authentication setup from the MailClaw CLI, run:

mailclaw domain:check --domain yourdomain.com --verbose

The --verbose flag outputs the full parsed SPF record, DKIM selector status, and DMARC policy in a readable format. If anything is misconfigured, MailClaw will surface a specific remediation suggestion — not just a generic "DKIM failed" error.

Blacklist Monitoring Across Major RBLs

Real-time blacklists (RBLs) are databases maintained by organizations like Spamhaus, Barracuda, and SURBL that track domains and IPs known to send spam. Getting listed on even one major RBL can halve your deliverability overnight.

MailClaw checks your sending domains and associated IPs against over 50 RBL providers on a configurable schedule. You can set check frequency per domain:

mailclaw domain:monitor --domain yourdomain.com --interval 6h --alert email

When a blacklist hit is detected, MailClaw pauses any active sequences using that domain and fires an alert — so you're not burning through your contact list while the problem exists. This automatic circuit-breaker behavior is one of the most practically valuable features for anyone running multi-account outreach at scale.

Bounce Rate and Complaint Tracking

High hard bounce rates signal to mailbox providers that you're sending to stale or purchased lists — a serious reputation red flag. MailClaw tracks bounce rates per domain across all your campaigns and surfaces a rolling 30-day trend in the dashboard.

Industry best practice: Keep hard bounce rates below 2% and spam complaint rates below 0.1%. Exceed those thresholds consistently and you risk getting throttled or blocked by Gmail's Postmaster Tools feedback loop.

If MailClaw's contact enrichment layer detects a contact's email address has a low confidence score or shows signs of being a role address (like info@ or admin@), it will flag it before your sequence even begins — reducing the chance of a bounce before it happens.

Setting Up the Domain Health Dashboard

Adding Your Sending Domains

Once MailClaw is running locally, navigate to localhost:3100/domains and click Add Domain. You can connect domains in three ways:

  1. OAuth (Gmail / Outlook) — Authorize via Google or Microsoft OAuth and MailClaw automatically pulls your verified sending domain and maps it to your account.
  2. SMTP Credentials — Paste your SMTP host, port, username, and password. MailClaw will resolve the sending domain automatically and begin monitoring.
  3. API Integration — If you're routing through SendGrid or Mailgun, connect via API key. MailClaw will pull event webhooks (bounces, complaints, opens) directly from those platforms into its unified health view.

Configuring Alerts and Thresholds

MailClaw's alert system is fully configurable through the mailclaw.config.json file in your project root. Here's an example configuration for a domain health alert profile:

{
  "domainHealth": {
    "bounceRateThreshold": 0.02,
    "complaintRateThreshold": 0.001,
    "blacklistCheckInterval": "6h",
    "alertChannels": ["email", "webhook"],
    "webhookUrl": "https://hooks.slack.com/services/YOUR/SLACK/WEBHOOK",
    "pauseSequencesOnAlert": true,
    "domains": [
      {
        "domain": "yourdomain.com",
        "dkimSelector": "mailclaw1"
      }
    ]
  }
}

The pauseSequencesOnAlert flag is particularly important — it automatically halts any sequence steps scheduled to send from a flagged domain until you manually review and clear the alert. This prevents you from compounding a deliverability problem while you're asleep or focused on other work.

Using AI Email Agents to Protect Reputation Proactively

MailClaw's AI email agents, powered by OpenClaw, don't just send emails — they actively participate in deliverability management. You can configure an agent to act as a deliverability watchdog with a prompt like:

mailclaw agent:create --name "DeliverabilityGuard" \
  --role "Monitor domain health metrics and recommend sequence adjustments when reputation signals degrade" \
  --trigger "domain_health_alert"

This agent will analyze the health data in context — cross-referencing bounce spikes with the specific sequences and contact segments that triggered them — and surface recommendations like "Consider warming up a secondary domain for outreach to this industry segment" or "Three contacts in this sequence have invalid MX records — remove before next send."

For teams that have CRM integrations set up with HubSpot or Salesforce, the agent can also push domain health notes back to deal records, giving sales reps visibility into whether an email thread may have been affected by a deliverability issue.

Domain Warming: The Proactive Side of Reputation Management

Why New Domains Need a Warm-Up Period

If you're launching outreach from a fresh domain — a common strategy for protecting your primary brand domain — you can't simply blast 500 emails on day one. Mailbox providers expect a gradual ramp-up that mirrors organic human behavior.

MailClaw's sequence builder includes a native warm-up mode. When you create a new sequence and assign a fresh domain, enable warm-up mode:

mailclaw sequence:create --name "Q3 Outreach" \
  --domain newdomain.com \
  --warmup true \
  --warmup-days 21 \
  --start-volume 10

This automatically calculates a daily sending ramp — starting at 10 emails per day and doubling approximately every 3–4 days until you hit your target volume — while the Domain Health Monitor watches reputation signals in real time and adjusts the pace if anything looks concerning.

Mixing Warm and Cold Traffic

A useful tactic during warm-up is to mix your outreach emails with a small percentage of internal or already-engaged contacts who are likely to open and reply. MailClaw's contact enrichment layer can tag contacts by engagement history, making it easy to build a warm-up segment:

mailclaw contacts:filter --tag "high-engagement" --export warmup-seed.csv

Add this segment to the front of your warm-up sequence so early sends go to receptive recipients — building a positive engagement history for your new domain before you start hitting cold prospects.

Reading Your Domain Health Score

The Domain Health dashboard at localhost:3100/domains distills all monitored signals into a single 0–100 health score per domain. Here's how to interpret it:

  • 90–100 (Green) — All authentication records valid, no blacklist hits, bounce and complaint rates within safe thresholds. Full send recommended.
  • 70–89 (Yellow) — One or more minor issues detected. Review the flagged items before running large campaigns. Sequences continue but with a warning banner.
  • 50–69 (Orange) — Significant issues present. MailClaw will throttle sequence volume automatically and recommend pausing new campaigns until resolved.
  • Below 50 (Red) — Critical issues. Active sequences are paused automatically. Immediate remediation required.

Because MailClaw runs entirely on your local machine and is open source, you have full visibility into exactly how that score is calculated — no black-box algorithms, no vendor lock-in. You can inspect the scoring logic, adjust weightings for your specific use case, and even contribute improvements back to the OpenClaw ecosystem.

The Bottom Line

Deliverability isn't a one-time setup task — it's an ongoing operational discipline. The best sequence in your history means nothing if it lands in spam. MailClaw's Domain Health Monitor treats reputation management as a first-class feature, not an afterthought, giving you the real-time visibility and automated safeguards you need to run outreach at scale without quietly burning your sending infrastructure.

Keep your domains clean, your sequences smart, and your agents watching — and your emails will actually get read.

articles.title: How to Diagnose and Fix Email Deliverability Issues with MailClaw
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how to diagnose and fix email deliverability issues using MailClaw's built-in monitoring tools, AI agents, and step-by-step troubleshooting techniques that keep your outreach landing in the inbox — not the spam folder.
articles.content:
Why Deliverability Is the Silent Killer of Email Campaigns

You've written a great sequence. Your subject lines are sharp. Your contacts are enriched, your timing is dialed in. But your open rates are sitting at 4%, replies are nonexistent, and you're starting to wonder if anyone is actually receiving your emails at all.

The answer might be: they're not.

Email deliverability is one of the most misunderstood and underdiagnosed problems in outreach. Most senders only notice it when it's already catastrophic — when a domain gets blacklisted or a Gmail account hits a sending wall. The good news is that with the right tooling and a systematic approach, deliverability issues are almost always diagnosable and fixable. This guide walks you through exactly how to do that using MailClaw's local dashboard, built-in monitoring tools, and AI-assisted analysis.

Understanding the Deliverability Stack

Before you can fix a problem, you need to understand what controls whether an email lands in the inbox. Deliverability is governed by three interacting layers:

  • Authentication — SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records prove to receiving mail servers that you're a legitimate sender.
  • Reputation — Your sending domain and IP have a score based on historical behavior, bounce rates, spam complaints, and engagement.
  • Content & Engagement — Spam filters analyze your email content, link patterns, and whether recipients actually open and reply.

A failure in any one of these layers can tank your campaign. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring surface tracks all three from the same local dashboard at localhost:3100, so you don't have to jump between tools to get a full picture.

Step 1: Run a Deliverability Audit from the Dashboard

Open your MailClaw dashboard and navigate to Deliverability → Health Check. This view gives you a per-account breakdown of your authentication setup, recent bounce rates, spam complaint signals, and inbox placement estimates.

If you prefer the CLI, you can pull a quick audit from your terminal:

mailclaw deliverability audit --account work@yourdomain.com

This command runs a full check against your connected sending accounts — whether that's a Gmail OAuth connection, an Outlook integration, or a custom SMTP provider like SendGrid or Postmark — and outputs a structured report:

✔ SPF record found and valid
✔ DKIM signing active (selector: mailclaw._domainkey)
⚠ DMARC policy set to p=none — consider upgrading to p=quarantine
✘ Domain found on 1 blocklist: spamhaus.org/zen
→ Bounce rate (last 7 days): 6.2% — exceeds recommended threshold of 2%
→ Spam complaint rate: 0.4% — exceeds Google's 0.1% threshold

Each flagged item links to a remediation guide directly within the dashboard. Let's work through the most common issues you'll encounter.

Fixing Authentication Failures

SPF, DKIM, and DMARC

If MailClaw flags missing or misconfigured authentication records, this is your first fix. Authentication failures are the fastest path to the spam folder — receiving servers like Gmail and Outlook will quietly deprioritize or reject unauthenticated mail.

For SPF, your DNS record should include all services you send from. If you're routing through SendGrid alongside MailClaw's SMTP, your record might look like:

v=spf1 include:sendgrid.net include:_spf.mailclaw.io ~all

DKIM requires generating a public/private key pair and publishing the public key as a DNS TXT record. MailClaw can generate and manage DKIM keys for your configured sending accounts:

mailclaw dkim generate --domain yourdomain.com --selector mailclaw
mailclaw dkim publish --domain yourdomain.com

For DMARC, start with a monitoring-only policy and tighten it once you've confirmed all legitimate sending sources are properly authenticated:

v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourdomain.com; ruf=mailto:dmarc-failures@yourdomain.com; fo=1

Once you're confident, move to p=quarantine or p=reject. MailClaw's DMARC report parser (under Deliverability → DMARC Reports) will automatically ingest and summarize your aggregate reports so you can monitor compliance over time without manually parsing XML files.

Diagnosing and Reducing Bounce Rates

A bounce rate above 2% is a red flag for most mail providers. High bounces signal to receiving servers that your list hygiene is poor, which degrades your sender reputation over time.

Using Contact Enrichment to Clean Your List

One of the most effective ways to reduce bounces before they happen is to validate and enrich your contacts before you send. MailClaw's contact enrichment layer, powered by OpenClaw, cross-references contact data against multiple sources to verify email validity and surface additional context — company size, role, LinkedIn data — that helps you personalize outreach as well.

mailclaw enrich --list prospects.csv --validate-emails --output enriched_prospects.csv

This removes role-based addresses (like info@ or support@), catch-all addresses that inflate your list, and hard-bounce-prone domains. Piping this step into your sequence builder workflow means you're only sending to contacts with a high deliverability confidence score.

Handling Bounces Automatically

MailClaw automatically processes bounce signals from connected accounts and suppresses hard-bounced contacts from future sends. You can review and export your suppression list at any time:

mailclaw bounces list --type hard --since 30d
mailclaw bounces export --output suppressed_contacts.csv

If you're syncing contacts with HubSpot or Salesforce, MailClaw's CRM integrations will push bounce status back to contact records, keeping your CRM clean without any manual work.

Dealing with Blacklisting

Finding your domain on a blocklist like Spamhaus or Barracuda is alarming but usually fixable. MailClaw's deliverability monitor checks your sending domains and IPs against major blocklist databases on a rolling basis and alerts you the moment something changes.

If you're blacklisted, the remediation process typically follows this order:

  1. Identify the cause — Was it a spike in complaints? A compromised account? A bad contact list? MailClaw's sending history view lets you trace exactly which campaign triggered the issue.
  2. Pause affected campaigns — Use the sequence builder to pause any active sends from the flagged account immediately.
  3. Submit a removal request — Most blocklists have a self-service removal form. MailClaw surfaces direct links to removal pages for each detected blocklist in the audit report.
  4. Warm up the domain again — After removal, use MailClaw's sending warmup scheduler to gradually ramp volume back up rather than resuming at full speed.
mailclaw warmup start --account work@yourdomain.com --days 14 --target-volume 200

Using AI Email Agents to Monitor and Adapt

One of MailClaw's most powerful — and underused — features for deliverability is its AI email agents. You can configure an agent to monitor deliverability signals across your active campaigns and automatically adjust sending behavior in response to early warning signs.

For example, you can set up an agent that watches for engagement drop-off patterns, rising bounce rates, or spam complaint spikes and pauses or throttles sequences before they cause lasting damage to your sender reputation:

mailclaw agent create \
  --name "Deliverability Watchdog" \
  --trigger "bounce_rate > 2% OR complaint_rate > 0.08%" \
  --action "pause_sequence AND notify slack:#email-ops"

This kind of proactive monitoring is what separates teams with consistently healthy deliverability from teams that only find out about problems after the damage is done.

Content and Sending Patterns That Hurt Deliverability

Even with clean authentication and a healthy list, certain content and sending behaviors will trigger spam filters. A few patterns to audit:

  • Link-heavy emails — Emails with more than 2–3 links, especially to redirects or URL shorteners, are flagged aggressively by Gmail and Outlook filters.
  • Image-to-text ratio — Purely image-based emails or emails where most content is embedded in images score poorly with spam filters.
  • Sending velocity spikes — Jumping from 50 emails/day to 500 without a warmup curve is a major reputation risk.
  • Generic subject lines — Patterns like "Quick question" or "Following up" are now overused enough that filters recognize them as low-quality sequences.

MailClaw's sequence builder includes a pre-send content score that runs your email copy through a deliverability heuristic before you launch a campaign. It won't catch everything, but it surfaces the most common red flags before they cost you.

Building a Deliverability-First Culture

The best deliverability strategy is a preventive one. Teams that maintain excellent inbox placement share a few common habits: they validate lists before every import, they never skip authentication setup on new domains, they monitor bounce and complaint rates weekly rather than monthly, and they treat their sender reputation like the asset it is.

Because MailClaw runs locally and is open source, you have full visibility into exactly what's being sent, from which accounts, and with what results. There's no black box, no vendor lock-in, and no mysterious "platform sending infrastructure" you can't inspect. That transparency is genuinely valuable when you're trying to debug a deliverability problem — you can trace the full path from sequence trigger to SMTP handshake to bounce signal, all from localhost:3100.

Deliverability isn't a one-time fix — it's an ongoing discipline. The teams with the best inbox placement rates aren't doing anything magical. They're just consistent about the basics, and they have tooling that makes it easy to catch problems early.

If you haven't already, run mailclaw deliverability audit against your active sending accounts today. You might be surprised what you find — and how quickly you can fix it.

articles.title: Using MailClaw to Calculate Customer Lifetime Value from Email
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to use MailClaw's AI email agents, contact enrichment, and sequence builder to calculate and act on customer lifetime value — turning your email data into a powerful revenue intelligence engine.
articles.content:
Why Customer Lifetime Value Starts in Your Inbox

Most teams think of email as a delivery mechanism — you send a campaign, you watch the open rate, you move on. But your email data is quietly accumulating one of the richest behavioral datasets you own. Every open, click, reply, and sequence completion is a signal about how a customer engages with your brand over time. When you connect those signals to purchase data and contact attributes, you get something genuinely powerful: a ground-level view of customer lifetime value (CLV) that you built yourself, without paying for another SaaS platform.

MailClaw — running locally on localhost:3100 — gives you the tooling to close this loop. Because it's open source and built on OpenClaw, you're not locked into a vendor's definition of "engagement." You own the data, the logic, and the enrichment pipeline. This guide walks through a practical approach to calculating CLV from email behavior using MailClaw's core features.

The CLV Formula (and Where Email Fits)

Customer lifetime value at its most straightforward is:

CLV = Average Order Value × Purchase Frequency × Customer Lifespan

Simple enough. The challenge is always sourcing the inputs. Average order value lives in your CRM or payment processor. Purchase frequency requires transaction history. Customer lifespan is often a guess. But email engagement adds a fourth variable that most teams ignore: behavioral propensity — how likely a customer is to keep engaging, and therefore keep buying.

A customer who opens every email, clicks through on product announcements, and consistently replies to nurture sequences has a fundamentally different CLV trajectory than someone who went cold after their second purchase. MailClaw lets you capture and act on that distinction.

Setting Up Your Contact Enrichment Pipeline

Before you can calculate anything, you need clean, enriched contact data. MailClaw's contact enrichment feature pulls in attributes from connected sources and appends them to your contact profiles automatically.

Connecting Your Data Sources

From your local dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to Contacts → Enrichment Sources. MailClaw supports direct integrations with HubSpot, Salesforce, and CSV imports from tools like Stripe or Shopify. For teams using Gmail or Outlook, the OAuth integration means your reply history is already being tracked — no extra setup needed.

A solid CLV enrichment profile should include:

  • Total purchases and average order value (from your CRM or payment processor)
  • First purchase date and most recent purchase date
  • Email engagement score — MailClaw calculates this automatically from opens, clicks, and replies across sequences
  • Sequence completion rate — what percentage of your nurture emails did they actually engage with?
  • Churn signals — how many re-engagement campaigns have they needed?

Once enrichment is running, every contact record becomes a living document. MailClaw's AI enrichment agent can also infer company size, industry, and job role from email domain patterns and public data, which is especially useful for B2B CLV modeling.

Building a CLV Scoring Sequence

Here's where MailClaw's sequence builder earns its keep. Rather than building CLV as a one-time calculation, you treat it as an ongoing score that updates based on email behavior. The sequence builder lets you define trigger conditions that move contacts between segments as their engagement changes.

Creating Behavioral Segments

Start by defining three baseline CLV tiers in your dashboard:

  1. High-value (Champions): Multiple purchases, high email engagement, short time between opens and clicks
  2. Mid-value (Growth candidates): 1–2 purchases, moderate engagement, occasional sequence drop-off
  3. At-risk: Purchased once, declining email engagement, triggered re-engagement sequences without conversion

In MailClaw's sequence builder, you can configure these as dynamic segments with conditions like:

# Example segment rule in MailClaw config
segment: "high_value_champions"
conditions:
  - field: "purchase_count"
    operator: "gte"
    value: 3
  - field: "email_engagement_score"
    operator: "gte"
    value: 75
  - field: "last_purchase_days_ago"
    operator: "lte"
    value: 90

These segments update automatically as contact data changes — so when a mid-value customer makes their third purchase and their engagement score crosses your threshold, they graduate to Champions without any manual work.

Running the CLV Calculation Agent

MailClaw's AI email agents aren't just for writing copy — they can be configured to run analytical tasks on your contact database. Using the OpenClaw agent framework, you can deploy a CLV calculation agent that runs on a schedule:

mailclaw agent run --task clv_score \
  --contacts all \
  --inputs purchase_history,engagement_score,sequence_completions \
  --output contact_field:clv_estimate \
  --schedule "0 8 * * 1"

This command runs every Monday at 8am, pulls the relevant fields for each contact, calculates a weighted CLV estimate, and writes it back to the contact record. You can view the updated scores in your local dashboard under Contacts → Custom Fields.

The weighting logic is configurable. By default, MailClaw applies a heavier weight to recency (last purchase and last email engagement) than frequency, following the well-established RFM model. You can adjust these weights in ~/.mailclaw/config/clv_weights.yaml:

clv_weights:
  recency: 0.40
  frequency: 0.35
  monetary: 0.25
  engagement_modifier: 1.2  # multiplier for high email engagement

Using CLV Data to Drive Smarter Outreach

Calculating CLV is only half the job. The payoff is using it to send the right message to the right person at the right moment.

Tailoring Sequences by CLV Tier

In your MailClaw sequence builder, create parallel sequence tracks for each CLV segment. Champions should receive early access offers, referral program invitations, and high-touch check-ins — not the same re-engagement drip you'd send to at-risk contacts.

A practical approach that works well:

  • Champions: 3-step VIP sequence — exclusive offer, loyalty reward, feedback request
  • Growth candidates: 5-step value nurture — educational content, case study, product highlight, testimonial, soft CTA
  • At-risk: 4-step re-engagement — "we miss you" hook, value reminder, objection-handling, final offer with deadline

Because MailClaw supports multi-account sending across Gmail, Outlook, and SMTP providers like SendGrid or Postmark, you can also route high-CLV contacts through your primary domain and at-risk contacts through a warmed secondary domain — protecting deliverability for your most valuable relationships.

Monitoring Deliverability by Segment

This is a nuance that most teams miss: your deliverability health is not uniform across your list. High-engagement contacts (your Champions) actually improve your sender reputation. At-risk contacts with low engagement can hurt it.

MailClaw's deliverability monitoring panel — accessible at localhost:3100/deliverability — breaks down bounce rates, spam complaints, and engagement metrics by segment. If your at-risk segment is generating disproportionate complaints, you can throttle that track's send volume or pause it entirely while you refine the messaging.

Protecting your sender reputation for high-CLV contacts is itself a CLV strategy. An email that doesn't reach the inbox generates zero revenue.

Connecting CLV Scores Back to Your CRM

Once MailClaw has calculated and enriched your CLV scores, you'll want to push them back to wherever your sales or customer success team works. MailClaw's export and webhook features make this straightforward.

For HubSpot or Salesforce users, the native sync pushes updated contact fields on a configurable interval:

mailclaw sync --destination hubspot \
  --fields clv_estimate,clv_tier,email_engagement_score \
  --filter "clv_estimate_updated_after:7d"

This means your sales team can sort their pipeline by CLV estimate, prioritize outreach to high-value accounts, and see the email engagement context that drove the score — all without leaving their CRM.

Making CLV a Living Metric, Not a Spreadsheet

The biggest mistake teams make with CLV is treating it as a quarterly calculation in a spreadsheet. Customer behavior changes week to week, and your outreach strategy should change with it. MailClaw's combination of automated enrichment, AI scoring agents, dynamic segments, and real-time deliverability monitoring gives you the infrastructure to make CLV a living, breathing part of your email program.

Because everything runs locally on your machine and the codebase is fully open source, you're not dependent on a vendor's roadmap or pricing tier to access the features that matter. You can extend the CLV agent, customize the weighting logic, or build entirely new scoring models — and run them all from a single command.

Start with a clean enrichment pass on your existing contacts, configure your three CLV segments, and let the Monday morning agent run for four weeks. By the end of the month, you'll have a data-driven view of who your best customers actually are — and a sequence strategy calibrated to keep them that way.

articles.title: How to Set Up Real-Time Email Analytics Alerts in MailClaw
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to configure real-time email analytics alerts in MailClaw so you can catch deliverability issues, track engagement spikes, and keep your outreach campaigns running at peak performance — all from your local dashboard.
articles.content:
Why Real-Time Alerts Change the Way You Run Email Campaigns

Most email marketers live in a reactive loop: send a campaign, wait a few days, check the numbers, wonder why open rates dropped. By then, the damage is done — a broken sequence has been running cold, a spam complaint threshold was crossed hours ago, or a key prospect bounced without anyone noticing.

MailClaw flips that dynamic. Because it runs entirely on your local machine at localhost:3100, every metric — opens, clicks, bounces, replies, spam complaints — flows through a single pipeline you control. Real-time alerts let you tap into that pipeline and get notified the moment something meaningful happens, without relying on a third-party dashboard you have to log into separately.

This guide walks you through configuring those alerts step by step, from the basics to more advanced threshold logic powered by MailClaw's AI email agents.

Understanding MailClaw's Analytics Event System

Before configuring alerts, it helps to understand how MailClaw tracks events under the hood. Every email sent through MailClaw — whether via Gmail OAuth, Outlook SMTP, or a transactional provider like SendGrid — generates a structured event object when something happens to it.

These events are stored locally in MailClaw's event log and exposed through both the dashboard and the CLI. The core event types you'll be working with include:

  • open — a tracked pixel was loaded
  • click — a tracked link was followed
  • reply — an inbound reply was detected via inbox polling
  • bounce_hard — permanent delivery failure
  • bounce_soft — temporary delivery failure
  • spam_complaint — the recipient marked your message as spam
  • unsubscribe — an unsubscribe link was triggered
  • sequence_completed — a contact finished an entire email sequence

Each of these can be used as an alert trigger. The power comes from combining event types with conditions — for example, alerting only when bounce rate on a specific sequence crosses 3%, not on every individual bounce.

Setting Up Your First Alert from the Dashboard

Open your MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100 and navigate to Analytics → Alert Rules. You'll see an empty rules list on a fresh install. Click New Alert Rule to open the alert builder.

Step 1: Choose Your Trigger Event

Select the event type from the dropdown. For a first alert, spam_complaint is the most critical — even a single complaint can damage your sender reputation, so you want immediate notice.

Step 2: Set Your Condition

Conditions let you add logic before the alert fires. Options include:

  • Any occurrence — fires on the first matching event (recommended for spam complaints)
  • Count threshold — fires when X events occur within a time window
  • Rate threshold — fires when the event rate (e.g., bounce rate) exceeds a percentage
  • Sequence-scoped — limits the alert to events within a specific sequence or campaign

For a bounce rate alert, set the condition to Rate threshold > 3% over a rolling 1-hour window, scoped to whichever sequence you're actively running.

Step 3: Configure Your Notification Channel

MailClaw supports four notification channels out of the box:

  1. Desktop notification — a native macOS notification via the MailClaw menu bar agent
  2. Email — sends an alert digest to an address you specify (useful if you're away from your machine)
  3. Webhook — posts a JSON payload to any URL, which enables Slack, Discord, HubSpot, or custom integrations
  4. Log file — writes alert events to a local log, great for auditing or piping into other tools

For most users, combining a desktop notification with a webhook to Slack covers the main use cases. We'll set up the webhook next.

Configuring Webhook Alerts for Slack and Other Tools

Webhooks are the most flexible alert channel in MailClaw. Once a webhook fires, you can route it anywhere — a Slack channel, a Zapier workflow that logs to a Google Sheet, a HubSpot workflow that updates a contact record, or even a custom script that pauses your sequence automatically.

Creating a Slack Webhook

In your Slack workspace, go to Apps → Incoming Webhooks and create a new webhook for the channel you want alerts delivered to. Copy the webhook URL — it'll look like https://hooks.slack.com/services/YOUR/SLACK/WEBHOOK.

Back in MailClaw's alert rule builder, select Webhook as the notification channel and paste your URL. You can customize the payload template to include the event type, contact name, sequence name, and timestamp:

{
  "text": "⚠️ MailClaw Alert: {{event.type}} on sequence '{{sequence.name}}'",
  "attachments": [
    {
      "fields": [
        { "title": "Contact", "value": "{{contact.email}}", "short": true },
        { "title": "Time", "value": "{{event.timestamp}}", "short": true },
        { "title": "Campaign", "value": "{{campaign.name}}", "short": false }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Hit Test Webhook to fire a sample payload and confirm it arrives in your Slack channel before saving the rule.

Using the CLI to Manage Alert Rules

If you prefer working in the terminal, MailClaw's CLI gives you full control over alert rules without touching the browser dashboard. This is especially useful for scripting alert configurations across multiple campaigns or sharing rule sets with your team via version control.

# List all current alert rules
mailclaw alerts list

# Create a new spam complaint alert with Slack webhook
mailclaw alerts create \
  --event spam_complaint \
  --condition any \
  --channel webhook \
  --webhook-url "https://hooks.slack.com/services/YOUR/SLACK/WEBHOOK..." \
  --name "Spam Complaint Immediate"

# Create a bounce rate alert scoped to a sequence
mailclaw alerts create \
  --event bounce_hard \
  --condition rate \
  --threshold 3 \
  --window 60m \
  --sequence-id seq_abc123 \
  --channel desktop,email \
  --alert-email you@yourdomain.com \
  --name "Cold Outreach Bounce Rate"

# Disable an alert without deleting it
mailclaw alerts disable alert_xyz789

# View recent alert history
mailclaw alerts history --last 24h

All alert rules are stored in MailClaw's local config at ~/.mailclaw/alerts.json, making them easy to back up, diff, and share.

Smarter Alerts with AI Email Agents

Standard threshold alerts are reactive — they tell you something went wrong. MailClaw's AI email agents take this further by analyzing patterns across your campaigns and predicting issues before they cross a hard threshold.

When you enable an AI agent on a sequence, it monitors the rolling analytics and can trigger a soft alert — a warning rather than a critical notification — when early indicators suggest a problem is developing. For example, if your open rate on a sequence drops 40% over two sends compared to your historical baseline, the agent flags it for review before your bounce or complaint rate climbs.

To enable AI agent monitoring on a sequence, open the sequence in the Sequence Builder and toggle AI Agent Monitoring under the Deliverability tab. You'll be prompted to set your sensitivity level:

  • Conservative — flags only significant deviations (best for mature, stable campaigns)
  • Standard — balanced detection, recommended for most outreach sequences
  • Aggressive — flags minor anomalies early, useful for high-stakes campaigns or new sender domains

AI agent alerts work best when MailClaw has at least two weeks of historical send data for a given account. For brand-new sender profiles, start with rule-based alerts and let the AI agent accumulate baseline data before relying on its anomaly detection.

Combining Alerts with Contact Enrichment Data

One of MailClaw's more powerful (and underused) features is triggering different alert logic based on contact enrichment data. Because MailClaw enriches contacts at send time — pulling in company size, industry, job title, and CRM status from integrations like HubSpot and Salesforce — you can create tiered alert rules that behave differently for high-value contacts.

For example, you might want an immediate desktop notification when any contact tagged as tier:enterprise replies to a sequence, but only a daily digest email for general list replies. Set this up by adding a contact filter to your reply alert rule:

mailclaw alerts create \
  --event reply \
  --condition any \
  --contact-filter "tag=tier:enterprise" \
  --channel desktop \
  --priority high \
  --name "Enterprise Reply — Immediate"

This kind of segmented alerting means your attention goes where it matters most, and you're not numbed by notification noise from lower-priority activity.

Recommended Alert Rule Set to Start With

If you're not sure where to start, here's a solid baseline configuration that covers deliverability protection and engagement tracking for most outreach use cases:

  • Spam complaint — any — immediate desktop + Slack
  • Hard bounce rate > 3% in 1 hour — Slack
  • Soft bounce rate > 8% in 3 hours — email digest
  • Reply from enterprise-tagged contact — immediate desktop
  • Sequence completion rate drops 25% vs. 7-day average — AI agent warning
  • Click rate spike > 3x baseline in 30 minutes — Slack (useful for catching tracking anomalies or bot clicks)

You can import this set directly using a MailClaw alert preset file. Save the following as baseline-alerts.json in your project directory and run:

mailclaw alerts import ./baseline-alerts.json

From there, tune the thresholds to match your sending volume and risk tolerance. A high-volume SendGrid-backed campaign will have different normal ranges than a low-volume personal Gmail sequence — MailClaw's per-account multi-sender support means you can maintain separate alert profiles for each connected account.

Keeping Alerts Useful Over Time

Alert fatigue is real. The most common mistake is setting thresholds too low and training yourself to ignore notifications. Review your alert history monthly using mailclaw alerts history --last 30d and look for rules that fire frequently without requiring action — those are candidates for higher thresholds or a daily digest instead of real-time pings.

Conversely, if you've gone weeks without a single alert on an active campaign, your thresholds may be set too high to catch genuine issues early. The goal is a signal, not silence and not noise.

With real-time alerts properly configured, MailClaw stops being just a tool you check and starts acting like a system that watches your campaigns for you — freeing you to focus on writing better sequences, enriching your contact lists, and closing the replies that actually matter.

articles.title: MailClaw Benchmarks: How Your Email Metrics Compare to Industry Averages
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Discover how your email open rates, click-through rates, and reply rates stack up against real industry benchmarks — and learn exactly how to use MailClaw's AI agents, sequence builder, and deliverability tools to close the gap.
articles.content:
Why Benchmarks Actually Matter (And When to Ignore Them)

Every email marketer has seen the generic stat floating around: "The average open rate is 21%." And every experienced sender has learned to treat that number with healthy suspicion. Industry averages are useful orientation points, not gospel. A 15% open rate might be a disaster for a SaaS onboarding sequence and a quiet triumph for a cold outreach campaign targeting enterprise procurement leads.

That said, benchmarks give you a starting line. Without them, you're optimizing in the dark — improving metrics without knowing whether you're approaching best-in-class or still sitting in the bottom quartile. This guide walks through the numbers that actually matter, what they mean for different campaign types, and how to use MailClaw's local toolchain to close the gap between where you are and where you want to be.

The Benchmarks You Should Actually Track

Open Rate

Open rate measures how many recipients opened your email, expressed as a percentage of delivered messages. Since Apple Mail Privacy Protection (MPP) launched in 2021, raw open rates have become noisier — Apple prefetches images, which triggers open pixels even when nobody actually reads anything. Factor that in when reading your numbers.

  • Cold outreach: 30–45% is strong; below 20% signals a subject line or deliverability problem
  • Newsletters: 20–35% is healthy across most industries
  • Transactional emails: 50–80% — these should always outperform everything else
  • Re-engagement campaigns: 5–15% is typical; if you're getting more, your list wasn't that cold

When you're pulling open rate data from MailClaw's localhost dashboard at localhost:3100, look at the Adjusted Open Rate metric, which filters out bot and privacy-proxy opens using MailClaw's heuristic layer. This gives you a cleaner signal than what HubSpot or Salesforce report out of the box.

Click-Through Rate (CTR)

CTR tells you how many people who received your email clicked at least one link. It's a stronger engagement signal than open rate because it requires actual intent.

  • B2B outreach: 2–5% is solid; above 8% is exceptional
  • E-commerce promotional: 3–6% is the standard range
  • Newsletters: 1–3% is realistic; high-quality niche newsletters often see 5–10%
  • Automated drip sequences: 4–7% in early stages, declining naturally in later steps

Reply Rate

For cold outreach and sales sequences, reply rate is king. Opens and clicks are vanity without a conversation.

  • Cold email sequences: 5–10% total reply rate across a sequence is respectable; above 15% is excellent
  • Warm outreach (existing contacts): 20–40% is realistic
  • Newsletter reply prompts: Even 1–2% indicates strong community engagement

Bounce Rate and Deliverability Health

Hard bounces above 2% are a red flag. Soft bounces above 5% suggest list hygiene issues. Spam complaint rates above 0.1% (Google's threshold) will get your sending domain flagged or your Gmail API access suspended.

Rule of thumb: If your bounce rate climbs above 3% or your spam rate crosses 0.08%, pause your campaign and run contact enrichment before sending another message. MailClaw's deliverability monitor will surface this automatically — but don't wait for the alert.

Diagnosing Your Gaps with MailClaw

Run a Campaign Health Check

From your terminal, pull a performance summary for any active campaign:

mailclaw campaign stats --id camp_abc123 --format table

This outputs open rate, CTR, reply rate, bounce breakdown, and an AI-generated health score powered by OpenClaw. The health score weights each metric against your industry vertical (set during account setup) so you get contextual benchmarking, not generic averages.

If you want to compare across all campaigns in a date range:

mailclaw campaign stats --all --since 2024-01-01 --until 2024-06-30 --export csv

Import that CSV into your dashboard at localhost:3100/analytics to visualize trends. The sequence builder view overlays benchmark bands directly on your charts — green for above-average, yellow for at-par, red for below-benchmark — so you can see at a glance which steps in a sequence are bleeding engagement.

Identify the Weak Step in a Sequence

Most multi-step sequences don't fail uniformly. Usually one step — often step 2 or 3 — is where engagement craters. Pull step-level metrics:

mailclaw sequence inspect --id seq_xyz789 --breakdown steps

You'll see per-step open, click, reply, and unsubscribe rates. If step 3 has a 40% drop in opens versus step 2, you likely have a subject line problem or a sending-time mismatch. If click rate drops but open rate holds, your CTA copy or offer isn't landing.

How to Move the Numbers

Low Open Rate: Fix Deliverability First, Copywriting Second

Before you rewrite your subject lines, verify your sending infrastructure is clean. In MailClaw, run:

mailclaw deliverability check --account work@yourdomain.com

This checks SPF, DKIM, DMARC alignment, domain reputation via multiple blocklist APIs, and your recent bounce history across connected accounts (Gmail via OAuth, Outlook via OAuth, or SendGrid via API key). If anything is misconfigured, MailClaw will output a fix checklist with exact DNS records.

Once infrastructure is healthy, focus on subject lines. Use MailClaw's AI email agent to generate and score subject line variants:

mailclaw agent run --task "generate 10 subject line variants for a cold outreach email targeting SaaS CTOs, tone: direct, goal: meeting booking" --model openClaw-3

The agent scores each variant on predicted open rate based on send volume data from the OpenClaw training corpus. Pick the top two and A/B test them in your next sequence step.

Low Click Rate: Simplify and Personalize the CTA

Emails with multiple links consistently underperform emails with one clear, personalized CTA. If your contacts are enriched, use that data to make the CTA contextual.

MailClaw's contact enrichment pulls LinkedIn role data, company size, tech stack signals, and recent funding events. You can reference enrichment fields directly in sequence templates:

Hey {{first_name}}, given that {{company_name}} recently {{enrichment.recent_event}}, 
I thought this [resource/demo/case study] might be timely — 
it's specifically for {{enrichment.industry}} teams at your stage.

Personalization at this level — not just first name, but context-aware relevance — routinely lifts CTR by 2–4 percentage points in B2B sequences.

Low Reply Rate: Rewrite the Ask

The most common reply-rate killer in cold outreach is asking for too much too soon. "Would you be open to a 30-minute call next week?" is a high-commitment ask from a stranger. "Does this problem sound familiar?" is almost free to answer.

Use MailClaw's AI agent to audit your sequence's call-to-action pattern:

mailclaw agent run --task "audit the following email sequence for ask friction and suggest lower-commitment alternatives" --input-file sequence_draft.txt

The agent will flag high-friction phrases and suggest micro-commitments that warm up the conversation before pushing for a meeting. This single change — reducing ask size in steps 1 and 2 — is the highest-ROI intervention in most cold sequences.

Multi-Account Benchmarking: What Changes Across Channels

If you're running outreach across multiple sending accounts — a common setup for agencies or growth teams using MailClaw's multi-account support — benchmark each account separately before aggregating. A Gmail account with 18 months of warm sending history will perform very differently than a fresh Outlook account set up last month, even with identical content.

In your dashboard, navigate to localhost:3100/accounts and enable per-account benchmark overlays. This prevents a high-performing account from masking a problem account in your aggregate stats — a mistake that's surprisingly common when teams manage outreach across five or more inboxes simultaneously.

Building a Feedback Loop

Benchmarks are only useful if you revisit them. Set a recurring review cadence — weekly for active campaigns, monthly for ongoing sequences — and use MailClaw's scheduled reporting to automate the data collection:

mailclaw report schedule --campaigns all --frequency weekly --output-dir ~/reports/mailclaw

Compare each week's numbers against both industry benchmarks and your own historical baseline. Your past performance is often a more actionable target than a generic industry average, because it controls for your specific audience, industry, and sending patterns.

The teams that consistently outperform benchmarks aren't the ones who read the most marketing blogs. They're the ones who run structured experiments, measure rigorously, and iterate on a tight loop. MailClaw's local-first architecture — running entirely on your machine, no data sent to third-party clouds, open source and auditable — makes that loop faster and more trustworthy than any SaaS dashboard can.

Your numbers are telling you something. The tools are here to help you listen.

articles.title: MailClaw vs Lemlist: Which Email Automation Tool Is Better
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: A detailed comparison of MailClaw and Lemlist across pricing, features, AI capabilities, and privacy — helping you decide which email automation tool is the right fit for your outreach stack.
articles.content:
The Case for Rethinking Your Email Automation Stack

If you've been running cold outreach or nurture campaigns for any length of time, you've probably landed on Lemlist as the go-to tool. It's polished, it's popular, and the liquid-based personalization is genuinely clever. But as AI-powered tooling matures and privacy concerns around SaaS platforms grow louder, more teams are asking a different question: do we actually need to send our contact data to a third-party cloud to run great email campaigns?

That's exactly the gap MailClaw was built to fill. It's an open-source, locally-run email automation platform powered by OpenClaw that runs on your Mac at localhost:3100. No per-seat pricing, no data leaving your machine unless you choose it to, and a surprisingly deep feature set that goes toe-to-toe with Lemlist in most areas — and beats it in a few that matter a lot.

Let's break down the real differences so you can make an informed call.

Pricing: Cloud Subscription vs. Running Free Locally

Lemlist's pricing starts at around $59/month per seat for their Email Outreach plan, climbing to $99/month for Sales Engagement and higher for team tiers. If you're a solo founder or a small team, those numbers add up fast — and you're paying whether or not you're actively sending.

MailClaw is open source and free to run locally. Your costs are your infrastructure — your own SMTP credentials, your API keys for enrichment providers, and whatever hardware you're already running. For teams already on SendGrid, Mailgun, or AWS SES, plugging those into MailClaw's SMTP integration takes minutes and you're sending at your own provider's rates, not a platform markup.

Bottom line: If you're sending at any meaningful volume and want to keep costs predictable, MailClaw's self-hosted model wins on economics alone. Lemlist's pricing makes more sense if you need a fully managed, zero-setup experience and don't mind the recurring cost.

Setup and Getting Started

Lemlist Onboarding

Lemlist is a standard SaaS onboarding flow: create an account, verify your email, connect your Gmail or Outlook via OAuth, and you're in their web dashboard. Fast, familiar, frictionless. The tradeoff is that your contact lists, sequences, and send behavior all live on their servers.

MailClaw Local Setup

MailClaw installs via a single CLI command and runs locally on your Mac. Getting started looks like this:

# Install MailClaw via npm
npm install -g mailclaw

# Initialize your local workspace
mailclaw init

# Start the local dashboard
mailclaw start
# → Dashboard running at http://localhost:3100

Once the dashboard is up, you connect your email accounts (Gmail via OAuth, Outlook via OAuth, or any SMTP provider), import your contacts, and you're ready to build your first sequence. The entire UI runs in your browser pointed at localhost — it feels like a SaaS product, except nothing leaves your machine until a send event fires.

Core Feature Comparison

Sequence Builder

Both tools offer multi-step email sequences with conditional logic. Lemlist's sequence builder is visual and drag-and-drop, which is approachable for non-technical users. MailClaw's sequence builder supports branching logic, wait conditions, and reply detection — you can build sequences that automatically skip follow-ups when a prospect replies, branch based on open behavior, or delay steps based on timezone-aware sending windows.

A simple MailClaw sequence config looks like this in the CLI:

mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "SaaS Founders Outreach" \
  --steps 3 \
  --delay "3d,5d" \
  --skip-on-reply true \
  --timezone-aware true

You can also define sequences directly in YAML if you're building programmatically or managing configs in version control — a workflow that Lemlist simply doesn't support.

AI Email Agents

This is where MailClaw pulls clearly ahead. Lemlist offers AI writing assistance to help you draft and rephrase emails, which is useful but fairly shallow. MailClaw's AI email agents, powered by OpenClaw, go much further.

You can deploy an agent that:

  • Monitors incoming replies and classifies them (interested, not now, unsubscribe, question)
  • Drafts context-aware follow-up responses based on the reply content
  • Automatically pauses sequences for contacts who express buying intent so a human can step in
  • Generates personalized first lines by pulling data from enriched contact profiles

To spin up a basic AI reply agent:

mailclaw agent create \
  --type reply-handler \
  --model openai/gpt-4o \
  --classify-replies true \
  --auto-draft true \
  --notify-on-intent true

This is the difference between email automation and email intelligence. You're not just scheduling sends — you're running an AI-assisted outreach operation that surfaces what matters and handles the routine.

Contact Enrichment

Lemlist integrates with some enrichment tools but treats enrichment as a bolt-on. MailClaw's contact enrichment is a first-class feature. You connect your preferred enrichment providers — Clearbit, Hunter, Apollo, or custom webhook endpoints — and MailClaw enriches contacts on import or on a schedule, appending job title, company size, tech stack, LinkedIn URL, and more to each profile.

# Enrich a contact list using Hunter + Clearbit
mailclaw enrich \
  --list "founders-q4.csv" \
  --providers hunter,clearbit \
  --fields email,title,company,linkedin

Enriched data feeds directly into your personalization tokens, so your AI agents and sequence templates can reference {{contact.company_size}} or {{contact.tech_stack}} without any manual cleanup.

CRM and Integration Support

Lemlist connects natively to HubSpot, Salesforce, and Pipedrive with a few clicks. These integrations are solid and well-documented, which is a genuine advantage if your team lives in those tools.

MailClaw handles CRM sync via webhook events and a REST API. If you're comfortable with a small amount of configuration, you can push engagement events (opens, clicks, replies) to HubSpot or Salesforce in real time:

# Push engagement events to HubSpot via webhook
mailclaw integrations add \
  --type webhook \
  --name hubspot-sync \
  --events open,click,reply \
  --url https://api.hubspot.com/crm/v3/...

It's slightly more setup than Lemlist's native connectors, but the flexibility means you're not locked into a specific CRM partner's implementation.

Deliverability Monitoring

Lemlist includes basic deliverability warnings and a warmup tool (Lemwarm, now built in). MailClaw's deliverability monitoring runs locally and gives you a real-time view of bounce rates, spam complaints, reply rates, and sender reputation scores across all your connected accounts — including multi-account setups where you're rotating sends across several domains.

For teams managing multiple sending domains on SendGrid or running dedicated IPs, MailClaw's deliverability dashboard at localhost:3100/deliverability shows per-domain health scores and flags issues before they become blacklist problems. You can also run seed tests directly from the CLI:

mailclaw deliverability test \
  --account founders@yourdomain.com \
  --seed-list default \
  --report true

Privacy, Data Ownership, and Compliance

This deserves its own section because it's often the deciding factor for teams operating under GDPR, CCPA, or internal data governance policies.

With Lemlist, your contact data — including email addresses, engagement behavior, and any enrichment data — is stored on their cloud infrastructure. Their privacy policy governs what happens to it. For most small teams this is fine. For agencies handling client data, or companies in regulated industries, it's a material concern.

MailClaw stores everything locally. Your contact database, sequence configs, engagement logs, and AI agent outputs all live on your machine. You can back them up however you like, encrypt them, or move them between environments. If you're building outreach on behalf of clients, you can run isolated MailClaw instances per client workspace — something Lemlist's multi-seat model makes awkward and expensive.

When to Choose Lemlist

  • You want a fully managed, zero-maintenance SaaS experience
  • Your team is non-technical and needs drag-and-drop everything
  • You rely heavily on LinkedIn steps and video personalization (Lemlist's standout differentiators)
  • Native CRM integrations with no configuration are a hard requirement

When to Choose MailClaw

  • You want to eliminate per-seat SaaS costs at any meaningful sending volume
  • Data privacy and local storage are requirements, not nice-to-haves
  • You want to run AI email agents that do more than rewrite subject lines
  • You're comfortable with a CLI and want to version-control your outreach configs
  • You're managing multiple client campaigns or rotating across many sending accounts
  • You want to extend and customize the tool — it's open source, fork it if you need to

The Verdict

Lemlist is a great tool — it earned its reputation. But it was built for a world where SaaS was the obvious default. MailClaw is built for a world where AI is table stakes, data ownership matters, and developers want infrastructure they actually control.

If you've been paying for Lemlist and feel like you're bumping against its limits — or just paying for features you don't use — MailClaw is worth an afternoon to evaluate. Run mailclaw init, connect your Gmail or Outlook account, drop in a CSV, and build your first sequence. By the time you've sent your first test campaign, you'll have a clear sense of whether the local-first, AI-native approach fits how your team actually works.

The dashboard is waiting at localhost:3100.

articles.title: MailClaw vs Apollo.io: Feature-by-Feature Comparison
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: A detailed side-by-side breakdown of MailClaw and Apollo.io across pricing, AI capabilities, deliverability, contact enrichment, and privacy — helping you decide which tool fits your outreach stack.
articles.content:
The Case for Rethinking Your Outreach Stack

Apollo.io has become one of the most recognizable names in sales outreach. It bundles a massive contact database, sequence tools, and analytics into a polished SaaS platform — and it charges accordingly. But as AI-native tooling matures and privacy concerns grow, a new class of locally-run, open-source alternatives is emerging that deserves serious consideration.

MailClaw is one of those alternatives. Built on the OpenClaw framework and running entirely on your Mac at localhost:3100, it brings AI email agents, contact enrichment, sequence building, and deliverability monitoring to a single CLI-powered tool — with no monthly seat fees and no data leaving your machine by default.

This isn't a hit piece on Apollo. It's an honest, feature-by-feature look at where each tool wins, so you can make a smarter decision for your team or solo operation.

Pricing: SaaS Subscription vs. True Ownership

Let's start with the number that usually ends the conversation fastest.

Apollo.io's pricing (as of 2024) starts at around $49/month per user for the Basic plan, climbing to $99/month on Professional and well beyond that for custom enterprise tiers. Contact enrichment credits, export limits, and advanced sequence features are often gated behind higher tiers. For a small team running multi-account outreach, costs compound quickly.

MailClaw is free and open source. You install it once, run it locally, and the only ongoing costs are your own SMTP provider (SendGrid, Mailgun, Postmark, or any SMTP relay you choose) and whatever LLM API keys you configure. If you already pay for OpenAI or Anthropic API access, MailClaw slots directly into that spend — no additional seat licensing.

For solo founders, indie hackers, and small sales teams, MailClaw can reduce tooling costs by hundreds of dollars per month while giving you more control over your data and workflows.

Contact Enrichment: Database vs. On-Demand Intelligence

Apollo's Approach

Apollo's core value proposition is its proprietary contact database — over 275 million contacts with emails, phone numbers, job titles, and firmographic data. This is genuinely powerful for prospecting from scratch. You can filter by industry, headcount, technology stack, and dozens of other signals. The tradeoff: you're working within Apollo's data, which may be stale, inaccurate, or simply absent for niche verticals.

MailClaw's Approach

MailClaw takes an on-demand enrichment model. Rather than maintaining a proprietary database, it connects to enrichment APIs you already use or trust — think Clearbit, Hunter.io, Clay, or custom enrichment endpoints — and runs enrichment jobs against your existing contact lists. This gives you flexibility to choose data sources that match your specific ICP.

To enrich a CSV of contacts via the MailClaw CLI, it looks something like this:

mailclaw enrich --input contacts.csv \
  --provider hunter \
  --fields email,company,linkedin \
  --output enriched_contacts.csv

The enriched output feeds directly into your sequence builder and AI agent workflows, keeping everything inside a single local pipeline. You own the data. It never hits a third-party SaaS database you don't control.

Email Sequences: Drag-and-Drop vs. Code-First Flexibility

Apollo Sequences

Apollo's sequence builder is polished and visual. You can build multi-step email + LinkedIn + call sequences with branching logic, set delays by business days, and A/B test subject lines. It's a solid tool for teams who want to move fast without writing any configuration files. The limitation is that you're constrained to Apollo's UX decisions — custom branching logic, webhook triggers, and deeply conditional flows require workarounds or aren't possible at all.

MailClaw Sequence Builder

MailClaw's sequence builder lives in your local dashboard at localhost:3100/sequences and supports a YAML-based sequence definition that you can version-control in Git alongside your codebase. This is a meaningful advantage for technical teams who want reproducible, reviewable outreach campaigns.

An example sequence definition:

sequence:
  name: "SaaS Founder Outreach - Q1"
  from_account: founders@yourdomain.com
  steps:
    - day: 0
      type: email
      subject: "Quick question about {{company}}"
      template: intro_v2.html
    - day: 3
      type: email
      subject: "Re: Quick question"
      template: followup_v1.html
      condition: not_opened
    - day: 7
      type: email
      subject: "Last note from me"
      template: breakup.html
      condition: not_replied

Conditional logic — like skipping a follow-up if someone opened but didn't reply — is first-class, not an afterthought. And because sequences are files, you can template, fork, and share them across projects trivially.

AI Capabilities: Bolt-On vs. Native Intelligence

This is where the gap between legacy SaaS and purpose-built AI tooling becomes most visible.

Apollo AI

Apollo has added AI-assisted email writing and some smart suggestions for send times and sequencing. These are useful quality-of-life features, but they're largely UI wrappers around general-purpose LLMs. You're not building agents; you're accepting suggestions in a text box.

MailClaw AI Email Agents

MailClaw's AI email agents — powered by OpenClaw — are a fundamentally different concept. Rather than helping you write one email, an agent can autonomously manage an entire outreach thread: responding to replies based on rules you define, escalating hot leads to a human, updating CRM fields in HubSpot or Salesforce via webhook, and adjusting messaging tone based on contact seniority.

You spin up an agent from the CLI:

mailclaw agent create \
  --name "inbound-qualifier" \
  --model gpt-4o \
  --goal "Qualify inbound leads, book a call if ICP match, otherwise send resources" \
  --inbox support@yourdomain.com \
  --crm hubspot

The agent watches the inbox, reads incoming replies, reasons about intent, and takes action — all running locally on your machine. For teams that receive high reply volumes, this is the difference between a tool that helps you write and a tool that actively works for you.

Deliverability: Monitoring and Control

Apollo gives you basic open and click tracking and some guidance on sending limits, but deliverability tooling is not its core focus. You're responsible for your own domain health and warming practices outside the platform.

MailClaw ships with a deliverability monitoring dashboard at localhost:3100/deliverability that surfaces:

  • SPF, DKIM, and DMARC record validation for each sending domain
  • Bounce rate tracking per account and per sequence
  • Spam trigger analysis on outbound templates using keyword scoring
  • Send volume pacing recommendations to avoid sudden spikes

You can also configure per-account daily send limits and randomized send windows to mimic human sending patterns — critical for cold outreach deliverability:

mailclaw account configure founders@yourdomain.com \
  --daily-limit 80 \
  --send-window "08:00-17:00" \
  --randomize-delays true

Multi-Account Support and Integrations

Apollo is fundamentally a single-account-per-user model. Multi-inbox rotation requires enterprise plans and custom setup.

MailClaw supports unlimited accounts out of the box via SMTP or OAuth (Gmail, Outlook, and any provider supporting OAuth2). Switching between accounts or running parallel campaigns across multiple sending domains is a first-class workflow, not an upgrade.

Integration-wise, MailClaw connects to:

  • CRMs: HubSpot, Salesforce, Pipedrive via webhook or native sync
  • SMTP providers: SendGrid, Mailgun, Postmark, Amazon SES
