It's not terrible, but it's not fast either. And those cron jobs? Miss one and your campaigns silently stall.

Listmonk

Listmonk is refreshingly simple. It's a single Go binary backed by PostgreSQL. If you've used Docker before, you can be running in under five minutes:

wget -O docker-compose.yml https://listmonk.app/docker-compose.yml
docker compose up -d

That's genuinely it. Listmonk earns enormous respect for this. The trade-off is that it's deliberately minimal — there's no built-in AI, no contact enrichment, and the sequencing logic is basic compared to the other two.

MailClaw

MailClaw takes a different philosophy entirely: it lives on your local machine. Powered by OpenClaw, it's built for developers and outreach professionals who want AI-assisted automation without spinning up infrastructure. Getting started is a single command:

npx mailclaw start

Your dashboard is live at localhost:3100 within seconds. Connect Gmail or Outlook via OAuth, or wire up SendGrid or any SMTP provider, and you're writing your first sequence in minutes. There's no server to manage, no cron jobs, no database to babysit.

Core Feature Comparison

Email Sequences and Campaign Logic

Mautic's campaign builder is genuinely sophisticated. You can build multi-step drip sequences with conditional branching, lead scoring, A/B tests, and behavioral triggers. If you need "send email 3 only if the contact visited the pricing page and didn't open email 2," Mautic can do it. The visual campaign canvas is one of its strongest assets.

Listmonk supports basic sequences and transactional email, but don't expect complex conditional logic. It's excellent for newsletters, announcement blasts, and high-volume sends where simplicity is a feature.

MailClaw's sequence builder hits a sweet spot between the two. You get multi-step sequences with conditional logic, but the real differentiator is that AI is embedded directly into the flow. You can write a prompt like "follow up if no reply in 3 days, personalize based on the contact's job title and company size" and MailClaw's AI email agents handle the execution. It's the kind of workflow that would take hours to configure in Mautic and simply isn't possible in Listmonk.

AI Capabilities

This is where the comparison gets asymmetrical. Mautic has no native AI. There are community plugins, but integrating something like GPT-based personalization requires custom development work. Listmonk similarly has no AI layer — it's intentionally a transport and list management tool.

MailClaw is built AI-first, powered by OpenClaw under the hood. Its AI email agents can:

  • Write and iterate on email copy based on your goals and audience
  • Decide autonomously when and how to follow up based on engagement signals
  • Enrich contacts in real-time — pulling job titles, company info, LinkedIn data, and tech stack details before sending
  • Adjust tone and messaging dynamically per recipient

The contact enrichment feature alone is worth highlighting. Before MailClaw sends an outreach email, it can automatically research the recipient and inject relevant context into your template. No more generic "Hi {{first_name}}" — instead you get personalization that actually reflects what the contact cares about.

Deliverability

Deliverability is where teams often make expensive mistakes. Mautic gives you some control — you can configure sending limits, manage bounce handling, and integrate with services like SendGrid or Amazon SES. But there's no proactive deliverability intelligence built in. You need to know what you're doing or you'll damage your sender reputation quietly.

Listmonk is similarly hands-off on deliverability guidance. It passes messages to your configured SMTP relay faithfully, but monitoring inbox placement, bounce trends, or spam score drift is entirely on you.

MailClaw includes a deliverability monitoring dashboard that surfaces real-time signals: bounce rates, open rates by domain, spam complaint indicators, and sending velocity warnings. If your Gmail sends are trending toward the spam folder, MailClaw surfaces that before it becomes a reputation problem. Combined with its multi-account support — which lets you spread sends across multiple Gmail and Outlook accounts to stay within provider limits — it's a meaningfully safer tool for outreach at scale.

Integrations

Mautic integrates with a wide ecosystem: Salesforce, HubSpot, Sugar CRM, Zapier, and dozens of others. If you're running enterprise marketing ops, this matters a lot.

Listmonk is API-first with a clean REST interface, making it straightforward to integrate with whatever your stack looks like.

MailClaw supports SMTP and OAuth integration natively (Gmail, Outlook, SendGrid out of the box) and exposes its own API for feeding contacts and triggering sequences programmatically. If your CRM is HubSpot or Salesforce and you want to trigger AI-powered sequences when a deal reaches a certain stage, MailClaw's API makes that a realistic weekend project rather than a multi-week integration effort.

When to Choose Each Tool

Choose Mautic if:

  • You're running enterprise marketing campaigns with complex multi-channel logic
  • You need deep CRM integrations (Salesforce, HubSpot) out of the box
  • You have DevOps capacity to manage and maintain a self-hosted server
  • Lead scoring and behavior-based segmentation are critical requirements

Choose Listmonk if:

  • Your primary use case is newsletter delivery or transactional email
  • You need to send high volumes cheaply with minimal operational overhead
  • Simplicity and performance are more important than automation depth
  • You're comfortable managing PostgreSQL and a Go binary

Choose MailClaw if:

  • You're doing sales outreach, cold email, or developer-led growth campaigns
  • You want AI agents to handle personalization and follow-up logic without custom code
  • You prefer running tools locally without provisioning servers
  • Contact enrichment and deliverability intelligence are first-class requirements
  • You want to move fast — from zero to a live sequence in under 10 minutes

A Practical Quickstart with MailClaw

If you want to try MailClaw today, here's a minimal end-to-end flow:

  1. Run npx mailclaw start and open localhost:3100
  2. Connect your Gmail account via OAuth under Settings → Accounts
  3. Import a CSV of contacts or paste them directly into the contact manager
  4. Open the Sequence Builder, describe your campaign goal in plain English, and let the AI draft your sequence steps
  5. Enable contact enrichment to auto-research your recipients before send
  6. Launch the sequence and monitor deliverability from the dashboard

Pro tip: Use MailClaw's multi-account support from day one. Distributing sends across two or three accounts keeps your daily send volume under Gmail and Outlook's per-account limits, protecting your sender reputation while you scale.

The Bottom Line

These three tools aren't really competing for the same user. Mautic is a marketing automation platform for teams with infrastructure and integration complexity. Listmonk is a fast, reliable delivery layer for list-based email. MailClaw is an AI-native outreach tool for people who want intelligent, locally-running automation without the ops burden.

If you're a developer, founder, or growth engineer who's tired of paying for Outreach.io or Apollo and wants full control over your email stack, MailClaw is the tool worth your attention. The open-source foundation means you own your data, your sequences, and your sending infrastructure — and the AI layer means you spend less time writing follow-ups and more time closing deals.

articles.title: MailClaw vs Clay: Enrichment and Outreach in One Tool
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: A practical comparison of MailClaw and Clay showing how MailClaw combines contact enrichment and email outreach in a single open-source tool you run locally — no per-seat pricing, no data leaving your machine.
articles.content:
Two Tools, One Job: Why the Stack Is Collapsing

For the past few years, the standard outbound stack looked something like this: Clay for enrichment, Instantly or Lemlist for sequences, a deliverability tool bolted on the side, and a CRM syncing everything together. It worked, but it was expensive, fragile, and slow. Data passed through four different APIs before a single email went out.

Clay is genuinely excellent at what it does. If you need to pull data from 50+ sources, run waterfalls, and pipe enriched rows into a downstream tool, it's hard to beat. But that downstream tool still has to exist. You're paying for Clay and your sequencer and your deliverability monitor, and you're hoping the integrations don't break mid-campaign.

MailClaw takes a different approach. Because it runs locally on your Mac at localhost:3100 and is built on OpenClaw, it can handle enrichment, sequencing, AI-driven personalization, and deliverability monitoring inside a single tool — one you own completely, with no per-seat pricing and no data leaving your machine.

What Clay Does Well (And Where It Stops)

To be fair about the comparison, Clay's strengths are real:

  • Waterfall enrichment: Try Provider A, fall back to Provider B, normalize the result. Clay handles this elegantly.
  • Data breadth: LinkedIn, Clearbit, Hunter, Apollo, Crunchbase — all accessible from one grid interface.
  • Formula-driven personalization: You can build complex icebreaker logic directly in the table.
  • Zapier/webhook exports: Relatively easy to push enriched rows to other tools.

But here's where Clay's model creates friction for outbound teams:

  • Credits evaporate quickly at scale. Enriching 10,000 contacts across three providers can cost hundreds of dollars in a single run.
  • There's no native sequencer. You're always exporting to something else.
  • There's no deliverability layer. You have no idea if your emails are landing in inbox or spam.
  • Everything runs in the cloud. Your prospect data — including personal emails, job titles, and company intelligence — lives on Clay's servers.

For teams doing low-volume, high-precision outbound, that stack works. For teams that want to move faster, cut costs, or keep data private, it starts to strain.

How MailClaw Handles Enrichment

MailClaw's contact enrichment runs through the OpenClaw engine, which orchestrates enrichment providers the same way Clay's waterfall does — but locally, with results stored in your own database.

Running an Enrichment Job from the CLI

Once MailClaw is running, you can kick off an enrichment job directly from the terminal:

# Enrich a single contact
mailclaw enrich --email jane@acmecorp.com --providers clearbit,hunter

# Enrich a CSV of contacts with waterfall logic
mailclaw enrich --file ./leads.csv --waterfall --output ./enriched.csv

# Enrich and immediately push to a sequence
mailclaw enrich --file ./leads.csv --waterfall --then sequence:q3-outbound

The --waterfall flag tells MailClaw to try providers in priority order and stop as soon as it gets a confident match on each field. This is the same logic Clay uses, but you control which providers are called and in what order — configured in your local mailclaw.config.js.

What Gets Enriched

A standard enrichment pass fills in:

  • Verified work email and personal email
  • Job title, seniority, and department
  • Company size, industry, tech stack, and funding stage
  • LinkedIn URL and recent activity signals
  • Phone number (where available from connected providers)

All of this lands in MailClaw's local contact database, visible in the dashboard at localhost:3100/contacts. You can filter, segment, and push directly into sequences without ever touching a CSV again.

The Sequence Builder: From Enriched Lead to Booked Meeting

This is where MailClaw pulls decisively ahead of Clay for outbound teams. Once your contacts are enriched, you build sequences inside the same tool — no export, no webhook, no waiting for Zapier to fire.

Building a Sequence via CLI

# Create a new sequence
mailclaw sequence create --name "Q3 SaaS Founders" --type email

# Add steps to the sequence
mailclaw sequence add-step "Q3 SaaS Founders" \
  --day 0 \
  --subject "Quick question about {{company}}" \
  --template ./templates/intro.html \
  --ai-personalize true

mailclaw sequence add-step "Q3 SaaS Founders" \
  --day 3 \
  --subject "Re: Quick question" \
  --template ./templates/followup-1.html

# Enroll enriched contacts
mailclaw sequence enroll --name "Q3 SaaS Founders" --from enriched.csv

The --ai-personalize true flag activates MailClaw's AI email agent on that step. The agent reads the enriched contact data — recent LinkedIn posts, company news, tech stack, funding announcements — and writes a personalized opening line for each recipient before the email sends.

Connecting Your Sending Infrastructure

MailClaw supports SMTP and OAuth authentication, so you can connect whatever sending setup you already have:

# Add a Gmail account via OAuth
mailclaw account add --provider gmail --oauth

# Add a SendGrid SMTP account
mailclaw account add --provider sendgrid \
  --smtp smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --port 587 \
  --user apikey \
  --pass YOUR_API_KEY

# Add an Outlook account
mailclaw account add --provider outlook --oauth

Multi-account support means you can rotate sending across several inboxes to protect deliverability, a technique Clay's native tooling can't help you with at all.

AI Email Agents: The Feature That Changes the Workflow

MailClaw's AI email agents go beyond simple variable substitution. An agent can:

  • Read enriched contact data and write a unique first sentence per recipient
  • Monitor replies and draft suggested responses in your dashboard
  • Detect out-of-office and bounce signals and pause the sequence automatically
  • Score replies by intent (interested, not interested, referral, timing objection) and route them to the right follow-up step

The agent doesn't just personalize at send time. It stays active throughout the sequence, adjusting timing and content based on how the prospect engages.

In Clay, you'd build personalization logic in a formula column before export. That logic is static — it runs once. MailClaw's agents run continuously, which means a prospect who opens your email three times in one hour can trigger a different follow-up path than one who hasn't opened at all.

Deliverability Monitoring Built In

This is the piece most Clay-based stacks are missing entirely. MailClaw includes a deliverability dashboard at localhost:3100/deliverability that tracks:

  • Open and click rates per sequence and per sending account
  • Bounce and complaint rates, with automatic suppression
  • Spam trap hits and blacklist checks
  • SPF, DKIM, and DMARC status for each connected domain
  • Inbox placement estimates across major providers (Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo)

When deliverability degrades, MailClaw surfaces the warning before you burn a domain. You can pause a sending account, swap to a backup, and keep the sequence running — all from the dashboard or CLI.

# Check deliverability health for all accounts
mailclaw deliverability check

# Pause a degraded account and redistribute to healthy ones
mailclaw account pause --email outbound@yourdomain.com --redistribute

CRM Sync: Closing the Loop with HubSpot and Salesforce

MailClaw isn't trying to replace your CRM. It syncs bidirectionally with HubSpot, Salesforce, and other tools so every enriched field and every sequence event flows back to where your team already works.

# Connect HubSpot
mailclaw crm connect --provider hubspot --api-key YOUR_KEY

# Sync enriched contacts to HubSpot
mailclaw crm sync --direction push --filter enriched:true

# Pull new HubSpot contacts into MailClaw for enrichment and outreach
mailclaw crm sync --direction pull --list "Q3 Targets"

Sequence events — opens, clicks, replies, bounces — are written back to the contact record in your CRM automatically, so your sales team has full context without logging into MailClaw at all.

The Real Difference: Ownership and Cost

Clay is a SaaS product. Your data lives in their cloud, their pricing scales with your usage, and if they change their API or credit model, your workflow changes too. For many teams, that's a fine trade-off. For teams at scale, or teams working with sensitive prospect data, or teams that simply want to control their own stack, it's a real constraint.

MailClaw is open source and runs on your machine. The code is auditable, the data stays local, and there's no per-seat cost. You pay for the enrichment providers you choose to connect — the same providers Clay charges a markup on — and you keep the rest.

If you're already paying for a Clay seat, a sequencer, and a deliverability tool, consolidating onto MailClaw likely cuts your tooling cost by more than half while giving you tighter control over every step of the outbound process.

Getting Started

If you want to run the comparison yourself, getting MailClaw running takes about five minutes:

  1. Install MailClaw: brew install mailclaw
  2. Start the local server: mailclaw start
  3. Open the dashboard: http://localhost:3100
  4. Connect a sending account and run your first enrichment job against a small list
  5. Build a three-step sequence with AI personalization enabled on step one

The whole flow — from raw CSV to personalized sequence with deliverability monitoring active — takes less than 30 minutes to set up the first time. After that, the CLI makes it repeatable in seconds.

Clay will remain the right choice for teams that need its full breadth of data integrations and are happy living in a SaaS model. But for teams that want enrichment and outreach in one place, want their data local, and want AI working on every email in the sequence — not just the first one — MailClaw is worth a serious look.

articles.title: 10 MailClaw Tips Every Email Power User Should Know
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Unlock the full potential of MailClaw with these 10 expert tips covering AI email agents, contact enrichment, sequence optimization, deliverability monitoring, and CLI shortcuts that most users never discover.
articles.content:
Most people who install MailClaw get as far as connecting their Gmail account and sending a basic sequence — and then stop. That's like buying a professional espresso machine and only using it to heat water. MailClaw, built on the OpenClaw engine and running entirely on your local machine at localhost:3100, is packed with features that can genuinely transform how you approach email outreach. Whether you're a solo founder running cold outreach, a growth marketer managing dozens of campaigns, or a developer who wants full control over your email stack, these ten tips will change how you work.

1. Use the CLI to Bootstrap Campaigns Without Touching the Dashboard

The local dashboard is beautiful, but the real power users live in the terminal. MailClaw ships with a full-featured CLI that lets you spin up campaigns, import contacts, and trigger sequences in a single command.

# Create and launch a new campaign from a YAML config
mailclaw campaign:create --config ./outreach-q3.yaml --launch

# Import a CSV of contacts and enrich them immediately
mailclaw contacts:import ./leads.csv --enrich --source hubspot

Pairing these commands with a simple shell script means you can trigger entire outreach workflows from a cron job, a CI pipeline, or even a GitHub Action. This is especially powerful if you're generating lead lists programmatically — pipe the output of a scraper directly into MailClaw without ever leaving your terminal.

2. Build AI Email Agents That Actually Understand Context

MailClaw's AI email agents are more than a "personalize the first line" gimmick. When you configure an agent correctly, it reads the contact's enriched profile — job title, company size, recent news, LinkedIn summary — and writes emails that sound like you actually did your homework.

Setting Up a Context-Aware Agent

  1. Navigate to Agents → New Agent in the dashboard at localhost:3100.
  2. Set the agent's persona: tone, signature style, goal (book a meeting, drive a demo, share a resource).
  3. Enable Contact Context Injection so the agent has access to enriched fields.
  4. Add a constraint prompt — for example: "Never mention pricing. Keep emails under 120 words. Always end with a single question."

The constraint prompt is the feature most people skip, and it's the one that makes agent output actually usable at scale. Without it, you'll get verbose, unfocused copy. With it, you'll get emails that feel hand-crafted.

3. Layer Contact Enrichment Before Your Sequence Starts

Sending a sequence to a raw, unenriched contact list is a waste of your sending reputation. MailClaw's contact enrichment pipeline can pull data from multiple sources before a single email goes out — and you can configure exactly what it fetches.

# Enrich a contact list and wait for completion before sequencing
mailclaw contacts:enrich --list campaign-leads --fields company,title,linkedin,funding
mailclaw sequence:start --name "Q3 SaaS Outreach" --wait-for-enrichment

The --wait-for-enrichment flag is easy to miss in the docs but critical: it pauses the sequence trigger until enrichment is complete, so no contact gets a generic email just because their data wasn't ready yet. If you're pulling from HubSpot or Salesforce, you can also sync enriched fields back to your CRM automatically using the webhook integration.

4. Master the Sequence Builder's Branching Logic

Linear sequences — Step 1, wait 3 days, Step 2, wait 5 days — are table stakes. What separates good campaigns from great ones is conditional branching. In MailClaw's sequence builder, you can branch based on opens, clicks, replies, link clicks, or even custom enrichment fields.

Example: If a contact opens your email three times but doesn't reply, they're interested but hesitant. Branch them into a softer follow-up that offers a resource instead of pushing for a call. If they never open at all, switch to a subject line variant and try a different angle.

To set this up, open any sequence in the builder and click Add Branch Condition on any step. You can stack multiple conditions with AND/OR logic, which lets you build genuinely sophisticated nurture paths without needing a separate marketing automation platform.

5. Connect Multiple Sending Accounts and Rotate Intelligently

One of MailClaw's most underrated features is multi-account support with smart rotation. You can connect Gmail accounts via OAuth, Outlook via OAuth, and custom SMTP providers like SendGrid or Postmark — all from the same dashboard — and let MailClaw distribute sending load across them automatically.

# Add a Gmail account via OAuth
mailclaw accounts:add --provider gmail --alias "outreach-1"

# Add a SendGrid SMTP account
mailclaw accounts:add --provider smtp --host smtp.sendgrid.net --port 587 --alias "sg-backup"

# Set rotation strategy for a campaign
mailclaw campaign:update --name "Q3 SaaS Outreach" --rotation round-robin

Use the round-robin strategy for volume, or weighted if you want your primary Gmail account to carry more of the load. This approach keeps individual account volumes low and your sender reputation healthy.

6. Monitor Deliverability From the Dashboard Before Problems Start

Most people only think about deliverability after they land in spam. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools let you stay ahead of the problem. From the dashboard, you can see:

  • Spam score estimates for each email in your sequence
  • DKIM, SPF, and DMARC status for connected domains
  • Bounce rate trends per sending account
  • Open rate anomalies that might indicate tab-open filtering (looking at you, Apple Mail Privacy Protection)

Set up deliverability alerts in Settings → Alerts so you get a local desktop notification the moment your bounce rate exceeds a threshold you define. Catching a bounce spike at 2% is a minor fix. Catching it at 12% is a crisis.

7. Use Template Variables Beyond Just First Name

Every email tool lets you use {{first_name}}. MailClaw lets you use any enriched field as a variable, including nested ones, with fallback values built in.

Hi {{first_name | fallback: "there"}},

I noticed {{company}} recently {{recent_news | fallback: "has been growing fast"}} —
thought this might be relevant to what you're building in the {{industry}} space.

The | fallback: syntax means your emails never awkwardly display a blank field. You can also create computed variables — for example, a variable that checks whether a contact is a VP or above and dynamically inserts either a peer-level tone or a more formal opener. Set these up in Templates → Variable Logic.

8. Expose MailClaw's API for Custom Integrations

Because MailClaw runs locally, its REST API is available at localhost:3100/api/v1 and requires no external authentication setup. This makes it trivial to integrate with internal tools, custom CRMs, or automation platforms like n8n or Zapier (via local webhook bridge).

# Trigger a sequence for a new contact via API
curl -X POST http://localhost:3100/api/v1/contacts \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email": "jane@acme.com", "first_name": "Jane", "sequence": "Q3 SaaS Outreach"}'

This is the pattern behind some of the most powerful MailClaw setups: a new lead fills out a form, your backend POSTs to MailClaw's API, the contact is enriched automatically, and a personalized sequence starts — all within seconds, all locally.

9. Version Control Your Campaigns With Git

Because MailClaw is open source and stores campaign configs as flat files, you can version control your entire outreach operation with Git. This is a game-changer for teams.

# Export all campaigns as YAML
mailclaw campaigns:export --output ./campaigns/

# Commit and push
git add ./campaigns/
git commit -m "Updated Q3 sequence — new branch for non-openers"
git push

Your team gets a full history of every campaign change, you can roll back a sequence that's underperforming, and onboarding a new person means cloning a repo instead of exporting a maze of settings from a SaaS dashboard. Pair this with a .env file for credentials (never committed) and you have a genuinely professional email ops setup.

10. Schedule a Weekly Deliverability and Performance Review

The last tip is more operational than technical, but it matters: build a weekly habit of pulling MailClaw's campaign reports and actually reading them. The CLI makes this easy to automate.

# Generate a weekly summary report
mailclaw report:weekly --format html --output ./reports/week-$(date +%Y-%W).html

Open the HTML report in your browser and look for patterns: Which subject lines drove the highest open rates? Which steps in your sequence see the biggest drop-off? Are there sending accounts where bounce rates are creeping up? MailClaw surfaces all of this data, but it only becomes valuable if you build the discipline to review it and iterate.

What to Look For Each Week

  • Open rate below 30%? Test a new subject line variant on your next batch.
  • Reply rate below 2%? The message isn't resonating — revisit the call to action or the offer.
  • Bounce rate above 3%? Pause that sending account and investigate the domain's reputation.
  • Click rate spiking without replies? Your content is interesting but your CTA isn't converting — rework the landing page or the ask.

MailClaw gives you all the tools. The compounding advantage comes from the habit of using them consistently. Start with two or three of these tips this week, build them into your workflow, and then layer in the rest. You'll quickly find that running a sophisticated, high-performing email operation from your local machine — no expensive SaaS subscriptions, no vendor lock-in, full control over your data — isn't just possible. It's genuinely better.

articles.title: Best Practices for AI-Powered Email Automation in 2026
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: A practical guide to getting the most out of AI-powered email automation in 2026, covering deliverability, sequence design, contact enrichment, and how to build intelligent email agents that actually convert.
articles.content:
The State of AI Email Automation in 2026

Email automation has crossed a threshold. What used to mean "send this template to everyone on Tuesday" now means deploying intelligent agents that read replies, adjust tone based on CRM signals, enrich contact data on the fly, and make branching decisions without human intervention. The tooling has caught up with the ambition — but only if you know how to use it well.

Whether you're running cold outreach for a SaaS product, nurturing leads from a HubSpot pipeline, or managing transactional sequences through SendGrid, the fundamentals of good AI-powered email automation remain consistent. This guide covers what actually works in 2026 — with practical examples you can implement today.

Build Your Sequences Around Intent, Not Intervals

The most common mistake in email automation is treating sequences as a calendar problem. "Send email 1 on day 0, email 2 on day 3, email 3 on day 7." This approach ignores the single most powerful input you have: what your contact actually did.

Intent-driven sequences use behavioral signals to determine the next step:

  • Opened but didn't click? Send a shorter, curiosity-driven follow-up with a single CTA.
  • Clicked but didn't reply? Trigger a sequence branch that addresses the specific link they clicked.
  • Replied with a question? Route to an AI email agent for an intelligent, contextual response.
  • No activity after 5 days? Switch to a re-engagement variant with a different subject line pattern.

In MailClaw's sequence builder, you can configure these branch conditions visually from your localhost dashboard at localhost:3100, or define them declaratively in a sequence config file:

mailclaw sequence create --name "SaaS Onboarding" \
  --trigger "contact.tag=trial_started" \
  --branch-on "open,click,reply,bounce" \
  --ai-agent "onboarding-agent-v2"

The --branch-on flag tells MailClaw to pause the linear sequence and hand off to conditional logic the moment a signal fires. This alone will improve reply rates significantly over fixed-interval drips.

Contact Enrichment Is Not Optional Anymore

Sending email to a name and an address is table stakes. Sending email to a person — with their role, company size, tech stack, recent funding round, or LinkedIn activity — is what separates a 3% reply rate from a 14% one.

Enrich Before You Write

The best time to enrich a contact is before your AI writes the first email, not after the sequence has already started. MailClaw's contact enrichment pipeline runs automatically when you import a list or add a contact via API:

mailclaw contacts import ./leads.csv --enrich --source clearbit,hunter

This command imports your CSV, runs enrichment against configured providers, and populates fields like company.size, contact.title, contact.linkedin, and company.tech_stack — all of which become available as dynamic variables in your email templates and as context for your AI agents.

Use Enrichment Data to Segment, Not Just Personalize

Personalization at the token level (Hi {{first_name}}) is expected and barely noticed. Segmentation at the sequence level is where enrichment data earns its keep. Use company size to route contacts to different sequences entirely. Use tech stack data to trigger sequences that speak directly to integration pain points. Use job title signals to adjust the authority level of your messaging.

Pro tip: If a contact's enriched data shows they're using Salesforce and their title includes "RevOps," your AI agent should know to lead with CRM workflow pain — not generic productivity messaging. Feed that context into your agent's system prompt.

Configuring AI Email Agents That Actually Sound Human

AI email agents in 2026 are capable of handling entire reply threads, objection sequences, and scheduling loops without human input. But poorly configured agents produce robotic, over-eager emails that destroy trust fast.

Define a Clear Persona and Scope

Every AI agent in MailClaw runs on an OpenClaw-powered inference layer, which means you have full control over the system prompt, persona, and behavioral constraints. Don't skip this configuration:

mailclaw agent create \
  --name "outreach-agent-v1" \
  --persona "You are a helpful sales rep at Acme Corp. Keep emails under 120 words. Never use the word 'synergy'. Always end with a single, specific question." \
  --scope "reply,follow-up" \
  --max-threads 3

The --max-threads flag limits how many back-and-forth replies the agent handles before escalating to a human. For cold outreach, 2-3 exchanges is usually the right threshold. For customer support sequences, you might push it higher.

Give Agents Access to the Right Context

An agent without context is just autocomplete. Connect your agents to your contact data, enrichment fields, and CRM notes so they can reference real information:

  • Sync MailClaw with HubSpot or Salesforce using the mailclaw sync command to pull deal stage, last activity, and contact properties.
  • Attach sequence history to agent context so it knows what's already been said.
  • Pass enrichment fields like company.recent_news or contact.recent_post as injected variables when available.

Deliverability Is a System, Not a Setting

You can have the best sequence in the world and still land in spam. In 2026, deliverability is an ongoing operational discipline, not a one-time checkbox.

Warm Up Every Sending Identity

Whether you're connecting Gmail, Outlook, or a custom SMTP account through SendGrid or Postmark, every new sending identity needs a warm-up period. MailClaw's deliverability tools include a built-in warm-up scheduler:

mailclaw account add --provider gmail --oauth \
  --warmup --warmup-days 21 --warmup-start-volume 10

This gradually ramps send volume from 10 emails/day to your target volume over 21 days, mixing real outreach with inbox-to-inbox warmup signals to build sender reputation before you hit full campaign volume.

Monitor What Matters

From the MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100/deliverability, you can track:

  • Bounce rate by domain — if a specific domain is bouncing hard, quarantine it before it damages your sender score.
  • Spam complaint rate — anything above 0.1% needs immediate attention.
  • Reply-to-send ratio — a strong positive signal that improves inbox placement over time.
  • SPF/DKIM/DMARC validation — MailClaw checks these on every connected account and alerts you to misconfiguration.

Rotate Sending Accounts Intelligently

For high-volume campaigns, multi-account rotation is essential. MailClaw's multi-account support lets you pool sending identities and distribute volume automatically:

mailclaw campaign launch --name "Q2 Outreach" \
  --sequence "saas-cold-v3" \
  --accounts "account1,account2,account3" \
  --rotate round-robin \
  --daily-limit 80

Keep each account under 80-100 sends per day for cold outreach on new domains. Established domains with strong reputation can handle more, but err conservative until your metrics prove otherwise.

Treat Open-Source as a Feature, Not a Footnote

Running MailClaw locally means your contact data, enrichment results, AI prompts, and sequence logic never leave your machine. For teams handling GDPR-sensitive data or enterprise prospect lists, this is a genuine compliance advantage — not just a nice-to-have.

Being open-source and OpenClaw-powered also means you can inspect exactly what your AI agents are doing, fork the inference layer, or swap in a different model without waiting for a SaaS vendor to ship the feature. That kind of transparency is increasingly valuable as AI behavior in sales contexts comes under more scrutiny.

The Checklist Before You Launch Any Campaign

  1. Contacts are enriched and segmented by intent signal or firmographic data.
  2. Sending accounts have completed warm-up and show healthy deliverability scores.
  3. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records are validated in the MailClaw dashboard.
  4. Sequence branches are configured for open, click, reply, and no-activity scenarios.
  5. AI agent persona and scope are defined, with max-thread limits set.
  6. Daily send limits are configured per account with rotation enabled.
  7. Unsubscribe handling is active and linked to your suppression list.
  8. You've sent a test sequence to a seed inbox and verified rendering across Gmail and Outlook.

Email automation done well is not about sending more — it's about sending smarter, with the right context, at the right moment, from a trusted identity. The tools are there. The differentiator in 2026 is the discipline to configure them properly and the patience to let the data guide your iterations.

articles.title: How to Write Cold Emails That Get Replies Using MailClaw AI
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to write cold emails that actually get replies by combining proven copywriting frameworks with MailClaw's AI email agents, contact enrichment, and sequence builder — all running locally on your Mac.
articles.content:
Why Most Cold Emails Fail Before They're Even Read

The average professional receives over 120 emails a day. Your cold email competes with newsletters, internal Slack notifications forwarded to inboxes, invoices, and a dozen other cold emails from people who had the exact same idea you did. The brutal truth is that most cold emails fail not because the product is bad or the timing is wrong — they fail because they were written for the sender, not the recipient.

Generic subject lines. Wall-of-text introductions. A pitch that leads with "we help companies like yours..." The delete key is milliseconds away, and readers will use it without guilt.

This guide walks you through the principles of cold emails that actually generate replies, and shows you how to use MailClaw's AI email agents and sequence builder to scale that quality — without sacrificing personalization.

The Anatomy of a High-Converting Cold Email

Before touching any automation tool, you need to understand what makes a cold email worth replying to. Every high-performing cold email shares five structural elements:

  • A subject line that earns the open — specific, curious, or relevant. Not clickbait.
  • A personalized opening line — something that proves you did your homework.
  • A clear, concise value proposition — what's in it for them, stated in one or two sentences.
  • Social proof or credibility signal — a name, result, or recognizable reference point.
  • A single, low-friction call to action — one ask, not three options.

Keep your email under 150 words. Shorter emails signal confidence. Long emails signal uncertainty — like you're afraid one reason won't be enough.

Subject Lines That Get Opened

Your subject line is doing one job: getting the preview pane click. It doesn't need to sell. It needs to create enough curiosity or relevance that the recipient thinks "okay, I'll give this ten seconds."

Frameworks that consistently outperform:

  • Name + specific trigger: "Saw your funding announcement, had a thought"
  • Mutual connection reference: "[Mutual contact] suggested I reach out"
  • Direct and honest: "Quick question about [Company]'s outbound process"
  • Curiosity gap: "The reason your reply rate dropped in Q3"

Avoid subject lines that include "synergy," "partnership opportunity," "touching base," or anything that sounds like it was written by someone who learned email from a 2009 sales training PDF.

Writing the Opening Line

The first sentence has to be about them, not you. This is where most cold emails collapse. Reps open with "My name is Jordan and I work at Acme..." — nobody asked.

Instead, reference something real and specific:

  • A recent blog post they published
  • A job posting that signals a business challenge
  • A LinkedIn comment they made
  • A company milestone or press mention

This is exactly where MailClaw's contact enrichment feature pays dividends. When you import a lead list — whether from HubSpot, Salesforce, or a CSV — MailClaw automatically enriches each contact with publicly available signals: recent activity, company news, LinkedIn data, and job title context. That data feeds directly into your AI-generated opening lines.

Using MailClaw's AI Email Agents to Personalize at Scale

Personalization at scale sounds like a contradiction, but it isn't — if you have the right tooling. MailClaw's AI email agents, powered by OpenClaw, let you define a prompt template that uses enriched contact data to generate a unique opening line for every recipient in your sequence.

Here's how to set up an AI-personalized sequence from your terminal:

# Start MailClaw if it's not already running
mailclaw start

# Import your lead list and trigger enrichment
mailclaw contacts import --file leads.csv --enrich

# Create a new sequence
mailclaw sequence create --name "Q1 Outbound" --ai-personalize

# Open your local dashboard to review enriched contacts
open http://localhost:3100

Once your contacts are enriched and your sequence is created, navigate to the AI Agent tab in your localhost dashboard at http://localhost:3100. Here you'll define your personalization prompt — for example:

Given the following contact data: {{contact.name}}, {{contact.company}}, 
{{contact.recent_news}}, {{contact.job_title}} — write a single opening 
sentence (max 20 words) that references something specific and real about 
them. Be direct. Do not use flattery.

The AI agent generates a unique first sentence for every contact, which gets stitched into your email template before sending. The result: emails that feel handwritten, even when you're sending to 500 people.

Building Your Sequence in MailClaw

A single cold email rarely converts. The real results come from a well-timed sequence — typically three to five touchpoints across two to three weeks. MailClaw's sequence builder lets you design multi-step outreach flows with conditional logic, delay rules, and automatic reply detection.

A high-performing cold outreach sequence looks like this:

  1. Day 1 — The initial email: Short, personalized, one clear CTA.
  2. Day 4 — The value-add follow-up: A relevant case study, article, or insight. No guilt-tripping about not replying.
  3. Day 9 — The bump: One sentence. "Just bubbling this up in case it got buried."
  4. Day 14 — The breakup email: "I'll stop reaching out after this — but wanted to share one last thought." Honest, human, no hard feelings.

MailClaw automatically stops the sequence the moment a contact replies, so you never send a follow-up to someone who already responded. Configure this in your sequence settings:

mailclaw sequence edit "Q1 Outbound" \
  --stop-on-reply \
  --stop-on-click \
  --unsubscribe-link required

Deliverability: The Hidden Variable That Kills Campaigns

You can write the best cold email in the world and still get zero replies if it lands in spam. Deliverability is the unsexy but critical foundation of any outreach campaign.

MailClaw's built-in deliverability monitoring tools give you a real-time health score for each sending account. Whether you're connected via Gmail OAuth, Outlook, or a dedicated SMTP provider like SendGrid or Postmark, MailClaw tracks:

  • Domain and IP reputation scores
  • SPF, DKIM, and DMARC configuration status
  • Bounce rates and spam complaint ratios per account
  • Inbox placement signals across major providers

Check your deliverability health before launching any sequence:

mailclaw deliverability check --account work@yourcompany.com

If your score drops below threshold, MailClaw flags it in the dashboard with specific remediation steps — whether that's warming up the domain, reducing send volume, or fixing a misconfigured DKIM record.

Multi-Account Sending and Inbox Rotation

For higher-volume outreach, MailClaw's multi-account support lets you distribute sends across multiple connected inboxes — Gmail, Outlook, or custom SMTP — reducing per-domain send volume and protecting your primary domain's reputation.

# Add a secondary sending account
mailclaw accounts add --email outreach@subdomain.com --smtp sendgrid

# Enable inbox rotation for a sequence
mailclaw sequence edit "Q1 Outbound" --rotate-accounts

This is especially important if you're sending more than 100 emails per day. Spreading sends across warmed-up accounts dramatically improves inbox placement rates.

What to Measure and How to Improve

Open rates are a vanity metric in 2024 — Apple Mail Privacy Protection has made them unreliable. Focus on what actually matters:

  • Reply rate: The north star. Anything above 5% is solid. Above 10% is excellent.
  • Positive reply rate: Replies that aren't unsubscribes or "remove me" responses.
  • Bounce rate: Keep hard bounces under 2%. MailClaw flags bad addresses during enrichment.
  • Sequence completion rate: How many contacts make it through without replying — a signal that your copy or targeting needs work.

MailClaw's dashboard at http://localhost:3100 surfaces all of these metrics per sequence and per step, so you can identify exactly which touchpoint is underperforming and run A/B variants against it.

The Mindset Shift That Changes Everything

Cold email is not about selling. It's about earning a conversation with someone who doesn't know you yet.

The best cold emails are genuinely helpful, honestly positioned, and respectful of the reader's time. They don't pretend to have a relationship that doesn't exist. They don't manufacture urgency. They make one clear, easy ask and then get out of the way.

MailClaw's AI agents and automation infrastructure give you the leverage to do this at scale — but the leverage only works if the foundation is solid. Write one great email template. Enrich your contacts properly. Let the AI personalize it. Let the sequence do the follow-up. Monitor deliverability so your emails actually land.

Because MailClaw runs entirely on your local machine — no SaaS subscription, no data leaving your infrastructure, fully open source — you maintain complete control over your outreach data and sending behavior. That's not just a privacy win; it's a trust signal that compounds over time.

Start with your best 50 leads. Run the sequence. Read every reply. Iterate. Then scale.

articles.title: MailClaw Email Etiquette: Guidelines for AI-Assisted Outreach
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: Learn how to use AI-assisted email outreach responsibly and effectively with MailClaw — covering personalization best practices, frequency guidelines, consent management, and how to configure your AI agents to send emails that get replies, not spam complaints.
articles.content:
Why Email Etiquette Matters More in the Age of AI

AI-powered email tools have made it possible for a solo founder to run outreach at the scale of an entire sales team. That's genuinely exciting — but it also introduces a real risk. When sending becomes effortless, the temptation to send more often wins out over the discipline to send better. The result? Inboxes flooded with templated, hollow messages that recipients tune out or, worse, mark as spam.

MailClaw was built on the belief that AI should make your outreach more human, not less. Running locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, it gives you full control over your campaigns — no third-party servers holding your data, no black-box algorithms deciding what gets sent. But control is only valuable when paired with good judgment. This guide lays out the etiquette principles that should govern every sequence you build, every agent you deploy, and every contact you enrich.

The Foundation: Consent, Context, and Clarity

Always Establish a Legitimate Reason to Reach Out

Before you build a single step in the MailClaw sequence builder, ask yourself: why does this person want to hear from me? A legitimate reason isn't just "they're in my target market." It means there's a genuine, contextual connection — they downloaded a resource, they're a past customer, they fit a specific problem you can credibly solve, or you have a warm mutual connection.

MailClaw's contact enrichment layer can pull in firmographic data, job titles, recent funding rounds, and social signals to help you understand who you're emailing. Use that intelligence to qualify before you send, not to blast a wider net. Enrichment is a tool for relevance, not volume.

Respect Regional Compliance Requirements

GDPR, CAN-SPAM, CASL, and Australia's Spam Act all carry real teeth. The rules differ by region, but the core principle is consistent: recipients should know who is contacting them, why, and how to stop it. Every sequence you configure in MailClaw should include:

  • A clear sender name and reply-to address (configurable under your SMTP or OAuth account settings)
  • A physical mailing address or registered business location in your signature
  • An unsubscribe mechanism that works instantly — MailClaw handles one-click unsubscribe headers automatically when deliverability tools are enabled
  • Honest subject lines that reflect the actual email content

If you're connecting MailClaw to Gmail or Outlook via OAuth, the sender identity is already verified, which strengthens deliverability and trust. If you're using a SendGrid or Postmark SMTP relay, make sure your domain has SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records properly configured — MailClaw's deliverability dashboard surfaces these checks at a glance.

Writing AI-Generated Emails That Don't Feel AI-Generated

Personalization Must Go Beyond the First Name

Inserting {{first_name}} into a subject line stopped being impressive around 2017. Today's recipients can smell a mail-merged template from the preview pane. Genuine personalization means referencing something specific and relevant — a recent company announcement, a role transition, a piece of content they published, or a shared context.

When configuring an AI email agent in MailClaw, you can pass enrichment fields directly into the agent's prompt context. A well-structured prompt might look like this:

You are writing a cold outreach email on behalf of {{sender_name}}.
The recipient is {{first_name}} {{last_name}}, {{job_title}} at {{company}}.
Recent context: {{enrichment.recent_news}}
Their company raised {{enrichment.funding_round}} in {{enrichment.funding_date}}.

Write a 3-sentence opening that references this context naturally.
Do not mention AI. Do not use the phrase "I hope this finds you well."
Tone: direct, specific, human.

The more structured context you give your agent, the more relevant the output. Garbage in, generic out.

Set Tone Guidelines for Your AI Agents

MailClaw's AI agents inherit a default persona, but you should override it to match your brand voice. In the agent configuration panel (accessible from your local dashboard), you can define tone instructions, prohibited phrases, length constraints, and even industry-specific vocabulary. Common etiquette-driven guardrails to add:

  • No false urgency: Avoid "act now," "limited spots," or artificial deadlines unless they're real
  • No manipulative framing: Don't imply a prior relationship that doesn't exist ("Following up on our conversation…" when there was none)
  • No excessive flattery: One genuine compliment is fine; three is suspicious
  • Match formality to industry: A cold email to a VP of Engineering at a startup reads differently than one to a General Counsel at a law firm

Sequence Design: Frequency, Timing, and Knowing When to Stop

The Right Cadence Is the One That Feels Human

A four-email sequence is almost always enough for cold outreach. The MailClaw sequence builder lets you set precise delays between steps — use them thoughtfully. A reasonable cold outreach cadence might look like:

  1. Day 1: Initial outreach — personalized, specific, short (under 100 words)
  2. Day 4: Brief follow-up — add a new angle, a case study, or a relevant resource
  3. Day 10: One more attempt — acknowledge you've reached out before, keep it light
  4. Day 18: Breakup email — give them an easy out, leave the door open

After four touches with no response, stop. Silence is an answer. Continuing past this point doesn't improve conversion rates — it damages your sender reputation and, more importantly, the recipient's perception of your brand.

Use MailClaw's Deliverability Tools to Catch Problems Early

Before a sequence goes live, run it through MailClaw's built-in deliverability checks. From the CLI, you can trigger a pre-send audit:

mailclaw sequence audit --id=seq_outreach_q1 --check=deliverability

This will flag common issues: missing unsubscribe headers, spam-trigger phrases in subject lines, sending domain health, and bounce rate thresholds from previous campaigns. Think of it as a spell-check for your outreach ethics — catching problems before they become complaints.

Warm Up New Sending Domains Properly

If you're launching outreach from a new domain, never start at full volume. Use MailClaw's multi-account support to rotate sending across warmed accounts, and configure a sending ramp in your sequence settings:

mailclaw account set --id=acct_domain2 --daily-limit=20 --ramp=true --ramp-days=14

Jumping to hundreds of emails per day from a cold domain is a fast path to the spam folder — and once you're there, it's difficult to recover. Slow ramps protect both your deliverability and your recipients' inboxes.

Managing Replies, Opt-Outs, and Relationships

Treat Every Reply as a Human Conversation

When an AI agent generates outreach, it's easy to forget that replies come back to a real person. Establish a clear handoff protocol: AI drafts and sends, but humans review and respond to replies. If you're using MailClaw integrated with HubSpot or Salesforce via webhook, you can trigger a CRM task the moment a positive reply is detected, ensuring no warm lead falls through the cracks.

Etiquette rule of thumb: The moment someone replies — even to say "not interested" — the AI sequence should stop and a human should take over. MailClaw's reply detection handles the former automatically. The latter is your responsibility.

Honor Opt-Outs Immediately and Permanently

When someone unsubscribes or replies with "remove me," that preference should propagate everywhere — not just the current sequence. MailClaw maintains a global suppression list across all your campaigns and accounts. You can inspect and export it anytime:

mailclaw contacts export --filter=suppressed --format=csv

If you sync contacts from an external CRM like HubSpot or a CSV import, always run an opt-out check against the suppression list before any sequence starts. MailClaw does this automatically on sequence launch, but it's worth building the habit of checking manually for large imports.

The Open-Source Advantage: Transparency You Can Actually Verify

One underappreciated benefit of using an open-source tool like MailClaw is that the etiquette principles described in this article aren't just policies — they're verifiable in the code. You can inspect exactly how suppression lists are maintained, how AI agent prompts are constructed, how deliverability checks work, and what data stays on your machine versus leaves it.

That transparency is worth something. When you tell a prospect that you're using a locally-run, open-source system to manage outreach, it's a meaningful signal that you take privacy seriously — both theirs and yours. In a world where every SaaS tool is training on your data in some opaque server farm, running MailClaw on localhost:3100 is itself an act of good faith.

A Checklist Before Every Campaign Launch

Use this as a final gate before you hit send on any sequence:

  • Does every contact have a legitimate reason to hear from me?
  • Is the email genuinely personalized beyond a name merge?
  • Is the subject line honest and non-manipulative?
  • Does the sequence stop at a reasonable number of touches?
  • Are unsubscribe headers and physical address included?
  • Has the sending domain been warmed appropriately?
  • Have I run the deliverability audit in MailClaw?
  • Is there a human ready to handle positive replies?
  • Are opt-outs synced across all accounts and CRMs?

Good outreach isn't about tricking people into opening emails. It's about finding the right people, saying something worth reading, and respecting their time and attention. MailClaw gives you the tools to scale that discipline — not to automate your way around it.

articles.title: 5 Common Mistakes When Setting Up Email Automation with MailClaw
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Setting up email automation seems straightforward until your open rates tank, contacts go stale, and sequences fire at the wrong time. This guide walks through five critical mistakes MailClaw users make and exactly how to fix them before they cost you deliverability or deals.
articles.content:
Why Your Email Automation Setup Might Be Working Against You

Email automation done right is one of the highest-leverage activities in any outreach strategy. Done wrong, it burns your sender reputation, annoys prospects, and buries your messages in spam folders before a human ever reads them. The frustrating part? Most of the damage happens silently, in configuration choices made in the first hour of setup.

MailClaw gives you powerful tools out of the box — AI email agents, contact enrichment, a visual sequence builder, and a full deliverability dashboard running locally at localhost:3100. But power without proper configuration is just a fast way to fail. Here are the five most common mistakes users make when first setting up MailClaw, and exactly how to avoid them.

Mistake #1: Skipping the Warm-Up Phase on New Sending Accounts

This is the single most common and most damaging mistake. You install MailClaw, connect your Gmail or Outlook account via OAuth, build a beautiful 5-step sequence, and immediately fire it at 500 contacts. Within a week, your open rates are in the single digits and your domain is flagged.

Email providers like Google and Microsoft use engagement signals to score sender reputation. A brand-new sending address that suddenly pushes high volume looks like a compromised account or a spam operation — because that's often exactly what it is.

What to Do Instead

Before running any sequence, use MailClaw's deliverability tools to establish a baseline. Navigate to Settings → Sending Accounts in your local dashboard and enable the warm-up schedule for any new account. A safe ramp looks like this:

# Example warm-up schedule via MailClaw CLI
mailclaw warmup --account hello@yourdomain.com \
  --start-volume 10 \
  --daily-increase 5 \
  --target-volume 100 \
  --days 18

This gradually increases your daily send volume over 18 days while MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered engine monitors bounce rates, spam complaints, and reply signals. For accounts connected through SendGrid or a dedicated SMTP relay, the same principle applies — the IP needs to build history before you push volume through it.

Rule of thumb: Never send more than 50 emails per day from a new account in the first two weeks, regardless of how good your copy is.

Mistake #2: Using Unverified or Unenriched Contact Data

Loading a raw CSV export from HubSpot, Salesforce, or a scraped list and pointing a sequence directly at it is a recipe for high bounce rates. Hard bounces above 2% will trigger spam filters across most major email providers. They're also a signal to MailClaw's deliverability monitor that something upstream is broken.

The less obvious problem is relevance. Contacts without enriched data mean your AI email agents are writing generic messages that convert poorly, because they have nothing specific to personalize against.

Run Enrichment Before Every Sequence

MailClaw's contact enrichment feature pulls in firmographic data, job titles, LinkedIn signals, and recent company activity before your sequence ever runs. Make this a mandatory step in your workflow:

# Enrich a contact list before importing to a sequence
mailclaw contacts enrich \
  --list ./prospects.csv \
  --fields company,title,linkedin,tech_stack \
  --verify-email true \
  --output ./enriched_prospects.csv

The --verify-email true flag runs each address through syntax validation, MX record checks, and mailbox verification. Contacts that fail get flagged rather than silently included. This alone can cut your bounce rate by 60–80% on cold lists.

Once enriched, these signals feed directly into MailClaw's AI email agents, which use the additional context to write first lines and subject lines that reference real details — a recent funding round, a tech stack match, a hiring signal — instead of defaulting to "I noticed you work at [Company]."

Mistake #3: Building Sequences Without Exit Conditions

The sequence builder in MailClaw makes it easy to chain together 4, 5, or 6 email steps with delays between them. What many users forget is setting the conditions that should stop the sequence, not just advance it.

Imagine a prospect replies to step 2 expressing interest. Without proper exit conditions, steps 3 through 6 still fire on schedule. Now you've sent a "just following up" email to someone who already responded positively. It signals that your outreach is automated and not human-monitored — and it's embarrassing.

Configure Smart Exit Triggers

In the MailClaw sequence builder, every sequence should have at minimum these exit conditions enabled:

  • Reply detected — pause the sequence immediately when any reply is received, regardless of sentiment
  • Link clicked — optionally pause or branch when a tracked link is clicked
  • Out-of-office detected — delay the next step rather than exit, so you follow up when they're back
  • Unsubscribe or bounce — hard exit and suppress the contact across all sequences
  • CRM stage change — if you're syncing with HubSpot or Salesforce, exit when a deal moves to a specific pipeline stage

You can configure these in Sequences → [Your Sequence] → Exit Rules from the dashboard at localhost:3100, or via the CLI:

mailclaw sequence update --id seq_abc123 \
  --exit-on reply,click,unsubscribe,bounce \
  --pause-on out_of_office \
  --crm-exit-stage "Meeting Booked"

Mistake #4: Letting AI Agents Run Without Review Gates

One of MailClaw's most powerful features is its AI email agents — autonomous agents powered by OpenClaw that can draft, personalize, and even send emails based on triggers and contact data. Used well, they're extraordinary. Used carelessly, they send things you'd never consciously approve.

The mistake here isn't using AI agents — it's setting them to auto-send before you've validated the output quality on a representative sample of your contacts.

Use Draft Mode First

When configuring an AI email agent for the first time, always start with --mode draft. This tells the agent to generate and queue emails without sending, so you can review them in the dashboard before anything goes out:

# Launch an AI agent in draft-review mode
mailclaw agent run \
  --agent outreach_agent_v1 \
  --contacts ./enriched_prospects.csv \
  --mode draft \
  --review-threshold 0.85

The --review-threshold 0.85 flag means any email the agent scores below 85% confidence (based on personalization quality and tone matching) gets flagged for manual review. Only emails above the threshold are queued for your approval batch.

After reviewing 20–30 drafts and making any prompt adjustments, you can increase your confidence in the agent's output and selectively move to --mode supervised or eventually --mode auto once trust is established.

"AI agents in MailClaw are teammates, not replacements. They work best when you set expectations clearly and check their work early."

Mistake #5: Ignoring the Deliverability Dashboard Until Something Breaks

Most users open the MailClaw deliverability dashboard reactively — after open rates drop, after a domain gets blacklisted, or after a client asks why their campaign underperformed. At that point, you're in damage-control mode instead of prevention mode.

The deliverability tools in MailClaw are genuinely powerful, but only if you're watching them proactively. They surface real-time data on:

  • SPF, DKIM, and DMARC alignment per sending account
  • Domain and IP blacklist status across major blocklists
  • Bounce and complaint rate trends by sequence and account
  • Inbox placement estimates for Gmail, Outlook, and Apple Mail
  • Engagement drop signals that precede deliverability degradation

Build a Weekly Deliverability Review Into Your Process

Set a calendar reminder to spend 10 minutes each week in your MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100/deliverability. Look specifically at:

  1. Complaint rate — should stay below 0.1% per sending account
  2. Hard bounce rate — flag anything above 1.5% for immediate list review
  3. DKIM/SPF pass rate — should be 100%; anything less means a DNS configuration issue
  4. Sequence-level engagement — compare open and reply rates across sequences to identify which ones are hurting your overall domain reputation

You can also schedule automated health reports via the CLI so they land in your inbox (or a Slack webhook) every Monday morning:

mailclaw report schedule \
  --type deliverability \
  --frequency weekly \
  --day monday \
  --output email \
  --recipient you@yourdomain.com

The Bottom Line

Email automation fails predictably. The same five mistakes show up across teams of all sizes — from solo founders using MailClaw on their MacBook to growth teams managing multi-account campaigns across dozens of domains. The good news is that every one of these mistakes is preventable with the right configuration upfront.

Warm up your accounts. Enrich and verify your contacts. Build sequences with smart exits. Review your AI agents before letting them run free. And treat the deliverability dashboard as a live instrument, not an alarm bell.

MailClaw is open source and built to give you full control over your outreach stack — no black boxes, no opaque sending infrastructure, just your machine, your data, and a powerful local toolset. Use that transparency to your advantage.

articles.title: How to Write Better Prompts for MailClaw AI Email Generation
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how to craft precise, effective prompts for MailClaw's AI email generation engine so your outreach sequences feel human, convert better, and land in the inbox every time.
articles.content:
Why Prompting Matters More Than You Think

Most people fire up MailClaw, type something like "write a cold email about my SaaS product" into the AI agent, and then wonder why the output sounds like every other forgettable pitch in their prospect's inbox. The problem isn't the model. It's the prompt.

MailClaw's AI email generation is powered by OpenClaw, which means it runs entirely on your machine at localhost:3100 — no third-party servers handling your contact data, no rate limits killing your momentum mid-campaign. But even the best locally-running model needs clear instructions to produce output worth sending. Think of prompting like briefing a talented copywriter: the more context you give, the better the result.

This guide breaks down exactly how to write prompts that get MailClaw producing emails your prospects will actually read.

The Four Pillars of a Strong MailClaw Prompt

Before we get into specific techniques, understand the four things every effective AI email prompt needs:

  • Role: Who is the AI writing as?
  • Context: What does the recipient care about?
  • Goal: What action should the email drive?
  • Constraints: Tone, length, format, and what to avoid.

When you leave any of these out, the model fills in the blanks with generic assumptions. That's how you end up with emails that open with "I hope this finds you well."

Using Contact Enrichment Data in Your Prompts

One of MailClaw's most powerful features is contact enrichment — the ability to pull in LinkedIn data, company details, tech stack signals, and recent news before generating your email. If you're not feeding that enriched data back into your prompt, you're leaving serious personalization on the table.

A Basic Prompt vs. An Enriched Prompt

Here's what a weak prompt looks like inside MailClaw's sequence builder:

Write a cold outreach email to a VP of Marketing at a B2B company.

Here's the same prompt rewritten to leverage enriched contact fields:

You are a senior account executive at a revenue intelligence company.

Write a concise cold email (under 120 words) to {{contact.first_name}}, 
the {{contact.job_title}} at {{contact.company_name}}.

Context:
- Their company recently {{contact.recent_news}}
- They use {{contact.tech_stack}} in their current stack
- Their company has {{contact.employee_count}} employees

Goal: Get them to agree to a 20-minute call to discuss how we help 
marketing teams reduce CAC by 30%.

Tone: Direct, peer-to-peer, no fluff. Do not use "I hope this email 
finds you well" or any similar filler phrases. End with one clear, 
low-friction CTA.

The difference in output quality is dramatic. MailClaw's enrichment pipeline can pull signals from HubSpot, Salesforce, and LinkedIn via its built-in connectors — make sure those fields are mapped correctly in your dashboard settings before building sequences.

Structuring Prompts for Email Sequences

When you're building a multi-step sequence in MailClaw's sequence builder, each email in the chain needs a prompt that's aware of the emails that came before it. This prevents repetition and keeps the narrative thread coherent across touchpoints.

The Sequence-Aware Prompt Pattern

Use a consistent structure across your sequence steps:

# Email 3 of 5 — Follow-Up After No Reply

Context: {{contact.first_name}} has not responded to two previous emails. 
Email 1 introduced our product and referenced their recent funding round.
Email 2 shared a relevant case study from their industry ({{contact.industry}}).

Your task: Write a follow-up email that:
- Acknowledges this is a follow-up without being apologetic
- Introduces a new angle: a specific pain point (pipeline visibility)
- Is 80 words or fewer
- Ends with a yes/no question to lower the response barrier

Tone: Confident, slightly informal, no corporate speak.
Subject line: Make it feel like a genuine reply thread (e.g., "Re: quick thought")

By keeping each prompt aware of the sequence's history, MailClaw generates a campaign that feels like a natural conversation rather than a series of disconnected blasts.

Prompting MailClaw's AI Email Agents

MailClaw's AI email agents go beyond one-shot generation — they can monitor replies, classify intent, and trigger follow-up actions automatically. To get the most out of agents, you need to write system-level prompts that define their behavior clearly.

Writing an Agent System Prompt

When configuring an agent in your local dashboard, treat the system prompt like a job description:

You are an outbound sales agent for [Company Name], a developer tools 
company targeting engineering managers at Series A–C startups.

Your responsibilities:
1. Draft initial outreach emails personalized to each contact's GitHub 
   activity and job posting signals
2. Classify inbound replies as: Interested / Not Now / Not Interested / Referral
3. If classified as "Interested," draft a calendar invite suggestion referencing 
   their timezone ({{contact.timezone}})
4. If classified as "Not Now," schedule a follow-up for 45 days out and 
   note the reason in the CRM

Rules:
- Never misrepresent our product's capabilities
- Always match the formality level of the prospect's reply
- Flag any reply that mentions a competitor for human review

This kind of structured agent prompt gives MailClaw the guardrails it needs to operate autonomously without going off-script. You can pair this with Gmail or Outlook OAuth and SendGrid delivery routing directly from the MailClaw config.

Tone and Voice: Getting Specific Enough to Matter

Telling the AI to write in a "professional tone" is nearly useless. Every model defaults to "professional." Instead, describe tone with specificity:

  • Instead of: "Professional and friendly"
  • Try: "Write like a founder talking to another founder — confident, direct, occasional dry humor, no buzzwords like 'synergy' or 'ecosystem'"
  • Instead of: "Keep it concise"
  • Try: "Maximum 3 sentences per paragraph. Total email body under 100 words. No bullet points."

You can save tone profiles in MailClaw's open-source config as reusable prompt fragments so you're not rewriting voice instructions for every new campaign.

A Reusable Tone Block Example

# tones/founder-to-founder.txt

Tone: Write as a startup founder, not a salesperson. 
Be direct and slightly casual. Use short sentences. 
Avoid passive voice. No filler phrases. 
One idea per paragraph. Sign off with first name only.

Reference this file in your MailClaw prompt templates using the --tone-file flag in the CLI:

mailclaw generate --template outreach-v2 \
  --tone-file tones/founder-to-founder.txt \
  --contact-list leads/q3-enterprise.csv \
  --sequence "cold-5-step"

Deliverability-Aware Prompting

Beautiful emails that land in spam folders are worthless. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools can flag problematic patterns, but you can prevent many issues at the prompt level itself.

Include deliverability guidance directly in your prompts:

"Avoid spam trigger words including: free, guaranteed, no risk, limited time, act now, click here. Do not use ALL CAPS for emphasis. Keep the email under 150 words to improve plain-text rendering across email clients including Gmail and Outlook."

For multi-account sending setups, you can also prompt the AI to vary sentence structure and vocabulary slightly between accounts — a useful technique when running parallel outreach across different sending domains managed within MailClaw's multi-account support.

Testing and Iterating Your Prompts

The best prompt is the one you've tested. MailClaw makes this straightforward because everything runs locally — you can iterate in seconds without burning API credits or worrying about data leaving your machine.

  1. Generate 5 variations of a prompt by adjusting one variable at a time (tone, length constraint, CTA phrasing).
  2. Run deliverability checks on each variant using MailClaw's built-in spam score analysis before launching.
  3. A/B test subject lines through the sequence builder by tagging variants and tracking open rates in the localhost dashboard.
  4. Review reply classifications from your AI agent after the first 50 sends — if "Not Interested" rates are high, revisit your value proposition framing in the prompt.

Good prompting is an iterative process. Keep a prompt changelog in your MailClaw project folder so you know what changed between campaign versions and why.

Quick Reference: Prompt Checklist

Before you submit any prompt to MailClaw's AI generation engine, run through this checklist:

  • ✅ Did you define the sender's role and company context?
  • ✅ Did you inject enriched contact fields (name, title, company, signals)?
  • ✅ Did you specify word count or paragraph constraints?
  • ✅ Did you describe tone with concrete examples, not vague adjectives?
  • ✅ Did you state the single goal of the email and the CTA clearly?
  • ✅ Did you include deliverability guardrails (words to avoid, formatting rules)?
  • ✅ Is this prompt sequence-aware if it's step 2 or later in a series?

Nail these elements consistently and MailClaw will generate outreach that sounds less like automation and more like something a real person spent time writing. That's the whole point.

articles.title: MailClaw Security Best Practices: Protecting Your Email Data Locally
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how to keep your email data, credentials, and contact lists secure when running MailClaw locally — with practical configuration tips, access controls, and best practices for SMTP, OAuth, and AI agent workflows.
articles.content:
Why Local-First Security Still Matters

Running MailClaw on localhost:3100 already puts you miles ahead of cloud-based email tools when it comes to data privacy. Your contact lists, email sequences, enrichment data, and API keys never leave your machine unless you explicitly send a campaign. But "local" doesn't mean "invincible." A misconfigured SMTP credential, an exposed dashboard port, or a carelessly stored API key can still create real problems — especially when you're connecting to production accounts on Gmail, Outlook, or SendGrid.

This guide walks through the concrete steps you should take to harden your MailClaw setup, whether you're a solo founder running outreach campaigns or a developer building AI email agents for a team.

Securing Your MailClaw Dashboard

Lock Down the Localhost Port

By default, MailClaw serves its dashboard at http://localhost:3100. This is intentionally local-only — nothing is exposed to the public internet out of the box. However, a few common mistakes can accidentally change that:

  • Binding to 0.0.0.0 instead of 127.0.0.1 — This exposes the dashboard on all network interfaces, including your local network. Anyone on the same Wi-Fi could access your campaigns and contacts.
  • Reverse proxying without authentication — If you've set up Nginx or Caddy to access MailClaw remotely, make sure you've added basic auth or an IP allowlist in front of it.
  • Leaving the port open on shared machines — If you're running MailClaw on a shared dev machine or a VM, restrict port 3100 to your user session only.

You can verify what interface MailClaw is binding to by checking your OpenClaw configuration file:

# ~/.mailclaw/config.yaml
server:
  host: 127.0.0.1   # ✅ Correct — local only
  port: 3100
  # host: 0.0.0.0   # ❌ Avoid — exposes to network

Enable Dashboard Authentication

MailClaw's open-source architecture means you can add a login layer directly in the config. Even on localhost, enabling a session password protects you from malicious browser extensions or cross-site request forgery attacks that target local services:

# ~/.mailclaw/config.yaml
auth:
  enabled: true
  session_secret: "use-a-long-random-string-here"
  password_hash: "$2b$12$..."  # bcrypt hash of your password

Generate a bcrypt hash quickly with the MailClaw CLI:

mailclaw auth hash-password --password "your-secure-password"

Protecting SMTP Credentials and OAuth Tokens

This is where most email tool breaches actually happen — not through the dashboard, but through leaked credentials. MailClaw supports both SMTP authentication and OAuth 2.0 for Gmail and Outlook, and each has its own security considerations.

Use OAuth Over SMTP Passwords Where Possible

If you're connecting a Gmail or Microsoft 365 account, always prefer OAuth integration over raw SMTP passwords. OAuth tokens are scoped, revocable, and don't expose your master account password. MailClaw stores OAuth refresh tokens encrypted on disk — but you should still understand where they live:

# Token storage location (macOS)
~/.mailclaw/credentials/
  gmail_oauth_token_account1.enc
  outlook_oauth_token_account2.enc

These .enc files are AES-256 encrypted using a key derived from your machine's hardware UUID combined with your session secret. Back up your session secret separately — if you lose it, you'll need to re-authenticate all your connected accounts.

Rotate Your SendGrid and Third-Party API Keys Regularly
