MailClaw integrates with SendGrid for transactional delivery and supports webhooks from tools like HubSpot and Salesforce for contact enrichment. Each of these connections uses an API key stored in your config. Treat these like passwords:

  • Create restricted API keys in SendGrid — grant only the permissions MailClaw actually needs (mail send, stats read).
  • In HubSpot and Salesforce, use dedicated integration users rather than your admin account credentials.
  • Rotate all third-party keys every 90 days, or immediately after any suspected exposure.
  • Never commit your ~/.mailclaw/config.yaml to a Git repository — add it to .gitignore if you version-control your dotfiles.
# Rotate a SendGrid key in MailClaw CLI
mailclaw accounts update --account sendgrid-main --rotate-key

# Verify current account connections
mailclaw accounts list --show-scopes

Securing Contact Data and Enrichment Pipelines

MailClaw's contact enrichment features pull data from a range of sources to build richer prospect profiles. This is powerful, but it also means sensitive data — email addresses, company info, LinkedIn handles — accumulates in your local database. Here's how to handle it responsibly.

Encrypt Your Local Contact Database

MailClaw stores contact data in a local SQLite database by default. On macOS, you can add a layer of protection by storing this database inside an encrypted disk image, or by enabling MailClaw's built-in encryption option:

# ~/.mailclaw/config.yaml
database:
  path: ~/.mailclaw/data/contacts.db
  encrypt: true
  encryption_key_source: keychain  # Uses macOS Keychain

With keychain as the key source, the database encryption key is stored in your macOS Keychain and unlocked only when your user session is active. This means the database is unreadable even if someone copies the file off your machine.

Audit What Your AI Email Agents Can Access

MailClaw's AI email agents — built on the OpenClaw engine — can autonomously read contact profiles, generate personalized sequences, and trigger follow-ups based on engagement signals. This is one of the platform's most compelling features, but it's also worth auditing carefully.

By default, AI agents have read access to all contacts and write access to sequence assignments. You can scope this down per agent:

# Define agent permissions in your agent config
agent:
  name: "outbound-sdr-agent"
  permissions:
    contacts:
      read: true
      write: false          # Agent can read but not modify contact records
      filter: "segment=cold-outreach"  # Limit to specific segment
    sequences:
      create: false
      assign: true          # Can assign contacts to existing sequences only
    enrichment:
      trigger: false        # Prevent agent from triggering paid enrichment calls

Principle of least privilege applies to AI agents too. An agent that only needs to send follow-up emails doesn't need write access to your entire contact database or the ability to trigger enrichment workflows that hit external APIs.

Network and System-Level Protections

Use macOS Firewall and App Sandbox Rules

Enable the macOS Application Firewall (System Settings → Network → Firewall) and ensure that MailClaw's outbound connections are limited to the domains it actually needs: your SMTP relay, OAuth endpoints, and any enrichment APIs you've explicitly configured. You can use a tool like Little Snitch or the open-source LuLu to monitor and control MailClaw's network activity at the application level.

Monitor Deliverability Without Leaking Data

MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools check your domain reputation, DKIM/SPF/DMARC alignment, and bounce rates. These checks involve making outbound requests to reputation services. Be aware that some third-party deliverability APIs log the domains and IP addresses you query. Prefer MailClaw's built-in local deliverability checks where available, and review which external services are enabled in your config:

# ~/.mailclaw/config.yaml
deliverability:
  local_checks: true        # DNS/SPF/DKIM checks run locally
  external_reputation: false  # Disable third-party IP reputation lookups
  bounce_tracking: local    # Store bounce data locally, not in external service

Practical Security Checklist

Before you send your next campaign, run through this quick checklist:

  1. Dashboard bound to 127.0.0.1 — not 0.0.0.0
  2. Dashboard authentication enabled with a strong session secret
  3. OAuth used for Gmail/Outlook instead of raw SMTP passwords
  4. SendGrid and enrichment API keys are restricted-scope and rotated regularly
  5. Contact database encryption enabled with macOS Keychain key storage
  6. AI agent permissions scoped to minimum required access
  7. config.yaml excluded from any version control system
  8. Firewall rules in place to monitor MailClaw's outbound connections
  9. External deliverability lookups reviewed and disabled if not needed

The Open-Source Advantage

One of MailClaw's core strengths — being fully open source and built on OpenClaw — means you can audit every line of code that handles your credentials, contact data, and AI agent logic. You're not trusting a black-box SaaS platform with your most sensitive outreach data. If you find a behavior you want to change or harden further, you can fork it, modify it, and run your own version.

That transparency is a security feature in itself. Take advantage of it: review the source before connecting production accounts, join the community to stay on top of security patches, and contribute hardening improvements if you find gaps. Your local MailClaw instance is only as secure as the time you invest in configuring it thoughtfully — but with the practices above, that investment pays off quickly.

articles.title: How to Measure the Impact of AI Email Automation on Your Sales
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to track, measure, and optimize the real revenue impact of AI email automation — with practical metrics, reporting workflows, and hands-on examples using MailClaw's local dashboard and AI email agents.
articles.content:
Why Most Teams Can't Answer "Is Our Email Automation Working?"

AI email automation promises a lot: more replies, shorter sales cycles, less manual work. But when a VP of Sales asks whether the new automated sequences are actually moving the needle, most teams go quiet. They can report open rates. Maybe click rates. But connecting email activity to pipeline and closed revenue? That's where the measurement usually falls apart.

The good news is that measuring impact isn't complicated — it just requires intentionality. You need the right metrics, the right tracking setup, and a consistent way to compare performance over time. This guide walks through exactly how to do that, using MailClaw as your measurement and execution hub.

The Metric Stack: What Actually Matters

Before you run a single sequence, get clear on which numbers you care about. There's a hierarchy here — vanity metrics at the top, revenue metrics at the bottom — and most teams live too far up the pyramid.

Tier 1: Activity Metrics (Necessary but Not Sufficient)

  • Open rate — A signal of subject line quality and sender reputation, not intent. With Apple Mail Privacy Protection inflating opens, treat this as directional only.
  • Click-through rate (CTR) — More meaningful than opens, especially if you're linking to a calendar, case study, or demo page.
  • Bounce rate — A direct indicator of list hygiene. High bounce rates hurt deliverability and skew every other metric.

Tier 2: Engagement Metrics (Where Intent Lives)

  • Reply rate — The single most important metric for cold outreach sequences. A reply — even a "not interested" — confirms a human read your email.
  • Positive reply rate — Replies that express interest, ask a question, or request a meeting. Tag these separately in MailClaw's contact enrichment layer.
  • Meeting booked rate — If you're using a Calendly or HubSpot Meetings link, track how many recipients go from email to scheduled call.

Tier 3: Revenue Metrics (The Real Score)

  • Pipeline generated per sequence — How much qualified pipeline did contacts from this sequence enter?
  • Opportunity-to-close rate by source — Do deals sourced from AI-automated sequences close at a higher or lower rate than inbound or other outbound?
  • Revenue attributed to email touchpoints — In a multi-touch attribution model, what percentage of closed deals had a meaningful email interaction in the sequence?

A 40% open rate means nothing if your reply rate is 0.3% and zero deals closed. Anchor your reporting to Tier 3 metrics and work backwards.

Setting Up Baseline Tracking in MailClaw

MailClaw runs locally on localhost:3100, which means your data stays on your machine and you're not shipping contact records to a third-party SaaS platform. This matters for baseline tracking because you own the raw logs.

Before launching any sequence, run a quick environment check from the CLI:

# Start MailClaw and verify your accounts are connected
mailclaw start

# List active SMTP/OAuth accounts
mailclaw accounts list

# Check deliverability health for each sender
mailclaw deliverability check --all

Make sure your sender accounts — whether Gmail via OAuth, Outlook, or a dedicated sending domain through SendGrid — are passing SPF, DKIM, and DMARC checks. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring panel in the dashboard surfaces these automatically, but a pre-launch CLI check catches issues before they corrupt your baseline data.

Tagging Sequences for Attribution

Every sequence you build should carry a UTM-style tag so you can filter results by campaign, persona, or experiment. In MailClaw's sequence builder, you can add metadata tags at creation time:

# Create a new sequence with attribution tags
mailclaw sequence create \
  --name "Q3 SaaS Founders Outreach" \
  --tag campaign:q3-outreach \
  --tag segment:saas-founders \
  --tag source:enriched-list \
  --steps 5

These tags flow through to the analytics view in the local dashboard, letting you slice performance by any combination. When you later sync pipeline data from HubSpot or Salesforce, you'll map these tags to the lead source field in your CRM.

Running a Controlled Experiment (Not Just a Launch)

The fastest way to prove AI email automation is working — or isn't — is to run an A/B test against a control group. This sounds obvious, but most teams skip it and then can't answer whether results improved because of the AI or because of the list quality or the timing.

Structuring Your Test

  1. Split your contact list evenly. Use MailClaw's contact enrichment to score and segment contacts first, then randomly split them. Don't let one group be "the good leads."
  2. Define one variable. Test AI-generated subject lines vs. manual, or an AI-personalized opener vs. a generic one. Change one thing at a time.
  3. Run for a full business cycle. For most B2B sequences, that means at least 3–4 weeks with a 5-step cadence fully completed.
  4. Measure at each tier. Record open rate, reply rate, meeting rate, and pipeline created for both groups.

MailClaw's AI email agents — powered by OpenClaw under the hood — can generate and personalize email variants automatically based on contact enrichment data like job title, company size, and recent funding events. This is where the AI actually earns its keep: not just sending faster, but adapting message angle to context.

# Generate AI variants for an existing sequence step
mailclaw agent generate \
  --sequence "Q3 SaaS Founders Outreach" \
  --step 1 \
  --persona "founder" \
  --variants 3 \
  --context "recent Series A funding"

The output gives you three distinct subject line and opener combinations. Load them into the sequence builder as variants, assign each to a contact segment, and let the experiment run.

Connecting Email Data to CRM Pipeline

This is the step most teams skip, and it's the only step that actually proves ROI to a CFO or board.

HubSpot Integration

If your team uses HubSpot, map MailClaw sequence tags to HubSpot's Original Source and Latest Source fields. Use the HubSpot API to push contact activity back when a reply or meeting is recorded:

# Sync a positive reply event to HubSpot
mailclaw crm sync \
  --provider hubspot \
  --event positive_reply \
  --contact-email "founder@example.com" \
  --sequence-tag "campaign:q3-outreach"

Once contact activity is in HubSpot, you can build a simple report: Deals created where lead source = MailClaw Q3 outreach, then filter by stage and close date. That's your pipeline attribution report.

Salesforce Integration

For Salesforce users, MailClaw can write to the Lead Source and Campaign fields on the Contact or Lead object. Work with your Salesforce admin to create a custom Campaign in SFDC for each MailClaw sequence, then use campaign member status (Contacted → Replied → Meeting Booked) to mirror your sequence funnel inside Salesforce's native reporting.

Reading Your Results: A Simple Reporting Framework

Once your experiment is complete and CRM data is synced, pull a structured report. Here's a simple framework to present results clearly:

  • Top of funnel: Emails sent → Opens → Clicks
  • Mid funnel: Replies → Positive replies → Meetings booked
  • Bottom of funnel: Opportunities created → Pipeline $ → Closed-won $
  • Efficiency: Cost per meeting (time + tooling / meetings booked), Revenue per contact touched

In MailClaw's local dashboard, the analytics panel displays the top and mid-funnel rows automatically. You'll add the bottom-funnel row manually by pulling from your CRM. Over time, as you run more sequences, you'll build a benchmark — your personal baseline for what "good" looks like for your audience and offer.

Red Flags to Watch For

  • High opens, low replies — Subject lines are working but body copy isn't. Test a more direct call to action or a shorter email.
  • High reply rate, low meeting rate — People are engaging but not converting. The CTA or offer may need refinement, or the handoff to a human rep is too slow.
  • Rising bounce rate over time — Your list is going stale. Use MailClaw's contact enrichment to re-verify email addresses before re-engaging older contacts.
  • Deliverability score dropping — Check MailClaw's deliverability monitoring dashboard. You may need to warm a new sending domain or rotate sender accounts using the multi-account support feature.

Iterating With Confidence

Measurement without iteration is just accounting. The real value comes when you use your data to make the next sequence meaningfully better. Because MailClaw is open source and runs locally, you can version-control your sequence configurations, store historical experiment results alongside your code, and build a compounding knowledge base of what works for your specific market.

Start with one well-instrumented sequence, measure it rigorously against all three metric tiers, sync your results to your CRM, and then make one deliberate change for the next run. Repeat that cycle six times and you'll have more reliable insight into your email-to-revenue engine than most sales teams accumulate in years.

The teams winning with AI email automation aren't the ones sending the most emails. They're the ones who know exactly why their emails work — and have the data to prove it.

articles.title: MailClaw Performance Tuning: Optimizing for High-Volume Sending
articles.author: Sarah Kim
articles.summary: Learn how to tune MailClaw for high-volume email sending — from SMTP connection pooling and sequence pacing to deliverability monitoring and AI agent optimization — so your outreach scales without hitting rate limits or spam filters.
articles.content:
Why Performance Tuning Matters Before You Scale

Most teams don't think about performance tuning until something breaks. Suddenly bounce rates spike, a Gmail account gets throttled, or a 10,000-contact sequence grinds to a halt at 2am. By then, the damage is done — sender reputation takes weeks to rebuild, and prospects have gone cold.

MailClaw's local-first architecture (running on localhost:3100 via OpenClaw) gives you a significant advantage here: full visibility and control over every layer of the sending stack, without being locked into a SaaS vendor's black box. But that control only pays off if you configure it thoughtfully.

This guide walks through the key levers you can pull — from SMTP connection settings and sequence pacing to AI agent load management and deliverability monitoring — so you can push volume confidently.

Optimizing Your SMTP Configuration

Connection Pooling and Concurrency Limits

The single biggest performance win for high-volume sending is configuring SMTP connection pools correctly. By default, MailClaw opens a new connection for each outbound message. At low volumes this is fine, but past a few hundred emails per hour, connection overhead becomes a real bottleneck.

Open your MailClaw config file (typically at ~/.mailclaw/config.yaml) and tune the SMTP pool settings per account:

smtp:
  accounts:
    - name: outreach-primary
      host: smtp.sendgrid.net
      port: 587
      pool:
        enabled: true
        max_connections: 10
        idle_timeout: 30s
        connection_timeout: 5s
      rate_limit:
        per_hour: 400
        per_day: 5000

For SendGrid and Mailgun, you can push max_connections up to 20–25 safely. For Gmail SMTP or Outlook/Microsoft 365, stay at 5–8 — these providers aggressively throttle concurrent connections from a single IP, and exceeding their soft limits triggers temporary blocks that hurt deliverability far more than they save in speed.

OAuth vs. SMTP Password Auth

If you're sending through Gmail or Outlook, always prefer OAuth over SMTP password authentication. OAuth tokens are less likely to trigger provider-side security alerts at volume, and MailClaw's OAuth integration handles token refresh automatically in the background. To set this up from the CLI:

mailclaw accounts add --provider gmail --auth oauth --alias team-outreach

Follow the browser prompt to authorize, and MailClaw stores the token securely in your local keychain — no plaintext credentials sitting in config files.

Sequence Builder: Pacing and Throttle Strategies

The Warm-Up Curve

Even with a healthy domain, dumping 5,000 emails into a new sending account on day one is a fast track to the spam folder. MailClaw's sequence builder lets you define a warm-up curve directly in a sequence definition:

sequence:
  name: Q3 Enterprise Outreach
  warmup:
    enabled: true
    schedule:
      - day: 1-3
        daily_cap: 50
      - day: 4-7
        daily_cap: 150
      - day: 8-14
        daily_cap: 400
      - day: 15+
        daily_cap: 1000

This gradual ramp signals to inbox providers that you're a legitimate sender building a real sending history — not a bulk spammer who bought a list and fired everything at once.

Staggered Send Windows

Sending 1,000 emails in a 60-second burst looks like bot activity to spam filters. Use MailClaw's send_window and jitter settings to spread sends naturally:

sequence:
  send_window:
    start: "08:00"
    end: "17:00"
    timezone: "America/New_York"
  jitter:
    min_delay: 45s
    max_delay: 180s

The jitter setting introduces a randomized delay between each send — mimicking human sending patterns. Combined with time-of-day windowing, this alone can lift open rates by keeping your domain out of bulk-send detection heuristics.

AI Email Agents: Managing Compute and API Load

MailClaw's AI email agents — powered by OpenClaw — can personalize messages at scale, handle reply classification, and trigger follow-up logic automatically. But at high volume, poorly configured agents become a throughput bottleneck.

Batching Personalization Requests

When an AI agent generates personalized opening lines for a 2,000-contact sequence, it's making thousands of LLM calls. Configure agents to batch these requests rather than running them inline at send time:

mailclaw agents run personalize \
  --sequence "Q3 Enterprise Outreach" \
  --batch-size 50 \
  --pre-generate \
  --cache-ttl 24h

The --pre-generate flag tells the agent to compute all personalizations ahead of the send window and cache them locally. This decouples LLM latency from SMTP throughput entirely — your send queue moves at full speed because the heavy lifting is already done.

Contact Enrichment at Scale

MailClaw's contact enrichment pipeline can pull data from sources like HubSpot, Salesforce, LinkedIn, Clearbit, and custom webhooks to flesh out contact records before personalization runs. At high volume, don't enrich inline — enrich in bulk as a pre-step:

mailclaw contacts enrich \
  --list enterprise-q3 \
  --sources hubspot,clearbit \
  --concurrency 20 \
  --on-conflict prefer-freshest

Setting --concurrency 20 parallelizes enrichment API calls without overwhelming rate limits on the provider side. The --on-conflict prefer-freshest flag ensures that if HubSpot and Clearbit disagree on a job title, the most recently updated record wins — keeping your personalization data clean.

Deliverability Monitoring at Volume

Sending fast is pointless if your emails land in spam. MailClaw's deliverability dashboard (available at http://localhost:3100/deliverability) surfaces the metrics you need to catch problems before they compound.

Setting Automated Alerts

Configure threshold-based alerts that pause sequences automatically if key metrics degrade:

mailclaw monitor set-alert \
  --metric bounce_rate \
  --threshold 3.5 \
  --action pause-sequence \
  --notify slack:#outreach-ops

Rule of thumb: Pause and investigate if hard bounce rate exceeds 2%, soft bounce rate exceeds 8%, or spam complaint rate exceeds 0.1%. These are the thresholds that trigger inbox provider penalties, and catching them early is far easier than recovering from a blacklist.

Multi-Account Load Balancing

MailClaw's multi-account support lets you distribute send volume across several sending identities, which is essential for sustained high-volume outreach. Rather than sending 5,000 emails from one domain, spread them across three or four warmed-up accounts:

mailclaw sequence distribute \
  --sequence "Q3 Enterprise Outreach" \
  --accounts outreach-1,outreach-2,outreach-3 \
  --strategy round-robin \
  --respect-per-account-limits

The --respect-per-account-limits flag ensures MailClaw honors the individual rate_limit settings you configured per account — no single account gets overloaded even if the others are fully utilized.

Dashboard and Observability Tips

The MailClaw local dashboard isn't just for monitoring — it's a control plane. A few things worth configuring before a major send:

  • Enable live queue view: Navigate to localhost:3100/queue to watch messages move through the pipeline in real time. This is invaluable for spotting SMTP hangs or retry storms early.
  • Export send logs: Use mailclaw logs export --format csv --last 7d to pull a week of send activity for offline analysis in a spreadsheet or BI tool.
  • Set up sequence snapshots: Before launching a high-volume push, run mailclaw sequence snapshot --name "pre-launch-Q3" to checkpoint your configuration. If something goes wrong, rollback is a single command.

A Pre-Launch Checklist

Before triggering any sequence over 1,000 contacts, run through this checklist using MailClaw's built-in validator:

mailclaw sequence validate --sequence "Q3 Enterprise Outreach" --strict

This command checks for:

  1. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records on all sending domains
  2. Unsubscribe links present in all email variants
  3. Contact list hygiene (duplicate emails, invalid addresses, suppression list conflicts)
  4. AI agent pre-generation status for personalized variants
  5. Per-account rate limit headroom relative to sequence volume and send window

If the validator returns warnings, treat them seriously — at scale, small misconfigurations become large problems fast. Fix everything flagged as an error before you proceed, and document your warnings-to-ignore list so you're making a conscious decision rather than an oversight.

The Bottom Line

High-volume email doesn't have to mean high-risk. Because MailClaw runs entirely on your local machine and gives you direct access to configuration, logs, and the full OpenClaw agent runtime, you have more tuning leverage than most teams realize. The key is treating performance configuration as a first-class part of campaign planning — not an afterthought when things go sideways.

Get the SMTP pools right, pace your sequences intelligently, pre-generate your AI personalizations, and keep a close eye on deliverability signals from the dashboard. Do those four things well, and you can scale outreach to tens of thousands of contacts per month without sacrificing inbox placement or sender reputation.

articles.title: How to Organize Email Campaigns for Maximum MailClaw Results
articles.author: James Rodriguez
articles.summary: Learn how to structure, segment, and launch email campaigns inside MailClaw for better open rates, cleaner sequences, and smarter AI-driven outreach — all from your local machine.
articles.content:
Why Campaign Organization Is the Foundation of Email Success

Most email automation problems aren't technical — they're structural. Campaigns that underperform usually suffer from the same root causes: contacts dumped into a single list, sequences built without a clear goal, and no system for tracking what's actually working. MailClaw gives you powerful tools to fix all of this, but only if your campaigns are organized well from the start.

This guide walks you through a practical framework for structuring campaigns in MailClaw so your AI email agents, contact enrichment, and sequence builder all work together — instead of against each other.

Step 1: Define Your Campaign Boundaries Before You Build Anything

Before you open the MailClaw dashboard at localhost:3100 or run a single CLI command, get clear on what each campaign is supposed to accomplish. A campaign should have one audience, one goal, and one measurable outcome.

The Three-Question Rule

  • Who is this for? Be specific. "SaaS founders in the US with fewer than 50 employees" is a campaign audience. "Leads" is not.
  • What do I want them to do? Book a call, download a resource, reply to an email, upgrade a plan — pick one.
  • How will I know if it worked? Define your success metric upfront: reply rate, click-through, conversion, or booked meetings.

Once you can answer all three clearly, you're ready to build. If you can't, you'll end up with a sequence that tries to do too many things and accomplishes none of them.

Step 2: Structure Your Contact Segments Before Importing

MailClaw's contact enrichment engine is most effective when your raw data is segmented before it enters the system. Dumping a 10,000-row CSV into one list and hoping the AI sorts it out creates noise that affects deliverability scoring and sequence targeting.

Recommended Segment Structure

Use a folder-style naming convention when creating contact groups. A clean naming system makes multi-campaign management much easier:

outbound-saas-founders-us-q3
inbound-trial-users-week1
nurture-cold-leads-enterprise
reengagement-churned-90days

When you're ready to import contacts from a CRM like HubSpot or Salesforce, use MailClaw's native integration to pull segmented lists rather than full contact exports. This keeps your campaigns clean from day one.

To import a CSV from the CLI:

mailclaw contacts import --file ./leads-saas-q3.csv --segment "outbound-saas-founders-us-q3" --enrich

The --enrich flag triggers MailClaw's contact enrichment pipeline, which automatically fills in missing job titles, company sizes, LinkedIn URLs, and technology stack data where available. This takes a flat CSV and turns it into a rich, actionable contact list without any manual research.

Step 3: Build Sequences With a Clear Narrative Arc

A sequence isn't just a series of emails — it's a conversation that unfolds over time. MailClaw's sequence builder lets you create multi-step flows with conditional logic, but the best sequences start with a simple narrative before any conditions are added.

The 4-Email Cold Outreach Framework

  1. Email 1 — The Opener: Short, relevant, no ask. Establish why you're reaching out and why now.
  2. Email 2 — The Value Add: Share something genuinely useful — a case study, a stat, a resource relevant to their situation.
  3. Email 3 — The Soft Ask: Introduce the specific action you want them to take. Keep the CTA low-friction.
  4. Email 4 — The Graceful Close: Make it easy to say no or opt out. This email often gets the highest reply rate.

Once you have this arc mapped, build it in the sequence builder. From the dashboard, navigate to Sequences → New Sequence, name it using the same convention as your contact segment (e.g., outbound-saas-founders-us-q3), and add your steps with appropriate wait times between them.

Using AI Email Agents to Write Sequence Copy

MailClaw's AI email agents — powered by OpenClaw — can draft each step of a sequence based on your goal, audience, and tone preferences. Rather than prompting the AI with vague instructions, give it structured context:

mailclaw agent write-sequence \
  --segment "outbound-saas-founders-us-q3" \
  --goal "book a 20-minute discovery call" \
  --tone "direct, no-fluff" \
  --steps 4

The agent will use enriched contact data from your segment to personalize subject lines and opening lines at scale. You review, edit, and approve each draft from the dashboard before anything goes live. You're always in control — the AI handles the first draft, you handle the judgment.

Step 4: Set Up Sending Infrastructure Before You Launch

Even the best-organized campaign will fail if your sending infrastructure isn't configured correctly. MailClaw supports both SMTP and OAuth-based sending, which means you can connect Gmail, Outlook, SendGrid, Mailgun, or any custom SMTP provider.

Multi-Account Sending for Volume and Deliverability

If you're running high-volume outreach, distribute sends across multiple accounts rather than blasting from one address. MailClaw's multi-account support lets you rotate sending accounts within a campaign, which spreads your sending reputation and reduces the risk of throttling or spam flags.

To add a sending account:

mailclaw accounts add \
  --name "outreach-account-1" \
  --provider gmail \
  --oauth

For SMTP providers like SendGrid:

mailclaw accounts add \
  --name "sendgrid-main" \
  --provider smtp \
  --host smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --port 587 \
  --user apikey \
  --pass YOUR_API_KEY

Once accounts are added, assign them to campaigns in the dashboard under Settings → Sending Accounts. You can set a daily send cap per account to stay within provider limits and protect your domain reputation.

Step 5: Monitor Deliverability Before and During Every Campaign

Deliverability monitoring is the one area most teams ignore until something breaks. MailClaw includes built-in deliverability tools that check DNS health, spam score, blacklist status, and inbox placement — all visible from the local dashboard.

Pre-Launch Deliverability Checklist

  • SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records are configured for your sending domain
  • Your domain warm-up is complete (new domains should ramp over 2–4 weeks)
  • Your contact list has been validated — no hard bounces from previous sends
  • Spam score for your email copy is below threshold (MailClaw flags this automatically)
  • Unsubscribe links are present and functional in all sequence steps

Run a deliverability check from the CLI before activating any campaign:

mailclaw deliverability check --campaign "outbound-saas-founders-us-q3"

This command audits your DNS records, tests your sending accounts, scores your email content, and returns a pass/warn/fail report. Fix any warnings before you hit send.

Step 6: Name and Tag Everything Consistently

This sounds mundane, but it's the difference between a dashboard that's genuinely useful and one that looks like organized chaos after three months of campaigns.

A Simple Naming Convention That Scales

Use this pattern for all campaigns, sequences, and contact segments:

[intent]-[audience]-[channel]-[quarter]

Examples:
outbound-founders-email-q3-2025
nurture-trial-users-email-q4-2025
reengagement-churned-email-q1-2026

Combine naming with MailClaw's tagging system to add cross-campaign labels like A/B-test, high-priority, or pending-review. Tags appear in the dashboard's campaign list and make filtering instant.

Pro tip: Create a private note on every campaign using the dashboard's notes field. Record what hypothesis you're testing, what audience you're targeting, and what success looks like. Three months from now, you'll thank yourself.

Putting It All Together

Great email campaigns aren't built — they're designed. The organizations that consistently outperform benchmarks aren't sending more emails; they're sending better-organized, better-targeted emails to people who are genuinely likely to care.

MailClaw gives you everything you need to operate this way from a single local instance: AI-assisted copy, enriched contact data, flexible sending infrastructure, and real-time deliverability monitoring. But the tool only amplifies what you bring to it. Start with clear campaign boundaries, clean segments, and a consistent naming system — and everything else will be easier to build, easier to analyze, and easier to improve.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your machine, you also get something most SaaS tools can't offer: complete data ownership and the ability to customize every part of the system. Fork it, extend it, and make it work exactly the way your outreach process demands.

articles.title: The Complete MailClaw CLI Commands Reference Guide
articles.author: Priya Patel
articles.summary: A complete reference guide to every MailClaw CLI command, from initial setup and contact enrichment to building AI email agents and monitoring deliverability — everything you need to run powerful email automation from your terminal.
articles.content:
Getting Started with the MailClaw CLI

MailClaw is built for people who prefer the terminal over clicking through yet another SaaS dashboard. Once you've installed it and the local server is running at localhost:3100, the mailclaw command becomes your central control point for everything — contacts, sequences, sending, monitoring, and AI agents. This guide covers every major command group with real examples so you can hit the ground running.

Before anything else, confirm your installation is healthy:

mailclaw status

You'll see a quick health check showing which services are active, your connected accounts, and whether the OpenClaw engine is loaded. If something's off, mailclaw doctor will diagnose common configuration issues automatically.

Core Setup Commands

Initializing Your Workspace

Run this once after installation to scaffold your config files, set up your local SQLite store, and launch the dashboard for the first time:

mailclaw init

You'll be walked through connecting your first email account. MailClaw supports both SMTP credentials and OAuth flows for Gmail and Outlook out of the box. For Gmail, the OAuth path is strongly recommended to keep deliverability clean:

mailclaw account add --provider gmail --oauth
mailclaw account add --provider outlook --oauth
mailclaw account add --name "SendGrid Transactional" --smtp smtp.sendgrid.net --port 587

Managing Multiple Accounts

MailClaw's multi-account support is one of its most practical features for agencies and teams running outreach across several domains. List, switch, and test accounts with:

mailclaw account list
mailclaw account use --name "SendGrid Transactional"
mailclaw account test --name "SendGrid Transactional"

Setting a default account means every command that sends email will use it unless you explicitly pass --account.

Contact Management and Enrichment

Importing Contacts

You can import contacts from a CSV, pull them directly from a CRM, or add them one at a time. MailClaw's enrichment engine — powered by OpenClaw — can fill in missing fields automatically after import:

mailclaw contacts import --file leads.csv
mailclaw contacts import --source hubspot --list "Q4 Prospects"
mailclaw contacts import --source salesforce --query "Industry = 'SaaS'"

Supported CRM sources include HubSpot, Salesforce, and any system that exports a standard CSV. The --map flag lets you define custom column mappings when your CSV headers don't match MailClaw's schema:

mailclaw contacts import --file export.csv --map "First Name=first_name,Company=company"

AI-Powered Contact Enrichment

This is where MailClaw really earns its place. The enrich command runs your contact list through OpenClaw's enrichment pipeline, adding job titles, company size, LinkedIn URLs, tech stack signals, and more — all locally, without shipping your data to a third-party API:

mailclaw contacts enrich --list "Q4 Prospects"
mailclaw contacts enrich --all --fields "title,company_size,linkedin"
Pro tip: Run enrichment before building sequences. Personalization tokens in your email templates pull directly from enriched contact fields, so the more data you have, the more specific your messaging can be.

Filter, tag, and segment contacts after enrichment to build precise lists for targeting:

mailclaw contacts filter --field company_size --gt 50 --tag "mid-market"
mailclaw contacts list --tag "mid-market" --export segment.csv

Building Email Sequences

Creating a New Sequence

Sequences in MailClaw are multi-step email workflows with configurable delays, conditions, and branching logic. Start by creating a named sequence:

mailclaw sequence create --name "SaaS Outbound Q4"

Then add steps. Each step is a plain-text or HTML email file (or an AI-generated draft) with a delay and optional send conditions:

mailclaw sequence add-step "SaaS Outbound Q4" \
  --subject "Quick question about {{company}}" \
  --body ./emails/step1.html \
  --delay 0

mailclaw sequence add-step "SaaS Outbound Q4" \
  --subject "Following up" \
  --body ./emails/step2.html \
  --delay 3d \
  --condition "not_opened"

mailclaw sequence add-step "SaaS Outbound Q4" \
  --subject "Last note from me" \
  --body ./emails/step3.html \
  --delay 5d \
  --condition "not_replied"

AI-Generated Email Drafts

Rather than writing step bodies by hand, you can have MailClaw's AI engine draft them for you. Describe the goal and tone, and OpenClaw generates a ready-to-use email:

mailclaw ai draft \
  --goal "introduce our project management tool to a VP of Engineering" \
  --tone "concise, peer-to-peer" \
  --output ./emails/step1.html

This is especially useful when you're spinning up sequences quickly or A/B testing subject lines across a large contact set.

Launching and Pausing Sequences

mailclaw sequence launch "SaaS Outbound Q4" --list "mid-market"
mailclaw sequence pause "SaaS Outbound Q4"
mailclaw sequence resume "SaaS Outbound Q4"
mailclaw sequence status "SaaS Outbound Q4"

AI Email Agents

MailClaw's AI agents go beyond static sequences. An agent can monitor replies, classify intent, trigger follow-up actions, and even draft personalized responses for your review — all running on your local machine through the OpenClaw runtime.

mailclaw agent create --name "Reply Handler" --sequence "SaaS Outbound Q4"
mailclaw agent set-rule "Reply Handler" --on replied --action classify_intent
mailclaw agent set-rule "Reply Handler" --on interested --action draft_reply --queue review
mailclaw agent start "Reply Handler"

With --queue review, drafted replies land in a local approval queue you can manage from the dashboard at localhost:3100 or directly from the CLI:

mailclaw agent queue list
mailclaw agent queue approve --id reply_29f3a
mailclaw agent queue edit --id reply_29f3a

Deliverability Monitoring

Running Deliverability Checks

Sending great emails means nothing if they land in spam. MailClaw's deliverability tools check your DNS records, sending reputation, and content score before you hit send:

mailclaw deliverability check --account "SendGrid Transactional"
mailclaw deliverability dns --domain yourdomain.com
mailclaw deliverability score --sequence "SaaS Outbound Q4"

The dns command validates SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records and outputs exactly what needs to be fixed. The score command runs your email content through a spam filter simulation and flags problematic phrases, excessive links, or image-to-text ratio issues.

Monitoring Live Campaigns

mailclaw campaign stats --sequence "SaaS Outbound Q4"
mailclaw campaign stats --sequence "SaaS Outbound Q4" --step 2
mailclaw campaign bounce-report --sequence "SaaS Outbound Q4"

You can tail live send activity in your terminal with:

mailclaw logs --sequence "SaaS Outbound Q4" --follow

Dashboard and Configuration

Opening the Local Dashboard

The MailClaw dashboard runs entirely on your machine — no cloud, no subscriptions, no data leaving your environment. Open it anytime with:

mailclaw dashboard

This launches your browser to localhost:3100, where you get a visual overview of campaigns, contact lists, agent queues, deliverability scores, and account health. It's especially useful for reviewing AI agent drafts and monitoring sequence performance at a glance.

Global Configuration

mailclaw config set default_delay 2d
mailclaw config set send_limit_per_day 150
mailclaw config set timezone "America/New_York"
mailclaw config list

All config values are stored in a plain .mailclaw/config.json file in your home directory — easy to version-control, back up, or share with a team.

Quick Reference Cheatsheet

  • mailclaw status — Check system health
  • mailclaw account add — Connect a new email account
  • mailclaw contacts import — Import from CSV or CRM
  • mailclaw contacts enrich — AI-powered data enrichment
  • mailclaw sequence create — Start a new email sequence
  • mailclaw sequence launch — Send a sequence to a list
  • mailclaw ai draft — Generate email copy with AI
  • mailclaw agent create — Build an AI email agent
  • mailclaw deliverability check — Pre-send deliverability audit
  • mailclaw campaign stats — Live campaign performance
  • mailclaw dashboard — Open localhost:3100 dashboard

MailClaw is under active development as an open-source project built on the OpenClaw foundation. If a command behaves unexpectedly, mailclaw --help and mailclaw [command] --help always surface the latest available flags. Contributions, command suggestions, and issue reports are welcome in the GitHub repository.

articles.title: How to Use MailClaw Templates Effectively for Different Audiences
articles.author: Mike Chen
articles.summary: Learn how to build, customize, and deploy MailClaw email templates that resonate with different audience segments — from cold outreach to customer onboarding — using AI agents, contact enrichment, and the sequence builder.
articles.content:
Why Templates Are Only as Good as the Audience They're Built For

Most email templates fail not because the writing is bad, but because they were written for everyone — which means they resonate with no one. A SaaS founder reading your cold outreach has completely different pain points than an HR manager at an enterprise company, even if you're selling them the same product.

MailClaw's template system is designed with this reality in mind. Because it runs locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, you get a fast, private environment to build, test, and iterate on templates without sending data to third-party servers. Powered by OpenClaw, the AI layer understands context — meaning your templates can be dynamically adapted, not just personalized with a first name.

This guide walks you through how to structure templates for different audience types, use MailClaw's contact enrichment and AI agents to tailor them at scale, and avoid the common pitfalls that tank deliverability.

The Foundation: Understanding Your Audience Segments

Before you write a single line of template copy, you need to define your audience segments clearly. In MailClaw, segments are built from enriched contact data. When you import a contact list — whether from a CSV, HubSpot, Salesforce, or a direct API connection — MailClaw's contact enrichment layer can append job title, company size, industry, seniority level, and recent activity signals.

Open your dashboard at localhost:3100, navigate to Contacts → Enrich, and run enrichment on your list before you build a single template. The data you get back will directly inform how you segment and what tone each template should take.

Common segments worth building separate templates for:

  • Cold prospects — No prior relationship, awareness is low
  • Warm leads — Downloaded something, attended a webinar, or replied to a prior touchpoint
  • Trial users — Active in your product, need guidance toward conversion
  • Churned customers — Had a relationship, something went wrong
  • Enterprise vs. SMB — Same product, wildly different buying processes

Building Templates in the Sequence Builder

MailClaw's sequence builder lets you create multi-step email flows visually. Each step can reference a named template, and those templates support dynamic variables drawn directly from your enriched contact fields.

Creating a Base Template

From your local dashboard, go to Templates → New Template. Give it a descriptive name that references both the use case and the segment — for example, cold-outreach-saas-founder or onboarding-day3-enterprise. Naming discipline here saves you significant confusion when you're managing 20+ templates across campaigns.

You can also create and manage templates directly from the MailClaw CLI:

# Create a new template from the command line
mailclaw template create --name "cold-outreach-saas-founder" --subject "Quick question about {{company_name}}'s growth stack"

# List all templates in your workspace
mailclaw template list

# Preview a template with sample contact data
mailclaw template preview --name "cold-outreach-saas-founder" --contact-id c_8821

The --contact-id flag is particularly useful. It pulls real enriched data from your local contact store and renders the template exactly as the recipient would see it — no guessing about how variable substitution will look.

Using Dynamic Variables Intelligently

MailClaw supports standard merge fields like {{first_name}} and {{company_name}}, but the real power comes from enrichment-based variables. Once contact enrichment runs, you have access to fields like:

  • {{job_title}} — "VP of Engineering", "Head of People Ops"
  • {{company_size}} — Used for conditional blocks
  • {{industry}} — "FinTech", "Healthcare", "eCommerce"
  • {{recent_signal}} — A hiring post, funding round, or product launch

Using these variables, a single template can produce meaningfully different emails without requiring you to maintain separate files for every micro-segment. The AI email agent layer in MailClaw can also take a base template and rewrite the core value proposition paragraph based on industry context — more on that below.

Tailoring Templates for Specific Audiences

Cold Outreach Templates

Cold email has one job: earn the right to a reply. Your template should be short (under 120 words), reference something specific about the recipient's world, and make exactly one ask.

Structure to follow:

  1. Relevance hook — Reference a recent signal from enriched data (funding, job post, product launch)
  2. What you do in one sentence — No jargon, no adjectives
  3. Why it matters to them specifically — Tie it to their role or industry
  4. Soft CTA — "Worth a 15-minute call?" or "Open to hearing more?"

In MailClaw, enable the AI email agent for this template type. The agent will use the {{recent_signal}} field to generate a unique relevance hook per contact, so you're not sending the same opening line to 500 people. Configure it under Agents → Cold Outreach Agent → Personalization Depth: High.

Onboarding Sequence Templates

Onboarding templates need to be structured around where the user is in their journey, not where you want them to be. A day-one email and a day-seven email should feel like they come from the same voice but address completely different contexts.

Use MailClaw's sequence builder to map these steps explicitly:

# Build a 5-step onboarding sequence
mailclaw sequence create --name "saas-onboarding-smb" \
  --steps "day0:template/welcome-smb,day3:template/first-value-moment,day7:template/feature-spotlight,day14:template/check-in,day21:template/upgrade-nudge"

# Attach sequence to a segment
mailclaw sequence attach --sequence "saas-onboarding-smb" --segment "trial-smb-users"

For enterprise accounts, the same sequence needs a different tone — more formal, more focused on ROI language, and often cc'ing a champion contact rather than speaking to just one person. Maintain separate enterprise variants and use the --segment flag to ensure the right template reaches the right audience automatically.

Re-engagement Templates for Churned Users

Churned or lapsed contacts require a completely different emotional register. Avoid sounding desperate or over-discounting immediately. Instead, lead with what's changed — a new feature, a resolved pain point, a product update that directly addresses the reason they left (if you know it).

"Re-engagement emails that acknowledge the gap perform 34% better than those that pretend the relationship never paused."

Use MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools before sending to a re-engagement list. Cold or aged contacts can damage your sender reputation if too many bounce. Under Deliverability → Pre-Send Check, run a list validation pass and remove contacts with high-risk scores before the sequence fires.

Connecting Templates Across Your Stack

MailClaw integrates with the tools you already use. If your CRM is HubSpot or Salesforce, you can sync contact fields directly into MailClaw's enrichment layer, ensuring your templates always draw from current data rather than a stale export.

For sending infrastructure, MailClaw supports SMTP and OAuth-based connections out of the box. Connect your Gmail workspace or Outlook account for low-volume personal outreach, or route high-volume campaigns through SendGrid or Postmark for better deliverability control. Each sending account can be configured under Settings → Accounts → Add Account, and you can assign specific sequences to specific sender accounts — useful when you want SDR outreach to come from individual rep addresses while transactional emails route through a dedicated IP.

# Add a SendGrid SMTP account
mailclaw account add --type smtp --name "sendgrid-campaigns" \
  --host smtp.sendgrid.net --port 587 --user apikey --pass YOUR_API_KEY

# Set account for a specific sequence
mailclaw sequence update --name "saas-onboarding-smb" --account "sendgrid-campaigns"

Testing Templates Before They Go Live

MailClaw's local-first architecture means you can test aggressively without fear of accidentally sending to real contacts. Use the built-in sandbox mode to fire a full sequence against a test contact list and inspect every rendered email in the dashboard before flipping to production.

A solid pre-send checklist for any template:

  • Preview with at least three different contact profiles (different industries, seniority levels)
  • Check that all variable fallbacks are set — {{first_name | "there"}} prevents blank greetings
  • Run the subject line through the deliverability scorer to avoid spam triggers
  • Verify that reply-to addresses are configured per account
  • Confirm unsubscribe links are present and functional for any marketing-classified template

Making Templates a Living System

The best-performing template today will plateau in three months. Build a habit of reviewing your template performance metrics in the MailClaw dashboard monthly — open rate, reply rate, and bounce rate per template give you the signal you need to know what to rewrite.

Because MailClaw is open source, you can also extend the template engine itself. If your team needs custom variable processors, conditional logic beyond the built-in syntax, or integration with a proprietary data source, the OpenClaw foundation makes that possible without waiting on a vendor roadmap.

Templates aren't a set-it-and-forget-it asset. Treat them like code: version them, review them, and improve them based on data. MailClaw gives you the local infrastructure to do all of that without your contact data or campaign logic ever leaving your machine.

articles.title: MailClaw for Remote Sales Teams: Maximizing Outreach Productivity
articles.author: Anna Liu
articles.summary: Learn how remote sales teams can use MailClaw's AI email agents, sequence builder, and contact enrichment tools to run high-performing outreach campaigns entirely from a local dashboard — no SaaS subscriptions required.
articles.content:
The Remote Sales Team Problem Nobody Talks About

Remote sales teams are distributed by design, but their tools rarely are. You've got SDRs in three time zones, a shared Gmail account someone set up in 2019, a HubSpot instance nobody fully configured, and a Salesforce export sitting in a Dropbox folder. Outreach happens in bursts, follow-up falls through the cracks, and nobody really knows which sequences are working.

The irony is that email — your highest-leverage outreach channel — is also the most fragmented part of the stack. MailClaw changes that. Because it runs locally on your Mac at localhost:3100 and is powered by OpenClaw's AI engine, your team gets a unified, private, and genuinely intelligent email automation platform without handing your contact data to another SaaS vendor.

This guide walks through how remote sales teams can set up MailClaw to maximize outreach productivity — from first install to running multi-touch sequences with AI-personalized copy.

Getting MailClaw Running in Under Five Minutes

Before anything else, you need MailClaw up and running. If you haven't installed it yet, the quickest path is through the CLI:

# Install MailClaw via npm
npm install -g mailclaw

# Initialize a new workspace
mailclaw init my-sales-workspace

# Start the local dashboard
mailclaw start

Once that's running, open your browser to http://localhost:3100. You'll see the MailClaw dashboard — a clean, fast interface for managing accounts, contacts, sequences, and campaigns. No login wall, no cloud sync delay. Everything is local and immediate.

Connecting Your Email Accounts

Remote teams typically spread outreach across multiple sender accounts to protect deliverability. MailClaw's multi-account support makes this straightforward. You can connect accounts via OAuth (ideal for Gmail and Outlook) or configure raw SMTP credentials for providers like SendGrid or custom mail servers:

# Add a Gmail account via OAuth
mailclaw account add --provider gmail --oauth

# Add a SendGrid SMTP account
mailclaw account add --provider smtp \
  --host smtp.sendgrid.net \
  --port 587 \
  --user apikey \
  --pass YOUR_SENDGRID_API_KEY \
  --label "SDR Outbound"

Once connected, each account appears in the dashboard with a live deliverability score, send limits, and warm-up status. For teams running cold outreach, this visibility alone is worth the setup time.

Building High-Converting Email Sequences

The sequence builder is where most sales teams spend their time. MailClaw's visual sequence editor (accessible at localhost:3100/sequences) lets you construct multi-step email campaigns with conditional logic — so follow-ups adapt based on whether a prospect opened, clicked, or replied.

A Practical 5-Step Outbound Sequence

Here's a sequence structure that consistently performs well for remote B2B sales teams targeting mid-market accounts:

  1. Day 1 — Cold intro: Short, personalized opening. Reference something specific about the prospect's company. Ask one clear question.
  2. Day 3 — Value bump: Share a relevant case study or insight. No ask — just value.
  3. Day 7 — Soft follow-up: Check in briefly. Restate the core problem you solve.
  4. Day 14 — Social proof: Name-drop a relevant customer or share a result. Include a low-friction CTA (a link, not a meeting request).
  5. Day 21 — Breakup email: Honest, human, short. Leave the door open without being pushy.

You can define this entire sequence in a YAML config file and import it directly — useful when your team lead wants to standardize sequences across reps:

# sequence-outbound-midmarket.yaml
name: "Mid-Market Outbound Q3"
steps:
  - day: 1
    subject: "Quick question about {{company}}"
    template: cold-intro
    ai_personalize: true
  - day: 3
    subject: "How {{competitor}} customers are switching"
    template: value-bump
    ai_personalize: false
  - day: 7
    subject: "Re: Quick question"
    template: soft-followup
    ai_personalize: true
  - day: 14
    subject: "What we did for {{similar_company}}"
    template: social-proof
    ai_personalize: false
  - day: 21
    subject: "Closing the loop"
    template: breakup
    ai_personalize: false
# Import and activate the sequence
mailclaw sequence import ./sequence-outbound-midmarket.yaml
mailclaw sequence activate "Mid-Market Outbound Q3"

The ai_personalize: true flag tells MailClaw's OpenClaw-powered AI engine to dynamically rewrite subject lines and opening sentences based on enriched contact data — more on that next.

Contact Enrichment: The Multiplier Nobody Uses Enough

Personalization at scale only works if you have data to personalize with. MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment pulls firmographic and professional data for each prospect before your sequences run — job title, company size, tech stack, recent funding, LinkedIn activity, and more.

# Enrich a single contact
mailclaw enrich contact --email jane@acmecorp.com

# Bulk enrich from a CSV
mailclaw enrich batch --file ./prospects-q3.csv --fields title,company,linkedin,techstack

Once enriched, those fields become available as dynamic variables in your templates. Your AI email agents can reference a prospect's specific tech stack or recent hiring activity to write opening lines that feel genuinely researched — not mail-merged.

"We saw a 34% lift in reply rates after switching from static templates to AI-personalized openers using enriched contact data. The difference is that it sounds like a human wrote it, not a sequence."

Syncing Contacts from HubSpot and Salesforce

If your team already tracks leads in HubSpot or Salesforce, MailClaw can pull contacts directly rather than requiring manual CSV exports:

# Sync contacts from HubSpot
mailclaw contacts sync --source hubspot --list "Q3 Outbound ICP"

# Sync from Salesforce with field mapping
mailclaw contacts sync --source salesforce \
  --object Lead \
  --filter "Status = 'Open - Not Contacted'" \
  --map "FirstName:first_name,LastName:last_name,Email:email,Company:company"

This keeps MailClaw in sync with your CRM without duplicating work. Replies and engagement data can be pushed back to HubSpot or Salesforce as activity records, keeping your reporting clean.

AI Email Agents: Your Async SDR

One of MailClaw's most powerful features for remote teams is the AI email agent system. Rather than just automating sends, an AI agent can monitor replies, classify intent (interested, not now, wrong person, unsubscribe), and trigger appropriate follow-up actions — all without a human in the loop.

For a remote team spread across time zones, this is transformative. A prospect in London replies at 8am GMT — before your US-based SDR is awake — and the AI agent can acknowledge the reply, send a relevant resource, and add a task to the rep's queue for a personal follow-up that morning.

# Create an AI agent for reply handling
mailclaw agent create \
  --name "OutboundReplyHandler" \
  --trigger reply \
  --sequence "Mid-Market Outbound Q3" \
  --actions classify,respond,notify

Agents are configured through the dashboard at localhost:3100/agents, where you can define response templates for each intent class, set escalation rules, and review every decision the agent makes before it becomes a sent email.

Deliverability: The Silent Campaign Killer

High reply rates mean nothing if your emails are landing in spam. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring dashboard gives remote teams real-time visibility into the health of every sending account — including spam score trends, bounce rates, SPF/DKIM/DMARC validation status, and blacklist checks.

Daily Deliverability Checks

Build a habit of running this before launching any new sequence:

# Run a full deliverability audit on all accounts
mailclaw deliverability audit --all-accounts

# Check a specific domain's sending reputation
mailclaw deliverability check --domain acme-sales.com --verbose

If an account's score drops below your threshold, MailClaw can automatically pause sends from that account and route traffic to a healthier sender — configurable in your campaign settings. For teams sending at volume through SendGrid or similar infrastructure, this prevents one bad batch from tanking an entire campaign.

Structuring Your Remote Team's Workflow in MailClaw

Here's a practical operating rhythm for a remote team of three to eight SDRs:

  • Monday: Sync fresh contacts from HubSpot, run enrichment batch, review AI agent activity from the previous week.
  • Tuesday–Thursday: Active sending days. Monitor the dashboard at localhost:3100 for deliverability flags and reply classifications.
  • Friday: Pull the weekly campaign report (mailclaw report weekly --export pdf), review sequence performance, A/B test new subject lines.

Because MailClaw is open source and runs locally, each rep can maintain their own instance with their own sender accounts, or a team lead can run a shared instance on a local network. Either way, there's no per-seat pricing and no data leaving your infrastructure — a meaningful advantage when you're handling prospect data across jurisdictions.

The Bottom Line

Remote sales teams don't fail at outreach because they lack effort — they fail because their tools create friction at every step. MailClaw removes that friction by putting AI-powered email automation, contact enrichment, deliverability monitoring, and multi-account management into a single local tool you actually control.

Start with one sequence, one account, and the daily deliverability check habit. Once you see how the AI personalization and agent-based reply handling change your reply rates, you'll wonder how you ran outreach any other way.

MailClaw is open source and free to use. Get started at localhost:3100 after install, and browse the full documentation to explore what OpenClaw's AI engine can do for your specific outreach use case.

articles.title: How to Avoid Spam Filters with MailClaw Smart Sending
articles.author: David Torres
articles.summary: Learn how MailClaw's smart sending engine helps you dodge spam filters, protect your sender reputation, and land in the inbox every time — with practical CLI commands, sequence tips, and deliverability best practices.
articles.content:
Why Spam Filters Are Getting Smarter (And How Your Outreach Can Too)

Spam filters have evolved dramatically. Modern inbox providers like Gmail, Outlook, and Apple Mail no longer just scan for suspicious keywords or blacklisted IPs — they analyze sending patterns, engagement rates, authentication records, content structure, and even behavioral signals from thousands of similar messages. If your outreach looks even slightly automated or bulk-sent, you can end up in the Promotions tab at best, or the spam folder at worst.

The good news: MailClaw was built with deliverability as a first-class concern. Because it runs locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, you have full control over every sending parameter — no black-box SaaS throttling your configuration or hiding your reputation data. This guide walks through the concrete steps you can take inside MailClaw to maximize inbox placement, from authentication setup to AI-powered personalization.

Start With the Foundation: Email Authentication

Before you send a single message, your domain needs to be properly authenticated. Spam filters treat unauthenticated email with deep suspicion, and rightfully so. MailClaw's deliverability dashboard (available at localhost:3100/deliverability) surfaces your current authentication status the moment you connect a sending account.

The Three Records You Must Have

  • SPF (Sender Policy Framework): Tells receiving servers which IP addresses are authorized to send on behalf of your domain. Add a TXT record to your DNS like v=spf1 include:sendgrid.net include:_spf.google.com ~all if you're sending through SendGrid or Gmail SMTP.
  • DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail): Cryptographically signs your outgoing messages. MailClaw will prompt you to install DKIM keys when you configure a new SMTP connection or OAuth account.
  • DMARC: Tells receivers what to do when SPF or DKIM checks fail. Start with a monitoring-only policy (p=none) and graduate to p=quarantine once you're confident in your setup.

To check your authentication status from the MailClaw CLI, run:

mailclaw deliverability check --domain yourdomain.com

This command hits standard DNS lookup endpoints and reports your SPF, DKIM, and DMARC configuration in one shot — no need to juggle third-party tools like MXToolbox separately (though cross-referencing is always smart).

Smart Sending: Throttling, Timing, and Warm-Up

Even with perfect authentication, blasting 500 cold emails in one hour will trigger rate-limit alarms at every major inbox provider. MailClaw's Smart Sending engine is designed to make your outreach look and behave like it came from a real human, because the best outreach actually does.

Configuring Send Delays and Daily Caps

Inside your sequence builder, you can set per-step sending windows and daily volume caps directly in your sequence config file:

# sequence.yaml
sequence:
  name: "Q4 Outbound"
  daily_cap: 80
  send_window:
    start: "09:00"
    end: "17:30"
    timezone: "America/New_York"
  delay_between_sends:
    min_seconds: 90
    max_seconds: 300
  steps:
    - step: 1
      template: "intro_email"
      delay_days: 0
    - step: 2
      template: "follow_up_1"
      delay_days: 3
    - step: 3
      template: "follow_up_2"
      delay_days: 5

The delay_between_sends randomization is particularly important. A perfectly uniform 120-second gap between every email is a machine pattern. Random variation mimics how a human sends messages throughout their day, and spam filters respond accordingly.

Account Warm-Up for New Domains

If you're sending from a domain less than 30 days old, or from an account with no prior sending history, you need to warm it up gradually. MailClaw includes a built-in warm-up mode:

mailclaw warmup start --account sales@yourcompany.com --days 21 --target-daily 150

This ramps your daily volume over the specified period, starting low and increasing incrementally. During warm-up, MailClaw's AI email agent monitors open rates and bounce signals, automatically pausing the ramp if negative signals spike — protecting your sender score before it becomes a problem.

Personalization That Actually Moves the Needle

Generic email copy is a double signal: it tells spam filters the message is bulk, and it tells your prospect they're just a name in a spreadsheet. MailClaw's contact enrichment and AI-powered personalization features address both problems simultaneously.

Enriching Contacts Before You Send

MailClaw can enrich your contact list with company data, recent news, LinkedIn signals, and role-specific context before a single email goes out. From the CLI:

mailclaw enrich --list prospects.csv --fields company,title,linkedin,recent_news --output enriched_prospects.csv

Once enriched, your AI email agent can reference that data dynamically — pulling in a contact's recent company announcement, their specific job function, or their tech stack to write genuinely personalized first lines. This isn't just good for conversions; emails with high engagement rates (opens, replies, link clicks) actively improve your sender reputation over time.

Using the AI Email Agent for Variation

One underappreciated spam filter trigger is content fingerprinting — when too many identical or near-identical emails come from the same domain in a short window, filters flag the pattern. MailClaw's AI email agent, powered by OpenClaw, generates subtle variation across your sequence at send time:

mailclaw agent run --template intro_email --variation-mode subtle --contacts enriched_prospects.csv

With --variation-mode subtle, the agent rewrites sentence structure, swaps synonyms, and adjusts paragraph order while keeping your core message and tone consistent. The result is a batch of emails that are functionally identical in intent but sufficiently varied to avoid content fingerprinting.

Managing Your Sending Infrastructure

Multi-Account Rotation

Sending all outbound email from a single account concentrates risk. MailClaw's multi-account support lets you distribute sends across several connected accounts — whether those are Gmail OAuth connections, Outlook accounts, or custom SMTP endpoints through SendGrid or Postmark:

mailclaw accounts list
# OUTPUT:
# [1] sales@yourcompany.com     (Gmail OAuth)    daily_sent: 42/80
# [2] hello@yourcompany.com     (SMTP/SendGrid)  daily_sent: 31/80
# [3] outreach@yourcompany.com  (Outlook OAuth)  daily_sent: 28/80

mailclaw sequence send --sequence "Q4 Outbound" --rotate-accounts

The --rotate-accounts flag distributes sends proportionally based on each account's remaining daily capacity and current reputation score, so your healthiest accounts carry proportionally more volume.

Monitoring Deliverability in Real Time

The MailClaw local dashboard at localhost:3100 gives you a live view of your deliverability health — bounce rates, spam complaints, open rates, and reply rates broken down by sequence, account, and time window. Pay close attention to:

  • Bounce rate: Keep hard bounces below 2%. Use MailClaw's list hygiene tools to validate addresses before sending.
  • Spam complaint rate: Anything above 0.1% is a red flag. Review your copy and targeting.
  • Reply rate: A healthy reply rate is a positive reputation signal. If it's dropping, your personalization may need refreshing.
mailclaw stats --sequence "Q4 Outbound" --range 7d --format table

Content Best Practices MailClaw Checks For You

MailClaw includes a pre-send content linter that flags common spam triggers before your sequence goes live. Run it any time:

mailclaw lint --template intro_email

"Warning: Subject line contains all-caps word (FREE). Consider rewriting. Warning: Link-to-text ratio is high — add more plain text content."

Beyond what the linter catches automatically, keep these principles in mind:

  • Avoid spam trigger words in subject lines: "free," "guaranteed," "act now," "no obligation," "click here."
  • Keep your HTML-to-text ratio balanced. Heavily designed HTML emails look like marketing blasts. Plain-text or lightly formatted messages look like human correspondence.
  • Include a physical mailing address in any bulk or marketing send — it's legally required under CAN-SPAM and GDPR, and its absence raises red flags with filters.
  • Use a custom tracking domain for link and open tracking rather than a shared subdomain. MailClaw supports custom tracking domains under Settings → Tracking.

Integrating With Your CRM Without Breaking Deliverability

If you're syncing contacts from HubSpot, Salesforce, or a CSV export, list quality becomes a deliverability issue. Old, stale, or improperly segmented lists generate bounces and spam complaints that drag down your entire domain's reputation.

MailClaw's enrichment pipeline can validate and score contacts as they're imported from your CRM:

mailclaw import --source hubspot --filter "last_activity_days < 180" --validate-email --output ready_to_send.csv

The --validate-email flag runs syntax checks, MX record lookups, and disposable-address detection before a contact ever enters your sequence. It's a small step that has an outsized impact on bounce rates.

The Open-Source Advantage

Because MailClaw is open source and runs entirely on your local machine, you're not sharing infrastructure — or a sender reputation — with thousands of other users the way you would on a shared SaaS platform. Your domain's reputation is yours alone to build and protect. Every configuration, every send log, and every deliverability metric lives at localhost:3100, visible and auditable by you.

That transparency is the real deliverability edge. When something goes wrong — a bounce spike, a complaint rate bump, an authentication failure — you see it immediately and can act on it, rather than waiting for a support ticket response from a platform that treats you as one account among millions.

Combine that ownership with MailClaw's Smart Sending engine, OpenClaw-powered personalization, and built-in deliverability tooling, and you have a system designed from the ground up to land in inboxes — not spam folders.

articles.title: Best Practices for MailClaw Email Sequences and Timing
articles.author: Ahmad Saroya
articles.summary: Learn how to structure high-converting email sequences in MailClaw, including optimal send timing, step spacing, and AI-assisted personalization strategies that keep your deliverability scores healthy and your replies flowing.
articles.content:
Why Sequence Structure and Timing Are the Difference-Makers

Most outreach campaigns don't fail because of bad copy — they fail because of bad timing. Sending three emails in 48 hours screams desperation. Waiting three weeks between touches lets your prospect forget you entirely. The sweet spot is intentional, and it's something MailClaw was built to help you find systematically.

Running locally on your Mac at localhost:3100, MailClaw gives you a full campaign control center without routing your strategy through a third-party SaaS dashboard. Your data stays local, your sequences stay flexible, and the AI email agents built on OpenClaw do the heavy analytical lifting. Let's walk through how to build sequences that actually work.

The Anatomy of a High-Converting Email Sequence

Before touching the MailClaw sequence builder, you need a mental model. A well-structured sequence has three distinct phases:

  • Awareness phase (Steps 1–2): Establish relevance and earn attention. No hard asks.
  • Engagement phase (Steps 3–4): Provide value, reference a specific pain point, and introduce your offer gently.
  • Decision phase (Steps 5–6): Clear CTA, social proof, and a low-friction next step.

A six-step sequence is a reliable baseline for cold outreach. Fewer than four steps and you're leaving conversions on the table. More than eight and you risk inbox fatigue — and potentially triggering spam filters from repeated contact patterns.

Spacing Your Steps: The Timing Framework

Here's a proven timing structure you can plug directly into MailClaw's sequence builder:

Step 1: Day 0       — Initial outreach email
Step 2: Day 3       — First follow-up (light touch)
Step 3: Day 7       — Value-add or case study
Step 4: Day 14      — Reframe or different angle
Step 5: Day 21      — Social proof or urgency nudge
Step 6: Day 30      — Breakup email / final ask

These aren't arbitrary gaps. The 3-day window after Step 1 catches people who meant to reply but got sidetracked. The jump to Day 7 gives breathing room. After Day 14, you're no longer in "follow-up" territory — you're running a nurture sequence, which means your content needs to carry more weight.

To configure this inside MailClaw, open the sequence builder from your dashboard and add steps with delay offsets:

mailclaw sequence create --name "Q4 Outreach" \
  --steps 6 \
  --delays "0,3,7,14,21,30" \
  --account gmail-primary

Using MailClaw's AI Email Agents for Smarter Personalization

Generic sequences get generic results. MailClaw's AI email agents — powered by OpenClaw — can analyze contact data, company signals, and even recent news to generate personalized email variants at scale. This isn't just mail-merge with someone's first name. It's contextual personalization that reads differently to each prospect.

Connecting Contact Enrichment to Your Sequences

Before your AI agent drafts anything, feed it good data. Use MailClaw's built-in contact enrichment to pull in LinkedIn roles, company size, tech stack, and funding history from your imported lists:

mailclaw enrich contacts --input leads.csv \
  --fields "company,title,linkedin,tech_stack,funding" \
  --output enriched_leads.csv

Once enriched, contacts flow into your sequence with attributes the AI agent can reference. For example, if your agent detects that a prospect's company recently raised a Series B, it can flag that for a relevance hook in Step 1. If the enrichment picks up that they use HubSpot, it can tailor your value proposition around your HubSpot integration story.

Setting Up AI-Assisted Draft Generation

With enriched contacts loaded, assign an AI agent to your sequence from the localhost dashboard under Agents → Assign to Sequence. You can configure the agent's tone, output length, and which enrichment fields to prioritize:

mailclaw agent assign \
  --sequence "Q4 Outreach" \
  --agent outreach-agent-v2 \
  --tone professional \
  --personalization-fields "company,title,tech_stack,recent_news"

The agent generates a unique draft per contact for human review before sending — or you can set auto-approval for contacts that score above a confidence threshold. Start with human review until you trust the outputs, then automate incrementally.

Send Time Optimization: When to Hit Send

Timing within the day matters almost as much as timing between steps. Data consistently points to a few reliable windows:

  • Tuesday–Thursday are the strongest days for cold outreach open rates.
  • 8–9 AM and 1–2 PM in the recipient's local timezone outperform evening sends by a significant margin.
  • Monday mornings are crowded and competitive — your email competes with weekend backlog.
  • Friday afternoons are a graveyard. Avoid unless you have a very specific reason.

MailClaw supports timezone-aware scheduling per contact. When you import your contact list, include a timezone column and MailClaw will adjust send times automatically:

mailclaw sequence schedule \
  --sequence "Q4 Outreach" \
  --send-time "09:00" \
  --timezone-aware true \
  --preferred-days "Tue,Wed,Thu"

Pro tip: If you're sending through Gmail or Outlook via OAuth, MailClaw respects per-account daily send limits automatically. You won't accidentally trigger rate limiting on your primary sending domain.

Protecting Deliverability Throughout Your Sequence

A beautiful sequence means nothing if your emails land in spam. MailClaw's deliverability monitoring tools watch your sending reputation in real time and surface warnings before your domain takes a hit.

Warm Up Before You Blast

If you're using a new sending domain with SendGrid, Mailgun, or a dedicated SMTP server, run MailClaw's warmup protocol first. This gradually increases your daily send volume over two to four weeks, building domain reputation organically:

mailclaw warmup start \
  --account sendgrid-outbound \
  --start-volume 20 \
  --target-volume 500 \
  --ramp-days 21

During warmup, MailClaw's deliverability dashboard will display your open rate trends, bounce rates, and spam complaint rates. Keep bounce rate below 2% and complaints below 0.1% — these are the thresholds that protect your sender score with major inbox providers.
